summary: A visual, story-driven course on object-oriented design patterns (Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Factory, Singleton, Command, Adapter, Facade, Template Method, Iterator, Composite, State, Proxy, MVC) and the design principles behind them.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Why changing requirements break inheritance-heavy designs, and how encapsulating what varies and favouring composition (Strategy) fix it.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: How a subject notifies dependent objects of changes without being tightly coupled to them.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: How wrapping objects adds behaviour at runtime while keeping classes closed to modification and open to extension.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: How Simple Factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory isolate object creation and invert dependencies on concrete classes.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: How to guarantee one instance with a global access point, and what multithreading does to the classic version.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: How wrapping a request as an object decouples the invoker from the receiver and enables undo, macros, queues and logs.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: How Adapter converts one interface to another and Facade simplifies a subsystem, guided by the Principle of Least Knowledge.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: How a superclass fixes an algorithm skeleton and lets subclasses supply steps, with hooks and the Hollywood Principle.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: How Iterator hides how a collection is traversed and Composite treats single objects and trees of objects uniformly.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: How an object changes behaviour by delegating to state objects, and how this differs from Strategy.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: How remote, virtual and protection proxies control access to another object.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: How patterns combine, with MVC as the model case built from Observer, Strategy and Composite.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: What a pattern really is, how to choose and keep one, and when not to use it.
unitSummaries.Appendix A: Nine further patterns (Bridge, Builder, Chain of Responsibility, Flyweight, Interpreter, Mediator, Memento, Prototype, Visitor) in brief.
unitSummaries.Whole book: Putting the patterns and principles together: choosing among them, telling similar ones apart, and knowing when none is needed.

concepts.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
concepts.title: Inheritance as the first tool for reuse
concepts.question: How does one Duck superclass let a simulator support many duck species with little code?

paragraphs: Inheritance lets a class receive the fields and methods of another class. The class that gives is the superclass, and each class that receives is a subclass. Code written once in the superclass works in every subclass without being copied.

SimUDuck, a duck pond game in the book, was built this way: its designers made one Duck superclass, and every duck species inherits from it. A new species needs only the code that makes it different. That is the reuse the early designers were counting on.
card.example: A company models trucks, vans and buses. Fuel tracking is identical for all three, so it is written once in a Vehicle superclass. A bus adds only a seat counter. Adding a new tow truck means writing a small subclass, not another copy of fuel tracking.
card.rule: Inheritance reuses code by writing it once in a superclass that every subclass receives.
card.limits: Every subclass receives everything the superclass holds, wanted or not. Reuse by inheritance works while all subclasses really share the code.

concepts.title: One change in a superclass reaches every subclass
concepts.question: Why did adding one fly() method to the Duck superclass produce flying rubber ducks?

paragraphs: Executives asked for flying ducks, and Joe added a fly() method to the Duck superclass. Every subclass inherits it, so every duck type could fly, including rubber ducks, which are inanimate objects. Joe had not noticed that not all Duck subclasses should fly.

The authors call this a localized update that caused a nonlocal side effect. Inheritance that looked like a good way to reuse code turned out poorly for maintenance, because a change meant for some subclasses landed on all of them.
card.example: A drawing program has a Shape superclass with Circle, Square and Text subclasses. A developer adds rotate() to Shape. Circle gains a pointless rotation, and Text now rotates in ways nobody asked for.
card.rule: Adding behavior to a superclass gives it to every subclass, so add it only where every subclass should have it.
card.limits: A new method in a superclass is safe when all subclasses really share it, such as a name every duck has. The risk comes from behavior that only some subclasses should have.

concepts.title: What inheritance costs when behavior varies
concepts.question: Which disadvantages appear when subclasses are the home for behavior that keeps changing?

paragraphs: The authors weigh inheritance as the way to give ducks their behavior and list its disadvantages. Code is duplicated across subclasses. Changing behavior while the program runs is difficult. It is hard to gain knowledge of every duck's behaviors. And changes can unintentionally affect other ducks.

All four come from one source: the behavior lives in the class definitions, fixed when the code is written. Notice that the list does not include things inheritance never promised, such as making ducks dance.
card.example: A report tool has PdfReport, HtmlReport and CsvReport subclasses, each pasting its own date formatting. Switching a finished report from PDF to HTML means building a new object. Fixing the date format means editing three classes.
card.rule: When behavior varies, inheritance costs duplicated code, hard runtime changes, scattered knowledge and unintended side effects.
card.limits: The list judges inheritance as the home for varying behavior, not inheritance in general. Stable code shared by all subclasses still belongs in a superclass.

concepts.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
concepts.title: Interfaces fix who gets a behavior but lose the code
concepts.question: Why does making only some ducks implement Flyable and Quackable trade one maintenance problem for another?

paragraphs: Joe's next idea was to pull fly() and quack() out of Duck and put them in Flyable and Quackable interfaces. Only ducks that really fly would implement Flyable. This solves part of the problem: no more inappropriately flying rubber ducks.

But a Java interface has no implementation code. Every class that implements it must write the behavior itself, so code reuse is destroyed. There may also be more than one kind of flying even among the ducks that fly. In the authors' words the result is a different maintenance nightmare.
card.example: A game has 30 character classes. Twelve implement a Healable interface and each writes its own healing code. When the healing rule changes, all twelve classes need editing.
card.rule: An interface decides which classes have a behavior but carries no code, so every implementer must supply its own.
card.limits: The lesson is not that interfaces are bad. They name a capability well. The trouble arises when they are the only place a varying behavior can live.

concepts.section: The one constant in software development
concepts.title: Change as the constant of software
concepts.question: What can a developer count on in every project, and what does it mean for design?

paragraphs: Joe's company wants an update every six months, in ways it has not yet decided on. The authors use this to make a point about all software: no matter where you work, what you build or which language you use, the one constant is change.

No matter how well an application is designed, over time it must grow and change or it will die. Users want new features, companies change suppliers or data formats, technology moves on, and teams learn how to do things better. A design should be judged by how well it takes the next change.
card.rule: Software must change to stay alive, so a design should be judged by how well it takes the next change.
card.limits: Not every part of a system changes at the same speed. Treating all of it as in flux wastes effort; the skill is to see where change is likely.

concepts.title: Two failed designs, one shared cause
concepts.question: What do the inheritance design and the interface design have in common that makes both hard to maintain?

paragraphs: Inheritance failed because duck behavior keeps changing across subclasses and does not suit every subclass. The Flyable and Quackable interfaces looked promising, but a Java interface has no implementation code, so there is no reuse. Whenever a behavior must change, you must track down every subclass that defines it, probably adding new bugs on the way.
Both designs put the varying behavior inside the duck classes themselves. When two different fixes fail in the same way, the shared feature is a better target than either fix.
card.example: Two spreadsheet add-ins crash. One reads a date column, the other reads a currency column. Both parse text with the same shared function. Fixing each add-in separately misses the shared function.
card.rule: When two designs fail the same way, find what they share and change that.
card.limits: Finding a shared cause works only if the failures really are the same kind. Two failures with different causes need different fixes.

concepts.title: Identify what varies and encapsulate it
concepts.question: What does the first design principle tell a designer to do with the parts of a program that change?

paragraphs: The first design principle reads: identify the aspects of your application that vary and separate them from what stays the same. To encapsulate what varies means to pull it out and give it its own place, so the rest of the code does not depend on its details.

The aim is that later you can alter or extend the parts that vary without affecting those that do not. The result is fewer unintended consequences from code changes and more flexibility. The authors call this the basis of almost every design pattern, since all patterns let some part of a system vary independently of the others.
card.example: A food-delivery app changes its delivery-fee formula every month, while order numbers and customer records stay stable. The formula is placed in its own set of classes. A new fee type is added there, and checkout and records are not touched.
card.rule: Find the parts of the code that change and put them behind their own boundary, apart from the parts that stay the same.
card.limits: The principle says to encapsulate what varies, not everything. Pulling out parts that never change adds structure without benefit.

concepts.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
concepts.title: Pulling fly and quack out of Duck
concepts.question: Which parts of the Duck class are moved out, where do they go, and what stays?

paragraphs: The team looked at the Duck class. Apart from fly() and quack(), it was working well, and no other part seemed to change often. So they left Duck mostly alone and pulled out only the two methods that vary from duck to duck.

Each pulled-out behavior gets its own set of classes, apart from Duck. One set holds all the ways of flying; another holds all the ways of quacking. For quacking, the set might hold one class that quacks, one that squeaks and one that is silent.
card.example: A music app's Playlist class stores tracks well, but sorting rules change often. The sort rules move into their own set of classes: by title, by artist, by date added. Playlist keeps storing tracks and is not rewritten.
card.rule: Move only the varying methods out, give each behavior its own set of classes, and leave the stable class where it is.
card.limits: Judging what varies rests on today's evidence. A part thought stable may start to vary, so the choice is a judgment, to be revised, not a one-time proof.

concepts.title: Program to an interface, not an implementation
concepts.question: What does the second design principle tell a designer about the type of a variable that holds a behavior?

paragraphs: The second design principle is: program to an interface, not an implementation. In the duck design, each behavior is represented by an interface, FlyBehavior or QuackBehavior, and the behavior classes implement it, not the Duck classes.

That way the Duck classes need not know any implementation detail of their behaviors. Before, behavior came from the Duck superclass or from a subclass, so each duck was locked into a specific implementation. Now a duck holds a variable typed as the behavior interface, and any class that implements it can be used.
card.rule: Declare the variable that holds a behavior with a supertype so the code does not depend on which implementation sits in it.
card.limits: Programming to a supertype adds a layer. Where nothing will ever vary, the extra interface buys little.

concepts.title: Interface as a concept versus a Java construct
concepts.question: What are the two meanings of the word interface, and which one does the second principle use?

paragraphs: The authors note that the word interface is overloaded. One meaning is the concept: what an object promises to do. The other is the Java construct, written with the keyword interface. You can program to an interface without using the Java construct.

So program to an interface really means program to a supertype. The declared type of a variable should be a supertype, usually an abstract class or an interface, so any concrete implementation can be assigned to it. The class that declares the variable then does not need to know the actual type of the object.
card.rule: Program to an interface means program to a supertype, which may be an abstract class or a Java interface.
card.limits: The supertype must still declare what the code calls on it. The principle fails if the declared type is a concrete class in disguise.

concepts.title: Assigning the concrete object at runtime
concepts.question: How does declaring a variable as a supertype let the actual object be chosen while the program runs?

paragraphs: The authors give an example with an abstract class Animal and concrete classes Dog and Cat. Declaring Dog d = new Dog() and calling d.bark() programs to an implementation, since the variable is typed as the concrete Dog.

Declaring Animal animal = new Dog() and calling animal.makeSound() programs to a supertype. Better still, the concrete object is assigned at runtime, as in a = getAnimal(). The code then does not know which animal it has; it only cares that the object knows how to respond to makeSound().
card.rule: Type the variable as the supertype and let the concrete object be assigned while the program runs.
card.limits: The calling code can only use what the supertype declares. A method found only in a subclass, such as bark(), is out of reach through the supertype variable.

concepts.title: Behaviors as classes of their own
concepts.question: What do the authors gain by putting each way of flying or quacking in its own class?

paragraphs: The reworked design has two interfaces, FlyBehavior and QuackBehavior, and classes that implement each concrete behavior. Because the behaviors no longer hide inside Duck classes, other objects can reuse them. New behaviors can be added without modifying any existing behavior class or any Duck class that uses flying.

The authors sum it up as reuse without all the baggage of inheritance. A behavior class is still a class: it can keep state, such as wing beats per minute, maximum altitude and speed. Duck itself stays an ordinary class, so specific ducks like MallardDuck still inherit common properties from it.
card.example: A shipping app has Standard, Express and Overnight pricing classes behind a PriceRule interface. A freight company reuses Express pricing in its own quote tool. A new Same-Day rule is added as one new class, and no pricing class is edited.
card.rule: Give every variant of a behavior its own class behind a shared interface, so it can be reused and added to without editing existing code.
card.limits: Each variant adds a class to maintain. For a behavior that will never have a second variant, a separate class family is more structure than it earns.

concepts.title: A Duck delegates to its behavior objects
concepts.question: How does a Duck perform flying and quacking when the code for them has been moved out of it?

paragraphs: To delegate is to hand a job to another object instead of doing it yourself. A Duck now holds two instance variables, flyBehavior and quackBehavior, declared with the interface types. The fly() and quack() methods are removed from Duck and its subclasses.

In their place the Duck class has performFly() and performQuack(). To perform the quack, a Duck lets the object referenced by quackBehavior quack for it. The Duck does not care what kind of object it is, only that it knows how to quack.
card.example: A Document class holds a variable typed PrintBehavior. Its print() method forwards to that variable. Assigning a PdfPrinter or a PlainPrinter changes how printing happens, and Document is not edited.
card.rule: Delegate by holding a reference typed as the behavior interface and forwarding the work to the object it refers to.
card.limits: A Duck can delegate only to an object it has been given. Delegation also adds one small forwarding method per behavior to the delegating class.

concepts.title: Giving a Duck its behaviors in the constructor
concepts.question: How does a MallardDuck get its flying and quacking behaviors, and what does the authors' admission about that tell you?

paragraphs: MallardDuck's constructor sets its inherited quackBehavior to a new Quack object and its flyBehavior to a new FlyWithWings object. So a mallard quacks like a real duck, not with a squeak or a silence, and flies with wings.

The authors admit this is a poor way to initialize, since concrete classes are hard-coded into the constructor. They promise later patterns that fix it. Still, because the variables are interface types, a different implementation can be assigned at runtime, so flexibility remains.
card.rule: A constructor can give an object its starting behaviors, but naming a concrete class there ties the object to it until the behavior is replaced.
card.limits: Hard-coding new Quack() into a constructor fixes the starting choice in code. Flexibility comes from the variable's interface type, not from the constructor.

concepts.title: The classes the duck code is built from
concepts.question: Which classes make up the working duck code, and what does each quack behavior do when it runs?

paragraphs: The test code is assembled from small parts: Duck and MallardDuck, the FlyBehavior interface with FlyWithWings and FlyNoWay, and the QuackBehavior interface with Quack, MuteQuack and Squeak. A MiniDuckSimulator test class runs them.

Each quack behavior is a tiny class with one quack() method that prints. Quack prints Quack. MuteQuack prints a message of silence. Squeak prints Squeak. Because every class implements the same interface, the Duck can call any of them the same way.
card.rule: Small classes behind one interface can be mixed and matched, so the Duck's calls never change as behaviors are swapped.
card.limits: A test like this shows the design works for a few cases. It does not show that every future behavior will fit the interface unchanged.

concepts.title: Changing a duck's behavior while the program runs
concepts.question: How can a duck's behavior change after it has been created, and what must the new behavior satisfy?

paragraphs: The authors add two setter methods to Duck, one for the fly behavior and one for the quack behavior. They can be called at any time to change a duck's behavior on the fly. To change a duck's behavior at runtime, just call the setter for that behavior.

Their example adds a new Duck type, ModelDuck, and a new FlyRocketPowered behavior. The test class then uses the setter to make the ModelDuck rocket-enabled. The new behavior works because it implements the right behavior interface.
card.rule: Call a setter with an object that implements the right interface, and the duck's behavior changes while the program runs.
card.limits: A setter changes only the one object it is called on. A rocket-enabled duck does not change the other ducks of the same class.

concepts.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
concepts.title: Behaviors as a family of algorithms
concepts.question: What makes a set of classes a family of algorithms, and where else could the same technique apply?

paragraphs: The authors suggest a change of wording. Instead of a set of duck behaviors, think of a family of algorithms: different ways of doing the same thing, such as different ways of flying or quacking. Each way is a class, and all of them share one interface.

The technique is not limited to ducks. The authors say the same approach could serve a set of classes that implement ways to compute state sales tax in different states. Seeing behaviors as algorithms makes it easier to spot the pattern in other problems.
card.example: A tax app has one class per state, each with its own rule for working out sales tax. All implement TaxRule, and checkout calls calculate() without knowing which state's rule it has.
card.rule: A family of algorithms is a set of interchangeable ways to do the same job, each in its own class behind one interface.
card.limits: Classes that do different jobs are not a family, even if they share a base. The members must be able to stand in for one another.

concepts.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
concepts.title: IS-A, HAS-A and IMPLEMENTS
concepts.question: What are the three relationships in the reworked class structure, and which arrow stands for each?

paragraphs: The reworked design has three kinds of link between classes. A MallardDuck extends Duck: this is IS-A, a mallard is a kind of duck. A FlyWithWings class implements FlyBehavior: this is IMPLEMENTS, a class that carries out an interface.

A Duck has a FlyBehavior and a QuackBehavior, to which it delegates flying and quacking. This is HAS-A. The authors urge careful attention to these links: in the class diagram each arrow should be labeled with one of the three.
card.example: In a vehicle program, a Truck extends Vehicle (IS-A). A Vehicle holds an EngineBehavior (HAS-A). A DieselEngine carries out EngineBehavior (IMPLEMENTS).
card.rule: IS-A means extends, IMPLEMENTS means carries out an interface, and HAS-A means holds a reference to another object.
card.limits: Choosing the wrong link gives a wrong design. A Duck is not a FlyBehavior, so IS-A would be a mistake there; the right link is HAS-A.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Composition
concepts.question: What is composition, and how do composed objects get their behavior?

paragraphs: Each duck has a FlyBehavior and a QuackBehavior, to which it delegates flying and quacking. When two classes are put together like this, you are using composition. Instead of inheriting behavior, the ducks get it by being composed with the right behavior object.

The authors call this an important technique. The composed object can be chosen when the duck is made and, because the part is held by interface, can be replaced later. Composition is the HAS-A link put to use.
card.rule: In composition an object gets its behavior from the objects it holds, not from classes it inherits from.
card.limits: Composition needs a part with a clear interface to hold. If there is no clean way to describe the part by an interface, composing it may be no easier than inheriting.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Favor composition over inheritance
concepts.question: What does the third design principle ask for, and what two benefits do the authors give?

paragraphs: The third design principle reads: favor composition over inheritance. The authors say creating systems with composition gives a lot more flexibility. It lets you encapsulate a family of algorithms into their own set of classes. It also lets you change behavior at runtime, as long as the object you compose with implements the correct behavior interface.

The duck design used this principle, though it was not named at the time. The authors add that composition appears in many design patterns, and that its advantages and disadvantages are covered throughout the book.
card.rule: Prefer giving an object its behavior by composing it with other objects over inheriting that behavior.
card.limits: The principle says favor, not forbid. Inheritance still fits stable, shared code, and the authors say composition has disadvantages as well as advantages.

concepts.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
concepts.title: Why reuse is not the highest aim
concepts.question: Why do the authors say effort should not go into reuse above maintainability and extensibility?

paragraphs: In the authors' dialogue, a student says the promise of object-oriented design is reuse, and that inheritance will cut development time. The master points out that we always spend more time maintaining and changing software than on first development.

The master then asks whether effort should go into reuse above maintainability and extensibility. The student agrees there is some truth in this, and the master tells him to think more about inheritance: it has problems, and there are other ways to reach reuse. The argument is: maintenance takes most of the time, so design for it.
card.example: A firm saves a week by copying one report module into six products. A year later a law changes and all six copies need edits. The saving in week one is far smaller than the cost in year two.
card.rule: Since most time is spent changing software after it is built, a design should be judged by how easily it can be maintained and extended.
card.limits: This is the authors' view, and it does not say reuse is worthless. Reuse that is easy to maintain remains valuable.

concepts.title: The Strategy Pattern in one sentence
concepts.question: What does the Strategy Pattern say in one sentence, and which parts of the duck design match it?

paragraphs: The pattern the authors have just walked through is the Strategy Pattern. Its formal definition: the Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.

In the duck design the family of algorithms is the set of fly or quack behaviors. Each one is encapsulated in its own class. They are interchangeable because they share an interface. The clients are the ducks, which hold a behavior and can have it changed without being edited.
card.rule: Strategy defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each, and makes them interchangeable so they vary independently of the clients that use them.
card.limits: Strategy suits a job that has several interchangeable ways of being done. Where the job has only one way, the pattern adds classes with no payoff.

concepts.title: A shared vocabulary shortens talk
concepts.question: What does a shared vocabulary between two people save, and what does it do for the listener?

paragraphs: At the diner, two customers place the same order. Alice uses twice the words and tries the cook's patience. Flo gets the same result in a few words, because she has a shared vocabulary with the short-order cook.

The shared vocabulary makes it easier to communicate and gives the cook less to remember, since the diner patterns are in his head. Design patterns give developers a shared vocabulary in the same way. It elevates thinking to the pattern level, away from the nitty-gritty of objects.
card.example: Two air traffic controllers say cleared to land, and a whole procedure is understood. Without the shared term, the same message would take a paragraph and invite mistakes.
card.rule: A shared vocabulary lets speakers say a complete idea in a few words because both already know what the words stand for.
card.limits: The saving exists only when both sides know the vocabulary. A pattern name said to someone who does not know it carries no meaning.

concepts.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
concepts.title: What a pattern name carries
concepts.question: What is communicated when a team says it uses a pattern, beyond the name itself?

paragraphs: When you speak in patterns you share more than lingo: you share a set of qualities, characteristics and constraints. Saying we are using the Strategy Pattern to implement our ducks' behaviors tells a listener that the behavior is encapsulated in its own classes, can be expanded easily and can be changed even at runtime.

The authors list the benefits. Patterns let you say more with less. They keep a discussion at the design level, instead of sliding into implementation details. They help a team move faster with less room for misunderstanding. And they motivate junior developers to learn, so you can build a community of pattern users.
card.rule: A pattern name stands for a whole design with its qualities and constraints, which lets a team discuss design at a higher level.
card.limits: This holds only while both sides mean the same thing by the name. Using a pattern name loosely brings back the misunderstanding it was meant to remove.

concepts.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
concepts.title: Patterns are not libraries
concepts.question: How does a design pattern differ from a library or framework, and where does a pattern first go?

paragraphs: Libraries and frameworks are code someone else wrote. You write against their APIs, compile them in and benefit from their functions, such as networking, GUI and IO. They do not help you structure your own application so that it is easier to understand, maintain and extend. Design patterns do.

A pattern is a higher-level idea: it says how to structure classes and objects to solve a certain problem, and it is your job to adapt it to your application. So patterns do not go straight into your code. They first go into your brain. Libraries and frameworks may use patterns inside, which helps you understand their APIs faster.
card.rule: A library supplies code you link in; a pattern supplies a design you learn and adapt to your own application.
card.limits: The two are related, not opposed. A library may be built on patterns, and knowing the pattern helps you learn the library.

concepts.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
concepts.title: Knowing OO basics is not enough
concepts.question: Why does knowing abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism not make a designer good at flexible systems?

paragraphs: A developer asks whether patterns matter for someone who already knows the OO basics. The guru calls this a misunderstanding: knowing the basics does not automatically make you good at building flexible, reusable, maintainable systems. Building such systems is not always obvious and was discovered through hard work.

Those discoveries were collected as design patterns. Knowing them puts you ahead, but design is an art with trade-offs. When no pattern fits, the OO principles that underlie the patterns help. One secret of maintainable systems is thinking about how they might change.
card.rule: OO basics are tools; flexible designs come from patterns and principles that were found through experience.
card.limits: Patterns do not guarantee a good design. The guru says design is an art and trade-offs remain, so judgment is still required.

concepts.title: The chapter in one view
concepts.question: What is the chapter's main claim about patterns, change and design, in a few sentences?

paragraphs: The chapter's bullet points can be gathered into one thread. Good OO designs are reusable, extensible and maintainable, and knowing the OO basics is not enough to get them. Patterns are proven OO experience: they show how to build such systems, and they give general solutions, not code, which you apply to your own application.

Patterns are discovered, not invented. Most patterns and principles address change, and most let some part of a system vary independently of the rest. A common move is to take what varies and encapsulate it. Patterns also give developers a shared language.
card.rule: Design for change: find what varies, encapsulate it, prefer composition, and use patterns as proven solutions and a shared language.
card.limits: A one-line summary leaves out the trade-offs the chapter mentions. Use it to recall the chapter, not to settle a design.

concepts.section: What do we know so far?
concepts.title: What the weather station must do
concepts.question: What does the weather application have to do, and what is already given to us?

paragraphs: The system has three players: the physical weather station that acquires readings, a WeatherData object that tracks those readings, and displays that show conditions to users. WeatherData offers getters for temperature, humidity and barometric pressure.

WeatherData also has a method, measurementsChanged(), that runs whenever new readings are available. The team is told not to worry about who calls it; its job is to fill that method so the displays update. Three displays are wanted: current conditions, statistics and a forecast.

The spec adds an open-ended requirement: other developers must be able to write their own displays, and users must be able to add or remove displays. This requirement about future change, more than the list of three, will drive the design.
card.rule: Before designing, separate what is given, what must be built, and what must stay open to change.
card.limits: A spec can be vague, so a list of what we know may be incomplete; the open requirement matters more than the three named displays, because the list of displays will grow.

concepts.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
concepts.title: Judging the hard-coded first attempt
concepts.question: Why does putting calls to each display directly inside measurementsChanged() make the application hard to extend?

paragraphs: The first attempt takes the hint and adds code to measurementsChanged(): it reads the three values and then calls update code on the current conditions, statistics and forecast displays by name. It works for the three displays the client listed.

The authors ask the reader to check it against the chapter 1 principles. The checklist covers: coding to concrete classes instead of interfaces, editing code for every new display, no way to add or remove displays while running, no shared interface among displays, and not encapsulating the part that changes.
Judging a design means testing it against the spec’s demands: who must be able to add displays, and when? The more the spec expects change, the more each of these flaws costs.
card.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.
card.limits: A small system that will never change may not need more, so the flaws only bite when the spec expects change. The checklist is a set of questions to ask, not a proof of which flaws a particular design has.

concepts.title: The newspaper subscription picture
concepts.question: How does a newspaper subscription work, and which of its parts will we reuse to understand the pattern?

paragraphs: A publisher starts printing newspapers. You subscribe to that publisher, and every time a new edition comes out it is delivered to you. As long as you stay subscribed, you keep getting editions.

When you unsubscribe, deliveries stop. While the publisher stays in business, people, hotels, airlines and other businesses keep subscribing and unsubscribing, so the set of recipients changes all the time.

The authors say that if you understand subscriptions you roughly understand the Observer Pattern. Keep three ideas: delivery goes only to the current subscribers, anyone can join or leave, and the publisher produces editions the same way whoever is on the list.
card.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.
card.limits: The picture shows who gets told, but not how the telling is coded. In software the publisher calls a method on each recipient, and the analogy says nothing about the interface that makes that possible.

concepts.title: Subject, observer and registering
concepts.question: What do the words subject, observer, register and notification mean, and who keeps the list?

paragraphs: In the Observer Pattern the publisher is called the SUBJECT and the subscribers are called OBSERVERS. The subject holds the state that matters and a list of its observers.

To register is to ask the subject to add you to its list. To remove yourself is to ask to be taken off it. A notification is what the subject sends to every observer currently on the list when its state changes.
Observers ask to join; the subject does not have to hunt for them. In the book’s walkthrough a Duck object tells the subject it wants to become an observer.
card.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.
card.limits: These words name roles, not kinds of class: one object can be a subject to some objects and an observer of others. Other systems use other names, for instance Swing calls observers listeners.

concepts.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
concepts.title: Registering, notifying and leaving
concepts.question: In what order do registering, notification and removal happen, and who receives which notification?

paragraphs: The book walks a subject through a sequence. A Duck object tells the subject it wants to be an observer, and the subject adds it to its list. When the subject gets a new data value, it sends a notification to every observer on the list.

Later a Mouse object, tired of receiving values, asks to be removed, and the subject takes it off the list. The next time the subject gets a new value, the notification goes to everyone still on the list, and the Mouse is skipped.
The Mouse secretly misses the values and may ask to be an observer again some day. Leaving is not permanent: an object can register again and will then be notified of later changes.
card.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.
card.limits: The walkthrough shows the list changing between notifications. It does not say what should happen if the list changes while a notification is being sent, so do not assume an answer from this story.

concepts.title: One object, two roles
concepts.question: Can one object be both a subject for some objects and an observer of another?

paragraphs: In the book’s skit Jill stops being an observer and collects a signing bonus, because her company no longer needed to pay a headhunter. Lori stays an observer of the headhunter.
Lori also builds her own call list and notifies her own observers. She is a subject and an observer at once: the roles describe a relationship, and one object can take part in several.
This lets notifications pass through a chain: the first subject tells Lori, and Lori tells those who depend on her. Each link depends on the one before it.
card.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.
card.limits: A chain of links is a possibility, not advice to build long chains. The skit does not discuss what long chains cost, so it should not be read as a recommendation.

concepts.title: The formal definition
concepts.question: What does the formal definition of the Observer Pattern claim about dependency and notification?

paragraphs: The textbook definition says the Observer Pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects, so that when one object changes state, all of its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

Read it in pieces. One object, the subject, holds the state; many objects, its dependents, rely on it. The trigger is a change of state. The effect is that every dependent is notified without anyone asking again.
The authors add that, depending on the style of notification, the observer may also be updated with the new values. Most implementations use Subject and Observer interfaces.
card.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.
card.limits: The definition states an intent, not code. How notices are sent, and whether values travel with them, differs between implementations, so one definition fits many different class designs.
card.example: A shared calendar event is changed. Every attendee’s calendar view shows the new time without anyone clicking refresh. One event (the one), many views (the dependents), a change (the trigger), everyone told (the effect).

concepts.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: One owner, many dependents
concepts.question: Why does the pattern speak of one subject and many observers, and what does dependence mean here?

paragraphs: With the Observer Pattern, the subject is the object that contains the state and controls it. So there is one subject with state. The observers use that state, even though they do not own it.

There are many observers, and they rely on the subject to tell them when its state changes. That reliance is the dependence: because the subject is the sole owner of the data, observers depend on it to update them.
The authors say this gives a cleaner object-oriented design than letting many objects control the same data.
card.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.
card.limits: The one is the owner of one piece of state. A system can contain many subjects, each with its own observers, and an observer can depend on several subjects.

concepts.title: Subject and Observer interfaces
concepts.question: What does each of the two interfaces contain, and which classes implement them?

paragraphs: Most implementations of the pattern revolve around two interfaces. The Subject interface has methods to register an observer, to remove an observer and to notify observers. The Observer interface has one method, update(), which the subject calls.

A concrete subject, such as WeatherData, implements the Subject interface and keeps the list. Each concrete observer, such as a display, implements the Observer interface so the subject can call update() on it.
Each interface lists what the other side may call on you: observers call the Subject interface to join or leave, and the subject calls the Observer interface to deliver news.
card.rule: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify; the Observer interface offers update.
card.limits: The book says there are a few ways to implement the pattern and that most use these two interfaces. The two-interface layout is common, not part of the definition itself.

concepts.title: Loose coupling
concepts.question: What does loosely coupled mean, and what does a subject know about its observers?

paragraphs: When two objects are loosely coupled, they can interact but have very little knowledge of each other. The Observer Pattern gives subjects and observers this property.
The only thing the subject knows about an observer is that it implements the Observer interface. It does not need to know the observer’s concrete class, what it does, or anything else about it.

The design principle the authors draw from this: strive for loosely coupled designs between objects that interact. Such designs build flexible systems that can handle change because they minimise the interdependency between objects.
card.rule: Loosely coupled objects interact while knowing as little as possible about each other.
card.limits: Loose coupling shrinks what each side knows, not whether they depend on each other. The subject still relies on the interface and observers still rely on the subject to tell them.

concepts.title: What loose coupling buys
concepts.question: Which changes can be made to subjects and observers without breaking the other side?

paragraphs: Because the subject depends only on a list of objects that implement the Observer interface, new observers can be added at any time. An observer can be replaced at run time by another, and observers can be removed at any time.

To add a new kind of observer, no change to the subject is needed: implement the Observer interface in the new class and register it. The subject delivers notifications to any object that implements the interface.
Subjects and observers can also be reused independently. Changes to either do not affect the other, as long as both still meet their obligations to implement the interfaces.
card.rule: While both sides keep to the interfaces, either can be changed, added, removed or reused without touching the other.
card.limits: The freedom lasts only while the interface contract is kept. Changing the interface itself reaches both sides, so this is not permission to change anything at all.

concepts.title: Three principles at work
concepts.question: How does the Observer Pattern apply the earlier principles of encapsulating variation, programming to interfaces and composition?

paragraphs: The authors’ answer to the principle challenge: what varies in Observer is the state of the subject and the number and types of observers. With the pattern you vary the dependents without changing the subject, which is separating what varies from what stays the same.

Both the subject and observers use interfaces. The subject tracks objects that implement the Observer interface, and observers register with the Subject interface. This is programming to an interface and keeps things loosely coupled.
The pattern uses composition to attach any number of observers to their subjects. The relationship is not set up by an inheritance hierarchy; it is set up at run time by composition.
card.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.
card.limits: The chapter later finds that the built-in java.util.Observable falls short on two of these principles, so using the pattern in name does not guarantee the principles are followed.

concepts.title: Applying Observer to the weather station
concepts.question: How do we apply Observer to the weather station: who is the subject, who are the observers, and how do they get the data?

paragraphs: Mary and Sue start by rereading the definition. WeatherData is the one, and the display elements are the many. WeatherData has state (temperature, humidity and pressure), and when it changes all displays must be told.
Sue proposes that displays register themselves with WeatherData to get the information they want. Once WeatherData knows a display, it can call a method to tell it the measurements.
Each display is a different type, so they should all implement the same interface. Every display will have an update() method that WeatherData calls, defined in the shared interface.
card.rule: Make WeatherData the subject and each display an observer behind a common interface with update().
card.limits: This is the team’s first answer. How the measurements travel to the observers is left open and revisited later in the chapter, so the mapping is not the end of the design.

concepts.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
concepts.title: WeatherData as a subject
concepts.question: What changes inside WeatherData when it implements the Subject interface?

paragraphs: WeatherData now implements the Subject interface. It keeps the list of registered observers and offers the methods to register and remove them.
The method measurementsChanged() no longer names the three displays. It tells the observers on the list instead, calling update() on each with the new measurements.
Because the displays are reached through the list, WeatherData does not care how many there are. One loop over the list covers any number of displays, including none.
card.rule: WeatherData keeps the observer list and, when measurementsChanged() runs, tells every observer on it.
card.limits: How the list is stored and how the loop is written are the implementer’s choices. The chapter’s code is not reproduced here, and the same idea fits other storage.

concepts.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
concepts.title: Displays that register themselves
concepts.question: What does a display do when it is built, and why does it keep a reference to the subject?

paragraphs: Each display implements the Observer interface so the subject can call update() on it. In the book’s current conditions display, the constructor receives the subject and registers the display with it, so the display puts itself on the list.

The display also stores a reference to the subject, even though it does not use it again after the constructor. The authors explain that in the future it may want to unregister itself, and holding the reference makes that easy.

In this display, update() stores the new values and calls display(). The authors say this is fine for a small example and that there are much better ways to organise display, which come with the Model-View-Controller pattern later.
card.rule: A display registers itself with the subject when built and keeps the subject so it can unregister later.
card.limits: Calling display() directly inside update() suits a small example only. The authors point to Model-View-Controller for a better separation of receiving data from presenting it.

concepts.title: Adding a display late
concepts.question: How can a new display, such as the heat index, be added to the weather station?

paragraphs: The CEO phones to say the station cannot ship without a heat index display. The heat index combines temperature and humidity into an apparent temperature, how hot it feels. The formula is supplied in a file.
In the Observer design the work is small: write a new HeatIndexDisplay class that implements the Observer interface and register it with WeatherData. The subject is not changed.
The new class takes the values it needs from each update, computes the index and shows it. It uses temperature and humidity and ignores pressure.
card.rule: To add a display, write one new observer class and register it; leave the subject alone.
card.limits: This works when the new display needs only data the subject already provides. A display that needs a value the subject does not hold forces a change to the subject.

concepts.title: Push and pull
concepts.question: What do push and pull mean for getting state to observers, and what does each cost?

paragraphs: There are two ways to get state from the subject to an observer. With push, the subject sends the state along with the notification, as the weather update() does with temperature, humidity and pressure. With pull, the subject notifies and each observer comes to it to fetch the state it wants.

The book stages a chat between a subject and an observer. The subject likes push: one notification carries everything, so the observer needs no extra calls. It worries that pull makes it open itself up through public getters.

The observer prefers pull. Many kinds of observer exist and the subject cannot anticipate them all; with pull, each takes only what it needs. If the subject gains state, the update calls on every observer need not change, as only getters are added.
card.rule: Push sends the state to every observer; pull lets each observer fetch what it needs.
card.limits: Each style has a price. Push gives all observers the same set and ties update() to it. Pull needs public getters and may need several calls to collect what an observer wants.

concepts.title: Is pull really better?
concepts.question: The authors call pull more correct than push: how sound are their reasons, and when do they hold?

paragraphs: In its summary the chapter says you can push or pull data from the Observable, and that pull is considered more correct. This is the authors’ view, not a definition of the pattern.

Their reasons come from the chat: observers differ and the subject cannot predict all their needs; observers fetch only what they need; and adding state later does not force changes to every update call.

To judge the claim, test each reason against the case. It is strong when observers are varied and the state is likely to grow. It is weaker when one small state is used in full by every observer, and the subject’s point about convenience then counts for more.
card.rule: Weigh the claim that pull is more correct by checking whether its reasons fit the situation.
card.limits: The authors give pull as a considered view, not a law. The subject’s counterpoint, that push is convenient and keeps state private, is real and wins in some cases.

concepts.title: Java’s built-in Observer support
concepts.question: What are java.util.Observable and java.util.Observer, and how do they differ from the hand-built version?

paragraphs: Java has built-in support for the Observer Pattern in several APIs. The most general is the Observer interface and Observable class in java.util. They resemble the hand-built Subject and Observer interfaces and give a lot of functionality out of the box, with either push or pull.

The main difference is that the subject, WeatherData, now extends the Observable class and inherits its add, delete and notify methods, instead of implementing a Subject interface and keeping its own list.
An observer implements the java.util.Observer interface and calls addObserver() on an Observable to join. To leave, it calls deleteObserver().
card.rule: Extend Observable to be a subject; implement java.util.Observer and call addObserver to observe.
card.limits: Observable is a class, so a subject must extend it. The chapter later shows this brings problems that limit its use.

concepts.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
concepts.title: The changed flag
concepts.question: What must a built-in subject do before notifyObservers() actually notifies, and why does that rule exist?

paragraphs: With the built-in support, notifying is a two-step process. First call setChanged() to signal that the state has changed. Then call one of the two notifyObservers() methods, with or without a data argument.

If notifyObservers() is called without setChanged() first, the observers are not notified. The flag exists to give the subject control over when to notify. If readings fluctuate by tenths of a degree, the subject can call setChanged() only when the temperature moves by more than half a degree.
Two more methods exist: clearChanged() sets the flag back to false and hasChanged() reports it. The authors say you may not use this often, but it is there if needed.
card.rule: No notification happens without setChanged(); use it to decide which changes deserve one.
card.limits: The flag is a gate that is easy to forget to open. If observers are not notified when you expect them to be, the missing setChanged() call is the first suspect.

concepts.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
concepts.title: Push and pull with the built-in classes
concepts.question: How does the built-in support let a subject push or pull data to observers?

paragraphs: The update() method of the built-in Observer has a different signature from our own. It receives the Observable that notified it, plus a data object.

To push, pass the data as an object to notifyObservers(arg). To leave it to the observers, call notifyObservers() without data and let each observer pull what it wants from the Observable it was handed.

The book reworks WeatherData and the displays this way. The displays pull temperature, humidity and pressure from the subject through its getters, and either style needs setChanged() to be called first.
card.rule: Pass a data object to notifyObservers(arg) to push, or notify without data and let observers pull from the Observable they receive.
card.limits: Pulling needs the subject to expose getters, and pushing with a data object means observers must know what the object contains.

concepts.title: Do not rely on notification order
concepts.question: Why can the output order differ between the hand-built and built-in versions, and what should our code assume about it?

paragraphs: Running the reworked weather station gives the same calculations, but the text appears in a different order. The built-in notifyObservers() notifies observers in a different order from the hand-built one.
The authors ask which is right and answer: neither. The two were simply implemented in different ways.

What would be incorrect is writing code that depends on a specific notification order. If the Observable or Observer implementation changes, the order could change and the application could produce wrong results, which is not loosely coupled.
card.rule: Do not depend on the order in which observers are notified.
card.limits: The advice is about order between observers. It does not claim that notifications happen in no order, only that the order is not part of what the pattern promises.

concepts.title: The dark side of Observable
concepts.question: What problems come from Observable being a class with a protected setChanged(), and which principles does that cut against?

paragraphs: The authors call this the dark side. Observable is a class, and it does not implement an interface. Because it is a class, a subject must subclass it, so you cannot add its behaviour to a class that already extends another superclass.
With no Observable interface you cannot write your own implementation that works with Java’s built-in Observer, and you cannot swap the java.util version for another, such as a multithreaded one.

Also, setChanged() is protected. You cannot call it unless you subclass Observable, so you cannot create an Observable instance and compose it with your own objects. This runs against favoring composition over inheritance.
card.rule: Judge a library class by whether it lets you follow the principles; Observable’s class form and protected method block reuse and composition.
card.limits: The authors say Observable still has some utility and may serve if you can extend it. These are potholes to watch for, not a ban on using the class.

concepts.title: Built-in or hand-built?
concepts.question: When should you use the built-in Observable, and when should you build your own?

paragraphs: The authors’ advice after the dark side: Observable may serve your needs if you can extend it. If you cannot, you may need to roll your own implementation as the chapter did at the start.
The summary adds: do not be afraid to create your own Observable implementation if needed. They also say that in many cases it is more flexible to build your own, and that it is not all that hard.
Either way, knowing the pattern well puts you in a good position to work with any API that uses it.
card.rule: Use the built-in class when you can extend it and its limits are tolerable; otherwise write an interface-based version of your own.
card.limits: This is the authors’ view. A hand-built version costs writing the list handling and does not plug into Java’s built-in Observer API, so the right choice depends on the constraints.

concepts.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
concepts.title: Observers in Swing
concepts.question: How do Swing listeners relate to observers, and what happens when a button is clicked?

paragraphs: Swing, Java’s GUI toolkit, uses the Observer Pattern. A JButton, through its superclass AbstractButton, has many add and remove listener methods. The listeners are the observers, and they listen for events on the component.

An ActionListener lets you listen for actions such as a button press. The book’s example has a button labelled Should I do it? with two listeners, AngelListener and DevilListener, each answering in its own way.
Listeners appear throughout Swing, and JavaBeans offers its own version, for instance the PropertyChangeListener interface. Many GUI frameworks use the pattern heavily.
card.rule: In Swing, a component is the subject and its listeners are observers added and removed through add and remove methods.
card.limits: Frameworks rename the roles and use their own method names and event objects. The match is by role, so a different toolkit may call the same thing by another name.

concepts.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
concepts.title: Lambdas as observers
concepts.question: How can a lambda expression act as an observer, and does it change the pattern?

paragraphs: Lambda expressions were added in Java 8. Instead of an inner class for a listener, you write a lambda expression, which creates a function object, and that function object is the observer.

When you pass it to addActionListener(), Java ensures its signature matches actionPerformed(), the one method in the ActionListener interface. Later, when the button is clicked, the button notifies its observers, including these function objects, by calling each listener’s actionPerformed().
You are still using the Observer Pattern: you just skip creating an ActionListener object. Readers unfamiliar with lambdas can keep using inner classes.
card.rule: A lambda that fits a one-method observer interface is an observer, and the pattern is unchanged.
card.limits: This applies where the observer interface has a single method, as ActionListener does. The pattern itself does not need lambdas, and inner classes still work.

concepts.title: One subclass per combination
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a shop gives every drink-and-extras combination its own subclass?

paragraphs: Starbuzz Coffee began with an abstract Beverage class and one subclass per drink. Customers can add extras such as steamed milk, soy, mocha and whipped milk, and each extra costs something, so the order system has to price every combination.

If each combination becomes its own subclass, the number of classes explodes. When the price of milk goes up, every class that includes milk must change, and a new topping such as caramel means yet more classes. The authors call the result a maintenance nightmare.
card.example: A florist sells bouquets of roses, tulips or lilies, each with optional ribbon, vase or card. Writing one class for every bouquet-and-extras combination gives dozens of classes, and a rise in the ribbon price means editing all of those that include ribbon.
card.rule: One subclass per combination multiplies the classes and scatters every price change across many of them.
card.limits: With a few fixed combinations that will not change, one subclass for each stays manageable; the trouble starts when options multiply or change.

concepts.title: Flags in the base class
concepts.question: Why does keeping a true-or-false flag for each extra in the base class still leave Starbuzz with problems?

paragraphs: A tempting fix keeps one Beverage base class with a flag for each extra: milk, soy, mocha and whip. The base cost() adds the price of every extra whose flag is on, and each drink subclass adds its own price on top.

This cuts the number of classes, but the trouble remains. When the price of an extra changes, the base class is edited. A new extra means a new flag and more changes to existing code. The authors also warn that functionality added to the base class may not be appropriate for some of the subclasses.
card.example: A print shop's Order base class has flags for lamination, binding and colour. When binding gets cheaper, Order is edited. When stapling is offered, Order gets another flag and another branch in its price method, and a poster subclass inherits a binding flag it can never use.
card.rule: Flags in the base class shrink the class count, yet every new or changed extra still edits existing code and burdens some subclasses.
card.limits: If the options are few, stable and fit every subclass, flags in the base class can be a reasonable, simple choice.

concepts.title: Static inheritance, runtime composition
concepts.question: How does behaviour gained by composition differ from behaviour inherited by subclassing, and when is each fixed?

paragraphs: Behaviour inherited by subclassing is set statically, at compile time, and every subclass must inherit the same behaviour. To change it, you edit code.

Behaviour added through composition and delegation can be assembled at runtime. Composition means one object holds others; delegation means it hands work on to them. This lets you add several new responsibilities, even ones the designer of the superclass never thought of, without touching that designer's code.

The authors' argument ends with maintenance: new functionality comes from writing new code instead of altering existing code, so the chance of bugs or side effects in code that already works is much reduced.
card.example: A music app builds playback effects by subclassing: Echo extends Player. A listener who wants echo plus bass boost forces a new class. If effects are objects that wrap a player, the app combines them while running, and a new effect is a new class that leaves the player untouched.
card.rule: Subclassing fixes behaviour at compile time for all subclasses; composition lets you add behaviour at runtime by writing new code.
card.limits: Composition adds more objects to create and coordinate, and when all variants share the same behaviour and nothing varies at runtime, plain inheritance is enough.

concepts.title: The Open-Closed Principle
concepts.question: What does the Open-Closed Principle ask of a class, and what does it buy?

paragraphs: The Open-Closed Principle says that classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Others may add new behaviour, yet code that has already been written and tested stays as it is.

The goal is to let a class take on new behaviour without changing its source. The authors say what you get is a design that is resilient to change and flexible enough to take on new functionality when requirements change.
Picture two signs on the class: one invites anyone to extend it with new behaviour, the other says the working code is not open to alteration.
card.example: A tax module has run correctly for years. When a new region's rules arrive, the team adds a new class for them and leaves the tested calculation code untouched. The module was open to the new rule and closed against edits.
card.rule: Design classes so new behaviour arrives as new code, while working code stays unchanged.
card.limits: A class without extension points is not broken; the principle is a goal pursued where change is expected, not a rule for every class.

concepts.title: Open and closed without contradiction
concepts.question: How can a class be open and closed at the same time without contradicting itself?

paragraphs: At first the phrase sounds contradictory, since the less modifiable something is, the harder it seems to extend. The contradiction fades once you see that each word is used in one sense about a different thing.

Open refers to adding behaviour: others can extend the class. Closed refers to editing source: the finished, tested code stays unmodified. With those two meanings, the phrase asks for one thing, extension through new code.
The authors' example is the Observer Pattern from Chapter 2: you can add new observers to extend a subject at any time without adding code to the subject.
card.example: A form-builder library lets you register new field types by writing a class and adding it to a list. The library's own files are not edited, yet developers extend what it can do.
card.rule: Open means behaviour can be added; closed means existing code is not edited, so the words do not collide.
card.limits: A design is open only along the extension points it provides; extending it any other way means editing its code.

concepts.title: Apply it where change is likely
concepts.question: Why do the authors say not to apply the Open-Closed Principle to every part of a design?

paragraphs: The authors say you usually cannot make every part of a design follow the principle. Making a design open to extension takes time and effort, and tying down every part would probably be wasteful.
Following the principle typically introduces new levels of abstraction, which adds complexity to the code. Applied everywhere, it can lead to complex, hard-to-understand code.
So concentrate on the areas of the design most likely to change. Spotting them comes partly from experience designing object-oriented systems and partly from knowing the domain you work in.
card.example: A shop's checkout has a stable receipt layout but changing tax rules and payment methods. The team adds extension points for tax and payment and leaves the receipt layout plain.
card.rule: Spend extensibility effort on the parts of the design most likely to change.
card.limits: Judging what will change takes experience and domain knowledge, so you will sometimes guess wrong; the principle gives no formula.

concepts.title: Decorating by wrapping
concepts.question: How do you build a Dark Roast with Mocha and Whip by decorating, without a new subclass?

paragraphs: Instead of a subclass for each combination, start with the plain beverage and decorate it with condiments at runtime. For a Dark Roast with Mocha and Whip, take a DarkRoast object, wrap it in a Mocha object, wrap that in a Whip object, then call cost().

Think of each decorator as a wrapper around another object. It holds the object it wraps. The customer's order is the outermost wrapper, inside it sit the others, and the chain ends at the plain drink.
A new extra, such as caramel, is just another wrapper class. No existing class changes, and an order may combine extras in any way.
card.example: A courier parcel starts as a plain Parcel. The customer wants insurance and a signature on delivery, so the system wraps the Parcel in an Insurance wrapper, then wraps that in a Signature wrapper. A fourth service later needs one new wrapper class.
card.rule: Start with the plain object and wrap it, one decorator per extra, at runtime.
card.limits: Wrapping builds an order from many small objects, and the code that assembles the chain must choose the extras and their order correctly.

concepts.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
concepts.title: Delegating inward
concepts.question: When cost() is called on the outermost wrapper, how does the total price come about?

paragraphs: To price the drink, call cost() on the outermost decorator, Whip in the drink order. Whip delegates the computation to the object it decorates, Mocha, which delegates to the DarkRoast. Each call travels inward until it reaches the plain drink.
When a cost comes back, each decorator adds its own charge on the way out: Whip receives Mocha's total and adds the whip charge. A decorator can do its work before delegating, after it, or both.
Delegation means handing a request on to another object. Each decorator needs to know only the one object it wraps, not the whole chain.
card.example: A report pipeline wraps a PlainReport in a Watermark, then in Encrypt. Calling render() on Encrypt asks Watermark to render, which asks PlainReport. The text comes back, Watermark adds its mark, and Encrypt scrambles the result, so Encrypt works after delegating.
card.rule: Call the outermost decorator; each decorator delegates inward and adds its own part.
card.limits: The order of wrappers can matter when each step works on the previous step's output, such as encrypting before or after adding a watermark.

concepts.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
concepts.title: Same supertype, so substitutable
concepts.question: Why can a decorated object be used anywhere the plain object was used?

paragraphs: A decorator has the same supertype as the object it decorates. A DarkRoast wrapped in Mocha and Whip is still a Beverage, so you can do with it anything you can do with a DarkRoast, including calling cost().
Because the types match, you can pass a decorated object wherever the original was expected. You can wrap an object in one decorator or several, and a wrapper can even wrap another wrapper.
Objects can be decorated at any time, so decorating at runtime with as many decorators as you like is possible. The authors flag this as a key point.
card.example: Application code takes any Sensor and calls read(). A SmoothedSensor wraps a Sensor and is itself a Sensor, so the application works with raw or smoothed readings without being changed.
card.rule: A decorator shares its component's type, so the wrapped object can replace the original anywhere.
card.limits: The substitution holds for code written against the shared type; code that checks for a specific concrete class will not see through the wrapper.

concepts.title: The pattern in one sentence
concepts.question: How does the book define the Decorator Pattern, and what does it offer instead of subclassing?

paragraphs: The book defines the Decorator Pattern as attaching additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators provide a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.
Dynamically means at runtime, while the program is running. The alternative to subclassing is wrapping: new behaviour comes from composing the object with a decorator, instead of from a new subclass.
The definition describes the role of the pattern. To see how to apply it, you need the class structure shown in the beverage example.
card.example: A photo app puts a border on the picture the user selected, while other pictures stay as they were. The border is attached to that object while the app runs; no BorderedPicture subclass is needed.
card.rule: The Decorator Pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object at runtime, as a flexible alternative to subclassing.
card.limits: The definition describes the role only; it does not tell you how to structure the classes, so use it together with the class structure, not alone.

concepts.title: Roles in the design
concepts.question: What do component, concrete component, decorator and concrete decorator each name in the beverage design?

paragraphs: The beverage design has four recurring roles. The abstract component is the shared type, Beverage. A concrete component is a real item that can be decorated, such as HouseBlend. The abstract decorator is CondimentDecorator, which extends Beverage. A concrete decorator, such as Mocha, adds one extra.

Read each term in one sense. Component names the thing being wrapped; decorator names the wrapper. A term like decorator names a job, not a kind of product, so it describes any object that wraps a component of the same type.
card.example: In a text toolkit, TextSource is the abstract component, FileText is a concrete component, TextFilter is the abstract decorator, and Uppercase is a concrete decorator that wraps another TextSource.
card.rule: Name each class by its role: abstract component, concrete component, abstract decorator or concrete decorator.
card.limits: Roles are jobs, not fixed classes: a decorator can itself be wrapped by another decorator, so one object can play both parts.

concepts.title: Inherit the type, not the behaviour
concepts.question: Why does CondimentDecorator extend Beverage when decorators do not get their behaviour from it?

paragraphs: In the class diagram CondimentDecorator extends Beverage, which looks like plain inheritance. The point is that decorators must have the same type as the objects they decorate, and here inheritance is used to achieve that type matching.

The behaviour does not come from the superclass. It comes from composing a decorator with a component and with other decorators. New behaviour is acquired by putting objects together, not by inheriting it.

That is why composition gives the flexibility to mix and match. With inheritance, behaviour is fixed at compile time and is only what the superclass gives or what is overridden. With composition, decorators combine in any way at runtime, and new ones can be added later.
card.example: UppercaseMessage extends Message so that it can stand in for a Message. It does not inherit its text from Message; the text comes from the Message object it wraps, which it then transforms.
card.rule: Decorators inherit the component's type, not its behaviour; the behaviour comes from composition.
card.limits: This reading holds when the superclass supplies only the shared type; if decorators also rely on inherited code, behaviour is coming from inheritance again.

concepts.title: Abstract class or interface for the type
concepts.question: Why did Starbuzz keep an abstract Beverage class when an interface could also supply the shared type?

paragraphs: Mary asks why Beverage is an abstract class if decorators only need the component's type, since an interface could supply a type too. Sue answers that the pattern traditionally specifies an abstract component, but in Java an interface could be used.
In Starbuzz's case, the code they received already had an abstract Beverage class. They try to avoid altering existing code, so they leave it alone as long as the abstract class works just fine.
In effect this is the Open-Closed Principle applied to the team's own habits: do not change what already works without a reason.
card.example: A team inherits an abstract PaymentMethod class from a vendor. Turning it into an interface would be tidier, but the existing class already gives decorators their type, so the team writes its decorators against it and leaves it alone.
card.rule: A decorator needs the component's type, supplied by an abstract class or an interface; keep the existing one if it works.
card.limits: When designing from scratch, the choice is open and an interface may be the lighter way to give the type; the argument for keeping applies to code you already have.

concepts.title: What a concrete decorator holds and does
concepts.question: What must a concrete decorator hold and implement to wrap a beverage and add its own extra?

paragraphs: A concrete decorator, such as Mocha, needs two things: a reference to the beverage it wraps, and its own versions of the component's methods. The wrapped drink is supplied when the wrapper is built.

Its cost() asks the wrapped beverage for its cost and adds the decorator's own charge. Its getDescription() works the same way: it asks the wrapped beverage for its description and adds the condiment's name, giving text such as Mocha, Whip, Mocha.
The Beverage class and the concrete drinks do not change. Each new condiment is a new class written to the same recipe: Soy and Whip follow Mocha.
card.example: A Discount wrapper around a Product holds that Product. Its price() returns the wrapped product's price reduced by ten percent, and its label() returns the wrapped label followed by on sale.
card.rule: A concrete decorator stores the component it wraps and implements each method by delegating to it and adding its own part.
card.limits: A decorator can only build on what the wrapped object returns; it cannot reach deeper into the chain, so reorganising descriptions needs extra code.

concepts.title: Code that checks concrete types
concepts.question: What happens to code that checks for a specific concrete component once decorators wrap it?

paragraphs: Decorators are transparent to code that uses only the abstract component type. A client calls cost() on a Beverage and neither knows nor cares whether decorators sit inside.
