Transparency stops when code relies on a concrete component's type. If code tests whether a drink is a HouseBlend in order to give a discount, wrapping the HouseBlend in decorators makes the test fail, because the outer object is a decorator.
The authors say that once you start writing code against concrete components, you should rethink your application design and your use of decorators.
card.example: A shipping function checks whether a Parcel is a FragileParcel to add padding. After an Insurance wrapper goes around the FragileParcel, the outer object is an Insurance wrapper, so the check fails and no padding is added.
card.rule: Write client code against the abstract component type; checks on concrete components break once decorators wrap them.
card.limits: The problem arises only for code that inspects concrete types; when all code uses the abstract type, decorators can be added with no change.

concepts.title: Chains, outermost objects and creation
concepts.question: Why is a decorator that needs to know every layer of its chain stretching the pattern?

paragraphs: Decorators are meant to add behaviour to the object they wrap. When a decorator must look several layers into its chain, for example to print Whip, Double Mocha instead of Mocha, Whip, Mocha, the authors say you are pushing it beyond its true intent.
It is still possible: a CondimentPrettyPrint decorator could parse the final description and tidy it, and getDescription() could return a list of descriptions to make that easier.

A second worry is that a client might hold a reference to an inner decorator, such as Soy, instead of the outermost one, Whip, so the Whip charge is lost. The authors admit that there are more objects to manage, and that errors of this kind are more likely.
card.example: A request pipeline wraps Cache with Auth, then Auth with Logging. A handler that kept a reference to the Auth layer instead of the Logging layer would bypass Logging, and nothing would be recorded.
card.rule: Let each decorator work with the one object it wraps, and hand clients only the outermost decorator.
card.limits: Features that need knowledge of the whole chain are possible with extra decorators, but they strain the pattern, so consider whether a different design suits better.

concepts.title: Decorators in Java I/O
concepts.question: How does the java.io package use the Decorator Pattern to add features when reading a file?

paragraphs: The java.io package is largely based on the Decorator Pattern. A typical set of objects for reading a file wraps a basic input stream in decorators that add functionality, such as buffering and line numbering.

BufferedInputStream and LineNumberInputStream both extend FilterInputStream, which acts as the abstract decorator class. The output streams have the same design, and the Reader and Writer streams, for character data, closely mirror the stream classes with a few differences.
Knowing the pattern, you can read an unfamiliar I/O class by asking which stream it wraps and what it adds.
card.example: To read a file with buffering and line counting, a program wraps a file input stream in a BufferedInputStream and that in a LineNumberInputStream. Like condiments around a coffee, each wrapper adds one feature to what is inside.
card.rule: In java.io, decorators such as buffering wrap an input stream; read the API by asking what each wrapper adds.
card.limits: The package has many small classes that can overwhelm newcomers, and the Reader and Writer streams mirror the byte streams only closely, with a few inconsistencies.

concepts.title: Weighing the costs of decorators
concepts.question: Which costs of the Decorator Pattern do the authors admit, and how should you weigh them?

paragraphs: A fair judgment of the pattern weighs its costs, and the authors name three. Decorator designs often contain many small classes, which can overwhelm developers, as Java I/O shows. Code that relies on concrete types can break when decorators are introduced. And the code that creates an object grows, because you must create the component and wrap it with several decorators.
The authors do not hide these costs. In an interview in the book the pattern itself lists them as its troubles and points to Factory and Builder to ease the creation burden.

To criticise fairly, ask whether the account leaves out anything relevant, and whether you can name a specific cost that outweighs the benefit for your case. Disliking the style of wrappers is not a criticism.
card.example: A team adds audit, retry and caching to a payment client. Decorators let them mix the three at runtime, but the code that builds the client now arranges three wrappers, and an old type check might stop working. The team weighs these costs before deciding.
card.rule: Weigh decorators' flexibility against many small classes, breakage of concrete-type checks and heavier creation code.
card.limits: Naming a cost is not a reason to reject the pattern; criticism must show that the costs outweigh the benefit in the case at hand.

concepts.title: When you see new, think concrete
concepts.question: What does a new expression tell you about the code that contains it?

paragraphs: Every new SomeClass() names a concrete class: one specific implementation, not an interface. The code containing it now depends on that exact class, so renaming it, replacing it or adding a sibling can force an edit right there.

The authors say there is technically nothing wrong with new. The culprit is change. When the class to build is picked at run time from a list of conditions, and that list keeps moving, every addition or removal means reopening the code that does the picking.
Code written to an interface keeps working with new classes that implement it, through polymorphism. Code that names many concrete classes does not.
card.example: A notification service builds an EmailSender, SmsSender or PushSender with new inside one method, choosing by a setting. Adding a chat-app sender means opening that method again, and any other method that repeats the same choice. Code that only called an interface method on a sender would need no edit.
card.rule: When you see new, think concrete: the code is tied to that class and must be reopened whenever the set of choices changes.
card.limits: The cost appears only where the choices vary. A class that is very unlikely to change can be created directly without harm.

concepts.title: Concrete choices break closed for modification
concepts.question: Why does code that picks among concrete classes fail to be closed for modification?

paragraphs: A design is open for extension and closed for modification when you can add behavior by adding code, without editing code that already works. The authors reviewed this principle in the previous chapter.
Code that chooses among concrete classes fails the test. To add or drop a variant you must open that code and examine what to add or delete, and the same choice often appears in several places.
The authors point to their first principle for a clue: identify the aspects that vary and separate them from what stays the same.
card.example: A report exporter has export(format) with branches for PDF, CSV and XML. Adding JSON means opening export() and adding a branch. A caller that only asked an Exporter interface for its output would not have to change.
card.rule: A piece of code is closed for modification only if adding a new concrete type needs no edit to it.
card.limits: Closed does not mean frozen. Bug fixes and genuinely new requirements still reopen code; the aim is that routine additions of variants do not.

concepts.section: But the pressure is on to add more pizza types
concepts.title: Finding the lines that vary
concepts.question: In an ordering method, which lines change as the menu changes and which stay the same?

paragraphs: The pizza store's orderPizza() method does two kinds of work. First it decides which pizza class to build from the type requested. Then it processes the pizza: prepare, bake, cut and box.
When competitors add Clam and Veggie pizzas and the Greek pizza sells poorly, the first part is edited again and again. The processing steps keep the same shape.

That split is the first principle in action: the creation lines are the aspect that varies, and they stop the method from being closed for modification. Once we know what varies, it is time to encapsulate it.
card.example: An invoice method picks a tax-rule class by country, then totals the lines, applies the rule and prints. Countries are added every month; totals and printing keep their form. The picking lines are the varying part.
card.rule: Find the lines that change with the menu and separate them from the steps that stay the same.
card.limits: Separate only what really varies. Moving stable code out adds indirection and gives nothing in return.

concepts.title: A factory handles creation
concepts.question: What is a factory in this chapter, and what does the old ordering method become?

paragraphs: The authors move the creation code out of orderPizza() into another object whose only concern is creating pizzas. They call that object a Factory: factories handle the details of object creation.
The old method becomes a client of the factory. When it needs a pizza it asks the factory to make one, so it no longer knows about Greek or Clam pizzas.
All it cares about is that the result implements the Pizza interface, so prepare, bake, cut and box can be called.
card.example: A notification app has sendAlert(kind). Creation moves to a NotificationFactory. sendAlert asks the factory for a notification of the requested kind and then calls send() on whatever comes back, without knowing which class it received.
card.rule: A factory is an object whose only job is to create other objects, so its clients ask for a product instead of building it.
card.limits: A factory does not remove concrete classes from the program. Some code, usually the factory, still names them; the gain is that the naming is gathered in one place.

concepts.title: Why one creation class helps
concepts.question: How does moving creation into one class help when it only seems to push the problem elsewhere?

paragraphs: SimplePizzaFactory has a createPizza(type) method holding the old chain of decisions. The ordering code asks it for a pizza and calls the pizza methods on the result.

The authors answer a natural objection, that the problem has only been pushed elsewhere. The factory may have many clients: a menu class that needs a pizza description and price, a home-delivery class that handles pizzas another way.
With creation in one class there is a single place to modify when the implementation changes, and the concrete instantiations leave the client code.
card.example: A parcel firm has a PriceCalculator, a LabelPrinter and a RouteMap, each choosing among Ground, Air and Sea carrier classes. A CarrierFactory replaces the three chains; adding Rail means one edit, in the factory.
card.rule: Put creation logic in one class so many clients share a single place to change.
card.limits: With one client, a short menu and no expected change the gain is small. The factory's own create method still changes when the menu does.

concepts.title: Static factory: convenient but fixed
concepts.question: What do you gain and lose by making the simple factory's create method static?

paragraphs: Some designs define the simple factory's method as static. This is often called a static factory. Callers use it directly with the class name, so no factory object has to be created.
The price is flexibility. A static method cannot be overridden by a subclass, so you cannot subclass the factory to change how it creates things.
An ordinary factory object, in contrast, is an instance that a client can be given, so a different factory can be passed in.
card.example: A ticket firm calls TicketFactory.create(kind) as a static method everywhere. When a holiday scheme needs different rules, there is no subclass to supply them; every call site would need an edit. An instance factory could be replaced at start-up.
card.rule: A static factory is convenient to call, but its creation behavior cannot be subclassed or swapped.
card.limits: If the creation rule will not need replacing, the convenience may outweigh the loss. The cost appears only when a different creator is needed.

concepts.title: The store holds its factory
concepts.question: How does the store hold its factory, and what could be swapped in?

paragraphs: The reworked PizzaStore receives a SimplePizzaFactory and keeps it in a field. Its orderPizza() method calls factory.createPizza(type) instead of building pizzas itself.
Because the store is composed with the factory, a different factory can be swapped in. The authors suggest New York, Chicago and California style pizza factories.
The store's own ordering logic stays the same; only the factory it was given differs.
card.example: A playlist builder is given a TrackSourceFactory when it is constructed. Online mode passes a streaming factory; offline mode passes a local-file factory. The builder's own code never changes.
card.rule: Give the client a reference to its factory so a different factory can be swapped in.
card.limits: Swapping the factory changes only how products are created. The store can still run its own steps its own way, which proves a weakness later.

concepts.title: Simple Factory is an idiom
concepts.question: Why do the authors give Simple Factory only an honorable mention instead of calling it a design pattern?

paragraphs: The authors state that Simple Factory is not actually a design pattern. They call it a programming idiom, widely used, and give it a Head First Pattern Honorable Mention.
They warn that some developers mistake the idiom for the Factory Pattern. Knowing the difference gives you something to say next time there is an awkward silence with another developer.
It is still worth studying: the authors treat it as a warm-up before two heavy-duty patterns that are both factories.
card.example: A team lead lists a class with a static create(type) method as a Factory Pattern on a design review. By the authors' view it is the Simple Factory idiom: one class that builds products from a type, with no subclass structure around it.
card.rule: Treat Simple Factory as a handy idiom, and do not confuse it with Factory Method or Abstract Factory.
card.limits: The label is the authors' judgment about what counts as a pattern, and the idiom is useful whatever it is called. Other writers may draw the line differently.

concepts.title: What implementing an interface means
concepts.question: What does the phrase implement an interface cover in design patterns, beyond the Java keyword?

paragraphs: The authors remind readers that in design patterns the phrase implement an interface does not always mean writing a class that uses the implements keyword with a Java interface.
In general use, a concrete class that supplies a method from a supertype is implementing that supertype's interface. The supertype can be a class or an interface.
So a subclass that provides the methods of an abstract class counts, even though it uses extends.
card.example: An abstract Shape declares area(). A Circle extends Shape and supplies area(). In design-pattern vocabulary Circle implements Shape's interface, though it never writes the implements keyword.
card.rule: To implement an interface is to supply the methods of any supertype's public contract, whether the supertype is a Java interface or a class.
card.limits: The broad sense is for reading design talk. In Java code the keyword implements still names a Java interface, so check which sense a speaker means.

concepts.title: Two needs at once
concepts.question: What two needs pull against each other when the pizza store becomes a franchise?

paragraphs: The store succeeds and everyone wants one in their neighborhood. As franchiser you want each franchise to use your time-tested code.
But regions differ. Each franchise may want its own style of pizza, such as New York, Chicago or California, depending on location and local taste.
Stated this way, the problem has two needs: freedom to vary the pizza style by region, and consistency in the way the store operates.
card.example: A coffee chain licenses its shop software. Local owners want regional menus; head office wants one checkout procedure. Naming both needs before choosing a design stops the team from solving only the louder one.
card.rule: State a design problem as its competing needs before choosing a solution.
card.limits: Naming the needs does not choose the solution, and some designs satisfy only one need well.

concepts.section: But you’d like a little more quality control...
concepts.title: Judging one factory per region
concepts.question: Does giving each region its own factory meet both of the franchiser's needs?

paragraphs: The first approach is to drop SimplePizzaFactory and write NYPizzaFactory, ChicagoPizzaFactory and CaliforniaPizzaFactory. Each store is composed with the right one and the franchise is ready.

Test-marketing showed a problem. Franchises used the factory to create pizzas, but began to use their own home-grown procedures for the rest: they baked differently, forgot to cut the pizza and used third-party boxes.

The approach meets the need for regional variety but fails the need for consistent operation, because nothing ties the store's procedure to its pizza creation. The authors want a framework that does both.
card.example: A bank gives each branch its own FeeCalculator but leaves the teller screens to each branch. Branches begin to round, approve and print differently. Fees vary as intended; the procedure does not stay consistent.
card.rule: Judge an approach against every stated need: this one varies creation but leaves the process uncontrolled.
card.limits: The test-market report is the authors' story, not data. The weakness exists only where franchises are free to edit or bypass the process.

concepts.section: A framework for the pizza store
concepts.title: Keep the process, vary one step
concepts.question: How can the pizza store keep its ordering process fixed yet let each region choose its pizzas?

paragraphs: The authors localize all pizza-making activities in the PizzaStore class again, while giving franchises freedom over style. They put createPizza() back into PizzaStore, but as an abstract method.
Then they create a PizzaStore subclass for each regional style. orderPizza(), the well-honed ordering routine, stays in the base class and is shared by every franchise.
What varies among stores is the style of pizza, and all of that variation is pushed into createPizza().
card.example: A report generator has a generate() routine that gathers data, formats a header and exports. The exporting step differs by format, so createExporter() is declared abstract and a PdfReport and CsvReport subclass supply it.
card.rule: Keep the fixed process in a base class and leave the varying step as an abstract method for subclasses.
card.limits: Inheritance fixes each variation when the subclass is chosen. Changing style while the program runs needs a different object, not just a different call.

concepts.title: What decide means here
concepts.question: When the pattern says subclasses decide which class to instantiate, who actually decides and when?

paragraphs: The orderPizza() method is defined in the abstract PizzaStore, while concrete pizza types are created only in the subclasses. When orderPizza() calls createPizza(), one of the subclasses is called into action.
Which pizza is made depends on the store you ordered from, a NYStylePizzaStore or a ChicagoStylePizzaStore. There is no real-time decision by the subclass.
So decide is a figure of speech. The person decides by choosing the store; the subclass then determines which pizza is made.
card.example: A document converter has an abstract Converter whose convert() calls createParser(). Choosing the HtmlConverter object sends every call to its HTML parser. The subclass was picked up front, and the parser follows.
card.rule: When the book says subclasses decide, it means the chosen subclass determines the product, not that code picks at run time.
card.limits: A creation method can also choose among several products using a parameter. That picking is separate from the sense of deciding by subclass.

concepts.title: The shape of a regional store
concepts.question: What does a regional store inherit, and what must it supply?

paragraphs: A franchise gets all the PizzaStore functionality for free by subclassing it. The regional store needs only to provide a createPizza() method that implements its style.
The base class's orderPizza() has no clue which Pizza is created. It knows only that it can prepare, bake, cut and box what comes back.
So the outline is: one shared ordering routine in the abstract class, one abstract creation method, and one subclass per region filling it in.
card.example: NYPizzaStore overrides createPizza(type) to return a NY style cheese, veggie, clam or pepperoni pizza depending on type. Chicago and California stores do the same with their own pizzas. None of them writes an order routine.
card.rule: A regional store inherits the whole ordering routine and supplies only the creation method for its style.
card.limits: If a regional store feels it must override the ordering routine, the framework is not doing its job. Style is what varies.

concepts.title: Declaring a factory method
concepts.question: What is a factory method, and what does it decouple?

paragraphs: A factory method is an abstract method declared in the base class, such as abstract Pizza createPizza(String type). It returns a product but contains no creation code there.
Subclasses implement it, so the object creation is encapsulated in a subclass. The client code in the superclass, orderPizza(), calls the method and works with the returned Pizza.

The authors summarize it this way: a factory method handles object creation and encapsulates it in a subclass, which decouples the client code in the superclass from the object creation code in the subclass.
card.example: An abstract GameLevel declares abstract Enemy createBoss(). ForestLevel returns a Wolf boss; CastleLevel returns a Knight boss. The level's play() calls createBoss() and uses an Enemy without knowing which one.
card.rule: A factory method is an abstract creation method that subclasses implement, keeping the superclass code ignorant of concrete products.
card.limits: It decouples the superclass from products, not from the subclass choice: someone must still pick which subclass to instantiate.

concepts.title: Tracing an order step by step
concepts.question: In what order do the pieces run when a customer orders a pizza in the factory method design?

paragraphs: Joel and Ethan each need a store: Joel instantiates a ChicagoPizzaStore and Ethan a NYPizzaStore. With a store in hand, each calls orderPizza() with the type, such as cheese or veggie.

To create the pizza, orderPizza() calls createPizza(), which is defined in the two subclasses. The NYPizzaStore builds a NY style pizza and the ChicagoPizzaStore a Chicago style pizza; either returns a Pizza to orderPizza().
orderPizza() has no idea what kind was created. It knows it has a Pizza, and prepares, bakes, cuts and boxes it.
card.example: Ethan orders a cheese pizza from the NY store. The same call from Joel to the Chicago store returns a thick-crust pizza. The ordering code is the same; only the store differs.
card.rule: Trace an order as: choose the store, call orderPizza, let the subclass create, then process the product.
card.limits: The trace shows the normal flow only. It does not show where the choice of store came from, which sits outside the pattern.

concepts.title: Creators and products
concepts.question: What are the four players of the pattern, and which one holds the factory method?

paragraphs: The pattern has two families of classes. The abstract Creator gives an interface with a method for creating objects, the factory method. Its other methods operate on the products that the factory method produces.

Only the subclasses, the concrete creators, implement the factory method and create products. In the pizza store, PizzaStore is the creator and NYPizzaStore and ChicagoPizzaStore are concrete creators.
On the other side stands the product: Pizza is the abstract product, and the NY and Chicago style pizzas are the concrete products. The creator is written against the abstract product.
card.example: A music app has an abstract PlaylistService (creator) that calls createTrack() (factory method) and plays what it gets. RockPlaylistService (concrete creator) returns RockTrack (concrete product). The abstract product is Track.
card.rule: Name the roles: the abstract creator holds the factory method, concrete creators implement it, and the abstract product is what the creator works with.
card.limits: Real designs rarely use these textbook names. Identify roles by what each class does: who declares creation, who implements it, who is created.

concepts.title: Two hierarchies side by side
concepts.question: How do the creator classes and the product classes mirror each other?

paragraphs: Another way to see the pattern as a framework: it encapsulates product knowledge into each creator. Draw the creators on one side and the products on the other, and the two hierarchies run in parallel.
NYPizzaStore knows how to make the NY style products; ChicagoPizzaStore the Chicago style ones. The factory method is the key to encapsulating this knowledge.
To add a California region you need a new creator and the matching set of products, one more strand in each hierarchy.
card.example: A car maker has creators TruckPlant and SedanPlant, each producing its own engine and body parts. A new ElectricPlant needs a new strand: the plant class plus its own parts, while the shared assembly routine is untouched.
card.rule: Pair every concrete creator with its concrete products; adding a region adds a strand to both hierarchies.
card.limits: Parallel hierarchies cost classes: each variation adds a creator and a product set. If variants are few, the extra structure may not pay off.

concepts.title: The Factory Method definition
concepts.question: What does the official definition of Factory Method say, and what does defer mean in it?

paragraphs: The official definition: the Factory Method Pattern defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.

As with every factory, it encapsulates the instantiation of concrete types. The abstract Creator offers an interface with the factory method; its other methods operate on products from that method. Only subclasses implement the factory method and create products.
Defer means the creator postpones the choice of concrete class and leaves it to a subclass.
card.example: A messaging app has an abstract Channel with a method createMessage(), used by a shared send() routine. SmsChannel and EmailChannel decide the message class. The base class defers the instantiation to them.
card.rule: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object and defers the choice of class to subclasses.
card.limits: It is one form of encapsulating creation, not the only one. Other factories, such as Abstract Factory, use composition instead of inheritance.

concepts.title: Forms a factory method can take
concepts.question: What forms can a factory method take, and why does it help even with one concrete creator?

paragraphs: The factory method does not have to be abstract. A default factory method can produce a concrete product, so the creator can create products even when it has no subclasses.
It may be parameterized, building several products from a parameter such as a type, as the pizza stores do. Often a factory produces only one product and takes no parameter. Both are valid forms.

Even with one concrete creator the pattern helps: the product's implementation is decoupled from its use, so adding or changing products does not affect the creator. A string parameter is not type-safe; enums, constants or parameter objects catch errors at compile time.
card.example: A ReportService has a default createExporter() returning a CsvExporter. It works without subclasses. A parameterized createExporter(Format) uses an enum Format so a misspelled format fails at compile time.
card.rule: A factory method may have a default, may be parameterized or single-product, and still decouples use from implementation with one creator.
card.limits: A string parameter pushes mistakes to run time. If many products are created from one method, a typed parameter keeps errors visible before the program runs.

concepts.title: Simple Factory versus Factory Method
concepts.question: How do Simple Factory and Factory Method differ, given that the concrete stores look like a simple factory?

paragraphs: The concrete stores look like SimplePizzaFactory, but they extend a class that declares createPizza() abstract. Each store defines the behavior; in Simple Factory the factory is a separate object composed with the store.

The authors call Simple Factory a one-shot deal. Factory Method creates a framework in which orderPizza() provides a general process that relies on a factory method, and the subclass you choose decides which products go into the pizza.
Simple Factory encapsulates creation, but there is no way to vary the products you create.
card.example: A script runner has run(). With a simple factory, the runner is handed a TaskFactory object. With Factory Method, the runner is subclassed, and createTask() inside each subclass supplies the task. In both the runner is free of concrete task names.
card.rule: Simple Factory composes a separate creator object; Factory Method places the creation step in subclasses of the class that uses the product.
card.limits: The two can look the same when written out. The difference is the relationship: a separate object versus an inheriting subclass.

concepts.title: Creation cannot be avoided
concepts.question: Is a factory merely hiding the concrete classes, and what does the master reply?

paragraphs: A student worries that although factories let him code to abstractions, his factory code still uses concrete classes to instantiate objects. Is he pulling the wool over his own eyes?

The master says object creation is a fact of life: we must create objects or never write a single Java program. The answer is to design so that the creation code is corralled, like the sheep whose wool you would pull over your eyes.
Once corralled, the creation code can be protected and cared for. If it runs wild, you can never collect its wool.
card.example: A team keeps all new calls for payment classes inside one PaymentFactory. When a payment provider changes, one class is reviewed and tested. Scattered new calls would need a hunt through the codebase.
card.rule: Concrete creation cannot be eliminated, only gathered in one place where it can be maintained.
card.limits: Corralling works only when the corral is the single place. Creation code that still lives elsewhere keeps the problem alive.

concepts.title: Counting what a class depends on
concepts.question: How do you count the concrete classes a piece of code depends on, and what happens when a variant is added?

paragraphs: When you directly instantiate an object you depend on its concrete class. The authors' very dependent PizzaStore creates every pizza object inside the store instead of delegating to a factory.
Draw that store and every pizza class it creates, and you get one arrow from the store for each concrete class. The store depends on all of them.
The count grows with the menu. If the store also made California style pizzas, it would depend on the new California classes as well. The same count shows how much a factory removes.
card.example: A travel app's BookingService builds a FlightBooking, HotelBooking or CarBooking directly. That is three concrete dependencies. Adding TrainBooking and BoatBooking makes five. After creation moves to a factory, the service depends on none of them.
card.rule: Count a class's dependencies by counting the distinct concrete classes it names; each new variant adds one.
card.limits: A count shows exposure, not damage. A dependency on a class that is very unlikely to change costs little.

concepts.title: Depend on abstractions
concepts.question: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle say, and how does it differ from program to an interface?

paragraphs: The Dependency Inversion Principle says: depend upon abstractions; do not depend upon concrete classes. It is a formal name for the idea that reducing dependencies on concrete classes is good.
It sounds like program to an interface, not an implementation, but is stronger. It says high-level components should not depend on low-level components; both should depend on abstractions.

A high-level component is a class whose behavior is defined in terms of other, low-level components. PizzaStore is high-level because its behavior is defined in terms of pizzas, which are the low-level components.
card.example: A ReportService prepares and sends monthly reports using PdfWriter objects. ReportService is high-level; PdfWriter is low-level. Under the principle, both depend on a Writer abstraction instead of ReportService depending on PdfWriter.
card.rule: Depend upon abstractions, and let both high-level and low-level components depend on them.
card.limits: The principle does not say that concrete classes disappear. It says the arrows between components should point at abstractions.

concepts.title: Where the inversion happens
concepts.question: How does applying Factory Method invert the dependencies, and what is inverted in your thinking?

paragraphs: The very dependent store was the problem because it instantiated every concrete pizza in orderPizza(). Pizza existed as an abstraction, but the store created concrete pizzas, so it gained little from it.

Applying Factory Method moves those instantiations out. Afterward the high-level store and the low-level pizzas both depend on the abstraction Pizza. Factory Method is not the only way to follow the principle, but it is a powerful one.

The inversion is in the direction. The low-level classes now depend on a higher abstraction, and the thinking flips too: instead of starting at the store and working down, start at the pizzas and ask what you can abstract.
card.example: A shop app's OrderScreen builds a concrete StripeCheckout. Start from the low level instead: abstract the checkouts as Checkout. Then the screen asks a factory for a Checkout, and Stripe and others implement the same abstraction.
card.rule: Start from the low-level classes, abstract what they share, and let both sides depend on that abstraction.
card.limits: Factory Method is one technique among others. It also adds classes, so for a stable class that is unlikely to change it can be more than needed.

concepts.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
concepts.title: Three guidelines for spotting violations
concepts.question: Which three guidelines help you avoid designs that violate the Dependency Inversion Principle?

paragraphs: First: no variable should hold a reference to a concrete class. If you use new you hold a reference to a concrete class, so use a factory to get around that.
Second: no class should derive from a concrete class. Deriving from a concrete class depends on it; derive from an abstraction such as an interface or abstract class.

Third: no method should override an implemented method of any of its base classes. If it does, the base class was not really an abstraction, since its implemented methods are meant to be shared by all subclasses.
card.example: A SmartLamp extends a concrete BasicLamp and overrides its turnOn(), and a Controller keeps a field of type SmartLamp. The code breaks all three guidelines: concrete reference, concrete parent, and overridden implementation.
card.rule: Check three things: concrete references held, concrete parents extended, and implemented methods overridden.
card.limits: These are warning signs, not proofs. A hit on one guideline marks a place to look, and calls for a judgment about whether the class is likely to change.

concepts.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
concepts.title: Guidelines to strive for
concepts.question: Must every program obey the Dependency Inversion guidelines, and when is breaking them acceptable?

paragraphs: The authors say these are guidelines you should strive for, not rules to follow all the time. Every Java program ever written violates them.
The value is awareness. If you internalize the guidelines, you know when you are violating the principle and you have a good reason for doing so.

For instance, a class that is not likely to change can be instantiated directly. We create String objects constantly without a second thought. That violates the principle, and it is acceptable because String is very unlikely to change. A class likely to change should be shielded with a technique such as Factory Method.
card.example: A team writes new ArrayList<>() inside a method without a thought, but keeps its own PricingRule class behind a factory because pricing rules change every quarter. The first is stable; the second is likely to change.
card.rule: Treat the guidelines as aims, and break them knowingly, only for classes unlikely to change.
card.limits: Knowing a class is stable is itself a judgment that can be wrong. A class once thought permanent can start to vary, and the cost of reopening code returns.

concepts.title: Keeping ingredients consistent
concepts.question: How can the franchiser guarantee that every franchise uses quality ingredients?

paragraphs: The framework works: franchises follow the procedures. But some franchises substitute inferior ingredients to lower costs and raise margins, which will hurt the Objectville brand in the long term.
The franchiser's answer is to build a factory that produces the ingredients and ships them to the franchises.
That works in outline, but there is one problem: regions differ, and what is red sauce in New York is not red sauce in Chicago. One set of ingredients goes to New York and a different set to Chicago.
card.example: A pharmacy chain finds some stores buying cheaper packaging than agreed. Head office decides to supply the packaging itself, with a different supply for each country because of labeling rules.
card.rule: Control quality by supplying the inputs yourself, in a form that still allows regional variation.
card.limits: Supplying inputs controls what goes in, not how it is used. The other controls, such as the shared process, are still needed.

concepts.title: A family of ingredients
concepts.question: What is a family of products, and why does each region need its own?

paragraphs: New York uses one set of ingredients and Chicago another. Popular as the business is, it will soon need another set for California, and perhaps Seattle after that.
To make this work, the design must handle families of ingredients. In the authors' case, a family is all the things needed to make a pizza: dough, sauce, cheese, meats and veggies.
The ingredients inside one family belong together. The thin crust dough of New York goes with its marinara sauce and Reggiano cheese, not with Chicago's plum tomato sauce.
card.example: A theme-park app has a WinterTheme family with a white background, a blue button and a snowflake icon, and a SummerTheme family with matching sunnier choices. A screen uses one family at a time.
card.rule: A product family is the set of related parts needed to make one whole thing, and a region chooses one family.
card.limits: Family is about parts that belong together. A group of unrelated products that are merely made by the same company is not a family in this sense.

concepts.title: Building the ingredient factories
concepts.question: What three steps build the ingredient factories and hook them into the store?

paragraphs: First, define an interface for the factory that creates the ingredients. The authors call it PizzaIngredientFactory, with a create method for each ingredient: dough, sauce, cheese, veggies, pepperoni and clam. An abstract class would do if there were common machinery to implement.

Step one: build a factory for each region, a subclass of PizzaIngredientFactory that implements each create method. Step two: implement the ingredient classes used by the factories, such as ReggianoCheese, RedPeppers and ThickCrustDough. These can be shared among regions where appropriate.
Step three: hook it all up by working the new ingredient factories into the old PizzaStore code.
card.example: A theme-park app defines ThemeFactory with createBackground(), createButton() and createIcon(). WinterThemeFactory returns white, blue and snowflake parts; SummerThemeFactory returns the summer ones. The screens are then given one factory.
card.rule: Define the factory interface, build one factory per region, then hook the factories into the client.
card.limits: Adding an ingredient to the family changes the interface and so every regional factory must be updated.

concepts.title: Pizzas built from the factory
concepts.question: How do pizzas use an ingredient factory, and why does one class per pizza suffice?

paragraphs: The abstract Pizza is reworked so that it only uses factory-produced ingredients. A pizza is composed with an ingredient factory and its prepare() method asks that factory for the dough, sauce and cheese.

When the authors wrote Factory Method, they had NYCheesePizza and ChicagoCheesePizza classes. The only difference was the regional ingredients: the pizzas are made the same way, dough plus sauce plus cheese. The same holds for Veggie, Clam and the rest.
So there is no need for two classes per pizza. The ingredient factory handles the regional differences, and the pizza is decoupled from them and ready for new regions.
card.example: A UI toolkit has a LoginDialog that asks a ThemeFactory for its background and button. One LoginDialog class works for Winter and Summer themes; with Factory Method alone there would be a WinterLoginDialog and a SummerLoginDialog.
card.rule: Give a product the factory that makes its parts, so one product class serves every region.
card.limits: This works when the products are built the same way and differ only in their parts. If the regions assemble differently, separate classes are still needed.

concepts.title: The Abstract Factory definition
concepts.question: What does the Abstract Factory Pattern provide, and what does the client stay free of?

paragraphs: The authors' definition: the Abstract Factory Pattern provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
A client uses an abstract interface to create a set of related products without knowing or caring which concrete products are produced. The client is decoupled from the specifics of those products.

From the abstract factory you derive one or more concrete factories that produce the same products with different implementations. By passing in a different factory you get different implementations while the client code stays the same.
card.example: A UI toolkit has a UiFactory interface that makes a window, a button and a menu. WindowsUiFactory and MacUiFactory produce platform versions. The application is handed one factory and builds its whole interface from it.
card.rule: Abstract Factory gives clients an interface for creating a whole family of related products, so they never name the concrete ones.
card.limits: The pattern pays off for families that vary together. For a single product, a plain factory method is lighter.

concepts.section: More pizza for Ethan and Joel...
concepts.title: Following an order through the ingredient factory
concepts.question: In what order do the store, pizza and ingredient factory act when a customer orders?

paragraphs: The first part of the order process has not changed. Ethan first needs a New York store, then orders by calling orderPizza(), which calls createPizza(), for instance with cheese.

From there things change, because an ingredient factory is involved. createPizza() builds the pizza and hands it the New York ingredient factory. When the prepare() method is called, the pizza asks that factory for its dough, sauce and cheese.
Finally the prepared pizza is returned and orderPizza() bakes, cuts and boxes it.
card.example: A UI app asks a MacUiFactory for a window. The window's own draw() asks the factory for a button when it is shown. The order is: choose factory, build window, window asks the factory for parts, draw.
card.rule: Trace the flow: choose a store, order, create the pizza with the factory, prepare from the factory, then bake, cut and box.
card.limits: The trace fits the chapter's code. A real system may pass the factory through other routes, but the idea that the product asks the factory for its parts holds.

concepts.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
concepts.title: Two factory patterns side by side
concepts.question: How do Factory Method and Abstract Factory differ in how they create objects and what they create?

paragraphs: Factory Method creates objects through inheritance: you extend a class and implement its factory method, so a subclass does the creating. Abstract Factory creates objects through object composition: you hand a factory object to code written against the abstract type.
Factory Method usually makes one product, so it needs one method. Abstract Factory makes a family of products, so it has a larger interface, and its methods are often implemented as factory methods.
In Factory Method the abstract creator often contains code that uses the products; in Abstract Factory the factory exists purely to create them. Both keep clients decoupled from concrete classes.
card.example: A parser class that subclasses to supply createToken() uses Factory Method. A UI toolkit that is given a factory object producing window, button and menu uses Abstract Factory.
card.rule: Factory Method creates one product by inheritance; Abstract Factory creates a family of products by composition.
card.limits: The two often appear together, and an Abstract Factory's methods are frequently factory methods. Real code rarely labels itself as one or the other.

concepts.section: Factory Method and Abstract Factory compared
concepts.title: Costs and choices
concepts.question: What does Abstract Factory cost when the family grows, and when should each factory pattern be chosen?

paragraphs: In the interview, Abstract Factory admits that if new products are added, its interface has to change, which people dislike. Factory Method points out that changing the interface means changing every subclass.
Abstract Factory replies that it needs a big interface because it creates whole families, while Factory Method creates one product and needs one method.

Their parting advice: use Abstract Factory when you have families of products and want clients to create products that belong together. Use Factory Method to decouple the client from concrete classes, or when you do not know ahead of time all the concrete classes you will need; to use it, subclass and implement the factory method.
card.example: A UI toolkit's UiFactory has three create methods. Adding createTooltip() means all of the Windows, Mac and Linux factories must be updated. A single factory method for one product would change only the creator's subclasses.
card.rule: Choose Abstract Factory for matching families and accept the cost of changing its interface; choose Factory Method when one product or unknown classes are the issue.
card.limits: The advice is a pair of speaking characters in an interview, not a measured study; for real work, consider how often the family grows.

concepts.title: Objects that must exist only once
concepts.question: Which kinds of objects should exist only once, and what goes wrong if a second copy appears?

paragraphs: Some objects stand for something there is only one of, or something that must stay consistent. The chapter lists thread pools, caches, dialog boxes, preference and registry settings, logging, and drivers for devices such as printers and graphics cards.

If a second instance of one of these appears, the authors warn of three kinds of trouble: incorrect program behavior, overuse of resources, and inconsistent results. Two settings objects, for example, could hold different values, so two parts of the program would disagree about the same fact.
The Singleton pattern is the chapter's answer: a class arranged so that only one object of it can ever exist. The rest of the chapter asks how to arrange that, and why it is harder than it sounds.
card.rule: Give a class a single instance when a second copy would cause wrong behavior, wasted resources or inconsistent results.
card.limits: Having one object is a cost as well as a benefit. The authors say Singletons are meant to be used sparingly, and a design with many of them deserves a hard look. Not every shared object needs to be one.
card.example: A print spooler queues jobs for one office printer. If two spooler objects each kept their own queue, two documents could reach the printer at once and come out mixed. One shared spooler keeps a single queue.

concepts.title: Why new cannot limit instances
concepts.question: Why can an ordinary class not promise that only one instance of it exists?

paragraphs: The new operator builds an object each time it runs. If a class is public, any code can call new on it, again and again. If the class is not public, only classes in the same package can, but they too may call new as often as they like.
So accessibility of the class cannot limit the count. The lever that is left is the constructor: who is allowed to call it decides who can create objects.
card.rule: Calls to new cannot be counted from outside, so limiting instances has to start with limiting who may call the constructor.
card.limits: Package-level access narrows who can call new but does not cap how many times they call it. Restricting callers is necessary for a single instance but not sufficient: something must also hand out the one object.
card.example: A class Spooler has a public constructor. Three different classes each run new on it and get three objects. Making the class package-level lets only its own package do this, yet two classes in that package still get two objects.

concepts.section: A small Socratic exercise in the style of The Little Lisper
concepts.title: A private constructor plus a static method
concepts.question: How can a class with a private constructor ever produce an object, and who may ask for it?

paragraphs: Declare the constructor private and no other class can run new on it. Only code inside the class can call that constructor. This looks like a dead end: to run code inside the class you seem to need an object of the class, and nobody can make one.

The way out is a static method. A static method belongs to the class, so you call it through the class name with no object, for example MyClass.getInstance(). Because the method is part of MyClass, it is allowed to call the private constructor.
Together the two features give a class that outsiders cannot instantiate directly and can still ask for an object through getInstance().
card.rule: Make the constructor private, then expose a static method so outsiders must ask the class for the object.
card.limits: Private construction closes the front door only. It says nothing about how many objects the static method builds, so a careless method could still return a fresh object on every call.
card.example: In a ticket machine program, class TicketCounter has a private constructor and a static method named current(). Code elsewhere cannot write new TicketCounter(), but it can call TicketCounter.current(), which runs inside the class and may build the object.

concepts.section: Dissecting the classic Singleton Pattern implementation
concepts.title: The classic implementation
concepts.question: What three pieces make up the classic Java Singleton, and what does getInstance do on the first call and later calls?

paragraphs: The classic Java Singleton combines three pieces: a private constructor, a static variable that holds the one instance, and a static method, conventionally getInstance(), that hands it out. The chapter's bullet points name exactly these.

On the first call getInstance finds the variable empty, builds the object with the private constructor, stores it, and returns it. On every later call the variable is already filled, so the method skips construction and returns the stored object. Every caller receives the same one.
The book warns readers not to type this version in blindly: it has issues, which later pages expose.
card.rule: Private constructor, static variable, static getInstance: build on the first request and return the stored object afterwards.
card.limits: The book itself marks this version as having issues that appear later in the chapter, so treat it as a starting point rather than finished code.
card.example: A LibraryCatalog class keeps a static variable called theCatalog, initially empty. The first caller of LibraryCatalog.getInstance() causes the object to be built and stored. The hundredth caller receives that same object and nothing new is built.

concepts.title: Why the chocolate boiler needs one instance
concepts.question: What can go wrong if a program holds two controller objects for one physical chocolate boiler?

paragraphs: The chapter's running case is an industrial chocolate boiler. Its controller takes in chocolate and milk, brings them to a boil, and passes the mix on. The class is careful: it must not drain 500 gallons of unboiled mixture, fill a boiler that is already full, or boil an empty one.

Those guards work by checking what the boiler is doing now. If that knowledge lives in one controller object, the checks protect only while every caller uses that object. With two controllers, each could hold a different idea of the boiler's state, and neither guard would fire when needed.
The authors invite the reader to suspect that two loose instances can cause very bad things, and they ask the reader to turn the controller into a Singleton.
card.rule: Safety checks that depend on an object's state only work if every caller shares the one object that holds the state.
card.limits: One instance protects the state only inside one running program and one copy of the class. The chapter later shows two ways the one-instance promise can still break: several threads, and several class loaders.
card.example: A greenhouse controller records that the vents are open and refuses to start the heater while they are. A second controller that believes the vents are closed would start the heater, and the safety check would never fire.

concepts.title: The Singleton pattern defined
concepts.question: What are the two promises in the Singleton definition, and who keeps them?

paragraphs: The authors define the pattern in one sentence: it ensures a class has only one instance, and provides a global point of access to it. Two promises sit inside, and a design must keep both.
First, the class manages a single instance of itself and stops other classes from creating one on their own. To get the object, anyone must go through the class.
Second, the class offers a global access point: wherever the object is needed, you ask the class and it hands back the one instance. The class diagram has a single class, the simplest of any pattern.
card.rule: Singleton means one instance, controlled by the class itself, plus one well-known way for anyone to reach it.
card.limits: Both promises are needed. A global variable offers the access without the one-instance guarantee, so reachability alone does not make a Singleton.
card.example: A theatre's SeatMap class holds the only seat map. It refuses outside construction (first promise), and any booking screen can obtain the map by calling SeatMap.getInstance() (second promise).

concepts.title: Lazy creation versus an up-front global
concepts.question: Why might building the single object only when first requested beat building it at startup?

paragraphs: If an object is assigned to a global variable, it may be created when the application begins. If it is resource-intensive and the program never uses it, the cost was wasted. The authors name this as a downside of the global-variable approach.

A Singleton can avoid the waste with lazy instantiation: the object is built only when someone first asks for it through getInstance. The authors call this especially important for resource-intensive objects.
Lazy instantiation means the program pays nothing for an object it never requests. The opposite choice, building early, is called eager creation and appears later in the chapter.
card.rule: Create the single instance on first request when it is expensive and may never be needed.
card.limits: Lazy creation is not free: the first request pays the whole cost, and the check that decides whether to build must stay correct when several threads call at once. When the instance is always needed, building early costs nothing extra.
card.example: A photo app has a heavy face-recognition engine that few users open. Built lazily, the engine costs memory only in sessions that call getInstance. Built at startup, every session pays for it.

concepts.section: Houston, Hershey, PA we have a problem...
concepts.title: How threads break the classic version
concepts.question: How can two threads running getInstance together end up with two different boiler objects?

paragraphs: The factory's boiler began filling while a batch was already boiling, spilling 500 gallons, even though the team had used the classic Singleton. The cause was threads: several paths of execution running the same code at once.

Look at the sequence inside getInstance: it checks whether the stored instance exists, and if not, builds one and stores it. Those are separate steps. One thread can pass the check and be paused; another can pass the same check while the variable is still empty. Each then builds an object.
The result is two boiler objects, each believing it is the only one. The one-instance promise held only for a single thread at a time.
card.rule: A check-then-create sequence can be interrupted, so two threads may both see no instance yet and each build one.
card.limits: The problem arises only when threads actually overlap during the first call, which makes it rare and hard to reproduce. A single-threaded program is safe, but the authors tell readers to consider every application multithreaded.
card.example: Two cashiers check a shared box for a spare key. Both see it empty, both cut a key and hand it to a customer. The check came before either finished, so two keys exist where the rule allowed one.

concepts.title: Synchronizing getInstance
concepts.question: What does making getInstance synchronized fix, and what does it cost on later calls?

paragraphs: The simplest repair is to declare getInstance as a synchronized method. Only one thread at a time may be inside it, so the check and the creation can no longer interleave. The authors call the fix almost trivial.

The price is paid on every call. Synchronization matters only the first time through, while the instance is still empty. Once it exists, calls still take their turn at the lock, which is unneeded overhead.
So the fix is correct and simple, but it protects something that is needed only once.
card.rule: Declare getInstance synchronized to make the first-time check and creation safe, accepting a lock on every call.
card.limits: Synchronization is needed only until the instance exists, so the price buys nothing afterwards. Where getInstance is called rarely this is harmless; on a busy path the cost matters.
card.example: A football club's Fixtures class has a synchronized getInstance. Two staff open it together on the first day, and the lock makes one wait while the other builds the object. After that, each lookup still queues briefly.

concepts.title: When the lock's cost is acceptable
concepts.question: Under what conditions do the authors say to leave a synchronized getInstance alone, and when to reconsider?

paragraphs: The authors list several ways to improve multithreading. Their first option is to do nothing if the performance of getInstance is not critical. Synchronizing is straightforward and effective.
They add a warning: synchronizing a method can decrease performance by a factor of 100. If a high-traffic part of the code begins to use getInstance, the choice may have to be reconsidered.
The decision therefore turns on measured needs and traffic, not on correctness. The synchronized version is correct either way.
card.rule: Keep the synchronized method while getInstance is off the busy path, and revisit the choice when traffic grows.
card.limits: The factor of 100 is the authors' warning about what can happen, not a measured cost for every program. Examine your own performance constraints before changing code that is correct.
card.example: A weekly payroll job calls Payroll.getInstance() three times per run. A shop-front site calls its Basket.getInstance() on every page view. The first can keep the lock without thought; the second should be looked at.

concepts.title: Eager creation at class loading
concepts.question: How does building the instance up front remove the thread race, and when is it a good fit?

paragraphs: The second option is to create the instance eagerly rather than lazily. The static variable is initialised with the object when the class is loaded, so getInstance only returns what is already there.
The authors say the JVM guarantees that the instance is created before any thread accesses the static variable. Threads therefore always find a ready object.
This suits programs that always create and use the instance, or where the cost of creating it is not onerous.
card.rule: Initialise the static instance when the class loads, so the JVM guarantees it exists before any thread uses it.
card.limits: Eager creation gives up laziness: a costly object is built even if never used. It is the wrong choice for a resource-intensive Singleton that the program might not need.
card.example: A parking app has a small FeeSchedule that every request reads. Initialising it when the class loads costs almost nothing, and getInstance simply hands it back with no lock and no check.

concepts.title: Double-checked locking
concepts.question: How does double-checked locking limit synchronization to the first calls, and which Java versions break it?

paragraphs: Double-checked locking checks whether the instance exists before taking any lock. Only if it is missing does the code synchronize, and then it checks again before building. The lock is therefore taken only on the first calls.

The technique relies on the volatile keyword. The authors warn that in Java 1.4 and earlier, many JVMs implement volatile in a way that allows improper synchronization, so double-checked locking does not work there.

If you must use a JVM earlier than Java 5, the authors advise using another method of implementing the Singleton. If getInstance performance is an issue, this method can drastically reduce the overhead.
card.rule: Check without locking first, lock only when the instance is missing, check again inside the lock, and use Java 5 or later.
card.limits: On Java 1.4 and earlier, many JVMs make the technique unsafe, so choose another method there. It also adds complexity, which is not worth paying when getInstance is not on a busy path.
card.example: A price-feed service Singleton is heavy and is asked for millions of times a second on a modern JVM. It tests the variable with no lock, and only when empty does it enter a synchronized block and test again.

concepts.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
concepts.title: Choosing a fix for the boiler
concepts.question: Does the authors' ranking of the three fixes follow from the facts they give about the boiler?

paragraphs: The authors weigh three fixes against the boiler. Synchronizing getInstance is straightforward and guaranteed to work, and since the boiler shows no performance concerns it is a good choice.

Eager instantiation also fits, because the code always instantiates the boiler, so building it at class loading adds no concern. It works as well as synchronizing, though it may be less obvious to a developer who knows the standard pattern.

Double-checked locking they judge overkill when performance is no concern, and it would require confirming that the program runs on Java 5 or later. The ranking follows from stated facts, so a reader can check it.
card.rule: Choose the simplest fix whose cost your actual constraints can bear.
card.limits: These verdicts hold for this boiler's constraints. Heavy traffic, or a costly object that may never be used, would change the ranking.
card.example: A flat-pack furniture app's Catalog is used by two staff once a day. The same facts that favour synchronizing for the boiler apply: little traffic, simple fix. A different app with heavy traffic would reverse the ranking.

concepts.title: Singleton versus a global variable
concepts.question: On what grounds do the authors say a Singleton beats a global variable or a plain convention?

paragraphs: A skeptic in the chapter asks whether a convention or a static variable could do the same job. The authors answer that the pattern is in many ways a convention, but a time-tested one that gives global access without the downsides.

They give grounds. A global variable may be created when the application starts, wasting a resource-intensive object that is never used. It provides access but not the guarantee of a single instance. And globals tend to encourage polluting the namespace with many references to small objects.
They add that Singletons do not encourage namespace clutter in the same way, but can be abused nonetheless.
card.rule: Judge a Singleton against a global by the stated reasons: lazy creation, a real one-instance guarantee, and less namespace clutter.
card.limits: These grounds are the authors' argument, not proof that globals are worse everywhere, and Singletons can be abused too. Weigh the reasons themselves instead of your taste for or against globals.
card.example: A company holiday calendar kept in a global variable is built at launch even in runs that never open it, and any code may build a second calendar. A Singleton calendar is built on first request and refuses outside construction.

concepts.title: A class made only of static members
concepts.question: Why do the authors advise against replacing a Singleton with a class where everything is static?

paragraphs: A reader may ask whether a class with only static methods and variables would be the same as a Singleton. The authors answer yes, if the class is self-contained and does not depend on complex initialization.
The difficulty is that static initializations in Java can get messy, especially when several classes are involved. The result is often subtle, hard-to-find bugs about the order of initialization.
According to the authors, unless there is a compelling need, it is far better to stay in the object world, that is, to use a real Singleton object.
card.rule: According to the authors, prefer a real Singleton object over an all-static class unless something compels otherwise.
card.limits: The warning concerns complex initialization or several classes. For a self-contained class with simple setup, the authors concede the two are equivalent.
card.example: A Settings utility with only static members reads its values from a file at load. Another class's static setup also reads Settings. Which loads first is not obvious from the code, and the wrong order gives empty values.

concepts.title: Class loaders and the one-instance promise
concepts.question: How can two class loaders produce two instances of a Singleton?

paragraphs: Each class loader defines a namespace. If a program uses two or more class loaders, the same class can be loaded several times, once in each loader.

If that class is a Singleton, there are then several versions of the class and so more than one instance of the Singleton. The one-instance promise therefore holds per loaded copy of the class, not for the whole program.
The authors say to be careful when using multiple class loaders together with Singletons.
card.rule: Remember that the one-instance promise holds per loaded copy of the class, so several class loaders can defeat it.
card.limits: The risk exists only when more than one class loader loads the class. In a program with a single loader the promise is unaffected, and the authors advise care rather than avoiding Singletons.
card.example: A plugin host loads each plugin through its own class loader. Two plugins both ship a PrefsStore Singleton. Each loader loads its own copy of the class, so two PrefsStore objects exist.

concepts.title: The garbage collector bug before Java 1.2
concepts.question: What did an old garbage collector bug do to Singletons, and when does it still matter?

paragraphs: Before Java 1.2, a bug in the garbage collector could destroy a Singleton prematurely if no global reference to it existed, for instance when the only reference to the Singleton was held by the Singleton itself.

After that, the next call to getInstance produced a new Singleton. State was mysteriously reset to its initial values, or things like network connections were reset, which made the symptoms confusing.
Since Java 1.2 the bug is fixed and a global reference is no longer required. The authors say rumours of Singletons being eaten by the garbage collector are greatly exaggerated.
card.rule: On Java 1.2 or later a Singleton needs no extra global reference to survive collection.
card.limits: On a pre-1.2 JVM the problem is real, and the authors advise a registry of Singletons there. On any modern JVM no precaution is needed.
card.example: A cache Singleton on a very old JVM is empty again after hours of use, though nobody cleared it. The collector reclaimed it, and the next getInstance built a fresh, empty one.

concepts.title: Singleton and one responsibility
concepts.question: Does a Singleton break the one-class-one-responsibility principle, and how do the authors weigh that?

paragraphs: The One Class, One Responsibility principle says a class should do one thing. A Singleton manages its own single instance and provides global access, and it also performs its main role in the application. The authors admit one could argue it takes on two responsibilities.
They answer with reasons: there is utility in a class managing its own instance, which makes the overall design simpler, and many developers know the Singleton because it is in wide use.
They also note that some developers feel the need to abstract the Singleton functionality out. The matter is left as a judgment.
card.rule: Weigh the extra responsibility against the simplicity and familiarity, and state which reasons carry your decision.
card.limits: The authors' reasons are about usefulness and familiarity, not a proof that the principle does not apply. Wide use does not make a design correct, so test their case instead of accepting it.
card.example: A BackupScheduler Singleton both decides when backups run and guards that only one scheduler exists. A team that values one-job classes might move the guarding into a separate holder class.

concepts.title: Subclassing a Singleton and using it sparingly
concepts.question: Why is subclassing a Singleton awkward, and what do the authors suggest asking before attempting it?

paragraphs: A Singleton's constructor is private, and a class with a private constructor cannot be extended. To subclass, you must make the constructor public or protected, but then other classes can instantiate it, and it is no longer a true Singleton.

The single-instance mechanism also rests on a static variable. With a straightforward subclass, all derived classes share that one variable, which is probably not intended. Making subclassing work takes extra machinery in the base class.

The authors suggest asking what you really gain from subclassing. They add that Singleton code is trivial to add to any class, and that Singletons are meant to be used sparingly; a design with many deserves a hard look.
card.rule: Before subclassing a Singleton, ask what the subclass gains, since the cost is a weakened guarantee or extra machinery.
card.limits: The advice is about subclassing, not about the pattern itself: the authors still say to use it wherever you must control the number of instances. Sparing use means counting your Singletons, not avoiding them.
card.example: A NotificationService Singleton gets two variants, one for email and one for text. Making its constructor protected lets the variants exist, but any class can now build a service, and both variants point to the same stored instance.

concepts.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
concepts.title: Wrapping a method call in an object
concepts.question: What does it mean to encapsulate a method invocation, and what does the caller gain from it?

paragraphs: The chapter starts from one move: take a method call, meaning the action and the object that performs it, and wrap it in an object of its own. The caller no longer runs the steps itself. It holds the wrapper and triggers it, and the wrapper knows how the work gets done.

Once a call is an object, it can be handled like any other object. It can be stored, handed to someone else, saved away for a log, or reused later to reverse what it did. The chapter builds on these uses: logging and undo.
card.rule: Wrap a request, together with the object that will carry it out, in an object so that the caller can trigger it without knowing the details.
card.limits: The wrapper pays off when the caller should stay ignorant of the details, or when requests must be stored, queued, logged or undone. For a single direct call that needs nothing of these, it only adds an object.

concepts.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
concepts.title: Vendor classes with no shared interface
concepts.question: Why is a remote control hard to design when every vendor class has its own methods?

paragraphs: The customer sends a set of vendor classes for lights, fans, hot tubs and audio gear. Besides on() and off(), they have methods such as dim(), setTemperature(), setVolume() and setInputChannel(). There is little industry effort to give them a common interface.

The customer also wants the remote to control current devices and any devices the vendors supply in future. So the design must cope with variety it has not yet seen, not only with the classes on the disc.
card.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.
card.limits: The difficulty is variety plus growth, not the number of classes. If the classes shared one interface, calling it would be enough and most of this problem would go away.

concepts.title: Keep the remote ignorant of the devices
concepts.question: What should the remote know, and what should it leave out, according to the team in the cubicle?

paragraphs: Mary frames the job as a separation of concerns: the remote should know how to interpret button presses and make requests, but not how to turn on a hot tub. Device know-how belongs somewhere else.

She rejects a remote built from if statements, such as if slot 1 holds a Light then call on(), else if it holds a Hottub then call jetsOn(). Sue adds the cost: every new vendor class would mean editing the remote, with the risk of new bugs.
card.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.
card.limits: Separating concerns says who should know what, not how a generic request reaches a specific device. The team still needs a mechanism for that link, which the next ideas supply.

concepts.title: A command object wraps a request and its target
concepts.question: What does a command object hold, and what does the remote do with it when a button is pressed?

paragraphs: Joe proposes command objects. A command object encapsulates a request to do something, such as turn on the light, on a specific object, such as the living room light. The remote keeps one per button.

When a button is pressed the remote asks the command object to do its work. The remote has no idea what the work is. The command object knows how to talk to the right object, so the remote is decoupled from the light.
Mary sums it up: command objects are loaded into button slots, the remote code stays simple, and each command holds how to do a task together with the object that does it.
card.rule: Store in each button an object that holds both the action and its target, and let the remote only ask that object to act.
card.limits: The remote stays simple only because the knowledge moved: some command object must still know the device own methods. Joe and Mary admit the pattern is hard to picture at first.

concepts.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
concepts.title: The order slip as a request object
concepts.question: Why can the waitress handle any order without knowing what is on it or who cooks it?

paragraphs: In the diner, an Order Slip encapsulates a request to prepare a meal. It is an object: it can be passed from the waitress to the order counter, or to the next waitress taking over her shift.
Its interface has one method, orderUp(), which encapsulates the actions needed to prepare the meal. The slip also holds a reference to the object that will prepare it, the cook.

So the waitress needs to know neither the contents of the order nor who prepares it. She passes the slip through the window and calls Order up. The authors admit a real waitress would care; in Objectville she does not.
card.rule: A request object carries its content and its performer inside it, behind one method, so whoever passes it on needs to know neither.
card.limits: The diner is a deliberate simplification: the authors note that a real waitress would care what is on the slip. Treat the picture as a model of the decoupling, not as advice that requesters never read content.

concepts.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
concepts.title: The waitress invokes, the cook performs
concepts.question: How are the waitress and the cook decoupled, and what links them?

paragraphs: The waitress takes order slips and invokes orderUp() on them. During the day her takeOrder() method is parameterized with different slips from different customers, but this does not faze her, because every slip supports orderUp().

The cook is the object that knows how to prepare meals. Once orderUp() is invoked he takes over. The authors stress that waitress and cook are totally decoupled: she holds slips, and he gets his instructions from the slip without talking to her.
The diner is a model for separating the object that makes a request from the objects that receive and carry it out.
card.rule: The requester only calls the one shared method on whatever request it holds, and the performer receives its instructions only through the request.
card.limits: The decoupling is between waitress and cook. The slip still refers to the cook, so the link has not vanished; it has moved into the request object.

concepts.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
