concepts.title: Matching the diner to the pattern roles
concepts.question: Which pattern role matches each diner player, and in what order is an invoker loaded and used?

paragraphs: The players stay the same; only the names change. The customer becomes the client, the order becomes the command, the waitress becomes the invoker and the short order cook becomes the receiver. The method orderUp() becomes execute(), and takeOrder() becomes setCommand().

Loading the invoker takes three steps. First, the client creates a command object. Second, the client calls setCommand() to store it in the invoker. Later, the client asks the invoker to execute the command.
Once loaded, a command may be used and discarded, or it may stay in the invoker and be used many times.
card.rule: The client builds a command, loads it into the invoker with setCommand(), and the invoker later calls execute() on it, which makes the receiver act.
card.limits: The roles describe jobs, not classes: one object can take more than one role in a small program. Check the jobs, not the names.

concepts.title: The Command interface has one method
concepts.question: Why do all command objects share one single-method interface, and what is that method called?

paragraphs: All command objects implement the same interface, and it consists of one method. In the diner this was orderUp(); in code the usual name is execute().
A single, device-free method is what lets the invoker treat every command alike. It needs to know only that execute() exists.
The variety of the vendor classes does not leak into the interface. Names like setVolume() or dim() appear only inside concrete commands that call them.
card.rule: Give every command the same one-method interface so that an invoker can run any of them without knowing which one it holds.
card.limits: The no-argument, no-result shape fits requests whose details are fixed when the command is created. A richer interface, such as one that adds undo, changes what every command must provide.

concepts.title: A concrete command binds a receiver to an action
concepts.question: What does a concrete command store, and what does its execute() method do?

paragraphs: A concrete command implements the Command interface. For a light, LightOnCommand takes the Light in its constructor and keeps it. Its execute() method calls on() on that light.

The garage door follows the same shape. GarageDoorOpenCommand keeps a GarageDoor and its execute() calls the door up() method. The command name states the request, while the vendor method name stays hidden inside.
So one concrete command ties one receiver to one action behind the common execute().
card.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.
card.limits: The command is the one place that knows the vendor method name. It adds nothing to the receiver, so a new method on the receiver, such as dim(), is not reachable until someone writes a command for it.

concepts.title: Loading and swapping a command in a one-slot remote
concepts.question: What happens when the one-slot remote is loaded with a command, pressed, and then loaded with another?

paragraphs: The simple remote has one button and one slot. Its setCommand() stores a command in the slot, and its buttonWasPressed() calls execute() on whatever command is there.

In the test, the client creates a Light, a LightOnCommand for it, loads the remote, and presses the button. Then it creates a GarageDoor and a GarageDoorOpenCommand, loads the remote again and presses again. The same remote code runs two different requests.
The slot does not care which command it holds, as long as it implements the Command interface.
card.rule: An invoker holds one command in its slot through setCommand(), and a button press calls execute() on whatever is there now.
card.limits: The slot keeps only the latest command, so loading a new one replaces the old one. Holding several commands at once needs more slots, which the seven-slot remote provides.

concepts.title: The Command Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Command Pattern do, and what four abilities does it give?

paragraphs: The Command Pattern encapsulates a request as an object. This lets you parameterize other objects with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.

A command object binds a set of actions to a specific receiver. It exposes one method, execute(). From outside, no other object knows which actions run on which receiver; they know that calling execute() services the request.

Parameterizing means loading an object with different requests: the waitress with various orders over a day, a remote slot first with light on and later with garage door open. Queuing, logging and undo come later, as does the Meta Command Pattern, which groups commands into macros.
card.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.
card.limits: A given use need not employ all four abilities. The authors say that logging would make no sense for a remote control, though it suits other applications.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: Where the decoupling comes from
concepts.question: How does the structure of the pattern keep the invoker and the receiver apart?

paragraphs: The invoker knows only the Command interface and its execute() method. The concrete command holds the reference to the receiver and calls its actions. The invoker never refers to the receiver.
The client creates the concrete command and gives it its receiver. So the knowledge of which receiver and which actions sits in one place, the command, and the invoker is free of it.
The invoker and receiver can then change independently, because the commands are the only link between them.
card.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.
card.limits: Coupling does not vanish; it moves. The command class depends on the receiver, and the client or setup code depends on the concrete classes. The gain is that the invoker is free of both.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
concepts.title: Binding each command to its own receiver
concepts.question: How does the remote tell the living room light from the kitchen light?

paragraphs: The remote has seven slots with an on and an off button each. Commands are assigned to the slots, for example onCommands[0] set to one command and offCommands[0] to another.

The remote does not know which light is which. When the commands are created, one is bound to the living room light object and another to the kitchen light object. The receiver of the request gets bound to the command that encapsulates it.
By the time a button is pressed, no one cares which light is which: the right thing happens when execute() is called.
card.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.
card.limits: A command acts on the receiver it was given. To act on another receiver you need another command object.

concepts.title: Seven slots: the remote as invoker
concepts.question: How does a seven-slot remote store its commands, and what happens when a button is pressed?

paragraphs: The plan is to assign each slot a command. That makes the remote control the invoker. Each slot has an on and an off button, so the remote keeps two arrays of commands, one for the on buttons and one for the off buttons, indexed by slot.
When a button is pressed, the remote calls execute() on the command stored for that button. That command invokes actions on its receiver, which may be a light, a ceiling fan or a stereo.
The remote code is the same for every device, because it never learns what is in a slot. Loading the slots is the client job.
card.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.
card.limits: The arrays hold only commands, and their size fixes the number of slots. The remote does not decide what a slot controls; the client code that loads the commands does.

concepts.title: A command can do several things
concepts.question: Can one command make several calls on its receiver, and what does the invoker see?

paragraphs: Some commands are simple. StereoOffCommand binds the stereo to its off() method. Turning the stereo on to play a CD takes more: StereoOnWithCDCommand turns the stereo on, sets the CD input and sets the volume to 11.
All of this goes inside execute(). The invoker still sees one method and makes one call.
The other vendor classes follow the same shape, so writing their commands is routine. The authors note that vendors will find such simple classes easy to write in future.
card.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.
card.limits: A command stays small only while it delegates to the receiver. Commands that grow their own logic are the smart commands discussed later, which cost some decoupling.

concepts.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
concepts.title: NoCommand: a command that does nothing
concepts.question: Why does the remote start every slot with a do-nothing command instead of leaving it empty?

paragraphs: If a slot could be empty, the remote would have to test each time it presses a button whether a command is loaded. That check would be repeated in every handler.

The fix is a command that does nothing: NoCommand implements Command, and its execute() is empty. The remote constructor puts a NoCommand in every on and off slot, so there is always a command to call.

This is an example of a null object. It is useful when you have no meaningful object to give but want to take the handling of null away from the client. It is sometimes listed as a design pattern in its own right.
card.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.
card.limits: The do-nothing object makes an empty slot silent: a press has no visible effect and gives no sign that nothing was loaded. Use it when doing nothing is an acceptable answer.

concepts.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
concepts.title: Judging the design against its stated goal
concepts.question: Does the design meet the goal the documentation states, and how would you check the claim?

paragraphs: The remote documentation says the primary design goal was to keep the remote code as simple as possible, so that it needs no changes as new vendor classes are produced. The means chosen was the Command Pattern, to decouple the RemoteControl class from the vendor classes.
The authors then say they believe this will reduce the cost of producing the remote and its upkeep. That is an expectation: a reader can test it by asking whether the means really delivers the goal.
The check is concrete: add a brand-new vendor class and see whether the remote must be edited.
card.rule: Judge a design by its stated goal: ask whether the chosen means delivers it, for example whether a new device needs no edit to the remote.
card.limits: A belief about lower cost is not a measurement. The authors also point out costs of the means, such as extra small classes, so weigh the benefit against them.

concepts.title: Undo mirrors execute
concepts.question: How does a command support undo, and what must the remote remember?

paragraphs: To support undo, the Command interface gains an undo() method that mirrors execute(): whatever execute() last did, undo() reverses. For the light, LightOnCommand.undo() calls off(), and LightOffCommand.undo() calls on().
The remote needs a small change. It adds an instance variable that tracks the last command invoked. When the undo button is pressed, the remote retrieves that command and calls its undo().
The remote does not know how to reverse anything. Each command knows how to reverse itself.
card.rule: Add undo() to the command so it reverses what execute() did, and have the invoker remember the last command to call it on.
card.limits: This version remembers one command, so it undoes one step. And a single opposite call works only when the earlier state is certain: a fan that could have been at any speed needs more.

concepts.title: Undo that needs remembered state
concepts.question: How can a command undo a change when the earlier state could have been any of several values?

paragraphs: Undo on the light was easy. Typically a command has to manage some state to support undo. The ceiling fan has several speeds and an off setting, so turning it to high must be reversed to whatever it was before.
The solution is to track the fan last speed setting and, when undo() is called, restore the fan to that previous setting. Each fan command, for high, medium, low and off, does this for itself.
The command therefore holds two things: the receiver and the earlier state of that receiver.
card.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().
card.limits: A command can restore only what it recorded. If something else changes the receiver between execute() and undo(), undo puts back the old record, not the newer situation.

concepts.title: A stack of commands for repeated undo
concepts.question: How can the remote undo several steps in a row instead of only the last one?

paragraphs: To let the user press undo many times, the invoker keeps a stack of the previous commands instead of one reference to the last command. Each time a command is executed it is pushed on the stack.
When undo is pressed, the invoker pops the top item off the stack and calls its undo(). The most recent command is reversed first, then the one before it, and so on.
card.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().
card.limits: Only the invoker changes; the commands stay as they are. The history holds only commands that went through the invoker, so an action performed directly on a receiver cannot be undone this way.

concepts.title: A macro command runs many commands
concepts.question: How can one button run several commands at once, such as a party mode?

paragraphs: Every remote needs a party mode: one button that dims the lights, turns on the stereo and the TV set to a DVD, and fires up the hot tub. The authors call the extension the Meta Command Pattern.

First create the commands for the parts. Then load them into an array and hand the array to a MacroCommand. Its execute() steps through the array and executes each command. A second array of off commands makes the matching off macro.
Finally assign the MacroCommand to a button like any other command. It is a Command, so the remote cannot tell it from a single one.
card.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().
card.limits: A macro holds no receiver of its own: its parts do the work, and the client chooses the parts when the macro is built. The macro is only as capable as the commands inside it.

concepts.title: Undoing a macro in reverse order
concepts.question: In what order should a macro undo its commands, and why?

paragraphs: When undo is pressed after a macro, every command that the macro invoked must undo its previous action. The macro does this by calling undo() on its parts.

In the authors solution, MacroCommand.undo() loops through the array from the last command down to the first, the opposite of execute(). A later step may rely on what an earlier step did, so it is taken back first.
Because a macro is a command, it can be undone as one unit, whether it holds two commands or twenty.
card.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.
card.limits: A macro can restore the earlier state only if every part can reverse itself. A part whose undo() does nothing leaves its effect in place.

concepts.title: Smart commands and macros: the authors view
concepts.question: What do you give up when a command does the work itself, and why do the authors favour macros?

paragraphs: In general, say the authors, aim for dumb commands that only invoke an action on a receiver. Smart commands implement most or all of the logic of the request themselves. They exist and are not uncommon, but then the invoker and receiver are less decoupled, and you can no longer parameterize commands with receivers.
For party mode, one could write a PartyCommand with the calls hard-coded. The authors prefer a MacroCommand: you decide dynamically which commands go in, and there is less new code.
card.rule: Prefer dumb commands that delegate and macros built from parts, and accept a smart command only when you can afford the lost decoupling.
card.limits: This is the authors recommendation, not a law. A smart command is legitimate where the decoupling it costs is not needed.

concepts.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
concepts.title: The cost: many small classes
concepts.question: What is the main cost of the plain pattern, and why are the extra classes so alike?

paragraphs: With the Command Pattern you end up with many small classes, the concrete Commands, each encapsulating the request for one receiver. In the remote, there are two per receiver class: LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand for the light, GarageDoorUpCommand and GarageDoorDownCommand for the garage door, and so on.

That is a lot of extra stuff for little bits of packaged computation. They all share one interface for the RemoteControl, and a command is only a piece of packaged-up computation giving common access to the behaviour of many receivers.
card.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.
card.limits: The cost counts the distinct requests, not the invokers. It is a cost of the plain form: a language feature that packages computation more compactly can reduce it, as the next ideas show.

concepts.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
concepts.title: Lambda expressions as commands
concepts.question: How can a lambda expression take the place of a concrete command class?

paragraphs: A lambda expression is a short way to write a method exactly where it is needed, without a separate class, an object made from it and a call. It was added in Java 8.

In the remote, instead of passing LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand objects to setCommand(), you pass lambda expressions holding the code from their execute() methods. The slot then holds a function object, and execute() runs the lambda.
This works because Command has exactly one method, execute(), taking no arguments and returning nothing. A lambda with a compatible signature fits, and the compiler checks the match.
card.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.
card.limits: It works only for an interface with a single method. A lambda replaces a method, not a whole object, so it cannot stand in for an interface with two.

concepts.section: Simplifying even more with method references
concepts.title: Method references and named lambdas
concepts.question: When can a method reference replace a lambda, and what do you do when the command has several steps?

paragraphs: When a lambda calls only one method, you can pass a method reference instead, a reference to the method itself. For the stereo off command, stereo::off replaces the lambda.

A command that does more than one thing cannot use a method reference. StereoOnWithCD turns the stereo on, sets the CD and sets the volume to 11. Write the lambda inline, or create it separately, give it a name, and pass that name to setCommand().
The separately created lambda has the type Command, which matches the parameter it is passed to.
card.rule: Use a method reference when the lambda only calls one method, and a lambda body, inline or named, when it does more.
card.limits: A method reference names one method, so it cannot cover a command with several calls. It is a convenience for the simplest case.

concepts.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
concepts.title: When lambdas are the wrong tool
concepts.question: Why do the authors advise against lambdas once the Command interface has an undo method?

paragraphs: Lambda expressions suit functional interfaces, those with a single method. With undo, the Command interface has two methods, execute() and undo(), and one lambda cannot replace two methods.

The authors say you could probably find a way, by making two kinds of commands, but the code would likely be more complex than the command objects used earlier. If you are working around the rule, lambdas are probably not the right solution.
Lambdas also have no nice class names: the runtime assigns them. A display that prints class names shows odd text, so a readable name has to be passed in.
card.rule: Use lambda commands while the interface has one method; keep command classes when it has more, such as execute() and undo().
card.limits: This is the authors judgment, worded as probably. Dropping the undo feature restores the single method. A workaround is allowed, and the question is whether it costs more than it saves.

concepts.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
concepts.title: Queuing requests
concepts.question: How do commands let a job queue and worker threads handle work they know nothing about?

paragraphs: A command packages a computation, a receiver and its actions, and passes it around as a first-class object. The computation may be invoked long after the command was created, even by a different thread. Schedulers, thread pools and job queues use this.
Commands go in at one end of a job queue. Threads at the other end remove a command, call execute(), wait for the call to finish, discard the command and fetch the next.
The queue and the threads are decoupled from the work. One moment a thread runs a financial computation, the next a network retrieval. They only call execute().
card.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.
card.limits: The queue runs only objects that implement the command interface. A worker discards each command after its run, so the queue serves work to be done once, not requests to be kept.

concepts.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
concepts.title: Logging requests for crash recovery
concepts.question: How can a log of command objects restore an application after a crash?

paragraphs: Some applications must log every action and recover after a crash by invoking those actions again. Commands support this with two added methods, store() and load(). In Java, serialization could implement them, with its usual caveats for persistence.
As commands run, a history is stored on disk. After a crash, the command objects are reloaded and their execute() methods invoked in batch and in order.

It makes no sense for a remote. It does suit applications with large data that cannot be saved on every change: log operations since the last checkpoint and replay them on it. A spreadsheet is the example. Extended to sets of operations, it gives transactions where all complete or none do.
card.rule: Log executed commands since the last checkpoint, and after a failure reload the checkpoint and execute the logged commands in order.
card.limits: It pays only when saving the whole data on each change is too costly. It does not suit a remote control, and serialization has its usual caveats as a way of storing commands.

concepts.title: What an adapter does
concepts.question: What does an adapter change, and what does it leave alone, when two things do not fit together?

paragraphs: Take a US laptop to Britain. Its plug does not fit the wall outlet. A travel power adapter sits between the two: the laptop is untouched, the outlet is untouched, and the adapter turns the outlet into something the plug can use.

The book puts it as changing the interface of the outlet into the one the laptop expects. The word interface here means the set of connections or calls that one side offers and the other side relies on.
Object-oriented adapters play the same role. They take one interface and adapt it to the interface a client, meaning the code that makes the calls, is expecting.
card.example: A British hotel room has three-pin sockets, and your charger has a two-pin plug. A plug adapter reshapes the socket. Neither the charger nor the hotel wiring is altered.
card.rule: An adapter changes the interface one side offers into the interface the other side expects, and leaves both sides as they were.
card.limits: An adapter only bridges a difference in interface. If the wrapped thing lacks what the client needs, the adapter cannot invent it.

concepts.title: The new vendor problem
concepts.question: How can a new vendor's classes join an existing system when neither your code nor theirs may be changed?

paragraphs: Suppose your system works with one vendor's classes, and a new vendor offers the same kind of service through differently designed interfaces. You do not want to change your existing code, and you cannot change the vendor's code.

The way out is to write a class that adapts the new vendor's interface into the one you already expect. This adapter is a middleman: it receives requests from your code and converts them into requests that make sense on the vendor's classes.
The book also points out a route that needs no code from you: ask the vendor to supply the adapter class.
card.example: Your shop app calls pay(amount) on every payment provider. A new provider only offers submitCharge(cents, currency). A small class with pay(amount) that calls submitCharge inside lets the app stay as it is.
card.rule: When you cannot change either side, put a middleman class between them that speaks your interface in front and the vendor's behind.
card.limits: An adapter is extra code that someone must write and maintain, so it earns its place only when changing the callers or the vendor is not realistic.

concepts.title: Client, target and adaptee
concepts.question: In an adapter design, which part is the client, which is the target interface, and which is the adaptee?

paragraphs: The pattern has named parts. The client is the code that makes the calls. The target interface is the interface the client is written against. The adaptee is the existing class whose interface does not match.

The adapter is the class between them: it implements the target interface and is composed with, meaning it holds a reference to, the adaptee. The book's duck example wraps a turkey so that it can be used where a duck is expected.
The book points out that the Client and the Adaptee are decoupled: neither knows about the other.
card.example: A navigation app (client) expects every map source to implement MapSource (target). A city's data feed (adaptee) offers different calls. A class implementing MapSource and holding the feed is the adapter.
card.rule: The client talks to the target interface, the adapter implements that interface, and the adaptee sits behind the adapter.
card.limits: The roles only matter when interfaces differ: a client that already speaks the adaptee's own interface has no use for the adapter.

concepts.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
concepts.title: How a request travels through an adapter
concepts.question: What happens, step by step, when a client uses an adapter, and what does the client know about it?

paragraphs: The book gives three steps. First, the client makes a request by calling a method on the adapter, using the target interface. Second, the adapter translates that request into one or more calls on the adaptee, using the adaptee's interface.
Third, the client receives the results of the call and never knows there is an adapter doing the translation.
Notice that one request on the target can become several calls on the adaptee. The adapter decides how to map them.
card.rule: The client calls the adapter through the target interface, the adapter makes the matching calls on the adaptee, and the client never sees the translation.
card.limits: The client is unaware of the adapter only while the adapter keeps up its end. When the translation is imperfect, the client may notice, as the remove() case later shows.

concepts.title: How much work an adapter needs
concepts.question: What decides how much work an adapter takes, and what shapes can an adapter have beyond wrapping one class?

paragraphs: The work of writing an adapter is proportional to the size of the target interface you must support. A large target means many methods to map.
Even so, the book's alternative is worse: reworking every client call to the new interface means a lot of investigation and many code changes, while an adapter puts all the changes in one class.

An adapter does not always wrap just one class. It may hold two or more adaptees when the target interface needs them. A Two Way Adapter implements both the old and the new interface, so it can act as either.
card.rule: Adapter effort grows with the size of the target interface, and an adapter may wrap several classes or serve two interfaces at once.
card.limits: An adapter that must map a huge target interface may cost more than editing a few callers. The book's comparison assumes the callers are many or cannot be changed.

concepts.title: The official definition
concepts.question: What is the Adapter Pattern's official definition, and what two benefits follow from it?

paragraphs: The book defines it this way: the Adapter Pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface the clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that could not otherwise because of incompatible interfaces.
The definition has two parts. The conversion part says what the pattern does. The purpose part says why: classes that could not cooperate can now work together.

One consequence is that the client is decoupled from the implemented interface. If the interface is expected to change over time, the adapter encapsulates the change, so the client does not have to be modified each time.
card.rule: The Adapter Pattern converts a class's interface into the one clients expect so that otherwise incompatible classes can work together.
card.limits: Converting an interface does not make a class's behavior suit the client. Two classes can match in signature and still disagree about what the calls mean.

concepts.title: Composition and coding to the target
concepts.question: Which design principles does the object adapter use, and what do they let you do?

paragraphs: The book says the Adapter Pattern is full of good design principles. First, it uses object composition: the adapter holds the adaptee inside and wraps it with an altered interface.
A benefit is that an adapter can work with any subclass of the adaptee, because anything of the adaptee's type can be held.

Second, the pattern binds the client to an interface, not an implementation. So you can use several adapters, each converting a different backend, or add new implementations later, as long as they adhere to the target interface.
card.rule: Wrap the adaptee by composition and code the client to the target interface, so any adaptee subclass or new backend can be fitted behind it.
card.limits: A backend that does not implement the target still needs its own adapter. Composition also adds one more object and a line of delegation per method.

concepts.title: Object adapter and class adapter
concepts.question: How does a class adapter differ from an object adapter, and why did this chapter cover only one of them?

paragraphs: There are two kinds of adapters. An object adapter uses composition: it holds the adaptee and passes requests to it. This chapter has covered object adapters.
A class adapter instead subclasses both the target and the adaptee. That needs multiple inheritance, which the book says is not possible in Java.
The book adds that you may meet a need for class adapters later in a language that does have multiple inheritance.
card.rule: An object adapter composes with the adaptee; a class adapter inherits from both the target and the adaptee and needs multiple inheritance.
card.limits: The book works through object adapters only, so details of class adapters here are only sketched. Which form is available depends on the language.

concepts.title: Weighing the two adapter forms
concepts.question: Before choosing between the object adapter and the class adapter, what does each side claim and what does each give up?

paragraphs: The book stages a fireside chat in which each form argues its case. The object adapter says that composition lets it adapt the adaptee and any of its subclasses. The class adapter admits it is committed to one specific adaptee class.

The class adapter replies with its own claims: it does not have to reimplement the whole adaptee, it can override the adaptee's behavior since it is a subclass, and there is just one object instead of two.

Before agreeing with either, restate what each claims in your own words, then check each claim against the facts of your situation. The book asks readers to think about how composition versus inheritance affects flexibility.
card.rule: Restate each form's claims and what it gives up, then weigh them against your language and your needs before taking sides.
card.limits: A debate staged between the two forms is not evidence by itself, since each speaker argues for itself. The book leaves the weighing to the reader.

concepts.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
concepts.title: Adapting Enumeration to Iterator
concepts.question: What do Enumeration and Iterator each offer, and how does an adapter let new code use legacy Enumerations?

paragraphs: Early Java collections such as Vector, Stack and Hashtable provide a method, elements(), that returns an Enumeration. It lets you step through the elements without knowing how the collection manages them.
Newer collection classes use the Iterator interface. Like Enumeration it steps through items, but it also adds the ability to remove them.

Legacy code still produces Enumerations while new code wants Iterators. So you build an adapter that implements the Iterator target and is composed with an Enumeration adaptee. The book calls it the EnumerationIterator adapter. The hasNext() and next() methods map straight through.
card.rule: To let new code use a legacy Enumeration, write an adapter that implements Iterator and wraps the Enumeration.
card.limits: The mapping works for the calls both sides have. Iterator offers an operation that Enumeration cannot support, which makes the adapter imperfect.

concepts.title: When the adaptee cannot do what the target asks
concepts.question: What can an adapter do when the target has an operation the wrapped class cannot support?

paragraphs: Enumeration is read-only, so there is no way to implement a fully working remove() on the adapter. The best that can be done is to throw a runtime exception.
Luckily the designers of Iterator foresaw this need. They defined remove() so that it may throw an UnsupportedOperationException.

The book calls this a case where the adapter is not perfect: clients must watch for exceptions. As long as clients are careful and the adapter is well documented, it is a perfectly reasonable solution.
card.rule: When the adaptee cannot do what the target allows to fail, throw the exception the target's contract permits and document it.
card.limits: This works because the Iterator contract was written to allow it. If a target promised that an operation always works, throwing would break the promise.

concepts.title: Is an adapter just a decorator?
concepts.question: Both adapters and decorators wrap an object. In what sense is 'an adapter is only a decorator' right, and in what sense wrong?

paragraphs: In the book's fireside chat, the Decorator claims that adapters are fancy decorators, since like decorators they wrap an object. The Adapter answers that it always converts the interface of what it wraps, while a decorator never does.
The Decorator in turn says it extends the behaviors or responsibilities of what it wraps, so it is not a simple pass-through.

They end by agreeing that they look somewhat similar on paper but are miles apart in intent. To judge a claim like this one, first find the sense in which it holds, here that both wrap, then ask whether it still holds for the purpose.
card.rule: A claim that one pattern is just another is judged by asking in what sense it holds: both wrap, but an adapter converts an interface while a decorator adds behavior.
card.limits: Similar structure does not mean the same purpose. The structural match makes the claim tempting, so check the intent before agreeing.

concepts.title: Adapter, decorator and facade by purpose
concepts.question: Which of adapter, decorator and facade converts an interface, which adds responsibility and which simplifies?

paragraphs: The next pattern in the chapter also alters an interface, but for a different reason: to simplify it. It is called the Facade Pattern because it hides the complexity of one or more classes behind a clean, well-lit facade.

The book sets the three wrapping patterns side by side. A decorator does not alter the interface but adds responsibility. An adapter converts one interface into another. A facade makes an interface simpler.

In the chapter's closing summary: an adapter wraps an object to change its interface, a decorator wraps an object to add behaviors and responsibilities, and a facade wraps a set of objects to simplify.
card.rule: An adapter converts an interface, a decorator adds responsibility while keeping the interface, and a facade simplifies.
card.limits: All three wrap something, so wrapping cannot tell them apart. Only what each does with the interface, and why, can.

concepts.title: The home theater problem
concepts.question: Why does using a collection of well-working components still become hard, as in the home theater example?

paragraphs: The book's example is a home theater: a DVD player, a projection system, an automated screen, surround sound and a popcorn popper. Each part works, and you have spent weeks wiring and tuning them.
Yet watching one movie takes thirteen tasks in order, from turning on the popper and dimming the lights to setting the amplifier and starting the DVD player.

That is only the start. Turning everything off means doing the steps again in reverse. Listening to a CD or the radio would be just as complex. After an upgrade, you would learn a slightly different procedure.
card.rule: When using a group of components takes many ordered calls that repeat and change with upgrades, the use itself has become the complexity.
card.limits: The example is a motivation, not a count. A short sequence on a few parts is usually not worth a new layer, and the book gives no threshold.

concepts.title: What a facade is for
concepts.question: What does a facade do for a complex subsystem, and what stays available to clients who need more?

paragraphs: A subsystem is a set of related classes that work together, like the home theater's parts. A facade is a class that provides one, more reasonable interface to that subsystem, so the subsystem becomes easier to use.
The facade takes the long sequence and gives it a short name. A client that only wants to watch a movie calls the facade and never meets the individual components.
The subsystem is still there. If you need the power of the complex subsystem, you can use it directly.
card.rule: A facade gives a complex subsystem one simpler interface while leaving the subsystem itself available.
card.limits: A facade makes using the subsystem simpler, not the subsystem itself. A facade that tries to expose every feature stops being simple.

concepts.title: A facade can be smart, and there can be several
concepts.question: Can a facade do more than forward calls, and can one subsystem have more than one facade?

paragraphs: A facade does not have to be a pass-through. The book says it is free to add its own smarts. Its home theater facade, for example, knows that the popcorn popper has to be turned on before it can pop, and it knows the details of staging a movie.
The book also says the pattern allows any number of facades for a given subsystem. A subsystem is not limited to one facade.
Both points follow from the facade's job: it is the place where knowledge about using the subsystem lives.
card.rule: A facade may hold its own knowledge, such as ordering, and a subsystem may have several facades.
card.limits: More smarts and more facades mean more code to keep correct. A facade also stays a client of the subsystem and does not repair it.

concepts.title: Building a facade by composition and delegation
concepts.question: How is a facade built, and why does a client coded to it survive a change of components?

paragraphs: To build the HomeTheaterFacade, the first step is composition: the facade holds the components of the subsystem. Then it implements simplified methods such as watchMovie() and endMovie(), which bring the components together into a unified interface.
The facade does its work by delegation. watchMovie() calls the individual components in the right order, and a client now makes one call.

The book adds that a facade decouples a client from the subsystem. If you upgrade to components with different interfaces and your client was coded to the facade, the client does not change, only the facade.
card.rule: Compose the facade with the subsystem's components, delegate through a few high-level methods, and code clients to the facade.
card.limits: Only clients that go through the facade are protected. A client that calls the components directly still depends on them.

concepts.title: Adapter or facade: count or intent?
concepts.question: Is the number of classes wrapped what separates an adapter from a facade, and how would you test such a claim?

paragraphs: A tempting rule says: an adapter wraps one class and a facade wraps many. The book answers no. An adapter may adapt many classes to one interface that a client expects, and a facade may simplify a single class that has a very complex interface.
The difference is intent. The intent of an adapter is to alter an interface so it matches the one a client expects. The intent of a facade is to provide a simplified interface to a subsystem.
To test a rule of thumb like the class count, look for a counterexample. One counterexample is enough to show the rule cannot define the difference.
card.rule: Tell an adapter from a facade by intent, converting versus simplifying, and not by how many classes are wrapped.
card.limits: The count is a fair hint in textbook examples, where adapters wrap one class and facades several. A hint is not a definition.

concepts.title: Talk only to your immediate friends
concepts.question: What does the Principle of Least Knowledge ask of an object, and what problem does it prevent?

paragraphs: The Principle of Least Knowledge is usually stated as: talk only to your immediate friends. It guides us to reduce the interactions between objects to just a few close friends.
In real terms: when designing a system, for any object, be careful of the number of classes it interacts with and also of how it comes to interact with them.
The principle prevents designs in which many classes are coupled together, so that changes in one part cascade to other parts. A web of dependencies is fragile.
card.rule: Principle of Least Knowledge: talk only to your immediate friends.
card.limits: The slogan does not by itself say who counts as a friend. The guidelines in the next idea do.

concepts.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
concepts.title: Who counts as a friend
concepts.question: From inside a method, which objects may you call, and which objects are off limits?

paragraphs: From any method of an object, the principle says to call only methods that belong to four kinds of objects: the object itself; objects passed in as parameters to the method; any object the method creates or instantiates; and any components of the object.
A component is any object referenced by an instance variable. In other words, it is a HAS-A relationship.
Notice what is missing: objects that were returned from calling other methods. Those are not friends.
card.rule: Inside a method, call only the object itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its own components.
card.limits: The guidelines concern reach, not whether the code works: a call on a returned object is out of bounds even when it is convenient.

concepts.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
concepts.title: Why a call chain through a returned object breaks the principle
concepts.question: What does a chain like station.getThermometer().getTemperature() cost the caller, and how is it fixed?

paragraphs: Take the code station.getThermometer().getTemperature(). The caller asks the station for a thermometer and then calls a method on what comes back. It therefore knows two classes: the station's and the thermometer's.

The principle's fix is to ask the object you already know to make the request for you. The station then makes the inner call, so the caller does not have to know about the station's component objects.
The book's Car class shows the allowed ways to call methods and still keep within the principle.
card.rule: Replace a chain through a returned object with a request to the object you know, and let it make the inner call.
card.limits: The rewrite shifts knowledge instead of removing it: the station still knows its thermometer. A method may freely call objects it creates itself.

concepts.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
concepts.title: Weighing the principle's costs and benefits
concepts.question: Should the Principle of Least Knowledge always be applied, and what does applying it cost?

paragraphs: The Principle of Least Knowledge is the same as the Law of Demeter, and the two names are used interchangeably. The authors say no principle is a law: principles are used when and where they are helpful, since all design involves trade-offs.
The benefit is fewer dependencies between objects, and the authors report that studies have shown this reduces software maintenance.
The cost is more wrapper classes written to handle method calls to other components. That can mean more complexity, more development time and slower runtime performance.
card.rule: Treat Least Knowledge as guidance to weigh: it cuts dependencies, but costs wrapper methods, complexity and some speed.
card.limits: The authors report the benefit but give no figures in this passage, so how large it is in your case is for you to judge.

concepts.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
concepts.title: How a facade supports Least Knowledge
concepts.question: How does a facade help a client keep to the Principle of Least Knowledge?

paragraphs: The book introduces the facade as a pattern that avoids tight coupling between clients and subsystems and helps us follow the Principle of Least Knowledge. A facade not only simplifies an interface, it decouples a client from a subsystem of components.
Put the two ideas together: a client that uses a facade deals with one friend. It no longer calls each component of the subsystem.
The facade itself may call every component, because the components are its own, held in instance variables.
card.rule: A facade lets a client talk to one friend instead of every component, which keeps the client within the Principle of Least Knowledge.
card.limits: Knowledge is concentrated, not removed: the facade still knows every component. Clients that bypass the facade get none of the benefit.

concepts.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
concepts.title: Duplicated recipes in Coffee and Tea
concepts.question: What problem is the author trying to solve by redesigning the Coffee and Tea classes?

paragraphs: The chapter opens with two classes, Coffee and Tea, that each hold a recipe method. The two recipes are written separately, yet they are so close that a lot of code appears twice.

Both boil water and both pour the drink into a cup in the same way. The steps that differ, such as brewing coffee grounds versus steeping a tea bag, or adding sugar and milk versus adding lemon, carry different details. The authors want the repetition gone, and a first redesign moves the identical steps into a common base class.
The authors then ask the reader whether that first cut was enough, and whether some other likeness between the two classes is still unused.
card.example: Two report classes, SalesReport and StockReport, both open a file, write a header and close the file. Only the body differs. Putting open, header and close in a base class removes the repeated methods.
card.rule: When two classes carry the same code, find what they share and move it to one place.
card.limits: A first cut that moves only the identical methods up removes some duplication, not all of it; what remains may be a repeated pattern around the steps that differ.

concepts.title: The recipes are one algorithm
concepts.question: What do the two recipes share beyond the methods they already have in common?

paragraphs: After moving the identical methods up, the authors look again and see that the two recipes follow one algorithm: boil some water, use the hot water to extract the coffee or tea, pour the result into a cup, and add the appropriate condiments.
Two of those four steps already sit in the base class. The other two are not shared in code, yet they play the same role in both drinks and differ only in which beverage they apply to.
So the next thing to abstract is the recipe method itself: the set of steps in order, not only single methods.
card.example: A MathExam class and an EssayExam class both collect papers, mark them, record scores and send results. Marking differs, but the four-step sequence is the same.
card.rule: Look for a shared sequence of steps, not only for shared methods.
card.limits: The sequence is shared only when the classes really run the same kinds of step in the same order; matching helper names called in different orders do not form one algorithm.

concepts.title: One neutral name for analogous steps
concepts.question: How does giving analogous steps one name let a single recipe method serve both drinks?

paragraphs: The first obstacle is that Coffee calls brewCoffeeGrinds and addSugarAndMilk, while Tea calls steepTeaBag and addLemon. Since the method names differ, one recipe method cannot call both.

The authors reason that steeping and brewing are analogous, and that adding sugar and milk is much like adding lemon: both add condiments. They invent a neutral name for each pair: brew and addCondiments.
With those names the recipe reads: boilWater, brew, pourInCup, addCondiments. It no longer mentions coffee or tea, so it can be written once.
card.example: A report tool has PdfExporter with drawPdfPages and HtmlExporter with writeHtmlTags. Both render the body of the document. Calling the step render lets one export method call render without knowing the format.
card.rule: Give analogous steps one general name so a shared sequence can call them without knowing the specific kind.
card.limits: A name should say what the step is for, not how one kind does it; if two steps are not truly analogous, a forced common name hides a real difference.

concepts.title: The recipe lives in the superclass
concepts.question: Which class holds the recipe, and what do Coffee and Tea still have to supply?

paragraphs: The authors now move prepareRecipe into the superclass, CaffeineBeverage. It calls boilWater, brew, pourInCup and addCondiments in that order. boilWater and pourInCup are written in the superclass; brew and addCondiments are left for the subclasses.

Coffee and Tea now supply only how to brew and which condiments to add. They no longer hold a recipe of their own. The authors say they have just built the Template Method Pattern, and the recipe method is the template method.
In the book's one-line wording, the template method defines the steps of an algorithm and lets subclasses provide the implementation of one or more of those steps.
card.example: A test framework runs setUp, runTest and tearDown for every test. A base class holds the method that calls the three in order, and each test class fills in its own steps.
card.rule: Write the algorithm once in the superclass and leave the varying steps to subclasses.
card.limits: The superclass can only call steps it has named in advance, so every variation must fit one of them; a variation that needs a different sequence calls for a different design.

concepts.title: Tracing a Tea through the template
concepts.question: Which class's code runs at each point when a Tea object makes its drink?

paragraphs: Take Tea myTea = new Tea() and then a call to prepareRecipe. The template method is found in CaffeineBeverage, so that is where the algorithm starts, and it stays in charge from there.
The steps run in order. boilWater runs in CaffeineBeverage. brew runs in Tea, because only the subclass knows how to steep. pourInCup runs in CaffeineBeverage again. addCondiments runs in Tea.
The superclass runs the show: it decides which step comes next, and the subclass is called only when its turn comes.
card.example: A ReportBase template calls loadData, formatBody and printFooter. HtmlReport supplies only formatBody. For an HtmlReport, the base class runs two steps and the subclass runs one.
card.rule: In a template method the superclass calls every step, and the subclass code runs only when the superclass reaches it.
card.limits: The trace holds when a subclass supplies only the steps left open; if it overrides a shared step or the template itself, the path through the code changes.

concepts.section: What did the Template Method get us?
concepts.title: What the template buys
concepts.question: What does the Template Method design give that the first Coffee and Tea design did not?

paragraphs: The book compares the old design with the new one in a table. Before, Coffee and Tea each ran their own algorithm, and code was duplicated across them. Now the superclass owns the algorithm and the subclasses reuse it.
A change to the algorithm is made in one place, instead of opening every subclass. The structure is also a framework: a new caffeine beverage only has to implement a couple of methods to plug in.
Knowledge of the algorithm sits in one class, which relies on the subclasses to supply the missing parts, instead of being spread across many classes.
card.rule: The template keeps the algorithm in one place, so reuse grows and changes stay local.
card.limits: These gains depend on the algorithm being really shared; if every new variant needs its own sequence, the central algorithm becomes a constraint instead of a help.

concepts.title: The pattern defined
concepts.question: How does the book define the Template Method Pattern, and what exactly is a template in it?

paragraphs: The official definition: the pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses. It lets subclasses redefine certain steps of the algorithm without changing the algorithm's structure.
A template, the authors explain, is a method that defines an algorithm as a set of steps. One or more of those steps is defined as abstract and implemented by a subclass.
This arrangement keeps the structure of the algorithm in place while the subclasses provide part of the implementation.
card.rule: A template method is a method that fixes the steps of an algorithm and defers some of them to subclasses.
card.limits: The pattern lets subclasses change how a step is done, not which steps exist or in what order; a change to the structure itself belongs in the superclass.

concepts.title: Concrete, abstract and hook methods
concepts.question: What kinds of method can the abstract class hold, and who supplies each?

paragraphs: The book says the abstract class that holds the template method may define three kinds of method: concrete methods, abstract methods and hooks.

A concrete method is written in the abstract class and shared by every subclass, as boilWater is. An abstract method is left empty and implemented by the subclasses. A hook has an empty or default body in the abstract class, and a subclass may override it.
So abstract methods are the steps a subclass has to supply, hooks are optional extras, and concrete methods are the shared work.
card.rule: The abstract class mixes shared concrete steps, required abstract steps and optional hooks.
card.limits: The kind is a design choice made step by step: moving a step from abstract to concrete removes a decision from subclasses, and moving it to a hook makes it optional.

concepts.title: Protecting the template with final
concepts.question: How can the template method be protected from subclasses that would change the algorithm?

paragraphs: The pattern promises that subclasses do not change the structure of the algorithm. The book's safeguard is to declare the template method final, so that subclasses cannot override it.

Without that, a subclass could replace the whole sequence with its own and the promise would be lost. With it, subclasses still supply the abstract steps and the hooks but cannot rewrite the template.
The book lists this among its summary points for the pattern.
card.rule: Declare the template method final so subclasses supply steps but cannot rewrite the algorithm.
card.limits: Final guards the sequence only; it does not stop a subclass doing poor work in its own steps, and it suits only an algorithm whose structure should be fixed.

concepts.title: What a hook is
concepts.question: What is a hook, and what does a subclass gain from it?

paragraphs: A hook is a method declared in the abstract class but given only an empty or default implementation. A subclass can override it to hook into the algorithm at that point, or ignore it.
This gives the algorithm optional extension points without forcing every subclass to write anything. A subclass that does not care leaves the default in place.
The template method decides where each hook is called.
card.rule: A hook is an empty or default method in the abstract class that a subclass may override to join the algorithm at that point.
card.limits: A hook is optional, so the algorithm must still work if every subclass ignores it; a step the algorithm cannot do without belongs among the abstract methods.

concepts.title: Three uses of hooks
concepts.question: In what ways can a hook be used inside the algorithm?

paragraphs: The book names several uses of hooks. A hook can make part of the algorithm optional: the subclass implements it if it wants that step.
A hook can let a subclass react to something about to happen or just done. The book's example is a hook called justReOrderedList, which lets a subclass redisplay a list after it is reordered.
A hook can also answer a question for the abstract class. In the drinks example, a hook asks whether the customer wants condiments, and the template adds them only when the answer is yes.
card.rule: Hooks let a subclass take an optional step, react to an event, or make a decision for the template.
card.limits: In each use the template still decides where the hook is called and what to do with its answer; the hook cannot reorder the algorithm.

concepts.title: Abstract method or hook?
concepts.question: When should a step be an abstract method and when should it be a hook?

paragraphs: The book gives a direct rule. Use an abstract method when the subclass must provide an implementation of the step. Use a hook when that part of the algorithm is optional.

Every concrete subclass has to implement all the abstract methods, so it gives a complete implementation of the undefined steps. With a hook the subclass may choose to implement it, but it does not have to.
The choice therefore sets how much each subclass has to write.
card.rule: Make a step abstract when every subclass must supply it, and a hook when it is optional.
card.limits: The test is whether the step is truly required: a step with a harmless default is a hook, but a step the algorithm cannot do without stays abstract even if some subclasses find it dull.

concepts.title: How fine to cut the steps
concepts.question: How fine should the steps of a template method be?

paragraphs: Every abstract step is work for each subclass. The authors therefore suggest keeping the number of abstract methods small, because otherwise writing a subclass is a big job.
One way is not to make the steps of the algorithm too granular. The authors admit this is a trade-off: less granularity means less flexibility.
Another way is to turn optional steps into hooks, which spares the subclasses from implementing them.
card.rule: Balance step size: fewer abstract steps are easier to implement, and more steps give more flexibility.
card.limits: There is no fixed number; the right size depends on how much subclasses really need to vary, and steps cut too coarse make the template too rigid to be useful.

concepts.title: The Hollywood Principle
concepts.question: What problem does the Hollywood Principle protect a design from?

paragraphs: The Hollywood Principle is summed up as: Don’t call us, we’ll call you.

It guards against dependency rot. That is what happens when high-level components depend on low-level ones, which depend on high-level ones, and on sideways ones, and so on. Once rot sets in, no one can easily understand how the system is designed.
The principle lets low-level components hook themselves into a system, while the high-level components decide when they are needed and how.
card.rule: High-level components decide when and how to call low-level components, not the other way round.
card.limits: The principle settles who is in charge; it does not remove every upward call, so judge the explicit dependencies between levels rather than each single call.

concepts.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
concepts.title: Template Method as Hollywood in action
concepts.question: How does Template Method apply the Hollywood Principle, and how does that differ from Dependency Inversion?

paragraphs: Designing with the Template Method Pattern tells the subclasses: don’t call us, we’ll call you. CaffeineBeverage is the high-level component. It controls the algorithm and calls on Coffee or Tea only when a step is needed.
Coffee and Tea do not decide when brew or addCondiments run; the superclass does. That is how the pattern keeps control in the high-level class.

The book relates this to the Dependency Inversion Principle. Both aim at decoupling, but Dependency Inversion is the stronger and more general statement: avoid concrete classes and work with abstractions. The Hollywood Principle is a technique for letting low-level components hook into a computation without creating dependencies between them and the higher layers.
card.rule: In Template Method the superclass decides when to call the subclass's steps.
card.limits: The Hollywood Principle is narrower than Dependency Inversion, and Template Method is only one of its uses; a design can follow it without following the pattern.

concepts.title: Arrays.sort in the wild
concepts.question: Is Arrays.sort a true Template Method, and why does it depart from the textbook form?

paragraphs: Java's Arrays class has a sort method that fixes the sorting algorithm but needs one piece from you: a way to compare two items. For ducks, you supply it by implementing compareTo, which says whether one object is less than, greater than or equal to another.

This is not the textbook pattern. A Java array cannot be subclassed, and the designers wanted sort to serve every array, so they made it a static method and deferred the comparison to the items, which implement the Comparable interface.
The authors judge that this is still in the spirit of Template Method: the algorithm is in one place and incomplete without the missing step.
card.rule: A method that owns an algorithm and defers one step to something supplied is in the spirit of Template Method, even without subclassing.
card.limits: Judging whether code counts as a pattern means asking what the pattern is for, not only whether it matches the textbook diagram; a look-alike can fit another pattern better.

concepts.title: Hooks in JFrame and applets
concepts.question: Where do hooks appear in Swing's JFrame and in applets?

paragraphs: The Java API holds further template methods. JFrame inherits a paint method that does nothing by default, because it is a hook. By overriding paint you insert yourself into JFrame's algorithm for displaying its area of the screen and add your own graphics.

An applet is a small program that runs in a web page. Every applet subclasses Applet, which provides several hooks that concrete applets use for their own behaviour. Because they are hooks, an applet is not required to implement them.
In both cases a framework runs the process and offers hooks where your code joins in.
card.rule: In a framework, override the hooks to add your behaviour; the framework decides when they run.
card.limits: Overriding a hook changes what happens at that point, not when it happens; and spotting hooks in real code means looking for methods the framework calls with an empty or default body.

concepts.title: Template Method versus Strategy
concepts.question: How do Template Method and Strategy differ, and what does each give up?

paragraphs: Both patterns encapsulate algorithms. Template Method does it by inheritance, and Strategy does it by object composition.

Template Method defines the outline of an algorithm and lets subclasses do some of the work, so it keeps control of the structure and puts shared code in the superclass. Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, each of which implements the whole algorithm.

In the authors' fireside chat, Strategy points out that it is more flexible, since a client can change algorithms at runtime by using a different strategy object. Template Method answers that it is a little more efficient and needs fewer objects.
card.rule: Template Method varies steps through inheritance; Strategy swaps whole algorithms through composition.
card.limits: These contrasts come from a playful dialogue and give the authors' view; real designs can blend both, as the sort method does.

concepts.title: Factory Method as a specialization
concepts.question: How is Factory Method related to Template Method?

paragraphs: The book says Factory Method is a specialization of Template Method. In that specialization, the steps that subclasses supply, the primitive operations, are used to create and return objects.

The book's matching exercise sets the two apart. In Template Method, subclasses decide how to implement the steps of an algorithm. In Factory Method, subclasses decide which concrete classes to instantiate.
card.rule: Factory Method is a Template Method whose varying step creates an object.
card.limits: Specialization points one way; the two patterns are not interchangeable, and the pair cannot be read as one pattern with two names.

concepts.section: Breaking News: Objectville Diner and Objectville Pancake House Merge
concepts.title: Two menus, two ways of storing items
concepts.question: What difficulty arises when two merged menus keep their own different ways of storing items?

paragraphs: In the story, a diner and a pancake house merge, and each keeps its own menu code. Both menus use the same MenuItem class, but one stores its items in an ArrayList and the other in an array. The chefs will not change this, because a lot of code depends on how each menu stores its items.

The difficulty appears as soon as one client must use both menus. The method that returns the items has a different return type in each, so the client cannot treat the two menus alike. The design question is how to let each storage choice stay while the client stays manageable.
card.rule: When two parts hold their data differently, any client that uses both inherits the difference unless something hides it.
card.limits: If only one menu existed, or both stored items the same way, there would be no difference to hide. The problem also assumes the owners refuse a rewrite; if one side could change cheaply, unifying storage might be the easier fix.

concepts.title: A client that must use both menus
concepts.question: What does a client have to do to print every item from menus stored in different structures?

paragraphs: The new company wants a Java waitress who can print a custom menu on demand and say whether an item is vegetarian. To print everything she asks each menu for its items. One menu returns an ArrayList and the other an array, so her code needs one loop for each kind of container.

Every other method in the Waitress would follow the same pattern: fetch both menus, then run two loops. If another restaurant with a third storage type were acquired, she would need three loops. The cost grows with every new storage type.
card.rule: Each distinct storage type forces its own traversal code into every client method that reads the items.
card.limits: The cost appears only when the client reads storage directly. If the client received items through one shared way of stepping through them, extra storage types would not add loops.

concepts.section: What’s the problem with having two different menu representations?
concepts.title: Three faults of a client that sees inside
concepts.question: Which design faults show up in a client that reads two storage types directly?

paragraphs: Reading both menus directly shows three faults. First, the Waitress codes to the concrete PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu classes, not to an interface. Second, she must know how each menu represents its items inside, which violates encapsulation. Third, the two loops are duplicate code, and a third menu would add a third loop.

A further consequence follows. If the Diner switched to a Hashtable, a lot of the Waitress's code would have to change. The faults are linked: each comes from the client being able to see inside the menus.
card.rule: A client that sees how its collaborators store things is tied to them, repeats code and breaks when they change.
card.limits: These are faults of the client's design, not of the menus: each menu's storage is fine inside its own class. Blaming the storage choice would point the repair at the wrong place.

concepts.title: The goal: one shared interface
concepts.question: What would the two menus need to share so the client can stop depending on either one?

paragraphs: The chefs will not rewrite their menus, yet the Waitress needs relief. The authors notice the menus are nearly alike already: both offer a method that returns the items, differing only in its return type. If both implemented one interface, the Waitress would need fewer concrete references and might lose the multiple loops.
The target is to decouple the Waitress from the concrete menu classes completely. She should concentrate on being a waitress and not have to think about what type of menu she is handling.
card.rule: Make the client depend on one shared interface so it need not know which concrete variation it holds.
card.limits: A shared interface helps only when the variations really do the same job. These menus already offer nearly the same operations; classes with unrelated jobs cannot be unified this way without more work.

concepts.title: Encapsulate the iteration
concepts.question: What is the part that varies in the menu code, and what can we do with it?

paragraphs: Earlier in the book we learned to encapsulate what varies. Here what varies is the iteration, since each menu hands back a different kind of collection. For the ArrayList we use size() and get(); for the array we use its length field and subscripts.

The idea is to create an object, called an Iterator, that encapsulates the way we step through a collection. We can build one for the ArrayList and another for the array. The client then asks the object for items one at a time and never touches the collection's own steps.
card.rule: Put the varying way of stepping through a collection into its own object, and let the client talk to that object.
card.limits: This helps when the stepping varies between collections. With a single collection type the iterator hides nothing worth hiding, and the iterator itself must still know the one collection it serves.

concepts.title: The Iterator interface
concepts.question: What operations does the Iterator interface offer so that one client loop can serve any collection?

paragraphs: The Iterator Pattern relies on an interface called Iterator. A version in Java offers hasNext(), which reports whether more items remain, and next(), which returns the next item. Because it is an interface, we can write an implementation for any kind of collection: arrays, lists, hashmaps, whatever you favour.

A client then needs only this interface. It loops while items remain and fetches one at a time, and the same loop works whichever concrete iterator sits behind it. Each concrete iterator holds the knowledge of one collection.
card.rule: Define a small interface for stepping through items and write one implementation for each kind of collection.
card.limits: The interface says nothing about order, so an iterator over an unordered collection promises none. A collection that cannot supply an iterator, like an array, still needs one written by hand.

concepts.section: Reworking the Diner Menu with Iterator
concepts.title: Each menu builds its own iterator
concepts.question: Who should create the iterator for a menu, and in what type should it be handed to the client?

paragraphs: An iterator class is not enough; the client must be able to get an instance. The authors add one method, createIterator(), to each menu. It builds the concrete iterator that fits that menu's storage and returns it to the client as an Iterator.

Each menu keeps its own storage and now also knows how to be walked. The cooks only had to add this one method, since the iterator classes were provided for them. The client never meets the concrete iterator class by name.
card.rule: Let each collection create the iterator that suits it and hand it out through the shared interface.
card.limits: The collection now depends on its iterator class, a small price paid in the one class that already knows the storage. A client that wants a different traversal needs the collection to offer it.

concepts.title: One printing method that takes an Iterator
concepts.question: How does the Waitress print any menu once she receives an Iterator instead of a menu?

paragraphs: The Waitress gets a printMenu() method that takes an Iterator. To print a menu she calls createIterator() on it and passes the result in. Inside, one loop does the work: while the iterator has more items, take the next one and print it.
Printing the two menus becomes two calls to the same method, and the duplicate loop is gone. The authors then write test drive code to confirm the Waitress works with both menus.
card.rule: Write the client's work once against the Iterator and feed it the iterator each collection produces.
card.limits: The Waitress still fetches each menu through its concrete class, so she is only partly decoupled, and each new menu still needs its own call. Fixing the loop did not fix those.

concepts.section: What have we done so far?
concepts.title: Before and after the Iterator
concepts.question: How do the Waitress's dependencies differ before and after iterators were added?

paragraphs: The authors compare the two designs point by point. Before, the menus are not encapsulated: the Diner uses an ArrayList and the Pancake House an array, and the Waitress can see it. After, the Waitress has no idea how the menus hold their items.

Before, two loops were needed and the Waitress was bound to the concrete collection types. After, one loop handles any collection implementing Iterator, and she uses an interface. One problem remains: the two menu classes have almost identical interfaces but no common type, so she is still bound to two concrete menu classes.
card.rule: Compare a design before and after a change along the same dimensions: what is visible, how many loops, and what the client is bound to.
card.limits: A before-and-after table can hide what the change left alone. Here the Waitress still depends on two concrete menu classes, so the table must be read for what remains as well as what improved.

concepts.title: What the iterator solution leaves unsolved
concepts.question: Which problem is still open after adding iterators, and how can we describe it precisely?

paragraphs: Judging a solution means asking whether it solved every problem it set out to solve. Iterators solved the exposure of the menus' storage and the duplicate loops. The authors point out one problem left: the two menu classes have the same interface in practice but no declared common interface.
So the Waitress still names two concrete menu classes, and the authors turn to fix that next. A fair review names the specific gap, rather than calling the solution incomplete without saying how.
card.rule: Judge a solution by listing the original problems, marking which are solved, and naming precisely any that remain.
card.limits: This only works if the original problems were stated fully at the start. A problem nobody wrote down can be marked neither solved nor open, so an incomplete list gives false comfort.

concepts.title: A small shared Menu interface
concepts.question: What does a shared Menu interface with one createIterator() method give the Waitress?

paragraphs: The Menu interface is small: it has one method, createIterator(). PancakeHouseMenu and DinerMenu both implement it, and the Waitress refers to each menu through the interface instead of the concrete class. She now programs to an interface, not an implementation, which reduces her dependency on the concrete classes.

Each menu class takes the responsibility of creating the iterator that suits its internal storage, so the Waitress no longer depends on how menu items are held. The authors keep addItem() out of the public interface, so that the chefs control their menus.
card.rule: Give the variations a small shared interface that exposes only what their clients need.
card.limits: A shared interface covers only what clients share. Anything a client needs beyond it must come from elsewhere, or the interface must grow, which couples more clients to more detail.

concepts.title: Use the standard java.util.Iterator
concepts.question: Why swap a homegrown Iterator for java.util.Iterator, and where must we still write our own?

paragraphs: The authors built their own Iterator interface to show how it works. They now switch to java.util.Iterator, because implementing the standard one gives a lot of leverage. Its methods are hasNext(), next() and remove().

ArrayList already has an iterator() method, so the PancakeHouseMenuIterator class can be deleted and one line changed. An array offers no iterator, so the DinerMenu still needs its own iterator class, now written to the java.util interface.
card.rule: Prefer the platform's standard iterator interface, and write your own iterator only for collections that lack one.
