card.limits: The standard interface fits only if its operations suit you. If your aggregates need more, you can extend the Iterator interface rather than abandon it.

concepts.title: Optional and unspecified parts of Iterator
concepts.question: What does the Iterator interface leave optional or unspecified, and how should a careful client react?

paragraphs: The standard interface includes remove(), but the authors call it optional. An iterator that will not allow removal should still provide the method and throw the runtime exception UnsupportedOperationException. A good client checks for that exception when calling remove().

The behaviour of remove() is also unspecified if the collection changes while you iterate over it, which matters in multithreaded code. The interface is therefore a contract with gaps, and a careful client reads what it promises before relying on it.
card.rule: Read an interface for what it leaves optional or unspecified, and write clients that survive those gaps.
card.limits: Gaps in a contract are not to be filled by guessing. A client that assumes removal works, or that iteration is safe while the collection changes, may break; check the documentation instead.

concepts.title: The Iterator Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Iterator Pattern provide, and what does it keep hidden?

paragraphs: The authors define it this way: the Iterator Pattern provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation. An aggregate here is any object that holds a group of elements, such as an array, a list or a hash map.

In the menu story, the Waitress steps through items one after another and never learns whether they sit in an array or an ArrayList. The traversal is done by the iterator object, which the aggregate creates.
card.rule: Access an aggregate's elements one after another through an iterator, without exposing how the aggregate holds them.
card.limits: Sequential access is what is promised, not any particular order or random access. A client that must jump to the fortieth element or sort by price gets no help from the pattern as defined.

concepts.title: Polymorphic iteration
concepts.question: What does a uniform way of stepping through every aggregate allow us to write?

paragraphs: Once every aggregate offers the same way of stepping through its elements, we can write polymorphic code that works with any of them. printMenu() is the example: it does not care whether items sit in an array, an ArrayList or anything else, as long as it can get hold of an Iterator.

The authors call this polymorphic iteration: methods that take Iterators as parameters. Such code iterates over any collection that supports Iterator, with no concern for how the collection is implemented.
card.rule: Write methods that take an Iterator, and they serve any collection that can supply one.
card.limits: Polymorphic code sees only what the Iterator offers. If a method needs something the interface lacks, such as the number of items in advance, the iterator alone cannot supply it.

concepts.title: Traversal belongs to the iterator
concepts.question: Which object should carry the job of traversal, and what does moving it do to the aggregate?

paragraphs: The pattern also moves a job. Traversal goes to the iterator object, not to the aggregate. The aggregate's interface and implementation become simpler because it no longer carries iteration methods.
The aggregate stays focused on what it should be focused on, which is managing a collection of objects. The authors say this puts the responsibility where it belongs.
card.rule: Give traversal to the iterator so the aggregate does only the job of holding and managing its elements.
card.limits: The move works when traversal can be separated from managing the elements. The iterator still needs to know enough about the aggregate to step through it, so the two are separate but not strangers.

concepts.title: Classic names and Java names
concepts.question: How do the classic iterator methods map onto the methods of java.util.Iterator?

paragraphs: Other books show the Iterator with the methods first(), next(), isDone() and currentItem(). These are the classic names and they have changed over time. In java.util.Iterator we have next(), hasNext() and even remove().

The classic next() and currentItem() were merged into one method. isDone() became hasNext(), with the sense turned around: done means no more items, while hasNext() reports that more remain. There is no counterpart of first(), since in Java we usually get a new iterator to start over.
card.rule: Read different iterator interfaces by mapping their methods onto the same few jobs: start, advance, read and test for the end.
card.limits: Mapping names works because the jobs agree. A method with no counterpart, like remove() in java.util.Iterator, is an extension, and the range of behaviours you can give an iterator is wide.

concepts.title: External and internal iterators
concepts.question: What is the difference between an external and an internal iterator, and which did the menus use?

paragraphs: An external iterator is controlled by the client, who calls next() to get each element. The menu example used this kind. An internal iterator controls the iteration itself, stepping through the elements and applying an operation that you give it.

An internal iterator therefore needs a way to pass an operation to it. It is less flexible, since the client does not control the iteration. Some argue it is easier to use, because you hand over the operation and the iterator does all the work.
card.rule: Choose an external iterator when the client needs control of the pace and path; consider an internal one when handing over the operation is enough.
card.limits: Neither style wins everywhere: the external one gives the client control, the internal one saves the client work. Choose by whether the caller needs to steer the traversal.

concepts.title: A class should have only one reason to change
concepts.question: Why does giving a class a second responsibility make it harder to keep stable?

paragraphs: Suppose the aggregate handled both its collection and the iteration. That gives the class two reasons to change: it changes if the collection changes in some way, and it changes if the way we iterate changes. This leads to a design principle: a class should have only one reason to change.

Every responsibility of a class is an area of potential change, so more than one responsibility means more than one area of change. Modifying code invites problems, and two ways to change raise the odds. The principle says to give each responsibility to one class, and only one class.
card.rule: A class should have only one reason to change, so give each responsibility to exactly one class.
card.limits: Separating responsibilities is one of the hardest jobs in design, because our minds group behaviours that are really two responsibilities. Only careful examination, and watching for signs that a class changes in more than one way, will find them.

concepts.title: Cohesion
concepts.question: How does cohesion relate to the Single Responsibility Principle, and what makes it high or low?

paragraphs: Cohesion measures how closely a class or module supports a single purpose or responsibility. A class has high cohesion when it is designed around a set of related functions, and low cohesion when it is designed around a set of unrelated functions.

Cohesion is a more general concept than the Single Responsibility Principle, but the two are closely related. Classes that follow the principle tend to have high cohesion and to be more maintainable than classes with several responsibilities and low cohesion.
card.rule: Aim for high cohesion: build each class around functions that belong together.
card.limits: Cohesion is a matter of degree and judgement, not a count of methods. A short class can be incoherent and a long one tightly focused; ask whether its parts serve one purpose.

concepts.title: Fitting a third menu into the framework
concepts.question: What three changes fit the Café menu, which stores items in a HashMap, into the framework?

paragraphs: The Café menu keeps its items in a HashMap. The authors list three things to do to fit it into the framework: implement the Menu interface, get rid of getItems(), and add createIterator() returning an iterator that steps through the HashMap's values.

This is easy because HashMap is one of the Java collections that supports Iterator, although not quite as ArrayList does. A HashMap holds keys and values, so you first retrieve its collection of values, which are the MenuItems, and then get the iterator from that.
card.rule: To fit a new collection into the iterator framework, implement the shared interface and return an iterator over the part that holds the elements.
card.limits: The route to an iterator differs by collection: a hash map gives one only through its values. Fitting a collection still needs someone who knows how it holds items to write its createIterator() code.

concepts.section: Adding the Café Menu to the Waitress
concepts.title: Decoupled and extensible
concepts.question: What did adding the Café menu show about the Waitress after the iterator work?

paragraphs: Because the Waitress now expects Iterators, adding the Café menu was easy. She takes one more menu and makes one more call to printMenu(), and the test drive prints breakfast, lunch and the Café's dinner. The Waitress is decoupled from how the menus are built.
She is also more extensible: a menu with any storage can be added by giving it createIterator(). The authors then look at what still remains in her code, which is where the next problem lies.
card.rule: Test a design by what it costs to add the next variation: a good design takes a small, local addition.
card.limits: Easy extension is relative. Adding the Café still meant opening the Waitress and adding a call, and the authors count that as a remaining cost; the design is extensible only up to that point.

concepts.title: The Collections Framework and Collection
concepts.question: What do ArrayList, Vector and similar classes share through java.util.Collection, and how does HashMap differ?

paragraphs: The Java Collections Framework is a set of classes and interfaces that includes ArrayList, Vector, LinkedList, Stack and PriorityQueue. Each of these implements the java.util.Collection interface, which has many useful methods for manipulating groups of objects.

Hashtable and HashMap support Iterator only indirectly. They hold two sets of objects, keys and values, so to iterate over the values you first retrieve the Collection called values and then obtain its iterator.
card.rule: Find the Collection that holds the elements you want, and get the iterator from it.
card.limits: Not every class takes the same route: maps hold two sets and need the extra step. Check which part you are iterating over before you ask for the iterator.

concepts.section: Is the Waitress ready for prime time?
concepts.title: The Waitress is still not ready
concepts.question: What weakness remains in the Waitress even though her menus are decoupled?

paragraphs: The Waitress has come a long way, but the three calls to printMenu() look ugly. Each time a new menu is added, her implementation must be opened and more code added. The authors call this a violation of the Open Closed Principle.

This is not her fault: the menu implementation was decoupled and the iteration extracted. What remains is that menus are handled as separate, independent objects, and a way to manage them together is needed. Putting them in a collection might do it, though the menu names would be lost unless added to each menu.
card.rule: After decoupling, check what still forces edits to the client when a variation is added, and look for a way to manage the variations together.
card.limits: Grouping the menus in a collection fixes the repeated calls but not everything. Names are lost unless each menu carries one, and a flat collection cannot hold menus inside menus, which is the next challenge.

concepts.section: Just when we thought it was safe...
concepts.title: When menus must hold menus
concepts.question: Why can the array-based Diner menu not take a dessert menu as one of its elements?

paragraphs: Just as the Waitress seemed settled, the Diner wants a dessert submenu. The design must now support several menus and menus within menus. It would be nice to make the dessert menu an element of the Diner menu's collection, but the Diner stores its elements in an array of MenuItem.

A dessert menu is not a MenuItem, so it cannot be assigned to the array. The authors conclude that the time has come to rework the chefs' implementation into something general enough for all menus and submenus, since otherwise no design could take further acquisitions or submenus.
card.rule: When a new requirement breaks the container's type assumptions, treat it as a sign the structure must change, not a case for a patch.
card.limits: Not every requirement justifies a rework. The authors reach for one because the complexity has risen so far that patching could not take further acquisitions or submenus; a one-off case may deserve a smaller fix.

concepts.title: Requirements for the new design
concepts.question: What three requirements must the new menu design meet?

paragraphs: The authors list what the new design needs. First, a tree-shaped structure that can hold menus, submenus and menu items. Second, a way to traverse the items in each menu that is at least as convenient as the iterators in use now.

Third, the ability to traverse more flexibly: for example, to iterate over only the Diner's dessert menu, or over the Diner's entire menu including the dessert submenu. Menus, nested submenus and items fit naturally into a tree.
card.rule: Before choosing a solution, list what it must provide: the structure, the convenience of access and the flexibility of traversal.
card.limits: A list of requirements reflects what is known now. This one comes from the dessert case, and later cases might add more, so treat it as a current outline rather than a final one.

concepts.title: The Composite Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Composite Pattern define, and what is a part-whole hierarchy?

paragraphs: The Composite Pattern allows you to compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. It lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly. The authors still keep Iterator as part of the solution, but menus now need something Iterator alone does not give.

For the menus, a tree can hold nested groups of menus and menu items in the same structure. This is a part-whole hierarchy: a tree made of parts, the menus and items, that can be treated as a whole, like one big über menu.
card.rule: Compose objects into a tree of parts and wholes, and let clients treat any node in the same way.
card.limits: The pattern fits only data that really is a hierarchy of parts and wholes. For a flat collection with no nesting, an Iterator is enough.

concepts.title: Treating parts and wholes uniformly
concepts.question: What does it mean to treat individual objects and compositions uniformly?

paragraphs: Any menu is a composition, because it can contain both other menus and menu items. The individual objects are the menu items, which hold no other objects. Treating them uniformly means the same operation, such as printing, can be applied to either.

With a tree of menus, submenus and perhaps subsubmenus plus items, one operation can be applied over the whole structure, or to any part of it. In most cases the client can ignore the difference between a composition and an individual object.
card.rule: Give compositions and individual objects the same operations so a client need not ask which one it holds.
card.limits: Uniformity has gaps: some operations make no sense on one kind, such as asking a leaf for its children. The pattern accepts this and handles such cases by design choices.

concepts.title: Component, composite and leaf
concepts.question: How are component, composite and leaf related in a composite structure?

paragraphs: A composite contains components. Components come in two flavours: composites and leaf elements. That sounds recursive, and it is: a composite holds a set of children, and those children may be other composites or leaves.

Organised this way, the data forms a tree, drawn upside down, with a composite at the root and branches of composites ending in leaf nodes. A leaf has no children; a composite does. A Component is any object in the structure, composite or leaf.
card.rule: Name the three roles: component for any node, composite for a node that holds children, leaf for a node that holds none.
card.limits: The roles describe positions in the structure, not kinds of thing in the world. If a leaf later needs to hold children, it has to become a composite, and its parent must still be able to treat it the same way.

concepts.title: The MenuComponent interface
concepts.question: What does the common component class offer, and what happens to operations a node cannot support?

paragraphs: To apply Composite to the menus, the authors create a component class that menus and menu items share, so the same method can be called on either. They start with the abstract class MenuComponent, which gives a default implementation for each method.

Some methods do not make sense on every node, such as getChild() on a leaf. Their default is to throw UnsupportedOperationException. A MenuItem or Menu implements only the methods that suit it and inherits the rest.
card.rule: Put every operation any node may need into one component type, with defaults that signal unsupported operations.
card.limits: Throwing defaults trade compile-time safety for uniformity: a client may call an operation its node does not support and learn only at run time. Sometimes the best a default can do is throw a runtime exception.

concepts.title: The leaf and composite classes
concepts.question: How do MenuItem and Menu differ in which MenuComponent methods they implement?

paragraphs: MenuItem is the leaf class: it implements the behaviour of the elements of the composite, such as getPrice() and isVegetarian(). The child-management methods stay as the inherited defaults, since a leaf has no children to manage.

Menu is the composite class. It can hold MenuItems or other Menus and implements the methods that manage its children. It does not implement getPrice() or isVegetarian(), because they make little sense for a Menu, so those fall back to the exception default.
card.rule: Let each class implement the operations that fit it and inherit the defaults for the rest.
card.limits: This split is a design choice. A Menu could have defined isVegetarian() in some way, but the authors leave it unsupported and discuss the alternatives later in the chapter.

concepts.title: Printing by recursion
concepts.question: How can a Menu print everything beneath it without the client walking the tree?

paragraphs: Because a Menu is a composite holding both MenuItems and other Menus, its print() should print everything it contains. If it did not, the client would have to iterate through the entire composite and print each item itself, which defeats the purpose of having a composite.

Implementing print() is easy because each component can print itself. The Menu iterates through its children and calls print() on each. If it meets another Menu, that Menu's print() starts its own iteration, and so on: the process is recursive.
card.rule: Let each composite perform an operation by asking its children to perform it, so the operation spreads over the whole tree.
card.limits: The recursive walk assumes every node can perform the operation. If one cannot, the call fails there unless the design supplies a default or a way to skip it.

concepts.section: Getting ready for a test drive...
concepts.title: Transparency traded for safety
concepts.question: What does the Composite Pattern trade away by putting child management and leaf operations in one interface?

paragraphs: A reader may say the Composite Pattern breaks the Single Responsibility Principle. The authors agree there is truth in this: the pattern trades that principle for transparency. Transparency means a client treats composites and leaves uniformly, so whether an element is a composite or a leaf is invisible to it.

The price is some safety: a client may try something meaningless, such as adding a menu to a menu item. You could go the other way and separate the responsibilities into interfaces. That is safer, because inappropriate calls are caught, but transparency is lost and the code needs conditionals and instanceof.
card.rule: Weigh transparency against safety in the component interface, and choose knowingly.
card.limits: Neither design is right everywhere. The authors call this a design decision and a classic tradeoff, and note a leaf can be seen as a node with zero children, which softens the apparent violation.

concepts.title: Iterating over a whole composite
concepts.question: Why does an external iterator over a composite need more than a simple loop, and what does it use?

paragraphs: The Waitress may want to iterate over the entire composite, for example to pull out the vegetarian items. To allow this, every component gets a createIterator() method, so a client can ask any node for an iterator.

The CompositeIterator is a serious iterator. It must step through the items of a component and also include child menus, and their child menus, and so on. As an external iterator it must keep its position so a client can call hasNext() and next(), and over a recursive structure it uses stacks to track where it is.
card.rule: To iterate externally over a tree, keep your position in stacks as you move up and down the hierarchy.
card.limits: Recursion inside print() is easier because the program's own call stack keeps the place for you. An external iterator gets no such help, which is why its code is hard to follow; the authors warn it can be mind-bending.

concepts.title: The Null Iterator
concepts.question: What should createIterator() return for a node that has nothing to iterate over?

paragraphs: A MenuItem has nothing to iterate over, so what should its createIterator() return? There are two choices. Choice one is to return null, but then the client needs conditional code to check whether null came back.

Choice two is to return an iterator whose hasNext() always returns false. This seems better, since the client never worries about null. The authors call it a no-op iterator, name it NullIterator, and mention that it is another example of the Null Object design pattern.
card.rule: When there is nothing to return, return an object that safely does nothing instead of null.
card.limits: This choice fits where having nothing to iterate is a normal answer, as it is for a leaf.

concepts.title: Unsupported operations: exception, false or type check
concepts.question: How did the authors handle isVegetarian() on a Menu, and what were the alternatives?

paragraphs: The Waitress goes through the whole composite and calls isVegetarian() on each element. A Menu does not support this, so its inherited method throws UnsupportedOperationException, which the Waitress catches before moving on. A reader may object that try/catch is for error handling, not program logic, and the authors agree in general.

There are alternatives. Checking with instanceof first would lose transparency. Menus could return false, which is simple and keeps transparency. The authors prefer the exception, because it says clearly that the operation is unsupported, which differs from false, and lets someone later implement a sensible isVegetarian() for Menu.
card.rule: When an operation does not apply to some nodes, choose among an exception, a default value and a type check by weighing clarity and uniformity.
card.limits: The authors' choice is a position, not a proof. It keeps uniformity and clarity but uses exception handling as part of program flow, which they concede is not its intended use.

concepts.section: The magic of Iterator & Composite together...
concepts.title: Implementation issues for composites
concepts.question: Which further issues can arise when implementing a composite, beyond the basic tree?

paragraphs: In an imagined interview, the Composite Pattern lists issues to consider. A component can hold a pointer to its parent, which makes traversal easier and lets a child be removed by asking the parent. Order matters too: a composite that must keep its children in a particular order needs a more careful scheme for adding, removing and traversing.

Caching is another issue. If the structure is complex or expensive to traverse and you constantly traverse it to compute a result, you can cache that result at the composite nodes and save traversals.
card.rule: When building a composite, decide about parent links, child order and caching, as well as the shape of the interface.
card.limits: These are options to weigh, not requirements. A menu whose items need no particular order needs no ordering scheme.

concepts.title: Iterator and Composite among the patterns
concepts.question: How do Iterator and Composite differ from the other patterns met so far, and what do they have in common?

paragraphs: The chapter adds two patterns to the toolbox, both for dealing with collections of objects. Iterator gives a way to traverse an aggregate without exposing its representation, and takes the job of iteration off the aggregate. Composite holds individual objects and composites in one structure and lets clients treat them uniformly.

Each pattern is told apart from the others by its purpose. Strategy encapsulates interchangeable behaviours and uses delegation, Adapter changes the interface of classes, Facade simplifies the interface of a group of classes, and Observer notifies objects when state changes. The new two concern traversal and uniform treatment.
card.rule: Know each pattern by its purpose: Iterator for traversal without exposure, Composite for uniform treatment of parts and wholes.
card.limits: A one-line purpose is a pointer, not the whole pattern. Each has tradeoffs the chapter spells out, such as an optional remove() in Iterator and transparency against safety in Composite.

concepts.title: States and transitions
concepts.question: What do the circles and the arrows of a state diagram stand for?

paragraphs: A state diagram draws a machine as circles and arrows. Each circle is a state: one configuration of the machine in which it behaves in a certain way. Each arrow is a transition: the move from one state to another that some action causes.

The chapter's gumball machine starts in No Quarter. Inserting a quarter moves it to Has Quarter. From there, turning the crank leads to Gumball Sold, while ejecting the quarter leads back to No Quarter.

The authors count four states and four actions (insert quarter, eject quarter, turn crank, dispense) but five transitions. Dispensing can end in either Out of Gumballs or No Quarter, depending on how many gumballs remain, so the machine has to keep that count.
card.example: A library book is Available, On Loan or Reserved. Checking it out moves it from Available to On Loan, returning it moves it back, and placing a hold on a book that is On Loan moves it to Reserved.
card.rule: Read a machine as states, which say how it behaves now, and transitions, which are the actions that move it between states.
card.limits: A diagram shows only the moves someone drew. It does not say what should happen when an action makes no sense in a state, and it does not hold the numbers, such as gumballs left, that pick between arrows.

concepts.title: A state machine with conditionals
concepts.question: How does a procedural state machine keep its current state and decide what each action does?

paragraphs: The chapter reviews a plain way to turn a diagram into code in four steps. First list the states. Next create an instance variable for the current state and give each state a value, for example a named constant.

Then list the actions that can happen. Finally write a class for the machine with one method per action. Inside each method, conditional statements look at the current state and choose the right behavior for it.
The book contrasts this with the State Pattern, which makes each state a full class instead of a value compared inside conditionals.
card.example: An elevator door has states Closed, Opening and Open. The elevator class holds a variable for the door's state, and a method for the action press button checks that variable to decide whether to open, wait or ignore.
card.rule: In a procedural state machine, one variable names the current state and every action method branches on it.
card.limits: The recipe works for small machines and the gumball tests passed. Its cost shows later, when states or actions are added and every branching method must be revisited.

concepts.title: Every action in every state
concepts.question: What must the code decide for each pairing of a state with an action, including pointless ones?

paragraphs: Joe and Frank warn that customers can do nonsensical things: eject a quarter when none is in, or insert a second quarter. For every possible action, the code must check which state the machine is in and act appropriately.
So the first gumball implementation handles inserting a quarter, ejecting a quarter, turning the crank and dispensing, plus the case of an empty machine. Each of those has an answer in each state.
That makes the work a grid of states against actions: every cell needs a defined response.
card.example: A turnstile has states Locked and Unlocked and actions insert coin and push arm. That is four pairings. Pushing while Locked and inserting a coin while Unlocked still need defined responses, even though a rider rarely does either.
card.rule: Give every action a defined response in every state.
card.limits: The grid grows with each new state or action: a machine with S states and A actions has S times A pairings. Many pairings simply refuse the action, but each still has to be written somewhere.

concepts.section: You knew it was coming... a change request!
concepts.title: The change request tests the design
concepts.question: Why does the 1-in-10 request put a working design under strain?

paragraphs: Mighty Gumball loaded the code into a new machine and the testers found it fine. The authors call the design nice and solid, built with a well-thought-out method. Then comes a change request: a contest in which one sale in ten releases two gumballs.
The authors ask the reader to draw the diagram for the contest first. The next pages argue that following a good method and passing the tests did not make the code easy to extend.
The argument runs: the design works now; a new requirement arrives; so the real test of the design is what that requirement forces you to change.
card.example: A payroll script passes every check this month. Next month tax rules change, and the team finds the rate is typed into twelve places. The script was correct, but it was costly to change.
card.rule: Judge a design by how a new requirement changes it, not only by whether it passes today's tests.
card.limits: One change request is a sample, not proof of a bad design. A program that will never change need not be judged on this, and the authors' verdict applies to the structure of this code.

concepts.title: Behavior scattered across states
concepts.question: What fault in the first design leads Judy and Frank to conclude that it must be refactored?

paragraphs: The authors give six statements about the first implementation and ask the reader to judge them. They touch on the Open Closed Principle, on whether anything that varies is encapsulated, on transitions buried in conditionals, and on bugs from further additions.

The conversation that follows draws the conclusion. Frank says the code must be refactored to be easy to maintain and modify. Judy says the behavior of each state should be localized, so that changing one state does not risk the others.
Put as an argument: the behavior of every state lives in shared methods; a change to one state edits those shared methods; so each state's behavior should be separated.
card.example: A shop's checkout code has one big function that handles card, cash and voucher payments with branches. A change to voucher rules means editing that function, and a typo can break card payments.
card.rule: When one change must edit code that other behaviors share, separate the behaviors.
card.limits: Separation has a price in structure and in the number of pieces. It helps most when the behaviors are likely to change independently. If they stay fixed, the shared code can be left alone.

concepts.title: Two principles behind the redesign
concepts.question: Which principles do Frank and Judy invoke, and which design move does each one justify?

paragraphs: Frank suggests putting each state's behavior in its own class, so that every state implements only its own actions. This applies the principle of encapsulating what varies: what differs from state to state is behavior, so it is pulled out of the machine.
Judy adds that the machine can delegate to the object for the current state. Frank names this favoring composition: the machine holds a state object rather than branching or inheriting.
Judy expects that a new state will still need code changes, but in a much smaller area: a new class and perhaps a few edited transitions.
card.example: A drawing editor lets the user pick a pen, an eraser or a selector. Each tool becomes its own class, and the editor passes every mouse event to whichever tool is current.
card.rule: Pull what varies into its own classes, then let the main object hold one of them and delegate to it.
card.limits: Adding a state still means writing code, and some neighboring transitions may need edits. The gain is a smaller area of change, not zero change.

concepts.title: The three-step redesign
concepts.question: What are the three steps of the redesign, and what happens to the conditional code?

paragraphs: The authors give a plan in three steps. First, define a State interface with a method for every action the machine can receive. Second, implement a State class for every state, each responsible for the machine's behavior when it is in that state.
Third, get rid of all the conditional code and delegate to the State class to do the work.
The authors then note that following the design principles has led to the State Pattern itself, which they define later in the chapter.
card.example: A help desk ticket is Open, Assigned or Closed, with actions assign, resolve and reopen. The plan gives an interface with those three methods, three classes that implement it, and a ticket that forwards each call.
card.rule: Make one State interface with a method per action, one class per state, and have the machine delegate instead of branching.
card.limits: The three steps are quick to state; the real work is deciding what each state does for every action. An action that matters in one state only still needs a reply from all the others.

concepts.section: Defining the State interfaces and classes
concepts.title: One interface, a class per state
concepts.question: What does each state class provide, and what does it need from the machine?

paragraphs: The State interface has one method for each action: insertQuarter, ejectQuarter, turnCrank and dispense. Each state class, such as the book's SoldOutState, implements all four. Every method says what happens in that state when that action arrives.

The same method name therefore does different things in different classes. In the sold-out state, inserting a quarter is refused with a message, because the machine has none left to sell. In the no-quarter state the same call accepts the coin.
The book's sold-out state also has a toString that names the state, which helps when reporting what the machine is doing.
card.example: A dishwasher has states Idle, Washing and Done. Each is a class with start, openDoor and finish methods. Washing's openDoor pauses the cycle, while Idle's openDoor allows access.
card.rule: Each state class implements every action of the State interface, answering correctly for its own state.
card.limits: A method name means nothing without its class: insertQuarter in one state and in another are different behavior. Reading a single method in isolation can mislead.

concepts.title: How a state moves the machine on
concepts.question: How does a state class change the machine's state, and how does it learn which state comes next?

paragraphs: Each state class follows the first version's code, but only the part for its own state. When an action should move the machine on, the state object asks the machine to switch its current state to the next state object.
In the authors' design the states decide what comes next. For example, in the sold state the choice between No Quarter and Sold Out depends on the number of gumballs at run time.
To find the next state object, a state calls a getter method on the machine rather than naming a concrete class.
card.example: In a video player, the Paused class handles play by resuming the sound and then asking the player to make Playing its current state, fetched through a getter on the player.
card.rule: A state class answers an action for its own state and, when the machine should move on, sets the machine's current state to the next state object.
card.limits: Because states choose the next state, they come to depend on one another. Fetching state objects through the machine's getters softens this, but does not remove it.

concepts.title: The machine just forwards
concepts.question: How does the reworked machine replace its integer state and its branches?

paragraphs: In the rework, the machine's state variables change from integers to state objects: one object for each state, plus a variable that holds the current one.

Each action method on the machine becomes a short forward. Inserting a quarter just calls the insert action on whichever state object is current. The branching that used to live in the machine now happens by polymorphism: the current object's class decides what happens.
One wrinkle remains. When the crank is turned unsuccessfully, the machine still calls dispense; the state refuses it, so nothing goes wrong, but the call is unnecessary.
card.example: A kiosk class holds Idle, Paying and Printing objects and a variable named current. Its pressStart method is one line: current.start().
card.rule: The context holds one object per state and a variable for the current one, and each action method calls the same action on that object.
card.limits: Forwarding looks the same whatever the state, so the cost shows up elsewhere: extra calls such as dispense after a failed crank turn are harmless only because the states refuse them.

concepts.section: Let’s take a look at what we’ve done so far...
concepts.title: Same behavior, new structure
concepts.question: What did the rework change, what did it keep, and which gains do the authors claim?

paragraphs: The authors stop to take stock. The new gumball machine is structurally quite different from the first, yet functionally exactly the same. Customers see no change.

They claim four gains. The behavior of each state is localized in its own class. The troublesome if statements are gone. Each state is closed for modification while the machine stays open to extension by new state classes. And the structure maps more closely to the diagram, so it is easier to read.
These four are the payoff of the argument made earlier: separate what varies and the next change becomes easier.
card.example: A shipping calculator is rewritten so each carrier's rules live in their own class. Quotes come out exactly as before, but adding a carrier now means adding one class.
card.rule: A good refactoring keeps behavior and changes structure so that behavior is localized, branching shrinks and extension is easy.
card.limits: The gains are the authors' claims for this redesign, and the price is more classes. Easier to read is a judgment: someone used to the first version may disagree.

concepts.title: The State Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the State Pattern's definition say an object can do?

paragraphs: The authors define the State Pattern in two sentences: it allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, and the object will appear to change its class. The object whose behavior changes is called the Context. Each state class that gives it behavior is a ConcreteState.
The first sentence follows from what the redesign does. The context delegates to the object for its current state, and the current state changes over time, so behavior changes with it.
The gumball machine shows it: insert a quarter in the no-quarter state and the machine accepts it; insert one in the has-quarter state and the machine rejects it.
card.example: A phone call object can be Ringing, Connected or OnHold. Pressing the hold button does one thing while Connected and another while Ringing, because the call forwards the press to its current state.
card.rule: The State Pattern lets a context change its behavior by delegating to a current state object that is replaced as its internal state changes.
card.limits: The pattern suits behavior that changes along with the object's own state. A behavior picked from outside and kept for life is another situation, the one Strategy covers.

concepts.title: Appearing to change class
concepts.question: What does it mean that an object appears to change its class, and what produces the appearance?

paragraphs: The definition's second sentence says the object will appear to change its class. The authors explain it from the client's side: if an object can completely change its behavior, then to a client it looks as if it were created from a different class.
In reality nothing like that occurs. The context uses composition, and it gives the appearance of a class change by simply referencing different state objects.
Clients usually know very little about the state objects, so the swap stays out of their sight.
card.example: A chat user object can be Online, Away or DoNotDisturb. A message sent to it is handled differently each time, yet the sender always deals with one user object.
card.rule: A client sees one object whose behavior changes; the change comes from swapping referenced state objects, not from changing a class.
card.limits: The class change is only an appearance, visible to a client that watches behavior. The context's real class stays the same throughout.

concepts.title: Same diagram, different intent
concepts.question: The State and Strategy patterns have the same class diagram; how do they differ?

paragraphs: The authors admit that the two class diagrams are essentially the same, and then argue that the patterns differ in intent. The argument turns on who picks the behavior object and how it changes.

With State, behaviors are encapsulated in state objects and the context delegates to one of them. Over time the current state changes across the set to reflect the context's internal state. The client usually knows little about the state objects.
With Strategy, the client usually specifies the strategy object that the context is composed with. It can be changed at run time, but often one strategy is the most appropriate for a given context.
card.example: A game enemy is given an aggressive or cautious plan by a designer at spawn and keeps it: Strategy. An order that moves from Placed to Paid to Shipped, answering cancel differently in each: State.
card.rule: Same structure, different intent: in Strategy the client configures the behavior, in State the context moves itself through states.
card.limits: Because the diagrams match, only the intent tells the patterns apart: who picks the object and why. A picture alone cannot name the pattern, and real code can sit between the two.

concepts.title: What each pattern replaces
concepts.question: What problem does each pattern solve, and when would you reach for each?

paragraphs: The authors give each pattern a problem. Think of Strategy as a flexible alternative to subclassing. If you use inheritance to define a class's behavior, you are stuck with that behavior even when it must change. With Strategy you change it by composing with a different object.
Think of State as an alternative to lots of conditionals in your context. By encapsulating behaviors in state objects, you change the behavior by changing the state object.
The Q&A adds a cost for the second alternative: without separate objects, a program with a lot of state ends up with very large conditionals that are hard to understand and maintain.
card.example: A tax calculator with a subclass per country is stuck with a country once created: Strategy lets it switch rules by composition. A document with many if-tests on Draft, Review and Final modes: State.
card.rule: Reach for Strategy when inheritance locks a behavior in place, and for State when conditionals on internal state pile up.
card.limits: Both rest on composition and delegation, so they overlap. If behavior never needs to change and no conditionals are piling up, neither is called for.

concepts.title: Who decides the transitions
concepts.question: Where should state transitions live, and what separates reasonable positions?

paragraphs: In the gumball machine the states decide what comes next, but the authors say they need not. The alternative is to let the Context decide the flow. They give a general guideline: fixed transitions suit the Context; dynamic ones usually go in the state classes.

In the gumball machine the move to No Quarter or Sold Out depends on the count of gumballs at run time, which is why the states hold it. The price is dependencies among the state classes, which the authors reduced with getter methods on the Context.
The authors leave a related question to the reader: would moving this logic to the machine be better, and what are the advantages and disadvantages?
card.example: A traffic light always runs Red, Green, Yellow in that order: fixed, so the controller can hold the order. A lift that picks its next stop from live requests: dynamic, so the states decide.
card.rule: Put fixed transitions in the context and dynamic ones in the states, and weigh the dependencies that each choice creates.
card.limits: The authors give a guideline, not a rule, and leave the choice open. Two designers can defend different placements, so the useful move is to state the issue and give reasons.

concepts.title: Clients, and sharing the states
concepts.question: Who talks to the state objects, and when can several contexts share them?

paragraphs: Clients do not talk to the states directly. All requests to the states come from the Context, which oversees its own state; a client changing it without the Context's knowledge is usually unwanted.

If an application holds many contexts, the state objects can be shared. This is a common scenario. The only requirement is that the state objects do not keep their own internal context. Each state is typically assigned to a static instance variable.
Sharing is aimed at applications that create many context instances.
card.example: A game with 500 enemies makes one Idle, one Chase and one Flee object and shares them. Each call passes in the enemy, so no state object remembers any single enemy.
card.rule: Clients talk only to the context, and state objects can be shared among contexts if they keep no context data of their own.
card.limits: Sharing fails when a state remembers anything about one particular context. Whatever varies per context, such as a count, must stay in the context and be reached through the reference passed in.

concepts.title: The price of more classes
concepts.question: Is the larger number of classes worth it, and how do the authors answer the objection?

paragraphs: A reader might object that the State Pattern increases the number of classes: look at how many more the gumball machine had. The authors agree that it does. In their words, more classes are often the price you pay for flexibility.

Their advice is to build with the extra classes unless the code is a one-off you are going to throw away. They add that what matters is often the number of classes exposed to clients, and that the extra ones can be hidden, for example by making them package visible.
So the objection is granted and answered by weighing a certain cost against a likely benefit.
card.example: A conference demo script with three states, used once and deleted, hardly needs a class per state. A booking system that will gain states for years does.
card.rule: Accept the extra classes when the code will live and change, and keep them out of the clients' sight.
card.limits: For a throwaway one-off the authors accept that the extra classes may not pay back. The advice also rests on a prediction that the code will change, which could turn out wrong.

concepts.title: Interface or abstract class
concepts.question: When would the State type be an abstract class instead of an interface?

paragraphs: The pattern's class diagram shows State as an abstract class. The gumball machine used an interface, because the authors had no common functionality to put in an abstract class. In your own design you may prefer an abstract class.

The sanity check points to a case. The sold state and the winner state hold a lot of duplicate code. If State were an abstract class with default behavior, the error replies, such as telling the customer a quarter is already in, could be generic and inherited.
The authors reason that those messages will not be seen by the customer, so one generic reply is acceptable.
card.example: A notification module has states Queued, Sending and Failed. Four of its five actions get the same reply 'not allowed now' in every state. A base class holding that reply removes twelve copies.
card.rule: Use an interface while states share no code, and an abstract State class when they repeat default behavior or methods may be added later.
card.limits: The gumball machine had nothing to share, so the interface was enough; the abstract class is something the authors suggest considering, not something they built.

concepts.section: We still need to finish the Gumball 1 in 10 game
concepts.title: Adding the contest as a new state
concepts.question: How does the 1-in-10 game fit into the state design, and what does that show?

paragraphs: To add the game, the authors add a state to the machine and then implement a WinnerState class. It is remarkably similar to the sold state, except that it dispenses two gumballs instead of one.
The last change is the chance itself. The random draw and the transition to the winner state go into the has-quarter state, because that is where the customer turns the crank.
The authors judge it simple: they added a state, implemented it, wrote the chance game and linked a transition. Their conclusion is that the new design is paying off.
card.example: A parking meter adds a promotion where one payer in twenty parks free. It gains a FreeParkState, and the state that handles the coin does the random draw.
card.rule: To add behavior to a state-based design, add a state class and change the transitions that lead into it.
card.limits: The change is small, not absent: the machine gains a new state variable, and the has-quarter state is edited. Changes that affect every state, such as a new action, still touch every class.

concepts.section: Demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball, Inc.
concepts.title: One state class or two
concepts.question: Should the winner behavior be its own state or part of the sold state, and how is such a trade-off judged?

paragraphs: The Q&A asks whether the sold state could simply dispense two gumballs. The authors say you could, since the two states are almost identical. The cost is that one class would then represent two states, the winner and the non-winner.

That sacrifices clarity in the state class to reduce duplicated code. It also gives the sold state two responsibilities, against the principle one class, one responsibility. They ask what happens when the promotion ends or the stakes change.
They close by calling it a trade-off that comes down to a design decision.
card.example: A shop has a Checkout state, and a Black Friday Checkout that differs only in a 20 percent discount. Separate classes let the discount be removed when the sale ends.
card.rule: Treat one state class or two as a trade-off between duplicated code and a class with two responsibilities, and decide with reasons.
card.limits: The authors do not name a winner. Their two considerations, clarity and single responsibility, favor a separate class, but they leave it as a design decision for the situation.

concepts.title: Adding an action: refill
concepts.question: How does the refill action get added to the state design?

paragraphs: The authors ask for a refill method that takes the number of gumballs added, updates the count and resets the machine's state. In the sold-out state the machine can do nothing until someone refills it.

Their solution adds refill to the State interface, so each state implements it. In every state except sold out, refill does nothing. In the sold-out state, it moves the machine to the no-quarter state.
The machine also gets a refill method. It adds to the count of gumballs, and then calls the current state's refill.
card.example: A ticket kiosk gains an addPaper action. The kiosk adds the sheets to its paper count, then calls the current state. Only the OutOfPaper state reacts, by returning the kiosk to Idle.
card.rule: A new action goes into the State interface and every state answers it, while the context updates its data and then delegates.
card.limits: The authors' version leaves refill as a quiet no-op outside the sold-out state. Another design might refuse with a message, or reject a refill when the machine is mid-sale.

concepts.title: A monitor that reports on machines
concepts.question: What does the first gumball report need, and where does each piece of its data come from?

paragraphs: The CEO wants a printed report on each gumball machine. The machine already has methods that give the count of gumballs and the current state, so the report needs only those two plus one new field: a location, so the CEO can tell machines apart.

The authors add location support to the GumballMachine class. They then write a separate class, GumballMonitor, that asks a machine for its location, its gumball inventory and its state, and prints them as a report. The monitor does its work only by calling methods on the machine it is given.
The team builds this quickly and expects the CEO to be delighted.
card.example: A bakery chain has an Oven class with methods for temperature and mode. A separate OvenMonitor is given an oven, calls those methods and prints one line per oven. Only the monitor knows how to format the report.
card.rule: Keep reporting in a separate monitor class that is given a machine and reads it through the machine's existing methods.
card.limits: This design relies on the monitor holding an ordinary reference to the machine, so it works only while both live in the same running program.

concepts.title: Right code, wrong place
concepts.question: Why does a correct monitor still fail to satisfy the CEO, and what does Joe propose to keep the code?

paragraphs: The first monitor is tested by giving a GumballMonitor a machine, and it works. The CEO wants more: to sit at his desk and monitor machines remotely. The monitor, however, runs in the same JVM as the gumball machine it watches, so it cannot see machines elsewhere.

A JVM is a Java Virtual Machine: one running Java environment with its own memory. Joe proposes to leave GumballMonitor as it is and hand it a proxy to a remote object instead. A proxy is a stand-in for a real object.
The proxy acts just like a gumball machine, yet behind the scenes it talks over the network to the real, remote machine.
card.example: A school has an AttendanceReport class that reads Classroom objects in the school server's program. The principal wants it on her home laptop. The report logic is right; only its position is wrong, so a stand-in for the classroom is the fix.
card.rule: When working code is in the wrong place, keep it and give it a stand-in for the distant object.
card.limits: A stand-in saves rewriting only when the existing code uses just the methods the stand-in can offer; code that reaches inside the object still needs changes.

concepts.title: The remote proxy
concepts.question: What is a remote proxy, and what do 'remote object' and 'local representative' mean in that definition?

paragraphs: A remote proxy acts as a local representative to a remote object. A remote object is an object that lives in the heap of a different Java Virtual Machine or, more generally, one running in a different address space.

A local representative is an object you can call local methods on, and the calls are forwarded to the remote object. The client behaves as if it makes remote method calls, but it only calls methods on a proxy object in its own heap. The proxy handles the low-level details of network communication.
card.example: A phone app calls a method on a local ProfileProxy object. The proxy sends the request to a Profile object on the company's server and passes the answer back. ProfileProxy is the local representative; Profile is the remote object.
card.rule: A remote proxy is a local object that forwards each call to an object in another JVM.
card.limits: The idea applies only when the real object lives in another address space; a stand-in for an object in the same JVM is not a remote proxy.

concepts.section: Adding a remote proxy to the Gumball Machine monitoring code
concepts.title: Why a reference cannot cross heaps
concepts.question: Why can't a program hold a variable referring to an object in another heap, and what does Java offer instead?

paragraphs: A variable such as Duck d can refer only to an object in the same heap as the code that runs the statement. You cannot write a line that sets d to an object living in another heap.
So the proxy cannot be built by grabbing a reference. Java's Remote Method Invocation, RMI, gives a way to find objects in a remote JVM and invoke their methods.
card.example: A server in one data centre holds a Customer record in its memory. Code on a second server cannot name that record in a variable, however it is declared. It must send a request that the first server carries out.
card.rule: A reference works only within one heap; to reach beyond it, use a mechanism such as RMI that finds and calls remote objects.
card.limits: RMI finds and calls remote objects, but the call still crosses a network; it does not bring the remote object into your heap.

concepts.title: Client helper and service helper
concepts.question: How do two helper objects let a client call a remote service as if it were local?

paragraphs: The client calls a method on a client helper, as if the client helper were the service. The client helper has the same method that the service advertises, but none of its real logic. Instead it contacts the server, sends the method name and arguments, and waits.

On the server side, the service helper receives the request through a socket connection, unpacks it, and invokes the real method on the real service object. To the service object the call is local: it comes from the service helper, not from a remote client.
card.example: At a hotel, a phone app calls unlock(412) on a LockHelper. LockHelper sends 'unlock, 412' to a server component, which calls unlock(412) on the real Door object. The Door sees a local call.
card.rule: The client calls a look-alike helper that ships the call to a second helper, which makes a plain local call on the real service.
card.limits: The client helper holds no service logic, so it can only forward; if the server is unreachable it has nothing of its own to answer with.

concepts.title: One remote call, six steps
concepts.question: In what order does a remote call travel from the client object to the service object and back?

paragraphs: The client object calls a method, say doBigThing(), on the client helper. The client helper packages up the call, with the arguments and the method name, and ships it over the network to the service helper. The service helper unpacks it, works out which method to call and on which object, and invokes the real method.

The service object returns a result to the service helper, which packages it up and ships it back over the network. The client helper unpackages the returned values and returns them to the client object. To the client object, all of this was transparent.
card.example: Asking a travel desk for a booking by post: you hand the clerk your request, the clerk letters it to head office, head office staff open it and act, reply by post, and your clerk reads the answer out to you.
card.rule: A remote call is a round trip: call, package, ship, unpack, run, package, ship, unpack, return.
card.limits: The six steps describe one successful round trip; they do not say what happens when the network fails part way.

concepts.title: What RMI builds for you
concepts.question: What does RMI build for you, and what are the client and service helpers called in RMI?

paragraphs: RMI builds the client and service helper objects, right down to a client helper with the same methods as the remote service. You write none of the networking or I/O code. With your client, you call remote methods just as you call normal methods on objects in your own JVM.
RMI also supplies the runtime infrastructure, including a lookup service the client uses to find remote objects. In RMI's own words, the client helper is a stub and the service helper is a skeleton.
card.example: Like a postal service, RMI handles sorting, transport and delivery. You write the letter, which here is the interface and the service, and the machinery between the two ends is built for you.
card.rule: RMI generates the stub, the skeleton and a lookup service, so you write ordinary calls instead of network code.
card.limits: RMI removes the networking code, not the network: calls still travel over a wire and can fail.

concepts.title: A call that looks local can fail
concepts.question: Should a remote call be fully transparent to the client, and what must the client still acknowledge?

paragraphs: Even though the call looks local to the client, the client helper sends it across the network, so there is networking and I/O. Networking and I/O are risky: they can fail, and they throw exceptions all over the place.

So the client has to acknowledge the risk. The authors ask the reader whether remote calls should be totally transparent and what might go wrong with that. To judge the claim that the call is transparent, ask what it leaves out: the call looks local, yet it is not, and the client must say so in its code.
card.example: A shop app reads stock from a branch through a proxy that looks like a local Stock object. A reviewer notes that the app treats the call as always working. The gap is the missing handling of a failure.
card.rule: A remote call looks local but is not; the client must acknowledge that it can fail.
card.limits: Acknowledging the risk means handling or declaring the failure; it does not mean the failure can be predicted or prevented.

concepts.title: The remote interface
concepts.question: What three rules must a remote interface follow so that RMI can use it?

paragraphs: Step one in making a remote service is a remote interface. It defines the methods a client can call remotely and is what the client uses as the type of the service. Both the stub and the actual service implement it. It must extend java.rmi.Remote, a marker interface with no methods but a special meaning for RMI.

Every method must declare that it throws RemoteException, because the stub does networking and I/O and the client must handle or declare the exceptions. Arguments and return values must be primitives or Serializable, since they are packaged and shipped across the network by serialization.
Strings, primitives and most API types, including arrays and collections, are fine. Your own types must implement Serializable.
card.example: A RoomService remote interface extends Remote. Its getOccupancy() returns an int and declares RemoteException. Its getGuest() returns a Guest object, so Guest must implement Serializable.
card.rule: A remote interface extends Remote, declares RemoteException on every method, and uses only primitive or Serializable types.
card.limits: Remote is a marker: extending it adds no behaviour, only meaning for RMI, and the interface declares what clients may call, not how.

concepts.title: The remote implementation
concepts.question: What must the class that does the real work do to be usable as a remote service?

paragraphs: Step two is the remote implementation, the class that does the real work. It must implement the remote interface. To get the functionality related to being remote, the simplest way is to extend UnicastRemoteObject, from java.rmi.server, and let that superclass do the work.

That superclass has one problem: its constructor throws a RemoteException. Whenever a class is instantiated, its superclass constructor is called, so your class must also declare the exception. That is why you write a no-arg constructor that declares RemoteException, even if it does nothing else.
card.example: A ParcelTrackerImpl implements ParcelTracker, extends UnicastRemoteObject and has a no-arg constructor that throws RemoteException. The tracking logic sits in its methods.
card.rule: A remote implementation implements the remote interface, extends UnicastRemoteObject and declares RemoteException on its constructor.
card.limits: Extending UnicastRemoteObject is described as the simplest way, not the only way; the constructor rule follows from the superclass constructor throwing.

concepts.title: Registry first, then the service
concepts.question: What does the rmiregistry do, and in what order are the pieces of a remote service started?

paragraphs: The remote service has four steps: make the remote interface, make the remote implementation, start the RMI registry, and start the service. The rmiregistry is like the white pages of a phone book: it is where a client goes to get the proxy, meaning the stub.

Start the rmiregistry from a terminal, in a directory with access to your classes. Then start the service, perhaps from a main() method in the implementation class, which instantiates the service and registers it with the registry using the static rebind() method of Naming. The registry must be running, or that line fails.
card.example: A TicketService developer starts rmiregistry in the classes directory first. Then she runs TicketServiceImpl's main(), which creates the service and registers it under a name. Clients can now look it up.
card.rule: Start the registry before the service, then register the service by name so clients can find it.
card.limits: The order is fixed by the registration line needing a running registry; the registry only helps once the service has registered.

concepts.section: How does the client get the stub object?
concepts.title: Getting the stub
concepts.question: How does the client obtain the stub it will actually call?

paragraphs: The client needs the stub, because it is the thing the client calls methods on. That is where the registry comes in. The client does a lookup, like going to the white pages, and essentially says, here is a name, give me the stub that goes with it.

In code, Naming.lookup is given an address and a name, for example rmi://127.0.0.1/RemoteHello. The registry returns the stub as the return value of lookup, and RMI deserializes it automatically. The client then invokes methods on the stub as if the stub were the real service.
card.example: A library kiosk wants the CatalogService. It asks the registry at 10.0.0.5 for the name Catalog and receives a stub. It calls the stub's search method exactly as if it held the service.
card.rule: Look up a name in the registry to get the stub, then call the stub as if it were the service.
card.limits: Lookup returns something only if the service registered that name; over the Internet the notes say some kind of locator service would be needed.

concepts.section: How does the client get the stub object?
concepts.title: Two common RMI mistakes
concepts.question: Which two mistakes do programmers most often make with RMI, and when does each show up?

paragraphs: The book names two mistakes. The first is forgetting to start the rmiregistry before starting the remote service. When the service registers with rebind(), the registry must already be running.
The second is forgetting to make arguments and return types serializable. You will not know until runtime, because the compiler does not detect it.
card.example: A team starts its order service before the registry and sees the registering line fail. Another team's new Seat class compiles, yet the first remote call fails because Seat is not Serializable.
card.rule: Start the registry first, and make every remote argument and return type serializable.
card.limits: These are the two mistakes the book names; it does not claim they are the only ones.

concepts.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
concepts.title: Making GumballMachine a service
concepts.question: Which three things must be done to turn GumballMachine into a service that remote clients can call?

paragraphs: To turn the existing machine into a service, the authors list three tasks. Create a remote interface for the GumballMachine, giving a set of methods that can be called remotely. Make sure all the return types in that interface are serializable. Then implement the interface in a concrete class.

The machine is already implemented, so it is not redesigned. It needs to do what it takes to implement the remote interface, which the authors say means adding only a couple of things, as in the RMI detour.
card.example: A CoffeeKiosk class already works locally. Its owner adds a remote interface listing the kiosk's methods, checks that each return type can be serialized, and has the existing class implement the interface.
card.rule: Give the existing object a remote interface, make its return types serializable, and implement the interface in the existing class.
card.limits: These steps prepare the machine to receive calls; no client can find it until it is started and registered.

concepts.section: Getting the GumballMachine ready to be a remote service
concepts.title: Serializing drags references along
concepts.question: Why is making State Serializable not enough, and what extra problem does its reference to the machine cause?

paragraphs: State is the type the machine returns from getState(), so State has to be made Serializable. The authors then point to a further problem: each State object keeps a reference to a gumball machine, so that it can call the machine's methods and change its state.

If State were serialized as it is, the machine it refers to would be serialized and transferred with it. The authors do not want the entire gumball machine sent across the wire along with the State object. They say there is an easy fix, which comes in the code.
card.example: A Receipt object holds a reference to the whole ShopSession so it can look up the shop name. Sending the receipt to a remote client would also send the session.
card.rule: Before marking a type Serializable, check what it points to, because shipping it can ship them too.
card.limits: The concern is the references the object holds; this card claims only the problem, and the fix is left to the book's code.

concepts.title: Registering the machine
concepts.question: What must a finished gumball machine service do before the monitor can find it?

paragraphs: With the machine now a complete service, it has to be started so it can receive requests. First it must be registered with the RMI registry, so that clients can locate it.

The authors add a little code to the test drive to take care of this, rather than changing the machine class itself. They then run several machines with the new code, so that the CEO's monitor will have more than one machine to find.
card.example: A factory runs ten packing-machine services. At startup each one registers itself with the registry. Without that line, the monitor would have no way to find any of them.
card.rule: A finished service is invisible until it is registered with the registry.
card.limits: Registration only makes lookup possible; a client still has to look up the stub, and the registry must be running.

concepts.title: Reusing the monitor with proxies
concepts.question: How does the original GumballMonitor keep working when the machines are remote?

paragraphs: The authors want to reuse GumballMonitor without rewriting it to work over a network. They make a few changes, and the test drive gets proxies to the remote machines, so the CEO can monitor a bunch of them.

The monitor calls methods on a proxy, which makes a remote call across the wire and returns a String, an integer and a State object. Because it uses a proxy, the monitor does not know or care that calls are remote, apart from having to worry about remote exceptions.
card.example: A TruckReport class prints each Truck's location and load. Given proxies to trucks in other depots, it keeps the same code, but its calls can fail on the network, so it must handle those failures.
card.rule: Hand the unchanged client proxies instead of local objects, and let it deal with remote exceptions.
card.limits: The monitor ignores where its machines live, but not that a call can fail; the book also says a few changes were still needed.

concepts.section: Another demo for the CEO of Mighty Gumball...
concepts.title: Following one request
concepts.question: What happens, step by step, when the CEO's monitor asks a remote machine for its state?

paragraphs: The CEO runs the monitor, which first grabs the proxies to the remote machines and then calls getState(), along with getCount() and getLocation(), on each. getState() is called on the proxy, which forwards the call to the remote service.

The skeleton receives the request and passes it to the gumball machine. The machine returns the state to the skeleton, which serializes it and transfers it back over the wire to the proxy. The proxy deserializes it and returns it as an object to the monitor.
card.example: A parcel-locker monitor calls getFreeSlots() on a proxy. The locker-side skeleton receives the request and calls the real locker, then sends the answer back by the same route.
card.rule: Proxy forwards, skeleton delivers, the machine answers, the skeleton serializes, the proxy deserializes.
card.limits: The walk-through follows getState(); the calls to getCount() and getLocation() take the same path.

concepts.title: The Proxy Pattern defined
concepts.question: What does the Proxy Pattern provide, and what does it mean for a proxy to control access?

paragraphs: The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object, to control access to it. The authors also call the proxy a representative for the other object, meaning an object that stands in for it.

Control of access can sound odd, but in the gumball case the remote proxy controlled access to the remote object because the monitor did not know how to talk to a remote object. The proxy handled the network details. The variations of the pattern mostly differ in the way the proxy controls access.
card.example: A video app shows a grey box where a film poster will appear. The box stands in for the poster and decides when the real image is used, which is control of access by a placeholder.
card.rule: A proxy is a representative of another object that controls access to it, whether by hiding the network, delaying creation or checking rights.
card.limits: Control of access does not always mean refusing a request; in the gumball case it meant making a remote object reachable.

concepts.title: Subject, RealSubject and Proxy
concepts.question: How do the Subject, the RealSubject and the Proxy relate in the pattern's structure?

paragraphs: The Subject provides an interface for both the RealSubject and the Proxy. Because the Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same interface, the Proxy can be substituted for the RealSubject anywhere it occurs.

The RealSubject does the real work and is the object the Proxy represents and controls access to. The Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject and clients interact with the RealSubject through the Proxy. In some cases the Proxy may be responsible for creating and destroying the RealSubject.
card.example: A LabResults interface is the Subject. FileLabResults does the real work. LabResultsGuard implements LabResults too, holds a FileLabResults and passes calls to it. A viewer typed to LabResults accepts either.
card.rule: The Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same Subject interface, and the Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject.
card.limits: Substitution works through the shared interface; a stand-in without the Subject interface cannot be dropped in.

concepts.title: Three ways to control access
concepts.question: Which three ways of controlling access does the chapter name, and what does each guard?

paragraphs: Variations of the Proxy Pattern typically revolve around how the proxy controls access. A remote proxy controls access to a remote object. A virtual proxy controls access to a resource that is expensive to create. A protection proxy controls access to a resource based on access rights.
The chapter says the Proxy Pattern has quite a few variations. The remote proxy is only one implementation of the general pattern, and the other two are covered next.
card.example: A calendar object on another continent needs a remote proxy. A heavy photo that should load only when opened suits a virtual proxy. A file that interns may read but not delete suits a protection proxy.
card.rule: Pick the proxy by what it guards: a remote object, an expensive resource or a resource needing rights.
card.limits: The three named forms are not a closed list; the book mentions further variants such as caching proxies.

concepts.title: The virtual proxy
concepts.question: How does a virtual proxy treat an object that is expensive to create, before and after it exists?

paragraphs: A virtual proxy acts as a representative for an object that may be expensive to create. It often defers creating the object until it is needed. It also acts as a surrogate for the object before and while it is being created. After that, it delegates requests directly to the real subject.

Compare this with a remote proxy, which is a local representative for an object in a different JVM; a call on it is transferred over the wire and the result returned. Both follow roughly the general proxy design.
card.example: A map app has a RoutePlanner that is slow to build. A planner proxy answers simple questions at once, builds the real planner only when a route is asked for, and forwards every request to it afterwards.
card.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
