card.limits: A virtual proxy hides the cost of creation but does not remove it: the real object must still be built when it is needed.

concepts.title: Waiting for a CD cover
concepts.question: What must a CD cover viewer show while an image downloads, and why does a virtual proxy fit?

paragraphs: A viewer shows a menu of CD titles and fetches the cover images from an online service. Depending on network load and bandwidth, retrieving a cover can take a while. The application should display something in the meantime, and should not hang the whole application while it waits.

A virtual proxy can stand in place of the icon, manage the loading in the background, and show 'Loading CD cover, please wait...' until the image arrives. Once it is loaded, the proxy delegates the display to the icon.
card.example: A recipe app shows a photo for each dish. The photo loads slowly, so a stand-in shows a short message in its place and the rest of the screen stays usable. When the photo arrives, the stand-in passes painting to it.
card.rule: When something slow must appear on screen, put a proxy in its place that shows a message and loads it in the background.
card.limits: The proxy hides the wait but does not shorten it; the real image still has to arrive before it can be shown.

concepts.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
concepts.title: How ImageProxy works
concepts.question: What are the four steps ImageProxy follows from the first request to a new image?

paragraphs: ImageProxy first creates an ImageIcon and starts loading it from a network URL. While the bytes arrive, it displays the message 'Loading CD cover, please wait...'.

When the image is fully loaded, ImageProxy delegates all method calls to the image icon, including paintIcon(), getWidth() and getHeight(). If the user requests a new image, a new proxy is created and the process starts over.
card.example: A slideshow proxy for a large PDF starts the download, shows a notice while pages arrive, forwards every call to the finished document, and starts a new proxy when another PDF is chosen.
card.rule: Start loading, show a message, delegate every call when loaded, and start over with a new proxy for a new image.
card.limits: The four steps describe one proxy's life; a new request does not reuse the old proxy.

concepts.title: Conditionals inside ImageProxy
concepts.question: What weakness do the conditionals in ImageProxy reveal, and how would the State Pattern address it?

paragraphs: ImageProxy has two situations, the image loaded and not loaded, and conditional statements decide between them. The authors set a design puzzle: could another pattern clean this up?

Their answer is the State Pattern. Implement two states, ImageLoaded and ImageNotLoaded, and move the code from the if statements into those states. The proxy starts in ImageNotLoaded and moves to ImageLoaded once the ImageIcon has been retrieved.
card.example: A document-upload widget checks 'if uploaded ... else ...' in every method. Moving the 'uploaded' and 'not uploaded' behaviour into two state classes removes those checks.
card.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
card.limits: The puzzle offers a possible clean-up; the version with conditionals still works, and the book does not call it wrong.

concepts.title: Running the viewer
concepts.question: What happens from the first paint to the moment the real image appears?

paragraphs: When paintIcon() is first called, ImageProxy fires off a thread to retrieve the image and create the ImageIcon. At some point the image returns and the ImageIcon is fully created.

After that, the next time paintIcon() is called, the proxy delegates to the ImageIcon. So the next time the display is painted, the image appears in place of the message. The authors suggest resizing the window during loading to see that the proxy does not hang the Swing window.
card.example: A news app proxy starts loading a photo on first paint. The photo is ready at 3 seconds. The screen next paints at 5 seconds, so the photo shows at that paint.
card.rule: The first paint starts a background load; the first paint after it finishes shows the real image.
card.limits: The image shows at the next paint after the load completes, not at the instant of arrival.

concepts.title: Proxy or Decorator?
concepts.question: How do Proxy and Decorator differ when both wrap an object and forward calls?

paragraphs: Proxy and Decorator can look alike, but their purposes differ. A decorator adds behaviour to a class; a proxy controls access to it. The loading message in ImageProxy may seem like added behaviour, yet its more important role is controlling access to the ImageIcon.

The proxy decouples the client from the ImageIcon. Without it the client would wait for each image before it could paint its whole interface. Before the icon exists the proxy offers another representation, and once it exists the proxy allows access.
People say a proxy wraps its subject, but that is not quite accurate. A remote proxy's subject lives on another machine, and a virtual proxy's subject may not exist yet.
card.example: A wrapper that adds a timestamp to every message in a chat object is a decorator. A wrapper that checks whether a user may edit a record before passing the call on is a proxy.
card.rule: Ask the intent of the wrapper: if it adds behaviour it is a Decorator, and if it controls access it is a Proxy.
card.limits: Structure alone cannot tell them apart, since both implement the same interface and forward calls; only the purpose does.

concepts.title: Proxy, Adapter, Decorator and Facade
concepts.question: How do Proxy, Adapter, Decorator and Facade differ in what they do to the objects they wrap?

paragraphs: Adapter and Proxy both sit in front of other objects and forward requests. An adapter changes the interface of the object it adapts, while a proxy implements the same interface. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour, and a facade wraps a bunch of objects to simplify their interface.

A protection proxy may offer only part of an interface to a client based on its role, which makes it similar to some adapters. A common way to make clients use a proxy is a factory that creates the subject, wraps it in a proxy and returns it, so the client never knows.
card.example: A class wraps an old PhoneBook so it fits where a Contacts interface is expected, converting method names. It changes the interface, so it is an adapter.
card.rule: Same interface and access control is Proxy; different interface is Adapter; added behaviour is Decorator; simplified interface is Facade.
card.limits: A protection proxy offering only part of an interface can resemble an adapter, so purpose, not shape, has to settle it.

concepts.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
concepts.title: Java's dynamic proxy
concepts.question: What is a dynamic proxy, and where does the code that says what the proxy does belong?

paragraphs: Java supports proxies in the java.lang.reflect package. It lets you create a proxy class on the fly that implements one or more interfaces and forwards method invocations to a class you specify. Because the proxy class is created at runtime, this is called a dynamic proxy.

Because Java creates the Proxy class, you cannot put the behaviour into it as in the classic pattern. Instead it goes in an InvocationHandler. The handler responds to every method call on the proxy; it is the object the proxy asks to do the real work after receiving the calls.
card.example: A team wants every call on any of three service interfaces to follow one access rule. Instead of writing three proxy classes, they ask Java for proxies and supply one handler that applies the rule.
card.rule: A dynamic proxy is a class that Java makes at runtime, and its behaviour is supplied by an InvocationHandler you write.
card.limits: The generated proxy holds none of your logic, so everything the proxy should do must live in the handler.

concepts.title: The protection proxy
concepts.question: What is a protection proxy, and which access rules does the matchmaking service need?

paragraphs: A protection proxy controls access to an object based on access rights. With an employee object, it might let an employee call some methods, a manager call more such as setSalary(), and a human resources employee call any method.

In the matchmaking service, PersonBean holds a person's information and a Hot or Not rating that other customers give. Customers must be able to set their own information but not other customers'. Others may set the rating, but not that customer. The getters return nothing private, so any customer may call them.
card.example: A hospital record object: a nurse may read and add notes, a doctor may also change the diagnosis, and a clerk may read only contact details. A protection proxy applies those rights per caller.
card.rule: A protection proxy lets each caller reach only the methods their role allows.
card.limits: The rules concern who is calling and which method, not the values passed; a proxy decides by role.

concepts.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
concepts.title: One bean, two proxies
concepts.question: How many proxies does the matchmaking service need, and which three steps build them?

paragraphs: There are two problems: customers should not change their own Hot or Not rating, and they should not change other customers' personal information. So the authors create two proxies, one for access to your own PersonBean and one for access to another customer's. Java creates the proxies and the developer supplies the handlers.

The steps are: create two InvocationHandlers, write the code that creates the dynamic proxies, and wrap any PersonBean in the appropriate proxy. A customer using their own bean is the owner, and one looking at someone else's is a non-owner.
card.example: A library has members who view their own account and staff who view members' accounts. It builds one proxy kind for self-access and one for other-access, each with its own handler.
card.rule: Make one proxy for the owner and another for the non-owner, and wrap the bean in whichever fits the situation.
card.limits: Which proxy applies depends on who is looking at whom; the same bean may need either one at different moments.

concepts.title: How a handler decides
concepts.question: How does a call on the proxy reach the handler, and how does the handler decide what to do?

paragraphs: When a method is called on the proxy, the proxy forwards it to your invocation handler, but not by calling the handler's matching method. The InvocationHandler interface has one method, invoke(). No matter which method is called on the proxy, invoke() is what gets called on the handler.

Typically invoke() examines the method that was called and decides from its name and possibly its arguments. The non-owner handler allows get methods and setHotOrNotRating, and refuses any other set method by throwing an IllegalAccessException. The handler is not itself a proxy; the proxy dispatches to it.
card.example: A guest handler for a document proxy allows methods whose names start with view and throws IllegalAccessException for methods whose names start with edit.
card.rule: Every call on the proxy arrives at invoke(), which looks at the method name and either passes the call on or refuses it.
card.limits: The handler decides only from what the call reveals, such as method name and arguments; it does not know who the caller is unless it was built with that information.

concepts.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
concepts.title: Creating the proxy
concepts.question: What does Java need to create a proxy for a PersonBean, and why is it called dynamic?

paragraphs: Step two is a method that takes a PersonBean and creates an owner proxy for it. It calls Proxy.newProxyInstance with three things: the class loader of the person's class, the interfaces of the person's class, and a new handler that is given the person. The result is cast to PersonBean.

The non-owner method has the same shape with the non-owner handler. The proxy is dynamic because its class is created at runtime from the set of interfaces you pass; before the code runs there is no proxy class.
card.example: To protect a Thermostat object, a method calls Proxy.newProxyInstance with the thermostat's class loader, its interfaces and a new handler built around it, then casts the result.
card.rule: Proxy.newProxyInstance takes a class loader, the interfaces to implement and a handler, and returns an object you can use as any of those interfaces.
card.limits: Dynamic refers to the class being created at runtime, not to the instance being set up at runtime.

concepts.title: Dynamic proxy fine print
concepts.question: What restrictions apply to the interfaces passed to newProxyInstance, and how can you tell a proxy class?

paragraphs: You can ask whether a class is a proxy class with the static method isProxyClass(), which returns true for a dynamic proxy class. Otherwise a proxy class acts like any other class that implements a given set of interfaces.

newProxyInstance takes an array of interfaces: only interfaces, no classes. All non-public interfaces must be from the same package, and two interfaces cannot have methods with the same signature. There are other minor nuances in the javadoc.
card.example: Two interfaces, Printer and Scanner, both declare void start(). Passing both to newProxyInstance breaks the rule about clashing method names.
card.rule: Pass only interfaces, keep non-public ones in one package, and avoid interfaces with clashing methods.
card.limits: The restrictions listed here are the major ones; the book points to the javadoc for further nuances.

concepts.title: A family still growing
concepts.question: What do the Proxy Zoo and the toolbox suggest about the list of proxies and about its costs?

paragraphs: The authors say that in the wild you will see many mutations of the pattern. Remote, virtual and protection proxies are only the ones studied; the zoo invites readers to add their own observations of other proxies.

The toolbox lists further variants: caching, synchronization, firewall and copy-on-write proxies. It also states a cost: like any wrapper, proxies increase the number of classes and objects in a design. A fair judgement of the pattern names both its range and its price.
card.example: A team puts a proxy in front of every object in its app because proxies are a pattern. The toolbox warns that each wrapper adds classes and objects, so proxies belong where access control is needed.
card.rule: Treat the three named proxies as examples of an open family, and weigh each proxy against the classes and objects it adds.
card.limits: The book states the cost in one line and gives no measure, so claim no more than that proxies add classes and objects.

concepts.title: Patterns working together
concepts.question: How can several patterns live in one design, and what does that look like?

paragraphs: Patterns are not used one at a time in separate boxes. In real designs they show up together: one pattern handles one need, and another handles the next. The more patterns you know, the more often you spot them side by side.

Chapter 12 rebuilds the duck simulator from scratch to show this. Each new request from the people using the simulator is met by a pattern that fits that request, and the earlier patterns keep working.
card.rule: Several patterns can share one design, each solving its own part of the problem.
card.limits: Using many patterns is a means, not a goal. A pattern earns its place only when it answers a real need in the design.
card.example: A transport app needs to read bus data from an old feed (one pattern) and also log every lookup (another pattern). Both patterns sit in the same code, each answering its own need.

concepts.title: Compound pattern or plain combination
concepts.question: What turns a group of patterns used together into a compound pattern?

paragraphs: A compound pattern combines two or more patterns into a solution to a recurring or general problem. The key word is general: the solution must be applicable over many problems, not just the one in front of you.

The duck simulator combines several patterns, but it was built for one scenario. The authors call it a set of patterns working together. Model-View-Controller is their example of a real compound pattern, because the same combination has been used over and over.
card.rule: A compound pattern is a combination of patterns that solves a general, recurring problem.
card.limits: Generality, not size, decides. A combination of six patterns built for one app is not compound, and a pair that answers a widespread problem can be.
card.example: Two teams each wire an adapter and a decorator around a payment gateway, in their own way, for their own app. That is patterns working together. A combination that thousands of apps reuse for the same general problem is a compound pattern.

concepts.title: A common interface for the flock
concepts.question: Why does the rebuilt simulator start with a Quackable interface?

paragraphs: The chapter rebuilds SimUDuck from scratch. This time the ducks implement a Quackable interface, so the simulator knows which things can quack: Mallard Ducks, Redhead Ducks, Duck Calls, and even a Rubber Duck.
The simulator creates a few such ducks and asks each to quack. All implement the same interface, yet each quacks in its own way. Every later pattern in the chapter works through this one shared type.
card.rule: A shared interface lets different things be used alike while each behaves in its own way.
card.limits: A shared interface only covers what it declares. A class with an unrelated method set, like the goose, does not fit until something adapts it.
card.example: A music app defines Playable. Songs, podcasts and radio streams each implement it, and the player calls play() on whatever it is given.

concepts.title: Adapting the goose
concepts.question: How can a goose that only honks join a simulator that expects Quackables?

paragraphs: The simulator expects Quackable. A Goose is not one: geese honk, they do not quack. Yet we want a Goose anywhere a duck can go.

The Adapter Pattern fits. A goose adapter implements Quackable and holds a Goose. When quack() is called on the adapter, it makes the goose honk. Create a Goose, wrap it in the adapter, and the simulator treats it as one more Quackable.
card.rule: An adapter implements the interface the client expects and translates each call into calls on the wrapped object.
card.limits: An adapter changes the shape of the call, not what the wrapped object can do. A goose still honks; it is only reached through quack().
card.example: A calendar app expects objects with an addToCalendar() method. A concert-ticket class offers saveEvent(). A small adapter implements the calendar's method and calls saveEvent() inside.

concepts.title: Counting quacks with a decorator
concepts.question: How can we add quack counting without touching any duck class?

paragraphs: The Quackologists want to know the total number of quacks made by a flock. We should not edit every duck class for that.

The Decorator Pattern adds behavior by wrapping. A QuackCounter implements Quackable and holds another Quackable. When quack() is called, it adds one to a count and then delegates the quack to the Quackable it wraps. The duck code never changes.
card.rule: A decorator wraps an object of the same interface, adds behavior around the call and delegates to the wrapped object.
card.limits: A decorator adds behavior only to the objects it wraps. Any duck created without the wrapper escapes the counting.
card.example: A shop wants to log every call to its price lookup. A logging wrapper implementing the same interface records the call and then passes it on to the real lookup.

concepts.title: You must wrap to get the behavior
concepts.question: What goes wrong when decorated behavior depends on every object being wrapped?

paragraphs: The authors point out a weakness: you have to decorate objects to get decorated behavior. In the simulator, every Quackable has to be wrapped in a QuackCounter at creation. If one is missed, ducks run around making uncounted quacks.
The problem is that the wrapping lives in the code that creates the ducks, scattered wherever ducks are made. Their answer is to take creation and decoration and localize it in one place.
card.rule: When behavior comes from wrapping, make sure the wrapping cannot be forgotten.
card.limits: This weakness matters where objects are created in many places. If one place creates every object, the wrapping can be put there once.
card.example: A shop adds a logging wrapper to each of its payment handlers. A new developer creates a handler directly and forgets the wrapper. That handler's payments are never logged.

concepts.title: A factory that always wraps
concepts.question: How does a factory guarantee that every duck is created already wrapped?

paragraphs: The authors use the Abstract Factory Pattern to produce a family of duck types. An AbstractDuckFactory declares methods that create each kind of duck. A plain DuckFactory creates ducks without decorators; a CountingDuckFactory wraps every duck it creates in a QuackCounter.

The simulator's simulate() method now takes a factory and uses it to create its ducks. Passing a different factory gives a different product family in the same method, so counted ducks come from one place and cannot be missed.
card.rule: Pass a factory into the code that makes objects, and the factory decides which family, wrapped or plain, is produced.
card.limits: A factory protects only objects it creates. Anything created directly with new, as the geese still were, bypasses it.
card.example: A diner app has a SandwichFactory. A PlainFactory returns sandwiches as they are; a PackedFactory returns every sandwich already in a bag. The ordering code takes a factory and never mentions bags.

concepts.title: The geese the factory missed
concepts.question: What gap does the duck factory leave, and how might it be closed?

paragraphs: The authors admit a gap: the simulator still creates geese by calling concrete classes directly. The factory covers ducks, but the adapted geese slip past it.

They ask for an Abstract Factory for geese that handles creating goose ducks, meaning geese already in their adapter. The suggested answers are to add a createGooseDuck() method to the existing duck factories, or to build a separate factory for families of geese.
card.rule: A factory design is complete only if every object that needs its treatment is created through it.
card.limits: Extending a factory with new methods is sensible when the products are one family. A very different family may deserve its own factory.
card.example: A bakery factory builds breads in bags, yet the rolls are still baked by a clerk's own hands and bagged by hand. Adding makeRoll() to the factory closes the gap.

concepts.title: A flock as a composite
concepts.question: How can a whole flock be treated like a single duck?

paragraphs: A ranger asks why ducks are managed one by one. The need is to talk about collections of ducks, and sub-collections for families, and to apply an operation across the whole set. The Composite Pattern lets a collection be treated like a single object.
A Flock implements Quackable and holds a list of Quackables. When quack() is called on the flock, it passes the call to every member. A member can itself be a flock, so flocks can nest.
card.rule: A composite implements the same interface as its parts and passes each call down to its children.
card.limits: The pattern says nothing about order or about who owns the children. Calling a method on a flock affects members only in the way the composite is written to pass it down.
card.example: A playlist implements the same play() as a song, and holds songs or other playlists. Playing a playlist plays each member in turn.

concepts.title: Safety versus transparency
concepts.question: What does a composite gain and lose by keeping add() only on the composite?

paragraphs: In the Composite chapter, menus and menu items shared the same methods, including add(). The benefit was transparency: a client did not need to know whether it held a leaf or a composite.

Here the authors keep child-management methods off the leaf nodes: only Flocks have add(). Nobody can call add() on a Duck, so the design is safer. The cost is lower transparency, because a client must know it holds a Flock to add to it. The authors say there are always trade-offs.
card.rule: Choosing which methods leaves share with composites trades safety against transparency.
card.limits: The authors do not call either choice the right one. The better choice depends on whether mistakes or uniform treatment hurt more in your design.
card.example: A file-system tool lets only Folder have addFile(). A call to addFile() on a plain File is a compile error, so a mistake cannot happen, but the tool must know it holds a Folder.

concepts.title: Letting Quackologists observe
concepts.question: How can the Quackologists be told every time a particular duck quacks?

paragraphs: The Quackologists want to observe individual duck behavior, which is what the Observer Pattern is made for. An Observable is the object being observed. It needs methods for registering observers and for notifying them. The authors leave out a removal method to keep the example short.

Quackable is changed to extend this Observable interface, so every kind of quacker can be watched. A Quackologist implements the Observer interface and registers with the ducks. Then each quack notifies all registered Quackologists.
card.rule: An observable lets observers register, and tells all of them when something happens.
card.limits: Observers learn that a quack happened only if they registered. An unregistered Quackologist hears nothing.
card.example: A shop's stock item can be watched. A purchasing screen registers with it, and each time the stock changes, the item tells every registered screen.

concepts.title: Putting observer code in a helper
concepts.question: How do many Quackable classes become observable without repeating the registration code?

paragraphs: Each Quackable class could implement registration and notification by itself, as in Chapter 2. Instead, the authors encapsulate that code in a helper class called Observable, and each Quackable is composed with an Observable.

The Quackable classes implement QuackObservable but only delegate to the helper. The real code is written once. Because Quackable now extends QuackObservable, every class that implements Quackable must change, including the QuackCounter decorator.
card.rule: Put shared observer code in one helper and have each class delegate to it.
card.limits: Delegating to a helper avoids duplicate code, but every class must still hold and call the helper, and a changed interface forces every implementer to follow.
card.example: A notification service class holds a list of listeners and a notify method. A dozen report classes each hold one and pass register and notify calls to it, instead of keeping twelve copies of the code.

concepts.title: Observing a whole flock
concepts.question: What does it mean to register an observer with a composite flock?

paragraphs: The authors ask what it means for a Quackologist to observe an entire flock. Their reasoning: if you observe a composite, you observe everything in it.

When you register with a flock, the flock makes sure you are registered with all its children, which may include other flocks. Then any quack by any member notifies you. Here two patterns, Composite and Observer, act together on one request.
card.rule: Registering with a composite registers the observer with all its children, nested flocks included.
card.limits: Registration covers the members at the time it is passed down. Members that are created without going through the flock are not covered.
card.example: A school notice board is the composite: it contains class boards. A parent registering with the school board is registered with every class board beneath it.

concepts.title: The pattern nobody mentioned
concepts.question: Where did the Iterator Pattern appear in the simulator without being announced?

paragraphs: The authors admit they snuck a pattern in: Iterator. A flock must apply quack() to each of its members, and it does so by using java.util's iterator over its ArrayList. The Observable helper does the same to notify each observer.
A pattern can therefore be present without being named. Iterator lets code walk a collection without knowing how the collection stores things.
card.rule: A pattern can be at work in a design without being named, and the collection class often provides it.
card.limits: Naming a pattern is useful only when it helps you reason; using a language's own collections does not make a design more clever.
card.example: A to-do app loops over its list of tasks to mark each one done. The loop is an iterator at work, even though the code never mentions the pattern.

concepts.title: The simulator in one pass
concepts.question: Which request in the simulator was answered by which pattern?

paragraphs: The story in one line: a bunch of Quackables; then a goose wants in (Adapter); then quacks should be counted (Decorator); then the decorator must not be forgotten (Abstract Factory); then the flock needs managing (Composite); then Quackologists want notice of each quack (Observer).
Iterator ran underneath Composite and Observer. The theme of the whole: each pattern answered one request, and the patterns cooperated because they shared the Quackable interface.
card.rule: State the unity of a design as a short chain: each need and the pattern that answered it.
card.limits: The chain shows how patterns can fit together, not how to design: the authors say you would not approach a real design this way.
card.example: A delivery app might read: foreign courier feed to fit (Adapter), timing added to every request (Decorator), a factory to ensure timing, route groups (Composite), and watchers told of each delivery (Observer).

concepts.title: Patterns are not the goal
concepts.question: Is applying patterns until a problem is solved a good way to design?

paragraphs: A reader asks if the lesson is to take a problem and apply patterns until a solution appears. The authors answer: wrong. The exercise showed how patterns cooperate; you would never really approach a design this way.

Parts of the simulator may be big-time overkill. Sometimes good OO design principles solve a problem well enough. Apply patterns where and when they make sense, never just for the sake of it. The authors call the simulator forced and artificial, though useful.
card.rule: Use a pattern when the problem calls for it, never in order to use a pattern.
card.limits: This is the authors' opinion, and it does not forbid patterns: where a need recurs, the pattern is often the best answer. The caution is against starting from the pattern.
card.example: A team builds a small tip calculator with a factory, an observer and a decorator, because a talk on patterns inspired them. A plain function would have done the job.

concepts.title: The three roles of MVC
concepts.question: What does each of the model, the view and the controller do in a music player?

paragraphs: Picture an MP3 player. You use its interface to add songs, manage playlists and rename tracks. The player keeps a small database of songs and plays them, and its screen keeps showing the current title and running time. Underneath sits the Model-View-Controller.

The model holds the data, the state and the application logic. The view is your window onto the model. The controller takes your actions, works out what they mean, and manipulates the model. The authors' secret for learning MVC: it is a few patterns put together.
card.rule: The model holds data and logic, the view displays it, and the controller turns user actions into changes to the model.
card.limits: The roles describe responsibilities, not necessarily three separate files. Small programs may place two roles in one class, at the cost of mixing their concerns.
card.example: In a thermostat app, the model holds the target temperature and the heating rules, the view is the dial on the screen, and the controller turns a tap on plus into a call that raises the target.

concepts.title: How an action moves through MVC
concepts.question: In what order do the user, view, controller and model react to a click?

paragraphs: You interact with the view. The view tells the controller what you did. The controller interprets the action and asks the model to change its state. It may also ask the view to change, for instance by enabling or disabling a button.

When the model's state changes, from your action or from inside, such as the next song starting, the model notifies the view. The view then asks the model for the state it displays, such as the new song name.
card.rule: Action flows from view to controller to model, and updates flow from model to view, which then asks for state.
card.limits: This is the classic flow. The authors note that the controller may also observe the model, and in other settings such as the web the update path differs.
card.example: In a banking app: you tap Transfer (view). The controller reads that as a request and tells the account model to move money. The model notifies the view, which asks the model for the new balance and shows it.

concepts.title: Why keep a controller
concepts.question: Why not put the control logic directly inside the view?

paragraphs: A reader asks: if the controller mostly calls a method on the model, why not do that in the view? You could, but the authors give two reasons not to.

First, the view would have two jobs, managing the interface and dealing with the logic of how to control the model. Second, the view would be tightly coupled to the model, so reusing it with another model would be out of the question. The controller separates control logic from the view and decouples the two.
card.rule: A controller keeps the view free of control logic and decoupled from the model.
card.limits: The reasons apply when a view might change or be reused. For a throwaway screen with one fixed model, the extra class may buy little.
card.example: A kitchen display shows orders. If the screen code also decided how a bump button changes order status, you could not reuse the screen for a different ordering system.

concepts.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
concepts.title: MVC is Observer, Strategy and Composite
concepts.question: Which three patterns make up MVC, and which part uses each?

paragraphs: Seen through patterns, MVC is a set of patterns working together. The model uses Observer to keep views and controllers updated about state changes. The controller is the strategy for the view: the behavior of the view, which can be swapped for another controller. The view uses Composite internally, to manage windows, buttons and other display components.
The authors say this is the best way to learn MVC, and the three patterns together decouple the three players.
card.rule: MVC is Observer in the model, Strategy for the controller, and Composite in the view.
card.limits: This is the classic reading. Real systems adapt it, as Model 2 does for the web, and not every framework shows each pattern as plainly.
card.example: In a weather app, the data model tells screens when it changes (Observer), a swappable input handler decides how taps behave (Strategy), and the screen is nested panels and buttons (Composite).

concepts.title: The model as Observer
concepts.question: How does the model keep views updated yet stay unaware of them?

paragraphs: The model notifies its observers when its state changes. It knows only that it has observers to notify, never what they are. This is why the model stays decoupled from views and controllers.

Observers can fetch the changed state themselves (pull), or the model can send the state with the notification (push). The authors note that the Observer chapter lists disadvantages of push. A controller may also register as an observer of the model, for example to enable or disable controls when model state demands it.
card.rule: The model announces changes to registered observers and knows nothing else about them.
card.limits: Pull and push are both possible. Push saves the view a call but ties the notification to what the observers want to know.
card.example: A stock model announces a price change to anything registered. A chart, an alert and a logger each register; the model knows none of their details.

concepts.title: The controller as Strategy
concepts.question: In what sense is the controller a swappable strategy for the view?

paragraphs: The view delegates behavior to a controller through an interface. In the DJ example this is ControllerInterface, which any controller plugged into the view must implement. The controller is the behavior of the view and can be exchanged for another to get different behavior.

The view concerns itself with presentation only, and the controller translates user input into actions on the model. Because the view talks to the interface, nothing in the view changes when the controller does.
card.rule: The view holds a controller through an interface, so swapping the controller swaps the view's behavior.
card.limits: A controller can only be swapped for another that fits the interface. A controller written for a different set of calls cannot be dropped in unchanged.
card.example: A text field passes keystrokes to an InputHandler interface. A strict handler rejects letters, a lenient one allows them. The field itself never changes.

concepts.title: The view as Composite
concepts.question: Where does the Composite Pattern sit in the view of an MVC program?

paragraphs: The view is made of nested display components: windows hold panels, panels hold buttons and labels. The view uses Composite to manage this, so asking a container to display itself makes it ask its members to do the same.

Today's GUI packages such as Swing hide this structure, and a browser turning markup into an interface hides it more. In the early days of MVC, building GUIs needed far more manual work, and the pattern was more obviously present.
card.rule: The view is a tree of nested components that are treated alike, which is the Composite Pattern.
card.limits: Composite is easy to miss because GUI libraries manage it for you. Not seeing it in your own code does not mean it is absent.
card.example: A form is a window containing panels, which contain labels and text boxes. Closing the window or redrawing it passes the call down through every level.

concepts.title: The BeatModel
concepts.question: What does the BeatModel hold, expose and leave out?

paragraphs: The BeatModel manages the beat. It holds the current beats per minute and the code that generates MIDI events for the sound. It exposes an interface through which the controller can manipulate the beat and the view and controller can read its state.

Because the model uses Observer, it also offers methods to register observers and to send notifications. It makes no assumptions about the view. A lightshow driven by the beat, or a text view naming the music genre from the BPM, could use the same notifications.
card.rule: A model holds state and logic, offers an interface to change and read them, and lets observers register.
card.limits: A model shaped this way serves many views, but its interface is also the only door in; whatever the view needs must be offered there.
card.example: A thermostat model holds target and current temperature and the heating logic, offers set and get calls, and lets screens register. It does not know whether a dial or a phone app watches.

concepts.title: The DJ view
concepts.question: How is the DJ view built, and what does it do with the model and controller?

paragraphs: The DJ view appears in two windows: one shows the current BPM and the beat pulse, and the other holds the controls, a text field and buttons. They are two parts of one class, DJView, split to show that the display of the model differs from the controls.

The view registers as an observer of the model, and uses the model's interface to read the BPM when notified. When you use a control, the view tells the controller what to do, and the controller tells the model. The view does not alter the model itself.
card.rule: The view displays what it learns from the model and reports user actions to the controller.
card.limits: Splitting the display and the controls into two windows is a teaching choice. Both live in one class, which shows that the roles are about responsibility, not about files.
card.example: A music app's now-playing panel shows the current track and hears model notifications. Its transport buttons just report the press to the controller.

concepts.title: The DJ controller
concepts.question: What does the BeatController do between the view and the model?

paragraphs: The controller sits between the view and the model. It takes input such as Start from the DJ Control menu and turns it into an action on the model. It also adjusts the view: after Start, it disables the Start item and enables Stop, and after Stop it does the reverse.
The controller holds no application logic. It implements behavior for the view and may work out which model calls to make, but the code that manages and manipulates the data lives in the model.
card.rule: The controller translates view actions into model calls and adjusts the controls, but keeps no application logic.
card.limits: The line between interpreting input and application logic can blur. The authors say a little work to choose the model calls is not application logic.
card.example: In a music app, pressing Play makes the controller call the player's start, then grey out the Play button. How playback works is the model's affair.

concepts.section: And now for a test run...
concepts.title: Tracing a change through the DJ tool
concepts.question: When the BPM is changed, which parts react and in what order?

paragraphs: In the test run, you change the BPM with the text entry and the increase and decrease buttons. The view display follows, even though it has no logical link to the controls. Observing the model is what keeps it current.

The beat bar also keeps up with the beat because it is an observer of the model. Start and Stop show the controller at work: it disables Start afterwards and, after Stop, disables Stop and enables Start. The path: control, controller, model, notification, view.
card.rule: To trace any change, follow it from control to controller to model to notification to view.
card.limits: Tracing works when the model is the single source of state. If a view kept its own copy of state, the trace would break.
card.example: In a thermostat app, pressing + calls the controller, the controller raises the model's target, the model notifies, and the display asks for the new target.

concepts.title: Adapting a model to an existing view
concepts.question: How can the DJ view be reused with a heart monitor that has a different interface?

paragraphs: The DJ view displays a beat rate and a pulse, much like a heartbeat. A HeartModel offers getHeartRate() where the view calls getBPM(), so the view cannot use it as it stands.

The authors adapt the HeartModel to the BeatModel interface with an adapter, a common technique with MVC: use an adapter to fit a model to existing controllers and views. The adapter's getBPM() calls getHeartRate(), and the view needs no change.
card.rule: Adapt the new model to the interface the existing view and controller expect.
card.limits: An adapter only translates. Where the new model cannot do what the old one did, such as set a heart rate, the adapter has nothing real to call.
card.example: A chart widget calls getValue(). A new sensor offers readNow(). A small class implementing getValue() and calling readNow() lets the old chart show the new sensor.

concepts.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
concepts.title: A controller for the heart
concepts.question: What does reusing the view with a HeartController show, and what does it leave unfinished?

paragraphs: With the HeartAdapter in hand, a HeartController is plugged into the same view. The view shows the heart rate and the beat bar looks like a pulse, because the HeartModel also supports BPM and beat observers. The adapter translates getBPM() calls into getHeartRate() calls.

The controller disables Start and Stop. The other buttons still appear and work, but have no effect, since the controller implements no-ops for them. The authors note the view could be changed to support disabling those items.
card.rule: A swapped-in controller can reuse a view fully, though controls it ignores remain visible.
card.limits: Reuse worked, but the result is not finished. The view still offers controls that do nothing, which the authors suggest fixing in the view.
card.example: A music app's view is reused with a read-only radio stream. The stream controller turns off Play and Pause, but the seek buttons stay on screen and do nothing.

concepts.title: Model 2: MVC on the web
concepts.question: How do a browser, a servlet and a JSP split the roles of MVC?

paragraphs: Soon after the Web appeared, developers adapted MVC to the browser and server model. The usual adaptation is called Model 2, which uses servlets and JSP technology. A browser sends an HTTP request, and a servlet receives and parses it. The servlet plays the controller and works on the model, usually a database.

The result is bundled into a JavaBean. The controller then forwards control to the view, a JSP, which generates the page showing the model's state and the controls for further actions. The page returns to the browser over HTTP.
card.rule: In Model 2, the servlet is the controller, the model is usually a database, and the JSP is the view.
card.limits: Model 2 fits the request and response style of the web. It differs from the desktop flow, where the model notifies the view at any time.
card.example: A user submits a login form. A servlet checks the account store, packs the result into a bean, and passes it to a page template that renders either a welcome or an error.

concepts.title: Why Model 2 helped web teams
concepts.question: What did Model 2 give web teams beyond a clean design?

paragraphs: The authors say Model 2 saved many web shops from sinking into chaos. It separates not only the components of a design but also production responsibilities. In the old days, anyone with access to the JSPs could write any Java code they liked, including people who knew HTML but not software.
With Model 2, developers who know servlets keep the controller work, and web producers are let loose on simple JSPs, where they have access only to HTML and simple JavaBeans.
card.rule: Separating model, view and controller also separates who works on what.
card.limits: The benefit is the authors' own account of the web shops of that time. It depends on view files being kept simple enough for non-programmers.
card.example: A company splits its site so engineers own the request handlers and designers own the page templates. Designers cannot break the handlers, and engineers do not fiddle with page text.

concepts.title: Reusing the model unchanged on the web
concepts.question: Why did the BeatModel need no change to move to the web?

paragraphs: In MVC the model knows nothing about views or controllers: it is totally decoupled. All it knows is that it may have observers to notify. It exposes an interface through which views and controllers get and set its state.

Because the BeatModel depends on no outside classes, no work was needed to use it on the web. The servlet controller translates HTTP input into model actions and passes control to a JSP view. The view uses the model's state and does not alter it, as in desktop MVC.
card.rule: A model that depends on no view or controller can be reused unchanged in a new setting.
card.limits: Reuse without change holds only while the model really has no dependencies on the old setting. One hidden reference to a screen class would break it.
card.example: A scoring model used by a phone app is also called by a web handler, with no change, since it knows nothing about screens or requests.

concepts.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
concepts.title: Where the patterns went in Model 2
concepts.question: Are Observer, Strategy and Composite still present in Model 2?

paragraphs: Model 2 does not look exactly like textbook MVC, but all the parts are still there, adapted to the browser model. The view no longer registers with the model, yet it receives the equivalent of notifications indirectly, when the controller passes it a bean. On the web, state is only needed when a response page is made.

The servlet is still the strategy, but it is not composed directly with the view; it still provides the view's behavior and could be swapped. The view is a nested set of components built by the browser from HTML, most likely a composite.
card.rule: Model 2 keeps all three patterns, adapted: indirect notification, a swappable servlet, and a browser-built composite.
card.limits: Model 2 departs from the classic form, so the patterns are less visible. The idea of the role remains, even when the original wiring is gone.
card.example: A site's page is only rebuilt when a request comes in. There is no point telling an already delivered page about model changes.

concepts.title: What MVC buys, and where it is loose
concepts.question: What does MVC achieve, and where do the authors admit it is looser than it looks?

paragraphs: The three patterns together decouple the model, view and controller, which keeps designs clear and flexible. The Adapter Pattern can fit a new model to an existing view and controller, and Model 2 adapts MVC to the web.

The authors also note loose ends. Some say the controller is a mediator, but the view reads the model's state directly, so it is not a pure mediator. In the DJ code the view has access to every model method, though it should not change the model. Giving it a narrower interface is a job for a pattern.
card.rule: MVC decouples its three parts, but judge a design by what each part can actually reach.
card.limits: These loose ends are the authors' own admissions in a simplified example. They do not make MVC unsound; they show where a real design should tighten.
card.example: A screen can read a stock model, yet it is also handed methods that set prices. A narrow read-only face on the model would remove the risk.

concepts.title: Context: the recurring situation
concepts.question: In the definition of a design pattern, what is the context and what must be true of it?

paragraphs: The book defines a pattern in one sentence: a pattern is a solution to a problem in a context. It then takes the three parts one at a time, starting with the context.

The context is the situation in which the pattern applies, and it should be a recurring situation. The book's example of a context is having a collection of objects. A context only sets the scene: it does not yet say what goes wrong or what to do about it.
card.example: A hospital ward changes shifts every eight hours, every day. That repeating situation is a context. Trouble at the handover would be the problem, and a handover routine the solution.
card.rule: Name the recurring situation first, because the context is where the pattern applies.
card.limits: A context is only a setting. Describing it tells you nothing about what to do, and a situation that will not come back is a poor context for a pattern.

concepts.title: Problem: goal plus constraints, called forces
concepts.question: What two things make up the problem part of a pattern, and what do pattern writers call them?

paragraphs: The problem is the goal you are trying to reach in the context, together with any constraints that occur there. The book's example: you need to step through a collection of objects without exposing how the collection is stored. Stepping through is the goal; keeping the storage hidden is the constraint.

Pattern writers call goals and constraints the forces, because they shape and control the solution. The goal is the light side and the constraints are the dark side. A pattern is useful only when its solution balances both sides.
card.example: A city wants buses to reach the airport fast (goal). The route may not cross the old town and the budget is fixed (constraints). A plan must satisfy all three to be useful.
card.rule: A problem is a goal plus its constraints, and a useful solution balances both.
card.limits: Reaching the goal while ignoring a constraint is not a solution. The term is lingo, though, and the book says not to let the word get in your way.

concepts.title: Solution: a general design anyone can apply
concepts.question: What kind of thing is the solution part of a pattern, and how does the book's collection example show it?

paragraphs: The solution is what you are after: a general design that anyone can apply, which resolves the goal and the set of constraints. In the book's collection example the solution is to encapsulate the iteration into a separate class.
Notice the word general. The solution is a design, a way of arranging things, and not the code of one program. That is why other developers can take it and use it on their own collection.
card.example: A shop wants every cashier to handle returns the same way, yet each branch has its own forms. A written routine of steps, who does what and when, resolves both and any branch can use it.
card.rule: A pattern's solution is a general design that resolves the goal and constraints.
card.limits: A solution that only fits one program is not a general design. A design that resolves the goal but breaks a constraint does not count as the solution either.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Why the car-window fix is not a pattern
concepts.question: A description has a context, a problem and a working solution. Why might it still fail to be a pattern?

paragraphs: The book tests its definition on an example. The problem is getting to work on time. The context is that your keys are locked in the car. The solution is to break the window, get in, start the engine and drive. All three parts are there, and the solution works. Yet the book says this is not a pattern.

The first reason is recurrence. A pattern must apply to a recurring problem, and breaking a window is not a solution you can apply over and over, once cost is balanced against the goal. Having all three parts is necessary but not enough.
card.example: A conference venue floods. The organiser rents boats to ferry guests in. It works, and there is a context, a problem and a solution, but nobody can apply it over and over.
card.rule: Before calling something a pattern, check that its solution can be applied again and again, not only that context, problem and solution are present.
card.limits: Recurrence is one test among several; the next idea adds two more. A problem that happens often is also not enough if the solution is too costly to repeat.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: A pattern needs a name and a transferable description
concepts.question: Besides recurrence, what two further weaknesses does the book find in the car-window description?

paragraphs: The book finds two more faults in the car example. First, you cannot easily take the description, hand it to someone and have them apply it to their own unique problem. Second, it has no name, and without a name it cannot become part of a vocabulary shared with other developers.

So a pattern's description must be usable by people who did not write it, and the pattern needs a name. The book adds that real pattern descriptions are more revealing than a bare problem, context and solution.
card.example: A recipe card that says ask Sam how she fixes the sauce fails both ways. Nobody else can follow it, and it has no name that other cooks can use.
card.rule: Give a pattern a name and describe it so that someone else can apply it to their own problem.
card.limits: A name alone does not make something a pattern, since recurrence and a general solution are still needed. A name also helps only as far as other developers share it.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Patterns are guidelines you may adapt
concepts.question: May you change a pattern's structure to fit your design, and what should you do when you do?

paragraphs: The book says you can alter a pattern. Like design principles, patterns are not meant to be laws or rules. They are guidelines that you can change to fit your needs.
When you adapt a pattern, it never hurts to document how yours differs from the classic design. Then other developers can quickly recognise the patterns you are using and see where yours departs.
card.example: A team drops one class from a well-known design because their app has no need for it. They note in a comment which class was dropped and why.
card.rule: Treat a pattern as a guideline you may adapt, and write down how your version differs from the classic one.
card.limits: Adapting is allowed, but undocumented changes leave the next developer unable to tell which pattern is in use or how it differs.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: How a catalog entry is laid out
concepts.question: Which sections does a pattern catalog entry have, and which question does each answer?

paragraphs: A patterns catalog takes a set of patterns and describes each one in detail, along with its relationship to the other patterns. Every pattern follows the same template, so you know where to look.

The book names these parts: a name; an Intent (what the pattern is, like a definition); Motivation and Applicability (when and where to use it); Structure and Participants (the class design, the classes and their roles); Implementation and sample code; uses in real systems; relations to other patterns; and Consequences, good and bad.
card.rule: Match your question to the section: intent says what, motivation and applicability say when, structure and participants say how, consequences say what it costs.
card.limits: The entry describes the classic design; your adapted version may differ. Catalog entries are also richer than the bare problem, context and solution definition, but they do not replace judgment about your own case.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Working through a catalog entry
concepts.question: In what order does the book's patterns user check a catalog entry before building the pattern into a design?

paragraphs: In the book's dialogue, Jim first gets familiar with all the patterns and their relationships. When a need arises, he returns to Motivation and Applicability to check that he has the right pattern, then reviews Consequences for unintended effects on his design.
Only then does he read Structure and Participants, work the pattern into his design with any alterations needed, and review Implementation and sample code for techniques and gotchas.
card.rule: Confirm the fit and the consequences first, then study structure and participants, then adapt and read the implementation notes.
card.limits: This is one practitioner's routine, not a rule of the catalog. The fixed points are to confirm the fit before adopting and to adapt the structure to your own design.

concepts.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition
concepts.title: Fundamental and domain-specific catalogs
concepts.question: What kinds of patterns catalogs exist, and how big is the classic one?

paragraphs: There is more than one patterns catalog. Some catalogs cover fundamental design patterns. Others cover domain-specific patterns, such as EJB patterns.
The classic fundamental catalog is Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, known as GoF. It lays out 23 fundamental patterns.
card.rule: Pick a catalog by its scope: the GoF catalog for the 23 fundamental patterns, a domain catalog for the patterns of one area.
card.limits: A catalog's scope is also its limit. A fundamental catalog does not cover the specific recurring problems of a domain, and a domain catalog does not teach the fundamentals.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Patterns are discovered, not created
concepts.question: Where do patterns come from, and who can write one?

paragraphs: The book says patterns are discovered, not created. Anyone can discover a design pattern and write its description. But it is not easy, it does not happen quickly, and it does not happen often. Being a patterns writer takes commitment.
The majority of people do not write patterns; they only use them. So the question to ask first is why you would want to write one.
card.rule: See a pattern as something found in recurring practice, and write one only if you are ready to commit.
card.limits: Finding a solution you like is not the same as having found a pattern. It still has to recur and to pass the tests the next ideas describe.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: The Rule of Three
concepts.question: When does the book say a candidate has earned the right to be called a pattern?

paragraphs: The book answers the question of when you really have a pattern: not until others have used it and found it to work. In general, a candidate must pass the Rule of Three.
The rule says a pattern can be called a pattern only if it has been applied in a real-world solution at least three times. The authors repeat it as a reminder in the advice to would-be writers.
card.rule: Call a candidate a pattern only after it has been applied in real-world solutions at least three times.
card.limits: The phrase in general marks it as a rule of thumb. Three uses is a minimum, not a proof, and the uses must be real-world solutions in which the pattern worked.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Study first, then reflect
concepts.question: What two things does the book tell a would-be patterns writer to do before writing anything down?

paragraphs: Do your homework. You need to be well versed in the existing patterns before you create a new one. Most patterns that appear new are in fact variants of existing patterns. Studying patterns makes you better at recognising them and at relating them to each other, and it keeps you from reinventing the wheel.
Then take time to reflect. Your experience, the problems you met and the solutions you used, is where ideas for patterns are born. Comb it for designs that recur.
card.rule: Study the existing patterns first, and expect most apparently new patterns to be variants of known ones.
card.limits: Most is not all: variants are far more common than new patterns, but new ones can appear. A find that does recur can also be too narrow to qualify as a real pattern.

concepts.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer
concepts.title: Write it down, let others try it, refine
concepts.question: How does the book say a pattern candidate should be written up and improved?

paragraphs: Get your ideas on paper in a way others can understand; a find is of little use if others cannot apply it. You do not need to invent a way to document it, because the GoF template already shows how to describe patterns.

Then have others try your pattern and refine it, and refine some more. Think of it as a work in progress. Let other developers review it, try it and give feedback, and use that feedback to improve the description.
card.rule: Write the candidate in an established template, let others try it, and refine it until they can read and apply it.
card.limits: The description will never be perfect; it needs to be solid enough for others to understand. Refining does not replace the Rule of Three, which still decides whether it counts as a pattern.

concepts.title: Why patterns are put into categories
concepts.question: Why do catalogs partition patterns into categories, and what does a reader gain?

paragraphs: As the number of discovered patterns grows, it makes sense to partition them into classifications. The book gives three reasons: to organise them, to narrow your search to a subset of all patterns, and to make comparisons within a group of patterns.

The book's Master adds a general point. Whenever we have a large collection of anything, we naturally find categories to put the items in, and this lets us think about the items at a more abstract level.
card.rule: Group a large collection into categories so that you can organise it, narrow a search and compare like with like.
card.limits: A classification is a tool. The book says the most important thing is to know the patterns and the relationships among them, and to use categories when they help.

concepts.title: Creational, structural and behavioral
concepts.question: Which three-way classification does the best-known scheme use, and what is it based on?

paragraphs: The best-known scheme, used by the first patterns catalog, partitions patterns into three categories based on their purpose: Creational, Behavioral and Structural.

The book describes two of them. Structural patterns describe how classes and objects are composed to create new structures or new functionality. Behavioral patterns are concerned with the communication and interconnection between objects.
card.rule: Classify a pattern by its purpose into creational, structural or behavioral.
card.limits: Many patterns seem to fit more than one category, and the book says everyone has trouble placing them. The scheme is a convenience, not a law.

concepts.title: Why Decorator is structural: look at intent
concepts.question: Decorator adds behavior, so why is it a structural pattern, and what is the key to placing a pattern?

paragraphs: Many developers say Decorator should be behavioral, since it adds behavior. The Gang of Four's thinking is that structural patterns describe how classes and objects are composed to create new structures or new functionality.

Decorator composes objects by wrapping one object in another to provide new functionality. Its focus is how objects are composed dynamically, not the communication and interconnection between objects, which is the aim of behavioral patterns. The intent of a pattern is often the key to its category.
card.rule: Decide a pattern's category from what its intent is about, not from whether its effect adds behavior.
card.limits: Intent usually settles the matter, but not always cleanly. Many people stay confused by the three categories, and a reasonable reader may disagree with a placement.

concepts.title: Other ways to classify patterns
concepts.question: Besides purpose, what other ways of classifying patterns does the book mention?

paragraphs: Patterns are often classified by a second attribute: whether the pattern deals with classes or with objects. This is separate from the three purpose categories.

The book also says these are not the only schemes. Others start with the three categories and add subcategories, such as Decoupling Patterns. You should know the most common schemes, and you are free to create your own if it helps you understand the patterns.
card.rule: Know the common schemes, and make your own grouping if it helps you understand the patterns.
card.limits: A private scheme helps your own understanding. When you talk with others, the common schemes are the shared vocabulary.

concepts.title: Looking past the categories
concepts.question: What further use of categories does the Master name, and how fixed is the number three?

paragraphs: Beyond talking about groups and comparing members, the Master names one more use: categories help us launch into new territory, the way a carmaker might aim at a sports car with a high-end performance for an economy price.

As for the number, the Master says three is a convenient number that many people find makes a nice grouping. Others have suggested four, five or more, so there are as many categories as you want to see.
card.rule: Use categories to reason about groups, and treat the number of categories as a convenience.
card.limits: Categories help you compare and explore, but many people are confused by them. The book says the most important thing is to know the patterns and their relationships.

concepts.title: Thinking in patterns takes practice
concepts.question: What does it mean to think in patterns, and why is knowing the theory not enough?

paragraphs: Contexts, constraints, forces, catalogs and classifications sound academic, the book admits. That knowledge is important, but if you understand it without experience and practice in using patterns, it will not make much difference in your life.
Thinking in patterns means being able to look at a design and see where patterns naturally fit and where they do not.
card.rule: Practise seeing where patterns fit and where they do not, because knowing the theory alone changes little.
card.limits: The theory is still worth having: the book says knowledge is power. Practice is what turns that knowledge into the skill of judging a design.

concepts.title: Keep it simple
concepts.question: What should your goal be when you design, and does that rule out patterns?

paragraphs: When you design, solve things in the simplest way possible. Your goal should be simplicity, not how to apply a pattern to the problem. The book abbreviates this as KISS, keep it simple.
That said, sometimes the best way to keep a design simple and flexible is to use a pattern. Simplicity does not forbid patterns; it makes them answer to the need.
card.rule: Aim for the simplest design that does the job, and use a pattern only when it is the simplest way to meet the need.
card.limits: Simplicity is not a ban on patterns. The book says the best way to keep a design both simple and flexible is sometimes a pattern.

concepts.title: Patterns are not a magic bullet
concepts.question: A pattern is well tested by many developers. Why must you still think about the rest of your design?

paragraphs: Patterns are general solutions to recurring problems, and they are well tested by lots of developers. When you see a need for one, you can sleep well knowing many developers have been there before and solved the problem with similar techniques.
But patterns are not a magic bullet. You cannot plug one in, compile and take an early lunch. To use patterns you must also think through the consequences for the rest of your design.
card.rule: Treat a pattern as a tested tool, and still think through its consequences for the rest of your design.
card.limits: A track record lowers the risk in the solution idea. It does not tell you how the pattern will affect your particular design.

concepts.section: You know you need a pattern when...
concepts.title: How to know you need a pattern
concepts.question: In what order should you decide whether, and which, pattern to use?

paragraphs: Introduce a pattern when you are sure it addresses a problem in your design. First give a simpler solution a chance. Once you are sure a simple solution will not meet your needs, consider the problem together with the constraints it must operate under; these help match it to a pattern.

If you know patterns well, you may know a good match. Otherwise survey patterns that might solve it; the intent and applicability sections of catalogs help. Then make sure the consequences are ones you can live with, and study the effect on the rest of the design. If all looks good, go for it.
card.rule: Rule out a simpler solution first, then match your problem and constraints to a pattern, and check its consequences before adopting it.
card.limits: The sequence has one stated exception: when you expect parts of your system to vary, a pattern can be right even if a simpler solution would work.

concepts.section: You know you need a pattern when...
concepts.title: The exception: expected variation
concepts.question: When does the book say to use a pattern even if a simpler solution would work?

paragraphs: There is one situation in which you will want a pattern even if a simpler solution would work: when you expect aspects of your system to vary. Identifying areas of change in your design is usually a sign that a pattern is needed.
The condition is that the change is practical: likely to happen. Add patterns for practical change that is likely, not for hypothetical change that may happen.
card.rule: Use a pattern despite a simpler option only when you expect part of the system to vary in practice.
card.limits: Change that is likely justifies a pattern; change that merely may happen does not. The next ideas say what that restraint is for.

concepts.title: Refactoring time is patterns time
concepts.question: What is refactoring, and why is it a good moment to consider patterns?

paragraphs: Refactoring is the process of making changes to your code to improve the way it is organized. Its goal is to improve the structure, not to change the behavior.

It is a great time to re-examine the design to see whether patterns could organize it better. The book gives two signs: code full of conditional statements might signal the need for State, and concrete dependencies might be cleaned up with a Factory.
card.rule: Use refactoring as a moment to ask whether a pattern would organize the code better, without changing what the code does.
card.limits: Entire books cover refactoring with patterns; the two signs here are a start. The signs suggest a pattern; they do not prove one is needed.

concepts.title: Taking a pattern out
concepts.question: When does the book say you should remove a pattern from a design?

paragraphs: No one ever talks about when to remove a pattern, as if it were blasphemy. The book says we are all adults and can take it: do not be afraid to remove a pattern from your design.
Remove one when your system has become complex and the flexibility you planned for is not needed. In other words, remove it when a simpler solution without the pattern would be better.
card.rule: Remove a pattern when the flexibility it was added for is not needed and a simpler solution would be better.
card.limits: Removal is for flexibility that is unused. A pattern that is still handling real change is earning its place.

concepts.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.
concepts.title: If you do not need it now, do not do it now
concepts.question: Why does the book tell developers to resist building patterns for changes that are only hypothetical?

paragraphs: Patterns are powerful, and it is easy to see ways to use them everywhere. Developers naturally love to create beautiful architectures that are ready to take on change from any direction. The book's advice is: resist the temptation.

If you have a practical need to support change today, go ahead and use a pattern. If the reason is only hypothetical, do not add the pattern. It will only add complexity to your system, and you might never need it.
card.rule: Add a pattern for a change you need to support now, and not for a reason that is only hypothetical.
card.limits: The Master also allows a pattern when you are quite sure it is needed to deal with a future change in requirements. Being sure is the standard, not hoping.

concepts.section: If you don’t need it now, don’t do it now.
concepts.title: Start from principles; let patterns emerge
concepts.question: What does the Master advise about where a design should start, and why still learn patterns?

paragraphs: In the Master's words, use your big guns only when you have to. Patterns are a tool, and should be used when needed. Start from your principles and create the simplest code that does the job. If you see the need for a pattern emerge, use it.

Do not make building from patterns your goal at the start of a design. Introduce a pattern when you are sure it is necessary to solve a problem, or quite sure it is needed for a future change in requirements.
card.rule: Start from design principles and the simplest code that works, and let a pattern emerge when the need appears.
card.limits: Emerge does not mean avoid. Patterns remain proven experience and a shared vocabulary; the point is that need, not enthusiasm, should bring them in.

concepts.title: The beginner and the intermediate mind
concepts.question: What does a beginner believe about patterns, and how does an intermediate designer's view differ?

paragraphs: The beginner uses patterns everywhere. This is good, because the beginner gets lots of experience and practice. The beginner also thinks the more patterns used, the better the design. The beginner will learn this is not so: designs should be as simple as possible, and patterns should be used only where needed for practical extensibility.

The intermediate mind starts to see where patterns are needed and where not. It still tries to fit too many square patterns into round holes, but begins to see that patterns can be adapted where the classic design does not fit.
card.rule: Notice the belief that more patterns make a better design, and test it against the need for each pattern.
card.limits: The stages describe attitudes. The book calls the beginner's use of patterns everywhere good practice, even though the belief behind it is wrong.

concepts.title: The Zen mind
concepts.question: How does the Zen mind approach patterns, compared with the beginner and the intermediate?

paragraphs: The Zen mind sees patterns where they fit naturally. It is not obsessed with using them; it looks for simple solutions that best solve the problem. It thinks in terms of the object principles and their trade-offs.
When a need for a pattern arises, the Zen mind applies it, knowing it may need adaptation. The book's sample thought for this mind is: this is a natural place for Decorator.
card.rule: Aim for the Zen mind: apply a pattern where it fits, adapted if needed, with simplicity and principles first.
card.limits: The stages describe attitudes to grow toward. Knowing many patterns does not bring the Zen mind by itself, and the Zen mind is not the same as using patterns less.

concepts.title: Weighing a pattern's costs and benefits
concepts.question: What are the costs of using a pattern, what are its benefits, and what should you do when a principle gives a simpler answer?

paragraphs: Overuse of patterns can lead to code that is over-engineered. Patterns often add classes and objects, so they can increase complexity. They can also add layers to a design, which adds complexity and inefficiency. Sometimes a pattern is overkill.

Many times you can fall back on design principles and find a much simpler solution. If that happens, do not fight it. When a pattern is the right tool, the advantages are many: it is time-tested, well documented and recognised by other developers.
card.rule: Weigh a pattern's costs against its benefits, and prefer the simpler principle-based solution when it does the job.
card.limits: Costs are not a reason to avoid patterns. When the pattern is the right tool, the book says the advantages are many.

concepts.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary
