concepts.title: The power of a shared vocabulary
concepts.question: Besides storing solutions, what is one of the biggest benefits of patterns, and what does it need from other people?

paragraphs: Patterns do not only load your brain with solutions; they also give you a shared vocabulary with other developers. The book calls this one of the biggest benefits of design patterns.

You now have a vocabulary of your own and a full set of OO principles from which to understand the motivation and workings of any new pattern. When your fellow developers also know patterns and use the shared vocabulary, it leads to better designs, better communication and saved time.
card.rule: Use patterns as a shared vocabulary as well as stored solutions, since it improves design, communication and time.
card.limits: A vocabulary works only when the other person shares it. A pattern name used with someone who does not know it communicates nothing.

concepts.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary
concepts.title: Five ways to share your vocabulary
concepts.question: In which five places does the book suggest using the pattern vocabulary?

paragraphs: The book lists five ways to share the vocabulary: in design meetings, with other developers, in architecture documentation, in code comments and naming conventions, and to groups of interested developers, for example in a brown-bag lunch talk or at a local user group.

In meetings, patterns help you stay in the design longer. In documentation they reduce how much you need to write. In code, comments should identify the patterns you use, and names should reveal the pattern underneath.
card.rule: Use pattern names in meetings, conversations, documentation, code names and comments, and talks.
card.limits: Names and comments help only if they are accurate. Identify the patterns you really use, and do not label code with a pattern it does not follow.

concepts.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four
concepts.title: The Gang of Four and their book
concepts.question: Who are the Gang of Four, and what is their place in the field?

paragraphs: The GoF, or Gang of Four, are Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, the group who put together the first patterns catalog and started a whole movement in the software field. No one knows for sure how they got the name.

Their book, Design Patterns, released in 1995, kicked off the field and is the basis for the patterns used in Head First Design Patterns. The field has grown a great deal since, so it is the first and most definitive text, not the last word.
card.rule: Know the GoF as the authors of the first patterns catalog, whose 1995 book is the starting point for the field.
card.limits: It is the first and most definitive catalog, not the last word. Many patterns and catalogs have appeared since.

concepts.title: Where patterns began, and where to go next
concepts.question: Where did the idea of patterns start, and where can you keep learning about them?

paragraphs: Patterns did not start with the GoF. They started with Christopher Alexander, a professor of architecture at Berkeley, an architect and not a computer scientist, who invented patterns for building living architectures such as houses, towns and cities. His books, The Timeless Way of Building and A Pattern Language, show direct analogies between creating living architecture and flexible, extensible software.
The community has resources: the Portland Patterns Repository, a wiki run by Ward Cunningham where anyone can take part, the Hillside Group site, and conferences such as PLoP and OOPSLA.
card.rule: Look to Alexander's architecture patterns for the origin of the idea, and to the community for places to keep learning.
card.limits: The analogy between buildings and software is the book's to draw. Alexander's patterns are about buildings, so software patterns borrow the idea, not the content.

concepts.title: The Patterns Zoo
concepts.question: Which domains does the book show patterns being used in, besides object-oriented design?

paragraphs: The patterns concept applies in many domains. The book's zoo shows a few. Architectural patterns create living architecture in buildings, towns and cities, where patterns began. Application patterns concern system-level architecture, such as many multi-tier architectures; MVC has been known to pass for one. Domain-specific patterns concern specific domains, like concurrent or real-time systems.

Business process patterns describe interactions between businesses, customers and data, for example making and communicating decisions. Organizational patterns describe the structures and practices of human organizations. User interface patterns address how to design interactive software.
card.rule: Match a recurring problem to its pattern domain: buildings, system architecture, a specific field, business processes, organizations or user interfaces.
card.limits: The zoo shows a few domains, not all. These domains also differ from the creational, structural and behavioral categories, which classify object-oriented design patterns by purpose.

concepts.title: Anti-patterns: documenting bad solutions
concepts.question: What is an anti-pattern, and why would anyone document a bad solution?

paragraphs: If a design pattern gives a general solution to a recurring problem in a particular context, an anti-pattern tells you how to go from a problem to a bad solution. An anti-pattern always looks like a good solution but turns out bad when applied.

Why document bad solutions? If a bad solution recurs for a common problem, documenting it prevents others from making the same mistake. Avoiding bad solutions can be as valuable as finding good ones. There are development, OO, organizational and domain-specific anti-patterns.
card.rule: Treat an anti-pattern as a documented, recurring, attractive bad solution, kept so that others can avoid it.
card.limits: An anti-pattern is not any mistake. It is a recurring bad solution to a common problem that looks good up front.

concepts.title: What an anti-pattern tells you
concepts.question: Besides naming the bad solution, what three things does a useful anti-pattern tell you?

paragraphs: An anti-pattern does three jobs. It tells you why the bad solution is attractive. No one would choose a bad solution if nothing about it seemed attractive up front, so it must warn you of the seductive aspect.
It tells you why the solution is bad in the long term, that is, where you will get into trouble. And it suggests other patterns that may give good solutions, so it points you in the right direction.
card.rule: A useful anti-pattern explains why the bad solution tempts, why it fails later, and which patterns to use instead.
card.limits: Knowing the temptation does not remove it, because the bad solution looks good up front. A warning without a way forward would be incomplete.

concepts.title: The Golden Hammer
concepts.question: How does the Golden Hammer anti-pattern work, and what does the book suggest as a cure?

paragraphs: The book's example anti-pattern is Golden Hammer. The problem: you must choose technologies and you believe exactly one technology must dominate the architecture. The context: new software that does not fit the technology the team knows. The forces: the team is committed to what it knows, is not familiar with others, sees unfamiliar technology as risky, and finds planning easy with the familiar one.

The supposed solution is to use the familiar technology anyway, applied obsessively, even where it is clearly inappropriate. The refactored solution is to widen developers' knowledge through education, training and book study groups. An observed example: web companies keep maintaining homegrown caching systems when open source alternatives are in use.
card.rule: Spot the golden hammer, the pull of the familiar technology, and cure it by widening what the team knows.
card.limits: The forces are real: familiarity does make planning easier. The anti-pattern does not call the familiar technology bad; it warns against applying it where it does not fit.

concepts.title: The closing toolbox
concepts.question: What are the book's closing pieces of advice for living with patterns?

paragraphs: The closing bullet points say: let patterns emerge in your designs and do not force them in; adapt and tweak patterns to your needs; use the simplest solution that meets your needs, even if it contains no pattern; study catalogs to learn the patterns and their relationships; and use classifications when they help.

They add: patterns writers need commitment, time, patience and lots of refinement; most patterns you meet are adaptations of existing ones; build your team's shared vocabulary; and do not let the patterns community's lingo hold you back, because after this book you know most of it.
card.rule: Let patterns emerge, adapt them, keep designs simple, study catalogs and build a shared vocabulary.
card.limits: These are guidelines, as the book says of patterns themselves. When enthusiasm and the simplest solution that meets the need conflict, the closing advice favours the simple one.

concepts.title: Reading each pattern's opening line first
concepts.question: What does the single sentence under each pattern's name tell you before you read its scenario?

paragraphs: The appendix gives nine patterns that are official but used less often than the ones in earlier chapters. Its goal is only a high-level idea of each, so you do not need every detail at once.

Each pattern opens with one sentence that starts with a phrase such as use this pattern when. That sentence states the purpose of the pattern. Reading all nine of these lines first gives you a quick map of which problem each pattern answers.
Only after that map do you read the scenario, the benefits and the drawbacks of the one or two patterns that match your problem.
card.rule: Read each pattern's opening purpose sentence first, to learn what problem it answers, and read the rest only for the patterns that match.
card.limits: An opening line is a lead, not understanding: two patterns can sound alike, so confirm with the scenario and the drawbacks before you choose.
card.example: Skimming for an undo feature, you read nine opening lines and find one about returning an object to a previous state. That is the Memento line, so you read the Memento scenario in full and skip the rest for now.

concepts.title: Bridge: vary the abstraction and the implementation
concepts.question: How can a design let both the abstraction and the implementation change without either one breaking the other?

paragraphs: In the remote-control scenario two things change. The remote's user interface is the abstraction and will be refined many times. The TV models are the implementations, one per model. If one hierarchy holds both, you can vary the TVs but not the interface.

Bridge places the abstraction and the implementation in two separate class hierarchies. The link between them is the bridge. Either side can then be extended on its own, and changes to the concrete abstraction classes do not affect the client.
card.rule: Put the abstraction and its implementation in separate class hierarchies so each can vary on its own.
card.limits: Bridge increases complexity. When only one of the two sides will ever vary, a single hierarchy or a plain interface is enough.
card.example: A messaging app has message kinds (alert, reminder, receipt) and delivery channels (email, text, push). Two hierarchies let any kind use any channel. Adding a channel means writing one class on the channel side.

concepts.title: Builder: construct a complex product in steps
concepts.question: How can a complex structure be built in varying steps without mixing the steps into the client or the structure?

paragraphs: In the Patternsland vacation planner, each guest's plan may include hotels, tickets, restaurant reservations and special events, in different numbers. You need a flexible structure and a sequence of possibly complex steps to make it.

Builder moves that construction into a separate builder object. The client asks the builder to build the structure, and the builder hides the structure's internal representation. This is the same idea the Iterator used for iteration.
card.rule: Hand the step-by-step construction of a complex product to a builder so the client never touches the product's internals.
card.limits: The client must know which steps to ask for, which takes more domain knowledge than calling a factory. If an object is made in one step, a factory is enough.
card.example: A custom computer shop lets a buyer pick a case, drives, a graphics card and extras. A builder takes those steps one by one and hands back the finished machine. A different builder can produce a different kind of product from the same steps.

concepts.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
concepts.title: Chain of Responsibility: pass the request along
concepts.question: How can a request reach whichever of several handlers can deal with it, without the sender knowing which one?

paragraphs: Mighty Gumball receives fan mail, complaints, requests for new machines and spam. Each kind goes to a different place. The sender should not need to know who handles what.

Chain of Responsibility links handler objects in a chain. Each handler has a successor. When a request comes in, a handler either handles it or forwards it to its successor. In the email example the SpamHandler comes first, then the FanHandler, and so on.
You can add or remove responsibilities by changing the members or the order of the chain.
card.rule: Link handlers so each either handles the request or passes it to its successor.
card.limits: A request may fall off the end if no handler takes it, and a long chain is hard to observe and debug at runtime.
card.example: A support desk passes each ticket to a billing agent, who handles billing tickets or forwards the rest to a shipping agent, who handles shipping tickets or forwards the rest on. The customer never picks an agent.

concepts.title: Flyweight: one instance, many virtual instances
concepts.question: How can a system with thousands of near-identical objects stay fast and small?

paragraphs: In the landscape application, a tree has an X-Y location and draws itself depending on its age. When a client makes large groves with thousands of tree objects, the app becomes sluggish.

Flyweight reduces the number of instances. You keep one Tree instance, and a client object maintains the state of all the trees. One instance then serves as many virtual instances, and state for all of them is in one place.
card.rule: Keep one shared instance and hold the differing state of every virtual instance in one place outside it.
card.limits: Once Flyweight is in place, a single logical instance cannot behave independently of the others, and with only a few objects the saving is small.
card.example: A map app shows 100000 identical street-lamp icons. It keeps one lamp object and a single list of positions in another object, instead of 100000 lamp objects.

concepts.title: Interpreter: a class for each grammar rule
concepts.question: How do a grammar's rules turn into classes that can run the sentences of a small language?

paragraphs: A grammar is a set of rules for what sentences of a language look like. In the Duck Simulator scenario, children control a duck with a simple language, so you write its grammar first.

Interpreter represents the grammar with classes: one class for each rule, mapped directly. Each expression class has an interpret method. It receives a context, which holds the input stream of the program being parsed, matches the input and evaluates it.
card.rule: Give each rule of the grammar its own class with an interpret method that takes the context.
card.limits: Interpreter suits a simple grammar where simplicity matters more than efficiency. With many rules it becomes cumbersome, and a parser or compiler generator may be better.
card.example: A language for a robot cleaner has the rules go with a number, turn, and a sequence of commands. You write a Go class, a Turn class and a Sequence class. Calling interpret on the sequence runs the commands against the context.

concepts.title: Mediator: centralize the coordination
concepts.question: Where should the rules about how related objects react to each other live?

paragraphs: Bob's auto-house has an alarm clock, a coffee maker and a sprinkler, and customers keep asking for new rules such as no coffee on weekends. Each appliance knows about the others, so it is hard to tell which rules live where.

Mediator adds one object that holds the control logic. The appliances tell the mediator when their state changes and respond to its requests. They no longer know about each other. A new rule or a new appliance means the logic goes into the mediator.
card.rule: Route all communication between related objects through one mediator that holds the coordinating rules.
card.limits: The mediator can itself become overly complex if it is not designed well, and for two objects with a simple link it adds an extra layer.
card.example: A booking form has a one-way checkbox, a return-date field and a price label. Each widget reports its change to a form controller, which disables the return date and updates the price. The widgets never call one another.

concepts.title: Three patterns that loosen links
concepts.question: Which of these patterns loosens links between objects, and what does each one separate?

paragraphs: Bridge, Chain of Responsibility and Mediator all reduce coupling, but each separates a different pair. Bridge separates an implementation from the interface it would otherwise be bound to. Chain separates the sender of a request from its receivers. Mediator separates related objects from one another.

To tell them apart, name the two things that are tangled. If it is an abstraction and its implementations, think Bridge. If it is a sender and several possible receivers, think Chain. If it is a group of peers that each know the others, think Mediator.
card.rule: Name what is tangled: abstraction and implementation points to Bridge, sender and receivers to Chain, a tangle of peers to Mediator.
card.limits: All three lower coupling, but each adds a cost: Bridge adds complexity, Chain is hard to debug, and Mediator can bloat. Lower coupling alone is not a reason to pick one.
card.example: A printing service has document types that change and printer models that change: Bridge. A help desk where a ticket may belong to one of several teams: Chain. A dialog whose widgets react to one another: Mediator.

concepts.title: Memento: save state and keep encapsulation
concepts.question: How can a game save and later restore an object's state without exposing the object's details?

paragraphs: In the role playing game, players want a save progress command that returns a resurrected player to the last completed level. Memento has two goals: save the important state of a key object, and keep the key object encapsulated.

With the single responsibility principle in mind, the saved state is kept in a separate object, called the Memento object. This keeps the key object cohesive and its data encapsulated, and it makes recovery easy to implement.
card.rule: Store the key object's state in a separate memento object so it can be restored without opening up the object.
card.limits: Saving and restoring state can be time consuming, so a very large state saved often makes the design slow. In Java, consider Serialization for saving a system's state.
card.example: A drawing app takes a snapshot of the canvas before each edit and stores it in a memento. Undo asks for the latest memento and restores the canvas from it, while the canvas fields stay hidden from the history list.

concepts.title: Prototype: make new objects by copying
concepts.question: How can a program create new objects without the client knowing which class they come from?

paragraphs: The role playing game needs an endless supply of monsters, whose traits change with the landscape, and advanced players want to create their own. Prototype creates new instances by copying existing ones.

In Java this typically means clone, or deserialization when deep copies are needed. A key aspect is that the client can make new instances without knowing which specific class is being instantiated. Copying can also be more efficient than creating in some circumstances.
card.rule: To make a new object, copy an existing prepared one instead of constructing it from scratch.
card.limits: Copying an object can sometimes be complicated, and copying is more efficient than creating only in some circumstances.
card.example: A billing system keeps a prepared invoice for each customer type. To create a new invoice, it copies the matching one and changes the customer name. The code that asks for the copy does not name the invoice class.

concepts.title: Memento or Prototype: restore or reproduce?
concepts.question: Memento and Prototype both work with an object's state; how do you tell which one a problem needs?

paragraphs: Memento brings an existing object back to an earlier state, as in undo or save progress, and keeps the object's data encapsulated. Prototype produces new objects by copying existing ones, when creating an instance is expensive or complicated.

Ask what you want at the end. If you want the same object restored to its old state, think Memento. If you want another object like an existing one, think Prototype. Their drawbacks differ too: Memento's cost is time to save and restore, Prototype's is that a copy can be complicated.
card.rule: Ask whether you need the old state back in the same object (Memento) or a new object like an existing one (Prototype).
card.limits: A system can need both, and the same technique, such as serialization, can serve either; decide by purpose, not by mechanism.
card.example: A level editor lets designers duplicate an enemy to tweak the copy: Prototype. The same editor lets them undo a change: Memento.

concepts.title: Visitor: add operations to a composite
concepts.question: How can new operations be added to a composite structure without editing its classes?

paragraphs: At the diner and the pancake house, customers ask for nutritional information, even per ingredient. Adding a method to each class means edits in two places each time, and a new class means a third place.

Visitor works with a Traverser. The Traverser knows how to navigate to every object in the Composite and guides the Visitor through it so the Visitor can collect state. The client can then have the Visitor perform operations, and new functionality only needs the Visitor to change.
card.rule: Put new operations in a visitor that a traverser carries through the composite, so the composite's classes stay unchanged.
card.limits: Visitor breaks the composite classes' encapsulation, and since traversal is involved, changing the composite's structure becomes harder.
card.example: A file tree has folders and files. A size-report visitor and a file-count visitor are each walked through the tree by a traverser. Neither report touches the Folder or File classes.

concepts.title: Reading the drawbacks lists
concepts.question: What do the drawbacks lists at the end of each pattern let you check before you adopt it?

paragraphs: Every pattern in the appendix ends with benefits and a uses and drawbacks box. Skimming the drawbacks gives you the price in a few seconds. Bridge increases complexity. Builder needs more domain knowledge in the client. Chain may leave a request unhandled and is hard to debug.

Flyweight instances cannot act independently. Interpreter gets cumbersome with many rules. Mediator can become overly complex. Memento can be slow to save and restore. Prototype copies can be complicated. Visitor breaks encapsulation and makes structure changes harder.
card.rule: Before choosing a pattern, read its drawbacks next to its benefits and check that the cost fits your problem.
card.limits: A listed drawback is a risk, not a verdict. The appendix says a request falling off the end of a chain can be an advantage or a disadvantage, depending on what you need.
card.example: A team wants to give 50000 dashboard widgets that each respond differently to events. The Flyweight drawbacks line shows that instances cannot behave independently, so Flyweight is ruled out in seconds.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Putting the book in one view
concepts.title: The book's unity in a few sentences
concepts.question: If someone asks what the whole book is about, what can you say in a few sentences?

paragraphs: To state a book's unity is to say what the whole book is about, briefly. For this book the answer starts with experience. A design pattern is a proven, general solution to a design problem that keeps recurring. It is not code to link in. You adapt it to your own application, so what you reuse is other designers' experience.

The authors add that knowing the object-oriented basics (abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) does not make you a good designer. Beneath the patterns sit design principles, such as separating what varies and favoring composition. Patterns and principles are two layers of one subject: building systems that stay reusable, extensible and maintainable.
A third layer is language. Patterns give a team shared names, so a whole design can be described in a word.
card.example: A cooking course might be summed up this way: it teaches proven techniques that recur across dishes, plus the principles of heat and timing behind them, so that cooks can adapt a technique to a new dish. Replace techniques with patterns and dishes with applications, and you have the shape of this book's statement.
card.rule: This book teaches proven solutions to recurring design problems, and the principles beneath them, so that you can build flexible systems by adapting experience instead of copying code.
card.limits: A feeling that you know what the book is about is not enough: say it in words and test it against the text. Even a good statement is only a summary, and it cannot tell you what any one pattern does.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Putting the book in one view
concepts.title: What each pattern lets vary
concepts.question: Which part of a system does each pattern let you change without disturbing the rest?

paragraphs: The first design principle says to separate what varies from what stays the same. The authors say most patterns apply it: each lets some part of a system vary independently of all the others. A quick way to see the whole book is to ask of each pattern what varies in it.

Strategy lets the algorithm a client uses vary. Observer lets the set of objects that depend on a subject vary. Decorator lets the responsibilities attached to an object vary. Factory Method lets the concrete class that gets created vary. Template Method lets individual steps of a fixed algorithm vary. Iterator lets the way a collection is walked through vary. State lets an object's behavior vary with its internal state.
Read this way, a list of names becomes one question you can put to any problem. If you can name the part that varies, you have narrowed the candidates.
card.example: A ride-hailing app prices trips by city rules that change often, while booking and payment stay the same. The rule is the varying part. It goes into its own interchangeable classes, which is Strategy, and the booking and payment code is left alone.
card.rule: To narrow the choice of pattern, name the part of the problem that varies, because each pattern is built to let one such part change on its own.
card.limits: The book says most patterns do this, not all, so the question narrows the choice without settling it. And a part that never changes gains nothing from being pulled out.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Putting the book in one view
concepts.title: Principles that recur across the patterns
concepts.question: Which design principles keep returning in the book, and which pattern shows each of them best?

paragraphs: The book names a small set of principles and keeps returning to them. Separate what varies, favor composition over inheritance, and program to an interface all come with Strategy in the first chapter. Strive for loosely coupled designs comes with Observer, and open for extension but closed for modification with Decorator.

Depend upon abstractions comes with the factory patterns. The Principle of Least Knowledge, talk only to your immediate friends, comes in the chapter on Adapter and Facade. The Hollywood Principle, don't call us, we'll call you, comes with Template Method, and the rule that a class has one reason to change comes with Iterator.
Each pattern leans on several principles at once, so this map shows emphasis and not a one-to-one table.
card.example: A report class holds a list of invoices and prints them in three formats. A format change edits the class, and so does a storage change. The one-reason-to-change principle says to give printing to another class, much as Iterator takes traversal away from the collection.
card.rule: Link each recurring principle to the pattern that shows it best, and expect every pattern to lean on several principles at once.
card.limits: Some principles overlap: Dependency Inversion is a stronger statement of program to an interface, not a separate idea. And the authors say a design may purposely depart from a principle once the effect is weighed.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Telling look-alike patterns apart by intent
concepts.question: Two patterns can have the same class diagram. What do you ask to tell which one a design is using?

paragraphs: Many patterns look alike on paper. State and Strategy have the same class diagram. Decorator and Proxy both implement the interface of the object they wrap and forward calls to it. Adapter, Decorator and Facade all wrap something. Simple Factory and Factory Method can read the same when written out. Structure alone cannot name the pattern.

What differs is intent, the problem the design solves. Strategy lets a client configure behavior, while State lets an object's behavior follow its own internal state. A decorator adds behavior, while a proxy controls access. An adapter converts an interface into the one a client expects, while a facade offers a simpler one.
Counting is a weak test. The book rejects the idea that an adapter wraps one class and a facade many: an adapter may adapt several classes, and a facade may simplify a single complicated one.
card.example: Two wrappers hold an Account and offer the same methods. One adds a timestamp to every statement it returns. The other checks the caller's role before passing a withdrawal on. The shape is the same, but the first adds behavior (Decorator) and the second controls access (Proxy).
card.rule: When two designs look alike, decide by intent, the problem each one solves, and not by the class diagram or the number of classes wrapped.
card.limits: Intent usually settles the question, but real code can sit between two patterns, and a reasonable reader may name it differently. When in doubt, say what problem the code solves; that is more useful than the label.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Adapter, Decorator, Facade or Proxy?
concepts.question: Given an object placed in front of another, what two questions sort it into Adapter, Decorator, Facade or Proxy?

paragraphs: Four patterns put something in front of another object: Adapter, Decorator, Facade and Proxy. The book separates them by what each does to the interface and why. The first question is whether the wrapper keeps the interface of what it stands in front of.

If the interface is different, the wrapper is an Adapter when it converts the interface into the one a client expects, and a Facade when it gives a simpler interface to a group of objects. If the interface is the same, the second question is the purpose: a Decorator adds behavior or responsibilities, and a Proxy controls access to the object.
Each answer names a purpose, so apply the sort to what the class is for. A proxy's subject may be on another machine or not yet created, so wrapping describes a proxy only loosely.
card.example: A shop's code calls pay(Order). A supplier's old class offers charge(amount, card). A class that implements pay(Order) and calls charge inside is an Adapter: a different interface converted to the expected one. If it implemented charge itself and added a receipt line to each call, it would be a Decorator.
card.rule: Keep the interface and add behavior: Decorator; keep it and control access: Proxy; change it to the expected one: Adapter; simplify a group of objects: Facade.
card.limits: A protection proxy that offers only part of an interface can resemble an adapter, and all four add classes to a design. The sort names the purpose; it does not say whether the wrapper is worth having.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Strategy, State or Template Method?
concepts.question: When behavior must vary, what three questions decide between Strategy, State and Template Method?

paragraphs: Strategy, State and Template Method all vary behavior, but they use different mechanisms. Strategy and State use composition: the object delegates to another object. Template Method uses inheritance: a superclass fixes the outline of an algorithm and subclasses fill in steps.

Ask three things. Does a whole algorithm change, or one step inside a fixed outline? A whole algorithm points to Strategy or State; a step points to Template Method. Who changes the behavior object? A client picks a Strategy, while in State the context moves between state objects as its own condition changes.

The third question is what is being replaced. Strategy replaces inheritance that locks a behavior in, State replaces a pile of conditionals on state, and Template Method replaces copies of the same outline.
card.example: An invoice can be Draft, Sent or Paid, and cancel() acts differently in each; the invoice moves itself between them: State. An exporter is handed a PDF writer or a CSV writer by its caller: Strategy. A monthly routine with fixed steps in which each department writes its own summary step: Template Method.
card.rule: Ask whether a whole algorithm or one step varies, who changes it, and what problem it replaces: Strategy and State compose, Template Method inherits.
card.limits: The patterns overlap: State and Strategy share a class diagram, and real code can blend Template Method with composition, as a sort method does. If behavior never has to vary and no conditionals are piling up, none of the three is called for.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Simple Factory, Factory Method or Abstract Factory?
concepts.question: Which factory form fits a creation problem, and how does Factory Method relate to Template Method?

paragraphs: All three factory forms move creation out of the code that uses the products, so that code depends on abstractions and not on concrete classes. They differ in how. Simple Factory hands creation to a separate object. It is an idiom, not a bona fide pattern, and it gives no way to vary the products.

Factory Method leaves creation in the class that uses the product, as an abstract method that subclasses implement, so the subclass chosen decides which concrete product appears. It makes one product by inheritance. Abstract Factory is passed to the client as an object and makes a whole family of related products, so products that belong together are used together.

Factory Method is also a specialization of Template Method: the step that subclasses supply is the one that creates an object. Choose by the need. One product with a subclass deciding: Factory Method. Matching families: Abstract Factory. Only moving new out of the client: Simple Factory.
card.example: A game builds fighters. A Fighter class creates its weapon through an abstract createWeapon(), and Knight and Archer subclasses return their own: Factory Method. A kingdom object that produces a matching weapon, shield and armor set and is passed to the game: Abstract Factory.
card.rule: Factory Method creates one product by inheritance, Abstract Factory creates a family by composition, and Simple Factory is a separate creator object.
card.limits: Real code rarely labels itself: an Abstract Factory's methods are often factory methods, and a factory method may supply a default product. The labels describe emphasis and not sealed categories.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation
concepts.title: From a symptom to a candidate pattern
concepts.question: How do you move from a design problem in front of you to a pattern worth trying?

paragraphs: The book gives an order for choosing. Try a simpler solution first and see whether it is enough. If it is not, state the problem together with its constraints, then match it to a pattern by reading catalogs for each pattern's intent and when it applies. Last, check the consequences for the rest of your design before you commit.

Symptoms in the code point to candidates. Conditionals piling up on an object's internal state suggest State. Concrete classes created with new suggest a factory. A change in one object that many others must follow suggests Observer. A request that should be separated from the code that performs it suggests Command.
An interface that does not match what a client expects suggests Adapter. A subsystem that is hard to use suggests Facade. Nested parts and wholes suggest Composite.
A symptom gives a candidate, not a verdict. The candidate still has to pass the first and the last step.
card.example: A support tool has a ticket object whose methods are full of if-else tests on its status, and the tests multiply whenever a status is added. That symptom points to State as the candidate. Before adopting it, the team asks whether statuses will keep changing and what a class per status would cost.
card.rule: Try a simpler solution first, then match the problem and its constraints to a pattern by intent, and check the consequences before adopting it.
card.limits: The sequence has one stated exception, expected variation: where change is practical and likely, a pattern can be right even if a simpler solution would work. Symptoms are hints, and one symptom can fit more than one pattern.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation
concepts.title: Choosing between two candidates
concepts.question: When two patterns both seem to fit, what do you compare to choose between them?

paragraphs: Sometimes two patterns both seem to fit. Compare them on what each separates or produces, and on what each costs. Name the two things that are tangled in your problem, then see which pattern separates exactly that pair.

Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementations, Chain of Responsibility separates a sender from several possible receivers, and Mediator separates peers that each know the others. Memento brings the same object back to an earlier state, while Prototype produces a new object by copying an existing one.
Iterator walks a collection without exposing it. Composite is for a tree of parts and wholes, and a flat collection needs only an iterator.

Then read each candidate's drawbacks. Bridge adds complexity, Chain may leave a request unhandled and is hard to debug, Mediator can become overly complex, Memento can be slow to save and restore, and a Prototype copy can be complicated.
card.example: A drawing editor needs an undo command and also a Duplicate Layer command. Undo wants the same object back in an earlier state: Memento. Duplicate wants another object like an existing one: Prototype.
card.rule: Choose between candidates by what each separates or produces, then read each one's drawbacks before you commit.
card.limits: A system can need both patterns, and one technique, such as serialization, can serve either, so decide by purpose and not by mechanism.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: When no pattern is the right answer
concepts.question: When is the right design choice to use no pattern at all, and what tells you a pattern is not earning its place?

paragraphs: The book's closing advice is to use the simplest solution that meets your needs, even if it contains no pattern. Patterns add classes and layers, so they cost complexity. Start from the principles and the simplest code that works, and let a pattern emerge when a need appears.

A pattern needs a practical reason: a change you must support now, or one you are quite sure will come. A reason that is only hypothetical does not justify one, because the pattern will add complexity and you might never need it.

Designing by applying patterns until a problem is solved is the opposite of this advice. The duck simulator showed patterns cooperating, but parts of it were overkill, and sometimes good principles alone solve a problem well enough.
card.example: A three-field settings screen gets a factory, an observer and a decorator because the team has just studied patterns. Nothing about it varies. A plain class with three fields would do, so the patterns add classes without adding flexibility.
card.rule: Use a pattern for a practical need, and if a simpler design that follows the principles does the job, use that.
card.limits: This is not a ban: when you expect part of the system to vary in practice, a pattern can be right even if a simpler solution would work. The test is need, not whether a pattern is present.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Principles and patterns as guidelines with costs
concepts.question: What should you do when a principle or a pattern pulls against another goal in your design?

paragraphs: The authors say principles and patterns are guidelines, not laws. Design is an art, and there will always be tradeoffs. A designer is guided by principles but must observe the effect they have on the design, and may purposely depart from one.

Composite is the book's example. Putting child management and leaf operations in one interface takes the one-reason-to-change principle and trades it for transparency, because clients can treat leaves and composites uniformly. The price is some safety: a client may try something meaningless, such as adding a menu to a menu item.

Every pattern carries costs, such as more classes, more layers or heavier creation code. Weigh them against the benefit in your case, and adapt the pattern to your needs where the classic design does not fit.
card.example: A team gives every Command its own class and ends with dozens of tiny classes. They weigh that cost against being able to queue and undo requests. Because the product needs undo, they accept the classes. For a one-off script with no undo, they would not.
card.rule: Treat principles and patterns as guidelines: name what a choice buys and what it costs in your design, then decide knowingly.
card.limits: Tradeoffs are not permission to ignore principles. A departure needs a reason you can state, and the costs are judged for the case at hand: extra classes can be worth it in a long-lived system and not in a throwaway one.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: A team models many kinds of ducks in a game, and all of them share most of their code. Which structure is the usual first choice in object-oriented design?
options: A separate copy of the shared code inside each duck class
A common superclass that every duck type inherits from
One class holding an if-statement for each duck type
A global file of functions called by name from each duck
optionExplain: Copying works at first, but every fix must then be made in each copy.
Right: shared code goes in one superclass and the subclasses receive it.
This puts every species into one class, so each new species means editing it.
Global functions share code but lose the link between a duck and what it can do.
questions.explain: Inheritance is the standard way to share code among related types. The card next shows how SimUDuck used it.
questions.rule: Shared code goes in a common superclass.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: In SimUDuck all duck types inherit from one Duck ____.
questions.explain: The designers made one Duck superclass from which every other duck type inherits.
questions.rule: Subclasses receive the superclass's code.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: A library app has Book, Magazine and DVD classes. All three need the same due-date and renewal code. What does the inheritance approach suggest?
options: Copy the due-date code into Book, Magazine and DVD
Write the code in Book and have Magazine and DVD call Book whenever they need it
Put the due-date code once in an Item superclass that the three extend
Make three interfaces, one per item type
optionExplain: Copies drift apart, and a fix has to be made three times.
Magazine and DVD are not kinds of Book, so a call to Book misstates the relationship.
Right: one copy in the superclass serves all three subclasses.
Interfaces declare methods but, in Java, carry no code to share.
questions.explain: A superclass is the single home for what the subclasses have in common. Each subclass then adds only what is different.
questions.rule: Write shared code once, in the superclass.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: Eight duck species already inherit from Duck. A ninth is added. What is the smallest amount of new code the inheritance design needs?
options: A full copy of every method in Duck
A new interface for each shared method
A change to each of the eight existing species so they know about the ninth
Only the code that makes the ninth species different
optionExplain: That is the copying that inheritance exists to avoid.
Interfaces would add a layer, not remove code.
Existing species are untouched by adding a new subclass.
Right: everything shared arrives by inheritance, so only the difference is new.
questions.explain: The cost of a new subclass is the size of its difference from the superclass, not the size of the whole class.
questions.rule: A new subclass pays only for what differs.
questions.teaches: A subclass can override an inherited method to replace the shared version with its own, so it writes code only where it differs.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: True or false: in a payroll program where Employee is the superclass of Manager and Intern, an Intern with its own overtime rule can override the inherited overtime method.
questions.explain: Overriding replaces the inherited version for that one subclass while the others keep the shared one. This is how a subclass handles its difference.
questions.rule: A subclass can override what it inherits.
questions.teaches: Overriding lets one subclass differ without touching the superclass or its siblings.

questions.section: It started with a simple SimUDuck app
questions.q: A Vehicle superclass has Truck, Bus and Bicycle subclasses. Sort each item: written once in the superclass, or written in a subclass?

items.t: Recording the owner's name
Tracking distance travelled
Counting a bus's seats
Calculating a truck's cargo limit
Storing the registration number
Ringing a bicycle's bell

questions.explain: Code that every vehicle needs belongs in the superclass. Code about one kind of vehicle belongs in that subclass; putting it higher would give it to vehicles that cannot use it.
questions.rule: Put it in the superclass only if all subclasses need it.

questions.q: True or false: a new method added to a superclass is received only by the subclasses whose authors ask for it.
questions.explain: Subclasses receive everything their superclass holds, whether or not anyone asked. The card next shows what that did to SimUDuck.
questions.rule: Subclasses cannot decline what the superclass gains.

questions.q: When Joe added fly() to the Duck superclass, every duck ____ received it, including rubber ducks.
questions.explain: Every subclass inherits what the superclass gains, including the ones it does not suit.
questions.rule: A superclass change spreads to all subclasses.

questions.q: A messaging app has a Message superclass with TextMessage, ImageMessage and VoiceNote subclasses. A developer adds a preview() method to Message that shows the first 100 characters. What is the likely result?
options: Only TextMessage receives preview(), since it holds the text
Message cannot gain methods once subclasses exist
All three subclasses automatically adjust the preview to their own content
ImageMessage and VoiceNote inherit a preview that has no text to show
optionExplain: Method delivery does not depend on the content of the subclass.
Adding a method to a superclass is allowed at any time.
Adjusting the preview would take extra code in each subclass; nothing does it automatically.
Right: inheritance does not check whether the method fits; the two non-text subclasses receive it anyway.
questions.explain: The developer meant to change text messages, but the change reached image and voice messages too.
questions.rule: Check every subclass before adding to a superclass.

questions.q: Which statement describes what the authors call a nonlocal side effect?
options: An edit that changes behavior only in the one class that was edited, and nothing else
A small, targeted edit that changes behavior in classes it was not aimed at
A bug that appears only on a slow computer
A change that is repeated by hand in many separate files
optionExplain: That is a local effect, the one intended.
Right: the edit was local, but its effect was felt elsewhere, as with the flying rubber ducks.
Speed of the machine has nothing to do with where the effect lands.
Repeating a change by hand is a different maintenance cost.
questions.explain: Joe's edit sat in one class, yet it altered behavior in subclasses far from his intention.
questions.rule: Judge a change by where it reaches, not by how small it is.
questions.teaches: A change can be small in size yet wide in reach: what matters is how many classes inherit from the one edited.

questions.q: In a payroll program, a developer adds a one-line method applyBonus() to the Staff superclass. Contractors and volunteers are also Staff subclasses. A colleague says the change is safe because it is only one line. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed, a one-line change cannot affect other classes
It is safe as long as the method has a descriptive name
Length does not decide reach: contractors and volunteers receive the bonus method too
It is safe because contractors and volunteers are unlikely ever to call the new method
optionExplain: Line count says nothing about which classes inherit it.
A clear name does not stop subclasses from receiving the method.
Right: reach is set by who inherits, so every Staff subclass gets applyBonus().
Even if unlikely, they now carry behavior they should not have.
questions.explain: Safety depends on whether every subclass should have the method, not on the edit's size.
questions.rule: Reach matters more than size.
questions.teaches: Code review of a superclass change should list every subclass, not just the class edited.

questions.q: True or false: adding getName() to an Animal superclass with Lion, Eagle and Penguin subclasses is a safe use of inheritance, because every subclass should have a name.
questions.explain: The danger in the card comes from behavior that only some subclasses should have. A name suits every animal, so putting it in the superclass is exactly what inheritance is for.
questions.rule: The danger is a mismatch, not superclass edits as such.

questions.q: Behavior that differs from one subclass to another is written inside each subclass. Which problems should you expect? Select all that apply.
options: The same code ends up copied into several subclasses
A change to a shared class can hit subclasses that did not need it
The compiler rejects subclasses that differ from each other
Changing an object's behavior while the program runs gets harder
optionExplain: Right: subclasses that need the same behavior each get their own copy.
Right: a change in a shared parent reaches all its children.
Subclasses are allowed to differ; the compiler does not object, which is why the problems appear only later.
Right: behavior fixed in the class is hard to swap on a live object.
questions.explain: Behavior fixed in class definitions is copied, scattered and hard to change on a live object. The card names four such costs.
questions.rule: Behavior fixed in subclasses is costly to copy and to change.

questions.q: According to the authors, one disadvantage of inheritance is that changing behavior at ____ is difficult.
questions.explain: Behavior defined in a subclass is fixed when the code is written, so changing it on a running program is hard.
questions.rule: Class-defined behavior is hard to change while running.

questions.q: A notification app has EmailAlert, SmsAlert and PushAlert subclasses. Each contains its own copy of the same retry logic. Which listed disadvantage does this show?
options: Changes affect other classes by surprise
Behavior cannot be known without reading every class
Behavior cannot be changed while running
Code is duplicated across subclasses
optionExplain: Surprise effects come from a shared parent being changed, which is not what happens here.
That cost is about finding out what each class does, which is not the point of this example.
Nothing here mentions switching behavior at runtime.
Right: three copies of the same logic is duplication, and a retry fix must be made three times.
questions.explain: Identical logic copied into sibling subclasses is the first cost on the list.
questions.rule: Identical code in sibling classes is duplication.

questions.q: A company has 6 duck species now and plans to add 10 more in the next year. Using inheritance for varying behavior, which cost grows with the number of species?
options: The effort to learn each species' behavior, since each class must be read
The compile time of the superclass, which gets slower with each subclass
The number of interfaces the language allows
The cost of reading the Duck superclass, which expands with each subclass
optionExplain: Right: knowledge is scattered across subclasses, so more subclasses mean more reading.
Compile time is not one of the listed costs.
Language limits on interfaces are not part of the problem.
The superclass is unchanged when a subclass is added, so its reading cost stays the same.
questions.explain: With behavior in subclasses, the whole picture exists only in the sum of the parts, which grows with each new part.
questions.rule: More subclasses mean more places to look.
questions.teaches: Costs of this design scale with the number of subclasses, so a design that is tolerable at 6 classes can become unmanageable at 16.

questions.q: Match each situation in a spreadsheet program to the cost it shows.
pairs: Ten chart subclasses each carry the same axis-label code
A chart on screen must switch style when the user clicks
A newcomer must open every chart class to know what each can do
Fixing the title code in one chart alters another chart
questions.explain: Each pair maps a symptom to one of the four listed costs: copies, a fixed behavior, scattered knowledge and spread of a change.
questions.rule: Learn each cost by the symptom you would see.
questions.teaches: The four costs are symptoms of one root cause: the varying behavior is tied to the class definitions.

questions.q: True or false: the authors criticise inheritance as the home for varying behavior, and still keep a Duck superclass in their final design.
questions.explain: The final design keeps Duck as a class from which MallardDuck and others inherit common properties. The criticism targets behavior that keeps changing.
questions.rule: The criticism targets varying behavior, not inheritance itself.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: Joe decides only the ducks that fly will implement a Flyable interface. What is the main drawback of this plan?
options: Each implementing duck must write its own flying code, so nothing is reused
Rubber ducks would still be able to fly
Java does not allow a single class to implement more than one interface at a time
Ducks could no longer be created at runtime
optionExplain: Right: an interface supplies no code, so every implementer writes its own copy.
The point of the plan is that rubber ducks would not implement Flyable.
Java allows a class to implement many interfaces.
Interfaces do not prevent creating objects.
questions.explain: The plan fixes which ducks fly but loses shared code. The card sets out why.
questions.rule: Interfaces carry no code to share.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: A Java interface, as the authors describe it, has no ____ code.
questions.explain: An interface only declares what must be done; the implementing class writes the body, so there is nothing to reuse.
questions.rule: No implementation code means no reuse.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: A drawing app has 12 shape classes that implement a Resizable interface. Each wrote its own resizing code. The resizing rule needs one fix. What must the developer do?
options: Edit the Resizable interface once
Edit nothing; interfaces update implementers automatically
Find and edit the resizing code in each of the 12 classes
Delete the interface so the shapes inherit the fix
optionExplain: The interface has no body to fix.
Implementers own their code; the interface does not push changes into it.
Right: the code was copied into each class, so each copy needs the fix.
Deleting the interface leaves the shapes with no behavior at all.
questions.explain: This is the maintenance problem the authors describe: a change repeated in every implementer, with a chance of missing one.
questions.rule: A fix in a copied behavior is made once per copy.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: Two ducks fly, one with wings and one with a rocket pack. Under the interface-only plan, how many flying implementations exist?
options: Exactly two, one for each kind of flying
One per implementing class, including copies of the same kind of flying
One, shared by every flying duck through the Flyable interface, so no copies exist
None, because interfaces cannot describe flying
optionExplain: Two kinds exist, but each class makes its own copy of its kind.
Right: each class that implements Flyable writes its own code, even when two do the same kind of flying.
The interface shares a name, not a body.
Interfaces can describe behaviors; they just hold no code.
questions.explain: Without a home for each kind of behavior, the number of copies tracks the number of classes, not the number of kinds.
questions.rule: The design needs one home per kind of behavior.
questions.teaches: A good design gives each variant of a behavior exactly one home, so a fix or a new variant is made once.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: A recipe app has Dish classes. Some dishes can be Frozen, some can be Fried. The designer makes Frozen and Fried interfaces and has each Dish class write its own freezing and frying steps. What is the likely outcome?
options: Each dish shares one copy of the freezing steps
Dishes that cannot be frozen are forced to implement the Frozen interface and run freezing steps anyway
The design cannot be compiled in Java
Two dishes that can both be frozen each write their own freezing steps, and a fix must be made twice
optionExplain: Sharing is what interfaces do not provide.
Only dishes that implement Frozen receive the capability.
The design compiles; the pain is in maintaining it.
Right: the interface forces each implementer to repeat the steps.
questions.explain: The same trade appears in any domain: selecting by interface fixes the who, but not the where-is-the-code.
questions.rule: Capabilities named by an interface still need a home for their code.
questions.teaches: Naming a capability and storing the code for it are separate jobs, and a design needs an answer for both.

questions.section: What would you do if you were Joe?
questions.q: True or false: a teammate is right that interfaces solve both of Joe's problems, since only the ducks that need a behavior implement it.
questions.explain: Interfaces stop the wrong ducks from flying, but each implementer still writes its own code, so the reuse problem is made worse. A fix must be repeated in every class.
questions.rule: Check a fix against both problems, not one.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: Which is the most dependable fact about a program that people keep using?
options: It will have to change as users and conditions change
A well-designed program stays the same once it is released to users
Its requirements are settled in the first month
Changes come only from programmers, not from users
optionExplain: Right: a program in use must grow or it will be replaced.
Even a good design must absorb change; that is what good design is for.
Requirements move as people use the system.
Users, companies and technology all drive change.
questions.explain: Every product in use is pushed by change, whatever its design. The card next states the authors' version.
questions.rule: Expect change.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: The authors say the one constant in software development is ____.
questions.explain: Whatever you build and whichever language you use, the authors say change is the constant.
questions.rule: The constant is change.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: A shop's online ordering system has run for three years. Which events would the authors count as drivers of change? Select all that apply.
options: The shop adds a new payment provider whose data format differs
The designers decide they can organise the code better now
The shop keeps its software untouched forever
Customers ask for a new delivery option
optionExplain: Right: a changed supplier or format forces new code.
Right: the authors list learning enough to do things better as a reason to change.
Staying untouched is not a driver of change; the card says an unchanged application will die.
Right: users wanting new functionality is the first driver listed.
questions.explain: The authors list customers wanting new things, changed suppliers or formats, changed technology and better ideas. Unchanged software is not a driver.
questions.rule: Customers, suppliers, technology and learning all drive change.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: A designer believes: a careful design finished today will not need to change. Which reply fits the authors' view?
options: A careful design prevents requirement changes from users, so it never has to change
Change matters only for large applications
Even a good design must be ready to change, or the application will die
Only a bad design needs to change
optionExplain: A design cannot control what users and suppliers decide.
The authors state the claim for any application.
Right: change comes from outside the code, so careful design means readiness, not immunity.
Good designs still change; they absorb it with less pain.
questions.explain: The measure of a design is its cost of change. A design that resists change is a design that dies.
questions.rule: Good design is ready for change, not safe from it.
questions.teaches: Design quality is measured by the cost of the next change, not by how complete the first release looks.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: A city plans a bus-timetable app. One planner says the schedule format is fixed, so the code can assume it. Another says the transport agency may change formats. By the authors' view, how should the code be written?
options: Assume the format will stay the same for ever, to save work now
So that a format change touches as little code as possible
Avoid releasing the app until the format is final
Rewrite the whole app each time the format changes
optionExplain: That bets against the one constant the authors name.
Right: the code should absorb a likely change in one place.
Waiting for permanent stability waits for something that does not occur.
A full rewrite is the costliest way to take a change.
questions.explain: Expecting change leads to keeping likely changes contained, which the next ideas turn into a principle.
questions.rule: Contain the changes you can foresee.
questions.teaches: Foreseeable change is cheapest to handle when it is planned for at design time.

questions.section: The one constant in software development
questions.q: True or false: the authors' claim that change is the constant implies that every part of an application is equally likely to change.
questions.explain: The claim is about software as a whole. Which parts change most is a separate question; the next ideas ask the designer to find those parts and separate them.
questions.rule: Find the parts that change and treat them apart.

questions.q: Two attempts to fix a program both fail, in the same way: every change has to be made in many places. What is the most useful next step?
options: Ask what the two attempts have in common
Repeat the first attempt with more care
Pick whichever attempt is shorter and defend it
Add more developers to make the many changes faster
optionExplain: Right: a shared feature of two failures points at the real cause.
Care does not remove a structural problem.
Length is not the issue; the failure is.
More people copy the same changes faster, but the cost remains.
questions.explain: A shared failure points to a shared cause. The card next shows the one the authors found.
questions.rule: Look for the shared cause.

questions.q: With the interface design, a change to a behavior forces you to track down and change it in all the different ____.
questions.explain: Each subclass wrote its own copy of the behavior, so a change must visit them all.
questions.rule: Copied behavior means a hunt for every copy.

questions.q: A shop's invoice code was fixed in two ways. In the first, each of 5 invoice types has its own tax code. In the second, each of 5 types implements a TaxRule interface with its own body. A tax law changes. What do both designs share?
options: The logic lives in one class that is used by all five invoice types
The tax logic sits inside each of the 5 invoice classes
Neither design needs any code to change
Only the interface needs editing
optionExplain: That would be the improved design, which neither of these is.
Right: in both designs the varying logic lives in every invoice class, so each must be edited.
The tax law changed; code that encodes it must change.
An interface has no body to edit.
questions.explain: Both designs spread the varying logic across the classes that use it.
questions.rule: Find where the varying code lives.

questions.q: Inheritance and interfaces both failed Joe. If the shared cause is that varying behavior lives inside the duck classes, what does that suggest the fix should do?
options: Add more duck subclasses so each behavior has its own
Replace every interface with an abstract class
Remove the Duck class and rewrite each species separately
Move the varying behavior out of the duck classes
optionExplain: More subclasses create more copies of the same behavior.
An abstract class would keep the behavior inside the duck hierarchy.
Rewriting each species increases duplication.
Right: if the problem is where the behavior lives, change where it lives.
questions.explain: Fix the location of the varying code, not the label on the container it sits in.
questions.rule: A problem of location needs a change of location.
questions.teaches: Changing the container (class to interface) did not help; moving the varying code out of the class that varies is what changes the outcome.

questions.q: A tour company's booking program has CoachTrip, BoatTrip and WalkTrip classes, each with its own cancellation-refund rule. A manager first adds a Refundable interface. Refund rules still change monthly and need edits in every trip class. What is the shared cause?
options: Trips are not given enough subclasses to hold their refund rules
The Refundable interface is spelled wrongly
Refund rules, which vary, are written inside each trip class
Cancellation is a poor feature to offer
optionExplain: More subclasses would spread the rule further.
Spelling has nothing to do with where the code lives.
Right: whether by inheritance or by interface, the rule lives in each trip class.
The feature is fine; its home is the problem.
questions.explain: The pattern repeats in any domain: the thing that varies is stuck inside the things that use it.
questions.rule: Varying code stuck in its users is the root cause.
questions.teaches: The diagnosis does not depend on the language feature used: class, subclass or interface can all trap varying code.

questions.q: True or false: if two failed designs fail for different reasons, finding what they share will reveal one cause for both.
questions.explain: A shared cause exists only when the failures are of the same kind. Different failures call for different diagnoses.
questions.rule: Check the failures match before merging the causes.

questions.q: A checkout program's discount rules change every season. Receipt printing and tax records have not changed in years. What is the best design instinct?
options: Spread the discount rules through every part of checkout to keep them close
Rewrite the receipt code each season for consistency
Keep the discount rules in a place of their own, apart from the stable code
Hard-code this season's rules and rewrite next year
optionExplain: Spreading them makes every seasonal change touch the whole program.
Rewriting the stable code adds risk with no gain.
Right: the part that changes belongs apart from the parts that do not.
Hard-coding repeats the pain every time rules change.
questions.explain: The part that changes needs a place of its own. The card next gives the authors' first design principle.
questions.rule: Separate the changing from the stable.

questions.q: The first design principle says: identify the aspects of your application that ____ and separate them from what stays the same.
questions.explain: The aspects that vary, meaning those that change with new requirements, are the ones to separate.
questions.rule: Separate what varies from what stays the same.

questions.q: A company says its delivery-fee formulas and shipping partners change often, while order numbers and the customer address format have not changed in ten years. Sort each part: separate it as something that varies, or leave it with the stable code?

items.t: Delivery-fee formulas
The choice of shipping partner
How order numbers are formed
The customer address format
Seasonal promotion rules, which the company changes quarterly
Storing a customer's name

questions.explain: The evidence in the scenario decides: parts reported to change go apart, and parts stable for years stay.
questions.rule: Use the evidence of past change to choose.

questions.q: Delivery fees have been encapsulated in their own classes. A new weekend-surcharge fee is added. What does the design aim for?
options: Only the fee classes change, and checkout code stays untouched
Checkout must be edited to recognise the new fee
Every stable class must be recompiled and retested by hand each time
All fees must be rewritten to match the new one
optionExplain: Right: the varying part absorbs the change on its own.
That would show the fee was not really separated.
Careful testing is sensible but the design aims at the change staying local.
Existing fee types are left alone when a new one is added.
questions.explain: If a change to the varying part forces edits in the stable part, the boundary has leaked.
questions.rule: A good boundary keeps a change inside it.
questions.teaches: A test of whether something is properly encapsulated is that adding a new variant needs no edit in the stable code.

questions.q: A weather app converts readings to Celsius, Fahrenheit or Kelvin, and users keep asking for more display formats. Sensor drivers have not changed in years. Which part is the better candidate to encapsulate?
options: The sensor drivers, since they are the oldest code in the app
The display formats, since new ones keep being requested
The whole app, to be safe
Neither, since both work today
optionExplain: Age alone does not mark a part as changing; this one is stable.
Right: the formats are the part that varies with requests.
Encapsulating everything gives structure with no benefit for stable code.
Working today does not tell you about tomorrow's requests.
questions.explain: Pick the part that the evidence says will vary, in any domain.
questions.rule: Evidence of change picks the candidate.
questions.teaches: Requests that keep arriving are the best evidence about what to encapsulate.

questions.q: True or false: the principle lets the designer leave parts that stay the same exactly where they are.
questions.explain: The principle targets what varies. Parts that stay the same are left alone, since extra structure for them adds cost and gives nothing back.
questions.rule: Encapsulate the varying, not everything.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: A Duck class works well except for two methods that differ by species. How much of the class should be rewritten?
options: The whole class, to keep it consistent
Only the two varying methods are pulled out; the rest stays
Nothing; the two methods should stay in the class
The class should be deleted and then rebuilt from scratch every time
optionExplain: Rewriting working code adds risk and no benefit.
Right: the parts that vary move, the rest stays.
Leaving the varying methods inside is what caused the trouble.
A rebuild wastes the parts that are fine.
questions.explain: Change is concentrated in two methods, so the work should be too. The card next shows how the team did it.
questions.rule: Move what varies; keep what works.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: To separate what changes, the team created two sets of classes, one for fly and one for ____.
questions.explain: Each set holds all the implementations of its behavior.
questions.rule: One set of classes per varying behavior.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: A car-rental class does well at storing cars and customers, but its price calculation changes with each promotion, and its insurance quote changes by country. Which should be pulled out? Select all that apply.
options: The price calculation
The storing of cars
The insurance quote
The storing of customers
optionExplain: Right: promotions keep changing it.
It works well and was not reported to change.
Right: it changes with the country.
It works well and was not reported to change.
questions.explain: The two behaviors that change are pulled out; the storage stays where it is.
questions.rule: Pull out only what is reported to vary.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: True or false: according to the authors, a designer can anticipate areas that will vary and build flexibility for them in from the start.
questions.explain: The authors say a designer need not always build first and separate later: often the varying areas can be anticipated. Principles and patterns apply at any stage of the development lifecycle.
questions.rule: Separate varying parts early when change is foreseeable.
questions.teaches: Encapsulation can be planned in the first design as well as applied in a later cleanup.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: A school's grading program has a Student class that has worked well for years. Grade formulas change every term, and the report layout changes every year. How many sets of classes does the approach in the card suggest?
options: One: a combined set holding formulas and layouts
Three: one for Student, one for formulas, one for layouts
None: Student should be extended with new subclasses
Two: one for grade formulas and one for report layouts
optionExplain: Combining the two ties together things that change for different reasons.
Student is stable, so it does not get a set of its own.
More subclasses would copy the changes into each, which is the problem in the card.
Right: each varying behavior gets its own set, and Student stays as it is.
questions.explain: One set per independent change keeps each change from touching the other.
questions.rule: One set of classes per independent variation.
questions.teaches: Behaviors that change for different reasons belong in separate sets, so a change to one does not touch the other.

questions.section: Separating what changes from what stays the same
questions.q: Six months later fly() turns out to be stable, but a new move() keeps changing. According to the card, what is the sound response?
options: Keep everything as it is, since the earlier choice has been proven right
Rewrite Duck from scratch to start clean
Treat move() as a new varying part and revisit the earlier choice
Pull every method out of Duck now, to be safe
optionExplain: The card says the choice rests on evidence, not on proof.
A rewrite is far larger than the change in evidence needs.
Right: the judgment of what varies follows the evidence, and the evidence changed.
Pulling out everything encapsulates parts that do not vary.
questions.explain: The split between varying and stable is a judgment, so new evidence can move the line.
questions.rule: Revise the split when the evidence changes.

questions.q: A Duck object needs a flying behavior that can differ from duck to duck. How should the Duck class refer to its behavior?
options: By the specific class of the flying behavior it uses today
By a copy of the flying code written in the Duck class
By an if-statement on the species name
By a general behavior type that every flying class fits
optionExplain: Naming one class ties the duck to it.
A copy inside Duck is the old design with its problems.
A species check adds a branch each time a species is added.
Right: a general type lets any flying class be plugged in.
questions.explain: Referring to a general type leaves the duck free to use any fitting behavior. The card names this the second principle.
questions.rule: Refer to the general type, not the specific class.

questions.q: The second design principle says to program to an interface, not to an ____.
questions.explain: The duck code relies on the interface, not on the implementation of a behavior.
questions.rule: Rely on the interface.

questions.q: A photo editor needs to apply filters, such as Sepia or Blur, to an image. Which declaration follows the second principle?
options: A variable typed as Sepia, with Blur and other filters handled by a separate copy
A variable typed as a general Filter that holds Sepia, Blur or any other filter
A variable typed as Blur, switched by an if-statement
