A separate variable for each filter, tested one by one
optionExplain: Typing the variable as Sepia ties the editor to one filter.
Right: the variable's type is the general Filter, so any filter fits.
Typing as Blur does the same; the if-statement grows with each filter.
A variable for each filter grows with each new filter.
questions.explain: The editor needs to know only that it has a Filter, not which one.
questions.rule: Type the variable as the general category.

questions.q: In the old design, a duck got its flying code from the Duck class or from its own subclass. What did the authors say that locked the duck into?
options: A specific implementation, with no room to change the behavior other than by writing more code
A specific library that had to be licensed
A fixed order of method calls that was decided at compile time for every duck in the whole program
A single species of duck for the whole program
optionExplain: Right: relying on an implementation locks it in.
No licensing is involved in the authors' description.
Order of calls is not the issue they raise.
Species are not limited by this problem.
questions.explain: The authors define the lock-in as relying on one implementation, either inherited or in the subclass.
questions.rule: Relying on an implementation locks you into it.
questions.teaches: The new design moves the choice of implementation out of the class code and into the object assigned at runtime.

questions.q: A navigation app computes routes. Today it uses a FastestRoute class. Walking and cycling routes will follow. A developer declares the route variable as type FastestRoute. What does the second principle suggest?
options: Keep FastestRoute, and add if-statements for walking and cycling routes
Declare it as Object, so anything fits
Declare it as a general Route type so other routes can be used later
Keep FastestRoute and copy it for each new route type
optionExplain: Each new type adds another branch in the app.
Object is too general: it says nothing the app can call.
Right: a general route type keeps the app open to new route classes.
Copies repeat the duplication that the design avoids.
questions.explain: A useful supertype is general enough to hold every variant, yet specific enough for the code to call.
questions.rule: Pick a supertype the code can call.
questions.teaches: The supertype must declare the methods the client calls; a type that is too general, such as Object, gives the client nothing to call.

questions.q: True or false: under the second principle, it is the behavior classes, not the Duck classes, that implement FlyBehavior and QuackBehavior.
questions.explain: In the new design the behavior classes implement the behavior interfaces. The Duck classes hold a reference typed as the interface.
questions.rule: Behavior classes implement the behavior interface; ducks hold a reference to it.

questions.q: True or false: programming to an interface is possible only by using the Java keyword interface.
questions.explain: The word interface has two meanings, and the principle is about the concept. An abstract class can also serve as the supertype. The card next sets out both meanings.
questions.rule: The principle is about supertypes, not a keyword.

questions.q: According to the authors, program to an interface really means program to a what?
options: A supertype
A Java keyword
A concrete implementation
A database schema
optionExplain: Right: the declared type should be a supertype.
The keyword is only one way to express a supertype.
That is the opposite of the principle.
Databases are not in this principle.
questions.explain: The authors rephrase the principle as program to a supertype.
questions.rule: Program to a supertype.

questions.q: A team writes an abstract class Logger with a write() method, and subclasses FileLogger and ScreenLogger. The app holds its logger in a variable typed Logger. Is the team programming to an interface?
options: No: only a Java interface keyword counts
No: abstract classes always depend on an implementation, so the supertype does not count
Yes: the variable is typed with a supertype, even though no Java interface is used
Yes, but only if the class Logger has no methods
optionExplain: That reads interface as only the Java construct, which the authors say is too narrow.
An abstract class defines a type that subclasses fill in; code that holds it is not tied to one subclass.
Right: an abstract class is a supertype, so the principle is met.
A supertype that declares nothing would be of no use to the client.
questions.explain: What matters is the declared type, not which language construct provides it.
questions.rule: An abstract class can be the supertype.

questions.q: Which of these declared types follow the advice program to a supertype for a variable that will hold any kind of Shape? Select all that apply.
options: Shape, an abstract class
Shape, a Java interface
Circle, a concrete class
Circle, a concrete class, with a cast whenever another shape is used
optionExplain: Right: an abstract class is a supertype.
Right: a Java interface is a supertype.
A concrete class locks the variable to one shape and its subclasses.
A cast hides the lock-in behind extra code; the variable is still typed to a concrete class.
questions.explain: Both an abstract class and a Java interface can serve; a concrete class cannot, since the variable would not accept other shapes.
questions.rule: Declare the variable with the supertype.
questions.teaches: Choosing between an abstract class and a Java interface as the supertype is a separate decision from the principle; either satisfies it.

questions.q: A bakery system has a class Oven with a heat() method. A developer declares a variable of type ConvectionOven because that is what the bakery owns. The bakery plans to add a wood-fired oven. What does the principle advise?
options: Keep ConvectionOven, and create a separate copy of that class for the wood-fired oven
Declare the variable as the general Oven type, so any oven class can be assigned
Remove the type, so the variable holds anything
Keep ConvectionOven until the new oven arrives, then decide
optionExplain: The copy duplicates what the supertype would share.
Right: the general type lets the new oven be added without touching the declaring code.
Holding anything leaves the system with nothing to call.
Waiting means changing the declaring code later, which the principle is meant to avoid.
questions.explain: Choose the supertype when the declaration is written, so later additions need no changes to it.
questions.rule: Choose the supertype at declaration time.
questions.teaches: The cost of choosing a concrete type is paid later, at the moment a second implementation shows up.

questions.q: Sort each declaration for a variable that holds a payment method: does it program to a supertype, or to an implementation?

items.t: PaymentMethod pay, where PaymentMethod is an abstract class
PaymentMethod pay, where PaymentMethod is a Java interface
CreditCard pay, where CreditCard is a concrete class
PayPalAccount pay, where PayPalAccount is a concrete class

questions.explain: The first two declarations accept any payment class. The last two lock the variable to one concrete class.
questions.rule: Look at the declared type, not the language keyword.

questions.q: A variable is declared with a general type, and the program picks which concrete object goes into it while running. What can the code that uses the variable depend on?
options: The exact class of the object, learned by checking each time
The order in which the objects were created
The memory address of the object
Only what the general type promises, not the actual class
optionExplain: Checking the class puts the dependency back in.
Creation order is irrelevant to the call.
Addresses are not part of the interface.
Right: the code uses the promised methods and nothing more.
questions.explain: That is what lets the actual object vary. The card next shows an example with animals.
questions.rule: Rely only on what the supertype promises.

questions.q: In the authors' example, the call animal.makeSound() works on whatever concrete ____ the variable holds.
questions.explain: The variable's type is Animal, and the object assigned can be a Dog, a Cat or another animal.
questions.rule: The object behind the variable is chosen apart from the code.

questions.q: A shape-drawing program has a variable typed Shape and calls draw() on it. A menu lets the user choose Circle, Square or Triangle, and the program assigns that object to the variable. What does the drawing code need to know?
options: Only that the object responds to draw()
Which of the three shapes the user chose
The number of shapes in the menu
How the circle computes its outline
optionExplain: Right: the call goes to whichever shape was assigned.
The point of the supertype is that this is not needed.
The menu size does not matter to a draw call.
Each shape handles its own outline.
questions.explain: The object is chosen at runtime; the calling code stays the same.
questions.rule: Call through the supertype and let the object decide.

questions.q: In the example, animal.makeSound() is called on a variable typed Animal that holds a Dog. Which object's version of makeSound() runs?
options: The Animal class's version, since the variable is typed Animal
No version runs, as the variable type and object do not match
The Dog's version, since the actual object decides
Both, one after the other
optionExplain: The type of the variable limits what can be called, not whose version runs.
A Dog is an Animal, so the types fit.
Right: the call is resolved on the object, not on the variable's type.
A single call runs a single method.
questions.explain: This is polymorphism: the same call, but a different behavior for each actual object.
questions.rule: The object, not the variable type, picks the version that runs.
questions.teaches: Polymorphism means one call on a supertype variable can run different code depending on the object it holds.

questions.q: A stock-trading app holds its pricing in a variable typed PriceSource. At startup it assigns either LivePrices or TestPrices. A developer adds code that checks which of the two is held and runs different calls for each. What is the effect?
options: It improves flexibility by making each case explicit and easy to read in one place
It is required for the supertype to work
It has no effect, since both implement PriceSource
It brings back the dependence on the concrete class that the supertype removed
optionExplain: Explicit cases look careful but must be edited for every new source.
The supertype works without any such check.
The check itself ties the code to the two classes.
Right: checking the class makes the calling code depend on the implementation again.
questions.explain: The benefit of the supertype is lost if the caller asks which implementation it has.
questions.rule: Do not ask the variable what it holds.
questions.teaches: Code that asks what class an object is, and acts on the answer, undoes the independence that a supertype gives.

questions.q: True or false: with the variable animal typed as Animal, the code may call bark(), since the object assigned is a Dog.
questions.explain: The variable's type limits the calls. bark() belongs to Dog, not to Animal, so only the methods declared on Animal, such as makeSound(), may be called through animal.
questions.rule: The variable type sets what may be called.

questions.q: A duck design needs a new way of flying. Which approach lets a developer add it without touching the existing flying code or the Duck classes?
options: Edit the Duck superclass to include the new flying
Write a new class that implements the shared flying interface
Add an if-statement to each existing flying class
Copy the closest existing flying class and edit the copy inside every duck
optionExplain: Editing the superclass touches all ducks, the problem from the start.
Right: a new class behind the interface leaves everything existing as it was.
Editing the flying classes changes code that works.
Copying inside every duck reintroduces duplicated code.
questions.explain: A new class adds without editing. The card next sets out why the new design allows it.
questions.rule: Add a variant with a new class.

questions.q: A class that adds rocket-powered flying to the app would implement the ____ interface.
questions.explain: Each concrete flying behavior is a class that implements FlyBehavior.
questions.rule: A new variant implements the behavior interface.

questions.q: A game has a Character class and a DamageRule interface. Fire, Ice and Poison are classes implementing it. A designer wants Lightning damage. What is the change?
options: Edit Fire, Ice and Poison so each can produce lightning damage
Add a lightning method to Character and each subclass
Make DamageRule a class and put Lightning inside it
Write one Lightning class implementing DamageRule
optionExplain: Existing variants should not change when a new one is added.
Spreading the new code across Character and subclasses is the old design.
Moving Lightning into the interface loses the separation.
Right: Lightning is a new variant, so it gets a new class.
questions.explain: One new class, no edits: the interface stays and the existing classes stay.
questions.rule: A new variant is a new class.

questions.q: True or false: a behavior class can hold state, such as a flying behavior with a maximum altitude and a speed.
questions.explain: The authors point out that a behavior is still a thing with state and methods. A flying behavior can keep instance variables for wing beats, altitude and speed.
questions.rule: A behavior class can hold its own state.
questions.teaches: A behavior class can carry settings of its own, so two variants of one behavior can differ in values as well as code.

questions.q: A toy company makes squeaky toys that are not ducks: a rubber frog and a rubber mouse. Its code has a Squeak behavior class like the one in the card. Which statement describes the benefit?
options: The toys can use Squeak without inheriting from Duck
The toys must become subclasses of Duck to use Squeak
Squeak can be used only by ducks whose fly behavior is set
Each toy needs its own copy of Squeak
optionExplain: Right: Squeak does not depend on Duck, so any object can use it.
Forcing a subclass relationship is the inheritance baggage the design avoids.
Quack and fly behaviors are independent of each other.
A copy per toy is the duplication the design avoids.
questions.explain: When behaviors stand outside their original owner, unrelated types can reuse them.
questions.rule: A free-standing behavior can serve unrelated types.
questions.teaches: Behavior classes can be reused by objects unrelated to Duck, because they depend only on the behavior interface.

questions.q: Rocket-powered flying is added to the app. Sort each class: must it be edited, or can it stay untouched?

items.t: The new FlyRocketPowered class
The existing FlyWithWings class
The existing MallardDuck class
The Duck superclass
The existing Squeak class

questions.explain: Only the new class is written. Existing behavior and duck classes are unchanged, since they depend on the interface, not on the new class.
questions.rule: Adding a variant should edit nothing that exists.

questions.q: A Duck should fly, but the flying code lives in another class. What should the Duck's flying method do?
options: Contain the flying code itself, copied from that class
Check the species name and then choose a block of code
Forward the request to the flying object it holds
Return nothing, and let callers find the flying class
optionExplain: Copying the code defeats the purpose of moving it out.
A species check ties the Duck to each species.
Right: the Duck passes the work to its flying object.
Callers should not need to know about the helper at all.
questions.explain: Handing the job to a held object is delegation. The card next shows how the Duck is built for it.
questions.rule: Forward the work.

questions.q: performQuack() lets the object referenced by quackBehavior ____ for the Duck.
questions.explain: The Duck forwards the call, and the referenced behavior object does the quacking.
questions.rule: The held object does the work.

questions.q: Put these steps in a sensible order for building the delegating Duck.
items: Declare flyBehavior and quackBehavior as interface-typed variables in Duck
Remove fly() and quack() from Duck and its subclasses
Add performFly() and performQuack() that forward to the variables
Set each subclass to reference the behavior objects it wants
questions.explain: The variables come first so there is something to forward to, then the old methods go, the new forwarding methods are added, and last each duck chooses its behaviors.
questions.rule: Variables first, then forwarding, then assignment.

questions.q: A Duck's performFly() forwards to flyBehavior. What does the Duck need to know about the object in flyBehavior?
options: Its exact class, so that the right method can be chosen at the call
Only that it implements FlyBehavior and knows how to fly
Whether it was created before or after the Duck
How many wing beats per minute it uses
optionExplain: Knowing the class would tie the Duck to it.
Right: the interface type is enough to forward the call.
Creation order plays no part in the call.
Wing-beat detail stays inside the behavior.
questions.explain: The Duck's code depends on the interface, so the held object can be replaced.
questions.rule: Depend on what the interface declares, nothing more.
questions.teaches: Because the Duck knows only the interface, a behavior object can be swapped for another without changing the Duck's code.

questions.q: A smart-home Alarm class used to contain its own ringing code. Its designer moves ringing into RingBehavior classes and gives Alarm a variable of that type. What should Alarm's trigger() method do?
options: Call ring() on the object held in its RingBehavior variable
Check which alarm model it is and run the matching code for it
Contain a loop that plays a sound file directly
Call the constructor of RingBehavior each time
optionExplain: Right: trigger() forwards to the held behavior.
A model check ties the Alarm to each model.
Direct sound code is the old design again.
Creating the behavior on every trigger loses the chosen behavior.
questions.explain: Any class can delegate in this way: one variable, one forwarding call.
questions.rule: One typed variable, one forwarding call.
questions.teaches: A class that delegates keeps the same outward behavior while the how is held in a replaceable object.

questions.q: True or false: after the redesign, the Duck class still contains the code that makes a duck fly.
questions.explain: The flying code lives in the FlyBehavior classes. Duck keeps only performFly(), which forwards to its flyBehavior variable.
questions.rule: The Duck forwards; the behavior class implements.

questions.q: A MallardDuck should start life flying with wings and quacking normally. Where could its starting behaviors be set?
options: In the FlyBehavior interface, which stores the starting choice for every duck
In its constructor, which assigns behavior objects to its two variables
In the QuackBehavior interface, with a flag for the species
In the Duck class, with the same behaviors for every duck
optionExplain: Interfaces hold no data like this.
Right: the constructor of the specific duck can assign the objects.
A flag in the interface reintroduces species checks.
That would give every duck the same behavior.
questions.explain: A constructor is a natural place for a starting choice. The card next shows the authors' MallardDuck.
questions.rule: Constructors set starting behaviors.

questions.q: MallardDuck's constructor assigns its flyBehavior an instance of ____.
questions.explain: The mallard flies with wings, so its flyBehavior becomes a FlyWithWings object.
questions.rule: A mallard gets FlyWithWings.

questions.q: A Chat app's Message class holds a SendBehavior variable. The constructor of TextMessage assigns new SmsSender(). Which statement is true of this design?
options: The message can never use any sender other than SmsSender
The variable's type is SmsSender, so only that class fits
The starting choice is fixed in code, though the variable could later hold another sender
The constructor makes the choice at runtime from user input, so no sender is fixed in code
optionExplain: The interface type allows other senders to be assigned later.
The variable is typed to the interface, not to SmsSender.
Right: the constructor names a concrete class, but the variable is typed to the interface.
The code is written in the constructor, with no user input.
questions.explain: Starting with a hard-coded choice is not the same as being stuck with it.
questions.rule: The variable type, not the constructor, keeps options open.

questions.q: The authors say the constructor approach is a poor way to initialize. What is the weakness they mean?
options: The concrete class is named in the code, so the starting choice cannot be changed without editing it
It makes the duck unable to fly
It allows only one duck to be created
It prevents any behavior from being replaced later
optionExplain: Right: new Quack() in the constructor names a concrete class.
The duck flies; the weakness is about flexibility.
Any number of ducks can be created.
Later replacement is still possible through the variable's type.
questions.explain: Hard-coding an instantiation is a smaller form of programming to an implementation.
questions.rule: Naming a concrete class ties the code to it.
questions.teaches: Even when variables are typed to an interface, a hard-coded new for a concrete class in the code brings back a link to an implementation.

questions.q: A thermostat object starts with a heating schedule created by new WinterSchedule() inside its constructor. The owner wants to change to a summer schedule on 1 June without recompiling. What does the card's reasoning suggest?
options: The constructor should be rewritten for each season
The thermostat should be replaced each season
The WinterSchedule class should be edited to include summer rules
The variable should be typed to a general schedule interface so another schedule can be assigned
optionExplain: Rewriting the constructor each season is the very rework the design avoids.
Replacement of the whole object is more than the change needs.
Editing the winter class mixes seasons in one place.
Right: the interface type allows a different object to be assigned at runtime.
questions.explain: The starting choice is only a starting point if the variable accepts other implementations.
questions.rule: Type the variable to the interface so the starting choice can change.
questions.teaches: The next idea shows the missing piece: a setter method lets the behavior be replaced after construction.

questions.q: True or false: because the constructor chooses Quack, a mallard's quackBehavior variable can hold only Quack objects.
questions.explain: The variable is typed QuackBehavior, so any class that implements that interface can be assigned to it, such as Squeak or MuteQuack.
questions.rule: The variable's type decides what it can hold.

questions.q: A team builds a test program with one quack interface and three classes that implement it, each printing a different sound. What must the code that calls them know?
options: The name of each class and its sound
The order in which the classes were written
Which class prints the loudest sound
Only the interface they share
optionExplain: Knowing each class would tie the caller to it.
Writing order is irrelevant.
Loudness plays no role.
Right: the shared interface is enough to call each.
questions.explain: The caller depends on one interface, not on each class. The card next lists the duck classes.
questions.rule: Call through the shared interface.

questions.q: Match each quack behavior class to what it does when quack() runs.
questions.explain: Quack makes the normal sound, Squeak the squeak, and MuteQuack a silence message instead of a sound.
questions.rule: Each class implements the same method in its own way.

questions.q: A duck's quackBehavior holds a MuteQuack object. A tester calls performQuack() on that duck. What is printed?
options: Quack, since the Duck's default is Quack
The silence message from MuteQuack
Squeak, since it is the next class in the list
Nothing at all, since MuteQuack has no method
optionExplain: There is no default; the duck uses whatever object it holds.
Right: the Duck forwards the call to the MuteQuack object it holds.
List order does not choose behavior.
MuteQuack does implement quack(); its version prints the silence message.
questions.explain: Whichever object is referenced decides what is printed.
questions.rule: The held object decides the output.

questions.q: A developer must add a Honk quack behavior to the test program. Which of these is needed?
options: A new Honk class that implements QuackBehavior
A change to the Quack class
A change to the Duck class and to MallardDuck as well
A change to the QuackBehavior interface
optionExplain: Right: the new class is all that is needed.
Quack is unaffected by a new behavior.
Duck and MallardDuck depend on the interface only.
The interface already declares quack(); it need not change.
questions.explain: A new behavior is a new class; no existing class changes.
questions.rule: Add by creating, not by editing.
questions.teaches: This is the open-for-extension idea at work: a new behavior is added by creating a class, not by changing a working one.

questions.q: A language-learning app has a Quiz class using a Hint interface, with classes FirstLetterHint, TranslationHint and NoHint. The team wants a new AudioHint. Which statement is accurate?
options: Quiz must be edited to recognise AudioHint
NoHint must be edited to allow audio
AudioHint implements Hint, and Quiz and the other hints stay as they are
Hint must be turned into a class that also contains AudioHint as a nested type
optionExplain: Quiz depends on the interface only, so it need not recognise a new class.
NoHint is a separate variant and has no link to the new one.
Right: the new class is added and nothing else is edited.
Folding a variant into the interface removes the separation.
questions.explain: The pattern works in any domain with a family of behaviors behind an interface.
questions.rule: A family behind an interface grows by addition.
questions.teaches: Extending a design by adding code, rather than changing code, keeps the working parts safe from new bugs.

questions.q: True or false: if a tester gives a duck a Squeak object in place of Quack, the Duck class's code must change to print the squeak.
questions.explain: The Duck forwards the call to whichever object it holds. A Squeak object prints Squeak with no change to Duck.
questions.rule: Swapping the held object changes the output without changing the Duck.

questions.q: A duck that cannot fly is later given a rocket pack in the middle of the simulation. Which design makes that straightforward?
options: A method that lets the duck's flying behavior be replaced by another object
A new subclass created for rocket ducks only
An if-statement in fly() that checks the clock
A restart of the program with a new Duck class that includes the rocket pack
optionExplain: Right: replacing the held behavior changes what the duck does.
A new subclass cannot turn an existing object into a different class.
A clock check adds a special case instead of letting the behavior vary.
Restarting loses the point of changing while running.
questions.explain: A setter makes the held behavior replaceable. The card next shows the authors' ModelDuck.
questions.rule: Let the behavior be replaced by a setter.

questions.q: To change a duck's behavior at runtime, call the duck's ____ method for that behavior.
questions.explain: The Duck class gains setter methods for the fly and quack behaviors.
questions.rule: Use a setter to replace behavior.

questions.q: In a game, a Character holds a MoveBehavior. After picking up skates, the character should glide. What should the game do?
options: Create a new character class called SkatingCharacter for the game
Call the character's setter with a new GlideMove object
Edit the WalkMove class so it glides
Remove the MoveBehavior variable
optionExplain: A new class cannot change an existing character object.
Right: the setter replaces the held behavior.
Editing WalkMove changes every character that walks.
Without the variable the character has no behavior to delegate.
questions.explain: The character keeps its identity while its behavior is replaced.
questions.rule: Replace the held object to change behavior.

questions.q: A game has three Character objects of the same class, all holding WalkMove. The code calls the setter on one of them with GlideMove. What do the other two do?
options: They glide too, since all three share the same class and so the same behavior
They stop moving until reset
They keep walking, since the setter changed only one object
They throw an error
optionExplain: Class membership does not link the held behavior of separate objects.
Their held behavior is untouched.
Right: the setter changes the reference held by that one object.
Nothing has failed for them.
questions.explain: Behavior belongs to the object that holds it, not to the class.
questions.rule: Behavior is per object.
questions.teaches: Because each object holds its own reference, behavior can differ between two objects of the same class and can change independently.

questions.q: A music player has a PlaybackMode variable. A user taps Shuffle. A developer proposes creating a new Player class for shuffle mode. Which reasoning fits the card?
options: Replace the Player object with an instance of a new class built for shuffle mode
Edit the Player class to hold both modes
Restart the player when the mode changes
Keep the Player and replace its PlaybackMode object with a ShuffleMode object
optionExplain: Replacing the whole object loses its state, such as the queue.
Holding both modes inside the Player reintroduces mode checks.
A restart is unnecessary when the held object can be replaced.
Right: the Player stays the same, and only the held behavior changes.
questions.explain: State such as a queue stays with the object while the behavior is replaced.
questions.rule: Replace the behavior, keep the object.
questions.teaches: Swapping the behavior object preserves the owner's other state, which replacing the owner would lose.

questions.q: True or false: a new FlyRocketPowered behavior can be given to a duck through the setter only if the Duck class is first edited to know about FlyRocketPowered.
questions.explain: The setter accepts any object that implements the FlyBehavior interface. The Duck class needs no edit to accept the new class.
questions.rule: The setter's parameter type is the interface, not a concrete class.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: Which set of classes is best described as different ways of doing the same job?
options: A class that stores users, one that prints invoices and one that sends email
A class for ducks, one for rubber ducks and one for decoys
Several classes, each computing sales tax by a different state's rule
A class for the user interface and one for the database
optionExplain: These classes do three different jobs.
These are kinds of things, not ways of doing one job.
Right: each class does the same job, computing tax, in its own way.
These cover two different jobs.
questions.explain: A family has one job and many ways. The card next uses the authors' term, family of algorithms.
questions.rule: A family means one job, many ways.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: The authors suggest thinking of the duck behaviors as a family of ____.
questions.explain: Different ways of flying and quacking are algorithms for the same job.
questions.rule: Think in terms of algorithms.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: A travel site computes ticket prices. Sort each item: could it be a member of a family of algorithms for calculating a fare, or does it do a different job?

items.t: Fare by distance
Fare by time of day
Fare with a student discount
Sending the ticket by email
Drawing the seat map
Checking passport numbers

questions.explain: A member computes a fare in a different way. Emailing, drawing and checking passports are other jobs with their own interfaces.
questions.rule: A family shares the job, not just a subject.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: A design has FareByDistance and FareByTime classes behind a Fare interface. The code that asks for a fare is told to use the FareByTime class in the morning. What does this show about the members of the family?
options: They can stand in for each other, since they share the same job and interface
They must be rewritten whenever the time of day changes in the running program
They cannot be changed once the code starts
They must be subclasses of each other
optionExplain: Right: interchangeability is what makes it a family.
Switching does not require rewriting.
The swap is possible, since both implement the interface.
They are siblings behind an interface, not subclasses of each other.
questions.explain: Interchangeability follows from a shared interface and a shared job.
questions.rule: Family members are interchangeable.
questions.teaches: The interface for a family should describe the job in a way that does not mention how any one member does it.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: A recipe app has three classes: BoilVegetables, SteamVegetables and RoastVegetables, all implementing a Cook interface with prepare(). It also has a class ShoppingList. Which belongs in the family of algorithms with the three cooking classes?
options: ShoppingList, since it also handles vegetables
A MenuPrinter class that prints recipe titles
A UserLogin class that checks passwords
A new FryVegetables class implementing Cook
optionExplain: Sharing the topic of vegetables is not sharing the job.
Printing titles is a different job.
Logging in is unrelated.
Right: Fry is another way of doing the same job.
questions.explain: Look for the shared job, not the shared subject.
questions.rule: Judge membership by the job done.
questions.teaches: A shared subject is not enough to make a family; the test is whether one member could replace another for the same caller.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: True or false: a class that calculates sales tax could join the family of algorithms of the duck behaviors, since both are algorithms.
questions.explain: The two do different jobs, so they cannot stand in for each other for any caller. Each belongs to a family of its own.
questions.rule: A family is defined by a shared job.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: A Car class contains a variable referring to an Engine object. How is the link from Car to Engine best described?
options: An IS-A link: the Car is an Engine
A HAS-A link: the Car holds an Engine
An IMPLEMENTS link: the Car carries out the Engine
No link, since the Engine is a separate class
optionExplain: A car is not a kind of engine.
Right: holding a reference is HAS-A.
IMPLEMENTS applies to a class carrying out an interface.
The variable creates a link between the two classes.
questions.explain: Holding a reference is HAS-A. The card next sets out all three links.
questions.rule: A held reference is HAS-A.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: Match each link in the duck design to its relationship.
questions.explain: Extending a class is IS-A, holding a reference is HAS-A, and carrying out an interface is IMPLEMENTS.
questions.rule: Name each arrow by its relationship.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: In a music app, a Playlist holds a SortRule. AlphabeticalSort carries out SortRule. A WorkoutPlaylist extends Playlist. Which pairing is right?
options: WorkoutPlaylist HAS-A Playlist, Playlist IS-A SortRule, AlphabeticalSort IMPLEMENTS Playlist
WorkoutPlaylist IMPLEMENTS Playlist, Playlist HAS-A AlphabeticalSort, SortRule IS-A AlphabeticalSort
WorkoutPlaylist IS-A SortRule, Playlist IMPLEMENTS SortRule, AlphabeticalSort HAS-A Playlist
WorkoutPlaylist IS-A Playlist, Playlist HAS-A SortRule, AlphabeticalSort IMPLEMENTS SortRule
optionExplain: The first and second links reverse the direction of the relationships.
Playlist holds a SortRule, not the other way round, and the interface does not extend its implementer.
A workout playlist is not a sort rule, and the links are mixed.
Right: each link follows its keyword: extends, holds, carries out.
questions.explain: Match the keyword to the relationship: extends is IS-A, holds is HAS-A, implements is IMPLEMENTS.
questions.rule: Keyword decides relationship.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: In the class diagram, which arrow label would be wrong for the link between Duck and FlyBehavior?
options: IS-A, since a Duck is not a kind of FlyBehavior
HAS-A, since a Duck holds a FlyBehavior
HAS-A, since the Duck delegates flying to it
HAS-A, since the Duck is composed with a behavior
optionExplain: Right: IS-A would say a Duck is a FlyBehavior, which it is not.
This label is correct.
Delegation is carried out through a HAS-A link.
Being composed with a behavior is HAS-A.
questions.explain: To test a link, say it aloud: a Duck is a FlyBehavior? A Duck has a FlyBehavior?
questions.rule: Say it aloud to test the link.
questions.teaches: Reading the link in a sentence, with is a or has a, is a quick test for whether the relationship is right.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: A bank's code has an Account class and a StatementFormat interface. Someone writes Account IS-A StatementFormat so the account can print itself. What does the three-link vocabulary suggest?
options: The link is fine, since an account prints statements
The link should be IMPLEMENTS, since both are part of the bank's own code
The link should be HAS-A: an Account holds a StatementFormat object
No link is needed, since printing is simple
optionExplain: Printing statements does not make an account a format.
IMPLEMENTS means carrying out an interface, which would turn the account into a format.
Right: an account is not a kind of format; it holds one.
A link is needed for the account to use the format.
questions.explain: Use HAS-A when one object uses another to do a job.
questions.rule: Use HAS-A for a used helper.
questions.teaches: IS-A claims the two things are the same kind of thing; choosing it for a helper gives the class the helper's whole interface.

questions.section: The Big Picture on encapsulated behaviors
questions.q: True or false: FlyWithWings carries out the FlyBehavior interface, so the link between them is HAS-A.
questions.explain: Carrying out an interface is IMPLEMENTS. HAS-A is the link between Duck and the behavior it holds.
questions.rule: Implements carries out; has-a holds.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A car gets its stopping behavior from a brakes object that it holds, rather than from a parent class. What is this technique called?
options: Composition
Inheritance
Overloading
Serialization
optionExplain: Right: getting behavior from held objects is composition.
Inheritance would take the behavior from a parent class.
Overloading means several methods with one name.
Serialization means turning objects into data.
questions.explain: Putting objects together this way has a name. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Composition is behavior from held objects.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Instead of inheriting their behavior, the ducks get it by being ____ with the right behavior object.
questions.explain: Being composed with a behavior object is composition.
questions.rule: Composed with the right object.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Which designs use composition? Select all that apply.
options: A Camera holds a FlashBehavior and calls it when a photo is taken
A Camera extends FlashCamera to receive its flash code
A Printer holds a PaperTray object and asks it for pages
A Printer copies the tray code into its own methods
optionExplain: Right: behavior comes from a held object.
That is inheritance, not composition.
Right: the printer uses a held tray.
That is duplication, not composition.
questions.explain: Composition means holding other objects and delegating to them.
questions.rule: Composition means holding objects.
questions.hint: Look for a held object that does the work.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A class gets its behavior through composition from an object typed to an interface. Which change is possible for this class that is difficult with inheritance?
options: Giving the class more methods than the parent class it would have inherited from
Replacing the behavior of an existing object while the program runs
Declaring the class abstract
Compiling the class without its parent
optionExplain: Adding methods is possible with inheritance.
Right: the held part can be swapped, and an inherited behavior cannot.
Abstract classes are an inheritance feature.
Compilation needs its parent whether through inheritance or not.
questions.explain: Held parts can be replaced; inherited parts are fixed by the class definition.
questions.rule: Held parts are replaceable.
questions.teaches: Composition moves the choice of behavior from class-definition time to object-creation or runtime.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A video-game enemy class gets its attack moves by extending MeleeEnemy or RangedEnemy. The designers want an enemy that switches from melee to ranged when its health drops. Which direction does the card point?
options: Add a third subclass, MeleeThenRangedEnemy
Make MeleeEnemy extend RangedEnemy
Give the enemy an AttackBehavior object that can be replaced
Create a new enemy object each time its health drops below a limit
optionExplain: A third subclass fixes one combination in the code.
Chaining classes mixes behaviors together without a switch.
Right: composition lets one object switch behavior.
A new object loses the state of the old one.
questions.explain: Switching during a life of one object calls for held, replaceable behavior.
questions.rule: Switching calls for composition.
questions.teaches: Behavior that must change during an object's life belongs in a held part, not in its class.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: True or false: composition means an object gets behavior by holding another object and delegating to it.
questions.explain: Composition means the object holds another object and delegates to it. Inheritance is the mechanism by which a class receives code from a superclass.
questions.rule: Composition holds; inheritance receives.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A designer must pick between inheritance and composition to give an object a behavior that may need to change later. Which will the authors favor?
options: Inheritance, since the child receives the code for free
Neither; behavior should be copied into each class
Whichever has fewer lines of code
Composition, since the held object can be replaced
optionExplain: Inheritance fixes the behavior in the class definition.
Copying is what both designs aim to avoid.
Line count is not a design principle.
Right: the authors favor composition for this reason.
questions.explain: Replaceable parts make change easier. The card next states the third principle.
questions.rule: Prefer replaceable parts.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: The third design principle: favor ____ over inheritance.
questions.explain: Composition is favored because it gives more flexibility.
questions.rule: Favor composition.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Which are benefits the authors give for favoring composition? Select all that apply.
options: A family of algorithms can be encapsulated into its own set of classes
A duck's behavior can be changed at runtime
Subclasses no longer exist in the program
Every pattern in the book uses only composition
optionExplain: Right: this is the first benefit named.
Right: a held part can be replaced when the object implements the right interface.
The duck design still has MallardDuck extending Duck.
The authors say composition appears in many patterns, not all of them.
questions.explain: The authors name encapsulating a family of algorithms and changing behavior at runtime.
questions.rule: Composition encapsulates families and allows runtime change.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: The authors write that composition is used in many patterns and its advantages and disadvantages will appear through the book. What does this tell you about the principle?
options: It is a leaning, with costs to weigh, not a ban on inheritance
It has no disadvantages at all, so it can be applied everywhere in a design
It is correct only for ducks
It replaces the first principle
optionExplain: Right: the word favor signals a preference with trade-offs.
The authors mention disadvantages explicitly.
They present it as a general principle.
It builds on the first principle rather than replacing it.
questions.explain: Design principles are leanings that need judgment.
questions.rule: A principle is a leaning, not a law.
questions.teaches: Design principles express preferences to be weighed against costs, not rules that settle every case.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A spreadsheet has a Cell class with subclasses NumberCell, DateCell and TextCell. Each inherits its own display code. Users want to switch a cell's display between plain and compact at any time. What does the third principle suggest?
options: Add PlainNumberCell, CompactNumberCell and similar subclasses for every pair
Give Cell a DisplayBehavior object that can be replaced, instead of subclassing each display style
Make DisplayBehavior a subclass of Cell
Add an if-statement to every Cell subclass
optionExplain: Subclass pairs multiply with each new type and style.
Right: composition lets one cell swap its display.
A behavior is not a kind of cell.
Branches in every subclass duplicate the switch.
questions.explain: Two independent variations call for composition, not a subclass for each combination.
questions.rule: Combine independent variations by composition.
questions.teaches: Inheritance multiplies classes when two independent choices vary together; composition combines them by holding one part per choice.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: True or false: the third principle is a preference that leaves room for inheritance where it fits.
questions.explain: The principle says to favor composition, which is a preference. The duck design keeps MallardDuck extending Duck.
questions.rule: Favor does not mean forbid.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Over the life of a program, when is most of the time spent?
options: Before any code is written, on planning and drawing designs
During the first month of coding
After the first release, on maintenance and change
On the final week of testing
optionExplain: Planning is a small part of the life of a program.
The first coding stretch is short compared with the years of upkeep.
Right: the authors' master says most time goes to maintaining and changing software.
Testing before release is brief against years of maintenance.
questions.explain: Most of a program's life is spent after the first release. The card next sets out the authors' dialogue.
questions.rule: Maintenance dominates.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: According to the master, software receives more time for maintaining and changing than for initial ____.
questions.explain: Maintenance exceeds initial development in the master's account.
questions.rule: Maintenance outweighs initial development.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: Two teams build a checkout module. Team A copies a tax routine into four products, saving a week. Team B puts it in one class the four products use. A tax law then changes. According to the authors' reasoning, which result is expected?
options: Team A is faster, since it saved time at the start
Team B changes one place, and Team A must change four
Both teams make the same number of edits
Team B must change four places, since each product differs
optionExplain: The head start in week one is outweighed by upkeep.
Right: maintenance cost decides, and copies multiply it.
Copies mean more places to edit.
One class means one place to edit.
questions.explain: Judging by maintenance changes which design looks cheaper.
questions.rule: Count the cost of change, not just the first build.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: The master does not tell the student to give up reuse. What does he suggest instead?
options: Drop object-oriented design altogether
Stop writing reusable code
Rewrite all code each time it is needed
Think more about inheritance, because there are other ways of achieving reuse
optionExplain: The dialogue never questions object-oriented design itself.
Reuse remains an aim in the dialogue.
Rewriting each time is the opposite of reuse.
Right: reuse is still wanted, by means that are easier to maintain.
questions.explain: The problem is the route to reuse, not the goal.
questions.rule: Keep reuse; pick a route that is easy to maintain.
questions.teaches: Composition is offered as a way to reach reuse without paying for it in maintenance.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: A university department wants one admissions form engine reused across ten faculties. Faculty rules change each year. Which design best fits the authors' priorities?
options: Keep each faculty's rules in separate replaceable classes behind one interface
Copy the engine into each faculty and then edit that copy there as rules change
Build one giant class with a branch for each faculty
Reuse the engine unchanged and ignore faculty rules
optionExplain: Right: reuse of the engine plus easy change of the rules.
Copies make yearly changes costly.
A giant class with branches makes every change risky.
Ignoring rules does not meet the faculties' needs.
questions.explain: Reuse and maintainability can both be met by separating what changes.
questions.rule: Separate what changes to reuse the rest.
questions.teaches: Reuse and easy change are not opposed: separating the changing part lets the stable part be reused unchanged.

questions.section: HAS-A can be better than IS-A
questions.q: True or false: the master points out that there are ways of achieving reuse other than inheritance.
questions.explain: The master says inheritance has problems and that there are other ways of achieving reuse. He does not dismiss reuse.
questions.rule: Reuse matters, but not above maintainability.

questions.q: A navigation app can find a route by fastest time, shortest distance or fewest tolls. The app should switch between them freely without changing the screen code. Which description fits?
options: One routing class with an if-statement for each option
Several interchangeable routing algorithms, each in its own class, used by a screen that holds one
A routing subclass for each screen in the app
A routing library that the screen copies and edits
optionExplain: Branches in one class are hard to extend and test.
Right: this is the shape of the Strategy Pattern.
Subclasses per screen duplicate the algorithms.
Copied code drifts apart.
questions.explain: This is the problem the Strategy Pattern solves. The card next gives the authors' definition.
questions.rule: Interchangeable algorithms in their own classes.

questions.q: Match each part of the Strategy definition to the part of the duck design.
pairs: The set of fly or quack behaviors
Each behavior has its own class
questions.explain: Each phrase of the definition maps to a part of the duck design.
questions.rule: Map the definition onto the design.

questions.q: A photo app applies compression to saved images: JPEG, PNG or WebP, chosen by the user. Which design matches the Strategy Pattern?
options: A Saver class with an if-statement inside it for each format the user can choose
A Saver subclass for each format
Three separate apps, one per format
A Compressor interface with a class per format, held by the saver and swappable
optionExplain: Branches inside one class mix all the formats together.
Subclassing ties each format to a Saver class.
Separate apps duplicate everything else.
Right: a family of interchangeable algorithms, each encapsulated.
questions.explain: The saver is the client; the formats are the family.
questions.rule: Name the family, the client and the interface.

questions.q: The authors' design puzzle has Character as an abstract class and WeaponBehavior as an interface. Each character uses one weapon at a time and can change weapons. Where does setWeapon() belong?
options: In each weapon class, so that the weapon picks its owner when it is created
In the WeaponBehavior interface
In the Character superclass, so every character can switch its weapon
In a separate class that handles all switching
optionExplain: A weapon does not choose its owner.
An interface declares what a weapon does, not what a character does.
Right: the solution places setWeapon() in the Character superclass.
Putting switching elsewhere adds a class with no purpose.
questions.explain: The client holds the strategy and exposes the setter.
questions.rule: The client owns the setter.
questions.teaches: In Strategy the setter belongs on the client that holds the strategy, so the superclass of the clients can provide it once for all of them.

questions.q: A pizza shop's cashier program calculates delivery charges. Which statement describes the Strategy Pattern here?
options: Delivery charge rules are separate interchangeable classes, and the cashier code can use any of them
The cashier code has a long if-statement over delivery zones
Each zone has a subclass of Cashier
Delivery charges are hard-coded in the receipt
optionExplain: Right: separate interchangeable rules, with the cashier as the client.
Branches put every rule into one place.
Subclasses fix a rule for each cashier type.
Hard-coding leaves no variation.
questions.explain: Strategy applies to any family of rules.
questions.rule: Recognize the pattern by its parts.
questions.teaches: You can recognize a pattern by its parts: a family, a shared interface, and a client that holds one member.

questions.q: True or false: the Strategy Pattern is a library of duck classes that a developer adds to a project.
questions.explain: A pattern is a general solution to a design problem, not code to add. The developer adapts the idea to the application.
questions.rule: A pattern is an idea, not a library.

questions.q: Two builders on a site use a short trade term for a standard foundation. A newcomer asks for a full explanation. What has the pair gained from their shared vocabulary?
options: A short phrase that stands for a complete, agreed procedure
A way to hide information from the newcomer
A promise that the work will be done faster by machine
A rule that all builders talk in single words
optionExplain: Right: the vocabulary packs a whole idea into a few words.
Concealment is not the aim of a vocabulary.
Speed of machines has nothing to do with it.
Short phrases are an option, not a rule.
questions.explain: That is the benefit the diner scene illustrates. The card next tells it.
questions.rule: A shared word stands for a whole idea.

questions.q: At the diner, Flo can order briefly because she has a shared ____ with the short-order cook.
questions.explain: Flo and the cook both know the diner's terms for orders.
questions.rule: Shared terms shorten talk.

questions.q: A hospital team uses a short alert phrase when a patient's heart stops. What does this phrase do for the team?
options: It delays action until everyone has been briefed
It stands for a complete response that all staff already know
It replaces training for new staff
It forces each nurse to design a response
optionExplain: Briefing would defeat the purpose of a shared term.
Right: the phrase carries a whole procedure.
New staff must still learn the term.
The response is agreed in advance.
questions.explain: A compact term stands for a rich, agreed meaning.
questions.rule: A term stands for an agreed meaning.

questions.q: The authors say the cook has 'less to remember' when orders use the diner's terms. What does the cook hold in his head instead?
options: Every ingredient of every customer's order, said aloud
The customer's life story
The diner's patterns, which each short order stands for
A list of each customer's name
optionExplain: Spelling out ingredients is what Alice does.
Nothing in the story concerns life stories.
Right: the cook keeps the patterns, and the short term points to one.
Names do not explain how the food is made.
questions.explain: Patterns held in memory make short communication possible.
questions.rule: Memorized patterns make short orders possible.
questions.teaches: A shared vocabulary works in two directions: it shortens the speaker's words and reduces what the listener must work out.

questions.q: A choir director calls out a short Italian term and the singers go back to the start. A visitor who cannot read music hears the same phrase. What does this show about a shared vocabulary?
options: A shared vocabulary works on anyone who hears it
The term is the problem, and should be avoided
Only the director needs to know the term
Its value depends on the listener already knowing the term
optionExplain: The visitor does not know the term, so it gives nothing.
The term works well for singers who know it.
Both sides need to know it.
Right: the term helps only those who share it.
questions.explain: Using patterns with colleagues who do not know them gains nothing until they learn them.
questions.rule: A vocabulary needs both sides.
questions.teaches: A team that wants the benefit of pattern names must teach the names to those who do not yet know them.

questions.q: True or false: Alice and Flo placed different orders at the diner.
questions.explain: The authors say the two orders are the same. Alice uses twice the number of words to say it.
questions.rule: Same order, different number of words.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: A colleague says the payment methods use a named design pattern, rather than a loose group of classes. What can the pattern name tell you?
options: The exact number of lines in the code
The names of the people who wrote it
A whole design shape, with its qualities and limits
Which database holds the payments
optionExplain: Line counts are not part of a pattern's meaning.
Authors' names are not part of the pattern.
Right: a pattern name stands for a known design.
A pattern does not name a database.
questions.explain: A pattern name stands for a known design, not a single class. The card next lists what is carried.
questions.rule: Names carry whole designs.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: Patterns let you say more with ____.
questions.explain: A pattern name replaces a long description of the design.
questions.rule: Say more with less.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: A team says: our ducks use the Strategy Pattern. Which can a listener infer from that statement? Select all that apply.
options: Duck behavior is encapsulated in its own set of classes
The behaviors are easy to expand with new classes
Every method in the program is a strategy
Behavior may be changed at runtime if needed
optionExplain: Right: this is one of the qualities the name carries.
Right: new behaviors are added as new classes.
The statement concerns the ducks' behaviors, not every method.
Right: the authors list runtime change among the qualities.
questions.explain: The authors list encapsulated behavior classes, easy expansion and runtime change as what the name conveys.
questions.rule: A pattern name implies its qualities.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: In a meeting, people debate the exact fields of a single class. A senior developer asks the group to agree which pattern fits first. What is the senior developer trying to do?
options: Return the discussion to the design level and away from the details
End the meeting without a decision
Move the debate to a different language
Hand the problem to the junior developers
optionExplain: Right: patterns let the discussion stay in the design.
The aim is to progress the decision.
The language is irrelevant here.
Nothing in the aim concerns who does the work.
questions.explain: Pattern talk keeps people at the level where design decisions are made.
questions.rule: Stay in the design.
questions.teaches: Talking at the pattern level stays at the design until the shape is agreed, and only then moves to implementation details.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: A bakery's head chef tells a new baker: 'Use the mother dough method for all the breads.' What does this do for the new baker, in the sense of a shared vocabulary?
options: It removes the need to learn any baking skill
It conveys a complete method with its steps and constraints in a few words
It guarantees every loaf is perfect
It makes the baker unable to try other methods
optionExplain: The term does not teach the skills it names.
Right: a short term carries a method.
A method names an approach; results still depend on the work.
The term does not forbid other methods.
questions.explain: A shared name works the same in baking as in software.
questions.rule: A name carries a method.
questions.teaches: A named method gives a newcomer a starting point to practise, but it does not replace the skill of applying it.

questions.section: The power of a shared pattern vocabulary
questions.q: True or false: a team that says it uses a pattern has told the listener nothing beyond the pattern's name.
questions.explain: The authors say a pattern name conveys a set of qualities, characteristics and constraints that the pattern represents.
questions.rule: The name stands for the qualities too.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A team wants to benefit from other developers' experience of structuring classes and objects. Which of these is a design idea to learn and adapt, not code to link in?
options: A networking library with a published API
A named way of structuring classes to let one behavior vary
A GUI framework with ready-made windows
A file-handling package that is added to the build
optionExplain: A library is code that you link into your program.
Right: a pattern is a design idea you learn and adapt.
A framework is also code written by someone else.
A package is code added to a build, not a design idea.
questions.explain: Libraries and frameworks are code; a pattern is a way of structuring classes and objects. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Code is linked in; a pattern is learned.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: Design patterns don't go directly into your code, they first go into your ____.
questions.explain: Patterns are applied by a developer who knows them, not added to the program as files.
questions.rule: Patterns go into your brain first.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A developer asks for a library of design patterns so as not to have to learn them. What do the authors say?
options: A library of patterns will be published soon
Patterns are the same as libraries, so any library will do
Patterns are too small to need adaptation
Patterns are higher level than libraries, and each must be adapted to the application
optionExplain: The authors say there is no library of patterns, only catalogs that list them.
The authors say libraries and frameworks are not patterns.
The authors say it is our job to adapt them.
Right: the authors say patterns tell us how to structure classes and objects, and we adapt them.
questions.explain: A pattern is a design to adapt, not a part to import.
questions.rule: Adapt the design to your application.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The authors say libraries and frameworks are not design patterns, yet may use them. What benefit follows for a developer who knows patterns?
options: They no longer need to read documentation
They understand APIs built around patterns more quickly
They can replace the library with a pattern
They can predict every bug in the library
optionExplain: Documentation is still needed.
Right: the authors say pattern knowledge speeds up understanding of such APIs.
A pattern is not a replacement for code.
Pattern knowledge does not reveal bugs.
questions.explain: Recognizing the pattern in a library tells you how its parts fit.
questions.rule: Patterns help you read other people's code.
questions.teaches: Recognizing a pattern inside a library lets you predict how its parts relate before reading its details.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A student learning to cook asks whether a recipe book is the same as the technique of emulsifying. By analogy with the card, which answer fits?
options: No: the book supplies finished recipes, and the technique is a method you learn and adapt
Yes: both are ingredients to add to the dish
Yes: the technique is a smaller recipe book
No: the technique cannot be adapted to new dishes
optionExplain: Right: finished recipes parallel libraries, and the method parallels a pattern.
Neither is an ingredient.
A technique is applied across dishes, which is its strength.
A technique can be adapted.
questions.explain: Finished parts and general methods differ in every field.
questions.rule: Parts are used; methods are adapted.
questions.teaches: Finished code gives you a result; a pattern gives you a method for reaching results in many situations.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: True or false: according to the authors, libraries and frameworks are themselves design patterns.
questions.explain: The authors say libraries and frameworks are not patterns; they are specific implementations that we link into our code, though they sometimes use patterns inside.
questions.rule: Libraries implement; patterns guide.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: A programmer knows classes, inheritance and polymorphism well. What can be said about the flexibility of their designs?
options: Knowing these basics does not by itself guarantee flexible, maintainable designs
It guarantees them, since the basics are the whole of design
It guarantees them, but only for small programs
It makes patterns useless for them
optionExplain: Right: the guru says the basics are not enough on their own.
The guru calls this a misunderstanding.
Size of program is not the guru's point.
The guru presents patterns as the collected experience.
questions.explain: Knowing tools is different from knowing how to use them to make flexible designs. The card next gives the guru's view.
questions.rule: Basics are necessary, not sufficient.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The guru says design is an art, and it involves ____ between competing goals.
questions.explain: Even with patterns, choices cost something and must be weighed.
questions.rule: Design involves trade-offs.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: Two developers face a design problem and neither can find a matching pattern. According to the guru, what should they use?
options: Nothing; without a pattern no design is possible
A library that happens to be close
The first design that comes to mind
The OO principles that underlie the patterns, including thinking about how the system might change
optionExplain: The guru says principles can guide them.
The authors say libraries are not patterns and do not cover design.
A first guess ignores the principles.
Right: the guru says principles help when no pattern is found.
questions.explain: Principles are the layer under the patterns.
questions.rule: Fall back on principles.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: The developer asks whether knowing patterns lets him skip the hard work and reach designs that are certain to work. How does the guru answer?
options: Yes, completely, so no judgment is needed
Yes, to an extent, but design is an art and trade-offs remain
No, patterns have nothing to offer
No, because patterns are discovered, not made
optionExplain: The guru adds a caution about trade-offs.
Right: patterns save effort but do not remove judgment.
The guru says well-tested patterns put you ahead.
The discovery of patterns is not the point of the answer.
questions.explain: Patterns shorten the path but do not do the choosing.
questions.rule: Patterns inform judgment; they do not replace it.
questions.teaches: The value of a pattern is that others have already paid for its lessons; the cost of choosing among patterns remains with the designer.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: An experienced pilot tells a student: 'Knowing the controls does not make you a good pilot. The checklists and the rules of flying came from hard experience.' Which part of the guru's view matches?
options: Anyone who knows the controls can fly well
Checklists remove the need for judgment
Basic knowledge is not enough; collected experience and principles add what is missing
Experience matters only for beginners
optionExplain: This is the misunderstanding the guru names.
The guru says trade-offs remain.
Right: the structure matches the guru's view.
The guru does not limit patterns to beginners.
questions.explain: The same relation between basics and experience appears in any craft.
questions.rule: Basics plus experience, not basics alone.
questions.teaches: In any craft, collected experience records what basic skills leave out; it speeds learning without removing the need for judgment.

questions.section: How do I use Design Patterns?
questions.q: True or false: the guru says a designer who knows the OO basics will automatically build flexible, reusable systems.
questions.explain: The guru calls that one of the true misunderstandings of object-oriented development.
questions.rule: Basics do not automatically give flexibility.

questions.q: Which sentence best sums up the main thread of a chapter on SimUDuck, Strategy and shared vocabulary?
options: Expect change, separate what varies, and use proven patterns as a shared language
Use inheritance wherever two classes share code
Never change working code after release
Write code first and decide the design later
optionExplain: Right: this captures the thread from the problem to the pattern.
The chapter shows the limits of inheritance.
The chapter says software must change.
The chapter shows the value of design thinking.
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a problem to principles to a pattern. The card next gathers the threads.
questions.rule: Change, separation, patterns.

questions.q: Match each idea from the chapter's summary to the sentence that expresses it.
questions.explain: The summary points: patterns are discovered, give general solutions rather than code, address change, and provide a shared language.
questions.rule: Know the chapter's summary points.

questions.q: A team builds a fitness app. Workout types differ, and new types are expected every quarter. Using the chapter's thread, what should the team do first?
options: Create a subclass for each workout and copy shared code
Write one big class with a branch for each type
Identify what varies, the workout types, and encapsulate it behind an interface
Wait for the first change request before designing
optionExplain: Copying shared code multiplies the cost of change.
Branches make every addition risky.
Right: expecting change, they separate what varies.
The chapter says to plan for change, not wait for it.
questions.explain: The chapter's main thread, applied to a new domain.
questions.rule: Expect change; separate what varies.

questions.q: Which statement about patterns would the chapter's authors accept?
options: A pattern is a finished class to be copied into the code
A pattern is a general solution that must be adapted to the application
A pattern is a law that settles every design choice
A pattern is a new invention for each project
optionExplain: The authors say patterns do not give you code.
Right: patterns give general solutions, not code.
The guru says trade-offs always remain.
The authors say patterns are discovered, not invented.
questions.explain: A pattern is a discovered, adaptable solution.
questions.rule: Adapt the pattern; do not copy it.
questions.teaches: Because patterns are discovered from repeated experience, a new design problem may resemble one that has been solved before.

questions.q: True or false: according to the chapter's bullet points, patterns give you code that you paste into your application.
questions.explain: The bullet points say patterns don't give you code, they give you general solutions to design problems, which you apply to your specific application.
questions.rule: Patterns give solutions, not code.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A client wants a dashboard whose panels refresh when sensor readings change, and wants outside developers to add panels later. What is the main pressure on the design?
options: Sensor readings must be saved in a database before any panel is shown
All panels must look identical to each other
Panels must be added and removed without rewriting the sensor code
Panels must refresh on a fixed timer, once a second, whatever the sensors do
optionExplain: Storage may be useful, but nothing in the request mentions saving readings.
Looks are not mentioned; the request is about who can add panels.
Right: the wish for outside developers to add panels is a demand about change.
A timer is one way to refresh, but the request is about reacting to changes, and a timer says nothing about adding panels.
questions.explain: The request stresses that new panels will come later from other people, so the design must absorb them without edits to the sensor code. The card next lays out this kind of requirement.
questions.rule: Before designing, separate what is given, what must be built, and what must stay open to change.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: WeatherData has getters for temperature, humidity and ____.
questions.explain: The three tracked values are temperature, humidity and barometric pressure.
questions.rule: Know the data the subject owns.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: The team cannot see the code that calls measurementsChanged(). What does the chapter have them do about that?
options: Rely only on the fact that it runs when new readings arrive
Rewrite it so that the displays themselves control when it runs and how often
Study the caller and copy its timing into each display
Replace it with a loop that checks readings repeatedly
optionExplain: Right: the contract is enough, and the callers are not their concern.
The team is asked to fill the method, not to take over its scheduling.
Copying the caller’s timing ties every display to details nobody asked them to know.
Polling is a different design and the spec gives no reason to change how the method is triggered.
questions.explain: The authors say we do not know or care how the method is called; we only know that it is, when data is available. A design can lean on a stated contract without knowing the code behind it.
questions.rule: Rely on the stated contract, not on the unseen internals.
questions.teaches: A design should depend on what a trigger promises (it fires when new data exists), not on how the code behind it works.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A greenhouse object has getters for temperature and moisture and runs readingsChanged() when its sensors report. Sort each item by whether the spec gives it or leaves it to our team.
groups: Left for our team to build

items.t: The getters for temperature and moisture
The sensors calling readingsChanged()
A moisture dashboard that updates itself
A fan panel that updates itself
A way for a grower to add a custom panel later
The sensor hardware that takes readings

questions.explain: The greenhouse object, its getters and the sensor calls are supplied. Every screen, and the ability to add more, is the team’s work.
questions.rule: Name what is supplied before deciding what to build.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: A client says: we need email and SMS alerts now, and other teams may add chat alerts later. Which statement should shape the design most?
options: The statement that email comes first in priority for the client
The statement that two channels exist today
The statement that alerts go to customers
The statement that more alert channels may be added later
optionExplain: The order of priority is not stated, and it would not change how new channels are added.
Today’s two channels are a snapshot; designing only for them is the trap in the first attempt.
Who receives alerts is a detail; it does not decide how channels are added.
Right: it tells the designer the set of channels is open, so a fixed list would break.
questions.explain: A requirement about future change outweighs the current list, because a design fitted to today’s list has to be reopened when the list grows.
questions.rule: Requirements about future change shape a design more than the current list.
questions.teaches: A requirement that says more variants will come tells the designer what to keep open, and outweighs the list of variants known today.

questions.section: What do we know so far?
questions.q: True or false: Suppose the spec said only three displays would ever exist and nobody could add or remove them. The requirement that outside developers can plug in displays would then no longer be part of the spec.
questions.explain: That requirement is exactly the one the spec states for the real project; with the three displays frozen it would disappear. The change tells you which requirement was driving the design.
questions.rule: Ask which requirement would vanish if conditions changed.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: True or false: A class that calls three named display classes one after another whenever its data changes is easy to extend with a fourth display.
questions.explain: Each added display needs another line in that class, so the class must be edited every time. The card next shows how the authors judge such a design.
questions.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: Which problem comes from hard-coding the calls to three display classes inside measurementsChanged()?
