options: The displays can no longer read the temperature
Each new display means editing that method
The method runs too slowly on every reading
WeatherData loses its getter methods
optionExplain: Reading values is unaffected; the displays receive them in the calls.
Right: the display list is fixed in the method body, so every change touches it.
Speed is not the issue the authors raise.
The getters stay; they are not touched by this choice.
questions.explain: The list of displays lives inside the code, so adding one means changing and recompiling that code.
questions.rule: The list of recipients should not be written into the sender’s code.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: With the hard-coded design, a user wants to switch off the forecast display while the program runs. Which flaw does this expose?
options: Displays do not store the measurements they are shown
No way to add or remove displays at run time
Humidity values are shown in the wrong units on screen
The getters return the wrong type of value to the caller
optionExplain: Storing is not at issue; the displays receive the values they show.
Right: the update calls are fixed when the code is written.
Units have nothing to do with who is updated.
Types of the getters are not the issue.
questions.explain: Because the calls are compiled into the method, the set of displays cannot change while the program runs. Changing it at run time needs the list held as data that can be altered.
questions.rule: A list fixed in code cannot change at run time.
questions.teaches: Whether recipients can change at run time depends on whether the list is data held by the sender or calls written into its code.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: A ticket system calls the concrete classes SmsSender and EmailSender by name whenever a ticket changes. Select the flaws that apply.
options: It codes to concrete classes instead of a shared interface
It keeps ticket text in a database
A new channel means editing the ticket class
It cannot reply to the customer
optionExplain: Right: the ticket class names the two concrete classes directly.
Where the text is stored is not part of the checklist.
Right: each new channel is a new edit to the ticket class.
Replying is a feature question, not a design flaw of this kind.
questions.explain: Naming concrete senders in the ticket class mirrors the weather example: concrete classes, and an edit for each new variant.
questions.rule: Concrete names in the sender mean edits for each new variant.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: True or false: A teammate defends hard-coded calls for a calculator with exactly two screens that are fixed for good. By this chapter’s reasoning, the flaws cost as much there as they do in the extensible weather application.
questions.explain: The flaws were judged against the weather spec’s demand for added displays. Where no change is expected, the same hard-coding costs little.
questions.rule: Weigh each design flaw by how much change the spec expects.
questions.teaches: A design flaw has a price that depends on how much change is expected; where change is not expected, the same hard-coding is cheap.

questions.section: Taking a first, misguided SWAG at the Weather Station
questions.q: A reviewer says: the hard-coded design is fine because each display really does receive its update. What is missing from this judgement?
options: It ignores that displays should be fast enough for readings arriving often
It forgets to count how many getters the measurement class has
It assumes the client’s CEO has already approved the whole design
It tests today’s behaviour, not what happens when displays are added or removed
optionExplain: Speed is not part of the argument.
The getter count is irrelevant to the judgement.
Approval is not a design criterion in the chapter.
Right: the design is judged against the demand for change, not for working once.
questions.explain: A design that works for the present list can still fail the spec’s requirement that the list change. Judging soundness means testing against the whole spec.
questions.rule: Judge a design by whether adding or removing a part forces edits to code that should stay stable.

questions.q: Which everyday arrangement is most like objects being told automatically whenever something changes?
options: A magazine subscription, with each issue sent to those signed up
A library catalogue, where you look up a book each time you need one
A phone book, where you search for a number when you want to call
A vending machine, where you ask for an item on each visit
optionExplain: Right: the source reaches out to its current list when something new exists.
In a catalogue the reader must go and look; nothing is sent.
A phone book is consulted on demand, not delivered.
A vending machine responds only to a request each time.
questions.explain: The source of change pushes news to those who signed up, instead of each person checking. The card next builds on this picture.
questions.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.

questions.q: True or false: Once you unsubscribe from a publisher, new editions stop being delivered to you.
questions.explain: Deliveries follow the current subscription list, so leaving the list ends them.
questions.rule: Delivery follows the current list.

questions.q: Hotels and airlines subscribe to the same paper as individuals. What does that suggest about how the publisher treats subscribers?
options: It prints a different edition for each type of subscriber it has
It checks each subscriber’s kind of business before delivering
It delivers the same edition to anyone on the list
It lets the subscribers decide when each edition is printed
optionExplain: Different editions per type would add knowledge about subscribers that the picture does not need.
Checking each subscriber is extra knowledge the picture never calls for.
Right: being on the list is all that matters to the publisher.
Subscribers receive editions; they do not control printing.
questions.explain: The publisher does not need to know what kind of recipient it has, only that the recipient is on the list. This is the seed of loose coupling.
questions.rule: The sender needs to know only who is on the list.
questions.teaches: The sender can treat every recipient alike because membership of the list is the only thing it has to know about them.

questions.q: Match each part of the newspaper picture to its counterpart in a podcast app.
pairs: A listener who follows the show
Tapping follow on the show page
questions.explain: The producer plays the publisher, followers are subscribers, following is subscribing and each episode is an edition.
questions.rule: Map the roles, not the surface details.

questions.q: A shop posts a sign saying come and check whether there is news. Customers drop in to look. How does this differ from a subscription?
options: It is the same, since customers still hear the news in the end
It is a subscription with a very large list of customers
Customers must check by themselves; nobody reaches them
It delivers news to some customers but not others on purpose
optionExplain: Hearing the news is not the point; who acts is.
There is no list and no delivery in the sign model.
Right: in a subscription the source reaches out; here the customer does the checking.
Selective delivery is not what the sign does.
questions.explain: A subscription flips who acts: the source reaches those on its list, rather than each interested party repeatedly checking the source.
questions.rule: Subscriptions put the work of telling on the source.
questions.teaches: In a subscription the source does the reaching out; with a notice board each interested party has to keep checking.

questions.q: A thousand more people subscribe to a newspaper overnight. What changes in how the publisher produces each edition?
options: Nothing about producing the edition; only the delivery list grows
The edition has to be redesigned for a much larger audience
The publisher must ask each new subscriber what it wants
Each existing subscriber must be told about all the newcomers
optionExplain: Right: producing the edition is independent of who receives it.
Content could change for other reasons, but a longer list does not require it.
The picture has no step where the publisher asks subscribers anything.
Subscribers do not need to know about each other.
questions.explain: Production and delivery are separate in the picture, so a longer list does not touch how editions are made.
questions.rule: Think of a subscription: delivery follows the current list, and recipients can join and leave at any time.

questions.q: A thermostat object changes its reading and several screens refresh. Which word best names the thermostat’s role in the Observer Pattern?
options: Observer, because it is watched by the screens
Listener, because it hears the room temperature
Client, because the screens use its reading
Subject, because it owns the state that changes
optionExplain: The screens are the observers; the thermostat is the thing being observed.
It listens to the room, but in this pattern “listener” is a synonym for observer, the receiving side.
“Client” is not one of the pattern’s role names.
Right: the thermostat holds the changing state the screens depend on.
questions.explain: The object that owns the changing state is the subject. The card next defines it with its partner term.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.q: Match each term of the pattern to its meaning.
pairs: The object that holds the state and the list
An object that wants to hear about changes
Ask to be put on the list
Ask to be taken off the list
questions.explain: Subject and observer are the two roles. Registering and removing are how observers join and leave the subject’s list.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.q: Who asks for an object to become an observer?
options: The subject searches for objects that look interested
The object itself asks the subject to register it
A third manager object assigns observers to subjects
The state is copied to every object automatically
optionExplain: The subject has no way to know who is interested without being told.
Right: the Duck tells the subject it wants in.
The card describes no manager; the observer asks.
Nothing is copied to objects that have not registered.
questions.explain: Registration is requested by the observer, so the subject only has to keep its list and does not need to find observers.
questions.rule: Observers sign themselves up.
questions.teaches: Registration is the observer’s request, which means the subject keeps no knowledge of who might want to join.

questions.q: A stock price feed tells a chart widget, an alert bell and a logger whenever a price changes. Sort each description by role.

items.t: The object that holds the current price
The object that keeps the list of who to tell
The object that asks to join the list
The object that receives each notification
The widget that redraws on a new price
The object that sends the notifications

questions.explain: The feed owns the price, keeps the list and sends notifications. The widget, bell and logger ask to join and receive notifications.
questions.rule: Subject owns and sends; observer joins and receives.

questions.q: In a smart-home app a door sensor reports open and a lamp and an alarm react. A teammate calls the lamp the subject because it is the visible part. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the visible object is always the subject
The subject is the sensor, the object that holds the changing state
The alarm should be the subject because it matters most
Neither lamp nor sensor is a subject; only the app is
optionExplain: Visibility does not decide the role; the sentence overgeneralises.
Right: roles follow who owns the state and who depends on it.
Importance does not decide the role either.
The sensor owns the state here; the app is only the setting.
questions.explain: The subject is picked by what it holds: the changing state. The lamp and alarm depend on it, so they are the observers.
questions.rule: Roles follow who owns the state, not who is most visible.
questions.teaches: Roles in the pattern are defined by who owns the changing state and who depends on it, not by importance or visibility.

questions.q: A new display object is created but does not ask to register. The subject’s state then changes. What happens?
options: The subject registers it as soon as its own state changes
The display receives the change after a short delay of some kind
The display is told once about the change and is then removed
The display receives nothing, since only registered observers are notified
optionExplain: The subject does not add objects by itself; observers ask.
No delay mechanism exists; being off the list means no notification.
Removal only happens when an observer asks.
Right: notifications go to the list, and the display is not on it.
questions.explain: Being on the list is what earns a notification, and joining is the observer’s own step.
questions.rule: The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies each when its state changes; observers join and leave by asking.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: An object has asked a subject to stop sending it updates, and then the subject’s state changes. What is the most likely outcome?
options: It is skipped for this change but can ask to join again later
It still gets this change but none of the ones after it, either
It is told about the change by a different object instead
It is blocked from ever observing that subject again
optionExplain: Right: removal takes effect for later changes, and rejoining is allowed.
Removal takes effect immediately, not after one more update.
The subject does the telling, and only to its list.
Nothing in the story bars a second registration.
questions.explain: Leaving ends notifications from then on, and joining again is possible. The card next walks through the story.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: Put these events from the book’s walkthrough in order.
items: An object asks the subject to make it an observer
The subject adds it to its list of observers
The subject gets a new data value
The subject notifies every observer on its list
The object asks to be removed
Later changes skip the removed object
questions.explain: The sequence is: join, be added, state changes, everyone on the list is notified, leave, and be skipped afterwards.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: True or false: Once an observer has removed itself, it is barred from observing the same subject again.
questions.explain: The Mouse may ask to be an observer again some day, and from then it would be notified of later changes.
questions.rule: Leaving can be undone by registering again.
questions.teaches: Removal is reversible: an object that left the list can register again and then receives later notifications.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A chat channel notifies members of each post. Ana joins at 9:00 and Bo at 9:05. Ana leaves at 9:10, then a message is posted at 9:15. Who is notified?
options: Ana only
Both Ana and Bo
Bo only
Nobody, since the membership changed recently
optionExplain: Ana left before the post, so she is skipped.
Ana was removed, so she is not on the list.
Right: Bo is on the list at 9:15 and Ana is not.
Membership changes do not suspend notifications; the current list is used.
questions.explain: The list at 9:15 holds Bo alone, because Ana was taken off at 9:10.
questions.rule: Notify the list as it stands at the moment of the change.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A flash-sale subject sends an update at 10:00. Cy registers at 10:30. Does Cy receive the 10:00 update?
options: Yes, since Cy is on the list now, past updates are re-sent
Yes, but only the update that came right before registering
No, Cy hears only about changes that happen after registering
Only if Cy also removes itself and joins again
optionExplain: Nothing in the story replays history to new observers.
There is no step in the story that sends one previous update.
Right: the walkthrough sends a notification when the state changes, to those on the list then.
Rejoining does not replay anything either.
questions.explain: Notification happens at the moment of a change, so a late observer misses earlier changes. A new observer may therefore need a way to learn the current state when it joins.
questions.rule: A new observer does not hear about past changes.
questions.teaches: Observers receive notifications only for changes after they register; the pattern as told does not replay earlier changes.

questions.section: A day in the life of the Observer Pattern
questions.q: A student summarises the walkthrough. Select the two statements that are wrong.
options: The subject notifies only the newest observer
A removed observer is skipped on later changes
An observer can register again after leaving
A removed observer still receives later notifications
optionExplain: Wrong: every observer on the list is notified.
Correct as told: the Mouse is skipped after removal.
Correct as told: the Mouse may ask again.
Wrong: removal ends later notifications.
questions.explain: Notification goes to the whole list, and removal ends it. The two wrong statements each break one of these facts.
questions.rule: Only the observers on the list at the moment of a change receive that change’s notification.

questions.q: In a group chat, the group object notifies members of new messages, and each member object also notifies a status bot when the member goes online. Is a member breaking the pattern?
options: No, a member can be an observer of the group and a subject for the bot
Yes, because an observer can never also serve as a subject for other objects
Yes, since the bot should observe the group object directly
No, because group members are neither subjects nor observers
optionExplain: Right: roles belong to relationships, so one object can hold several.
The pattern places no such ban on an object.
The bot may observe the group too, but the pattern does not require it.
Members are observers of the group, so they do take a role.
questions.explain: The roles are about relationships, so an object can have one role in one and another elsewhere. The card next shows the book’s example.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: True or false: In the skit, Lori ends up only as an observer, with no observers of her own.
questions.explain: Lori keeps observing the headhunter and builds her own call list, so she is also a subject.
questions.rule: Lori is both.

questions.q: A news agency tells a regional paper, which tells its readers. If the agency stops publishing, what do the readers receive?
options: New items, since the paper itself becomes the subject for the readers
Items from the agency, delayed by the paper’s own work
The paper’s own items, which are unaffected by upstream
Nothing new, because the paper has nothing from upstream to relay
optionExplain: The paper stays a subject, but only has what it receives or produces itself.
There is nothing to be delayed once the agency has stopped.
The paper might produce its own items, but this chain is about relayed ones.
Right: each link depends on the one before it.
questions.explain: In a chain, each object depends on the one upstream, so a break upstream silences what depends on it.
questions.rule: In a chain every link depends on the one above.
questions.teaches: A chain relays changes through layers, and each layer depends on the one before, so an upstream break silences everything below it.

questions.q: A warehouse sensor tells a stock tracker when a shelf is empty. The tracker tells a purchasing screen and a supplier emailer when stock runs low. Select the true statements.
options: The stock tracker is an observer of the sensor
The stock tracker is a subject for the screen and the emailer
The purchasing screen is a subject for the sensor
The sensor is an observer of the stock tracker
optionExplain: True: it depends on the sensor’s reports.
True: it keeps its own list and tells them.
False: the screen only receives what the tracker sends.
False: the sensor does not depend on the tracker.
questions.explain: The tracker sits in the middle with both roles. The screen and emailer are only observers; the sensor is only a subject.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: A spreadsheet cell B1 depends on A1, and cell C1 depends on B1. Which description fits B1?
options: A subject for A1 and an observer of C1
An observer of A1 and a subject for C1
A subject only, since it holds a value
An observer only, since it depends on A1
optionExplain: This reverses both directions.
Right: it follows A1 and is followed by C1.
It holds a value, but C1 depends on it too, so it also observes.
C1 depends on B1, so B1 is also a subject.
questions.explain: A chain of dependent values lets a change ripple through layers, and each layer chooses what to pass on.
questions.rule: Chained dependencies let one change ripple through several layers.
questions.teaches: Chained links let a change ripple through several layers, and each middle object is both an observer and a subject.

questions.q: Lori stops observing the headhunter but keeps her own call list. What happens to her observers?
options: They keep hearing the headhunter’s news through her anyway
They hear nothing about the headhunter, though she can announce her own news
They are removed from her own list automatically, as well
They become observers of the headhunter directly at once
optionExplain: She has stopped receiving it, so there is nothing to relay.
Right: she no longer receives it, so she cannot relay it.
Nothing removes observers except their own request.
Nothing moves them; they stay on her list.
questions.explain: What she relays depends on what she receives, while her own news is still hers to announce.
questions.rule: An object can observe one subject while acting as the subject for others.

questions.q: The Observer Pattern defines a one-to-____ dependency between objects.
questions.explain: One object, the subject, has many dependents. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.

questions.q: True or false: In the Observer Pattern, the dependents are notified when the state of the one object changes.
questions.explain: The trigger in the definition is a change in the state of the one object.
questions.rule: The trigger is a change of state.

questions.q: Does the definition require the subject to send the new values along with its notification?
options: Yes, a notification must always contain the new values themselves
No, because observers never need any values from the subject at all
Yes, but only for the very first notification that is sent
No, it leaves open how the values reach the dependents
optionExplain: This treats one common style as the definition itself.
Observers usually do need values; the point is how they get them.
Nothing in the definition separates a first notification.
Right: the definition leaves the style of notification open.
questions.explain: The definition fixes that dependents are told about a change, not how the data reaches them. Sending values along and letting observers fetch them are two styles.
questions.rule: The definition fixes who is told and when, not how the data travels.
questions.teaches: The definition leaves open whether the new values travel with the notification or the observer fetches them afterwards.

questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it fits the Observer Pattern or not.

items.t: A fitness tracker refreshes a watch face and phone widget when steps change
A calendar event update refreshes every attendee’s view
A calculator returns a result when asked
A function sorts a list and hands it back
A group chat pushes each new message to every member
A converter turns one file into another on request

questions.explain: The fitting cases have one changing source and many dependents told automatically. The others are on-demand requests with a single caller.
questions.rule: Look for one changing source and many dependents told automatically.

questions.q: An operations room has staff who must refresh their screens by hand after a change. Which word of the definition does this arrangement fail?
options: Automatically, because the change itself does not cause the update
One-to-many, because there are many screens on the wall
Dependency, because the screens depend on the data they show
State, because the shared data has no state of its own
optionExplain: Right: here a person must act after every change.
There are many screens, so this part holds.
The screens still depend on the data.
The data has state; the failing part is how the screens learn of changes.
questions.explain: Automatic means the change itself causes the notification, with no manual step or checking by the dependents.
questions.rule: Automatic means no manual step by the dependents.
questions.teaches: Automatic in the definition means that the notification follows from the change itself, with no manual step or polling by the dependents.

questions.q: A student restates the pattern: many objects change state and one object is notified. What is wrong?
options: It leaves out the word dependency, which is the only word needed
It says state where the definition says value, which changes the meaning
It reverses the direction: one object changes and many are notified
Nothing is wrong, since both directions describe the same pattern
optionExplain: Dependency matters, but the main fault is the reversed direction.
The definition uses state; this is not the fault.
Right: the one is the source of change and the many are notified.
The directions are not interchangeable.
questions.explain: The subject is the one source of change and the observers are the many dependents who are told.
questions.rule: Observer is when one object’s state change automatically notifies all its dependents.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A playlist is edited by its owner and shown on several devices. Where should the playlist data be controlled?
options: In every device, each one editing and keeping its own copy
In whichever device made the latest edit, switching over to others as time goes on
In one object that owns it, with the devices depending on that object
In a copy per device, with none treated as the real one
optionExplain: Many editable copies would drift apart.
The owner would change from edit to edit, and no one could rely on it.
Right: one owner means one place where the truth lives.
Without an authoritative copy, devices cannot agree.
questions.explain: A single owner gives the other objects one place to rely on. The card next names this relationship.
questions.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Because the subject is the ____ owner of the data, the observers depend on it for updates.
questions.explain: The subject alone owns and controls the state, so every observer relies on it.
questions.rule: One owner, many dependents.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Why do the authors call one owner a cleaner design than many objects controlling the same data?
options: Only one place can change the state, so none disagree
Fewer classes are needed in total, so the design is smaller overall
Observers become faster at reading the data they depend on
The data can be stored in less memory than before
optionExplain: Right: a single owner removes conflicting changes by different objects.
The count of classes is not the argument.
Speed is not what the authors claim.
Memory is not what the authors claim.
questions.explain: With one owner there is one place where changes are made and one source of truth. Shared control would let objects change the same data in conflicting ways.
questions.rule: One owner, one source of truth.
questions.teaches: A single owner means one place to change the data and one source of truth, while shared control lets objects make conflicting changes.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: One flight record is shown on a gate screen, an airline app and an airport board. Select the true statements.
options: The flight record is the one that owns the state
Each screen edits its own copy of the status
The screens depend on the flight record for changes
Adding a fourth screen creates a second subject
optionExplain: True: it owns the status.
False: that would give many owners.
True: they rely on it to be told.
False: a new screen is one more observer; the subject stays one.
questions.explain: The record is the single owner, and the screens are dependents. A new screen adds a dependent and does not add a subject.
questions.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A school has 200 classroom attendance lists, and a district dashboard watches all of them. Does this break the idea of one subject and many observers?
options: Yes, because a dashboard can only observe a single subject at a time
Yes, because there are now 200 owners sharing one piece of state
No, because the dashboard becomes the owner of every attendance list
No, each list is its own subject and the dashboard watches many
optionExplain: Nothing limits an observer to one subject.
Each list owns its own state, so each state still has one owner.
The dashboard only reads; the lists remain the owners.
Right: the one-to-many relationship holds for each list separately.
questions.explain: One-to-many describes each subject’s relationship to its observers, and an observer may watch several subjects.
questions.rule: The rule is one owner per piece of state.
questions.teaches: The one-to-many count is per subject, so an observer can depend on several subjects without breaking the idea of one owner per piece of state.

questions.section: The Observer Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Two objects both edit the same state, and observers watch both. How does this compare with the pattern?
options: It is the same pattern, with two subjects in place of one
It loses the single owner the authors prefer, so changes can conflict
It is better, since changes arrive twice as fast as before
It is the same pattern, since observers cannot tell who edits
optionExplain: Two subjects would each own different state; here the state is shared.
Right: shared control is the arrangement the authors warn is less clean.
Speed is not the issue; control is.
The design differs even if the observers cannot tell.
questions.explain: The point of the pattern is a single owner of each piece of state. Shared editing gives up that benefit.
questions.rule: One object owns and controls the state; many others depend on it for updates.

questions.q: To let any object be notified, what should a subject require of it?
options: That it extends the subject’s own class so it can reach its data
That it implements a shared interface that has an update method
That it exposes all of its fields to the subject directly
That it is created by the subject when the program starts
optionExplain: Extending the subject class would tie observers to one class family.
Right: a shared interface lets the subject call every observer the same way.
Exposing fields is far more than the subject needs.
Creating observers would tie the subject to their concrete classes.
questions.explain: A shared interface is the only thing the subject has to rely on. The card next shows the two interfaces.
questions.rule: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify; the Observer interface offers update.

questions.q: Match each piece of the design to its role.
pairs: Methods to register, remove and notify observers
The update method the subject calls
A concrete class implementing the subject interface
A concrete class implementing the observer interface
questions.explain: The two interfaces describe what each side offers. WeatherData and the displays are concrete classes that implement them.
questions.rule: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify; the Observer interface offers update.

questions.q: Every display shows different things. Why must they all implement the same interface?
options: So that every display shows the same values as all the others
So that displays can call each other’s methods when needed
So that the subject can change what each display shows on screen
So the subject can call update on each the same way
optionExplain: Each display is free to show what it likes.
Displays have no need to call each other in this design.
What a display shows is the display’s own business.
Right: one shared method lets the subject treat a mixed list the same way.
questions.explain: One shared call is all the subject needs, so a list holding many concrete types can be notified through the interface alone.
questions.rule: Share a method signature, not a class family.
questions.teaches: A shared update method lets the subject notify a list of mixed concrete types through the interface alone.

questions.q: A ride-share Trip object must notify a map, a receipt maker and a driver-rating prompt. Which design gives all three a shared entry point?
options: An interface with one update method, implemented by each of the three
A separate method on Trip for each one of the three classes, called by name
Making each of the three classes a subclass of Trip
Three lists inside Trip, each with its own calling code
optionExplain: Right: one interface lets Trip notify all three in one way.
This ties Trip to each concrete class by name.
Subclassing Trip couples them and wastes the one inheritance slot.
Separate calling code is the hard-coding the chapter moved away from.
questions.explain: A shared interface keeps the subject unaware of concrete classes and keeps its notify step the same for any number of observers.
questions.rule: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify; the Observer interface offers update.

questions.q: An observer wants to leave a subject. Which side’s interface does it call, and on which object?
options: It calls the update method of the Observer interface, on itself
It calls the notify method, on the subject
It calls the remove method of the Subject interface, on the subject
It calls the remove method of the Observer interface, on another observer
optionExplain: Update is what the subject calls on the observer, not the way around.
Notify sends news; it does not remove anyone.
Right: leaving is requested from the subject.
Observers do not manage each other.
questions.explain: Each interface lists what the other side can call: observers call the Subject interface to join or leave, and the subject calls the Observer interface to deliver news.
questions.rule: Join and leave go to the Subject interface; news goes to the Observer interface.
questions.teaches: Each interface holds the methods the other side calls on you, so observers join and leave through the Subject interface and the subject delivers news through the Observer interface.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new display class that implements the Observer interface means changing the Subject interface.
questions.explain: The Subject interface offers register, remove and notify, none of which depend on which observer classes exist. A new observer only has to implement update().
questions.rule: New observers do not change the Subject interface.

questions.q: Two objects must work together. Which arrangement leaves them least tied to each other?
options: Object A knows B’s class and reads its private fields directly
Object A is written inside the body of B’s class
Object A knows only that object B offers one agreed method
Object A copies B’s code into itself and keeps its own version
optionExplain: Knowing the class and fields ties A to B’s internals.
Writing A inside B ties them most tightly.
Right: A depends on a small agreement and nothing else.
Copying code ties A to the details of B at one moment.
questions.explain: The less each side must know, the looser the coupling. The card next gives the term.
questions.rule: Loosely coupled objects interact while knowing as little as possible about each other.

questions.q: Loosely coupled objects can interact but have very little ____ of each other.
questions.explain: The definition is that they can interact while knowing very little about each other.
questions.rule: Loose means little knowledge.

questions.q: The subject knows an observer implements the Observer interface. Does it know what the observer does with an update?
options: No, what an observer does with a notice is its own business
Yes, it must know in order to choose which observer to call
Yes, it records each observer’s behaviour for later reference
Only for observers that it created itself, not for others
optionExplain: Right: the subject’s knowledge ends at the interface.
Choosing is not needed; every observer on the list is called.
Recording behaviour would be extra knowledge the pattern does not require.
The subject does not create observers; they register themselves.
questions.explain: The subject’s knowledge ends at the interface, so what an observer does with a notice stays inside the observer.
questions.rule: The interface is the edge of what the subject knows.
questions.teaches: The subject’s knowledge stops at the interface, which keeps what an observer does with a notice private to the observer.

questions.q: A parcel locker system notifies customers. Sort each description by the coupling it shows.

items.t: The locker calls notify on anything that implements a Notifiable interface
The locker class names the SmsSender class and reads its private fields
The locker keeps a list of Notifiable items and loops over it
The locker checks the customer’s phone model before notifying
The locker is unaware of which classes sit behind the interface
The locker is edited whenever a new messaging app appears

questions.explain: Loose cases rely on the interface only. Tight cases name concrete classes, read internals or need edits when the world changes.
questions.rule: Rely on the interface and nothing else.

questions.q: Loose coupling means the two objects no longer depend on each other at all. Is this right?
options: Yes, that is the whole point of the idea, and its main promise
Yes, though only after the program has been compiled and linked
No, because loose coupling means depending on the concrete class
No, they still depend on an agreed interface, but a small one
optionExplain: The idea shrinks dependency; it does not remove it.
Compilation does not remove the agreement.
A concrete class dependency is the tight kind.
Right: the dependency shrinks to a small, stable agreement.
questions.explain: Loose coupling narrows a dependency to a small agreement; it does not erase it.
questions.rule: Loose is small, not zero.
questions.teaches: Loose coupling does not remove dependence; it narrows it to a small, stable agreement such as an interface.

questions.q: The Observer interface changes so that update() takes an extra argument. What follows for the coupling?
options: Nothing, since loose coupling protects the design against any change at all
The subject and every observer must change with it
Only the subject changes, since observers ignore such details anyway
Only one observer changes, namely the first one on the list
optionExplain: Loose coupling does not protect the agreement itself.
Right: the freedom lasts only while the interface stays the same.
Observers implement the method, so they must change too.
No observer is special; they all implement the method.
questions.explain: The interface is the one thing both sides depend on, so a change to it reaches everyone who uses it.
questions.rule: Loosely coupled objects interact while knowing as little as possible about each other.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new kind of observer to an Observer-style design requires editing the subject.
questions.explain: The subject knows only the interface, so a new class that implements it can register without any edit to the subject. The card next lists such benefits.
questions.rule: While both sides keep to the interfaces, either can be changed, added, removed or reused without touching the other.

questions.q: Select the benefits the book gives for loose coupling between subject and observer.
options: New observers can be added at any time
Observers can be removed at any time
Subjects and observers can be reused independently
Observers can read the subject’s private fields
optionExplain: Listed in the book: add any time.
Listed in the book: remove any time.
Listed in the book: independent reuse.
Not a benefit: reading private fields would be tight coupling.
questions.explain: The book lists adding, replacing and removing observers and independent reuse. Reading private fields is the opposite of loose coupling.
questions.rule: While both sides keep to the interfaces, either can be changed, added, removed or reused without touching the other.

questions.q: An observer is swapped at run time for a different one while the subject keeps running. What does the swap require?
options: Stopping the whole program in order to recompile the subject
Remove the old observer and register the new one
Making the new observer extend the old observer’s class
Telling every other observer about the swap in advance
optionExplain: A recompile is only needed if the subject is edited.
Right: replacement is a removal plus a registration.
Extending the old class is not required; the interface is enough.
Other observers are not affected.
questions.explain: Replacement is a removal plus a registration, so a running system can change which objects it informs.
questions.rule: A swap is a removal plus a registration.
questions.teaches: Swapping an observer at run time is a removal followed by a registration, so a running system can change who it informs.

questions.q: A payment service tells a receipt printer when a sale is made. A shop wants SMS receipts too. Put the steps in order.
items: Write a class that implements the observer interface
Make an instance of the new class
Register the instance with the payment service
On the next sale it receives the notification
questions.explain: Only the new class and its registration are needed. The payment service does not change.
questions.rule: Add an observer by writing a class and registering it.

questions.q: A weather subject is lifted out of one app and used in a stock-price app with a completely different set of observers. What makes this possible?
options: The subject was written to hold every possible kind of observer
The observers were copied into the new app along with it
The new app is made a subclass of the old app
The subject knows nothing about its observers beyond the interface
optionExplain: No subject can be written to hold every kind; it holds the interface.
Copying observers is not needed; they can be new.
Subclassing the app is unrelated to reuse here.
Right: nothing in the subject refers to a specific observer.
questions.explain: Independent reuse is a direct result of the subject not knowing its observers.
questions.rule: Reuse follows from not knowing.
questions.teaches: Reuse of a subject with entirely different observers works because the subject refers to its observers only by the interface.

questions.q: A developer renames update() in the Observer interface and edits only the subject, saying loose coupling means no other change is needed. What is wrong?
options: Observers implement update(), so they break at once
Nothing is wrong, since the subject alone owns the interface
Only the subject should have been left alone by the change
The rename should have been made in the observers only
optionExplain: Right: the interface is the shared agreement and both sides rely on it.
Owning the data does not make the subject the owner of the agreement.
The rename itself is the issue, not which class is left alone.
The rename in observers only would break the subject.
questions.explain: Loose coupling allows changes that keep the interface obligations. Changing the interface is a change both sides feel.
questions.rule: While both sides keep to the interfaces, either can be changed, added, removed or reused without touching the other.

questions.q: Which principle is applied when a sender holds a list of objects typed by a shared interface rather than by concrete classes?
options: Favor inheritance over composition
Hide the sender from every receiver in the system
Program to an interface, not an implementation
Keep each class as large as possible
optionExplain: The pattern favours composition, the reverse.
The sender is known to receivers when they register.
Right: the list is typed by the interface.
Size is not a principle in the chapter.
questions.explain: Typing the list by an interface is what programming to an interface means. The card next ties three principles to the pattern.
questions.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.

questions.q: Match each principle to how the Observer Pattern applies it.
pairs: The number and kinds of observers can change without editing the subject
Subject and observers meet through interfaces
Observers are attached to subjects at run time
The subject knows only that observers implement the interface
questions.explain: Each principle shows up in a different part of the pattern: varying observers, interface use, run-time composition and minimal knowledge.
questions.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.

questions.q: Why is the link between a subject and its observers set up by composition rather than by inheritance?
options: Composition is shorter to type than a class hierarchy is to write
Inheritance cannot be combined with interfaces in any design
Composition can change while the program runs; a hierarchy cannot
Composition makes the observers run faster than inheritance would
optionExplain: Length is not the reason.
Inheritance and interfaces can be combined; this is not the reason.
Right: run-time change is the reason the authors give for composition.
Speed is not the reason.
questions.explain: A hierarchy is decided when the code is written, while a list of observers can grow and shrink at run time.
questions.rule: Run-time change needs composition.
questions.teaches: Composition lets the set of observers change while the program runs, which a class hierarchy fixed in the code cannot do.

questions.q: A team makes EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier subclasses of Order so that they get its status. Which principle does this go against?
options: Favor composition over inheritance
Program to an interface
Strive for loose coupling by using more inheritance
Encapsulate what changes by merging classes
optionExplain: Right: notifiers attached by subclassing are tied to Order at write time.
Interfaces are not the issue in this proposal.
More inheritance tightens coupling.
Merging classes does not separate what varies.
questions.explain: Subclassing fixes the relationship in code. The pattern composes observers with the subject at run time instead.
questions.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.

questions.q: A sensor tells a log writer and a dashboard through objects behind one interface, registered at run time. Select the principles this follows.
options: Encapsulate what varies
Program to an interface
Favor composition over inheritance
Share behaviour through a deep class hierarchy
optionExplain: Followed: the set of listeners can vary without editing the sensor.
Followed: the sensor refers only to the interface.
Followed: listeners are attached at run time.
Not followed: the design avoids hierarchies.
questions.explain: A single design can satisfy all three principles, because in Observer they push in the same direction.
questions.rule: The principles reinforce each other here.
questions.teaches: The three principles are not separate costs; in this design they point the same way and one structure satisfies all of them.

questions.q: A subject keeps its list typed by a concrete display class instead of the Observer interface. What is the likely result?
options: No effect at all, since the displays would still get their updates as before
The subject becomes faster because it checks fewer things
The displays no longer need to register with the subject
Each new kind of observer would need edits, so loose coupling is lost
optionExplain: Updates may still arrive, but the design inherits the first attempt’s flaw.
Speed is not the point.
Registration remains necessary.
Right: the subject is tied to specific classes again.
questions.explain: Replacing the interface by a concrete class brings back the first attempt’s flaws.
questions.rule: Observer separates what varies (the observers), programs to interfaces, and links subject and observers by composition.

questions.q: A weather app has one object that tracks readings and several displays that show them. In the Observer Pattern, which is the subject?
options: Each display, since it presents the data
The object that tracks the readings
The physical weather station
The user watching the screen
optionExplain: Displays depend on the data; they are observers.
Right: it owns the changing state.
The station feeds data in; the tracking object holds the state.
Users are outside the object design.
questions.explain: The subject is the owner of the changing state. The card next shows how the team reasons to this.
questions.rule: Make WeatherData the subject and each display an observer behind a common interface with update().

questions.q: In Mary and Sue’s plan, WeatherData is the one and the display elements are the ____.
questions.explain: The definition’s one-to-many relationship maps to one WeatherData and many displays.
questions.rule: One-to-many maps to WeatherData and displays.

questions.q: What is the first move Mary makes when she applies the pattern to the project?
options: She writes the display classes first and looks for a pattern afterwards
She rereads the definition and finds the one, the many and the state
She asks the CEO which displays to build first of all, then designs
She copies the publishing system of a newspaper company directly
optionExplain: This reverses the order; the pattern tells her what the classes need.
Right: the definition tells her what to look for.
Priorities are not the issue here.
The newspaper picture is a way to understand the pattern, not code to copy.
questions.explain: Applying a pattern means mapping each part of its definition to a part of the problem.
questions.rule: Map the definition’s words onto the problem.
questions.teaches: A pattern is applied by mapping each part of its definition (the one, the many, the state, the trigger) to a part of the problem.

questions.q: Apply the same mapping to a bike-share station. Match each part of the pattern to the bike-share part.
pairs: A map app, a kiosk and a fleet manager
questions.explain: The station owns the dock count, and the three consumers depend on it. Each change of the count is the trigger.
questions.rule: Find the one, the many, the state and the trigger.

questions.q: A game’s score object must tell a heads-up display, a sound player and a save system when the score changes. What must the three share?
options: The same superclass, so they inherit one common behaviour
The same file of source code, kept together in one place
The same colour theme, so they look alike on screen
The same observer interface with an update method
optionExplain: A shared superclass would not be needed and would limit what they can extend.
Source files are irrelevant to the call.
Looks have no bearing on notification.
Right: the score object calls update on each in the same way.
questions.explain: The three classes do different things, so what they share is a method signature rather than a parent class.
questions.rule: Share a method signature, not a parent.
questions.teaches: The subject’s call must look the same for every observer, so what they share is one method signature rather than a class lineage.

questions.q: A new reading, wind speed, is added to the subject while update() passes only temperature, humidity and pressure. What follows?
options: update() and every display that implements it would have to change
Nothing changes, since the displays fetch wind speed on their own later
Only the subject changes, because the displays are unaffected
Only the new wind speed display changes, and nothing else
optionExplain: Right: the shared method signature is the agreement.
Displays only get what the signature gives them.
The signature is used by all displays, so the subject alone cannot change it.
Old displays use the same signature and would break too.
questions.explain: The team’s choice to pass the measurements directly ties them to the signature. The book returns to this choice later.
questions.rule: Make WeatherData the subject and each display an observer behind a common interface with update().

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: In a reworked weather class that uses the Observer Pattern, what should measurementsChanged() do?
options: Call the three display classes by name, one after another
Clear all of the stored measurements after each reading
Tell every registered observer about the new measurements
Ask each display for its own readings and then merge them
optionExplain: Naming the displays is the first attempt it replaces.
Clearing readings would lose the data.
Right: it passes the news to everyone on the list.
The displays do not hold the readings; the subject does.
questions.explain: The method now tells whoever is on the list. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: WeatherData keeps the observer list and, when measurementsChanged() runs, tells every observer on it.

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: Each registered observer is told through its ____ method.
questions.explain: The shared Observer interface has the single method update(), which the subject calls on each observer.
questions.rule: The subject calls update on each observer.

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: What replaces the three named display calls in WeatherData?
options: A separate method for each possible display
A switch on the type of each display
A single loop over the list of observers
A call to a central display manager
optionExplain: This is the first attempt in another form.
Type checks tie the subject to concrete types.
Right: the loop works for any number of observers, including zero.
A manager would add a layer the pattern does not need.
questions.explain: One loop works for any number of observers, including none, because it simply goes through whatever is on the list.
questions.rule: One loop covers any number of observers.
questions.teaches: A single loop over the list covers any number of observers, including zero, because it goes through whatever is registered.

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: A forum subject tells observers of each new post. Put the steps in order.
items: A new post is stored
The subject starts its notify step
The loop goes through the observer list
Each observer’s update is called
questions.explain: The state change comes first, then the notify step, then the loop, then each call to update.
questions.rule: State changes, then loop and update.

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: A 3D printer controller must tell a progress bar and a log writer when a layer finishes. Which two things must the controller hold?
options: A list of observers and a step that goes through it calling update
A copy of the progress bar and the log writer classes
A timer that wakes both of them every second to check
A separate flag for each of the two, switched on and off
optionExplain: Right: storage plus a notify step is all a subject needs.
Copies of concrete classes tie the controller to them.
A timer would be polling, not notification.
Flags per observer would bring back one case per class.
questions.explain: A subject needs only storage for its observers and a notify step that visits them.
questions.rule: A subject needs a list and a notify step.
questions.teaches: A subject needs two pieces: storage for its observers and a step that visits each one and calls update.

questions.section: Implementing the Subject interface in WeatherData
questions.q: The observer list is empty when measurementsChanged() runs. What happens?
options: An error is raised because no display exists to be updated
The subject registers a default display so something is shown
The measurements are discarded because nobody was there to read them
The loop has nothing to call, so no display is updated and nothing breaks
optionExplain: Nothing in the design requires a display to exist.
The subject does not create displays.
The data stays in the subject.
Right: the loop simply goes through zero items.
questions.explain: An empty list is a normal case for the loop and needs no special handling.
questions.rule: WeatherData keeps the observer list and, when measurementsChanged() runs, tells every observer on it.

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: A new display object wants to receive updates from a subject. What is the usual way it gets onto the subject’s list?
options: The subject scans all objects in the program and adds the interested ones
It registers itself, for example in its constructor, using the subject it was given
A main program adds every display by hand, one at a time
The display extends the subject’s class, so it shares its list
optionExplain: Scanning would require the subject to know its prospective observers.
Right: the display asks to join, so nothing else needs to know about it.
A main program could do it, but the book’s displays register themselves.
Extending the subject would tie the display to the subject’s class.
questions.explain: In the book’s design the display makes the request itself. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: A display registers itself with the subject when built and keeps the subject so it can unregister later.

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: True or false: In the book’s current conditions display, the stored reference to the subject is not used again after the constructor.
questions.explain: The authors confirm this and explain the reference is kept so the display can unregister later.
questions.rule: Keep the subject if you may need to leave.

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: The book calls display() from update() in this small example. How do the authors rate that choice?
options: It is the best design possible, and nothing better exists at all
Fine for the example, with better ways coming later in the book
It is wrong, and it breaks the Observer Pattern altogether
It is required by the Observer interface for every observer
optionExplain: The authors say better ways exist.
Right: they point forward to Model-View-Controller.
Nothing breaks the pattern here; it is a design preference.
The interface only requires update().
questions.explain: Receiving a notice and presenting data are two separate jobs, and the Model-View-Controller pattern later separates them properly.
questions.rule: Receiving and presenting are separate jobs.
questions.teaches: Receiving a notice and presenting data are different jobs, and the Model-View-Controller pattern separates them more cleanly than doing both in update().

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: A StockAlert class implements the Observer interface. Order what its constructor does.
items: Receive the price feed as a parameter
Save a reference to the price feed
Register itself with the price feed
questions.explain: The feed arrives first, the reference is saved for later, and registration puts the alert on the feed’s list.
questions.rule: Take the subject, keep it, register.

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: A chart widget should stop receiving updates when the user closes its panel. What makes this easy?
options: The feed tracks which panels are currently open on screen
The widget deletes itself, and the feed notices on its own
The feed stops notifying everyone when any single panel closes
The widget kept a reference to the feed, so it can call remove
optionExplain: The feed knows nothing about panels.
An object that is deleted without leaving would stay on the list.
Nothing makes the feed stop for all observers.
Right: leaving requires the subject, so keeping it helps.
questions.explain: Observers tied to windows or panels should unregister when they close; otherwise the subject keeps notifying objects nobody can see.
questions.rule: Unregister when the observer goes away.
questions.teaches: Observers whose life is tied to a panel or window should unregister when it closes, or the subject keeps notifying objects nobody sees.

questions.section: Now, let’s build those display elements
questions.q: A display did not keep its subject and later needs to leave. What must it do first?
options: Find the subject again by some other route before it can unregister
Nothing, since leaving needs no subject to be involved
Ask the other observers on the list to leave for it
Wait for the subject to remove it when it feels like it
optionExplain: Right: removal is requested from the subject.
Removal is requested from the subject, so the subject is needed.
Other observers cannot remove it.
The subject removes observers only when asked.
questions.explain: Without the reference, the display has no handle for the remove request. That is the cost the stored reference avoids.
questions.rule: A display registers itself with the subject when built and keeps the subject so it can unregister later.

questions.q: Weather-O-Rama asks late for a heat index display in a station built on the Observer Pattern. What must change in WeatherData?
options: Its measurementsChanged() method must gain a new line of code
Its class must be rewritten from scratch to allow the display
Nothing; the new display is a new class that registers itself
Every existing display must be edited to make room for it
optionExplain: That is the first attempt’s approach.
A rewrite is unneeded.
Right: the subject does not depend on which observers exist.
Existing displays are unaffected by a new peer.
questions.explain: A new observer needs no edit to the subject. The card next shows the steps.
questions.rule: To add a display, write one new observer class and register it; leave the subject alone.

questions.q: Put the steps for adding the heat index display in order.
items: Write HeatIndexDisplay to implement the Observer interface
Compute the index from temperature and humidity in its update
Register it with WeatherData
It is updated on every change
questions.explain: Write the class, give it the computation, register it, and it receives every later notification.
questions.rule: To add a display, write one new observer class and register it; leave the subject alone.

questions.q: The heat index display ignores pressure but still receives it. What does this show?
options: The subject should send different values to each separate display
The display is written incorrectly and should be fixed before use
An observer can ignore part of what the subject sends it
Pressure should be removed from the update() method altogether
optionExplain: The subject does not know what each display wants.
Ignoring a value is acceptable.
Right: with a fixed set of values, each observer takes what it needs.
Other displays may need pressure.
questions.explain: When the subject passes a fixed set of values to every observer, some observers take only part of it. This is a cost of sending state to everyone.
questions.rule: Observers may use only part of what they are sent.
questions.teaches: When the subject sends the same fixed set of values to every observer, some observers use only part of it.

questions.q: A hospital monitor object sends pulse and oxygen readings to its screens. The team adds an alarm for low oxygen. What change does the Observer design need?
options: A new alarm class that implements the observer interface and registers
A new branch inside the monitor itself that handles the alarm too
A rewrite of every existing screen that shows the readings
A second monitor class that is built only for the alarm
optionExplain: Right: only a new observer is needed.
This brings back hard-coding.
Existing screens are unrelated to the alarm.
Another monitor would split the single source of the readings.
questions.explain: The monitor is the subject, and the alarm is another observer. The existing screens and the monitor stay as they are.
questions.rule: To add a display, write one new observer class and register it; leave the subject alone.

questions.q: The client now wants a wind speed display, but WeatherData does not hold wind speed. Does adding one observer class still suffice?
options: Yes, because any display can be added without touching the subject
Yes, because the display can compute wind speed itself from pressure
No, but only the old displays need editing
No, the subject needs a new value, and update() may have to carry it
optionExplain: The rule has this limit.
Wind speed cannot be derived from pressure alone.
The subject must change; old displays are affected only if the signature changes.
Right: the free addition applies only to data the subject already has.
questions.explain: Adding observers is free only when the data they need already exists in the subject. A new kind of data is a change to the subject.
questions.rule: Adding observers is free only for data the subject already has.
questions.teaches: A new observer costs nothing only when it needs data the subject already holds; new kinds of data require a change to the subject.

questions.q: True or false: Two HeatIndexDisplay objects are registered with the same WeatherData. Both are updated on every change.
questions.explain: The subject notifies every observer on its list, so each registered object gets every notification.
questions.rule: Every registered observer is notified.

questions.q: A news app can (A) send the full article with each alert, or (B) send a short alert and let each reader’s app fetch the parts it wants. Which one is called pull?
options: A, because the full article is pulled to the reader
B, because the receiver fetches what it needs
Both, since the reader gets the article either way
Neither, since news apps use a different pattern
optionExplain: In A the sender supplies the article, which is push.
Right: in pull, the receiver asks for the state.
The difference is who carries the data.
Alerts like these are an example of the pattern.
questions.explain: Pull means the receiver goes and gets the state. The card next compares it with push.
questions.rule: Push sends the state to every observer; pull lets each observer fetch what it needs.

questions.q: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: The subject sends state with the notification
The observer fetches the state it wants
What pull needs the subject to expose
A fixed update with all the values
questions.explain: Push sends state to observers; pull lets observers fetch it, which needs getters on the subject.
questions.rule: Push sends the state to every observer; pull lets each observer fetch what it needs.

questions.q: The subject fears that pull opens it up. What does pull require of the subject?
options: A separate copy of its own state kept ready for each observer
Public getters through which observers can read its state
Knowledge of each observer’s class
A timer to check what has changed
optionExplain: Copies are not needed for pull.
Right: observers can only pull what the subject exposes.
Pull does not need the subject to know its observers.
A timer would be polling.
questions.explain: Pull widens the subject’s public surface, while push keeps its state private but fixes the update signature for every observer.
questions.rule: Pull exposes getters; push fixes the signature.
questions.teaches: Pull widens what the subject exposes through getters, while push keeps state private but locks the update signature.

questions.q: Sort each description of a feed-to-observer arrangement into push or pull.

items.t: The notification carries price and volume with it
The observer calls a getter on the feed to read the price
Each observer reads only the one value it needs
Every observer receives the same set of values
Adding a new value changes every observer’s update signature
Adding a new value means adding a getter on the feed

questions.explain: Push sends a fixed set to all and ties the signature to it; pull moves the choice to each observer and the cost to the getters.
questions.rule: Push fixes what is sent; pull lets observers choose.

questions.q: A subject has 50 observers, and 49 of them need only one field. A new field is added for one observer. Which style needs fewer edits?
options: Push, because it avoids the need for any getters at all
Neither; both would change every one of the 50 observers
Push, because new fields fit into the existing update signatures with no edits
Pull, because only a getter is added and most observers are untouched
optionExplain: Push avoids getters but changes the signature for all.
Pull confines the change to the subject and the one observer.
Signatures must be changed to carry a new field in push.
Right: change spreads less when observers fetch for themselves.
questions.explain: With pull, observers that do not need a new field are not affected, so a change spreads less.
questions.rule: Pull keeps change local.
questions.teaches: With pull, observers that do not need a new field are untouched, so a state change spreads to fewer places than with push.

questions.q: An observer claims that pull has no downside. What does the subject’s reply point out?
options: Observers may need several calls and getters on the subject
Pull cannot work at all with more than one observer on a subject
Pull makes the subject slower for every observer it has to serve
Pull needs the subject to know each observer’s class beforehand
optionExplain: Right: these are the costs the subject raises.
Pull works with any number of observers.
Speed is not the reply’s point.
The subject still knows only the interface.
questions.explain: The subject’s concerns are the exposure of state and the several calls an observer may need.
questions.rule: Push sends the state to every observer; pull lets each observer fetch what it needs.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors’ summary, push is the more correct way to give state to observers.
questions.explain: The summary says pull is considered more correct. The card next sets out their reasons.
questions.rule: Weigh the claim that pull is more correct by checking whether its reasons fit the situation.

questions.q: The chapter’s summary says pull is considered more ____ than push.
questions.explain: The summary uses the word correct, in quotation marks, to signal a considered view.
questions.rule: Know the claim before judging it.

questions.q: What kind of claim is pull is more correct?
options: A rule that holds in every design that uses the pattern
A fact about how Java’s library classes are built inside
A considered judgement with reasons, to test in each case
A matter of taste with no reasons behind it at all
optionExplain: They present it as a view; a rule would not need reasons.
It is not about Java’s mechanics.
Right: the authors give reasons, so the claim can be tested.
Reasons are given, so it is more than taste.
questions.explain: Design advice comes with reasons, and a reasoned claim can be weighed against the case in hand.
questions.rule: Test advice against reasons and the case.
questions.teaches: Design advice is a judgement with reasons, and judging it means checking whether those reasons hold in the case at hand.

questions.q: Select the situations where the authors’ reasons for pull are strong.
options: Many different kinds of observers each need different parts of the state
The subject’s state is likely to grow over time
One observer uses the whole of a tiny, fixed state
The subject must hide every part of its state
optionExplain: Strong: the subject cannot predict varied needs.
Strong: new state need not change every update call.
Weak: nothing needs to be anticipated.
Weak: pull requires getters, so it exposes state.
questions.explain: The reasons concern variety of observers and growth of state, so they apply where those conditions hold.
questions.rule: Weigh the claim that pull is more correct by checking whether its reasons fit the situation.

questions.q: A reviewer rejects pull because an observer may need several calls to collect what it wants. How should this be judged?
options: As false, since pull does not need several calls at any point
As decisive, since one cost alone ends the whole matter
As a fair point, the subject’s own, to weigh against how often state grows
As irrelevant, since the number of calls does not matter
optionExplain: Several calls can happen, as the subject notes.
One cost does not decide the matter by itself.
Right: the cost is real and needs weighing, not dismissing.
The subject itself cites the extra calls.
questions.explain: A fair judgement sets the costs of an option against its benefits for the case in question.
questions.rule: Weigh the costs against the benefits for the case.
questions.teaches: A sound judgement sets an option’s costs against its benefits in the case at hand, rather than letting one cost or one benefit decide.

questions.q: A student writes: since the authors prefer pull, push is wrong in every design. Where is the error?
options: Preferred is not forbidden; push can suit a small shared state
The authors prefer push, not pull, in their summary of the chapter
The authors treat both styles as equally correct in every case
Pull is wrong for any design that has more than one observer
optionExplain: Right: the authors state a preference with reasons, not a ban.
The summary says pull is considered more correct.
They do rank pull higher.
Pull fits many observers well.
questions.explain: A preference with reasons leaves room for cases where the reasons do not apply.
questions.rule: Weigh the claim that pull is more correct by checking whether its reasons fit the situation.

questions.q: In Java’s built-in Observer support, how does a class become a subject?
options: By implementing an interface named Subject
By registering itself with the Observer class
By calling a static method on java.util
By extending a class named Observable
optionExplain: The built-in support provides a class, not a Subject interface.
Observers register with the subject, not the other way round.
There is no such static method in the description.
Right: the subject inherits its observer-handling methods.
questions.explain: The built-in version gives subjects a ready-made superclass. The card next gives details.
questions.rule: Extend Observable to be a subject; implement java.util.Observer and call addObserver to observe.

questions.q: Match each part of the built-in support to its job.
pairs: Registers an observer with the subject
Removes an observer from the subject
questions.explain: A subject extends Observable; observers implement Observer and join or leave with addObserver() and deleteObserver().
questions.rule: Extend Observable to be a subject; implement java.util.Observer and call addObserver to observe.

questions.q: What does a subject gain by extending Observable?
options: A guarantee that its observers will be loosely coupled to it
The add, delete and notify methods, inherited ready-made
Automatic push of data to every observer it has registered
The ability to extend a second class as well as Observable
optionExplain: Loose coupling comes from using interfaces.
Right: the list handling is inherited.
Pushing needs an argument to notifyObservers().
Extending Observable uses up the subject’s one superclass.
questions.explain: Inheritance supplies the list handling, at the price of using the class’s single superclass.
questions.rule: Inheriting list handling uses up the superclass slot.
questions.teaches: Extending Observable supplies list handling ready-made but uses up the class’s single superclass.

questions.q: A Doorbell must notify a Chime using the built-in support. Who extends and who implements?
options: Doorbell implements Observer; Chime extends Observable and registers
Doorbell extends Observable; Chime implements Observer and registers
Both extend Observable and then call each other’s methods
Chime extends Observable and registers the Doorbell with itself
optionExplain: This swaps the roles.
Right: the subject extends, the observer implements and registers.
Only the subject extends Observable.
The Doorbell is the source of change, so it is the subject.
questions.explain: The source of change extends the class and the receiver implements the interface and joins.
questions.rule: Extend Observable to be a subject; implement java.util.Observer and call addObserver to observe.

questions.q: The hand-built subject has register and remove methods. Which statement about the built-in names is right?
options: The built-in version has no way at all to remove observers
The built-in names are identical to the hand-built ones
The built-in version has no notify step, only an update step that observers call
The names differ, such as addObserver and deleteObserver, but the roles match
optionExplain: Removal is available as deleteObserver().
The names are not identical.
There is a notify step; the chapter shows it.
Right: the same jobs have different names.
questions.explain: Pattern roles stay the same across implementations even when method names change, so a reader should look for roles, not names.
questions.rule: Match roles, not method names.
questions.teaches: Pattern roles stay the same across implementations even when the method names differ, so match roles to roles when reading unfamiliar code.

questions.q: True or false: In the built-in version, the subject class writes and stores its own list of observers.
