questions.explain: The subject inherits the observer handling from Observable. The hand-built version is the one that stores its own list.
questions.rule: The list handling is inherited.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: True or false: In Java’s built-in support, calling notifyObservers() is enough on its own to notify observers.
questions.explain: A flag must be set first or no one is notified. The card next explains the rule.
questions.rule: No notification happens without setChanged(); use it to decide which changes deserve one.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: Put the steps of a built-in notification in order.
items: The subject’s state changes
The subject calls setChanged()
The subject calls notifyObservers()
Each observer’s update method is called
questions.explain: The change comes first, then the flag, then the notify call, and then the observers are called.
questions.rule: No notification happens without setChanged(); use it to decide which changes deserve one.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: Why does the built-in version have a changed flag at all?
options: So the subject can choose which changes are worth a notification
So observers can tell whether they have been removed or not
So the subject can store the old values for later
So notifications arrive in a fixed order every time
optionExplain: Right: the flag separates something changed from tell everyone.
Removal is handled by deleteObserver().
The flag does not store values.
Order is a separate matter.
questions.explain: The flag lets the subject filter out noise, such as tiny fluctuations, before bothering observers.
questions.rule: The flag filters which changes get announced.
questions.teaches: The flag separates something changed from tell everyone, so a subject can filter noise before notifying.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: A GPS subject updates its position hundreds of times a second, but observers need news only after a move of more than 10 metres. What should the subject do?
options: Call notifyObservers() on every reading without ever calling setChanged() first
Call clearChanged() on every single reading it receives
Call setChanged() and notifyObservers() only once the move passes 10 metres
Remove all of the observers until a move occurs
optionExplain: Without setChanged() no one is notified at all.
Clearing the flag cancels notifications.
Right: the flag is the gate for the threshold.
Removing observers is not needed.
questions.explain: The threshold test decides whether to set the flag, so only meaningful moves reach the observers.
questions.rule: No notification happens without setChanged(); use it to decide which changes deserve one.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: A developer’s observers do not fire. The subject calls notifyObservers() after each reading. What is the most likely cause?
options: The observers were not meant to receive readings
notifyObservers() needs an argument
setChanged() was never called before notifying
The observers must be removed first
optionExplain: Nothing suggests that.
The call works without an argument.
Right: without the flag, no one is notified.
Removing observers prevents notifications.
questions.explain: Missed notifications with the built-in class point first to the changed flag, and hasChanged() lets you inspect it.
questions.rule: Check the flag when notifications go missing.
questions.teaches: When built-in observers are not notified, the changed flag is the first thing to check, and hasChanged() reports its state.

questions.section: How Java’s built-in Observer Pattern works
questions.q: True or false: Raising the threshold from half a degree to two degrees means editing every observer.
questions.explain: The threshold sits in the subject’s test before setChanged(), so observers are not touched.
questions.rule: The filter lives in the subject.

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: With Java’s built-in support, how might a subject push data to its observers?
options: By passing a data object when it calls its notify method
By setting a global variable the observers watch
By restarting each observer with fresh data
By storing data in the Observer interface
optionExplain: Right: the notify call can carry a data object.
A global would couple everything together.
Observers are not restarted.
Interfaces do not carry data in this design.
questions.explain: The notify call is the channel for pushed data. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Push by passing a data object to notifyObservers(arg).

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: Match each call to what it does.
pairs: Pushes a data object to observers
The object an observer pulls from
Must be called before either notify
questions.explain: Pushing passes data, pulling uses the Observable handed to update, and the flag gates both.
questions.rule: Passing data pushes; notifying without data lets observers pull.

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: If a subject notifies without data, how does an observer get the readings?
options: By reading a copy that the subject made for it earlier
By waiting for a second notification that comes with data
By asking the other observers for the readings they received
By calling getters on the Observable handed to update
optionExplain: No copy is made for pull.
A second notification is not part of the design.
Observers do not share data with each other.
Right: update receives the source subject to pull from.
questions.explain: Because update receives the source subject, pulling needs no stored reference to it.
questions.rule: The update call hands over its source.
questions.teaches: The built-in update receives the subject that sent the notification, so pulling does not need a stored reference.

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: A Robot subject extends Observable and has a getBattery() getter. Sort each action into push or pull.

items.t: The robot calls notifyObservers with a battery reading attached
The battery bar calls getBattery() on the robot given to update
The robot sends the same data object to every observer
Each observer reads only what it needs from the robot
The robot builds a data object before notifying
The observer ignores the data argument and uses the robot

questions.explain: In push the subject builds and sends the data object. In pull the observer uses the robot it receives.
questions.rule: Push builds a payload; pull uses the source.

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: One observer is registered with two subjects of different classes. How can its update method tell which subject called it?
options: It cannot tell, since update carries no source
It compares the Observable object handed to it
It reads the time of the notification
It counts the notifications so far
optionExplain: The source is part of the call.
Right: the source subject is handed to update.
Time does not identify a subject.
Counting does not identify the source.
questions.explain: Because update receives its source, one observer can watch several subjects and tell them apart.
questions.rule: The source subject travels with the call.
questions.teaches: The source subject is passed to update, so one observer can watch several subjects and tell which one is calling.

questions.section: Reworking the Weather Station with the built-in support
questions.q: A subject pushes data with notifyObservers(arg) but skips setChanged(). What happens?
options: Observers are called, but they receive no data with the call
No observer is called, push or not, because the flag was not set
Observers are called and they receive the data as well
Only the first observer on the list is called
optionExplain: The flag does not affect data only.
Right: the flag gates every notification.
Setting the data does not replace the flag.
The flag is not about observer order.
questions.explain: The rule applies to both styles, since the gate comes before the call.
questions.rule: Without setChanged(), notifyObservers() notifies nobody.

questions.q: A team swaps one observer-handling class for another and the output lines appear in a different order. How should this be read?
options: The new class is faulty and should be reversed
The old class defines the correct order for the pattern
The observers must have been registered twice
Neither order is right, unless the code relied on one of them
optionExplain: The new order is not a fault in itself.
No order is defined by the pattern.
Double registration is not implied.
Right: the pattern does not promise an order.
questions.explain: The pattern fixes who is told, not in what order. The card next discusses this.
questions.rule: Do not depend on the order in which observers are notified.

questions.q: True or false: The book says the order of the built-in Observable is wrong and the hand-built order is right.
questions.explain: The authors say neither is right; they were implemented differently.
questions.rule: Neither order is the right one.

questions.q: Why is code that depends on notification order not loosely coupled?
options: It relies on a detail of one implementation that another could change
It uses too many observers for one subject to be able to manage them all
It forces the subject to know its observers’ classes
It makes the output appear on the wrong screen
optionExplain: Right: an unpromised behaviour has become a hidden dependency.
The count of observers is irrelevant.
It does not reveal classes, only a hidden expectation.
Screens are not the issue.
questions.explain: When code leans on behaviour nobody promised, that behaviour becomes a hidden dependency and a changed implementation breaks the code.
questions.rule: Do not lean on unpromised behaviour.
questions.teaches: Behaviour that nobody promised becomes a hidden dependency once code relies on it, and a changed implementation then breaks that code.

questions.q: A receipt-logging observer must run before an email observer, because the email reads the log. The developer registers the logger first and counts on that. Select the true statements.
options: Registration order is not a promised notification order
The dependency between the two steps is hidden
Registering the logger second would fix the problem
The pattern promises that the first registered is notified first
optionExplain: True: the pattern fixes who is told, not the order.
True: nothing states or enforces that the log comes first.
False: that would be the same bet in reverse.
False: the pattern makes no such promise.
questions.explain: The email step needs the log, and that dependency rests on an order nobody promised.
questions.rule: Do not depend on the order in which observers are notified.

questions.q: The email step needs what the logger produces. Which design avoids relying on notification order?
options: Register the logger a second time to make it run first
Add a short delay in the email observer before it runs
One observer does both steps, or the email draws on the subject
Remove the logger from the subject so that only the email runs
optionExplain: A second registration does not promise order.
A delay is a guess about timing.
Right: the sequence is put in one place instead of being spread across observers.
Removing the logger loses the data.
questions.explain: Steps that must follow one another belong together in one observer, or should draw on data the subject holds, rather than depend on the order of independent observers.
questions.rule: Put ordered steps in one place.
questions.teaches: Steps that must run in sequence should live in one observer, or all draw on the subject’s data, rather than rely on the order of independent observers.

questions.q: True or false: An application whose displays produce the same results in any notification order keeps working when the Observer implementation is swapped.
questions.explain: Such an application makes no assumption about order, so a different order does not change its results.
questions.rule: Order-independent code survives a swap.

questions.q: A helper class has no interface and must be subclassed to be used. What restriction follows?
options: It cannot be used with any object in the program
It can be used only once per program run
Classes that already extend another class cannot use it
It must be used through composition instead of inheritance
optionExplain: Subclassing allows it to be used.
Nothing limits the count of uses.
Right: a class can have only one superclass.
Composition is what the restriction rules out.
questions.explain: A class that must be subclassed claims the one superclass slot. The card next applies this to Observable.
questions.rule: A class that must be subclassed cannot be reused by classes with a parent.

questions.q: Select the problems the authors name with java.util.Observable.
options: It is a class and implements no interface
setChanged() is protected
It cannot notify more than one observer
It cannot remove observers
optionExplain: Named by the authors.
Named by the authors.
Not a problem raised; it notifies many observers.
Not a problem raised; deleteObserver() exists.
questions.explain: The two problems are that it is a class without an interface, and that setChanged() is protected.
questions.rule: Judge Observable by the principles it blocks.

questions.q: A team wants to replace java.util.Observable by a multithreaded version. What makes this hard?
options: No interface exists, so code naming the class must be edited
The multithreaded version cannot notify more than a few observers
Observable forbids a second subclass anywhere in the program
Observers cannot be removed from an Observable once added
optionExplain: Right: without an interface there is nothing to swap behind.
Nothing says that.
Observable can be subclassed more than once.
deleteObserver() removes observers.
questions.explain: Swapping an implementation needs an interface that both versions satisfy. Without one, every user of the class must change.
questions.rule: No interface, no easy swap.
questions.teaches: Swapping implementations needs a shared interface; without one, code that names the class has to be edited.

questions.q: True or false: A class that already extends another class can add Observable behaviour by also extending Observable.
questions.explain: A class has one superclass, so it cannot extend both. This is the reuse limit the authors name.
questions.rule: One superclass limits reuse.

questions.q: A designer wants a notification helper held inside her class by composition. Why does Observable resist this?
options: Its notify method is private, so nothing outside can call it
It cannot hold more than one observer at a time in its list
It only works inside a graphical program that has windows
Its setChanged() is protected, so outsiders cannot call it
optionExplain: The book names setChanged() as protected.
It can hold many observers.
The setting does not matter.
Right: protected methods are for subclasses.
questions.explain: Composition needs the helper’s key methods to be callable by its owner, and a protected method restricts them to subclasses.
questions.rule: Composition needs callable methods.
questions.teaches: Composition needs the helper’s key methods to be callable from its owner, and a protected method limits them to subclasses.

questions.q: A colleague says Observable is useless and must be avoided. How does the chapter differ?
options: It says Observable is the best choice in every case that arises
It says Observable has some use if you can extend it
It says the Observer Pattern itself is flawed and unusable
It says only the Swing version of the pattern ever works
optionExplain: They list problems, so not best everywhere.
Right: the authors call the problems potholes, not a ban.
The criticism is of one class, not the pattern.
Swing is a separate example.
questions.explain: The authors weigh limits against utility and leave the choice to the situation.
questions.rule: Observable has some use when you can extend it.

questions.q: A class already extends a framework base class and now needs observer behaviour. Which choice fits?
options: Extend Observable as well as the base class it already has
Write its own subject interface and list handling
Give up on notifying other objects and find another design
Copy the base class into Observable so it can be extended
optionExplain: A second superclass is not allowed.
Right: the hand-built route has no superclass limit.
Notification is still needed.
Copying classes would not remove the limit.
questions.explain: When the built-in class cannot be extended, building your own is the route. The card next gives the advice.
questions.rule: When the class cannot extend the built-in one, write your own.

questions.q: If you cannot extend Observable, you may need to roll your ____ implementation.
questions.explain: The authors advise creating your own implementation if needed.
questions.rule: Rolling your own is an accepted option.

questions.q: If you use the built-in classes, what does knowing the pattern still give you?
options: Nothing, since the library does all of the work for you
A guarantee that the library you use is correct
A way to avoid ever having to call setChanged()
The ability to work with any API that uses the pattern
optionExplain: Understanding is still useful to read and fix usage.
Understanding does not prove a library correct.
The flag is part of the built-in class.
Right: the authors say you are in a good position to work with such APIs.
questions.explain: Understanding the pattern lets you read and use observer APIs whether built in or not.
questions.rule: Know the pattern, not only the class.
questions.teaches: Understanding the pattern lets you read and use any observer API, built in or not, because the roles stay the same.

questions.q: Match each situation to the choice the authors’ advice suggests.
pairs: A new class with no superclass needing basic notification
A class that already extends a framework base class
A wish to swap in a multithreaded notifier later
A wish to learn the pattern thoroughly
questions.explain: The built-in class suits simple, free-standing cases. Other constraints push toward an interface-based version of your own.
questions.rule: Match the choice to the constraint.

questions.q: A library method accepts only java.util.Observable arguments. Can a hand-built subject be passed to it?
options: No, a hand-built subject is not an Observable
Yes, any subject can be passed to such a method
Yes, if it registers its observers by name
Only if it has exactly the same method names
optionExplain: Right: it is outside Java’s built-in Observer API.
Having the same role does not make it the same type.
Registering by name does not change its type.
Matching names does not make it the same type.
questions.explain: A hand-built subject stands outside Java’s built-in API, so code written for the built-in types will not accept it.
questions.rule: Hand-built subjects are outside the built-in API.
questions.teaches: A hand-built subject is not a java.util.Observable, so code written for the built-in types will not accept it.

questions.q: A team chose the built-in Observable and later needs a multithreaded notifier. What follows?
options: Nothing changes, since the new notifier slots in without edits
Only the subject changes, and every other class is untouched
Every place that names Observable must be edited
The observers must all be rewritten from scratch, one by one
optionExplain: A swap without an interface is not possible.
Code that names the class is wider than the subject.
Right: the missing interface makes the switch costly.
Observers need not be rewritten, only places naming the class.
questions.explain: The choice of a class over an interface returns later as an edit across every user of the class.
questions.rule: Naming Observable everywhere ties code to its limits.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: In a GUI toolkit a button lets code add click handlers. In Observer terms, what is the button?
options: An observer, since it reacts to the actions of the user
A listener, since it hears the mouse as it moves
The subject, since the handlers depend on its events
Neither; click handlers are not observers in this sense
optionExplain: The handlers observe the button.
The handlers are the listeners; the button is what they listen to.
Right: it owns the event that the handlers care about.
Handlers are the observers here.
questions.explain: The button is the source of the events. The card next gives the toolkit’s names.
questions.rule: In Swing, a component is the subject and its listeners are observers added and removed through add and remove methods.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: Match each Swing part to its Observer Pattern role.
questions.explain: The button is the subject; listeners implement ActionListener and are added with addActionListener().
questions.rule: In Swing, a component is the subject and its listeners are observers added and removed through add and remove methods.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: Both AngelListener and DevilListener are added to the button. What happens on a click?
options: The button notifies both, and each responds in its own way
Only the first added listener is called
The listeners vote on one answer
The button decides which listener answers
optionExplain: Right: every registered observer is notified.
Every observer on the list is notified.
No voting exists in the pattern.
The button does not choose.
questions.explain: Two observers of one subject receive the same notification and may respond differently, as the Angel and Devil do.
questions.rule: Same notification, different responses.
questions.teaches: Observers of one subject receive the same notification, and each is free to respond to it differently.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: A text field lets code register handlers for text changes, such as a validator and a character counter. Sort each item by role.

items.t: The text field
The validator handler
The character counter handler
The object that holds the text
The object called when the text changes
The object that lets handlers be added and removed

questions.explain: The field holds the text and manages handlers. The validator and counter are called when the text changes.
questions.rule: The source of change is the subject.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: In an unfamiliar framework, a class has addPriceListener and removePriceListener methods. What should you suspect?
options: A singleton that restricts the class to a single instance
A factory that makes new price objects on request
A decorator that wraps the class to add behaviour to it
An observer relationship, with the listeners as observers
optionExplain: A singleton limits instances, which is not suggested.
A factory creates objects.
A decorator wraps behaviour.
Right: add and remove for listeners is the usual sign.
questions.explain: Method names such as add and remove listener are a clue to look for observer roles, even in code you have never seen.
questions.rule: Look for the roles behind the names.
questions.teaches: Add and remove listener methods are a strong clue that a class is a subject, so look for observer roles behind unfamiliar names.

questions.section: Other places you’ll find the Observer Pattern in the JDK
questions.q: The AngelListener is removed from the button, and the user clicks. What happens?
options: Both still answer
Only the DevilListener answers
Neither answers
The button asks the user which to use
optionExplain: Removal ends notifications.
Right: removal takes a listener off the list.
The remaining listener is still on the list.
The button does not ask anyone.
questions.explain: Notification goes to the list as it stands, so a removed listener is skipped.
questions.rule: In Swing, a component is the subject and its listeners are observers added and removed through add and remove methods.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: True or false: Using a lambda expression for a Swing listener means the code no longer uses the Observer Pattern.
questions.explain: The lambda is still an observer registered with a subject. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A lambda that fits a one-method observer interface is an observer, and the pattern is unchanged.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: A lambda expression creates a function ____ that serves as the observer.
questions.explain: The function object is what gets registered and later called.
questions.rule: The lambda creates the observer.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: What does Java check when a lambda is passed to addActionListener()?
options: That it has the same name as an inner class would have had
That its signature matches the interface’s one method
That the body of the lambda contains no button code at all
That it was written before the button was created, not after
optionExplain: Lambdas have no class name to match.
Right: the lambda stands in for that one method.
Content of the body is up to you.
Timing of writing is irrelevant.
questions.explain: The lambda supplies the interface’s single method, so the compiler matches it by signature.
questions.rule: A lambda stands in for a single method.
questions.teaches: The lambda stands in for the interface’s single method, and Java matches it by signature rather than by class name.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: A Timer has addTickListener(listener) where the listener interface has a single method, onTick(). Which registers an observer by lambda?
options: Subclassing Timer so that its tick method writes to the log
Calling removeTickListener with a function that writes to a log
Passing the whole Timer object to itself as a listener
Passing a short function that writes to a log on each tick
optionExplain: Subclassing is not needed.
Removal is the opposite of registering.
The Timer is the subject, not the observer.
Right: the function is the observer.
questions.explain: A one-method listener interface is a place where a function can serve as the observer.
questions.rule: A lambda that fits a one-method observer interface is an observer, and the pattern is unchanged.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: An observer interface has three methods. Can one lambda expression stand in for it?
options: Not directly, because a lambda supplies a single method
Yes, a lambda can supply any number of methods at once
Yes, but only if the same lambda is passed twice
Yes, if the subject is a button in a graphical program
optionExplain: Right: the match is for single-method interfaces.
A lambda stands in for one method.
Passing it twice does not add methods.
The kind of subject does not matter.
questions.explain: Lambdas replace single-method observer interfaces; interfaces with several methods need a class that supplies them.
questions.rule: Lambdas fit single-method interfaces.
questions.teaches: A lambda replaces an interface with a single method, so observer interfaces with several methods need a class that supplies them.

questions.section: The updated code, using lambda expressions
questions.q: True or false: With a lambda observer, the button still notifies each observer by calling the interface method on it.
questions.explain: The button calls each listener’s actionPerformed(), including those created from lambdas.
questions.rule: The notification step is unchanged.

questions.q: A coffee shop sells four drinks, and customers can add any mix of four extras. How does a design with one class for each drink-and-extras combination behave as extras are added?
options: The number of classes climbs steeply with each extra
Each extra adds one class, so growth stays small
The number of classes stays the same, because drinks stay the same
Only the drink classes grow, never the extras
optionExplain: Each extra multiplies the combinations, so classes pile up quickly.
Adding one class per extra sounds natural, but every extra can pair with every existing combination.
The drinks do stay the same, but the combinations are what get classes.
Extras are part of each combination, so they multiply the classes too.
questions.explain: Every extra can be present or absent in each combination, so the combinations multiply. The card next shows why this hurts maintenance.
questions.rule: Combinations multiply as options are added.

questions.q: Because Starbuzz would have to change many classes whenever a price moves, the authors call that design a ____ nightmare.
questions.explain: The authors say Starbuzz has created a maintenance nightmare for itself: price changes and new toppings spread across many classes.
questions.rule: Many combination classes make every change costly.

questions.q: A laptop shop offers 3 models, and each of 5 extras (case, mouse, warranty, dock, bag) is either included or not. If every combination gets its own subclass, how many classes are needed?
optionExplain: This adds 3 models and 5 extras twice over, but combinations multiply, they do not add.
This treats each extra as having three states; with included or not, each has two.
Each model has 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32 extras combinations, and 3 x 32 = 96.
This adds models and extras (3 + 5); extras combine with each model, so the count multiplies.
questions.explain: Five yes-or-no extras give 32 combinations for each of 3 models, so 96 classes.
questions.rule: Count combinations by multiplying the choices.

questions.q: The shop adds a sixth extra (a screen protector) to the same 3-model laptop menu. How many classes would the one-class-per-combination design need now?
optionExplain: This adds 3 classes, as if the new extra paired with each model only on its own.
A sixth extra doubles the combinations per model from 32 to 64, so 3 x 64 = 192.
This adds 6 classes; the new extra pairs with every existing combination, not just once per model.
This adds a single class; the new extra doubles every earlier combination.
questions.explain: Each extra that can be on or off doubles the number of combinations.
questions.rule: Each new optional extra doubles the combinations.
questions.teaches: Every additional optional extra doubles the number of combination classes, so growth is exponential rather than a steady addition.

questions.q: A developer defends the design: 'With a class per combination, a price change is made in one place.' Which statement shows the flaw in this?
options: The price is stored in the base class, which becomes too large, and every subclass then depends on that one file
The compiler cannot store prices in classes
Prices must change at runtime, which subclasses forbid
The price of an extra is repeated in every class that includes it, so each of those classes must be edited
optionExplain: The scheme in question has no flags in the base class; the prices sit in the combination classes.
Classes can hold prices, which is exactly the problem: they hold them many times over.
The point is how many places change, not when.
Each combination class carries the price of its extras, so the same number appears in many places.
questions.explain: If milk appears in half of the combinations, a milk price change touches half of the classes.
questions.rule: One fact stored in many classes means many edits.
questions.hint: Where does the price of milk live in each combination class?

questions.q: True or false: A kiosk sells exactly three fixed meal deals that will not change, so the class explosion described for Starbuzz applies to it to the same degree.
questions.explain: The explosion comes from options that multiply and change. Three fixed deals give three classes, and nothing else needs editing.
questions.rule: Judge a design by how its options grow, not by the pattern alone.
questions.teaches: Counting the combinations your options allow, and asking whether the list will grow, tells you whether one class per combination will hold up.

questions.q: True or false: Moving the extras into the base class as flags means that adding a new extra needs no change to existing code.
questions.explain: The base class must gain a flag and price logic for the new extra, so existing code changes. The card next walks through this design.
questions.rule: New extras still mean edits.

questions.q: In the flag design, the base class cost() adds the price of each extra whose flag is ____.
questions.explain: Each flag records whether the extra was ordered, and cost() adds only the prices of extras that are on.
questions.rule: Flags record which extras were ordered.

questions.q: A bakery's Cake base class has flags for icing, sprinkles and candles. The bakery starts offering glitter. What does the flag design require?
options: A new flag and price logic added to the existing Cake class
A new subclass only, with no change to Cake
Nothing, because flags can be added at runtime without code
A rewrite of all the existing cake subclasses
optionExplain: The base class holds every extra, so supporting one more means editing it.
That would be true if extras lived in subclasses, but here they live in the base class.
A flag has to exist in the class before it can be switched on.
Subclasses inherit the base class, so they need no rewrite for this change.
questions.explain: Extras live in the base class, so a new extra changes that class.
questions.rule: New extra means new flag in the base class.

questions.q: A customer asks for double sprinkles. Why is that awkward with a true-or-false flag?
options: Sprinkles cannot be priced by a flag
Flags can only be used for one extra at a time
A flag records only on or off, so repeating an extra needs a count or other new structure
Doubling needs a new subclass for every cake, so each flavour would need its own double version
optionExplain: A flag can trigger a price; it just cannot say how many.
Several flags can be on at once.
A boolean can say sprinkles were added, not how many times.
A subclass is not needed; the limit is the flag itself.
questions.explain: An on-or-off flag has two states, so a double portion means changing what the base class stores.
questions.rule: A flag records presence, not quantity.
questions.teaches: A true-or-false flag cannot express repeated extras such as double sprinkles, so the base class must change again to hold counts.

questions.q: Which problem belongs to which design?

items.t: The number of classes multiplies with each new option
Some subclasses inherit features that do not suit them
A new extra requires many new subclasses
A new extra requires a new flag and edits to the base class
A price change must be made in every class that contains the extra
The base class cost() grows another branch for each extra

questions.explain: The first design spreads each fact over many classes; the second piles every extra into one class that all subclasses share.
questions.rule: Know which weakness belongs to which design.

questions.q: A ticket app has three ticket types and two add-ons, insurance and fast-track. Every type supports both add-ons, and the list is stable. Which design fits best?
options: Twelve subclasses, one for each type and add-on combination, so every price change is repeated many times
Flags for the two add-ons in the base class, because the add-ons suit every type and rarely change
A separate app for each ticket type
Prices set by hand at the counter for every sale
optionExplain: This works, but twelve classes repeat the same prices for little gain.
Two flags cover all twelve combinations and nothing is inherited that does not fit.
Splitting the app multiplies the maintenance without fixing anything.
This removes the problem by removing the system.
questions.explain: Where options are few, stable and fit every subclass, the flag design is reasonable.
questions.rule: Match the design to how stable the options are.
questions.teaches: With flags the code grows by one flag per option, while one class per combination grows by a doubling per option.

questions.q: When is the behaviour a class receives by inheritance decided?
options: When the program runs, each time an object is created
When the code is compiled
When the user places an order
When the object is deleted
optionExplain: The object is created at runtime, but what it inherits was already fixed.
The subclass relationship is written into the source, so the inherited behaviour is fixed before the program runs.
User actions choose among existing objects; they do not change what a class inherits.
Deletion has no part in deciding inherited behaviour.
questions.explain: The inheritance relationship is part of the source code, so it is settled at compile time. The card next compares this with composition.
questions.rule: Inheritance is fixed at compile time.

questions.q: Behaviour added by composition and delegation can be assembled at ____, which inheritance cannot do.
questions.explain: The student tells the master that composition lets him extend an object's behaviour dynamically, at runtime.
questions.rule: Composition assembles behaviour while the program runs.

questions.q: A chat app lets users toggle bold, italic and emoji conversion on each message as they type. Which design fits that need best?
options: Small objects for each effect that are wrapped around the message when it is sent
One subclass of Message for each possible combination of effects
A single Message class with every effect hard-coded in one method, chosen when the app is built
A new application release for every combination
optionExplain: Effects are chosen at runtime for each message, which composition supports.
Compile-time subclasses must be written ahead of time for every combination.
This hides the choices in one class and invites edits whenever an effect changes.
Releasing code for each combination is the inflexibility composition avoids.
questions.explain: The user's choices arrive while the program runs, so the behaviour must be assembled then.
questions.rule: Choices at runtime call for composition.

questions.q: Your team does not own the source code of a payment class. According to the student's argument, can you still add a new responsibility to its objects?
options: No, because only the owner of a class can extend it
Yes, but only by copying the whole class and then changing the copy to add the responsibility
No, because behaviour is decided at compile time
Yes, by writing new classes that compose with it, since no existing code is touched
optionExplain: Ownership matters if extension means editing, but composition adds from outside.
Copying is itself a modification route; composition avoids it.
That describes inheritance; composition adds behaviour at runtime.
Extension needs only new code, so code you cannot edit does not block it.
questions.explain: The authors say the technique can give someone else's objects new responsibilities without code changes to the underlying classes.
questions.rule: New code can extend code you cannot edit.
questions.teaches: Because extension needs only new code, composition can add behaviour even to classes whose source you cannot change.

questions.q: True or false: Mia argues that subclassing is flawed because it keeps changing a class's behaviour unpredictably at runtime, and this is an accurate description of inheritance.
questions.explain: Inherited behaviour is fixed at compile time, so it does not change at runtime. The weakness of inheritance is rigidity, not unpredictable change.
questions.rule: Inheritance is rigid, not unpredictable.

questions.q: Two product lines share one pricing rule that does not differ between them and does not change at runtime. According to the authors, is inheritance a poor choice there?
options: Yes, because inheritance makes every design rigid, so it should be avoided whenever any other choice is available
No; the authors call inheritance one form of extension, though not necessarily the best way to get flexibility
Yes, because composition is required in every design
No, because composition cannot work with shared rules
optionExplain: The authors say inheritance is not necessarily best, not that it is always rigid.
The authors do not ban inheritance; they caution that it is not always the best route to flexible designs.
No such requirement is stated.
Composition can share rules too; it is simply not needed here.
questions.explain: When behaviour is shared and fixed, inheritance's static nature is no handicap.
questions.rule: Inheritance is not wrong, only not always best.
questions.teaches: The authors treat inheritance as one form of extension that is not necessarily the best way to achieve flexibility, rather than as a mistake to avoid.

questions.q: A thoroughly tested class must support a new rule next month. Which approach puts the working code at the least risk?
options: Editing the tested class directly to include the new rule, then retesting it
Copying the class and editing the copy
Adding new code that extends its behaviour while leaving it unedited
Rewriting the class from scratch
optionExplain: This is quick, but it risks breaking behaviour that already works.
Copying leaves two versions to maintain and fix.
Untouched code cannot pick up new bugs from the change.
A rewrite throws away the testing the class has already had.
questions.explain: Adding without editing keeps the proven code as it was. The card next names this idea.
questions.rule: Add new code; leave working code alone.

questions.q: The principle says classes should be open for ____ but closed for modification.
questions.explain: Open for extension, closed for modification: new behaviour comes in, existing code stays unchanged.
questions.rule: Open for extension, closed for modification.

questions.q: A video editor has a tested exporter. Users now ask for a new filter. Which design change follows the principle?
options: Add an if branch inside the exporter for the new filter
Add a new Filter class that the exporter can use without changing the exporter
Replace the exporter with a brand new exporter that has the new filter built into it
Tell users to apply the filter in another program
optionExplain: This modifies the closed class for each new filter.
The exporter stays closed while the filter extends what it can do.
Replacing the class throws away tested code.
This sidesteps the design question.
questions.explain: New behaviour is supplied as a new class, so the exporter is not edited.
questions.rule: New filter, new class; exporter untouched.

questions.q: Which situation does the principle prepare a design for?
options: A requirement that nobody has specified yet
A measured speed problem found in production
A request to rename a variable
A change of programming language
optionExplain: The design offers a way in for additions that cannot be foreseen in detail.
Performance problems are a different concern from extending behaviour.
Renaming is a small edit unrelated to adding behaviour.
A language change is a rewrite, which the principle does not address.
questions.explain: The authors write that requirements will change; the design should be ready for additions it cannot predict.
questions.rule: Prepare for change you cannot specify yet.
questions.teaches: The principle targets changes you expect but cannot yet describe, so an extension point must be general enough for additions nobody has imagined.

questions.q: Match each part of the principle to what it means.
pairs: Existing tested code is not edited
A design that survives changing requirements
questions.explain: Open concerns adding; closed concerns editing; the payoff is resilience to change.
questions.rule: Open means add, closed means do not edit.

questions.q: Which of these is closest to the spirit of the principle?
options: A browser whose developers edit the core code for each user's feature request as it arrives
A browser that lets users install add-ons without anyone changing the browser's own code
A browser that refuses add-ons and ignores feature requests
A browser rebuilt from scratch each year
optionExplain: This keeps the core open to modification, the opposite of the principle.
New features arrive as new code from outside while the core is untouched.
This is closed in both senses; nothing can be extended.
Rebuilding is wholesale modification, not extension.
questions.explain: The idea reaches beyond classes: any component that is costly to change safely can be given a way in for additions.
questions.rule: Extension points protect the core.
questions.teaches: The principle's spirit applies beyond classes: any system whose core is costly to change safely can offer extension points, as with plug-ins.

questions.q: The phrase open for extension, closed for modification sounds self-contradictory. What is the most likely way out?
options: Only one of the two can hold, and the authors favour closed
Open applies during design before release, and closed applies only after the release ships
It is a joke about naming that should not be taken literally
The two words describe different things: adding behaviour versus editing existing code
optionExplain: A design is meant to satisfy both.
The words describe what is allowed, not stages of a project.
The authors state it as a serious design principle.
Once each word has its own meaning, both can hold together.
questions.explain: Extension and modification are different acts. The card next explains how a design allows the first and blocks the second.
questions.rule: Different words, different acts.

questions.q: By adding new observers you can extend the ____ without adding code to it.
questions.explain: In the Observer Pattern, observers register with the subject, so the subject gains new behaviour without editing.
questions.rule: Observers extend the subject without editing it.

questions.q: A ride app supports card and cash payment. Which way of adding a wallet payment keeps the checkout both open and closed?
options: Write a new class that follows the shared payment type and register it
Add a wallet branch to the existing checkout code beside the card branch
Copy the checkout and replace card with wallet
Remove card payment and use wallet only
optionExplain: Checkout needs no edits because it already works with the shared type.
This edits the closed class.
Copying leaves two checkouts to maintain.
This removes existing behaviour instead of extending it.
questions.explain: A shared payment type acts as the extension point.
questions.rule: Add a class; do not edit checkout.

questions.q: A team wants to extend an existing class that offers no shared type, hook or registration list. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The class is already open, so extension is automatic for any team
They can extend it by editing the compiled program
They must edit the class or redesign it to offer a way in
They can add behaviour with no effort from outside
optionExplain: Open needs a way to add behaviour, which has to be provided.
Editing the compiled program is itself modification, only less safe.
With no extension point, new behaviour has nowhere to attach.
Without an entry point, outside code has nothing to attach to.
questions.explain: Openness does not come free; it exists only where the design gives new code a place to attach.
questions.rule: Provide the extension point.
questions.teaches: Openness has to be designed in by providing an extension point, such as a shared type, a registration list or a wrapper.

questions.q: True or false: In the phrase open for extension, closed for modification, the word closed means that nobody may add behaviour to the class.
questions.explain: Closed is about editing the existing source. Adding behaviour is exactly what open allows.
questions.rule: Closed forbids edits, not additions.

questions.q: A spreadsheet app lets users add custom functions through plug-in files, but the app must still contain code that loads plug-ins. Does that code break the principle?
options: Yes, because any code that handles extensions is itself a modification of the application
Yes, because a plug-in system cannot be closed
No, because the principle only applies to games
No; it is written once as the way in, and each later function needs no edit to it
optionExplain: The loader is the extension point; it is not changed per addition.
Plug-ins are a standard way to be open and closed together.
The principle applies to any designed system.
The principle is met when each addition leaves the existing code untouched.
questions.explain: Some code must provide the way in; the test is whether each later addition needs edits to it.
questions.rule: Write the way in once.
questions.teaches: Some code has to be written once to provide the way in; the principle is met when each later addition needs no edit to it.

questions.q: True or false: A good designer makes every class in a system open for extension.
questions.explain: Extension points cost effort and complexity, so a designer spends them selectively. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Extend where change is likely.

questions.q: According to the authors, the new levels of abstraction that the principle usually introduces add ____ to the code.
questions.explain: The authors say the principle usually introduces new levels of abstraction, which adds complexity.
questions.rule: Abstraction costs complexity.

questions.q: A mobile game's scoring rules change each season, but its splash-screen layout has stayed the same for six years. Where should the team build extension points?
options: In the splash screen, since it is seen first
In both, so that nothing in the game is ever closed to change
In the scoring rules, and probably not in the splash screen
In neither, since games should never change
optionExplain: Visibility does not make something likely to change.
Applying it everywhere is the waste the authors warn about.
Scoring is likely to change, and the splash screen is not.
The scoring rules do change, so they are a good place for a way in.
questions.explain: Concentrate on the area with a history of change.
questions.rule: Past change predicts future change.

questions.q: A junior designer asks how to get better at picking which areas to open for extension. What do the authors suggest?
options: Study other examples of designs to learn to spot areas of change
Memorise a list of the classes that always change in every kind of design
Make every area extensible and prune later
Wait for management to decide
optionExplain: Examples help you recognise which parts tend to change.
No such list is offered.
This is the wasteful approach the authors warn against.
The authors point to experience and domain knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors say that looking at other examples will help you learn to identify areas of change in your own designs.
questions.rule: Study examples to learn where change happens.
questions.teaches: Looking at other examples of designs helps you learn to identify likely areas of change in your own.

questions.q: A reviewer says: 'To follow the principle, wrap every class in an extension layer.' What is wrong with that advice, judging by the authors' remarks?
options: It makes the code run slower in every case, whatever the application does
It forbids the use of classes
It cannot be done in an object-oriented language
It adds abstraction and complexity to code where change is unlikely
optionExplain: The authors raise complexity, not speed.
The principle says nothing against classes.
The authors say it can be done, just not everywhere.
The authors say applying it everywhere is wasteful and can make code hard to understand.
questions.explain: The authors say the principle applied everywhere can lead to complex, hard-to-understand code.
questions.rule: Do not extend everything.

questions.q: A team adds extension points to every module of a small invoicing tool, though most modules rarely change. Which of these costs follow?
options: Extra abstraction that readers must understand
The effort of designing and testing each way in
The compiler refuses to build the project
Code that is easier to follow in every module
Little payoff in modules that never change
optionExplain: Each extension point adds a layer that someone must learn.
The authors note that extensibility takes time and effort.
Extra abstraction does not break compilation.
Unneeded layers make the code harder to follow, not easier.
Where nothing changes, the extension points repay nothing.
questions.explain: Flexibility that is never used still has to be written, read and tested.
questions.rule: Unused flexibility is not free.
questions.teaches: Flexibility that is never used still costs effort and readability, so an extension point is only worth its price where change is likely.

questions.q: A customer orders a drink with two extras. Which approach avoids writing a class for that exact combination?
options: Write a subclass named for the drink and both extras
Edit the drink class to include both extras
Wrap the drink object in an object for each extra
Ask the customer to choose a different drink
optionExplain: This is the combination class the question wants to avoid.
This changes existing code and fits one order only.
Each extra becomes a layer around the drink instead of a class of its own.
This avoids the question by removing the choice.
questions.explain: Layers can be combined while the program runs. The card next shows the layering.
questions.rule: Wrap instead of subclassing.

questions.q: Put the steps for a Dark Roast with Mocha and Whip in order.
items: Take a DarkRoast object
Wrap it with a Mocha object
Wrap the result with a Whip object
Call cost() on the outermost wrapper
questions.explain: You build from the inside out, then ask the outermost object for the result.
questions.rule: Build inside out; ask the outside.

questions.q: A sandwich shop starts with a veggie sandwich and adds bacon, then avocado, as wrappers. Which describes the finished object?
options: A veggie sandwich inside a bacon wrapper, inside an avocado wrapper
A single BaconAvocadoVeggie subclass
A veggie sandwich with two true-or-false flags
An avocado object that extends the bacon class, which extends veggie
optionExplain: The plain sandwich is at the centre; the last extra added is the outermost layer.
This is the combination class that wrapping replaces.
Flags belong to the earlier base class design, not wrappers.
The wrappers hold the object they wrap; they do not extend each other.
questions.explain: Each extra wraps what exists so far.
questions.rule: The last extra wrapped is the outermost.

questions.q: The shop adds pickles as a fifth extra. How many new classes does the wrapper design need so that pickles can go on any sandwich with any other extras?
options: One per existing sandwich type
Twice as many as before
One for every combination of extras
One new wrapper class for pickles
optionExplain: Wrappers are not tied to a particular sandwich.
Doubling is what happens with a class per combination, not with wrappers.
Combinations are made at runtime, not written as classes.
A wrapper works with any sandwich or other wrapper, so one class is enough.
questions.explain: Wrapper classes grow one per extra instead of doubling.
questions.rule: One new extra, one new class.
questions.teaches: With wrappers, the class count grows by one for each new extra, instead of doubling as it does with a class per combination.

questions.q: True or false: A shop wraps a sandwich in a Bacon decorator and then wraps that in a second Bacon decorator, so double bacon needs a new DoubleBacon class.
questions.explain: Two Bacon wrappers each add their charge, so double bacon is a combination, not a new class.
questions.rule: Repeat a wrapper to repeat the extra.

questions.q: A developer assembles each order's wrapper chain by hand in a dozen places in the code. Which concern follows from this?
options: The wrappers will no longer fit the drink type, so the order cannot be priced at all
The program can no longer use composition
Mistakes in the order or choice of wrappers become easy to make and hard to find
Each order needs its own new class
optionExplain: Wrappers fit any drink of the shared type.
Building chains by hand still uses composition.
Many copies of the assembly code can drift apart.
Orders are built from existing classes.
questions.explain: The authors say a much better way of creating decorated objects comes with the Factory and Builder patterns.
questions.rule: Gather chain assembly in one place.
questions.teaches: Assembling chains by hand across the code invites mistakes, which is why the authors point to the Factory and Builder patterns for creating decorated objects.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: A chain of three wrappers surrounds a plain drink. Which object should the client call to get the price of the whole order?
options: The plain drink at the centre
The outermost wrapper
Each wrapper in turn, with the client adding the results
The wrapper added first to the chain
optionExplain: The centre knows nothing of the extras, so it would price the drink alone.
It asks each inner object in turn and gets the whole price.
The client would then have to combine the results itself.
The first wrapper is inside the others and misses the later extras.
questions.explain: The outermost layer reaches everything inside it. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Ask the outermost wrapper.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: Whip computes its cost by ____ the calculation to the object it decorates and then adding its own charge.
questions.explain: Delegation passes the request inward; the decorator adds its own part to what comes back.
questions.rule: Delegate inward, then add your part.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: A parcel costs 5.00. An Insurance wrapper adds 2.00 and an Express wrapper adds 3.50. The parcel is wrapped in Insurance, then in Express, and cost() is called on Express. What is the result?
optionExplain: This forgets the Express charge.
This forgets the Insurance charge.
This is the plain parcel alone.
Express delegates to Insurance, which delegates to the parcel (5.00); on the way out 2.00 and then 3.50 are added.
questions.rule: Add each layer's charge on the way out.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: True or false: The parcel is wrapped in Express first and Insurance second instead. With charges that only add, the total price changes.
questions.explain: Addition gives the same total in any order. The text each layer builds is where the order shows, for instance in a description listing the extras.
questions.rule: Totals that only add do not depend on order.
questions.teaches: The wrapping order shows up in text each layer builds, such as a description that lists extras in the order they were wrapped, even when the total price is unchanged.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: A student describes the pricing like this: the client calls cost() on the DarkRoast, then asks Mocha for its charge, then asks Whip for its charge, and adds them. Where does this depart from the pattern?
options: The client should not call cost() on any object, because only the decorators may ever be asked for a price
Mocha and Whip should not have charges
The client does the combining, instead of calling the outermost decorator and letting delegation do it
The DarkRoast should be priced last
optionExplain: The client does call cost(), on the outermost object.
Each decorator has its own charge.
In the pattern, the combining happens inside the chain.
The order of adding is not the issue; who combines is.
questions.explain: The client would need to know the whole chain, which defeats the point.
questions.rule: The chain does the combining.

questions.section: Constructing a drink order with Decorators
questions.q: A Cache decorator wraps a slow price lookup. When it already has a stored answer, it returns it. What does the Cache decorator do on such a hit?
options: It delegates first, then discards the result
It returns the stored answer without delegating to the object it wraps
It adds a charge to the wrapped lookup
It fails, because a decorator must always delegate to the object it wraps first
optionExplain: Delegating on a hit would waste the stored answer.
The decorator replaces the delegated call with its own answer.
A cache supplies an answer; it does not add a charge.
A decorator may substitute its own answer for the call.
questions.explain: The authors note that decorators may add behaviour before and/or after calls, or even in place of them.
questions.rule: A decorator may skip delegation.
questions.teaches: A decorator may act in place of the delegated call, answering by itself, as the authors note when they say decorators can work before, after or in place of the call.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: True or false: A drink wrapped in a Mocha decorator can be passed to code that expects a plain Beverage.
questions.explain: The wrapped object has the same supertype, so it fits where a Beverage fits. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Same type means substitutable.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: Which statements do the authors list among what we know about decorators?
options: Decorators have the same supertype as the objects they decorate
You can use one or more decorators to wrap an object
A decorator adds its own behaviour before and/or after delegating
A decorator must be a subclass of the concrete component it wraps
An object can be decorated only at the time it is created
optionExplain: This is the first point on the authors' list.
A chain may be as long as needed.
Work can come before or after the delegated call.
A decorator shares the abstract type, not a particular concrete component.
Objects can be decorated at any time.
questions.explain: Three of these statements appear among the authors' points; the other two reverse them.
questions.rule: Same type, many wrappers, any time.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: A downloader app has a Downloader type. Rana writes ThrottledDownloader, which wraps a Downloader. What must hold for it to be passed into code that expects a Downloader?
options: ThrottledDownloader must itself be a Downloader
It must be a subclass of the specific downloader it wraps
The receiving code must be told it is a wrapper
It must copy all the methods of the wrapped downloader
optionExplain: Shared supertype is what lets it stand in for the original.
The wrapper must match the shared type, not the particular wrapped class.
Transparency means the receiving code needs no such knowledge.
It may delegate some or all; copying is not the requirement.
questions.explain: The decorator shares the component's type, so existing code accepts it.
questions.rule: Be a Downloader to replace a Downloader.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: A decorator wraps another decorator, which wraps a plain component. Does the outer decorator need to know whether what it wraps is a plain component or another decorator?
options: Yes, it must check first to choose how to delegate
No; both have the shared type, and the outer one works only with that type
Yes, because decorators can only wrap plain components and never other decorators
No, because the inner object is always a decorator
optionExplain: Delegation works the same on any object of the shared type.
Chains can be any length because every layer sees the same type.
Decorators may wrap other decorators.
The innermost object is a plain component.
questions.explain: Since both have the shared type, the outer wrapper cannot tell the difference and has no need to.
questions.rule: Layers see only the shared type.
questions.teaches: An outer decorator cannot tell whether it wraps a plain component or another decorator, and need not care, which is why chains may be any length.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: True or false: A Mocha decorator wrapped around a DarkRoast is a Mocha and therefore cannot be passed to code that expects a Beverage.
questions.explain: A Mocha decorator is also a Beverage, since it shares the component's supertype. Being a Mocha does not stop it being a Beverage.
questions.rule: A decorator is also a component.

questions.section: Okay, here’s what we know so far...
questions.q: Team A wrote a Retry wrapper for the Service type. Team B wrote a Logging wrapper for Service. Can one Service be wrapped by both without either team changing its code?
options: Yes; both wrappers depend only on the Service type, so they can be stacked
No, because wrappers can only be written by one team
No, because two wrappers confuse the type
Yes, but only if the two teams first merge their wrappers into a single class
optionExplain: Wrappers written independently can combine through the shared type.
Authorship does not matter to the pattern.
Any number of wrappers may be used.
Merging is not needed.
questions.explain: The shared type is the contract that lets independent decorators fit together.
questions.rule: Independent decorators stack through the shared type.
questions.teaches: Decorators written independently of each other can be stacked, because each depends only on the shared type and not on any other decorator.

questions.q: The Decorator Pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object ____.
questions.explain: The word is dynamically, meaning at runtime. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Attach responsibilities dynamically.

questions.q: According to the authors, decorators are a flexible alternative to what?
options: Subclassing
Delegation
Interfaces
Abstract classes
optionExplain: The definition names subclassing as the alternative.
Delegation is the technique decorators rely on.
Interfaces can supply the shared type for decorators.
An abstract class is how Starbuzz supplies the shared type.
questions.explain: Decorators extend functionality without creating a new subclass.
questions.rule: Alternative to subclassing.

questions.q: A forum wants a gold badge on the posts of certain moderators, chosen while the site runs. Which matches the definition of the pattern?
options: Write a ModeratorPost subclass and recompile
Attach a Badge wrapper to those post objects at runtime
Edit the post class to show a badge on every post
Delete the post and create a differently coloured one with a badge
optionExplain: Subclasses are fixed at compile time.
The extra responsibility is attached dynamically to chosen objects.
This changes every post and edits existing code.
Replacing posts does not attach behaviour to existing objects.
questions.explain: Wrapping adds the badge to chosen objects while the site runs.
questions.rule: Attach a wrapper at runtime.

questions.q: True or false: Decorating one beverage object changes the behaviour of every other object of the same class.
questions.explain: A decorator is attached to a particular object. Other objects of the same class stay as they were, so two objects of one class may differ.
questions.rule: Decoration affects one object.
questions.teaches: Decoration applies to an individual object, not to a whole class, so two objects of the same class can carry different decorations.

questions.q: Which description fits subclassing, and which fits decorating?

items.t: Behaviour is chosen when the code is compiled
A wrapper is added to one object while the program runs
Every instance of the class gets the new behaviour
Different objects of one class can have different extras
A new class is written for each combination
Several extras are stacked by wrapping repeatedly

questions.explain: Subclassing decides statically for the whole class; decorating attaches behaviour dynamically to chosen objects.
questions.rule: Static for the class, dynamic for the object.

questions.q: A script needs one fixed variant of a report and needs no others. Does the definition of the pattern point to wrapping for this script?
options: No; nothing needs to be attached dynamically, so plain code is enough
Yes, because every class should be wrapped
Yes, because subclassing is not allowed
No, because decorators cannot be used on reports
optionExplain: The pattern pays off where extras vary independently at runtime.
The definition does not ask for every class to be wrapped.
Subclassing is allowed; decorating is an alternative.
Decorators suit any objects with a shared type.
questions.explain: With one fixed variant, nothing varies, so wrapping adds structure without a gain.
questions.rule: Use the pattern where extras vary.
questions.teaches: The pattern's value comes when extras vary independently; with a single fixed variant there is nothing to attach dynamically.

questions.q: In a design with Beverage, HouseBlend, CondimentDecorator and Mocha, which class would you call the concrete decorator?
options: Beverage
HouseBlend
Mocha
CondimentDecorator
optionExplain: It is the shared type that everything else conforms to.
It is a plain drink that gets wrapped, not a wrapper.
It wraps a drink and adds one extra.
It is the abstract decorator, which sets the common wrapper shape.
questions.explain: Mocha is a specific wrapper. The card next names all four roles.
questions.rule: The concrete decorator is a specific wrapper.

questions.q: Match each Starbuzz class to its role.
questions.explain: Beverage is the shared type, HouseBlend is a drink, CondimentDecorator is the wrapper base and Mocha is a specific wrapper.
questions.rule: Name classes by role.

questions.q: A notification system has Notifier, SmsNotifier, NotifierWrapper (extends Notifier and holds a Notifier) and EncryptedNotifier (extends NotifierWrapper). The concrete decorator is ____.
questions.explain: EncryptedNotifier is the specific wrapper that adds one extra. Notifier is the abstract component, SmsNotifier a concrete component and NotifierWrapper the abstract decorator.
questions.rule: The concrete decorator is the specific class that adds one extra.

questions.q: A Dark Roast is wrapped in Mocha and then in Whip. Which object is the concrete component?
options: The Whip
The Dark Roast
The Mocha
CondimentDecorator
optionExplain: It is a concrete decorator.
It is the real drink at the centre of the chain.
It is a concrete decorator.
It is an abstract class, not an object in the chain.
questions.explain: Every chain ends at a concrete component, which supplies the base work no wrapper can supply on its own.
questions.rule: Every chain ends in a concrete component.
questions.teaches: Every wrapper chain ends at a concrete component, which does the base work that no decorator can supply on its own.

questions.q: Which description fits a decorator but not a concrete component?
options: It can be passed anywhere the component type is expected by the client
It has a cost() method that returns a price
It holds a reference to another object of the shared type
It extends the abstract component type
optionExplain: Both can be passed there.
Both implement cost().
A decorator wraps something.
Both share the type.
questions.explain: Holding the wrapped object is what makes a decorator a decorator.
questions.rule: A decorator holds what it wraps.

questions.q: A Logging wrapper wraps a Service. A Retry wrapper then wraps the Logging wrapper. From Retry's point of view, what is the Logging wrapper?
options: The component it wraps, even though the Logging wrapper is itself a decorator
An abstract decorator, because it wraps something
Nothing, because only plain objects are components
A second copy of Retry
optionExplain: Roles are relative to the wrapper: the thing wrapped is its component.
Wrapping makes it a decorator to the object inside it, not to Retry.
Anything of the shared type can be wrapped.
Logging and Retry are different wrappers.
questions.explain: One object can be a decorator to what it wraps and a component to what wraps it.
questions.rule: Roles are relative.
questions.teaches: Roles are relative: the object being wrapped is a component to the wrapper around it, even when that object is itself a decorator.

questions.q: In the Starbuzz class diagram, CondimentDecorator extends Beverage. What is the main reason for that inheritance?
options: So that condiment decorators can inherit the cost of each drink they wrap
So that decorators have the same type as the beverages they wrap
So that Beverage can be hidden from the client
So that Beverage can be changed by each decorator
optionExplain: Inherited code would give fixed, compile-time prices.
Sharing the type lets a wrapped drink replace a plain one.
Beverage is the type clients use.
Decorators are meant to leave Beverage unchanged.
questions.explain: The inheritance supplies a type, not behaviour. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Inheritance here gives the type.

questions.q: True or false: Decorators get their added behaviour by inheriting it from the component's superclass.
questions.explain: Decorators get behaviour from composition. Inheritance only gives them the shared type.
questions.rule: Behaviour from composition, type from inheritance.

questions.q: Mara writes AuditedAccount, which extends Account and wraps an Account. Where does the audit behaviour come from?
options: From methods it inherits from Account when AuditedAccount is created
From the compiler, which adds auditing
From AuditedAccount's own code, combined with the Account it wraps
From every Account in the program
optionExplain: Account supplies the type; the wrapped Account supplies the work.
Compilers do not add auditing.
The decorator adds its part and delegates the rest to the wrapped account.
Only the wrapped Account is involved.
questions.explain: The wrapper's added behaviour is its own; the rest is delegated.
questions.rule: Added behaviour is the wrapper's own.

questions.q: A new condiment decorator is added to Starbuzz. According to the authors, what does the abstract Beverage class need?
options: A new method for the new condiment
A flag for the new condiment
A rewrite to include the new condiment's price in the class
No change; it stays as Starbuzz's original design
optionExplain: Behaviour lives in the decorator, not in Beverage.
Flags belong to the earlier design.
The price belongs to the decorator.
The decorator takes only the type from Beverage, so the base can stay untouched.
questions.explain: Because decorators acquire behaviour by composing, the superclass can stay as it was. The authors say Beverage does not need to change from Starbuzz's original design.
questions.rule: The base type stays unchanged.
questions.teaches: Because decorators take only the type from the superclass, adding new decorators leaves the abstract component unchanged.

questions.q: In the decorator design, which things come from inheritance and which from composition?

items.t: The shared type that lets a wrapped drink replace a plain one
The charge a Mocha decorator adds to a drink
Being accepted by code that expects a Beverage
Stacking extras in any order while the program runs
The price of the drink inside the wrapper
The Beverage type itself

questions.explain: Inheritance supplies the type; composition supplies the behaviour and the mixing.
questions.rule: Inheritance gives type, composition gives behaviour.

questions.q: A designer writes SaleDecorator extends Product. Its price() calls a method inherited from Product that reads a global discount table. Is the discount behaviour coming only from composition?
options: Yes, because it wraps a Product
No; part of it comes from inherited code, which departs from the pattern's approach
Yes, because it extends Product
No, because discounts cannot be decorators
optionExplain: Wrapping is present, but the discount logic is inherited.
Behaviour inherited from the superclass is fixed at compile time.
Extending Product gives the type; inherited code adds behaviour.
A discount is a fine decorator when its logic is its own.
questions.explain: Check where the behaviour comes from: the decorator's own code and the wrapped object, not an inherited method.
questions.rule: Look for inherited behaviour.
questions.teaches: A useful check on a decorator is where its behaviour originates: it should come from its own code and the object it wraps, not from inherited methods.

questions.q: True or false: In Java, the shared type that decorators use could be an interface instead of an abstract class.
questions.explain: The authors say that in Java an interface could be used. The card next explains why Starbuzz did not.
questions.rule: Interface or abstract class can give the type.

questions.q: The authors say that traditionally the Decorator Pattern specifies an ____ component.
questions.explain: Sue says the pattern traditionally specifies an abstract component, though in Java an interface could be used.
questions.rule: Traditionally the component is abstract.

questions.q: A team inherits a vendor's abstract Report class that works well. They want to add decorators. According to the reasoning in the conversation, what should they do?
options: Write the decorators against Report and leave it as it is
Refactor Report into an interface first
Wait to use decorators until the vendor changes Report
Copy Report into a new interface and abandon the original
optionExplain: The abstract class already provides the shared type and works fine.
This alters code that works, which the authors try to avoid.
Nothing about Report blocks decorators.
Copying creates two versions to maintain.
questions.explain: Sue's point is that a working abstract class does not need fixing.
questions.rule: Do not fix what works.

questions.q: In what ways can a decorator come to share the type of the component it decorates, according to the authors' summary?
options: Only by inheritance from the concrete component
Only by copying the component's code
By being created before the component
By inheritance or by implementing an interface
optionExplain: The shared type is the abstract one, and an interface also works.
Copying does not make it the same type.
Order of creation has nothing to do with type.
Either route gives it the same type.
questions.explain: The authors write that decorators are the same type as the components they decorate, either through inheritance or interface implementation.
questions.rule: Same type by inheritance or interface.
questions.teaches: Either route, extending a class or implementing an interface, gives a decorator the same type as its component; what matters is the shared type.

questions.q: True or false: Pat says the Decorator Pattern cannot be used in Java unless the component type is an interface.
questions.explain: The Starbuzz design uses an abstract class, and the authors say an interface could also be used. Both give the shared type.
questions.rule: Both routes work.
