questions.rule: Product knowledge sits in the subclass.
questions.teaches: The wording decide reflects where product knowledge lives: the creator is written without it, so the subclass holds all of it.

questions.q: A drawing program has an abstract Tool with draw() calling createBrush(). PenTool and ChalkTool supply different brushes. A user picks ChalkTool, and a colleague says the program decided to use chalk. Which reply fits the book's sense?
options: The program decided, by inspecting what was drawn on the screen
The brush decided by itself, since it knows which tool needs it
The base class decided, by examining the type of brush before drawing
The user decided by picking a tool; the subclass fixes the brush
optionExplain: Nothing in the program inspected the drawing; the subclass chosen by the user fixed the brush.
A brush is a product and does not choose; the subclass that creates it fixed the choice.
The base class names no brush type; the subclass chosen by the user fixes the brush.
Right: the user's pick of a tool settled the brush, the same pattern as choosing a pizza store.
questions.explain: The user decided by picking ChalkTool, and that subclass fixes the brush through createBrush(). This mirrors the pizza stores, where choosing the store settles the pizza.
questions.rule: Choice up front, product follows.
questions.teaches: The choice of subclass is often made by a user or by program setup, before any creation call happens; creation itself involves no further choosing.

questions.q: A developer says: since subclasses decide at run time, I can let a subclass change its mind halfway through orderPizza(). What is the flaw?
options: No decision happens at run time; the chosen subclass fixes the product
Subclasses cannot create objects, so the base class must do it
orderPizza() cannot be called twice on the same store object
Subclasses decide only when the program is compiled, not when it runs
optionExplain: Right: the subclass is chosen up front and fixes the product, so there is no later decision to change.
Subclasses do create the products, by supplying createPizza().
Calling orderPizza() repeatedly on one store is a separate matter and not the flaw here.
The choice is made when the object is chosen.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the subclass decision is made when the store object is chosen, and that subclass then fixes what createPizza() returns. orderPizza() has no later point at which a subclass can change its mind halfway through.
questions.rule: No mind-changing.

questions.q: A franchise subclasses PizzaStore. How much of its own code must it write to take orders?
options: A full ordering routine of its own for taking orders
A new Pizza interface covering its own regional pizzas
Only the creation method for its own pizza style
Nothing at all, since the base class does everything
optionExplain: It inherits the ordering routine from PizzaStore, so writing a second one is unnecessary.
The Pizza interface is shared by all stores, so a franchise does not write a new one.
Right: ordering comes with the base class, so only the creation method for its style is needed.
It must still supply the creation method that says which pizzas it makes.
questions.explain: A franchise inherits the whole ordering routine from PizzaStore and only supplies the creation method for its own style. The card next outlines the parts.
questions.rule: Inherit the process, supply the product.

questions.q: Put these steps of a regional store's order into the right sequence.
items: The customer picks a store
orderPizza() is called with a type
createPizza() in the subclass builds the pizza
orderPizza() prepares the pizza
orderPizza() bakes, cuts and boxes it
questions.explain: Choosing the store comes first, then the shared orderPizza() routine calls createPizza() in the subclass, and only after the pizza exists does it prepare, bake, cut and box it.
questions.rule: Store, order, create, then process.

questions.q: A pet-store franchise subclasses a Store with an abstract createAnimal(). A DogStore needs to sell puppies. What is the minimum it must provide?
options: A complete selling routine of its own
A createAnimal() that returns a puppy
A replacement for the Animal class
A new interface that describes sales
optionExplain: The selling routine is inherited from Store, so DogStore need not write its own.
Right: a createAnimal() that returns a puppy is the only thing the subclass must supply.
Animal is shared by all stores, so DogStore does not replace it.
The selling routine already exists in Store, so no new interface describing sales is needed.
questions.explain: DogStore inherits the selling routine from Store, so the only thing it must provide is the abstract createAnimal(), returning a puppy.
questions.rule: One method to supply.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a new pizza type to NYPizzaStore requires a change to orderPizza() in the base class.
questions.explain: orderPizza() never names pizza types, so adding a new type to NYPizzaStore changes only that subclass's createPizza(). The base-class routine stays untouched.
questions.rule: Products change in the subclass only.
questions.teaches: A new product added to one regional subclass leaves the base class and the other subclasses untouched, because only the subclass knows its own pizza types.

questions.q: A software firm has an abstract ReportService with run() that calls createExporter(). AccountingReportService and SalesReportService each supply their own exporters. What does each subclass inherit and supply?
options: It supplies run() and inherits createExporter()
It supplies both run() and createExporter()
It inherits run() and supplies createExporter()
It inherits both run() and createExporter()
optionExplain: That reverses the roles: run() is the shared routine and createExporter() is the abstract step.
If each subclass wrote its own run(), nothing would be shared and consistency would be lost.
Right: run() is inherited as the shared routine while each subclass supplies createExporter().
If both were inherited, the subclasses would have no exporter of their own, so nothing would vary.
questions.explain: Each subclass inherits run() from ReportService, which stays shared, and supplies its own createExporter(). That is the same outline as the pizza stores.
questions.rule: Inherit the routine, supply the creator.
questions.teaches: The same outline applies to any class with a fixed routine and one varying creation step, regardless of what is being created.

questions.q: A developer says: my regional store overrides orderPizza() to add a coupon step. Which comment fits the chapter's framework idea?
options: It weakens the shared routine, so franchises may drift apart
It is the recommended way to add features to a regional store
It is needed in every region so each can add its own steps
It is impossible in Java because the method is inherited
optionExplain: Right: overriding weakens the shared routine, so franchises may drift apart.
The framework keeps one shared routine, so overriding it is not the recommended way to add features.
It is not needed in any region; a region varies only through its creation method.
It is possible in Java, but it undermines the consistency the framework provides.
questions.explain: Overriding orderPizza() in a regional store breaks the idea of one shared routine, because each store could then change the process and the franchises may drift apart.
questions.rule: Do not override the shared routine.

questions.q: What is the best name for an abstract method that returns a product and is implemented by subclasses?
options: A static method call
A constructor
A singleton
A factory method
optionExplain: Static methods cannot be overridden, so subclasses could not implement one.
Constructors are not inherited or overridden, so a subclass cannot implement one from the superclass.
A singleton limits a class to one instance; it is not an abstract method returning a product.
Right: it creates the product and subclasses implement it, which is what a factory method is.
questions.explain: Creation can be a method that subclasses supply, and an abstract method that returns a product is called a factory method. The card next gives the name.
questions.rule: Name the method.

questions.q: In the pizza store, the code that builds a concrete pizza lives in the ____ that implements createPizza().
questions.explain: createPizza() is abstract in PizzaStore, so the code that builds a concrete pizza is pushed down into the subclass that implements it.
questions.rule: Subclass creates.

questions.q: An abstract GameLevel declares abstract Enemy createBoss(). Where is a Wolf boss created for the forest level?
options: In GameLevel's play() routine itself
In ForestLevel's createBoss()
In the Enemy class
In the player's code
optionExplain: play() is shared code that calls createBoss() and does not name bosses.
Right: the subclass ForestLevel implements the factory method, so the Wolf is created there.
Enemy is the product type that is created, not the place where creation happens.
The player's code only plays the level and never creates the boss.
questions.explain: GameLevel only declares createBoss(); ForestLevel implements it, so the Wolf is created there. The factory method sits in the subclass.
questions.rule: Subclass creates the boss.

questions.q: True or false: A factory method may have a default implementation in the base class that creates a basic product.
questions.explain: The book notes the factory method is not always abstract; a default gives a way to create products even with no subclass.
questions.rule: Defaults are allowed.
questions.teaches: A factory method may have a default implementation that creates a basic product, so the base class can work even with no subclass.

questions.q: A text editor has an abstract Document with open() calling createView(). TextDocument and TableDocument supply different views. Which part is the factory method?
options: open()
createView()
Document
TableDocument
optionExplain: open() is the client code that uses the view.
Right: createView() creates the product, and TextDocument and TableDocument implement it.
Document is the abstract creator class that declares the factory method, not the method itself.
TableDocument is a concrete creator that implements the factory method, not the method itself.
questions.explain: createView() is the factory method: the abstract creation method that subclasses implement. open() is the client code using the view, Document is the creator, and TableDocument is a concrete creator.
questions.rule: The creation method is the factory method.
questions.teaches: Any method whose job is to return a new product for the rest of a class to use can be a factory method; the pattern is found by role, not by name.

questions.q: Which statement about a factory method is mistaken?
options: It encapsulates object creation inside a subclass of the creator
It decouples the superclass code from the creation code
It returns an abstract product type that the superclass can use
It lets the superclass name the concrete products it creates
optionExplain: True: encapsulating creation in a subclass of the creator is its job.
True: decoupling the superclass code from the creation code is its benefit.
True: the superclass works with the abstract product type and never needs the concrete one.
Right: this is the mistaken statement, since the superclass stays ignorant of the concrete products it never names.
questions.explain: A factory method decouples the superclass from the creation code: a subclass encapsulates creation and the superclass works only with an abstract product. Letting the superclass name concrete products would defeat that.
questions.rule: Superclass stays ignorant.

questions.q: A customer orders a pizza from a store whose base class has a shared ordering routine and an abstract creation method. Which event happens last?
options: The pizza is prepared, baked, cut and boxed
The creation method builds the pizza for the order
The ordering routine is called with the pizza type
The store object is chosen by the customer
optionExplain: Right: processing needs the finished product, so it follows creation.
Creation comes before the pizza can be processed.
The ordering routine is called first, so it starts the sequence rather than ending it.
The store has to exist before anything is ordered.
questions.explain: Processing needs a product, so it comes after creation. The card next traces the whole order.
questions.rule: Create before you process.

questions.q: orderPizza() calls createPizza(), which is defined in the ____ of PizzaStore.
questions.explain: The two regional subclasses define createPizza(); the base class orderPizza() only calls it, so it never knows which concrete pizza it receives.
questions.rule: createPizza lives in the subclasses.

questions.q: A report service has an abstract ReportService with run(type) calling createReport(type). A client creates a SalesReportService and calls run. In what order do the pieces run?
options: createReport, then the object is created, then run, then the shared steps
Shared steps first, then createReport, then run is called last
Object created, run called, createReport in the subclass, then shared steps
Run is called, then the shared steps run, and createReport is called last of all
optionExplain: createReport is a method of the subclass object, so the object must be created before it can run.
The shared steps need the report, so they cannot run before createReport.
Right: object created, run called, createReport in the subclass, then the shared steps.
The report must exist before processing, so createReport cannot come last.
questions.explain: The client creates the SalesReportService and calls run, which calls createReport in the subclass, and only then do the shared steps process the report. This is the same flow as the pizza stores.
questions.rule: Object, call, create, process.

questions.q: True or false: When createPizza() returns, orderPizza() knows whether the pizza is New York or Chicago style.
questions.explain: orderPizza() only knows it has a Pizza, which is why the same routine works for every store.
questions.rule: Only the abstract type is known.
questions.teaches: The base class never learns which concrete product came back, which is why the same routine works unchanged for every store.

questions.q: In a delivery app, the base class calls createRoute() and then follows the route. A BikeCourier subclass returns a bike route. Which step is reached through the subclass?
options: followRoute()
The base class constructor
The courier's phone
createRoute()
optionExplain: followRoute() is a shared step in the base class, not one reached through the subclass.
The base class constructor is not the creation hook that subclasses supply.
The courier's phone is not part of the call flow between the base class and the subclass.
Right: createRoute() is the creation hook, so the call reaches BikeCourier's version.
questions.explain: createRoute() is the hook reached through the subclass: the base class calls it, and BikeCourier supplies the bike route. followRoute() is the shared step.
questions.rule: The hook runs in the subclass.
questions.teaches: In any trace of this pattern, exactly one step passes into the subclass, and control returns to the base class straight after.

questions.q: A trace states: orderPizza() asks the customer which concrete pizza class to instantiate. What is wrong?
options: It never learns the concrete class; the subclass's createPizza() supplies the pizza
orderPizza() should ask the customer, but only for the pizza's crust style
orderPizza() asks the Pizza class itself which concrete class to build
orderPizza() chooses the concrete class by reading the store's name
optionExplain: Right: the base class stays ignorant of concrete classes, since the subclass's createPizza() supplies the pizza.
orderPizza() asks for nothing; the subclass's createPizza() decides what is built.
The Pizza abstraction does not build anything; the subclass does.
The base class has no knowledge of concrete classes; the subclass supplies the pizza.
questions.explain: orderPizza() never learns the concrete class; it calls createPizza(), and the subclass supplies the pizza. The trace wrongly has the base class asking for a class to instantiate.
questions.rule: Base class stays ignorant.

questions.q: In a design where an abstract class declares a creation method and works on what it returns, what is that abstract class called in the Factory Method pattern?
options: The product
The client
The creator
The observer
optionExplain: The product is what is created.
In this chapter the creator itself uses the product.
Right: it declares the creation method.
That belongs to a different pattern.
questions.explain: The class that declares creation is the creator. The card next names all four players.
questions.rule: Creator declares creation.

questions.q: Match each pizza store class to its role in the Factory Method pattern.
questions.explain: Creators sit on one side, products on the other, each with an abstract and a concrete level.
questions.rule: Four roles, two hierarchies.

questions.q: A shipping system has an abstract Shipment with a factory method createLabel(), plus AirShipment and SeaShipment subclasses that return AirLabel and SeaLabel. What is AirShipment?
options: The abstract product
A concrete creator
A concrete product
The abstract creator
optionExplain: The abstract product would be Label, the type that AirLabel and SeaLabel share.
Right: it implements the factory method, so it is a concrete creator.
The concrete product here is AirLabel, which AirShipment creates rather than is.
The abstract creator is Shipment, the class that declares createLabel().
questions.explain: AirShipment extends the abstract creator Shipment and implements the factory method createLabel(), returning AirLabel. That makes it a concrete creator.
questions.rule: Concrete creator implements the method.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a pizza type only for NYPizzaStore requires a new abstract creator.
questions.explain: It needs a new concrete product and an edit to NYPizzaStore; the abstract creator and abstract product stay.
questions.rule: One new product, one edit.
questions.teaches: Adding a product to one region touches only that region's concrete creator and the new concrete product class; the abstract creator and abstract product are unaffected.

questions.q: A hospital system has abstract WardManager with createBed(), used in admit(). SurgicalWard returns SurgicalBed and MaternityWard returns MaternityBed. Which pair are a concrete product and its abstract product?
options: SurgicalWard and WardManager
Bed and WardManager
SurgicalBed and Bed
MaternityWard and MaternityBed
optionExplain: SurgicalWard and WardManager are both creators, not products.
Bed is an abstract product but WardManager is an abstract creator, so the pair mixes the two hierarchies.
Right: SurgicalBed is a concrete class and Bed is its abstract supertype.
MaternityWard is a concrete creator and MaternityBed a concrete product, so that pair crosses hierarchies.
questions.explain: SurgicalBed is a concrete product and Bed is the abstract product type; the wards are the creators.
questions.rule: Classify by job.
questions.teaches: Roles can be assigned in any domain by asking three questions: who declares creation, who implements it, and what comes out.

questions.q: A reader says: PizzaStore is the product because it produces pizzas. What is wrong?
options: PizzaStore is the creator; the product is what it creates, Pizza
PizzaStore is a concrete creator, since it creates pizzas
PizzaStore is an interface that the pizza classes implement
PizzaStore is the client, because it uses the pizzas that Pizza creates
optionExplain: Right: PizzaStore is the creator, and the product it creates is Pizza.
PizzaStore is abstract, so it is the abstract creator, not a concrete one.
PizzaStore is an abstract class, not an interface that the pizza classes implement.
PizzaStore declares the creation method, so it is the creator and Pizza is the product, not the reverse.
questions.explain: PizzaStore is an abstract creator: it declares the factory method and produces pizzas through its subclasses. The product is what gets created, which is Pizza.
questions.rule: Creator creates, product is created.

questions.q: A franchise network adds a new region. In a design with a creator hierarchy and a product hierarchy, what has to be added?
options: Only a new concrete product for the region
Only a new concrete creator for the region
A new copy of the base class for the region
A new concrete creator and its concrete products
optionExplain: A product alone is never created without a creator that returns it.
A creator alone has nothing to return unless the region's products exist.
The base class is shared by all regions, so no copy is needed.
Right: both hierarchies grow, with a concrete creator and its concrete products.
questions.explain: A new region adds a pair: a concrete creator plus its concrete products, one new strand in each hierarchy. The card next calls this parallel hierarchies.
questions.rule: Add a pair.

questions.q: True or false: In the pizza stores, the factory method is where each creator's knowledge of its own products is encapsulated.
questions.explain: That is the authors' remark: the factory method is the key to encapsulating this knowledge.
questions.rule: Knowledge lives in the factory method.

questions.q: A car maker has TruckPlant and SedanPlant creators with their own parts. It now wants an ElectricPlant. What must be added?
options: Nothing, because the shared assembly can build anything
An ElectricPlant creator and its own concrete parts
Edits to TruckPlant and SedanPlant to cover the new plant
A change to the abstract part type used by all plants
optionExplain: The shared assembly works with parts, so a plant must still provide the electric parts.
Right: an ElectricPlant creator with its own concrete parts is a new strand in each hierarchy.
TruckPlant and SedanPlant are unrelated to the electric plant and need no edit.
The abstract part type stays as it is, because the new parts implement it.
questions.explain: Adding ElectricPlant means a new creator and its own concrete parts, one new strand in each hierarchy. TruckPlant, SedanPlant and the abstract part type stay as they are.
questions.rule: One strand per variant.

questions.q: True or false: Two concrete creators may return the same concrete product class.
questions.explain: The parallel shape is typical, not required; when regions overlap, creators can share products.
questions.rule: Products may be shared.
questions.teaches: The parallel hierarchies are the typical shape, not a requirement: concrete creators may return the same concrete product when regions overlap.

questions.q: A game has Forest, Desert and Castle levels, each with its own enemies and each exposing createEnemy(). A fourth level, Space, is requested. What is added?
options: A new base Level class that the four levels share
A Space level creator and a set of space enemies
A change to every other level to make room for it
A change to the Enemy interface that all enemies use
optionExplain: The base Level class already exists and is shared by the three levels.
Right: a Space level creator and a set of space enemies add one strand on each side.
Forest, Desert and Castle are independent of Space, so they need no change.
The Enemy interface stays as it is, because space enemies implement it.
questions.explain: Space needs its own creator and a set of space enemies, one new strand on each side. The existing levels, the shared Level base and the Enemy interface stay unchanged.
questions.rule: Level plus enemies.
questions.teaches: The cost of this pattern grows with the number of variants: each new variant is a pair of new classes rather than a one-line change.

questions.q: When do parallel creator and product hierarchies pay for their extra classes? Select all that apply.
options: Several variants are expected over time
Each variant needs its own product knowledge
Only one variant is planned
No variant differs from another
optionExplain: Right: the structure absorbs each expected variant as a new strand.
Right: the creator is the place to keep each variant's product knowledge.
With only one variant planned, the extra classes buy nothing.
If no variant differs from another, there is nothing to separate and the hierarchies add only cost.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Parallel hierarchies cost extra classes, and they pay when several variants are expected and each needs its own product knowledge. With one variant or no differences there is nothing to separate.
questions.rule: Skip it for a single fixed variant.

questions.q: Factory Method lets a class ____ instantiation to its subclasses.
questions.explain: The class postpones the choice of concrete class and leaves it to subclasses. The card next gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Defer instantiation to subclasses.

questions.q: Which statement matches the official definition of Factory Method?
options: It creates families of related objects without naming their concrete classes
It ensures that a class has only a single instance anywhere in the program
It lets objects register with a subject so they are told whenever it changes
An interface for creating an object, with subclasses deciding which class to instantiate
optionExplain: That describes Abstract Factory, the pattern later in the chapter.
That belongs to a different pattern.
That describes the Observer pattern.
Right: this is the definition as the authors give it.
questions.explain: The official definition says Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The other options describe Abstract Factory, Singleton and Observer.
questions.rule: Interface plus subclass choice.

questions.q: A messaging app has an abstract Channel whose shared send() calls createMessage(). SmsChannel and EmailChannel implement createMessage(), so instantiation is deferred to the ____.
questions.explain: The shared send() uses messages that SmsChannel and EmailChannel create in createMessage(), so instantiation is deferred to the subclasses. The base class only uses what they create.
questions.rule: Defer means the subclass creates.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a PushChannel subclass requires editing the Channel base class.
questions.explain: The base class defers the choice, so a new subclass is enough. That is the closed-for-modification payoff.
questions.rule: New subclass, no base edit.
questions.teaches: Because the base class defers the choice, adding a new variant means adding a subclass without editing the base class at all, which is the closed-for-modification payoff.

questions.q: A mapping app has an abstract MapView with a shared render() that calls createTile(). StreetView and SatelliteView supply different tiles. Which words describe MapView in the definition?
options: It creates every tile type itself in render()
It forbids subclasses from creating tiles
It defers instantiation of tiles to its subclasses
It is the product that the subclasses create
optionExplain: MapView does not create tiles itself in render(); the subclasses create them.
Forbidding subclasses from creating tiles would defeat the pattern, since subclasses are the point.
Right: render() uses tiles while the subclasses create them.
MapView is the creator, not the product that its subclasses create.
questions.explain: MapView defers instantiation of tiles to its subclasses: render() uses the tiles while StreetView and SatelliteView create them. That is the wording of the definition applied to maps.
questions.rule: Defer to subclasses.
questions.teaches: The definition covers any class that uses a product but leaves its creation to subclasses, whatever the domain.

questions.q: A developer defines Factory Method as a pattern in which the user picks a product at run time. What is wrong?
options: Users cannot pick products in any pattern, so the claim is meaningless
Products cannot be chosen at run time, so no pattern allows it
Factory Method has no subclasses; it relies on parameters alone
It concerns subclasses supplying creation, not run-time user choice
optionExplain: Users can pick a subclass indirectly, so the claim is not meaningless; it just misdescribes the pattern.
Products can be chosen at run time by other means such as a parameter, so some designs allow it.
Factory Method depends on subclasses supplying creation; it does not rely on parameters alone.
Right: the pattern concerns subclasses supplying creation, and any choice is made by selecting a subclass.
questions.explain: Factory Method is about subclasses supplying creation, not about run-time user choice. A user can indirectly cause a choice by selecting a subclass, but that is not the definition.
questions.rule: Subclass supplies creation.

questions.q: True or false: A factory method must be abstract.
questions.explain: A factory method does not have to be abstract: it may have a default implementation that subclasses can override. The card next lists the forms it can take.
questions.rule: Defaults are allowed.

questions.q: A factory method that can make more than one product depending on an argument is called a ____ factory method.
questions.explain: A factory method that makes more than one product depending on an argument is parameterized. The pizza stores work this way, using the type they are passed.
questions.rule: A parameter selects the product.

questions.q: A parameterized factory method takes a String naming the pizza. A caller passes CalmPizza, which is not on the menu. According to the authors, when does this mistake surface?
options: At compile time, because the compiler checks every String
Only when the pizza is first baked, because the name is checked at that point
At run time, because a String is not checked by the compiler
When the Pizza class is defined
optionExplain: The compiler cannot know which strings are valid.
A String is not checked until the method runs, so the error appears then, not at some later baking step.
Right: a String is not checked by the compiler, so the mistake surfaces at run time.
The Pizza class is defined before any caller passes an argument, so it cannot be the point of failure.
questions.explain: A String is not checked by the compiler, so passing CalmPizza is only caught while the program runs. The authors call this a runtime error.
questions.rule: Strings defer errors.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing the String parameter with an enum lets the compiler catch a misspelled pizza type.
questions.explain: An enum has a fixed list of values, so a misspelled pizza type no longer compiles, whereas a String is accepted and only fails at run time.
questions.rule: Prefer typed parameters.
questions.teaches: Typed parameters such as enums, static constants or parameter objects turn an invalid product request into a compile-time error instead of a run-time failure.

questions.q: A library has a single concrete creator, BookLoader, whose factory method returns a Book. A new format adds a new Book subclass. What is affected?
options: Every method of the creator must be rewritten to know the new format
The new subclass is added; the creator's other code does not change
Every client of the library must be rewritten to know about the new subclass
The Book interface must be changed to describe the new format
optionExplain: The creator's other methods work with the Book type and do not name products, so they need no rewrite.
Right: the new subclass is added, and the creator's other code is decoupled from products so it does not change.
Clients work with the Book type and do not name its subclasses, so they need no rewrite.
The Book interface stays as it is, because the new subclass implements it.
questions.explain: BookLoader's factory method is the only code that names Book subclasses, so a new format adds one subclass and the creator's other code stays unchanged. One concrete creator still benefits from the decoupling.
questions.rule: Decoupling helps even with one creator.
questions.teaches: The pattern's benefit does not depend on having several creators; with one, products can still change without affecting the creator's code.

questions.q: A developer says: since I only have one concrete creator, the pattern gives me nothing. Where does this go wrong?
options: The pattern needs at least two creators to work
One creator cannot exist, since the pattern needs a hierarchy
It ignores the decoupling of product implementation from use
The pattern applies only to parameterized methods
optionExplain: The authors say a single concrete creator is fine, so the pattern needs no minimum of two.
A single concrete creator is possible, so the pattern does not demand a hierarchy of creators.
Right: the benefit of decoupling the product's implementation from its use remains with one creator.
It applies to single-product factory methods as well, not just parameterized ones.
questions.explain: Even with one concrete creator, the product's implementation stays decoupled from the code that uses it, so the pattern still gives something.
questions.rule: One creator is fine.

questions.q: One design hands a class a separate object that creates products. Another subclasses the class to supply the creation step. Which one is Factory Method?
options: The subclassing design
The separate-object design
Both are Factory Method
Neither is Factory Method
optionExplain: Right: Factory Method gets its creation step through subclassing, which is inheritance.
Handing over a separate creating object is composition, which is the Simple Factory idiom.
Only the subclassing design is Factory Method, so they are not both.
The subclassing design is Factory Method, so the answer cannot be neither.
questions.explain: Subclassing the class to supply the creation step is Factory Method, which uses inheritance. Handing the class a separate creator object is Simple Factory, which uses composition. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Subclass means Factory Method.

questions.q: The authors call Simple Factory a one-____ deal, because it gives no way to vary the products.
questions.explain: A one-shot deal encapsulates creation once; Factory Method adds a framework in which subclasses vary the products.
questions.rule: One-shot versus framework.

questions.q: A script runner is given a TaskFactory object at construction. Which pattern is this?
options: Factory Method
The Simple Factory idiom
Abstract Factory
The Observer pattern
optionExplain: Factory Method would subclass the runner and have each subclass supply the task, not hand it an object.
Right: a separate creator object is composed with the runner.
That would add an interface for a family of products.
That is about notifying dependents.
questions.explain: Because the runner is handed a separate TaskFactory object, the creator is composed with it rather than subclassed. That is the Simple Factory idiom, not Factory Method.
questions.rule: Separate creator object.

questions.q: True or false: A runner that is subclassed, with each subclass overriding createTask(), is using Factory Method.
questions.explain: Creation sits in the subclass, so the relationship is inheritance, which is the mark of Factory Method.
questions.rule: Subclass creation is Factory Method.
questions.teaches: The same task-creation job can be done either way; the pattern is named by the relationship between the class that uses the product and the code that creates it.

questions.q: In a payment module, one class receives a ProcessorFactory in its constructor. Another is subclassed, with each subclass supplying createProcessor(). Which one lets you vary the processor by choosing a different subclass of the user itself?
options: The constructor-supplied factory
Both equally, since each one uses a creator
Neither, since a user class cannot be varied
The subclass-supplied createProcessor()
optionExplain: That is Simple Factory, which varies by passing a different object.
Only one varies through subclassing.
A user class can be varied by subclassing it, which is what the second design does.
Right: createProcessor() is supplied by each subclass, which is Factory Method.
questions.explain: Factory Method varies the processor by choosing a different subclass of the class that uses it, with each subclass supplying createProcessor(). The constructor-supplied ProcessorFactory varies by passing a different object.
questions.rule: Subclass supply.
questions.teaches: With a separate factory you vary products by passing a different object, whereas with a subclass you vary them by choosing a different subclass of the user itself.

questions.q: A developer says: our NYPizzaStore is only SimplePizzaFactory under another name. What is wrong?
options: The store inherits an abstract createPizza(); a simple factory is a separate object
The store cannot create pizzas itself, so it must be a different kind of class
SimplePizzaFactory is an interface, so it cannot be compared with a store class
The two are identical in structure; only the names differ, as the authors admit
optionExplain: Right: Factory Method uses inheritance (a subclass decides what to create); Simple Factory is a separate object used by composition.
The store does create pizzas, through its own createPizza().
SimplePizzaFactory is a concrete class, so it can be compared with a store.
They differ in structure: one is inherited, the other is a separate object.
questions.explain: A Simple Factory is a separate object the store uses; Factory Method is an abstract method the store subclass implements.
questions.rule: Subclass versus composition.

questions.q: A student says: my factory still uses new on concrete classes, so I have gained nothing. Which reply is most apt?
options: You have gained nothing, since concrete classes remain
Stop using concrete classes entirely and rely on interfaces
Gather creation in one place, since it cannot be avoided
Use more factories until no concrete class is named anywhere
optionExplain: Gathering creation in one place helps even though concrete classes remain, so gained nothing is wrong.
Dropping concrete classes entirely is impossible, because something must be created somewhere.
Right: creation cannot be avoided, so gathering it in one place is the master's idea of corralling.
Adding factories until no concrete class is named is not the point; creation has to live somewhere.
questions.explain: Factories still use new, but they gather creation in one place, which is the master's idea of corralling. Creation cannot be avoided, so the gain comes from where it lives.
questions.rule: Corral, do not eliminate.

questions.q: True or false: The master tells the student that the creation of concrete objects can be removed from a program altogether.
questions.explain: The master replies that we must create objects or we will never write a program, so creation cannot be removed altogether. It can only be gathered.
questions.rule: Creation is unavoidable.

questions.q: A team keeps all new calls for payment providers in one PaymentFactory. When a provider changes its interface, ____ place(s) need review.
questions.explain: All the new calls for payment providers are corralled in PaymentFactory, so when a provider changes its interface there is a single place to review.
questions.rule: A corral gives a single place.

questions.q: True or false: A factory still protects you fully if some classes keep creating payment providers with new instead of using it.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a factory only protects you where it is used. Classes that still create payment providers with new leave the same maintenance trouble in those places.
questions.rule: One corral, no strays.
questions.teaches: A factory protects you only to the extent that all creation goes through it; stray new calls elsewhere leave the same maintenance trouble as before.

questions.q: A gardener says: fencing the sheep does not remove the sheep, so the fence is pointless. Which reply parallels the master's answer?
options: The fence keeps the sheep, but gathered, they are easy to care for
The fence should be taken down, since the sheep are still there
The sheep can be eliminated, so no fence will be needed
The fence is useful only if the sheep are made to disappear
optionExplain: Right: the fence does not remove the sheep, but gathered, they are easy to care for.
That leaves the sheep running wild.
The sheep cannot be eliminated, just as creation cannot, so the fence cannot depend on that.
The fence is useful because it gathers the sheep, not because they disappear.
questions.explain: The master's answer is that creation cannot be eliminated, but gathering it into one place makes it easy to care for. Fencing the sheep works the same way: the sheep stay, and the fence makes them manageable.
questions.rule: Gather to care.
questions.teaches: Judging a design by whether it removes something is the wrong test when the thing cannot be removed; the useful test is whether it makes the thing easier to manage.

questions.q: A reader says: the student's worry shows factories are a trick that gains nothing. How should that judgment be assessed?
options: It is fully right, since the concrete classes remain inside the factory and nothing is gained
It is fully wrong, since a factory does not need to name any concrete class
It is half right: factories do use concrete classes, but it ignores the value of one place
It cannot be assessed, since the master gives no reply to the student's doubt
optionExplain: The conclusion ignores the benefit of gathering.
Factories do name concrete classes, as the student says, so claiming they need none is false.
Right: the observation is accurate, but the conclusion that nothing is gained goes too far.
The master does reply at length to the student's doubt.
questions.explain: The student's observation is accurate, since factories do use concrete classes, but the conclusion goes too far because gathering creation in one place is a real benefit.
questions.rule: Accurate premise, over-reaching conclusion.

questions.q: A class contains code that creates a cheese pizza, a veggie pizza and a clam pizza, each as a concrete class. How many concrete classes does it depend on?
options: One, because all three are pizzas of the same type
Three, one for each concrete pizza class it creates
None, because the pizzas implement an interface
Two, because the first one named is exempt
optionExplain: The shared supertype does not remove the dependency on each creating line.
Right: each distinct class it names is one dependency.
The interface covers later calls; the creating lines still name classes.
No class is exempt; each one named counts.
questions.explain: Each creating line names one concrete class, so code that creates a cheese, a veggie and a clam pizza depends on three classes. The card next shows how the count grows.
questions.rule: One dependency per named concrete class.

questions.q: A class that creates 8 different concrete product classes directly has ____ concrete dependencies.
questions.explain: Each distinct concrete class named by the code is a dependency, so a class that directly creates 8 product classes has 8 concrete dependencies.
questions.rule: Count the classes you name.

questions.q: A travel app's BookingService builds FlightBooking, HotelBooking and CarBooking with new. Product asks for TrainBooking and BoatBooking too. How many concrete classes will BookingService depend on?
options: Three, because new ones will be created by subclasses
Two, because only the new ones count
Five
One, because all are bookings
optionExplain: No subclasses are involved; the service builds them itself.
The three existing dependencies stay, so counting only the new ones undercounts.
Right: the three existing classes plus the two new ones make five.
They share a supertype but each creating line names its own class.
questions.explain: BookingService already names three concrete bookings and the two new ones add two more, so it depends on five. Dependencies add up with each variant it creates with new.
questions.rule: Add one per new variant.

questions.q: If two regions share one cheese pizza class that the store already creates, the dependency count grows by ____.
questions.explain: The store already depends on that class; the count is of distinct classes, not mentions.
questions.rule: Count distinct classes.
questions.teaches: The dependency count is the number of distinct concrete classes named, so a class used in several places counts once, though its repeated creations increase the edit sites.

questions.q: A weather app's DashboardScreen creates AndroidTile, IosTile and WebTile directly. A rewrite hands creation to a TileFactory that returns a Tile. How many concrete tile classes does DashboardScreen depend on afterwards?
options: None: it names only the Tile type and the factory
Three, because the tiles still exist in the program
One, because the factory counts as a tile too
Four, which is three tiles plus the factory
optionExplain: Right: the screen names only Tile and the factory, and the factory is the only code left that names the three classes.
They exist, but the screen no longer names them.
The factory creates tiles but is not one, so it adds no concrete tile dependency.
The screen no longer names any concrete tile.
questions.explain: After the rewrite only TileFactory names AndroidTile, IosTile and WebTile, so DashboardScreen depends on none of them. It names the Tile type and the factory instead.
questions.rule: Counts drop to zero in the client.
questions.teaches: Moving creation to a factory does not remove the dependencies from the program; it moves them from the client to the factory, which is now the only code exposed to the tile classes.

questions.q: True or false: A class that depends on 8 stable, rarely changed concrete classes must be refactored at once.
questions.explain: The count measures exposure; the cost depends on how often the classes change, and stable ones cost little.
questions.rule: Weigh the count by how often classes change.

questions.q: Which statement is closest to the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: Depend upon the most stable concrete class you can find
Depend upon abstractions; do not depend upon concrete classes
Avoid creating objects anywhere in the program or its libraries
Keep every class in a single shared package for easy access
optionExplain: Stability helps, but the principle asks for abstraction.
Right: this is the principle as the authors state it.
Creation is needed somewhere; the principle concerns what code depends on.
Packaging is a different concern.
questions.explain: The principle says to depend upon abstractions and not upon concrete classes. The name sounds technical but the idea is short. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Depend on abstractions.

questions.q: Match each item in the pizza example to its role in the Dependency Inversion Principle.
questions.explain: The store's behavior is defined in terms of pizzas, and both sides should rely on the abstraction between them.
questions.rule: High-level uses low-level; both use the abstraction.

questions.q: A ReportService uses a PdfWriter directly. Which redesign follows the principle?
options: Make PdfWriter a subclass of ReportService so they stay together
Make ReportService create more writer classes for other formats
Rename PdfWriter to a more general name such as Writer
Add a Writer abstraction that both ReportService and PdfWriter depend on
optionExplain: This ties the two together more tightly.
More concrete creation does not help.
A name does not change a dependency.
Right: both components then depend on the abstraction.
questions.explain: The principle says to depend on abstractions: a Writer abstraction between ReportService and PdfWriter lets both depend on it. Renaming or adding classes leaves the direct dependency in place.
questions.rule: Put an abstraction between high and low.

questions.q: True or false: The principle is satisfied when only the high-level component depends on an abstraction, even if the low-level class ignores it.
questions.explain: The principle asks both high-level and low-level components to depend on abstractions.
questions.rule: Both ends depend on the abstraction.
questions.teaches: Program to an interface secures only the user's side; the principle also requires the low-level class to be written against the abstraction, so the arrows meet at the abstraction.

questions.q: A weather app's Dashboard shows data from an AndroidSensor class directly. Which sentence fits the principle's vocabulary?
options: Dashboard is high-level, AndroidSensor low-level, and both depend on a Sensor abstraction
AndroidSensor is high-level because it is closer to the hardware layer
Dashboard should depend on AndroidSensor directly, because that gives the best speed
No abstraction is needed for hardware classes, since they are stable
optionExplain: Right: roles are assigned by use and the abstraction sits between them.
Hardware proximity does not decide the level.
Speed is not what the principle is about; it is about depending on abstractions.
Hardware classes change too, so they still need an abstraction between them and high-level code.
questions.explain: In the principle's vocabulary, Dashboard is the high-level component and AndroidSensor the low-level one, and both should depend on a Sensor abstraction. Level is assigned by use, not by closeness to hardware.
questions.rule: Level follows use.
questions.teaches: High-level and low-level are relative: a class is high-level when its behavior is defined in terms of the classes it uses, regardless of where it sits in an architecture diagram.

questions.q: A reader says the principle is the same thing as program to an interface. Which is the most accurate correction?
options: It is weaker, since it only covers constructors and says nothing about classes
It is about program speed, not design, so the two cannot be compared
It is stronger: both high-level and low-level components depend on abstractions
It is identical to the interface rule, only written in more formal words
optionExplain: It is not weaker; it covers more than constructors and applies to whole components.
It concerns design structure, not program speed, so the two can be compared.
Right: both high-level and low-level components depend on abstractions, so the principle governs both sides.
The authors call it a stronger statement.
questions.explain: The principle is stronger than programming to an interface: it asks both high-level and low-level components to depend on abstractions, not only the code that calls them.
questions.rule: A stronger statement.

questions.q: A store class depends on every concrete pizza class. Which change makes both the store and the pizzas depend on one abstraction?
options: Add more concrete pizza classes so that each region has a pizza of its own
Make the store a subclass of one pizza so it knows what to bake
Hide the pizza class names in comments so the code looks abstract
Move creation to a factory method so the store uses only the Pizza abstraction
optionExplain: More concrete pizza classes would increase the store's dependencies rather than reduce them.
The store would depend on more, not less.
Names in comments do not change the code.
Right: with creation in a factory method, the store and the concrete pizzas both point at the Pizza abstraction.
questions.explain: The store and the pizzas can both depend on the Pizza abstraction if creation moves to a factory method, so think about which type both sides can share. The card next shows the move.
questions.rule: Both sides share the abstraction.

questions.q: After the inversion, the high-level store and the low-level pizzas both depend on the ____ Pizza.
questions.explain: After the inversion both the high-level store and the low-level pizzas point at the Pizza abstraction, which turns the old top-to-bottom dependency chart around.
questions.rule: Arrows point at the abstraction.

questions.q: An OrderScreen builds a concrete StripeCheckout with new. Applying the authors' bottom-up thinking, what is the first step?
options: Add more checkout classes so that every payment method has one
Move OrderScreen into the Stripe class so that they share code
Look at the checkouts and abstract what they share into a Checkout type
Write comments on the new calls to explain the dependency
optionExplain: This does not abstract anything.
This merges the two instead of separating them.
Right: start at the low level and ask what the concrete classes share, then abstract it.
Comments do not change dependencies.
questions.explain: The bottom-up step is to look at the concrete checkouts and ask what they share; that shared part becomes the abstraction OrderScreen depends on.
questions.rule: Abstract from the bottom.

questions.q: True or false: A store that uses a factory method but still casts the returned Pizza to NYStyleCheesePizza has inverted its dependencies.
questions.explain: Casting the returned Pizza to NYStyleCheesePizza names a concrete class again, so the store depends on it once more and the dependencies are not inverted.
questions.rule: Do not cast to the concrete type.
questions.teaches: Using a factory method does not by itself invert dependencies; the client must also work only through the abstraction, because a cast to a concrete class re-creates the dependency.

questions.q: A music app's Player builds a Mp3Decoder directly. Which design inverts the dependency?
options: Mp3Decoder extends Player so that the decoder inherits its settings
A Decoder type that Player uses and Mp3Decoder implements, with a factory
Player stores decoder names as strings and converts them when needed
Player gets a second concrete decoder class to share the load
optionExplain: Subclassing makes the coupling tighter.
Right: Player uses a Decoder type that Mp3Decoder implements, so both sides rely on Decoder.
Strings still require creation by class somewhere in the player.
A second concrete decoder only adds another dependency for Player to carry.
questions.explain: Player and Mp3Decoder both depend on the Decoder abstraction, so the arrow from Player to the concrete class is gone.
questions.rule: Introduce the shared abstraction.
questions.teaches: The inversion applies to any pair of components: introduce an abstraction that the higher level uses and make the lower level implement it, so the arrows point at the abstraction.

questions.q: A reader says: Factory Method is the only way to follow the Dependency Inversion Principle. What does the book say?
options: It is the only technique the authors give for the principle
It has no connection to this principle, which is about subclassing
It is not the only technique, though it is one of the more powerful
It is a weak technique that the authors recommend against
optionExplain: The authors say it is just one technique, not the only one.
It is a technique for following the principle, which is about depending on abstractions, not merely subclassing.
Right: the authors say it is not the only technique, though it is one of the more powerful.
The authors call it one of the more powerful techniques, not a weak one.
questions.explain: The book presents Factory Method as one technique for following the Dependency Inversion Principle, and one of the more powerful, but not the only one.
questions.rule: One powerful technique among others.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: Which of these does the Dependency Inversion Principle's guidance advise against? Select all that apply.
options: Holding a reference to a concrete class in a variable
Deriving a class from a concrete class
Calling a method through an interface
Declaring a method in an abstract class
optionExplain: Right: a reference to a concrete class ties the code to that class.
Right: the child depends on its concrete parent.
Calling a method through an interface is the preferred style, so the guidance does not advise against it.
Abstract declarations are what the principle favors.
questions.explain: The guidance disfavors depending on concrete classes: holding a reference to one and deriving from one both do that. Calling through an interface and declaring methods in an abstract class are the preferred style.
questions.rule: Avoid concrete references and parents.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: No class should derive from a concrete class; derive from an ____ such as an interface or abstract class.
questions.explain: Deriving from an abstraction such as an interface or abstract class keeps the new class depending on a stable contract instead of on a concrete implementation.
questions.rule: Derive from abstractions.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A SmartLamp extends a concrete BasicLamp, overrides its turnOn(), and a Controller holds a field of type SmartLamp. How many guidelines does this break?
options: Three: a concrete reference, a concrete parent and an overridden method
One, since only the field holding the SmartLamp reference counts
Two, since overriding a method is allowed for any subclass
None, since the guidelines were written about pizza stores only
optionExplain: Right: a concrete reference, a concrete parent and an overridden method each break one guideline.
The field is only one issue; the concrete parent and the override also break guidelines.
Overriding an implemented method is what the third guideline advises against, so it counts.
The guidelines are general advice for any design, not only for pizza stores.
questions.explain: Checking each guideline in turn: Controller holds a reference of the concrete type SmartLamp, SmartLamp derives from a concrete class, and it overrides an implemented method. That breaks all three guidelines.
questions.rule: Check all three.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: If a subclass has to override an implemented method of its base class, the base class was not really an abstraction to start with.
questions.explain: Implemented methods in a base class are meant to be shared by all subclasses; overriding shows they were not.
questions.rule: Overriding signals a leaky base.
questions.teaches: Having to override an implemented method suggests the base class does not capture what its subclasses share, so the abstraction itself may be the thing to repair.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: In a spreadsheet tool, a ChartPanel keeps a field of type ConcreteBarChart. Which guideline does this break, and what fix do the authors suggest?
options: A class derives from a concrete class; make ChartPanel final to stop it
A method overrides an implemented method; delete the overriding method
None, because a field is allowed to hold a reference to any class it uses
A variable holds a concrete class; type it as Chart and use a factory
optionExplain: ChartPanel is not deriving from a concrete class; it holds a field, so that guideline does not apply.
The scenario describes no overriding method, so that guideline is not the one broken.
The guideline explicitly covers variables holding references to concrete classes, so a field is not exempt.
Right: this is the guideline about variables holding concrete classes, and the fix is to type it as Chart and use a factory.
questions.explain: ChartPanel's field of type ConcreteBarChart breaks the guideline against holding a reference to a concrete class. The fix is to type the variable as the Chart abstraction and obtain the object from a factory.
questions.rule: Variable type reveals dependency.
questions.teaches: Guidelines are symptom checks: each points at a different place, field types, parent classes or overridden methods, where a hidden concrete dependency can be found.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A developer says: I derive from an abstract base class and override its concrete helper methods all the time, so I follow the guidelines. What is wrong?
options: Abstract parents are not allowed under the guidelines, so the design fails
Overriding implemented methods breaks the third guideline, abstract parent or not
Helper methods cannot be concrete in an abstract parent, so the design fails
The guidelines apply only to interfaces, so this code is outside their scope
optionExplain: Abstract parents are encouraged by the guidelines, so that is not what fails.
Right: overriding implemented methods breaks the third guideline, whether or not the parent is abstract.
An abstract parent can contain concrete helper methods; the guidelines caution against overriding them.
The guidelines apply to all classes and not only to interfaces, so this code is in scope.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Deriving from an abstract base class is fine under the guidelines, but overriding its implemented helper methods breaks the third guideline. The abstraction is not the problem; the overrides are.
questions.rule: Overrides are the warning.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A developer calls new String() inside a method. How should this be judged by the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: It does not violate the principle, since String is part of the language
It violates the principle but is acceptable, as String is unlikely to change
It is a serious fault, so String creation should go behind a factory
It is acceptable because strings are small and cheap to create anywhere
optionExplain: It names a concrete class, so it does.
Right: it violates the principle but is acceptable, since String is unlikely to change.
The cost of a violation depends on how often the class changes, and String rarely does.
Size and cheapness do not decide; what matters is how likely the class is to change.
questions.explain: String is a concrete class, so new String() technically violates the principle, but it is unlikely to change, so the violation is harmless. The cost depends on how often the class changes; the card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Judge by likelihood of change.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every Java program ever written violates these guidelines.
questions.explain: The authors say every Java program violates these guidelines, to stress that they are guidelines to aim for rather than absolute rules.
questions.rule: Guidelines are aims.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: Sort these creation sites by what the authors' reasoning suggests.

items.t: A String built inside a method
A list built inline in a helper
A small value class that has not changed in years
A pricing rule that changes every quarter
Payment provider classes that vary by country
Enemy types added every release

questions.explain: Classes unlikely to change can be created directly; classes likely to change deserve a technique such as Factory Method.
questions.rule: Shield what changes.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: True or false: A factory placed around a class that later proves stable for ten years was a serious design error.
questions.explain: Likelihood of change is a prediction made in advance; a protective factory that turned out unnecessary is a small cost.
questions.rule: Judge by what was known then.
questions.teaches: Whether a class is likely to change is a prediction made in advance, so a protective factory around a class that later proves stable is a small cost, not an error.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A game developer creates Vector2 objects directly everywhere but puts Enemy creation behind a factory. A reviewer wants Vector2 behind a factory too. What reply fits the authors' reasoning?
options: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so direct creation is fine; Enemy varies
The reviewer is right, since no concrete creation is acceptable
The developer is wrong to use any factory at all in the game
Both should be created directly, since factories add needless classes
optionExplain: Right: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so direct creation is fine, while Enemy varies.
The authors accept violations for stable classes, so not every concrete creation must be removed.
Classes that vary, like Enemy, do need a factory, so using one is right.
Enemy varies, so it does benefit from a factory and should not be created directly.
questions.explain: Vector2 is unlikely to change, so creating it directly is acceptable by the same reasoning the authors give for String. Enemy varies, so it belongs behind a factory.
questions.rule: Stable classes can be created directly.
questions.teaches: The test for dropping the guideline is the class's expected stability, not its category; a small value class is usually stable, while a domain class with many variants is not.

questions.section: A few guidelines to help you follow the Principle...
questions.q: A reader concludes: the authors admit all programs violate the guidelines, so the guidelines are worthless. Where does the conclusion fail?
options: The authors themselves said the guidelines are worthless in practice
The authors only meant that a few programs violate them, so the admission is narrower
It ignores that guidelines tell you when and why you are breaking them
The guidelines apply only to String objects, so they say nothing else
optionExplain: The authors never called the guidelines worthless; they present them as guidelines to follow where reasonable.
The authors say every Java program violates them, so the admission is not narrower; the flaw lies elsewhere.
Right: guidelines tell you when and why you are breaking them, and that awareness is the value.
The guidelines apply to class design generally, not only to String objects.
questions.explain: The guidelines are valuable because they tell you when and why you are breaking them, so you break them knowingly. Admitting that violations are common does not make that awareness worthless.
questions.rule: Guidelines give awareness.

questions.q: A franchiser finds that some franchises use cheaper ingredients than agreed. Which response gives the franchiser direct control over ingredient quality?
options: Ask franchisees to be more careful with their ingredients
Remove the regional styles from the franchise menu
Let each franchise choose its own supplier of ingredients
Supply the ingredients from the franchiser's own source
optionExplain: Asking franchisees to be careful is only a request, and requests do not enforce quality.
Regional styles are not the cause of the cheaper ingredients, so removing them fixes nothing.
Letting each franchise pick its own supplier invites exactly the cheaper-ingredient problem.
Right: supplying ingredients from the franchiser's own source gives direct control over their quality.
questions.explain: Controlling the source controls the quality, so the franchiser supplies the ingredients itself. The card next shows how the book does it.
questions.rule: Control the supply.

questions.q: True or false: In the book, the ingredient problem appears after the ordering framework was already in place.
questions.explain: The franchises were following the procedures, but some were substituting inferior ingredients.
questions.rule: Process was fine, inputs were not.

questions.q: A pharmacy chain finds some stores buying cheaper packaging than agreed. The chain wants one supplier but needs different labels per country. What does the pizza solution suggest?
options: Supply the packaging from head office, with a set for each country
Ban country-specific labels so one packaging set fits every store
Let each store decide on quality, since stores know their customers
Ship one identical set everywhere and ignore the labeling differences
optionExplain: Right: head office supplies the packaging, with a regional set for each country.
The regional differences are real.
Letting each store decide brings back the original problem of stores buying cheaper packaging.
One identical set ignores that labeling rules differ by country.
questions.explain: As with the pizza ingredients, head office supplies the packaging centrally and provides a set for each country. That keeps one supplier while allowing the labeling to differ.
questions.rule: Central source, regional sets.

questions.q: True or false: If every region could use exactly the same sauce, the book's design would still need a separate sauce set for each region.
questions.explain: The need for several sets comes from regional differences; one shared sauce needs only one set.
questions.rule: Sets follow differences.
questions.teaches: The need for several parallel sets comes from regional difference; where regions share an ingredient, one shared class serves them all.

questions.q: A coffee chain wants consistent beans in every shop, but each country has different import rules. Which problem structure does this match?
options: Process variation with a single set of inputs
A static factory that every shop calls directly
Centralized supply with a separate set per region
A cache that stores the beans between shops
optionExplain: A single set of inputs does not fit, because the sets differ by region.
Static calls are not the structure here; the problem is central supply with regional sets.
Right: this matches the pizza ingredients, with centralized supply and a separate set per region.
A cache between shops is unrelated to the supply and regional-set structure.
questions.explain: Consistent beans from central supply, with a separate set for each country's import rules, has the same structure as the pizza ingredients: one control point and regional sets.
questions.rule: Central supply, regional sets.
questions.teaches: The ingredient problem is a general shape: a central party controls inputs, but each context needs its own matching set, which is what families of products later model.

questions.q: Which measures help keep pizzas consistent across franchises, according to the chapter's design? Select all that apply.
options: A shared ordering and preparation procedure
Regional ingredient sets supplied from a factory
Letting each franchise choose its own supplier
Removing the regional styles
optionExplain: Right: the framework keeps the ordering and preparation process the same.
Right: the franchiser controls what goes into each pizza through the factory.
Letting each franchise choose its own supplier invites the substitution problem.
Regional variety is a goal, not the cause, so removing regional styles does not help consistency.
questions.explain: Consistency needs control of both the process and the inputs: a shared procedure keeps the steps the same, and regional ingredient sets from a factory keep the franchiser in charge of what goes in.
questions.rule: Inputs and process.

questions.q: A pizza needs dough, sauce and cheese, and each region has its own versions of all three. What is the set of one region's versions called?
options: A singleton shared by every region
A decorator layered over the ingredients
A family of related ingredient classes
A proxy standing in for the ingredients
optionExplain: A singleton is a different concept about instance counts.
A decorator wraps an object to add behavior.
Right: the related parts needed for one region's pizza.
A proxy stands in for another object.
questions.explain: Dough, sauce and cheese are a set of parts that belong together for one region, and a set of related parts like that is a family. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Family means parts that belong together.

questions.q: Which of these belong to the pizza ingredient family in the book? Select all that apply.
options: Dough
Sauce
Cheese
The franchise's phone number
The shop's opening hours
optionExplain: Right: dough is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
Right: sauce is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
Right: cheese is one of the ingredients needed to make a pizza.
A phone number has nothing to do with making a pizza, so it is not in the ingredient family.
Opening hours are not an ingredient, so they are not part of the family.
questions.explain: The ingredient family is everything needed to make a pizza, such as dough, sauce and cheese. A phone number and opening hours are not ingredients.
questions.rule: Family means all the parts.

questions.q: A theme-park app has WinterTheme with a white background, blue button and snowflake icon, and SummerTheme with matching summer choices. A screen uses the white background from WinterTheme and a summer icon. What is wrong?
options: The parts come from different families, so they may not belong together
Nothing is wrong, because a theme is only decoration for the screen
The screen should use more families so that the parts can be mixed
The icon should be removed, because only one icon is allowed
optionExplain: Right: parts from different families may not belong together, and mixing them breaks consistency.
A theme is more than decoration: its parts are designed to match, and mixing them spoils that.
Using more families so parts can be mixed would make the inconsistency worse.
The issue is mixing families, not the icon itself; each family has its own icon.
questions.explain: WinterTheme's background and SummerTheme's icon come from different families, which are designed so that their parts match. Mixing them breaks the consistency a family provides.
questions.rule: One family at a time.

questions.q: True or false: Two families may share an ingredient class, such as a Seattle family that reuses New York's dough.
questions.explain: What makes a set a family is that its parts belong together; individual parts can be reused across families.
questions.rule: Families may share parts.
questions.teaches: Families may share ingredient classes; what makes a set a family is that the parts are chosen to belong together, not that every part is unique to it.

questions.q: A car configurator offers a Sport package with stiff suspension, sports seats and low-profile tires, and a Comfort package with soft suspension, plush seats and tall tires. What is each package, in the book's terms?
options: A single large product
A static method call
A constructor parameter
A family of related parts
optionExplain: A package is not a single product; it is made of many parts chosen to go together.
A static method call is a code construct and does not describe a set of related parts.
A constructor parameter is a single value passed in, while a package is a set of parts.
Right: the parts are chosen to go together, so each package is a family of related parts.
questions.explain: Each package is a set of parts chosen to go together, such as suspension, seats and tires. That is a family of related parts in the book's sense.
questions.rule: Families are sets of related parts.
questions.teaches: A family is defined by the parts' relationship, not by the domain: any product built from several parts that must match each other forms one.

questions.q: A developer says: a family means all the products a class can possibly create. What is wrong?
options: Families only apply to food products such as ingredients
A family is a set of related parts that belong together
Families must have exactly three parts, like dough, sauce and cheese
Classes cannot create families, only single objects
optionExplain: Families apply to any related parts, not only to food products.
Right: a family is a set of related parts that belong together, and relatedness is what defines it.
A family can have any number of related parts; the three in the pizza example are only an illustration.
A class can create a whole family of related products, not just single objects.
questions.explain: A family is defined by relatedness: a set of parts that belong together, like dough, sauce and cheese. It is not simply everything a class can create.
questions.rule: Family means related.

questions.q: A franchiser must provide regional ingredient sets. Which approach lets any store get its region's ingredients through one common type?
options: One big class that uses an if for each region and each ingredient
An interface with a create method per ingredient and a factory per region
A static method for each ingredient that the store calls by name
A separate unrelated class for each region, with no shared type
optionExplain: Branches return the edit problem.
Right: one shared type, one implementation per region.
Static blocks swapping regions.
With no shared type the store would have to name each region.
questions.explain: A shared type with regional implementations is the shape. The card next lists the steps.
questions.rule: Interface plus one factory per region.

questions.q: What does the PizzaIngredientFactory interface declare?
options: A method that bakes the pizzas for each region
A single method that returns a whole pizza
A constructor for each region of the franchise
A create method for each ingredient in the family
optionExplain: Baking is not creation of ingredients.
Pizzas are built from ingredients.
Constructors belong to classes, not interfaces.
Right: the interface has one create method per product in the family.
questions.explain: PizzaIngredientFactory declares one create method for each ingredient in the family, such as createDough(), createSauce() and createCheese(). Each regional factory implements them.
questions.rule: One method per product.

questions.q: The theme-park app has ThemeFactory with createBackground(), createButton() and createIcon(). How many classes does a new AutumnThemeFactory implement?
options: One class, implementing all three create methods
Three classes, one for each create method
None, because it inherits from the winter factory
Two, covering background and button only
optionExplain: Right: one concrete factory class implements all three create methods for the whole family.
One factory covers the whole family, so there is no class per create method.
It does not need to inherit from the winter factory; it implements the ThemeFactory interface itself.
All three methods must be implemented, so covering only background and button leaves the family incomplete.
questions.explain: A concrete factory covers the whole family, so AutumnThemeFactory is a single class that implements createBackground(), createButton() and createIcon().
questions.rule: One factory, all methods.

questions.q: True or false: Adding a createSound() method to the factory interface requires every concrete factory to be updated.
questions.explain: Adding createSound() to the interface means each concrete factory that implements it must supply the new method, which is a real cost of this design.
questions.rule: Adding to the interface means updating all.
questions.teaches: Adding a product to a family changes the factory interface and so forces an update to every concrete factory, a real cost of this design.

questions.q: Put the steps of building regional factories for an office suite's dialogs in the order the authors' recipe suggests.
items: Define a UiFactory interface with createWindow, createButton and createMenu
