questions.q: True or false: If the program must run on a JVM at Java 1.4, double-checked locking is a safe choice.
questions.explain: The authors warn that many 1.4 JVMs implement volatile in a way that allows improper synchronization, so another method should be considered.
questions.rule: Java 5 or later only.

questions.q: An engineer removes the first, unlocked check from a configuration loader and keeps only the check inside the synchronized block. What is the effect?
options: It stays correct, but every call takes the lock again, losing the saving
It becomes incorrect, because a single check cannot find an empty variable at all
It becomes faster, because there are now fewer checks for each call to make
It works only on Java 1.4 and earlier, where checks are handled differently
optionExplain: The first check is what avoids the lock on later calls.
One check inside the lock is enough for correctness.
Each call now waits for the lock.
The version issue is unrelated to this change.
questions.explain: The code is then equivalent to a synchronized method. The unlocked first check is the whole point of the technique.
questions.rule: The first check buys the speed.
questions.teaches: The unlocked first check is what saves the cost; removing it leaves a correct but fully locked method.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: The boiler has no performance concerns and is instantiated in every run. Which fix would the authors call overkill?
options: Double-checked locking
Synchronizing getInstance
Eager instantiation
All three fixes are equally overkill
optionExplain: It adds complexity and a Java 5 requirement for no needed gain.
They call it straightforward and a good choice.
They say it works as well as synchronizing.
They recommend two of them for this case.
questions.explain: Complex techniques are justified by needs the boiler does not have. The card next gives the full verdicts.
questions.rule: Match the technique to the need.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: Match each fix to the authors' verdict for the boiler.
pairs: Works as well, but may be less obvious to some developers
Overkill here, and needs Java 5 or later
questions.explain: Each verdict ties the fix to the facts: no performance concerns, always instantiated, and a version requirement.
questions.rule: Know each verdict and its reason.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: An airport tracker Singleton is heavy and needed in only some deployments. Scanners call it 100,000 times a second on Java 17. Which fix fits the authors' reasoning?
options: Synchronizing getInstance
Eager instantiation
Double-checked locking
Keeping the classic unsynchronized version
optionExplain: The lock would be taken 100,000 times a second.
The object is heavy and not needed everywhere.
It keeps lazy creation and avoids a lock on most calls.
It is not thread-safe.
questions.explain: The constraints reverse the boiler's: heavy traffic and an object that may never be needed. The same reasoning picks a different fix.
questions.rule: Different constraints, different fix.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: Which fact about the boiler makes eager instantiation harmless for it?
options: The boiler is a small object with only a little data
The code instantiates the boiler anyway
The boiler runs on Java 5 or later in the factory
The boiler is controlled by a single trained operator
optionExplain: Size is not the stated reason.
Early creation costs nothing extra if the object would be built regardless.
The version matters for double-checked locking, not eager creation.
Operators are not mentioned as the reason.
questions.explain: A verdict is only as good as the fact behind it. If the boiler were not always created, eager creation would waste the build.
questions.rule: A recommendation depends on its premise.
questions.teaches: A verdict is only as good as the facts behind it: the endorsement of eager creation depends on the boiler always being instantiated.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: True or false: If the boiler controller became a hot path with thousands of calls a second on Java 5 or later, the authors' reason for rejecting double-checked locking would no longer hold.
questions.explain: They rejected it because performance was no concern. When that premise changes, the verdict can change.
questions.rule: Change the premise, change the verdict.

questions.section: Meanwhile, back at the Chocolate Factory...
questions.q: A colleague says: the authors chose synchronization for the boiler, so use it everywhere. Which reply fits the chapter?
options: They are right, because the authors would not give weak advice to their readers
They are wrong, because synchronization is always the slowest of the possible options
They are right, because the other fixes were shown to be incorrect in the chapter
Their choice rested on the boiler's facts; other constraints could favour another fix
optionExplain: Authority is not the test; the reasons are.
The chapter says it can be a good choice.
The chapter presents all three as working.
Advice is tied to the case it was given for.
questions.explain: A generalisation from one case needs the case's conditions to hold elsewhere. The authors stress examining performance and resource constraints.
questions.rule: Generalise only where the conditions match.
questions.teaches: A choice recommended for one case is not a rule for all cases; the recommendation holds only where the same constraints hold.

questions.q: A developer says a global variable does everything a Singleton does. Which gap is the real one?
options: It cannot be read from other classes, only from the class that declares it
It can only hold primitive values and cannot hold objects at all
It gives access to an object but cannot ensure only one instance exists
It is created at compile time, long before the program itself begins to run
optionExplain: Globals are readable from other classes.
Globals can hold objects.
Access is covered; the one-instance guarantee is not.
Objects are created when the program runs.
questions.explain: A global offers reachability. Nothing about it stops a second object from being built. The card next lists the authors' grounds.
questions.rule: Access is not control of the count.

questions.q: Which disadvantages of global variables does the chapter name or imply? Choose three.
options: The object may be created at startup even if it is never used
Nothing in a global variable prevents a second instance
They encourage polluting the namespace with many references
They can only be read by classes in the same package
They run noticeably slower than any method call
optionExplain: Right: the lazy-versus-eager problem the Guru raises.
Right: a global provides access but not the one-instance guarantee.
Right: the Q and A mentions namespace pollution with small objects.
Globals in Java are static references reachable from other classes; the chapter does not claim this.
The chapter makes no claim about speed against method calls.
questions.explain: The chapter's three grounds are startup creation, no guarantee of a single instance, and namespace clutter.
questions.rule: Three grounds against globals.

questions.q: A teammate proposes a global static reference to a 2 GB translation table filled at launch, saying it is the same as a Singleton. Which difference matters most?
options: The table is built at launch even in runs that never use it; a lazy Singleton waits
The global cannot be shared between classes, while a Singleton can be shared
The global is stored on disk, while a Singleton is stored in the memory
The global holds only one language, while a Singleton can hold several of them
optionExplain: This is the lazy-versus-eager difference the Guru names.
Globals are shared between classes.
Both live in memory.
Content is not what differs.
questions.explain: A global filled at launch spends the cost in every run. A lazily built Singleton spends it only when the table is first requested.
questions.rule: Cost at launch versus cost at first use.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Singletons can still be abused, even though they avoid some problems of global variables.
questions.explain: The authors argue for the pattern without claiming it is free of faults. A reader who accepts the grounds should still watch for abuse.
questions.rule: Better is not flawless.
questions.teaches: Singletons avoid some drawbacks of globals but not all: the authors warn that they can be abused, so the grounds for preferring them are comparative, not absolute.

questions.q: Which review comment gives a showable ground rather than a reaction?
options: Global variables feel sloppy to me, so I would avoid this design in new code
Everyone says Singletons are outdated, so we should drop it from this project
I have never liked static methods, so I think the design is weak overall
This object is built at startup though most runs never use it, wasting memory
optionExplain: A feeling, not a ground.
Popularity of an opinion is not a reason.
A dislike, not an argument about this case.
It points to a cost that can be checked in the code.
questions.explain: A good critique names something that can be shown wrong or costly in this design. Taste and common opinion cannot be tested.
questions.rule: Give grounds you can show.

questions.q: A small holiday-calendar object is cheap, used in every run at launch, and not duplicated in practice. Which of the authors' grounds still favours a Singleton over a global?
options: Avoiding the cost of building an object that is never used
The guarantee that no second instance can be built
Avoiding namespace pollution from many small references
None of them, since a global is better in every such case
optionExplain: The object is always used, so there is no waste.
The lazy-creation ground weakens, but the guarantee remains.
One object does not pollute the namespace.
The guarantee still differs.
questions.explain: When creation cost is irrelevant and only one object exists anyway, the remaining benefit is that the class enforces the count. Whether that is worth the pattern is a judgment.
questions.rule: Weigh which grounds apply to the case.
questions.teaches: Which grounds for a Singleton apply depends on the case: for a cheap, always-used object only the one-instance guarantee remains, so the benefit is smaller.

questions.q: True or false: A class whose members are all static can behave like a Singleton in some cases.
questions.explain: The authors say yes, if the class is self-contained and does not depend on complex initialization. The card next gives the catch.
questions.rule: It can work, but with conditions.

questions.q: According to the authors, the all-static approach can cause subtle bugs involving the ____ of initialization.
questions.explain: Static initialization across several classes can run in a hard-to-see order, which creates subtle bugs.
questions.rule: Initialization order is the hazard.

questions.q: Which scenario most strongly warns against an all-static class?
options: A text-formatting helper that holds no data and reads nothing when it loads
A configuration class whose static setup depends on the fields of three other classes
A constants class holding fixed numbers that are set directly in the code itself
A small utility with a single method that converts inches into centimetres
optionExplain: Self-contained with simple setup is the safe case.
Several classes with initialization dependencies are the risky case.
No dependencies, no ordering problem.
A self-contained utility is not at risk.
questions.explain: The warning applies when initialization is complex or spans several classes. A self-contained class avoids the ordering problem.
questions.rule: Dependencies create ordering bugs.

questions.q: Class A's static setup reads a static field of class B. What risk do the authors' warning point to?
options: A and B become one single object, so that both of their values are overwritten
B is created twice, once by itself and once more by the setup code of A
A cannot be loaded at all, because it depends on a static field of B
A may read B's field before B has finished its setup, giving a wrong value
optionExplain: Static classes do not merge.
Static classes are not instantiated.
Dependencies themselves are allowed.
This is an order-of-initialization bug.
questions.explain: When initializations depend on each other, the order decides the values. The bug is subtle because the code may work or fail depending on which class is loaded first.
questions.rule: Order decides the value.
questions.teaches: When one class's static setup reads another's, the order in which they initialise decides what is read, which is the subtle bug the authors mean by order of initialization.

questions.q: True or false: If the class is self-contained with no complex initialization, the authors say an all-static class would be the same as a Singleton.
questions.explain: The warning is conditional. With simple, self-contained setup, the authors accept the all-static design.
questions.rule: The warning depends on the conditions.

questions.q: A colleague says the authors condemn all-static classes outright. Which response is accurate?
options: They accept them when self-contained, and prefer a Singleton object otherwise
The colleague is right, since the authors call them far worse in every single case
The colleague is wrong, since the authors recommend all-static classes as the first choice
The authors do not discuss the topic anywhere in the whole of the chapter
optionExplain: The advice is conditional, not a ban.
The authors allow the self-contained case.
They recommend staying in the object world.
The Q and A addresses it directly.
questions.explain: A careful reader separates what an author says conditionally from what is claimed in general. Here the preference follows from the order-of-initialization risk.
questions.rule: Quote the conditions, not only the verdict.
questions.teaches: An author's preference can be conditional: the authors favour the object world because of initialization risk, while accepting that the simple self-contained case works.

questions.q: True or false: A Singleton has one instance no matter how many class loaders a program uses.
questions.explain: The chapter says that with several class loaders there can be several instances. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: One loader, one copy of the class.

questions.q: Each class loader defines a ____.
questions.explain: Because each loader has its own namespace, the same class can be loaded once per loader.
questions.rule: A loader is a namespace.

questions.q: A plugin host loads two plugins with separate class loaders, and both include the class PrefsStore, a Singleton. How many PrefsStore instances may exist?
options: Exactly one, since the class is a Singleton
Exactly one per plugin thread
Up to two, one for each loaded copy of the class
None, since the host refuses duplicate class names
optionExplain: The promise holds per loaded copy, not per name.
Threads are not the cause here.
Each copy of the class has its own Singleton.
The loaders do not refuse; each loads its copy.
questions.explain: The class name is the same, but two loaders mean two loaded classes, so each has its own instance.
questions.rule: One instance per loaded copy.

questions.q: What workaround do the authors mention for the class loader problem?
options: Declare the Singleton constructor protected
Make getInstance synchronized in every copy
Build the instance at class loading in every loader
Specify the class loader yourself
optionExplain: The constructor's access does not control which loader loads the class.
A lock inside each copy does not join the copies.
Each loader would still build its own.
The chapter says one way around it is to specify the class loader yourself.
questions.explain: If you control which loader loads the class, all code shares one copy and so one instance.
questions.rule: Control the loader to control the count.
questions.teaches: The authors' way around the class loader problem is to specify the class loader yourself, so that all code uses the same loaded copy of the class.

questions.q: True or false: In an application that uses a single class loader for everything, the class loader warning does not apply.
questions.explain: The problem is multiple copies of the class. With one loader there is one copy, so the promise holds.
questions.rule: One loader, no duplicate copy.

questions.q: A team synchronized getInstance yet still sees two instances in an application server with two class loaders. Why?
options: The synchronization was written incorrectly in the first copy of the class by the team
Synchronization coordinates threads within one loaded copy; there are two copies
Class loaders disable all of the synchronized methods in the classes they load
The server removes the private constructor when it loads the classes of the application
optionExplain: The cause is not a coding error in one copy.
Locks cannot join two separate copies.
They do not.
Nothing removes constructors.
questions.explain: Threads and class loaders are different causes of duplicates. A fix for one does not repair the other.
questions.rule: Match the fix to the cause.
questions.teaches: Synchronization guards against overlapping threads within one copy of a class; it cannot repair duplicates caused by two loaded copies of the class.

questions.q: On a very old JVM, a Singleton's state suddenly resets to its initial values. What could explain it?
options: Two threads built two objects at the same moment in the program
A subclass replaced the instance with an instance of its own class
The Singleton was collected, and a new one was built on the next request
The class loader loaded the class a second time and kept the new copy
optionExplain: That produces two objects, not a reset.
Subclassing is not involved.
This is the bug described before Java 1.2.
Class loaders cause duplicates, not resets.
questions.explain: A premature collection followed by a new build looks like a reset. The card next describes the bug.
questions.rule: Reset state can mean a rebuilt Singleton.

questions.q: True or false: Since Java 1.2 a Singleton needs a separate global reference to avoid being collected.
questions.explain: The bug was fixed in Java 1.2, and a global reference is no longer required.
questions.rule: Modern JVMs need no extra reference.

questions.q: A team maintains software on a JVM from before 1.2. Network connections held by a Singleton reset at random. Which diagnosis fits the chapter?
options: The Singleton is being collected; the next getInstance builds a fresh one
Two threads are building two different Singletons at exactly the same time
The constructor of the Singleton is public, so other classes build their own
The class is being loaded twice by two separate class loaders in the host
optionExplain: This matches the reset symptoms.
That gives two objects, not a reset.
That gives extra objects, not a reset.
That gives two objects living together.
questions.explain: The collector destroys the unreferenced Singleton, and getInstance quietly makes another with initial state.
questions.rule: A reset can mean a lost Singleton.

questions.q: On a JVM earlier than 1.2, how do the authors suggest defeating the collector?
options: Create a registry of Singletons
Make the constructor protected
Call getInstance twice at startup
Declare getInstance synchronized
optionExplain: The chapter's bullet points advise a registry of Singletons.
Constructor access does not affect collection.
Calling twice does not keep a reference.
Locks do not stop collection.
questions.explain: A registry keeps a reference to each Singleton, so the collector sees it as in use.
questions.rule: A registry keeps the instance reachable.
questions.teaches: On a JVM earlier than 1.2 the remedy is a registry of Singletons that keeps each one referenced so the collector does not reclaim it.

questions.q: On Java 8 no registry of Singletons is needed, because the garbage collector bug was fixed in Java ____.
questions.explain: The collection bug exists only on JVMs before 1.2, so later JVMs need no precaution.
questions.rule: Java 1.2 or later: no precaution.

questions.q: After hours of uptime on a very old JVM, a settings Singleton is back to defaults and no error appears. Why is this failure hard to notice?
options: The old object keeps running beside the new one and both answer callers
The JVM prints a warning that nobody reads when the object is lost
The next getInstance call quietly builds a new object, so callers see no error
The new object is a copy of the old state, so nothing visibly changes
optionExplain: The old object is destroyed.
The chapter describes confusing behaviour, not warnings.
The replacement happens silently.
It starts from initial values.
questions.explain: Because getInstance builds when the variable is empty, a lost Singleton is replaced without a signal. Only the changed behaviour reveals it.
questions.rule: Silent replacement hides the cause.
questions.teaches: The failure is silent: callers simply receive a fresh object and nothing signals that the earlier one was lost.

questions.q: Which two jobs does a Singleton class carry?
options: Creating its own subclasses and deleting its old instances over time
Managing its own single instance and doing its main role in the application
Handling several threads and handling several class loaders at once
Counting its callers and logging every one of the requests they make
optionExplain: Neither is part of the pattern.
Instance management is the added job.
These are hazards, not jobs of the class.
The pattern does not do this.
questions.explain: The Singleton does its ordinary job and also controls its own count and access. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: Two jobs in one class.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a Singleton can be argued to have two responsibilities.
questions.explain: They agree one could argue it manages its own instance and also performs its main role.
questions.rule: The authors admit the tension.

questions.q: Which two reasons do the authors give in defence of the Singleton against the one-responsibility objection?
options: A class managing its own instance makes the overall design simpler
Many developers are familiar with the pattern because it is widely used
The principle only applies to classes that use inheritance
Java requires every global object to manage itself
Responsibilities are not counted for static methods
optionExplain: Right: utility and simplicity are their first reason.
Right: familiarity is their second reason.
The authors do not say this; the principle applies to classes in general.
Java has no such requirement.
The authors give no such exemption.
questions.explain: The authors rely on simplicity and familiarity. Neither claims the principle is wrong.
questions.rule: Simplicity and familiarity.

questions.q: What do some developers do about the Singleton's second responsibility?
options: Give the class a second instance so that the two can share the work
Make every method of the class static so that no object is needed
Declare the constructor public so that access is spread to more classes
Abstract the Singleton functionality out of the class
optionExplain: This defeats the pattern.
This does not separate the responsibilities.
This weakens the pattern.
The chapter says some developers feel the need to do this.
questions.explain: Moving instance management elsewhere restores one job per class but gives up some of the simplicity the authors value.
questions.rule: Separate if the principle matters more.
questions.teaches: Some developers abstract the Singleton functionality into separate code, trading the simplicity of a self-managing class for one job per class.

questions.q: A reviewer says Singleton breaks the one-responsibility principle, so it is bad. Which reply is a reasoned reply rather than a reaction?
options: You dislike patterns in general, so your objection does not count for much here
Everyone uses Singletons, so the principle must not apply to this kind of class
It takes on two jobs, but self-managing simplifies the design, so the trade may be worth it
The principle is outdated and does not deserve to be taken seriously by a team
optionExplain: Attacks the person, not the argument.
Popularity does not answer the objection.
It concedes the point and weighs it.
An assertion with no reason.
questions.explain: A reasoned reply grants what is true in the objection and answers it with grounds. Dismissal and popularity are not grounds.
questions.rule: Grant what is true, then weigh.

questions.q: A team separates instance management from the main job of a Notifier class. What price do the authors' reasons suggest they pay?
options: They lose some of the simplicity of a class that manages its own instance
They lose the one-instance guarantee completely, whatever else the new code does
They lose the ability to use static methods anywhere in the new classes
They break the one-responsibility principle for the new holder class they create
optionExplain: This is the benefit the authors cite for the Singleton.
The guarantee can still be kept by the separate holder.
The separation does not forbid static methods.
The holder would have one job.
questions.explain: Every design choice here trades something. The authors name the simplicity of a class that manages itself as what the Singleton gains.
questions.rule: Each option has a price.
questions.teaches: Separating the instance management from the class's main job restores one job per class, at the price of the simplicity of a self-managing class.

questions.q: Several subclasses extend a Singleton base class built in the classic way. Why might they all share one instance?
options: Each subclass is forced to call the base constructor only once during a run
The compiler merges all of the subclasses of a Singleton into one single class
Subclasses of a Singleton are not allowed to have constructors of their own
The instance is held in one static variable that all of them share
optionExplain: Constructors are not limited this way.
Compilers do not merge classes.
They can.
Static variables belong to the base class, not to each subclass.
questions.explain: A single static variable in the base class is shared by everything derived from it. The card next explains the consequence.
questions.rule: One static variable, one shared instance.

questions.q: To let a subclass call the constructor, you must change it from private to public or ____.
questions.explain: The authors say the constructor must become public or protected, which weakens the Singleton.
questions.rule: Opening the constructor weakens the guarantee.

questions.q: A team makes the constructor of its SoundManager Singleton protected so that WinSound and MacSound can extend it. Which problems follow, according to the chapter?
options: None at all, since protected still blocks every class that lies outside the hierarchy
Other classes can instantiate it now, and the subclasses share one static variable
The subclasses cannot access getInstance, since static methods are never inherited
Only the loss of lazy creation, since protected forces the class to be created eagerly
optionExplain: The authors say that other classes can then instantiate it.
Both consequences are named in the chapter.
The chapter does not claim this.
Constructor access does not force eager creation.
questions.explain: Opening the constructor lets other classes build instances, and the static variable remains one shared slot.
questions.rule: Open constructor, shared variable.

questions.q: What do the authors say is needed to make subclassing a Singleton work?
options: A second static variable declared in each subclass by hand
A registry of sorts in the base class
A synchronized constructor
A public getInstance method in every subclass without any registry
optionExplain: The authors name a registry, not per-subclass variables.
The chapter says this is required.
Locks do not solve the shared variable.
Without a registry the shared variable remains.
questions.explain: A registry lets the base class track one instance per derived class. The extra machinery is part of the cost.
questions.rule: Subclassing needs extra machinery.
questions.teaches: Making subclassing work requires a registry of sorts in the base class, so that each derived class can have its own instance instead of sharing one static variable.

questions.q: True or false: If an application defines dozens of Singletons, the authors suggest taking a hard look at its design.
questions.explain: Singletons are meant to be used sparingly. A large number suggests the pattern is applied where it is not needed.
questions.rule: Use it sparingly.

questions.q: A team wants three variants of a Notifier Singleton that share behaviour. Which alternative do the authors' remarks point to?
options: Subclass one Singleton and let all three variants share its static instance variable
Make the constructor public so that all of the variants can reuse it directly
Replace the three variants with one all-static class that serves every purpose
Add the Singleton code to each class that needs it; the code is trivial to add
optionExplain: The shared variable is the problem they name.
This ends the Singleton guarantee.
The authors prefer to stay in the object world.
The chapter says Singleton code is trivial to add to any class.
questions.explain: Because the pattern code is small, repeating it in each class is a cheap alternative to a registry in a base class.
questions.rule: Ask whether repeating a little code is simpler than inheriting.
questions.teaches: Because Singleton code is trivial to add to any existing class, repeating it in each class is an alternative to subclassing and a registry.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: A scheduler must keep the request switch on the heater until 6 a.m. Which design lets it keep that request itself?
options: Give the scheduler its own copy of the heater control code
Let the scheduler poll the heater every minute to ask whether it is time to turn on yet
Represent the request as an object that the scheduler stores and triggers later
Add a branch to the scheduler for every device in the house, to be edited as devices change
optionExplain: This works for one device but ties the scheduler to heater details.
Polling stores no request; the heater would need to know the schedule.
An object can be stored until needed, so the scheduler never has to know how heating works.
This stores nothing and forces edits for each new device.
questions.explain: A request kept as an object can wait until it is needed. The card next shows how the chapter builds this.
questions.rule: A request held as an object can be stored and triggered later.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter opening, wrapping a method invocation in an object lets the invoking object avoid worrying about how the work is done.
questions.explain: The invoker uses the wrapped piece of computation and leaves the how to it.
questions.rule: The caller triggers; the wrapper knows how.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: A coffee kiosk has one touch button per drink. Which design applies the idea of an encapsulated invocation?
options: Each button holds a request object and triggers it, leaving the brewing to that object
Each button contains the grinder and boiler steps for its own drink
One method inspects the pressed button and runs matching steps in a conditional
The touch screen inherits from the boiler class to reach its methods
optionExplain: The button knows only that it holds something to trigger; the request object holds the brewing details.
This puts the how inside the button, so the button must change whenever a recipe or machine changes.
The details still sit with the caller, in a branch for every drink.
This welds the screen to one machine instead of hiding the details.
questions.explain: The button should hold a wrapped request and trigger it, leaving the how to the request object.
questions.rule: Each button holds a request object and just triggers it.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: A request object is created at 9:00 and triggered at 9:05 by a different part of the program. Why can it still run correctly?
options: The runtime remembers the state of the program at 9:00 and restores it
The part that triggers it looks up the right device again at 9:05
The creator stays blocked until the wrapper is triggered
It carries the action and its target, so nothing else is needed when it runs
optionExplain: Nothing is restored; the wrapper simply holds what it needs.
If it had to look the device up, it would not be ignorant of details.
Creating and triggering are separate steps, and the creator need not wait.
Everything the work needs travels inside the wrapper.
questions.explain: The wrapper is self-contained, so making it and running it can happen at different times and in different places.
questions.teaches: Because a request object is self-contained, creating it and running it can be separated in time and in place: the one who makes it need not be the one who runs it.
questions.rule: The request object carries both the action and its target.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: A game lets players rebind keys to actions. Which fact about encapsulated requests makes rebinding easy to build?
options: Each key stores the action source code and recompiles it on assignment
The key holds only a request object, so a different object changes its behaviour
The game checks a list of all actions at every key press
Actions are saved as text names and parsed at each press
optionExplain: Nothing needs recompiling; only the held object changes.
The key never knew the action, so a swap touches nothing in the key.
A lookup of every action would make the key depend on all of them.
Text parsing adds work and still needs someone who knows each action.
questions.explain: Because the trigger only holds a request object, the behaviour behind a key can be swapped freely.
questions.teaches: The trigger depends only on holding a request object, so new actions and swapped actions work without any change to the trigger.
questions.rule: Rebinding swaps the request object a key holds.

questions.section: Free hardware! Let’s check out the Remote Control...
questions.q: Sort each situation: does wrapping the call in a request object help, or is a direct call enough?

items.t: Reversing the last action of a remote control
Running requests later on worker threads
Replaying logged actions after a crash
Calling a helper once and using its result on the next line
Writing a status line inside a loop
Reading a value from a field in the same class

questions.explain: Storing, queuing, logging and undoing are the reasons to wrap a call. A one-off call whose result is used at once gains nothing from a wrapper.
questions.rule: Wrap when requests must be stored, passed around, logged or undone.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: A remote must drive lights, fans and hot tubs from different vendors, and new device kinds will arrive. What is the central design difficulty?
options: A remote cannot call methods on objects written by another vendor
The devices differ and more will come, so the remote cannot assume a fixed set
There are too few devices to justify a shared design
Buttons can only be tied to on and off actions
optionExplain: Calling is possible; the trouble is knowing what to call.
Variety that keeps growing is what the design has to survive.
Even a few devices with unrelated methods cause trouble, and more are coming.
The buttons are the easy part; the devices behind them differ.
questions.explain: The mix of different methods and unknown future devices is the heart of the problem. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: The vendor classes offer methods such as dim(), setTemperature() and ____(), so they share no common interface.
questions.explain: The chapter lists dim(), setTemperature(), setVolume() and setInputChannel() as examples of the variety.
questions.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: A fitness app reads data from heart straps, power meters and step counters made by different firms with different method names, and more firms keep appearing. Which requirement should drive the design?
options: Rewrite each maker class to use the app method names
Support the three known makers and extend later by editing the app
Pick the most popular maker and drop the rest
App code must keep working for makers it has never seen
optionExplain: The classes belong to the makers; rewriting them is not a plan for future makers.
This invites a change in the app for every newcomer.
This dodges the requirement rather than meeting it.
This is the same pressure as the remote: unknown future variety.
questions.explain: Like the customer, the app must handle devices that do not exist yet.
questions.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: Which test best shows that a remote design meets the requirement about future devices?
options: A brand-new device kind can be added without editing the remote existing code
The design handles every vendor class that happens to be on the disc supplied today
Every vendor class on the disc has an on method and an off method of its own
The remote compiles with no warnings
optionExplain: Only a case that is not yet written proves the claim.
Today classes alone cannot show readiness for later ones.
The classes do not all share such methods, and this says nothing of the future.
Compiling says nothing about adding new devices.
questions.explain: A requirement about the future is met only if a new device can be added without touching what already works.
questions.teaches: A requirement about the future is tested against a case not yet written: the design passes only if a new device needs no edit to old code.
questions.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: A school timetable tool must show lessons from systems with different method names, with three more systems promised. Where should each system method names live?
options: In the display code, as one branch per system
In the display code, but only for the systems that exist at the moment
In small separate pieces per system, so the display never names them
In the head of each teacher, who types the matching call in by hand each time
optionExplain: The display would change with every new system.
The three promised systems would still force edits.
Keeping the vendor knowledge at the edge protects the core.
This removes the problem from the program and puts it on the users.
questions.explain: Vendor-specific knowledge belongs in per-vendor pieces at the edge, so the core stays free of it.
questions.teaches: Method names of each vendor should be kept in per-vendor pieces at the edge of the program, so the core code stays vendor-free.
questions.rule: Treat future variety as a requirement: the remote must not depend on any particular vendor class.

questions.section: Taking a look at the vendor classes
questions.q: True or false: Suppose every vendor class shared one interface with a single method. Then the remote could call that method without knowing the device kind.
questions.explain: With a shared interface the remote needs no per-device knowledge. The chapter problem comes from the lack of one.
questions.rule: A shared interface removes much of the variety problem.

questions.q: True or false: A remote that checks which device is in a slot and calls that device own method is a good design when new device types keep arriving.
questions.explain: Each new type would force an edit to the remote. The card next explains why the team rejects it.
questions.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.

questions.q: Which job belongs to the remote in Mary separation of concerns?
options: Knowing how to switch the hot tub jets on
Keeping each vendor volume scale in mind
Deciding which vendor classes the remote supports
Interpreting button presses and making requests
optionExplain: This is device knowledge, which the remote should not hold.
Scales are vendor details, not button handling.
A fixed list is exactly what the remote should not carry.
This is the remote one concern.
questions.explain: The remote reads buttons and makes requests; the devices know how to do the work.
questions.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.

questions.q: Sort each job of a vending machine: does it belong to the front panel, or to the dispensing mechanism?

items.t: Detecting which key was pressed
Turning a key press into a request
Showing the code that was typed
Spinning the coil of row C
Cooling the cold compartment
Counting the coins it dropped

questions.explain: The panel deals with the person and makes requests. Moving parts belong to the mechanism, in the same split as remote and devices.
questions.rule: Interpreting input and performing the work are separate concerns.

questions.q: Which changes would force edits to a remote built as a chain of if statements? Select all that apply.
options: A vendor adds a new device class
A vendor renames a method the remote calls
The remote button labels change colour
A device is replaced by a newer model of the same class with the same methods
optionExplain: The chain needs a new branch for it.
The remote names that method in its branch, so it must follow.
Colour has no link to device calls.
The branch still matches, so no edit is needed.
questions.explain: A chain names every vendor class and method it calls, so vendor-side changes reach the remote.
questions.teaches: A chain of if statements makes the remote depend on every vendor class and method it names, so vendor changes ripple into the remote.
questions.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.

questions.q: A word processor holds a branch for each printer model commands. Which complaint from the cubicle talk applies, and what is the cost?
options: The printers expose private fields to the editor, which breaks data hiding
Concerns are mixed: the editor knows printer details, so every new model forces an edit
The editor cannot reverse a print, so undo is missing
Print jobs wait too long, so a queue is needed
optionExplain: The problem here is knowledge in the wrong place, not exposed fields.
The editor should hand over a generic request and leave model details out.
Undo is a separate matter and is not the issue here.
Waiting time is a different concern.
questions.explain: Any program that mixes handling user actions with device specifics pays at every new device.
questions.teaches: A common remedy is that the editor produces one generic kind of print request and leaves model-specific commands to per-model code.
questions.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.

questions.q: The team adopts Mary rule, so the remote knows nothing of hot tubs. Which question does the rule leave open?
options: Whether the remote should still read button presses
Whether vendor classes may keep their own method names
How a generic request reaches the specific device
Whether the remote needs a battery
optionExplain: Reading presses stays its job.
They do keep them; nothing in the rule changes that.
The rule says who should not know; the link still has to be designed.
Power has nothing to do with the rule.
questions.explain: The rule removes device knowledge from the remote, which creates the next question: how does a request reach a device?
questions.rule: Give the remote only the job of turning button presses into requests, and keep device knowledge out of it.

questions.q: Each remote button must trigger a different device action. What could a button hold so that the remote stays ignorant of devices?
options: An object that knows the device and what to ask it
The device class name as text, looked up at each press
A copy of the device source code
A counter of how often it was pressed
optionExplain: The button holds a ready-made request.
A lookup still needs knowledge of every class.
Copying code ties the button to the device again.
A counter says nothing about what to do.
questions.explain: The idea is a ready-made request. The card next names it.
questions.rule: A button holds an object that knows the device and the action.

questions.q: A command object encapsulates a request to do something on a specific ____.
questions.explain: The example is the living room light object: the command is tied to one particular target.
questions.rule: A command is bound to its receiver object.

questions.q: A thermostat app has a Cosy button that sets the living room to 21 degrees. What should the button hold?
options: A command bound to the living room thermostat, setting 21
The living room thermostat alone, with the app calling its methods
A list of all the thermostats in the house for the app to loop over
The number 21, applied to the nearest device
optionExplain: The command holds both the action and its target.
Then the app must know the thermostat methods.
The app would have to choose among devices itself.
A bare number carries neither target nor action.
questions.explain: The button holds a request that is already tied to its target.
questions.rule: The button holds a command bound to its target.

questions.q: True or false: In the basic form of the pattern, the command object relays the work to the device own method rather than doing the device work itself.
questions.explain: In the light example the command asks the light to act. This keeps commands small and leaves device logic in the device.
questions.rule: The command relays; the device does the work.
questions.teaches: In the basic form the command only relays to the device, so the real knowledge stays in the device and the command stays small.

questions.q: A spreadsheet toolbar has Bold, Italic and Merge buttons. Which statements fit the command-object idea? Select all that apply.
options: Each button can hold a command bound to the sheet selection
The toolbar needs no knowledge of how bolding works
One button class can serve many different actions
The toolbar must contain a branch per formatting action
optionExplain: The command ties the action to its target.
It only asks the command to act.
The button differs only in the command it holds.
That is the if-chain design the idea avoids.
questions.explain: A toolbar button is only a requester, so the same wrapping lets one button serve many actions.
questions.teaches: Even interface elements like toolbar buttons are plain requesters, so one button class can serve many actions when each holds its own command.
questions.rule: Each button holds a command; the toolbar only asks it to act.

questions.q: A slot is loaded with a command that works on a different device. What must change in the remote code?
options: The branch for that slot must be edited
The remote must learn the new device method names and call them
Nothing: the remote still only asks the command to act
The slot needs a new kind of button
optionExplain: There are no branches in this design.
Those names live in the command.
The remote never knew the device.
The button is unchanged.
questions.explain: Swapping the command changes the behaviour; the remote code stays as it was.
questions.rule: The remote only asks the command to act.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: In a diner, a waitress passes slips to the counter and calls Order up. What lets her do this for any meal?
options: She memorises the recipe of each dish
All slips answer to one call, so she needs no knowledge of meals
She stays next to the cook and relays what each customer said
She prepares the simple meals herself and passes on the rest
optionExplain: Then she would depend on every dish.
A uniform call hides the content of each order.
Direct relaying keeps her tied to the cook.
Splitting the work this way still needs her to know the meals.
questions.explain: A single shared call is what lets her ignore the content. The card next shows the slip.
questions.rule: One method on every slip hides the content of the request.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: The Order Slip interface has a single method, ____().
questions.explain: The slip exposes only orderUp(); everything else is hidden inside it.
questions.rule: The slip exposes a single method, orderUp().

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: A print shop clerk hands a job ticket to the press operator. Which feature of the ticket matches the diner order slip?
options: It lists every press setting that the clerk must adjust by hand
It must be read by the clerk, who then tells the operator what to do
It is thrown away unread because the operator works from memory
It carries the job and the operator, so the clerk can pass it on unread
optionExplain: Then the clerk would carry the details.
This adds a middleman who needs the content.
Then it would carry no request at all.
The ticket is a self-contained request.
questions.explain: Like the slip, the ticket carries both the job and its performer, so it can be passed unread.
questions.rule: The ticket carries both the job and its performer.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: The slip can be handed to the next shift waitress. What does this show about a request object?
options: It stops working until the first waitress comes back
The new waitress must retake the order from the customer
It stays valid in other hands, as it does not depend on its creator
It must be copied once for each waitress
optionExplain: Nothing in the slip refers to its first carrier.
The point of the slip is that she need not.
The slip carries all it needs.
One slip serves whoever holds it.
questions.explain: A request object is independent of its creator, so it can change hands and still work.
questions.teaches: A request object does not depend on its creator, so it can change hands (and, in code, change threads or queues) and still work.
questions.rule: A request object stays valid in whoever's hands it passes to.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: Match each diner element to its counterpart in a courier company.
questions.explain: The ticket carries the job, the clerk passes it on unread, and the driver does the work. Finding who triggers, what is passed and who does the work reveals the structure.
questions.teaches: Mapping a familiar scene onto new roles is a way to recognise the same structure in unfamiliar code: find who triggers, what is passed on and who does the work.
questions.rule: Map each diner element to its counterpart role.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: The authors say a real waitress would care what is on the slip. What does this note tell us about the diner as a model?
options: The ignorance is a deliberate simplification to show the decoupling
The pattern only works for requesters that never read the content of requests
The diner is wrong and should be replaced by another scene
Real slips must hide their content so the waitress cannot be influenced by it
optionExplain: Objectville is a teaching device.
The note says nothing about limits of the pattern.
The authors keep the scene because it helps.
Nothing is said about hiding content; the note only says the waitress's ignorance is a simplification.
questions.explain: The diner shows the decoupling in pure form; real settings may let the requester read more.
questions.rule: The diner deliberately simplifies to show the decoupling.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: True or false: In the diner model, the waitress and the cook talk to each other about every meal.
questions.explain: The authors stress that they are totally decoupled. The card next shows what stands between them.
questions.rule: The requester and performer meet only through the request.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: Match each diner element to what it does.
pairs: Carries the request and a reference to the cook
questions.explain: The waitress triggers, the cook performs and the slip links them.
questions.rule: Each diner element has one role in the exchange.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: A radio producer drops a cue card on the desk and says go; the sound engineer does what the card says. Which statement matches the waitress and cook decoupling?
options: The engineer must ask the producer what each cue means
The producer must be told each sound effect before saying go
The card is useless unless producer and engineer are in the same room
The producer needs no knowledge of the engineer kit; the card carries it all
optionExplain: Then they would not be decoupled.
Then the producer would hold the details.
The card is what removes that need.
The card is the only link between them.
questions.explain: The card plays the role of the order slip: it carries the instructions between the two.
questions.rule: The requester calls one method; the card carries the instructions.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: The diner adds a new dish. Which parts must change?
options: The waitress, who must learn each new dish before she can pass its slip along
A new slip and a cook who can prepare the dish; the waitress is unchanged
All three, since they interact
Neither slip nor cook, as slips are generic
optionExplain: She never knew any dish.
The waitress depends only on orderUp().
Interaction through one method does not spread changes.
Someone must still describe and cook the dish.
questions.explain: Knowledge of the dish lives in the slip and the cook, so the requester is untouched.
questions.teaches: Because the requester depends only on the shared method, new kinds of work need new request objects and performers but no change to the requester.
questions.rule: New dishes touch the slip and the cook, not the waitress.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: A smart speaker turns a spoken request into an action object and calls run() on it; a service then does the work. A new service is added. What must the speaker layer change?
options: A new branch that names the new service and calls its methods
Nothing, as long as the new action object offers run()
The microphone code that hears requests
The run() method name, one per service
optionExplain: That is the if-chain design the chapter avoids.
The layer depends only on the one method.
Hearing has nothing to do with the new service.
Different names would break the shared call.
questions.explain: The middle layer depends only on the one-method interface, not on the services behind it.
questions.teaches: What the middle layer depends on is only the shared one-method interface, so services can be added behind it without changing it.
questions.rule: The caller needs only the shared method of the action object.

questions.section: The Objectville Diner roles and responsibilities
questions.q: True or false: The slip holds a reference to the cook, so the waitress and the cook are not decoupled.
questions.explain: The waitress never refers to the cook. Only the slip joins the two, so the decoupling holds between waitress and cook.
questions.rule: The slip joins them; the waitress and cook stay apart.

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: In the diner, the waitress takes slips and calls orderUp() on them. Which Command Pattern role does she play?
options: Receiver
Client
Command
Invoker
optionExplain: The receiver performs the work, which is the cook.
The client creates the request, which is the customer.
The command is the slip she holds.
She triggers requests without performing them.
questions.explain: She triggers requests. The card next names all the roles.
questions.rule: The invoker calls execute() on the command it holds.

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: Put the steps of loading and using an invoker in order.
items: The client creates a command object
The client calls setCommand() to store it in the invoker
Later the client asks the invoker to execute the command
The command execute() makes the receiver perform its actions
questions.explain: Create, load, trigger, then the command makes the receiver act.
questions.rule: Build the command, load it, then the invoker calls execute().

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: A library patron fills in a request slip, a desk clerk sends slips to the stacks, and a page fetches the books. Match each to its pattern role.
questions.explain: The patron makes the request, the slip is the command, the clerk triggers it and the page performs it.
questions.rule: Match the roles: client, invoker, command and receiver.

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: Which invoker is most likely to keep one command for many uses?
options: A remote control slot that is pressed again and again
A worker that takes a job from a queue and runs it once
A timer that fires once at midnight
An installer step that runs only on first start
optionExplain: A button needs its command each time it is pressed.
The job is discarded after one run.
A single firing needs the command once.
It runs once and is done.
questions.explain: Whether a command is kept or discarded depends on the invoker job.
questions.teaches: Whether a command is single-use or reusable depends on the invoker job: a button keeps its command for repeated use, while a worker taking jobs from a queue discards each after running it.
questions.rule: An invoker slot may keep one command for repeated use.

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: In a text editor, a menu item calls execute() on a stored object, and that object changes the document. Which role does the document play?
options: Invoker
Client
Receiver
Command
optionExplain: The menu item triggers the request.
The client is the code that builds and loads the commands.
The document is the object that is acted on.
The command is the stored object with execute().
questions.explain: The menu item triggers, the stored object is the command, and the document performs.
questions.teaches: The invoker is what triggers, the receiver is what is acted on, and the client is the wiring code that creates commands and loads them, such as the code that builds the menu.
questions.rule: The receiver is the object that actually does the work.

questions.section: From the Diner to the Command Pattern
questions.q: One step in this account is wrong. 1: the client creates a command bound to a receiver. 2: the client stores it in the invoker with setCommand(). 3: later the invoker calls execute() on the receiver. 4: the receiver actions run. Which step?
options: Step 1
Step 2
Step 4
Step 3
optionExplain: The client does create the command and bind a receiver.
Loading the invoker is done with setCommand().
The receiver does perform the actions once asked.
The invoker calls execute() on the command, never on the receiver.
questions.explain: The invoker only knows the command. The command calls the receiver actions.
questions.rule: Check the order: build, load, then the invoker calls execute().

questions.q: Which interface would let a remote run any device action without knowing the device?
options: One method per device kind, such as lightOn() and hotTubJetsOn()
One method with no device-specific part, such as execute()
A method that takes the device name and action name as text
No interface; the remote checks the class of each object
optionExplain: Per-kind methods bring the variety back into the interface.
A uniform call hides the device.
The remote would still have to know names.
Class checks are the if-chain design.
questions.explain: A uniform one-method call keeps the invoker ignorant. The card next confirms this.
questions.rule: One device-free method lets an invoker run any command.

questions.q: True or false: In the chapter, the Command interface consists of a single method, which is usually named execute().
questions.explain: The diner called it orderUp(), but code uses execute().
questions.rule: One method, usually execute().

questions.q: A pottery studio kiln controller must let a panel start any firing program. Which command interface follows the chapter?
options: A method per program, such as startBisque() and startGlaze()
A method that takes the kiln model and temperature as arguments
A single method with no arguments, such as execute()
A method that returns the kiln state to the panel
optionExplain: The panel interface would grow with each program.
The panel would have to know kiln details.
Every program looks the same to the panel.
The panel would depend on kiln state.
questions.explain: A uniform no-argument method lets the panel start any program without knowing it.
questions.rule: A single argument-free execute() lets a panel start any program.

questions.q: The method execute() takes no arguments. Where must a command get the device it works on?
options: From its constructor, when the command is created
From the invoker, at each call
From a global lookup by device name that it performs on each call
From the button label that was pressed
optionExplain: The wiring happens at creation.
The invoker does not know the device.
A lookup would add knowledge of names.
A label carries no device.
questions.explain: With nothing passed at call time, everything the command needs is supplied when it is created.
questions.teaches: Since execute() takes nothing, everything a command needs, such as its receiver, is supplied when the command is created.
questions.rule: A command receives its receiver through its constructor.

questions.q: An admin panel has refund, ship and archive actions, all behind one execute() method. Which statements describe a design that matches the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The panel treats refund, ship and archive commands alike
Each action has its own concrete command class
The panel switches on the action name
The shared interface lists refund(), ship() and archive()
optionExplain: Only execute() is visible to it.
The variety lives in the concrete commands.
That is the branching the interface avoids.
This would put variety into the interface.
questions.explain: The interface stays generic and the variety lives in the concrete commands.
questions.teaches: Naming each action is the job of its command class, not of the interface or the panel, so a new action adds a class and leaves the panel untouched.
questions.rule: Behind one execute() method, the invoker cannot tell commands apart.

questions.q: The interface later adds a second method, undo(). What does that mean for each command class?
options: Each must now provide both methods
Only commands for devices with a power switch must change
None, because the second method is optional
Only the invoker, which now calls two methods
optionExplain: Every class implementing the interface must fill in all its methods.
The interface applies to all implementers.
Methods of an interface are not optional for implementers.
The commands implement the interface.
questions.explain: Changing the interface changes every class that implements it.
questions.rule: Adding undo() means every command class must provide it.

questions.q: A command that turns a light on calls the light ____ method when it is executed.
questions.explain: The light has on() and off(); the on command calls on(). The card next shows how the command is built.
questions.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.

questions.q: A concrete command stores its ____ when it is constructed, so that execute() can act on it later.
questions.explain: The constructor receives the receiver, such as the Light, and keeps it for execute().
questions.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.

questions.q: A garden sprinkler class has valveOpen() and valveClose(). Which command for switching it on matches the chapter?
options: A command whose execute() takes the sprinkler as an argument each time it runs
A command that calls the sprinkler methods inside its constructor
A command that stores the sprinkler and calls valveOpen() in execute()
A command that extends the Sprinkler class and overrides execute()
optionExplain: This changes the shared interface.
The call would happen at creation, not when executed.
It binds receiver and action behind execute().
This welds the command to the sprinkler class.
questions.explain: Store the receiver in the constructor and call its method in execute().
questions.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.

questions.q: GarageDoor opens with up(), yet the command is named GarageDoorOpenCommand. What does this show?
options: Vendor methods must be renamed so that they match the commands that call them
The command name states the request, and the vendor method name stays inside
The remote must translate up() into open
A command name must repeat the receiver method name
optionExplain: The vendor class is left as it is.
The command gives the request its own meaningful name.
The remote knows neither name.
The two names differ here.
questions.explain: The command is a translation layer between a meaningful request and an arbitrary vendor method.
questions.teaches: A command gives a request a meaningful name of its own, so odd vendor method names such as up() are hidden behind names such as Open.
questions.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.

questions.q: A student writes a light command with no constructor, whose execute(Light light) method receives the light. What is the flaw?
options: A command may not call a light method such as on(), since only the invoker calls receivers
The class should extend the Light class
The class needs a second method to turn the light off again
Its execute() no longer matches the shared interface
optionExplain: A command exists to call its receiver, and on() is exactly what it calls; the problem is the signature.
Inheritance is not the issue.
On and off are separate commands.
The invoker only knows the no-argument method.
questions.explain: A command needing an argument at call time breaks the invoker, which knows only the argument-free execute().
questions.teaches: A command that needs an argument at execution time cannot be called by an invoker that knows only the argument-free execute().
questions.rule: A concrete command stores its receiver when it is constructed and, in execute(), calls the receiver own method.

questions.q: True or false: The Light class gains a new method dim(). LightOnCommand will then be able to dim the light.
questions.explain: The command still calls on(). A dim feature needs its own command that calls dim().
questions.rule: New receiver methods need new commands.

questions.q: True or false: A remote slot can hold a light command at one moment and a garage door command at another with no change to the remote code.
questions.explain: The slot cares only that the held object has execute(). The card next walks through this test.
questions.rule: The slot holds whichever command was loaded last.

questions.q: Pressing the button of the simple remote calls ____() on the stored command.
questions.explain: The button handler calls execute() on whatever command is in the slot.
questions.rule: A button press calls execute() on the stored command.

questions.q: A client wants an alarm panel with one button to sound a siren. Put the steps in order.
items: Create the siren object
Create a command bound to the siren
Load the command into the panel with setCommand()
Press the panel button
questions.explain: Receiver first, then the command bound to it, then loading, then the press.
questions.rule: Create the command, load it, then press the button.

questions.q: The test loads the light command, presses, then loads the garage command. What does the slot hold after the second load?
options: Two commands, because both stay loaded
Nothing, until the button is pressed again
One command: the garage command, which replaced the light command
The light command, which stays until the garage command is pressed
optionExplain: One slot cannot hold two.
Loading stores the command at once.
A single slot has room for one command.
Loading replaces the old command immediately.
questions.explain: setCommand() replaces what the slot held before.
questions.teaches: Setting a command replaces the previous one; to keep several at once, an invoker needs several slots, as the seven-slot remote has.
questions.rule: Loading a new command replaces the one in the slot.

questions.q: A one-button kiosk must print tickets by day and reset a counter by night. Which implementation uses the idea of this card?
options: Scheduling code swaps the stored command at the change of shift
The button checks the time at every press and branches on the result
Two buttons are built, each with its own code
The reset code is copied into the ticket printer class
optionExplain: The behaviour changes by changing the held command.
This puts mode logic inside the button.
This duplicates the invoker for each mode.
This mixes two requests into one object.
questions.explain: Time-dependent behaviour can come from swapping the stored command rather than adding mode checks.
questions.teaches: Behaviour that changes with the situation can be produced by swapping the stored command, rather than by mode checks inside the invoker.
questions.rule: Swapping the stored command changes what the button does.

questions.q: A teammate says the simple remote can run the light command and the garage command with one press. What stops this?
options: Commands cannot be stored in a remote
The garage command does not implement Command
The light must be switched off first
It holds only one command at a time
optionExplain: It stores one command at a time.
It implements Command like the other.
Nothing in the design requires this.
The slot stores a single command.
questions.explain: One slot holds one command; combining commands needs another mechanism, which comes later.
questions.rule: A slot holds one command at a time.

questions.q: Which abilities does wrapping a request as an object give? Select all that apply.
options: Parameterizing other objects with different requests
Queuing or logging requests
Supporting undoable operations
Making every method call run faster
optionExplain: An invoker can be loaded with various requests.
Requests held as objects can be stored and recorded.
A request object can carry the way to reverse itself.
Wrapping adds an object and gives no speed-up.
questions.explain: The pattern is about handling requests as things. The card next states the definition.
questions.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.

questions.q: The pattern encapsulates a request as an object so that other objects can be ____ with different requests.
questions.explain: Parameterizing an object means loading it with different requests, as the waitress and the remote slot show.
questions.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.

questions.q: A photo editor wraps each edit as an object. Which feature does the definition say this wrapping makes possible?
options: Faster processing of the pixels in each picture
A history in which edits can be undone
Automatic colour correction
Encryption of saved files
optionExplain: The definition claims nothing about faster pixel processing; wrapping edits is about undo and queuing.
Undoable operations are one of the four abilities.
The pattern does not decide what edits do.
Security is outside the pattern.
questions.explain: Wrapped edits can be recorded and reversed.
questions.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.

questions.q: A remote slot command is replaced according to a choice the user makes while the program runs. Which claim does this show?
options: Commands must be fixed when the invoker class is compiled and built
An invoker can be loaded with commands dynamically, at run time
Commands can be replaced only by stopping the program and restarting it
Replacing a command needs a new invoker class to be written and built
optionExplain: Nothing fixes them at compile time.
The slot can be reloaded while running.
Later commands replace earlier ones while the program runs; no restart is needed.
The same invoker takes any command.
questions.explain: Parameterizing is done at run time, not in the source code of the invoker.
questions.teaches: Parameterizing happens at run time: an invoker can be given a new command while the program runs, with no rebuild.
questions.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.

questions.q: A bank app keeps a journal of transfer request objects, and after a crash it re-runs them in order. Which ability is used, and how does it differ from queuing?
options: Queuing: the journal holds requests waiting to run, as a queue does
Parameterizing: the journal is loaded with different requests
Undo: the journal reverses each transfer in turn
Logging: a log holds requests already run; a queue holds requests waiting
optionExplain: The journal is of requests already run.
Parameterizing is loading an invoker, not recording.
Replay re-runs requests rather than reversing them.
The journal records past requests for replay.
questions.explain: A queue looks forward to what will run; a log looks back to what ran.
questions.teaches: A queue holds requests waiting to be run; a log holds requests that have already run, kept so they can be replayed after a failure.
questions.rule: Wrap a request as an object and you can parameterize invokers with it, queue it, log it and undo it.

questions.q: True or false: Every use of the pattern must provide all four abilities: parameterizing, queuing, logging and undo.
questions.explain: The authors say logging would make no sense for a remote control, though it suits a spreadsheet. The abilities are available, not compulsory.
questions.rule: The abilities are available, not compulsory.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: In a remote design with command objects, which object holds a reference to the light?
options: The command created for the light
The remote itself
The button
The Command interface that all commands share
optionExplain: The command is bound to its receiver.
The remote is meant to be ignorant of lights.
The button holds a command only.
An interface holds no object.
questions.explain: The command holds the receiver. The card next explains why that decouples.
questions.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: True or false: In the Command Pattern, the invoker holds a direct reference to the receiver.
questions.explain: The invoker holds a command; the command holds the receiver.
questions.rule: Invoker to command to receiver.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A DJ app has pads, which trigger sample players. Which dependency would break the decoupling?
options: A command class importing the sample player
The pad class importing the Command interface to hold its commands
The pad class importing and calling the sample player methods
The setup code that creates the commands for each of the players
optionExplain: This is where the receiver knowledge belongs.
The invoker should know the interface.
The pad would then know the receiver.
The client is the right place for this wiring.
questions.explain: Only commands and setup code should know the receiver.
questions.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A vendor renames a method of a receiver class. Which class needs editing?
options: The invoker
Every command in the program that uses any receiver
The Command interface
The concrete command that calls that method
optionExplain: The invoker never named the method.
Only commands for that receiver call it.
The interface is generic.
The command is the only caller.
questions.explain: Changes in a receiver reach only its commands.
questions.teaches: Coupling is contained: a change in a receiver affects only the commands for that receiver, not the invoker or other receivers.
questions.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A notification system has a bell button, a command that sends email, and an email sender class. Which pieces may depend on the email sender? Select all that apply.
options: The command that sends the email
The setup code that builds the command
The bell button
The Command interface
optionExplain: It calls the receiver.
It supplies the receiver at creation.
The button knows only commands.
The interface is generic.
questions.explain: The command and the setup code are where concrete classes meet; the rest stays independent.
questions.teaches: Concrete classes should meet in a few places, the commands and the setup code, so the rest of the program can stay independent of them.
questions.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Where does the coupling to the receiver go once the pattern is used?
options: It disappears entirely
Into the command classes and the setup code
Into the Command interface
Into the invoker setCommand() method, which stores each command
optionExplain: Someone must still know the receiver.
