The two places where receiver is named.
The interface stays generic.
That method takes a command only.
questions.explain: The pattern relocates the coupling away from the invoker.
questions.rule: Keep the receiver reference inside the command so that the invoker depends on the Command interface alone.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A remote has two slots, one for the living room light and one for the kitchen light, both of class Light. How can the remote tell the two apart?
options: It reads the name stored in each light
It keeps a table of room names and the lights that go with them
It cannot and need not: each command is bound to its own light
It asks the user which light is meant each time a button is pressed
optionExplain: This makes the remote depend on light details.
The table would be device knowledge.
The binding is in the commands.
This puts the burden on the user.
questions.explain: The remote only presses; the command knows the light. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: The receiver of the request gets ____ to the command it is encapsulated in.
questions.explain: Binding the receiver to the command is what lets the remote stay ignorant.
questions.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: A hotel has one lamp command class and 40 rooms. Which plan fits the chapter?
options: Create 40 objects of one command class, each bound to a room lamp
Write 40 different command classes, one per room
Write one command that asks which room at each press
Let the kiosk switch on the room number at each press
optionExplain: One class, many bindings.
The class does not need to differ.
The command then needs extra input.
The kiosk would hold room knowledge.
questions.explain: The binding sits in the object, so one class serves all rooms.
questions.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Two LightOnCommand objects sit in two slots, one per room. What differs between them?
options: Only the Light each was created with
Their class
The code of their execute() method
Their position in the Command interface
optionExplain: The binding differs; the code does not.
They are the same class.
Both objects run the same execute() code; only the Light each is bound to differs.
Both implement the interface alike.
questions.explain: The objects differ in their receiver; the class is shared.
questions.teaches: One concrete command class can serve any number of receivers of the same type; the binding lives in the object, not in the class.
questions.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: Valves A and B are both class Valve. Slot 1 holds OpenValveCommand bound to A, slot 2 holds one bound to B. A technician swaps the two commands between the slots. What happens when slot 1 is pressed?
options: It opens valve A, because slot 1 is tied to A
Nothing, because the swap leaves the commands unbound to any valve
It opens valve B, because the command now in slot 1 is bound to B
Both valves, because the commands are the same class
optionExplain: The slot is tied to no valve.
A swap does not unbind.
The binding goes with the command.
Each command acts on its own valve.
questions.explain: A command carries its receiver wherever it is moved.
questions.teaches: A command carries its binding with it, so rearranging commands among slots never changes what a given command does.
questions.rule: Choose the receiver when you create the command, and the invoker then needs no idea which receiver it drives.

questions.section: The Command Pattern defined: the class diagram
questions.q: True or false: A command bound to the living room light can be made to switch the kitchen light by loading it into a different slot.
questions.explain: The binding is inside the command. Another slot changes which button triggers it, not which light it controls.
questions.rule: The slot does not choose the receiver.

questions.q: A remote has seven on buttons and seven off buttons. How can it store what each button does?
options: One list of devices, with the button deciding which method to call on each
Two lists of commands indexed by slot number, one for on and one for off
Seven classes, one per slot, each hard-coded for its device
A table of device names and method names kept as text
optionExplain: The remote would then know every device method.
Each button gets its own ready-made request.
Slots would be tied to devices in the source code.
The remote would parse text and still need device knowledge.
questions.explain: Each button needs its own stored request. The card next shows the arrays.
questions.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.

questions.q: The remote keeps two arrays of commands, one for the ____ buttons and one for the off buttons.
questions.explain: The remote indexes its on-command array by slot and calls execute() on the entry when a button is pressed.
questions.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.

questions.q: A stage console has 12 channels, each with a start and a stop button. By the remote design, what should the console hold?
options: Twelve sound-module objects that the console asks for their state
One array of twelve device names that it looks up at each press
Twelve console subclasses, one for each channel
Two arrays of 12 commands, one for start and one for stop
optionExplain: The console would depend on the modules.
Name lookups bring device knowledge back.
Subclassing the invoker for each channel is needless.
This mirrors the on and off arrays of the remote.
questions.explain: One command per button, held in arrays by slot.
questions.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.

questions.q: For a slot that controls a stereo, which arrangement fits the design?
options: One command with a flag that the buttons flip
The on button holds the stereo itself and the off button a command
Different commands on the on and off buttons, both bound to the same stereo
Both buttons hold the identical on command
optionExplain: The remote would need to know about the flag.
The remote would then know stereo methods.
Each button has its own command.
Off would then turn the stereo on.
questions.explain: Each button is separate; two commands can share one receiver.
questions.teaches: On and off are separate command objects, possibly of different classes, and both may be bound to the same receiver.
questions.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.

questions.q: A customer wants nine slots instead of seven. Which part of the design must change?
options: Only the array sizes and button pairs; the commands stay as they are
Every command class, since each of them is tied to the number of slots
Every vendor class, since they must offer one action per slot
The Command interface
optionExplain: Slot count belongs to the invoker.
Commands do not know about slots.
Vendor classes are not involved.
The interface has nothing to do with the number of slots.
questions.explain: The number of slots is a property of the invoker storage, apart from commands and receivers.
questions.teaches: The slot count is a property of the invoker storage alone, independent of the commands and receivers it holds.
questions.rule: Keep one command per button in arrays indexed by slot, and make a press call execute() on the matching entry.

questions.q: True or false: The remote itself decides which device each slot controls.
questions.explain: The client creates the commands and loads them. The remote only stores and triggers them.
questions.rule: The client loads; the remote triggers.

questions.q: Playing a CD needs the stereo to be switched on, the CD selected and the volume set. Where can these three calls go so the remote needs one press?
options: Inside the remote button handler
In three commands loaded on the same button
In the constructor of the Stereo class
Inside one command execute() method
optionExplain: The remote would then know stereo details.
A button holds one command.
Constructing a stereo should not play a CD.
The remote sees one request.
questions.explain: One request can hide several steps. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.

questions.q: StereoOnWithCDCommand makes three calls on the stereo: on, ____ and set the volume.
questions.explain: The command turns the stereo on, sets the CD and sets the volume to 11.
questions.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.

questions.q: A projector needs power on, input selection and a brightness setting. The panel has one Present button. What fits the chapter?
options: A button handler in the panel that makes the three calls
A projector command whose execute() makes all three calls
Three projector classes, one for each step
A command that takes the input name at each press
optionExplain: The panel would hold projector knowledge.
The panel sees a single request.
Splitting the receiver does not help the button.
The interface has no argument.
questions.explain: One command can package several calls on one receiver.
questions.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.

questions.q: Why will vendors have little trouble writing command classes for their devices?
options: The Command interface contains the logic of every device
Each is a small class that keeps the receiver and calls it in execute()
They can reuse the code of the remote control
The classes are generated automatically from the vendor classes
optionExplain: The interface holds only the method signature.
The class is simple and uniform.
The remote knows nothing of devices.
Nothing in the chapter mentions generation.
questions.explain: Commands are small and uniform, which the authors say makes them easy for vendors to write.
questions.teaches: Because commands are small and uniform, the vendors themselves can supply them with new devices, so the integration work falls on those who know the device best.
questions.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.

questions.q: A drive-mode command sets the speed limit, the suspension and the display on a single car object. How does the infotainment screen invoke it?
options: With three calls, one for each step
With a loop that builds the steps from the car object it holds
By reading the car state and choosing the step
With one execute() call, without seeing the three steps
optionExplain: The screen would hold the steps.
This makes the screen assemble the request.
The screen would be choosing among car actions.
The steps are hidden in the command.
questions.explain: The invoker sees one call however many steps lie behind it.
questions.teaches: The size of the request behind execute() is hidden, so a request can grow from one call to many without any change to the invoker.
questions.rule: Let execute() make as many receiver calls as the request needs, and name the command for the whole request.

questions.q: True or false: The stereo gains a new method setBass(). StereoOnWithCDCommand must now change to call it.
questions.explain: The command changes only if its request is meant to include the bass setting. It calls what its request needs.
questions.rule: A command calls what its request needs.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: A remote slot may be empty. How can the remote press every slot safely without a check on each press?
options: Fill each slot at the start with a command that does nothing
Catch the error each time a press fails
Remove the buttons of the empty slots
Reload every empty slot with the last command pressed
optionExplain: There is always something to call.
The check moves into an error handler, which is no simpler.
Buttons cannot be removed from a built remote.
This would run an unrelated action.
questions.explain: A harmless default removes the check. The card next names this idea.
questions.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: True or false: NoCommand implements Command, and its execute() method does nothing.
questions.explain: It is a command that does no work, used as the default for every slot.
questions.rule: A default that obeys the interface and does nothing.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: A game has an equipped-item slot that may be empty, and attack code calls use() on the item. Which design follows the chapter?
options: Attack code checks for an empty slot before each use() call it makes
An empty slot holds null, and the attack code catches the resulting exception
An empty slot holds a do-nothing item whose use() does nothing
An empty slot is filled with a copy of the item that was equipped last
optionExplain: The check is spread through the code.
A null slot makes use() fail, and exception handling then spreads through the attack code.
Attack code needs no check.
A copy of the old item would keep acting as if it were still equipped, which is unwanted.
questions.explain: A do-nothing item spares the callers.
questions.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: A do-nothing default object like NoCommand is an example of a ____ object.
questions.explain: The chapter calls NoCommand a null object: it stands in where no meaningful object exists.
questions.teaches: A null object moves the nothing-here case into an object that obeys the same interface, so the client code has no special case for it.
questions.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: A service takes an optional Logger. Which design uses the null object idea?
options: Pass null and test it before each log call
Create a new subclass of the service for each level of logging wanted
Drop the Logger interface and print directly to the console instead
Pass a Logger whose methods do nothing when no logging is wanted
optionExplain: Every call site carries a check.
This multiplies classes without removing the check.
The service would then log whether or not it should.
The service calls a Logger every time.
questions.explain: An optional collaborator can be replaced by a do-nothing implementation.
questions.teaches: The null object idea is general: any optional collaborator can be replaced by a do-nothing implementation of its interface.
questions.rule: Fill unused places with an object that obeys the interface and does nothing, so the caller needs no check.

questions.section: Now, let’s check out the execution of our remote control test...
questions.q: True or false: Pressing a button whose slot still holds NoCommand has no visible effect.
questions.explain: execute() is empty, so nothing happens and nothing signals that the slot was empty.
questions.rule: A null object is silent.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: A design note claims its main goal is code that needs no changes when new devices appear. What would best support the claim?
options: A list of all the devices supported today
Showing that a new device needs new classes but no edits to old ones
A statement that the code is clean, tidy and well organised throughout
A diagram with many boxes and arrows
optionExplain: Today devices say nothing about tomorrow.
This tests the goal directly.
Style does not show the stated goal is met.
A diagram is not evidence of the goal.
questions.explain: A claim about change is tested by a change. The card next uses this check.
questions.rule: Judge the design by evidence that it delivers the goal.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: The documentation says the primary design goal was to keep the remote control code as ____ as possible.
questions.explain: The goal was simplicity of the remote code, so that it need not change for new vendor classes.
questions.rule: The stated goal was keeping the remote code simple.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: A payments team says its goal is that adding a bank needs no change to checkout, and proposes a design in which checkout calls a bank interface. Which question best tests the claim?
options: Does checkout have fewer lines of code than it had in the earlier version?
Do all of the banks use method names that look similar to one another?
Can a new bank be added by one new class, with no edit to checkout?
Do other companies use the same design?
optionExplain: Length says little about change.
Similar names are not the goal.
This is the stated goal turned into a test.
Popularity is not evidence for this design.
questions.explain: Turn the goal into a test of the claimed means.
questions.rule: Ask whether the means delivers the goal: one new class per bank.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: The authors write that they believe the design will reduce cost. What kind of statement is that?
options: An expectation, which a reader can test against costs and savings
A measured result from a production line
A guarantee that the vendors will cooperate
A proof that no other design could possibly do better than this one
optionExplain: It states a hope that can be checked.
No measurement is given.
The text speaks of belief, not guarantee.
No comparison is made.
questions.explain: A belief is a claim awaiting a test.
questions.teaches: An expectation about cost is a prediction, not a result, so a reader should look for what would confirm or weaken it.
questions.rule: A belief about cost is an expectation to test.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: A team proposes the Command Pattern for a calculator whose four buttons are fixed for good. Which judgement fits a goal-based review?
options: The goal of change-free growth is not at stake, so the benefit is small
Patterns should be used wherever they fit, so it is worth doing
More classes mean better decoupling, so add many
A calculator cannot use any design pattern
optionExplain: The means serves a goal this calculator lacks.
Fit alone does not justify the cost.
Class count is not a measure of decoupling.
Nothing prevents it; the question is whether it pays.
questions.explain: A means is worth its costs only when the goal it serves is actually at stake.
questions.teaches: A design means is worth its costs only when the goal it serves is actually at stake in the case at hand.
questions.rule: A benefit counts only where the stated goal is at stake.

questions.section: Putting the Remote Control through its paces
questions.q: True or false: If adding a new vendor class forces edits to the remote code, the design has missed its stated goal.
questions.explain: The goal was a remote that needs no changes when vendor classes are added, so a forced edit shows the goal was missed.
questions.rule: Test the goal with a new device.

questions.q: A remote has a global undo button. What must the remote remember to reverse the last action?
options: A snapshot of every device in the house
The name of the last button pressed
The command that was invoked last
The time of the last press
optionExplain: A snapshot is heavy and unnecessary.
A name is not enough to reverse the action.
The command knows how to reverse itself.
Time says nothing about what to reverse.
questions.explain: The command knows its own reversal. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: The invoker remembers the last command to undo it.

questions.q: The undo() method of a command ____ whatever its execute() method last did.
questions.explain: undo() mirrors execute() by reversing its effect.
questions.rule: undo() reverses what execute() did.

questions.q: A door lock command has execute() calling lock(). Which call should its undo() make?
options: lock() again, to confirm that the door state is right
unlock(), the opposite of what execute() did
checkStatus(), to see what happened
toggle(), which flips the door to whatever state it is not in
optionExplain: Repeating execute() reverses nothing.
Right: undo mirrors execute, so a command that locked the door undoes itself by unlocking it.
Reading state does not reverse it.
A toggle can land on the wrong state if the door changed in between; undo should make the exact opposite call.
questions.explain: Reverse with the opposite call.
questions.rule: undo() makes the opposite call to execute().

questions.q: A remote remembers only the last command. The user presses light on, then undo, then undo again. What does the second undo do?
options: It reverses an earlier command that came before the light
It turns the light back on
It does nothing because the remote cleared the command
It calls undo() on the same command again, as the remote still holds it
optionExplain: The remote has no record of earlier commands.
The second call repeats the reversal.
Nothing in this design clears it.
Only one command is remembered.
questions.explain: With one remembered command, the second undo repeats the first reversal.
questions.teaches: Remembering only the last command gives a single level of undo: pressing undo again repeats the same reversal instead of stepping further back.
questions.rule: The remote still holds the last command, so undo repeats on it.

questions.q: In a menu-driven app, where should the last executed command be remembered for undo?
options: In each receiver
In the client code that creates the commands and loads them into slots
In the invoker, which sees every command and updates its record
In the Command interface
optionExplain: A receiver does not see commands as a series.
The client does not see each execution.
The invoker is the one place that triggers them all.
An interface stores nothing.
questions.explain: The invoker keeps the record and each command knows its own reversal.
questions.teaches: Undo bookkeeping lives in the invoker, which sees every command, while each command knows how to reverse itself.
questions.rule: The invoker, which sees every command, keeps the last one.

questions.q: True or false: Calling off() is enough to undo a command that set a fan to high, whatever speed the fan had before.
questions.explain: The fan may have been on medium or low before. Turning it off does not restore that earlier state.
questions.rule: A bare opposite call needs a certain earlier state.

questions.q: A fan is on medium and the user presses a button that sets it to high. After undo, what should the fan do?
options: Go back to medium
Turn off
Stay on high speed
Go to low
optionExplain: Undo restores the state before the change.
Off is not the earlier state.
Then nothing would have been undone.
Low is not where it started.
questions.explain: Undo restores what was there before. The card next shows how a command can know it.
questions.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().

questions.q: True or false: To undo a ceiling fan speed command, the command must keep track of the fan previous speed.
questions.explain: Without the old speed it cannot restore the earlier setting.
questions.rule: Remember the earlier state to restore it.

questions.q: A volume command sets the volume to 7 while it is at 3. Which plan lets it undo correctly?
options: Set the volume to 0 in undo()
Remember 7 and set it to 7 again in undo()
Subtract one from 7 in undo()
Remember 3 before the change, and restore 3 in undo()
optionExplain: Zero is not where it was.
This repeats execute().
The old value is 3, not 6.
Undo restores the recorded value.
questions.explain: Record the old value, restore it in undo.
questions.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().

questions.q: The command must record the previous state ____ it changes the receiver.
questions.explain: After the change the old value is gone from the receiver, so it must be captured first.
questions.teaches: The earlier state must be captured at the moment just before the change, because afterwards the old value is no longer in the receiver.
questions.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().

questions.q: A spreadsheet cell holds 40. Command A sets it to 55, then command B sets it to 70. The user undoes B. What does B restore?
options: 40, the first value the cell ever had
55, the value B found when it ran
70, the value B wrote
15, the difference between the value B wrote and the value A wrote
optionExplain: B only saw the value 55 that A left, so it never knew the cell once held 40.
B recorded the state it saw.
That is what B did, not what it replaced.
Undo restores a saved value, not a difference between two values.
questions.explain: Each command saves the state it saw just before it ran.
questions.teaches: Each command saves the state it saw just before it ran, so undoing in reverse order steps back through the earlier states.
questions.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().

questions.q: A fan command recorded medium before setting high. Someone then sets the fan by hand to low, and undo is pressed. What does undo restore?
options: Low, the current speed
Medium, the speed it recorded, even though the fan changed since
Off, the safe state
Nothing, as the command notices the hand change and cancels the undo
optionExplain: That would not change anything.
Undo puts back its record.
The command knows nothing of safety.
Commands do not watch the receiver.
questions.explain: A command restores its record, which can be out of date if others change the receiver.
questions.rule: When a command changes a receiver, have it remember the earlier state and put it back in undo().

questions.q: Users want to press undo several times in a row to step back through their actions. What does the invoker need?
options: A larger undo button
A copy of every receiver
A longer undo() method in each command, to hold more steps
A history of earlier commands, not a single reference
optionExplain: The button is not the limitation.
Copies of receivers are not needed.
The method length has no bearing.
Each press needs the next earlier command.
questions.explain: Stepping back needs a record of several commands. The card next names the structure.
questions.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a history of undo operations can be kept by a stack of previous commands.
questions.explain: The invoker pops the first item off the stack and calls its undo().
questions.rule: Stack the commands; pop to undo.

questions.q: In a text editor the user runs commands A, B and C in that order, then presses undo three times. Put the commands in the order in which they are undone.
items: Command C is undone
Command B is undone
Command A is undone
questions.explain: A stack gives last in, first out, so the most recent command is undone first.
questions.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().

questions.q: Command C was popped and undone a moment ago. The user presses undo again. Which command is undone?
options: Command B, the next one on the stack
Command C again, as it was the latest
Command A, the oldest one
No command, until a new one is executed
optionExplain: Popping removed C from the history.
C is no longer on the stack.
B lies above A on the stack, so B is undone before A.
B is still stored on the stack, so there is a command to undo.
questions.explain: Popping removes the command, so repeated undo keeps stepping backward.
questions.teaches: Popping removes the command from the history, so repeated undo keeps stepping backward instead of repeating the same reversal.
questions.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().

questions.q: A browser back button steps through visited pages one at a time. Which structure does this resemble?
options: A single remembered page
A queue in which the oldest page comes back first
A stack of past entries, each press popping the latest
A log replayed in order after a crash
optionExplain: Back could then go only once.
Back would then jump to the first page.
Both step backward from the latest.
A log replays forward.
questions.explain: Stepping backward fits last-in, first-out ordering.
questions.teaches: Last in, first out is the natural order for stepping backward, while a queue, which is first in, first out, suits work waiting to be done.
questions.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().

questions.q: Which action can a stack-based undo not reverse?
options: One performed by a command that has an undo() method
One performed by the most recent command
One performed by a macro of several commands
One performed directly on a receiver, outside any command
optionExplain: It is on the stack and can be reversed.
The top of the stack is undone first.
A macro is a command and can be undone.
It was never pushed on the stack.
questions.explain: Only what went through the invoker is on the stack.
questions.rule: Keep executed commands on a stack and, on each undo, pop the top one and call its undo().

questions.q: A remote needs one Party button that dims lights, starts the stereo and TV, and fires up the hot tub. What is the best way to build it?
options: A fifth hard-wired party routine inside the remote
A command that holds the other commands and runs them all
A button that must be pressed four times quickly
A command that copies the code of the other four
optionExplain: The remote would then know the devices.
One button, one request, many parts.
Four presses do not make one request.
Copying repeats the code and ties it together.
questions.explain: The idea is a command made of commands. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().

questions.q: A MacroCommand holds an array of commands, and its execute() runs ____ of them.
questions.explain: It steps through the array and executes every command in it.
questions.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().

questions.q: A smart kitchen needs a Morning button that runs existing lights, kettle and radio commands. Which design reuses them?
options: A new command class that repeats the three device calls
Three buttons that the user presses in turn
A macro command built from the three existing commands
An edit of each device command so that it also calls the other two
optionExplain: This duplicates what the commands already do.
This is not one request.
The parts are reused as they are.
This ties the commands to each other.
questions.explain: A macro reuses existing commands without changing them.
questions.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().

questions.q: The remote treats a MacroCommand like any other command. Why can it?
options: MacroCommand implements Command, so the remote sees execute()
The remote has a special slot type for macros
The macro copies the remote code inside itself
The remote checks the type of each command and adapts
optionExplain: It looks like any command from outside.
No special slot exists.
The macro does not copy the remote's code; it only holds commands and calls their execute().
Type checks would reintroduce knowledge.
questions.explain: The macro is a Command, so no change to the remote is needed.
questions.teaches: Because MacroCommand is itself a Command, the invoker cannot tell a macro from a single command, so adding macros needs no change to the remote.
questions.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().

questions.q: A video editor builds an Apply Look macro from [crop, colour, sharpen] in that order. Which step runs first?
options: Crop, the first in the array
Sharpen, the last in the array
All three at the same moment
Whichever step takes the least time, since the macro orders its parts for speed
optionExplain: The macro steps through the array from the start.
Sharpen is last in the array, so it runs last, after crop and colour.
The loop runs them one after another.
The macro does not reorder its parts; the array order decides.
questions.explain: The macro runs its parts in list order.
questions.teaches: A macro runs its parts in the order of its list, so the order of that list is part of the macro design.
questions.rule: Make a command that holds a list of commands and runs each of them in its execute().

questions.q: True or false: A MacroCommand needs a receiver of its own to hold the actions it runs.
questions.explain: Its parts are commands, and each has its own receiver. The macro only holds the commands.
questions.rule: A macro holds commands, not a receiver.

questions.q: A macro ran steps 1, 2 and 3 in that order. In what order should undo reverse them?
options: Any order, as the steps are independent
optionExplain: This repeats the order of execution.
There is no reason for this order.
Back out the latest step first.
Steps can depend on each other.
questions.explain: Reversing runs the other way. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.

questions.q: A macro executed its first, second and third commands. Put the undo calls in the order the macro makes them.
items: Undo the third command
Undo the second command
Undo the first command
questions.explain: The loop in undo() runs from the last command down to the first.
questions.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.

questions.q: A deployment macro ran: stop the service, update the files, start the service. Which undo order matches the chapter?
options: Undo the stop, then undo the update, then undo the start
Undo the start, then undo the update, then undo the stop
Undo the update, then undo the start, then undo the stop
Undo only the update, because the other steps are routine
optionExplain: This follows the order of execution.
The last step is reversed first.
The start came after the update, so it should be undone first.
Every step must be reversed for the earlier state to return.
questions.explain: Reverse the steps in reverse order.
questions.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.

questions.q: Why does reverse order make sense when undoing a macro?
options: Forward order would run more slowly
The array can only be read backward during undo
Each undo() may be called only in the order opposite to execute()
A later step may rest on an earlier one, so later steps come off first
optionExplain: Speed plays no part; the reason for reverse order is that later steps depend on earlier ones.
Arrays can be read either way.
This is not a rule of the language.
Undoing out of order could act on a state that no longer holds.
questions.explain: Later steps rest on earlier ones, so they come off first.
questions.teaches: A later step may depend on the state an earlier step left, so undoing later steps first keeps each reversal acting on the state it expects.
questions.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.

questions.q: One command in a macro has an undo() that does nothing. What happens when the macro is undone?
options: The macro skips it and still restores everything that it changed
The remote reverses that step itself
That step stays in effect, so the earlier state is not restored
Undo is unaffected
optionExplain: Nothing would restore its effect.
The remote knows no commands.
The macro calls it, but it reverses nothing.
The result is incomplete.
questions.explain: A macro is as undoable as its weakest part.
questions.teaches: A macro is only as undoable as its weakest part: one step that cannot reverse itself leaves the earlier state incomplete.
questions.rule: Undo a macro by calling undo() on its parts from the last to the first.

questions.q: True or false: If a macro holds three commands, its undo() calls the undo() of each of them once.
questions.explain: The loop visits each command one time, from last to first.
questions.rule: One undo per part, in reverse.

questions.q: A command execute() contains all the logic of the request instead of calling a receiver. According to the authors, what is the main cost?
options: Less decoupling, and no parameterizing commands with receivers
The command can no longer be executed twice
The invoker can no longer call execute()
The command cannot be stored in a slot
optionExplain: The receiver was what kept the two apart.
Nothing prevents repeated execution.
The interface is unchanged.
Storing needs only the interface.
questions.explain: A command without a receiver loses some flexibility. The card next states the authors view.
questions.rule: A smart command gives up decoupling from the receiver.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, smart commands that carry out the request themselves are not uncommon in practice.
questions.explain: They say so in the chapter summary, while preferring dumb commands in general.
questions.rule: Smart commands exist and are common.

questions.q: A music app has these commands. Sort each: does its execute() delegate to a receiver, or do the work itself?

items.t: PlayCommand calls player.play()
MuteCommand calls speaker.mute()
ShuffleCommand calls playlist.shuffle()
ImportCommand parses the file and updates the library itself
ReportCommand computes totals itself
ConvertCommand re-encodes the audio itself

questions.explain: The first three hand the work to a receiver. The last three contain the logic, so they have no receiver to swap.
questions.rule: Dumb commands delegate; smart commands carry the logic.

questions.q: Party mode could be a PartyCommand with hard-coded calls or a MacroCommand with a list. Which do the authors prefer, and why?
options: PartyCommand, because hard-coding the calls makes it run faster in practice
PartyCommand, because a macro cannot support undo in the way a single command can
Neither, as party mode needs a new invoker
MacroCommand: its parts are chosen dynamically, with less new code
optionExplain: Speed is not discussed.
The chapter shows macro undo.
The remote needs no change.
Right: the list of parts is chosen dynamically, so the combination needs less new code.
questions.explain: A macro lets the combination be decided when the program runs.
questions.teaches: Choosing at run time which commands go into a macro is the flexibility that a hard-coded combined command lacks.
questions.rule: Prefer a macro of parts over a hard-coded smart command.

questions.q: A coffee app wants users to build their own presets from existing commands. Which design supports this?
options: A new preset class written for each user
A macro command built at run time from the commands users pick
A smart command with all of the weekend steps written inside its execute()
A preset button with a branch for each user
optionExplain: Users cannot write classes.
The list is built when the user chooses.
This is fixed in code.
Branches grow with the users.
questions.explain: Run-time assembly lets end users define combined actions.
questions.teaches: Assembling macros at run time lets end users, not programmers, define combined actions.
questions.rule: Macros built from existing commands let users compose presets.

questions.q: Which statement about the authors preference is accurate?
options: Smart commands are forbidden by the pattern
A general recommendation; smart commands remain legitimate
Every command must be built from a macro
A command must have a receiver to be a command
optionExplain: No such ban is stated.
The authors call smart commands not uncommon.
Macros are an extension, not a requirement.
A smart command has none yet is a command.
questions.explain: The preference weighs flexibility against convenience; it is not a prohibition.
questions.rule: Dumb commands are preferred, but smart ones stay legitimate.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: A remote uses commands for a light, a garage door, a stereo and a hot tub, each with an on and an off request. About how many command classes does the plain pattern produce?
options: Two, one on-command and one off-command shared by every device
Four, one for each device, handling both its on and its off request
Nine, eight request classes plus one more for the remote itself
About eight, two for each receiver
optionExplain: On and off are requests on different receivers, so two shared classes cannot cover all eight combinations.
A command class carries one request, and on and off are separate requests, so one class per device is too few.
The remote is the invoker, not a command, so it adds no command class.
One class per request and receiver.
questions.explain: Each request gets its own small class. The card next states this cost.
questions.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: True or false: In the chapter remote, each receiver class has two command classes, one for each of its two requests.
questions.explain: The examples are LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand, GarageDoorUpCommand and GarageDoorDownCommand.
questions.rule: Roughly two classes per receiver.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: A game has five unit types, each with an attack request and a defend request wrapped as commands in the plain form. How many command classes result?
options: Ten, two for each unit type
Five, one for each unit type
Two, one for attack and one for defend
Seven, five types plus two actions
optionExplain: One class per request and receiver.
Each type has two requests.
Each is bound to a different receiver type.
The classes are multiplied, not added.
questions.explain: Count requests times receivers.
questions.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: What explains the strong resemblance among the many command classes?
options: They were generated from the same source file
The invoker requires identical code in all of them
Each is a piece of packaged computation behind one shared method
Java forbids classes that differ
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter says so.
The invoker sees only the interface.
They differ in the receiver and the call inside.
Classes may differ freely.
questions.explain: Uniform shape and tiny size make the repetition obvious.
questions.teaches: Because each command is only a bit of packaged computation behind one shared method, the repetition invites a more compact way to write it.
questions.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: An email client wraps archive, delete and flag as command classes. Which complaints are fair? Select all that apply.
options: Every new action adds another small class
Many classes look alike because they share one interface
The toolbar must change for every new class
Commands can no longer be stored in toolbar buttons
optionExplain: The classes grow with the number of distinct requests.
Each differs mainly in its receiver call.
The toolbar depends only on the interface.
Storing needs only the interface.
questions.explain: The cost is in the number of small classes, not in the invoker.
questions.teaches: The cost of the plain pattern grows with the number of distinct requests, not with the number of invokers.
questions.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.

questions.section: The Command Pattern means lots of command classes
questions.q: A program has only two requests to wrap in command objects. How much does the extra class count matter?
options: A lot: the pattern then cannot be used
Moderately: the invoker must be rewritten for each of the two requests
Greatly: every command needs its own invoker class as well
Little: two small classes cost little
optionExplain: Nothing prevents using it.
The invoker works with any command through the shared interface, so it needs no rewrite for each request.
Commands need no invoker class of their own; the cost is one small class per request.
The cost scales with requests.
questions.explain: The cost matters when requests are many.
questions.rule: Expect about one small class per request and receiver when the pattern is written in its plain form.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: Which is the smallest piece of code that could take the place of a LightOnCommand object in the remote?
options: A subclass of the Light class
A short expression that calls the light on() when it runs
A copy of the whole remote class
A string that names the method to call, looked up by the remote
optionExplain: A light is not a command.
It is the body of execute() written in place.
The remote is the invoker.
A string cannot run by itself; the remote would have to look up and call the named method.
questions.explain: Only the computation is needed. The card next shows how Java allows it.
questions.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: A lambda expression can stand in for a Command object because the interface has exactly ____ method.
questions.explain: With only execute(), there is one method for the lambda to match.
questions.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: An interface Greeter has a single method greet() that takes nothing and returns nothing. What follows?
options: Only a class that implements Greeter can be passed to a Greeter parameter
A lambda needs an extra method named run()
A lambda with no parameters and no result can be passed in its place
A lambda cannot call methods on other objects, only on its own fields
optionExplain: A compatible lambda can also be passed.
It needs no extra method.
Right: a lambda with no parameters and no result matches greet(), so it can be passed in its place.
It can call any accessible method.
questions.explain: A compatible lambda replaces the single method.
questions.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: What does the compiler check when a lambda is passed to a Command parameter?
options: That the interface has one method with a matching signature
That the lambda is named execute
That the lambda extends the Command class and inherits from it
That the lambda is stored in an array
optionExplain: Signature, not name, decides.
A lambda has no name to check.
A lambda is not a subclass.
Storage is irrelevant.
questions.explain: The match is by signature against the single method.
questions.teaches: The compiler matches the lambda to the interface single method by its parameters and return type, not by name, which is why the lambda needs no name.
questions.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: A listener interface has one method that takes one event argument and returns nothing. Can a lambda replace a listener class?
options: Yes, if the lambda takes one argument and returns nothing
No, because lambdas cannot take parameters or return values
Yes, whatever its parameters
No, because listeners must be objects
optionExplain: The signature matches.
They can have parameters and return values.
The signature must match.
The lambda becomes a function object.
questions.explain: Lambdas may have parameters and return values, provided they match the single method.
questions.teaches: Lambdas can have parameters and return values, provided their signature matches the interface single method.
questions.rule: Where an interface has exactly one method, pass a lambda with a compatible signature instead of writing a class.

questions.section: Simplifying the Remote Control with lambda expressions
questions.q: True or false: A lambda whose parameter list differs from the interface single method can still be used, because the compiler adapts it.
questions.explain: The compiler checks for a compatible signature and rejects a mismatch.
questions.rule: The signature must be compatible.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: A command needs only to call stereo.off(). What is the shortest way to pass it?
options: A lambda with three statements
A new class named StereoOffCommand with its own execute()
A reference to the off method of the stereo
The Stereo object itself
optionExplain: One call needs no three statements.
Writing a whole StereoOffCommand class is the long way when one call is all that is needed.
Naming the method is enough.
The slot needs something with execute().
questions.explain: One call can be named directly. The card next shows the notation.
questions.rule: A lambda that only calls one method can be a method reference.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: A method reference to the off method of the stereo is written stereo____off.
questions.explain: The double colon joins the object and the method name.
questions.rule: A method reference is written with the :: notation.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: Which of these lambdas could be replaced by a method reference?
options: A lambda that calls fan.start() and then fan.setSpeed(2)
A lambda that only calls fan.start()
A lambda that prints a message and then calls fan.start()
A lambda that calls fan.start() twice in a row
optionExplain: It makes two calls, start() and setSpeed(2), so one method reference cannot express it.
It calls exactly one method.
It does something besides the call.
It makes the same call twice, so a single method reference cannot express it.
questions.explain: A method reference suits a lambda that makes just one call.
questions.rule: Only a single-call lambda can become a method reference.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: A three-step stereo command is needed in two slots. How can it be written once?
options: Use one method reference that names all three of the methods at once
Copy the lambda body into each slot where the sequence is needed, by hand
Write a subclass of Stereo for the sequence
Declare the lambda once as a Command with a name, and pass the name
optionExplain: A reference names one method.
This repeats the code.
This adds a class and does not help the slots.
A named lambda is an ordinary value.
questions.explain: A lambda stored under a name can be reused.
questions.teaches: A lambda assigned to a variable of the interface type is an ordinary value that can be reused, with the type Command giving it its meaning.
questions.rule: A lambda that does more needs a body, which can be named.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: A scheduler accepts an object with one method run(). To schedule printing a report, where printing is a single call report.print(), what fits?
options: A subclass of the scheduler
A lambda with extra statements added for safety
A reference to the print method of the report
The report object itself, with no change
optionExplain: The scheduler needs no subclass.
Extra statements are not needed.
One call can be named directly.
It has no run() method.
questions.explain: Method references work for any one-method interface with a matching signature.
questions.teaches: Method references are not specific to commands: any one-method interface accepts a reference to a method with a matching signature.
questions.rule: A single call to print fits a method reference.

questions.section: Simplifying even more with method references
questions.q: True or false: A command that makes three calls can be written as a method reference to one of them.
questions.explain: A reference names a single method, so the other two calls would be lost.
questions.rule: One reference, one method.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: The Command interface now has execute() and undo(). Can lambda expressions replace the concrete command classes?
options: Not directly: a lambda covers one method and there are two
Yes, a lambda can implement two methods at once
Yes, but only for execute()
No, since lambdas cannot call methods
optionExplain: Right: a lambda implements one method, so it cannot cover both execute() and undo() directly.
A lambda implements a single method, so it cannot implement execute() and undo() at once.
The object would still lack undo().
Lambdas can call methods; the limit is the number of methods to implement.
questions.explain: The count of methods decides. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A lambda covers one method; execute() plus undo() needs a class.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if you find yourself working around the one-method rule to support undo, lambdas are probably not the right solution.
questions.explain: They say the resulting code would probably be more complex than using command objects.
questions.rule: Do not fight the tool.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: Which of these interfaces could take a lambda expression? Select all that apply.
options: Task, with the single method run()
Greeter, with the single method greet()
Job, with the two methods start() and stop()
Command, with the two methods execute() and undo()
optionExplain: One method, so one lambda can replace it.
One method, so one lambda can replace it.
One lambda is one method, not two.
The two-method version is the case the authors warn about.
questions.explain: Only a single-method interface can take a lambda.
questions.rule: A lambda fits an interface with only one method.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: The authors say two kinds of commands could let lambdas support undo, yet they advise against it. Why?
options: It cannot compile in Java
Undo cannot be written in Java by any means, with or without lambdas
Lambdas run more slowly than classes, which matters in a remote
It would probably be more complex than using command objects
optionExplain: The authors say you could probably find a way.
Undo was written with command objects.
Speed is not mentioned.
The workaround costs more than it saves.
questions.explain: A technique should be dropped when working around its limits costs more than it gains.
questions.teaches: A technique is worth dropping when the workaround for its limits costs more than the technique saves.
questions.rule: Lambda undo would be more complex than command objects.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: A pipeline replaces its stage classes with lambdas, and the logs printed stage class names. What changes in the logs?
options: The logs gain clearer stage names, since each lambda carries its own readable name
The names come from the runtime and are unreadable unless labels are added
The logs stop working
The names stay the same as before
optionExplain: The names get worse, not clearer, because lambdas carry no meaningful class names.
Lambdas have no meaningful class names.
They still print, but with odd names.
The old classes are gone.
questions.explain: Display code that relies on class names needs explicit labels once lambdas are used.
questions.teaches: A lambda has no meaningful class name, so any display that relies on class names needs explicit labels supplied by the programmer.
questions.rule: Lambdas lose meaningful class names, so logs need labels.

questions.section: Test the remote control with lambda expressions
questions.q: True or false: If the undo feature were dropped, so that execute() is the only method, lambda expressions could again replace the command classes.
questions.explain: The single-method condition would hold again.
questions.rule: One method makes lambdas possible.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: A web server wants worker threads to handle whatever tasks arrive, such as computing or fetching. What lets the workers treat all tasks alike?
options: Each worker is written for one kind of task
Each task is a command with the same execute() method
The queue stores task names and the worker picks the code
Tasks are run by the thread that created them
optionExplain: Workers would then not be interchangeable.
The uniform call hides the task.
Names bring the knowledge back.
Then there would be no queue.
questions.explain: A uniform call lets workers be generic. The card next describes the queue.
questions.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: Put the steps of a worker thread in order.
items: Remove a command from the queue
Call its execute() method
Wait for the call to finish
Discard the command and fetch a new one
questions.explain: The worker removes, executes, waits, discards and repeats.
questions.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: A print spooler gets jobs from many programs. Which design follows the job queue idea?
options: Each program prints directly and waits for the printer
Jobs are stored as text files that the spooler parses by type
One worker per job type, hard-coded
Jobs are queued as command objects, and workers take one and call execute()
optionExplain: Printing directly and waiting forms no queue of jobs for workers to take.
The spooler would know every type.
Workers would not be interchangeable.
The spooler knows only execute().
questions.explain: Commands make the jobs uniform.
questions.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: Why can the queue classes ignore what the commands compute?
options: They only call execute(), so the content stays behind it
They compute everything themselves
Commands announce their type to the queue first
The queue accepts only one kind of command
optionExplain: The interface hides the work.
Then commands would not be needed.
This would be extra knowledge for the queue.
The point is that any kind fits.
questions.explain: The queue knows only the interface.
questions.teaches: The queue and workers are reusable infrastructure: one queue can serve unrelated kinds of work because it depends only on execute().
questions.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: An alarm app schedules a command for 7:00. What does the scheduler need to know about the command?
options: Which receiver it uses
Which actions it performs
Only that it has execute()
Whether it is a light or an audio command
optionExplain: That is hidden in the command.
That is hidden in the command.
The scheduler waits for the time and calls it.
The kind is of no concern to the scheduler.
questions.explain: A scheduler is a queue ordered by time and needs only the one method.
questions.teaches: A scheduler is a queue ordered by time: it needs only the time and execute(), never what the command does.
questions.rule: Put commands in a queue and let worker threads take each one and call execute(), whatever it computes.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: queuing requests
questions.q: True or false: A worker thread can run an object placed in the queue even if it does not implement the command interface.
questions.explain: The worker calls execute(), so the object must have it. The queue accepts only commands.
questions.rule: No execute(), no run.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: A spreadsheet is too large to save in full after every edit. How could it still recover after a crash?
options: Save nothing and ask the user to redo the edits
Save the full spreadsheet after every edit anyway
Keep the edits in memory, since memory survives crashes
Save a checkpoint now and then, and log each later edit as a command
optionExplain: Asking the user to redo the edits loses their work.
This is the cost the log avoids.
Memory is lost in a crash.
Replaying the log rebuilds the lost work.
questions.explain: A log of edits plus a checkpoint is the idea. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A checkpoint plus a command log recovers lost work.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: To support logging, commands gain two methods, store() and ____().
questions.explain: store() writes the command to disk and load() reads it back.
questions.rule: Logging adds store() and load() to commands.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: A note-taking app crashed. Put the recovery steps in order.
items: Load the last checkpoint
Reload the logged command objects
Execute the commands in the order they were logged
questions.explain: Start from the checkpoint and replay the logged commands in order.
questions.rule: Reload the checkpoint, then execute the logged commands in order.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: Why must the logged commands be replayed in order?
options: Commands are stored on disk in alphabetical order of the names of their classes
Each acts on the state earlier ones left, so order can change results
The disk can only be read in the forward direction, from the start to the end
Order matters only for the first command
optionExplain: Storage order has no such rule.
Later commands rest on earlier ones.
Disks can be read in any order.
It matters throughout.
questions.explain: Replay must rebuild the same sequence of states.
questions.teaches: Each command acts on the state the earlier ones left, so replaying them in a different order can produce a different result.
questions.rule: Replay in order because each command acts on earlier state.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: A bank transfer is a debit followed by a credit. Which goal does the chapter mention for sets of operations?
options: The first completes and the rest are optional
Each completes at its own time with no link between them
All the operations complete, or none of them do
Each is retried separately until it succeeds, in whatever order that happens
optionExplain: The pair belongs together.
Then half a transfer could happen.
This is the transactional goal.
Retrying separately does not keep the debit and credit together, and order matters.
questions.explain: Logging commands extends to transactions where the set completes as a whole.
questions.teaches: Commands can be extended to sets of operations in a transactional manner, so that the whole set completes or none of it does.
questions.rule: Logged operations complete as a whole, or not at all.

questions.section: More uses of the Command Pattern: logging requests
questions.q: True or false: The authors say logging commands would make sense for a remote control.
questions.explain: They say this kind of logging would not make sense for a remote control, though it suits applications with large data.
questions.rule: Log when the data is costly to save.

questions.q: You carry a laptop from the US to Britain, where the wall outlet has a different shape. What does a travel power adapter do?
options: It rebuilds the laptop's plug into the shape that the outlet needs
It swaps the wall outlet for a new one made for the laptop
It presents the outlet in a form that the plug fits
It makes electricity for the laptop on its own, without the outlet
optionExplain: Rebuilding the plug sounds possible, but the adapter leaves the laptop alone.
The outlet stays in the wall; the adapter does not replace it.
Right: it sits between plug and outlet and presents the outlet in the shape the plug expects.
The power still comes from the outlet; the adapter only changes how it is presented.
questions.explain: The adapter sits in the middle and leaves both ends unchanged. The card next shows the same idea in software.
questions.rule: An adapter changes the interface one side offers into the interface the other side expects, and leaves both sides as they were.

questions.q: An object-oriented adapter takes one interface and adapts it to the interface that a ____ expects.
questions.explain: The client is the code that makes the calls. The adapter lets it keep calling the interface it was written for.
questions.rule: Adapters serve the client's expected interface.

questions.q: A travel adapter changes nothing inside the laptop or inside the wall. What does that suggest about adapting two software parts?
options: A part you cannot modify can still be used, via a go-between
Both parts must first be edited so that they share a common design
Only the newer of the two parts needs any changes to be compatible
The go-between must replace one of the two parts that it connects
optionExplain: Right: since the adapter modifies neither side, it works even when one side belongs to someone else.
Editing both is the cost an adapter exists to avoid.
Changing the newer part is just another edit; the adapter needs none.
The adapter sits between the parts; the wrapped part stays in use.
questions.explain: Because the adapter changes neither side, it fits cases where one side is not yours to change.
questions.rule: Adapt around what you cannot edit.
questions.teaches: An adapter is the answer when one side of the mismatch is outside your control, because it needs no edits to either side.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it plays the adapter role (it makes one interface usable where another is expected).
groups: Does not play the adapter role

items.t: Travel plug that lets a US laptop use a British outlet
Dongle that lets a wired headphone jack connect to a USB-C phone
Class that lets old code call a new library through the methods the old code already uses
Extension cord with the same plug and socket shape at both ends
Wall hook that holds chargers in one place
Class that adds a new feature but keeps the same methods as the class it wraps

questions.explain: The first three change what one side looks like to the other. The cord and the hook do not change any interface, and the last item changes behavior, not the interface.
questions.rule: No change of interface, no adapter role.

questions.q: A simple adapter only reshapes a socket and passes the current straight through. The device needs less voltage than the outlet supplies. What follows?
options: The simple adapter will adjust the voltage by itself as needed
No adapter can help, so the device cannot be used
The device must be rebuilt to take the higher voltage
A more complex adapter that adjusts the power is needed
optionExplain: A pass-through adapter does exactly that: it passes things through.
Some adapters do the extra work, so this gap can be bridged.
Rebuilding the device is the change an adapter is meant to avoid.
Right: the book notes that some adapters are more complex inside and step power up or down.
questions.explain: How much an adapter does depends on how large the gap is. Shape alone is simple; matching power needs more inside.
questions.rule: The wider the gap between interfaces, the more work the adapter does.
questions.hint: Think about which kind of adapter the book says exists besides the simple kind.

questions.q: A data pipeline's report tool reads rows through one fixed set of calls. A legacy system offers its data through different calls and cannot be edited. Which component plays the adapter role?
options: A copy of the legacy system in which every data field has been renamed for the tool
A class offering the report tool's calls and answering them with the legacy calls
A new report tool built from scratch around the legacy system's own calls
A script that exports the legacy data to files once a year for the tool
optionExplain: Copying and renaming changes the data, not the interface the tool sees.
Right: it presents the legacy system in the form the report tool already expects.
Rebuilding the tool changes the client, which the adapter leaves alone.
An export moves data around but does not adapt one set of calls to another.
questions.explain: The adapter role is about interfaces. It appears wherever something translates one side's calls into the other's, in hardware or in software.
questions.rule: The adapter is a role that any translating go-between can play.
questions.teaches: The adapter idea is a role, not a particular library: anything that translates one side's calls into the form the other side expects plays it.

questions.q: Your code calls vendor A's classes. Vendor B's classes do the same job under different method names. You cannot edit either vendor's code. What is a sound plan?
options: Edit vendor B's classes so that their method names match the ones you use
Write a middleman class that takes your calls and passes them to vendor B
Change every call in your code so that it uses vendor B's method names
Copy vendor B's source into your project and rename its methods there
optionExplain: You said you cannot edit the vendors' code.
Right: a middleman leaves your code and B's code as they are.
That is exactly the widespread change you want to avoid.
Copying is still editing code that is not yours, and it forks B's work.
questions.explain: A middleman between your code and the vendor avoids touching either. The card next names it.
questions.rule: When you cannot change either side, put a middleman class between them that speaks your interface in front and the vendor's behind.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, the adapter acts as a middleman that receives requests from the client and converts them into requests that make sense on the vendor classes.
questions.explain: That is the adapter's job in the book's account: it receives the client's requests and translates them.
questions.rule: The adapter translates the client's requests for the vendor.

questions.q: The book mentions one way to avoid writing any extra code to integrate the new vendor's classes. Which is it?
options: Have the vendor rewrite its interface for each client
Wrap your own old classes in new ones first
Delete the old calls and call the new ones directly
Ask the vendor to supply the adapter class
optionExplain: A rewrite for each client is far more work than shipping one adapter.
Wrapping your own classes is still extra code on your side.
Direct calls to the new interface mean changing your existing code.
Right: if the vendor ships the adapter, your team writes none.
questions.explain: The cost of the mismatch can sit with whoever is best placed to carry it, and the book suggests the vendor.
questions.rule: Someone has to write the adapter; it need not be you.
questions.teaches: Writing the adapter is a cost that can be pushed onto the vendor, so the pattern does not always mean extra code on your side.

questions.q: A school timetable app calls getFreeSlots() on every room source. The library's booking system, run by another department and not editable, offers only listOpenTimes(). Which design fits the adapter approach?
options: A class with getFreeSlots() that calls listOpenTimes() inside
A new method listOpenTimes() added to the timetable app
A copy of the booking system with listOpenTimes() renamed
A rule that the library must adopt getFreeSlots() by next term
optionExplain: Right: the timetable keeps its calls, and the library system stays as it is.
That changes the app's calls to match the library, which is the widespread change to avoid.
A renamed copy edits code that belongs to the library, and the copy drifts away from the original.
Demanding that the other department change is not something the app's team controls.
questions.explain: The new class presents the interface the app expects and hides the library's calls behind it.
questions.rule: Put the translation in one new class, not in the callers.

questions.q: An adapter sits between your app and a vendor. The vendor ships a new version that renames its methods. Where does the fix land?
options: In every class of your app that makes a call to the vendor's code
In both the adapter and in each of your app's other classes
In the adapter alone, with the rest of your code untouched
Nowhere, because the adapter updates itself when the vendor does
optionExplain: That would be true without an adapter; the adapter is there to prevent it.
Your classes call the adapter's stable interface, so they need no change.
Right: the adapter holds the only code that knows the vendor's names.
An adapter is ordinary code and must be edited when the vendor's calls change.
questions.explain: The adapter encapsulates the change, so the rest of the system does not have to follow the vendor's renames.
questions.rule: Vendor changes stop at the adapter.

questions.q: A timetable app asks a middleman for free slots, and the middleman uses a room calendar it cannot change. Put these steps in the order they happen.
items: The timetable calls getFreeSlots on the middleman
The middleman calls listOpenTimes on the room calendar
The room calendar returns its open times to the middleman
The middleman returns the slots to the timetable in the form it expects
questions.explain: A request goes in through the expected interface and is translated on the way to the vendor. The answer comes back and is translated again.
questions.rule: An adapter translates the request on the way in and the answer on the way out.
questions.teaches: The middleman translates in both directions: the request on its way to the vendor and the vendor's answer on its way back.

questions.q: A scheduler is written to call a Printer interface. A fax machine class has other methods, and someone wraps it so the scheduler can use it. What is the wrapped fax machine called?
options: The client
The target
The scheduler
The adaptee
optionExplain: The client is the scheduler's side: the code making the calls.
The target is the Printer interface the scheduler expects.
The scheduler is the client, not the class that gets wrapped.
Right: it is the existing class with the incompatible interface.
questions.explain: The wrapped class is the adaptee. The card next names all the parts.
questions.rule: The client talks to the target interface, the adapter implements that interface, and the adaptee sits behind the adapter.

questions.q: Match each part of the Adapter Pattern to its description.
pairs: Code that makes calls through the target interface
The interface the client is written against
The existing class with the incompatible interface
Implements the target and delegates to the adaptee
questions.explain: Each name labels a position in the design: caller, expected interface, wrapped class and the wrapper that joins them.
questions.rule: Four parts: client, target, adaptee, adapter.

questions.q: The book also asks for an adapter that converts a Duck to a Turkey. In that design, what do the client's expectations make the target?
options: Duck, because ducks were the first class in the example
Turkey, because the client now expects turkeys
Neither, because the adapter picks its own interface
Both, because every wrapped class is a target too
optionExplain: Which class came first has no bearing on the roles.
Right: the target is whatever the client is written against.
The adapter implements the target; it does not choose it.
Only one interface is the one the client calls; the other is the adaptee.
questions.explain: Reversing the direction swaps the roles. The target is set by the client, and the adaptee is the thing wrapped.
questions.rule: The client decides which interface is the target.
questions.teaches: Roles belong to a design, not to a class: reverse the direction of adaptation and the target and the adaptee swap places.

questions.q: A navigation app expects every map source to implement MapSource with getRoute(). A team wraps a city's open-data feed class, which offers fetchPath(), in a class that implements MapSource. Which assignment is right?
options: MapSource is the adaptee and the feed class is the target
The feed class is the client and the app is the adaptee
MapSource is the target and the feed class is the adaptee
MapSource is the adapter and the feed class is the client
optionExplain: This swaps the two: the app calls MapSource, so that is the target.
The app is the client, and the feed is what gets adapted, not the caller.
Right: the app is written against MapSource, and the feed is the existing class that is wrapped.
The wrapper class is the adapter; MapSource is only the interface it implements.
questions.explain: The app is the client, MapSource the target, the feed the adaptee, and the new class the adapter.
questions.rule: Name the caller first, then the interface it uses, then the wrapped class.

questions.q: True or false: A new client written directly against the feed class's own methods still needs the adapter in order to call the feed.
