questions.explain: The adapter exists for clients that expect the target interface. A client that already speaks the feed's methods can call the feed directly.
questions.rule: No mismatch for a client, no need for an adapter.

questions.q: A reporting tool asks each data source for rows(). Its team adds a mainframe whose class offers only readRecord(). Who should know about readRecord()?
options: Only the adapter that wraps the mainframe
The reporting tool and the adapter together
Every source class the tool already uses
Anyone who writes reports with the tool
optionExplain: Right: the reporting tool and the mainframe are decoupled, so the adapter holds the only link.
The tool calling readRecord would mean it knows the adaptee, which defeats the adapter.
Other sources have nothing to do with the mainframe's calls.
Report writers use the tool, which knows only rows().
questions.explain: Since client and adaptee do not know each other, the adaptee's calls stay inside the adapter. That is also why a different mainframe could later replace this one by changing only the adapter.
questions.rule: Only the adapter knows the adaptee's calls.
questions.teaches: The adaptee's own calls are hidden inside the adapter, so replacing the adaptee later means changing only the adapter.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: A client calls a method on an adapter. Which statement best describes what happens next?
options: The client calls the wrapped class itself and the adapter only watches
The adapter hands the client a copy of the wrapped class to use
The adapter makes calls on the wrapped class and returns the outcome
The wrapped class calls back into the client to finish the job
optionExplain: The client does not call the wrapped class; the adapter stands in front of it.
Handing over the wrapped class would expose the incompatible interface again.
Right: the adapter does the translating on the client's behalf.
Nothing in the pattern has the wrapped class calling the client.
questions.explain: The adapter takes the client's call and does the work on the wrapped class. The card next lists the steps.
questions.rule: The client calls the adapter through the target interface, the adapter makes the matching calls on the adaptee, and the client never sees the translation.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: Put the three steps of the client's use of an adapter in order.
items: The client calls a method on the adapter using the target interface
The adapter translates the request into calls on the adaptee
The client receives the results and never knows an adapter translated
questions.explain: The call enters through the target interface, is translated for the adaptee, and the result comes back with the translation hidden.
questions.rule: Call in, translate, result out.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: A client asks a trip adapter for one fare estimate. The adapter has to call the old pricing service three times to build it. Is that consistent with the pattern?
options: Yes: one request on the target may become several adaptee calls
No: each target call must map to exactly one call on the adaptee
No: the client would need to know about all three of the calls
Yes, but only if the client makes the three calls by itself
optionExplain: Right: the book says the adapter translates a request into one or more calls.
The book says one or more calls, so one-to-one is not required.
The client sees only its single call; the three calls are the adapter's business.
If the client made the calls it would be talking to the adaptee, which the adapter is hiding.
questions.explain: The adapter owns the mapping, and it may be one call or several.
questions.rule: One target call can fan out to several adaptee calls.
questions.teaches: An adapter may combine several adaptee calls to answer one target call, so the mapping is not necessarily one-to-one.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: A smart-home app asks a lamp adapter to turnOn(). The adapter calls the vendor's setPower(true) and then setBrightness(80). What does the app see?
options: Two separate calls it must make, one for power and one for brightness
A note listing the vendor methods that the adapter used on the lamp
A copy of the vendor lamp object for the app to use afterwards
One call to turnOn() that returns, with no sign of the vendor calls
optionExplain: That would put the vendor's interface back in the app's code.
Reporting the vendor's methods would leak the adaptee to the client.
The vendor object stays behind the adapter; the client is never given it.
Right: the translation is hidden behind the target interface.
questions.explain: The client calls only the target interface and receives only the result, in line with the third step.
questions.rule: The client sees the target interface and nothing behind it.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: True or false: If the vendor replaces the lamp with a different model, a client that calls turnOn() on the adapter must be edited to use the new model's method names.
questions.explain: The client only knows the target interface. The adapter absorbs the new model's names, so the client's code stays the same.
questions.rule: Changes behind the adapter stay behind it.

questions.section: Here’s how the Client uses the Adapter
questions.q: A mail app lets users call send(message) on any provider object. For one provider, the adapter must first log in, then upload, then confirm delivery. What does the mail app itself need to do about the login and the confirmation?
options: Call login and confirm itself around every send()
Nothing: they happen inside the adapter's send()
Check which provider is in use before each send()
Ask the user to log in before sending anything
optionExplain: That would spread the provider's procedure through the app.
Right: the adapter hides provider-specific steps behind the one call.
Branching on the provider moves the mismatch back into the client.
The adapter can handle the login; users need not be asked.
questions.explain: Because the adapter can wrap a whole procedure in one target call, the client stays simple. The same hiding makes it possible to add another provider without touching the client.
questions.rule: Provider-specific steps belong inside the adapter.
questions.teaches: An adapter can hide a whole provider-specific procedure, such as login, upload and confirmation, behind one target call.

questions.q: You must support a target interface of forty methods with an adapter. What mostly decides how much work the adapter is?
options: How many clients will use the adapter once it is written
The number and complexity of the target methods to be mapped
How old the wrapped class is and how long it has existed
How many lines the client's main method contains in total
optionExplain: More clients do not add mapping work; the adapter is written once.
Right: the book ties the effort to the size of the target interface.
Age does not set the number of methods to map.
The client's code does not set how many target methods must be implemented.
questions.explain: The effort follows the size of the interface being supported. The card next gives the book's comparison.
questions.rule: Adapter effort grows with the size of the target interface, and an adapter may wrap several classes or serve two interfaces at once.

questions.q: According to the book, the job of implementing an adapter is ____ to the size of the target interface.
questions.explain: The book says the work is proportional to the size of the target interface you need to support.
questions.rule: Bigger target, more mapping.

questions.q: Besides a one-class adapter, the book notes that an adapter can hold more than one adaptee. When is that useful?
options: When the client wants to call each of the classes by its own name
When two clients need two different target interfaces at once
When one class is too large to be wrapped by a single adapter
When the target needs functions spread across several classes
optionExplain: Calling classes by their own names is exactly what the adapter hides.
Serving two interfaces is the Two Way Adapter, a different matter.
Size alone does not call for more adaptees.
Right: the adapter can gather several classes to present one target interface.
questions.explain: The book says an adapter may hold two or more adaptees needed to implement the target.
questions.rule: One adapter may gather several adaptees.
questions.teaches: Wrapping one class is the common textbook case, not a rule: an adapter may combine several adaptees to meet one target interface.

questions.q: A clinic's old billing code calls the vendor's invoice interface. Half the clinic's new code calls a newer interface. The team wants one object usable by both halves. Which fits the book?
options: A Two Way Adapter that implements both interfaces
An adapter that implements only the older interface
A decorator that adds the newer interface's methods
A rewrite of the old code to call the newer interface
optionExplain: Right: implementing both interfaces lets it act as either.
That would serve only the old half and leave the new half unserved.
A decorator does not convert one interface into another.
Rewriting is the broad change the adapter is used to avoid.
questions.explain: The book describes a Two Way Adapter as implementing both interfaces involved.
questions.rule: Implement both interfaces to serve both halves.

questions.q: A team compares two options for a new library: rewrite 300 call sites in the app, or write one adapter class. The library's interface has three methods. Which is the likely outcome?
options: The adapter is the larger job, since adapters are always heavy
Both options cost the same, since each changes all call sites
The adapter is small, since the target interface is small
The rewrite is quicker, since it avoids a new class
optionExplain: The book says adapter effort is proportional to interface size, not always heavy.
An adapter changes none of the call sites.
Right: effort follows the size of the interface, and three methods is little.
300 call sites need far more investigation than three methods.
questions.explain: A small interface makes a small adapter, and the adapter keeps the changes in one class.
questions.rule: A small interface means a cheap adapter.

questions.q: True or false: A wrapper that translates one fixed interface into another is called an adapter only if it wraps exactly one class.
questions.explain: The book says adapters may hold two or more adaptees. The role depends on converting an interface, not on a count of wrapped classes.
questions.rule: Count of classes does not define an adapter.
questions.teaches: Whether something is an adapter depends on what it does to the interface, not on how many classes it wraps, a point that matters again when comparing it with a facade.

questions.q: Which statement best captures what the Adapter Pattern is for?
options: Making a class run faster than it did before the change
Adding new behavior to objects at runtime without editing them
Creating only one instance of a class for the whole program
Letting classes with incompatible interfaces cooperate
optionExplain: Speed is not what an adapter is about.
Adding behavior is the decorator's purpose.
That describes a different pattern, which controls instances.
Right: it converts one interface into the one a client expects.
questions.explain: The adapter's concern is the interface. The card next gives the book's definition.
questions.rule: The Adapter Pattern converts a class's interface into the one clients expect so that otherwise incompatible classes can work together.

questions.q: The Adapter Pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface the ____ expect.
questions.explain: That wording is the book's definition: the target interface is the one the clients expect.
questions.rule: Convert to the interface clients expect.

questions.q: The book says an adapter helps when an interface is expected to change over time. Why?
options: The adapter freezes the interface so that it can never change again
The adapter encapsulates the change, so the client stays unmodified
The client is rebuilt each time by the build tool automatically
The adaptee is changed to follow whatever the client expects
optionExplain: The adapter cannot stop the adaptee from changing; it absorbs the effect.
Right: the change lands in the adapter, and the client stays as it was.
Nothing is rebuilt for the client in the pattern.
The adaptee is not edited; the adapter bridges the difference.
questions.explain: Encapsulating the change in the adapter protects the client from a shifting backend.
questions.rule: The adapter absorbs interface change.
questions.teaches: The adapter protects against change as well as mismatch: when the backend's interface moves, only the adapter is edited.

questions.q: A fitness app's code expects getSteps(). Its wearable vendor changes the method name to stepCount() in every release. What does the pattern recommend?
options: Edit the app's code at each release to use the vendor's latest name
Ask users to stay on an old release of the app
A class offering getSteps() that calls the vendor's current name
Make the app check the vendor's method name at every call
optionExplain: That touches client code on every release, the very cost the adapter removes.
Holding users back postpones the problem and leaves them with old software.
Right: the fix is localized, and the app keeps its stable getSteps().
Checking names inside the app spreads the mismatch through the client.
questions.explain: The adapter holds the vendor-specific names so that the app stays unchanged.
questions.rule: Keep the churn in one adapter.

questions.q: True or false: A student claims that an adapter makes two classes compatible by editing the wrapped class's source so that its methods match the client. The claim fits the Adapter Pattern.
questions.explain: The adapter converts the interface by wrapping the class. The wrapped class stays as it is.
questions.rule: Adapters wrap; they do not edit.

questions.q: Two payroll classes have identical method names but the first returns pay in dollars and the second in cents. Both are called through the same interface. Does the adapter definition fix this?
options: No: the definition covers the interface, not the meaning of values
Yes: matching names means the interface has been converted correctly
Yes: the adapter converts units as a standard part of its job
No: an adapter cannot be used with payroll classes at all
optionExplain: Right: matching signatures do not guarantee matching meanings.
Same names with different units still disagree about what the call returns.
The definition says nothing about converting units; that would be extra work for the adapter.
Nothing prevents an adapter from being used with payroll classes.
questions.explain: An interface is more than names. Where meanings differ, the adapter needs to convert values, which goes beyond renaming calls.
questions.rule: Check meanings, not just names.
questions.teaches: An interface mismatch can hide in the meaning of values such as units, so a faithful adapter may have to convert data as well as rename calls.

questions.q: True or false: An adapter that wraps a class by composition can be used only with exactly that class, not with its subclasses.
questions.explain: Composition lets the adapter hold anything of the adaptee's type, subclasses included. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Wrap the adaptee by composition and code the client to the target interface, so any adaptee subclass or new backend can be fitted behind it.

questions.q: The object adapter wraps the adaptee using object ____.
questions.explain: Composition means the adapter holds the adaptee as a component and passes requests to it.
questions.rule: Object adapters wrap by composition.

questions.q: Why can an object adapter built for a class also accept one of that class's subclasses?
options: The adapter copies every subclass into itself when it is built
The subclass has to be edited to match the adapter first
A subclass object can stand where its parent class is expected
The adapter ignores which class it is given altogether
optionExplain: Nothing is copied; the adapter just holds a reference.
Subclasses are not edited for the adapter to accept them.
Right: because the adapter holds the adaptee type, a subclass instance fits there too.
The adapter depends on the adaptee type; it just accepts any subtype of it.
questions.explain: A subclass is a kind of its parent, so a reference to the parent's type can hold it.
questions.rule: Substitutability makes composition reusable.
questions.teaches: A reference typed as a class can hold any subclass instance, which is why composing with the adaptee extends the adapter to every subclass.

questions.q: A drone app is coded to a Camera interface. A CameraAdapter wraps VendorCam. The vendor ships NightVendorCam, a subclass of VendorCam. What must the team do to use it?
options: Hand the night camera to the existing adapter, as a kind of VendorCam
Write a fresh adapter from scratch for the new night camera model
Rewrite the whole drone app against NightVendorCam's own calls
Copy the existing adapter and rename it for the night camera
optionExplain: Right: the adapter accepts any VendorCam, including its subclasses.
A new adapter is unnecessary when the existing one accepts the subclass.
Rewriting the app would remove the benefit of coding to Camera.
A copy duplicates code that already works.
questions.explain: The existing adapter already wraps the parent type, so it serves the subclass too.
questions.rule: One adapter can serve a class and its subclasses.

questions.q: A Camera-based app later needs a cloud camera with entirely different calls, and the cloud camera does not implement Camera. What is needed?
options: A rewrite of every class in the app that uses Camera
A change to the existing adapter so it also wraps the cloud camera
Nothing, since Camera adapters cover any camera
One new adapter implementing Camera for the cloud camera
optionExplain: The app is coded to the interface, so its classes need no change.
The old adapter is written for VendorCam; stretching it would mix two backends.
The existing adapter does not know the cloud camera's calls.
Right: the app is coded to Camera, so a fresh adapter plugs the new backend in.
questions.explain: Binding the client to an interface lets new backends be added after the fact, each with its own adapter.
questions.rule: New backend, new adapter, same client.

questions.q: A booking site is coded to a Payment interface and has one adapter per payment company. Which benefits does coding to the interface give it? Select two.
options: It can use several adapters, each converting a different company's classes
It can add a new company later by writing another adapter for the same interface
It can let each page call a company's own methods whenever convenient
It no longer needs any adapter once the interface exists
optionExplain: Right: each adapter converts a different backend behind the same interface.
Right: new implementations can be added after the fact if they adhere to the interface.
Calling a company's own methods from pages would bypass the interface and bring back the coupling.
The adapters are what connect each company to the interface.
questions.explain: The two benefits are the ones the book names: several adapters for several backends, and later additions that follow the interface.
questions.rule: Code to the interface and each backend stays swappable.
questions.teaches: Because the client knows only the interface, backends can be swapped or added at any time without editing the client.

questions.q: A class adapter needs a language feature that, according to the book, Java does not have. Which is it?
options: Generic type parameters
Multiple inheritance
Interface declarations
Garbage collection
optionExplain: Generics have nothing to do with how the adapter is built.
Right: a class adapter subclasses both the target and the adaptee.
Interfaces are present in Java and the adapter pattern uses them.
Memory management is not involved in the choice.
questions.explain: Class adapters inherit from two classes at once. The card next compares both forms.
questions.rule: An object adapter composes with the adaptee; a class adapter inherits from both the target and the adaptee and needs multiple inheritance.

questions.q: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: Holds the adaptee and passes requests to it
Subclasses both the target and the adaptee
What a class adapter needs and Java lacks, per the book
questions.explain: The two forms differ in how they reach the adaptee: by composition or by inheritance.
questions.rule: Composition for object adapters, inheritance for class adapters.

questions.q: In the book's fireside chat, the class adapter says there is only one of it, not an adapter and an adaptee. What explains that?
options: It copies the adaptee's data into itself and discards the adaptee
It is itself a subclass of the adaptee, so no separate adaptee exists
It shares a single object with every other class adapter in use
It runs the adaptee inside a separate process on the same machine
optionExplain: The class adapter does not discard anything; it extends the adaptee class.
Right: because it inherits from the adaptee, adapter and adaptee are one object.
Each class adapter is its own object.
No separate process is involved; it is plain inheritance.
questions.explain: With inheritance the adapter and the adaptee are one and the same object at runtime.
questions.rule: Class adapter: one object. Object adapter: an adapter plus an adaptee.
questions.teaches: A class adapter is a single object, whereas an object adapter always pairs two objects, adapter and adaptee.

questions.q: A developer works in a language that lets a class extend two classes. She writes ReceiptPrinter, which extends both the Printer target and the LegacyTicketMachine adaptee. Which form is this?
options: An object adapter
A Two Way Adapter
A facade
A class adapter
optionExplain: An object adapter holds the adaptee as a field instead of inheriting from it.
A Two Way Adapter implements two interfaces; it does not inherit from the adaptee.
A facade simplifies a subsystem and is not built this way.
Right: it subclasses both the target and the adaptee.
questions.explain: Inheriting from both target and adaptee defines a class adapter.
questions.rule: Inherit from both: class adapter.

questions.q: True or false: The duck-and-turkey adapter in this chapter is a class adapter, because it makes a turkey look like a duck.
questions.explain: Making one thing look like another does not decide the form; how the adapter reaches the adaptee does. The chapter covers object adapters, which use composition.
questions.rule: Judge the form by how the adapter reaches the adaptee.

questions.q: A team moves to a language with multiple inheritance. They need an adapter for a ticket library and ask whether the Java limit still rules out a class adapter. What is the sound answer?
options: The limit comes from Java, so a class adapter is possible there
Class adapters are invalid in every programming language
Only object adapters are able to implement a target interface
Multiple inheritance forbids adapters of any kind in a design
optionExplain: Right: the book says you may need class adapters when using a language with multiple inheritance.
The book rules class adapters out for Java only.
A class adapter also implements the target, by inheriting from it.
Multiple inheritance is what makes class adapters possible.
questions.explain: Which form you can use is a property of the language, so choices made for Java need not carry over.
questions.rule: The pattern is the same; the available forms depend on the language.
questions.teaches: Pattern forms are constrained by language features, so a choice that is forced in one language can be open in another.

questions.q: A teammate says: 'Class adapters are better, since there is only one object instead of two.' What is the best first move?
options: Accept it, since fewer objects always means better design
Reject it, since composition is always preferable
Ask what that one object gives up in exchange
Ask for a vote and follow the majority
optionExplain: Fewer objects is one advantage; it may come with a cost.
Rejecting it by rule is as unexamined as accepting it by rule.
Right: a claim can be true and still leave out a cost.
A vote shows opinion, not whether the claim holds.
questions.explain: Understand the claim and its price before judging. The card next sets out both sides.
questions.rule: Restate each form's claims and what it gives up, then weigh them against your language and your needs before taking sides.

questions.q: Sort each claim by the form that makes it in the fireside chat.

items.t: It can adapt the adaptee and any of its subclasses
It prefers composition, for flexibility
It is a single object rather than an adapter plus an adaptee
It can override the adaptee's behavior
It does not have to reimplement the whole adaptee

questions.explain: Each form argues from what its construction gives it: composition for reach, inheritance for reuse and overriding.
questions.rule: Class adapter: override and reuse; object adapter: reach subclasses.

questions.q: The object adapter says it prefers composition over inheritance. What reason does it give?
options: Composition runs faster than inheritance at runtime
Inheritance is not allowed with adapters in any language
Composition needs no target interface to work
A little delegation code keeps things flexible
optionExplain: The chat concedes the class adapter may be more efficient, since it has one object.
The class adapter is an accepted form; Java simply lacks multiple inheritance.
Composition still uses the target interface.
Right: writing a little code to delegate is the price for flexibility.
questions.explain: The object adapter accepts a little extra delegation code in return for flexibility.
questions.rule: Flexibility is bought with some delegation code.
questions.teaches: The object adapter's argument is design preference as well as technique: it accepts a little more code and an extra object for flexibility.

questions.q: Using the language's multiple inheritance, a team can build either form to adapt LegacyScanner, which has three subclasses used in different offices. Which form lets one adapter serve all three?
options: The class adapter, which inherits from all three subclasses at once
The object adapter, which holds a LegacyScanner and accepts subclasses
Either form, since both forms reach every subclass equally well in practice
Neither form, since an adapter can serve only one specific class
optionExplain: A class adapter is committed to one specific adaptee class.
Right: composition lets the adapter work with the adaptee and any subclass of it.
The chat says the class adapter has trouble with subclasses.
The book says an object adapter can serve subclasses of the adaptee.
questions.explain: The subclass advantage belongs to composition.
questions.rule: Need subclass reach: compose.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chat, the class adapter and the object adapter are equally flexible.
questions.explain: The class adapter admits it is committed to one specific adaptee class, which the object adapter is not.
questions.rule: Check the concessions as well as the boasts.

questions.q: In a language with multiple inheritance, a team must adapt an adaptee that has no subclasses and needs one of its methods overridden. Using the chat's claims, which form fits that situation?
options: The object adapter, since it can override the adaptee's methods directly
The object adapter, since it is a single combined object at runtime
The class adapter, since it overrides directly and subclasses are absent
Neither, since this situation rules out all forms of adapters
optionExplain: The chat credits overriding to the class adapter, not the object adapter.
Having a single object is the class adapter's claim.
Right: the class adapter's strengths match this case and its weakness does not arise.
Nothing about this case rules out adapters.
questions.explain: Weighing means matching each side's strengths and weaknesses to the facts at hand. Here the weakness, subclasses, does not apply.
questions.rule: Match claims to the facts of the case.
questions.teaches: A trade-off is settled by the facts of the situation: a form's weakness does not count against it where the condition that triggers it is absent.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: Legacy code hands you an Enumeration, but your new code is written to use an Iterator. In an adapter between them, which is the target?
options: Iterator
Enumeration
Vector
Collection
optionExplain: Right: the new code expects an Iterator, so that is the interface the adapter implements.
Enumeration is the adaptee, the thing being wrapped.
Vector is one legacy collection that produces Enumerations.
Collection is not the interface being adapted.
questions.explain: The new code decides the target. The card next names both interfaces.
questions.rule: To let new code use a legacy Enumeration, write an adapter that implements Iterator and wraps the Enumeration.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: Match each item to its role in the legacy example.
pairs: Older way to step through a collection, returned by elements()
Newer way to step through a collection that also adds removal
An early collection type that returns an Enumeration
Adapter that makes an Enumeration usable as an Iterator
questions.explain: Enumeration is the older interface, Iterator the newer, and the adapter bridges them.
questions.rule: Iterator is the target; Enumeration the adaptee.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: The book says hasNext() and next() are straightforward to map from target to adaptee. What does that mean for the adapter's code on those two?
options: It must rebuild each of those behaviors from scratch inside the adapter
It must refuse both calls and rely on remove() to do the work
It can pass each call straight through to the matching Enumeration call
It must copy the whole collection into a new list before each call
optionExplain: Rebuilding would be needed only for operations with no counterpart.
remove() is not usable on an Enumeration, so it cannot carry the load.
Right: they mean the same thing on both sides, so delegation is enough.
Copying is not part of the book's design.
questions.explain: Where both interfaces have an operation that means the same thing, the adapter only delegates.
questions.rule: Same meaning on both sides: pass through.
questions.teaches: Work concentrates on the methods without a counterpart: those with the same meaning on both sides need only be passed through.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: New reporting code uses Iterator. An old Hashtable-based class returns an Enumeration from elements(). Which wiring uses the pattern?
options: Wrap the Enumeration in an EnumerationIterator for the reporting code
Give the Enumeration itself to the reporting code and hope it works
Change the reporting code to call Enumeration's methods instead
Convert the Hashtable into a Vector before it is passed to the reporting code
optionExplain: Right: the adapter makes the Enumeration look like the Iterator the reporting code expects.
The reporting code was written to a different interface and cannot use it directly.
Changing the client undoes the purpose of the adapter.
Another legacy class would still produce an Enumeration.
questions.explain: The adapter sits between the legacy producer and the new consumer.
questions.rule: Wrap the legacy interface, not the client.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: True or false: If legacy client code expects an Enumeration and the data supports Iterator, the target is still Iterator and the adaptee is still Enumeration.
questions.explain: The client's expectation sets the target. With the direction reversed, Enumeration is the target and Iterator the adaptee. The book's exercise asks for exactly this adapter.
questions.rule: Whoever the client expects is the target.

questions.section: Adapting an Enumeration to an Iterator
questions.q: A playlist player is written against a Playlist interface with next() and skip(). A legacy jukebox class has only next(). What is true of an adapter between them?
options: Both calls pass through unchanged, so no design decision is needed at all
skip() passes straight through to the jukebox and next() must be rebuilt
No adapter is possible because the two interfaces differ in size
next() can be passed through, but skip() has no counterpart to call
optionExplain: skip() has nothing to pass through to on the jukebox.
next() exists on both sides and passes straight through.
Interfaces that differ are what adapters are for.
Right: matched operations pass through, and the unmatched one is where the design effort goes.
questions.explain: The same pattern appears in the Iterator case: the target asks for more than the adaptee has, so one operation has no counterpart.
questions.rule: Find the operations the adaptee cannot support.
questions.teaches: When a target interface asks for more than the adaptee offers, some operations have no counterpart, and the adapter must decide what they do.

questions.q: Your adapter's target has a remove() operation, but the wrapped class is read-only. What is the best the adapter can do?
options: Ignore the call silently and report success to the caller
Throw a runtime exception when remove() is called
Remove the item from a private copy of the collection
Delete remove() from the target interface for every client
optionExplain: Reporting success would mislead the client.
Right: it cannot truly remove, so it signals that clearly.
A private copy is not the collection the client meant.
Changing the target would change what the client expects.
questions.explain: With nothing to delegate to, the honest option is to signal that the operation is unsupported. The card next gives the book's view.
questions.rule: When the adaptee cannot do what the target allows to fail, throw the exception the target's contract permits and document it.

questions.q: Because Enumeration is a ____ interface, the adapter cannot truly implement remove().
questions.explain: Enumeration only lets you step through items; it has no way to remove them.
questions.rule: No removal on the adaptee, no true remove() on the adapter.

questions.q: The book calls throwing an exception here reasonable. What makes it acceptable?
options: An exception is the right response to any missing method at all
The Iterator designers let remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException
Clients do not call remove() on an Iterator in any practical case
The adapter can recover from the missing method by calling next() instead
optionExplain: Whether an exception fits depends on what the target's contract allows.
Right: the contract of the target interface permits this failure.
Clients may call remove(); that is why the possibility needs warning.
next() moves forward and does not remove anything.
questions.explain: The target contract anticipated that some implementations cannot remove.
questions.rule: Fail the way the contract allows.
questions.teaches: Whether an imperfect adapter is acceptable depends on whether the target's contract allows the operation to fail.

questions.q: A notes app's Exporter interface has save() and delete(). Its contract says delete() may throw UnsupportedOperationException. A legacy archive class is write-once and cannot delete. What should the adapter's delete() do?
options: Return quietly so that callers believe the note has been deleted
Overwrite the note with blank text and then report success to callers
Call save() with an empty note and treat the deletion as done
Throw UnsupportedOperationException and be documented as doing so
optionExplain: Returning quietly would leave the note and mislead the caller.
Blanking the note is a different operation than deleting it.
Saving an empty note changes data instead of deleting it.
Right: the contract allows the failure, and documenting it lets clients guard against it.
questions.explain: The adapter is imperfect, so it states the limit openly instead of faking the behavior.
questions.rule: Signal the gap; do not fake the behavior.

questions.q: True or false: If the Exporter contract promised that delete() succeeds, throwing UnsupportedOperationException from a legacy archive would still be consistent with that contract.
questions.explain: The exception approach relies on a contract that allows failure. Take that permission away and the approach stops working.
questions.rule: The exception trick depends on the contract.

questions.q: A team writes an adapter that exposes a read-only weather map service as a Cache interface that includes put(). Which practice from the Enumeration case carries over?
options: Document that put() can fail so clients can guard against it
Hide the failure so that clients never see an exception at all
Remove put() from the cache interface for every client that uses it
Trust that no client will ever call put() on the cache
optionExplain: Right: the book pairs the exception with good documentation and careful clients.
Hiding a failure removes the warning that careful clients rely on.
Changing the interface for everyone is beyond the adapter's job.
Hoping clients avoid the call is not a design.
questions.explain: An adapter's gaps become part of its documented behavior, so they are known and not discovered in production.
questions.rule: Known gaps belong in the documentation.
questions.teaches: The limits of an imperfect adapter are part of its behavior, so they must be documented where clients can find them.

questions.q: Someone says: 'An adapter is only a decorator, since both wrap an object.' Which reply does the book support?
options: That is right, because both are wrappers, and wrappers are all one pattern
That is wrong, because neither of them actually wraps another object at all
Both wrap, but an adapter converts the interface and a decorator adds behavior
That is right, because both patterns change the interface of what they wrap
optionExplain: Wrapping is shared, but that is not the whole story; intent differs.
Both wrap an object, so denying wrapping gets the facts wrong.
Right: shared wrapping is true but does not settle what each is for.
A decorator does not change the interface it wraps.
questions.explain: Part of the claim is true, and part is not. The card next sets out each side.
questions.rule: A claim that one pattern is just another is judged by asking in what sense it holds: both wrap, but an adapter converts an interface while a decorator adds behavior.

questions.q: In the chat, the Adapter says it ____ the interface of what it wraps, while a decorator does not.
questions.explain: Converting the interface is the adapter's defining act in the chat.
questions.rule: Adapters convert; decorators keep.

questions.q: In the chat, the Decorator and Adapter finally agree on how their patterns differ. On what basis?
options: On line count, since adapters need a great deal more code to write
On language, since only one of the two patterns works in Java at all
On age, since decorators were invented before adapters existed
On intent, since they look alike on paper but serve different purposes
optionExplain: Both complain about the amount of code they need, but that is not what separates them.
Both patterns work in Java; the book uses both there.
Age is not mentioned as a difference.
Right: the chat concludes that their structures look alike but their intents are miles apart.
questions.explain: Intent is what tells similar-looking patterns apart.
questions.rule: Tell patterns apart by intent, not by structure.
questions.teaches: Two patterns can share a structure, such as wrapping an object, and still differ in intent, which is what defines the pattern.

questions.q: A logging class wraps an Email sender, offers exactly the same methods and also records each message sent. Is it more like an adapter or a decorator?
options: An adapter, since it wraps another class that sends the mail
A decorator, since it keeps the interface and adds behavior
An adapter, since it adds a feature to the class it wraps
Neither, since it wraps a class that only sends mail messages
optionExplain: Wrapping alone does not make an adapter; the interface must change.
Right: unchanged interface plus new behavior is the decorator's mark.
Adding a feature is the decorator's job.
Wrapping a mail sender is no obstacle to being a decorator.
questions.explain: Check what the wrapper does to the interface and to the behavior.
questions.rule: Same interface, extra behavior: decorator.

questions.q: True or false: A wrapper whose methods have different names from the object it wraps, and which adds no behavior, is an adapter in the book's terms.
questions.explain: Changing the interface without adding behavior is the adapter's purpose. A decorator would keep the interface and add behavior.
questions.rule: Changes the interface: adapter.

questions.q: A project lead says: 'Our Cache class and our Index class both hold a Store inside and forward calls to it, so they are the same pattern.' What should you check before agreeing?
options: Whether both classes are in the same source file
Whether both classes forward at least one call
What each does with the interface, and why
Whether both were written by the same person
optionExplain: File location says nothing about pattern.
Forwarding is the shared structure that makes them look alike.
Right: structure is shared, so the open question is intent.
The author is irrelevant to the design.
questions.explain: The adapter-and-decorator chat shows that shared structure can mislead; intent settles the question.
questions.rule: Similar shape is not the same pattern.
questions.teaches: A shared structure is weak evidence that two classes are the same pattern; compare what each does with the interface and why it exists.

questions.q: Which wrapping pattern exists to make a complicated interface easier to use?
options: Facade
Adapter
Decorator
Observer
optionExplain: Right: a facade presents a simpler interface.
An adapter converts an interface rather than simplifying it.
A decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior.
Observer is about notifications, not wrapping.
questions.explain: Simplifying is the facade's job. The card next compares all three.
questions.rule: An adapter converts an interface, a decorator adds responsibility while keeping the interface, and a facade simplifies.

questions.q: Match each pattern to its intent.
pairs: Does not alter the interface but adds responsibility
questions.explain: Three wrapping patterns, three purposes: convert, add, simplify.
questions.rule: Convert, add, simplify.

questions.q: Which of the three patterns leaves the interface it wraps unchanged, and what follows from that?
options: The adapter, so the client never notices the class that it wraps
The facade, so the subsystem can be used exactly as it was before
The decorator, so a decorated object can replace the original
All three, since none of them actually wrap another object
optionExplain: The adapter changes the interface; the client only does not notice the conversion.
The facade presents a different, simpler interface.
Right: unchanged interface means the wrapped object and its decorated version are interchangeable.
All three wrap objects, and two of them change the interface.
questions.explain: Only the decorator keeps the interface, which is why it can sit anywhere the plain object could.
questions.rule: Decorator keeps the interface; adapter and facade present a different one.
questions.teaches: A decorator can stand in wherever the original was used because its interface is unchanged; an adapter or a facade presents a different interface.

questions.q: A smart-home class has one method, startDay(), that opens the blinds, heats the coffee maker and switches on the radio by calling each device. Which role does it play?
options: A facade, since it turns several devices into one call
An adapter, since it changes one interface into another
A decorator, since it adds new behavior to the radio device
An adapter, since it wraps more than one device class
optionExplain: Right: one simple call over several components is the facade's job.
No client interface is being matched; the aim is to simplify.
It does not add behavior to one object while keeping its interface.
Wrapping several classes does not make an adapter; its intent would be conversion.
questions.explain: The wrapper offers a simpler, higher-level interface over a group of parts.
questions.rule: One simple call over many parts: facade.

questions.q: A teammate calls a class a facade because it hides a Fahrenheit thermometer. In fact the class presents the thermometer through the Celsius interface the app already uses, with no simplification. What is the mistake?
options: Facades may not hide classes from their callers at all
It is a decorator, since it wraps exactly one other object
It is neither of them, since it wraps a thermometer class
It converts the interface, so it is an adapter
optionExplain: Hiding classes is not the question; the intent is.
A decorator keeps the interface, and this one changes it.
Nothing about thermometers rules out an adapter.
Right: the interface is being converted to match the client, not simplified.
questions.explain: Hiding something is not the same as simplifying it. Look at what the wrapper does to the interface.
questions.rule: Ask what the wrapper does with the interface.

questions.q: Which of these wrappers alter the interface of what they wrap? Select all that apply.
options: A class that makes a vendor's calls look like the ones the app already uses
A class that offers one start() call in place of twelve separate setup calls
A class that times each call while keeping exactly the same methods
A class that adds a surcharge to a price while keeping getPrice()
optionExplain: Right: this is an adapter, which changes the interface into the one expected.
Right: this is a facade, which presents a simpler interface.
This keeps the interface and adds behavior, which is a decorator.
This also keeps the interface and adds behavior, which is a decorator.
questions.explain: Adapters and facades present a different interface. Decorators keep it.
questions.rule: Adapter and facade change the interface; decorator does not.
questions.teaches: Altering the interface separates the decorator from the other two, but not the adapter from the facade; only their purposes, convert versus simplify, separate those.

questions.q: Every component of a home theater works well, yet starting a movie is a long list of steps. What is the underlying difficulty?
options: Each component is badly designed and needs to be replaced by a better one
Using the system needs knowledge of many components and their call order
The components should be merged into one large class with a single owner
The owner has not read the manuals for each component closely enough
optionExplain: Nothing says the parts are poor; they work.
Right: the burden comes from coordinating many parts.
Merging them would not simplify using each one.
The difficulty is built into the number of coordinated steps.
questions.explain: The cost is in coordinating the parts. The card next gives the book's count.
questions.rule: When using a group of components takes many ordered calls that repeat and change with upgrades, the use itself has become the complexity.

questions.q: In the book's example, watching a movie the hard way takes ____ separate tasks.
questions.explain: The book lists thirteen numbered tasks, from turning on the popcorn popper to starting the DVD player.
questions.rule: Thirteen steps to start one movie.

questions.q: Besides starting a movie, which further burdens does the book name? Select all that apply.
options: Turning everything off means repeating the work in reverse
Listening to a CD or the radio would be as complex
An upgrade means learning a slightly different procedure
The projector cannot work with the amplifier
The popcorn popper must be rewired for each movie
optionExplain: Right: the book says you would have to do it all over again in reverse.
Right: the book says it would be as complex to listen to a CD or the radio.
Right: the book says an upgrade means a slightly different procedure.
The book does not claim the components are incompatible.
The book does not mention rewiring the popper.
questions.explain: The pain repeats at every shutdown, every new activity and every upgrade.
questions.rule: Complexity repeats with each use and each change.
questions.teaches: The cost of a many-step procedure is multiplied by every new use and every upgrade, not paid once.

questions.q: A photo studio's interns learn an eleven-step start-up for lights, backdrop and camera. The studio switches light brands, and every intern must relearn the start-up. Which of the book's burdens is this?
options: Turning everything off means repeating the work in reverse
An upgrade means a slightly different procedure
Using another source needs the same amount of effort
Every component must be wired by hand
optionExplain: Shutdown in reverse is a different burden, and nothing here is about shutdown.
Right: swapping components changed the procedure, and everyone has to relearn it.
A different source is not what happened; the equipment was swapped.
Wiring was not what the interns had to relearn.
questions.explain: The changed brand altered the steps that every user follows.
questions.rule: Upgrades ripple to everyone who follows the steps.

questions.q: An owner watches only movies, does not upgrade and does not listen to CDs. Which of the book's burdens still applies?
options: The procedure changes after each upgrade of a component
Playing a CD is as complex as playing a movie from the DVD
None of them, since only upgrades make the system hard to use
Starting and stopping each movie still takes many steps
optionExplain: That burden needs an upgrade, which this owner never makes.
This owner never listens to CDs.
The long start-up and shutdown remain.
Right: even a fixed setup has the long start-up and shutdown.
questions.explain: Removing two of the burdens leaves the first: the procedure itself.
questions.rule: Even a fixed setup has a long procedure.

questions.q: A ward's nurses start a patient monitor by switching on five devices in a set order, and the order changes whenever a device is replaced. What does the home theater suggest as a way forward?
options: Offer one simpler interface that runs the start-up sequence
Train every nurse more thoroughly on all five of the devices
Buy five devices that are certain never to need replacing
Remove two of the devices to shorten the start-up list
optionExplain: Right: moving the sequence to one place spares every user and every change.
Training leaves the burden on every nurse and returns at each change.
No set of devices is guaranteed to stay unchanged.
Removing devices changes the clinical equipment, not the complexity of using it.
questions.explain: Putting the sequence in one place means users and changes meet it once. That is the direction the book takes next.
questions.rule: Put the procedure in one place.
questions.teaches: The remedy is to move the sequence out of every user and into one place, so that users and changes meet it once.

questions.q: A group of related classes is awkward to use. Someone adds a class with one reasonable interface that coordinates them. What is that class called?
options: An adaptee
A client
A facade
A target
optionExplain: An adaptee is the class an adapter wraps.
A client is the code that makes the calls.
Right: it fronts a complex subsystem with a simpler interface.
A target is the interface a client expects from an adapter.
questions.explain: The class that simplifies a subsystem is the facade. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: A facade gives a complex subsystem one simpler interface while leaving the subsystem itself available.

questions.q: A facade gives a complex subsystem one more ____ interface.
questions.explain: The book describes the facade's job as providing one, more reasonable interface.
questions.rule: A facade simplifies the way in.

questions.q: True or false: A facade hides the subsystem classes, so clients cannot use them directly.
questions.explain: The book says the subsystem classes remain available for clients that need their more specific interfaces. The facade is a shortcut, not a wall.
questions.rule: The facade is a shortcut, not a wall.
questions.teaches: A facade adds a simple way in without closing the lower-level way in, so expert clients keep full access.

questions.q: A video app's export uses Encoder, AudioMixer, Subtitler and Uploader. The product team wants a one-button Publish. Which design fits the book?
options: Merge the four classes into one class and delete the originals
Move publish() into Uploader and make the other three classes private
Ask users to call the four classes in the right order themselves
A class with publish() that coordinates the four, which stay usable
optionExplain: Deleting the parts would remove the power that experts rely on.
Making the others private would hide them from clients who need them.
That leaves the burden of the order with every user.
Right: one simple call for common needs, with the parts still available.
questions.explain: A facade coordinates the subsystem for the common case and leaves the rest untouched.
questions.rule: Simplify the common case; keep the parts.

questions.q: A power user needs an audio setting that publish() does not expose. What can they do?
options: Nothing, because publish() is the only way in to the subsystem
Use AudioMixer directly, since the subsystem is available
Ask for publish() to be replaced by the mixer for everyone
Wait until publish() has gained every setting the mixer offers
optionExplain: That would be true only if the facade encapsulated the subsystem away.
Right: the facade does not close the lower-level access.
Replacing the facade would take away the simple way in for everyone else.
A facade that grows every setting loses its simplicity.
questions.explain: Direct access remains for specific needs, as the book notes.
questions.rule: Rare needs go straight to the subsystem.

questions.q: A game engine has a facade with play(level). The team debates adding forty more methods so that every engine feature can be reached through the facade. What is the weakness of that plan?
options: It would stop the engine from working as soon as the extra methods are added
It would force clients to learn the facade and nothing else about it
It would stop being simple, and the engine is available directly anyway
It would make the engine's features unavailable to all other clients
optionExplain: Adding methods to the facade does not break the engine.
Learning a larger facade is the cost, but the larger issue is lost simplicity.
Right: the point of a facade is the simpler interface, and rare needs can use the engine itself.
The engine's features stay available; they would just be duplicated.
questions.explain: A facade is aimed at the common use. It need not mirror everything.
questions.rule: Keep the facade small; let rare needs go to the subsystem.
questions.teaches: A facade stays useful by staying small and aimed at the common use, since the rare needs can go directly to the subsystem.

questions.q: True or false: A facade can only pass each request on to the subsystem, and a subsystem can have only one facade.
questions.explain: The book says a facade may add its own smarts and that a subsystem may have any number of facades. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A facade may hold its own knowledge, such as ordering, and a subsystem may have several facades.

questions.q: According to the book, the home theater facade knows that the popcorn popper has to be turned on before it can ____.
questions.explain: The book names this detail: the popper must be on before it can pop.
questions.rule: A facade knows the order of use.

questions.q: Why might one subsystem reasonably have two facades?
options: Different clients may need different simplified views
Every subsystem must have exactly one facade for each class
Two facades make the whole subsystem run faster overall
A second facade is needed to repair the first facade's bugs
optionExplain: Right: simplification is relative to what a client needs.
Nothing ties facade counts to class counts.
Speed is not part of the book's account.
A facade does not need a second one to work.
questions.explain: Because each facade is a view aimed at certain uses, the same subsystem can be given more than one.
questions.rule: One subsystem, as many views as clients need.
questions.teaches: Each facade is a view of the subsystem aimed at certain clients, so one subsystem can carry several views.

questions.q: A print subsystem has Spooler, Renderer and Tray. A facade's print(doc) first checks that the tray has paper, then renders, then spools. Which statement is true?
options: The facade is only forwarding the same call on to each class in turn
The facade is converting one interface to another for the client
The facade is using its own ordering knowledge, beyond forwarding
The facade is adding a new responsibility to the Spooler class
optionExplain: It does more than forward: it sequences and checks.
The intent is simplifying, not matching a client's expected interface.
Right: the order and the paper check are knowledge the facade holds.
Nothing is added to Spooler; the facade sits in front of the group.
questions.explain: A facade may decide the order of calls and carry the conditions for them.
questions.rule: Sequencing knowledge belongs in the facade.

questions.q: True or false: Once the print subsystem has one facade, the pattern does not allow a second facade for a different use of the same subsystem.
questions.explain: The book says the pattern allows any number of facades for a given subsystem. A second use can get its own facade without disturbing the first.
questions.rule: A new use can get its own facade.

questions.q: A reviewer says: 'A facade should be a plain list of forwarded calls; putting ordering logic in it breaks the pattern.' How does the book's account compare?
options: The book allows a facade to add its own smarts, like ordering
The book agrees, because facades are not allowed to hold logic of their own
The book agrees, but only when the logic is about ordering calls
The book is silent on what a facade may contain besides calls
optionExplain: Right: the book's facade knows the popper has to be on before it pops.
The book says the facade is free to add its own smarts.
The popper example is exactly an ordering detail, and the book accepts it.
The book addresses the question directly.
questions.explain: Keeping sequencing in the facade puts that knowledge in one place instead of in every client.
questions.rule: Put the sequencing in the facade.
questions.teaches: Placing ordering knowledge in the facade keeps it in one place, instead of repeating it in every client.

questions.q: How does a facade get access to the components of its subsystem?
options: It inherits from every component class
It copies each component's code into itself
Its clients pass in the components on every call
It holds them as parts of itself (composition)
optionExplain: Inheriting from all of them would be unwieldy and is not the book's approach.
Copying code would lose the components' own behavior.
That would put the burden back on the clients.
Right: the facade is composed with the components.
questions.explain: The facade holds its components and uses them. The card next gives the book's construction.
questions.rule: Compose the facade with the subsystem's components, delegate through a few high-level methods, and code clients to the facade.

questions.q: The facade uses ____ so that it has access to all the components of the subsystem.
questions.explain: The facade holds the components in its own fields.
questions.rule: A facade is composed with its subsystem.

questions.q: Besides watchMovie(), which method does the book implement on its facade, and why is it useful?
options: pauseMovie(), so the projector can be adjusted mid-film
endMovie(), so one call covers the shutdown steps
rewireTheater(), so components can be replaced later
buyPopcorn(), so supplies are ordered ahead of time
optionExplain: The book does not give a pauseMovie method.
Right: the reverse procedure is also placed behind one call.
The facade does not rewire anything; it uses the existing components.
Supplies are not part of the facade.
questions.explain: A facade can hide both the start-up and the shutdown procedure.
questions.rule: Hide both directions of the procedure.
questions.teaches: A facade simplifies both directions of a procedure, so the shutdown sequence is as hidden as the start-up.

questions.q: A greenhouse subsystem has Vent, Heater and Sprinkler. Which sketch of a GreenhouseFacade matches the book's construction?
options: It extends Vent, Heater and Sprinkler and overrides every method of each
It holds a Vent, Heater and Sprinkler, and nightMode() calls each in turn
It is empty, and clients pass the three parts to nightMode() each time
It places nightMode() inside Vent and has the other two parts call it
optionExplain: Inheriting from all three is not how a facade is built.
Right: composition plus delegation gives a facade.
That puts the knowledge in the clients again.
That moves the knowledge into one component and tangles the others.
questions.explain: The facade owns the components and delegates through a simpler method.
questions.rule: Own the parts, delegate through a simple method.

questions.q: The owner replaces the projector with a model that has different calls. The family's client code calls only watchMovie(). What needs to change?
options: Every client that calls watchMovie() on the facade
Nothing, since a facade adapts itself to new components
Both the facade and every client that calls it
The facade's code for the projector, and not the client
optionExplain: The client is coded to the facade and stays as it was.
A facade is ordinary code and must be edited for the new calls.
The clients are protected by the facade.
Right: the facade absorbs the change.
questions.explain: The book notes the client code does not need to change, just the facade.
questions.rule: Change lands in the facade.

questions.q: True or false: A script that calls the lights and projector directly is protected from a projector upgrade by the mere existence of a facade.
questions.explain: The protection comes from going through the facade. A script that calls the components directly still depends on them.
questions.rule: Protection comes from using the facade, not from its existing.
questions.teaches: A facade protects only the clients that use it: direct callers of the components stay coupled to them.

questions.q: A colleague says: 'If a wrapper hides one class it is an adapter, and if it hides several it is a facade.' What does the book say?
options: Either can wrap one class or several; intent differs
The colleague is right, since the count of classes decides
The colleague is right for facades but not for adapters
Neither pattern is allowed to wrap more than one class
optionExplain: Right: intent, not count, separates them.
The count is not what the book uses.
The book says a facade may simplify a single complex class and an adapter may adapt many.
Both patterns can involve several classes.
questions.explain: The book rejects the count rule and points to intent. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Tell an adapter from a facade by intent, converting versus simplifying, and not by how many classes are wrapped.

questions.q: The book says that the difference between an adapter and a facade is not how many classes they wrap but their ____.
questions.explain: The adapter's intent is to match an expected interface; the facade's is to simplify.
questions.rule: Intent separates them.

questions.q: Which scenario contradicts the rule of thumb that a facade must wrap several classes?
options: A wrapper that simplifies ten separate classes in one subsystem
A wrapper that converts one class to a different interface for a client
A wrapper that simplifies one class with a complex interface
A wrapper that adds logging to a class and keeps its methods
optionExplain: Ten classes fit the rule rather than contradict it.
A converting wrapper is an adapter, not a facade.
Right: a facade for a single complex class contradicts the rule.
A logging wrapper is a decorator.
questions.explain: One case where a facade wraps a single class is enough to break the rule.
questions.rule: One counterexample refutes a rule.
questions.teaches: One clear counterexample is enough to refute a rule of thumb, which is why the count rule fails as a definition.

questions.q: A wrapper takes a vendor's three classes and presents them through the single interface the app is already written against. Nothing is meant to be simpler. What is it?
options: A facade, since it wraps three classes from the vendor
A decorator, since it adds the app's interface to the vendor
A facade, since it hides the vendor from the rest of the app
An adapter, since it matches the interface the app expects
optionExplain: The count is not what defines a facade.
A decorator keeps the wrapped interface instead of matching a different one.
Hiding the vendor is a side effect of any wrapper.
Right: its aim is to match the expected interface, though it wraps several classes.
questions.explain: Intent decides, and the intent is matching.
questions.rule: Matching an expected interface: adapter.

questions.q: A student argues: 'This class wraps six classes, so it must be a facade.' Where is the reasoning weak?
options: Facades may wrap at most five classes before they become adapters
The class count says nothing about intent; it may be an adapter
Six classes can only be wrapped by a decorator, not by facades
Adapters never wrap more than one class, whatever the interface
optionExplain: The book sets no limit on how many classes a facade wraps.
Right: the class count does not tell you what the wrapper is for.
A decorator is defined by adding behavior, not by a count.
The book says adapters may hold two or more adaptees.
questions.explain: The student's premise is true, but it does not lead to the conclusion.
questions.rule: A true premise can fail to support the conclusion.

questions.q: Sort each wrapper by its intent. Both groups include wrappers of one class and of several.
groups: Adapter intent: match the interface the client expects
Facade intent: provide a simpler interface

items.t: Makes ten sensor classes appear as the single Sensor interface the dashboard was built for
Gives the dashboard one refreshAll() call over ten sensor classes
Lets a legacy class with eighty methods be driven through five simple methods
Lets one modern class be used where a different interface is demanded

questions.explain: The same ten classes could be wrapped by either, depending on what the client needs. The intent separates them.
questions.rule: Same classes, different wrapper: ask what the client needs.
questions.teaches: The same set of classes can be fitted with an adapter or with a facade, depending on whether the client needs a matching interface or a simpler one.

questions.q: In a design, one class talks to many others and, through them, to still more. What is the main risk of that design?
options: The classes will run out of memory at runtime
The code can no longer be compiled or linked
A change in one part can cascade into others
Each class will lose some of its own methods
optionExplain: Memory use is not the issue the principle names.
Such code compiles; the trouble is that it is fragile.
Right: many dependencies let changes spread.
Classes keep their methods; their dependencies are the issue.
questions.explain: Dependencies carry change from one place to another. The card next gives the principle.
questions.rule: Principle of Least Knowledge: talk only to your immediate friends.

questions.q: Principle of Least Knowledge: talk only to your immediate ____.
questions.explain: That is the usual statement in the book.
questions.rule: Talk only to immediate friends.

questions.q: The book calls a system with many dependencies between classes fragile. What else does it say about such a system?
options: It is costly to maintain and complex for others to read
It is faster to run but much harder to compile and link
It is easy to maintain but quite hard to test and debug
It is simple for others but costly to extend later on
optionExplain: Right: the book lists maintenance cost and complexity for others.
Speed and compile time are not part of the book's concern.
The book says dependencies make it costly to maintain, not easy.
The book says such a system is complex for others, not simple.
questions.explain: Dependencies hurt the people who must change and read the code, not only the code.
questions.rule: Coupling costs maintenance and understanding.
questions.teaches: Heavy coupling harms people as well as code: it raises maintenance cost and makes the system harder for newcomers to understand.

questions.q: A checkout class reaches through order.getCustomer().getAddress() to get a city. Which change leaves checkout knowing fewer classes?
options: Store the customer in a global variable for checkout to use
Add a second chain that goes through the customer's account
Ask the order for the shipping city with a method on order
Copy the address class into the checkout class itself
optionExplain: A global does not reduce what checkout knows; it hides the dependency.
A second chain adds more classes to know.
Right: checkout then knows only the order.
Copying the class would make checkout depend on it even more.
questions.explain: Fewer classes known means a smaller circle of friends.
questions.rule: Know one friend, not the whole chain.

questions.q: True or false: If Address renames getCity(), checkout code that reaches it through order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() may need an edit.
questions.explain: The chain makes checkout depend on a detail of Address, so a change there travels to checkout.
questions.rule: Long chains carry change far.

questions.q: Which everyday situation best matches talking only to immediate friends?
options: A diner tells the waiter the order and does not deal with the kitchen
A diner asks the waiter who the chef is and then phones the chef directly
A diner walks into the kitchen and starts to cook the meal personally
A diner asks the chef to pass the orders on to the waiter
optionExplain: Right: the diner knows one person, and the kitchen can change unseen.
Phoning the chef widens the circle of people the diner deals with.
Entering the kitchen drops all separation.
That reverses the route and still has the diner reach past the waiter.
questions.explain: Dealing through one friend means the people behind that friend can change without your noticing.
questions.rule: Let the friend deal with the people behind it.
questions.teaches: A friend in the middle lets everything behind it change unseen, so the number of people you deal with, not the size of the system, sets your exposure.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: Which object may a method call without leaving the circle of friends?
options: An object that another method returned
An object a parameter's method returned
An object found by following two getters
An object passed in as a parameter
optionExplain: A returned object is not a friend.
An object returned by a parameter's method is still a returned object.
Following getters leads to objects returned by other calls.
Right: parameters are among the four kinds of friends.
questions.explain: Friends are objects you already hold or made. The card next lists the four kinds.
questions.rule: Inside a method, call only the object itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its own components.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: A component of an object is any object referenced by an instance variable, which is a ____ relationship.
questions.explain: Holding an object in a field is a HAS-A relationship.
questions.rule: A component is something the object has.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: Why does the principle rule out calling methods on objects returned from other calls?
options: It would make the call slower, since returned objects are costly to reach
It adds a request to another object's subpart and widens the objects you know
It would let the called object delete its own methods during the call
It would change the type of the object that is returned to the caller
optionExplain: Speed is not the reason the book gives.
Right: each such call widens your circle of known objects.
Calling a method does not delete anything.
The type of the returned object does not change.
questions.explain: Counting is what matters: the principle keeps the circle of known objects small.
questions.rule: Every extra object you call is another object you know.
questions.teaches: The principle measures exposure by counting objects you directly know, so each call into a returned object adds to the count.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: In Studio.shoot(Lens lens), a method calls camera.capture() on a field, lens.focus() on its parameter, f.expose() on a Film it newly created, and camera.getSensor().calibrate(). Which call is outside the circle of friends?
options: camera.capture()
camera.getSensor().calibrate()
lens.focus()
f.expose()
optionExplain: camera is a field, so it is a component.
Right: the sensor was returned by a call, so it is not a friend.
lens is a parameter of the method.
f was created inside the method.
questions.explain: Field, parameter and created object are friends; an object returned by getSensor() is not.
questions.rule: Fields, parameters, creations: friends. Returned objects: strangers.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: True or false: A Studio that keeps its Sensor in a field set at construction and calls sensor.calibrate() on that field stays within the principle's bounds.
questions.explain: An object referenced by an instance variable is a component, and components are among the allowed friends.
questions.rule: How you reach an object decides whether it is a friend.

questions.section: How NOT to Win Friends and Influence Objects
questions.q: A library app does member.getAccount().getBalance(). Which fix keeps within the guidelines?
options: Make the account a public global so that any class can use it freely
Pass the account into every method of the app that needs it
Call getBalance() twice on the account to be sure of the value
Add getBalance() to member, which asks its own account for the result
optionExplain: A global makes the account reachable by everyone, not a friend of anyone.
Passing the account in turns it into a parameter friend, but spreads the account through many signatures.
Calling twice does not change whom you know.
Right: the member is the friend and handles the inner call.
questions.explain: The fix moves the inner call into an object that already holds the account as a component.
questions.rule: Ask the friend to make the inner call.
questions.teaches: The usual fix adds a method to the object you already know, so that it makes the inner call for you.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: A method calls station.getThermometer().getTemperature(). How many classes does the caller come to know?
options: Two, the station's and the thermometer's
One, the station's class and nothing else
None, since the call returns only a number
Three, including the type of number returned
optionExplain: Right: the caller must know what a station offers and what a thermometer offers.
The second call is made on a Thermometer, so the caller knows that class too.
The call still depends on both classes to get the number.
The number type is not one the caller reaches through.
questions.explain: The chain couples the caller to both classes. The card next shows the fix.
questions.rule: Replace a chain through a returned object with a request to the object you know, and let it make the inner call.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: True or false: In station.getThermometer().getTemperature(), the second call is made on an object that was returned from another call.
questions.explain: getThermometer() returns the thermometer, and getTemperature() is then called on that returned object, which is what the guidelines rule out.
questions.rule: Calls on returned objects reach beyond your friends.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: How does asking the station to supply the temperature itself help the caller?
options: The thermometer is deleted from the program once the station exists
The caller must now hold the thermometer object itself as a field
Only the station knows the thermometer; the caller knows the station
The station becomes a subclass of the class that calls it
optionExplain: The thermometer still exists; it is simply hidden.
Holding it would increase what the caller knows.
Right: the inner call moves into the station, which already holds the thermometer.
No subclassing is involved.
questions.explain: The inner call happens where the thermometer is a component, which is allowed.
questions.rule: Let the object that holds the part make the call.
questions.teaches: The inner call is legal inside the station because the thermometer is the station's own component, so the same call moves from outside to inside.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: In a library app, a notification calls loan.getBook().getShelf().getRoom(). Which rewrite fits the principle?
options: Call loan.getBook() and keep the result in a global
Call getShelf() on the library object instead of the loan
Add a second notification that makes the same chain
Call loan.getRoom(), which asks its book and shelf internally
optionExplain: A global still leaves the caller reaching through the book.
That swaps one reach for another without shortening it.
Doubling the chain doubles the exposure.
Right: the notification now knows only the loan.
questions.explain: The loan is the friend and takes over the chain.
questions.rule: Shorten the chain to one friend.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: A weather team replaces the thermometer class with a sensor class inside the station. Which code is likely to need edits? Select two.
options: Code that chains through getThermometer()
Code that only calls station.getTemperature()
The station's own code that uses the thermometer
Code that never touches a station
optionExplain: Right: it knows the thermometer class directly.
It knows only the station, which keeps its own interface.
Right: the station holds the thermometer, so its inner code changes.
