It does not depend on the station or the thermometer.
questions.explain: Exposure follows knowledge: callers that know the thermometer class and the station's own inner code feel the change.
questions.rule: Know less, break less.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: In a retail system, 40 screens call order.getCustomer().getEmail(). After a rewrite to order.getCustomerEmail(), how many places outside Order know about the Customer class's email method?
options: Forty, as before
None: only Order does
One, the first screen
Forty, since screens still ask for email
optionExplain: The 40 screens used to depend on Customer; they no longer do.
Right: the screens now know Order only.
No screen is special; none of them reaches into Customer any more.
The screens ask Order, not Customer.
questions.explain: One count tells the benefit: how many places depend on the inner class.
questions.rule: Count the places that know the inner class.
questions.teaches: A good way to measure the benefit of the rewrite is to count the places that know the inner class: here that drops from forty to one.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: A reviewer says: 'This call chain breaks a design principle, so it must be changed.' What fits the book's attitude to principles?
options: Any broken principle must be fixed before the next release
Principles apply only to very large systems with many teams
A principle is guidance to weigh against its costs, not a law
A principle matters only if a code-checking tool reports it
optionExplain: That treats the principle as a law, which the authors reject.
The book does not tie principles to system size.
Right: the authors say no principle is a law.
Tools are not the test; the helpfulness in the case is.
questions.explain: The authors ask for judgment. The card next gives their reasons.
questions.rule: Treat Least Knowledge as guidance to weigh: it cuts dependencies, but costs wrapper methods, complexity and some speed.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: The Law of Demeter and the Principle of Least ____ are, in the book's words, one and the same.
questions.explain: The book says the two terms are used interchangeably.
questions.rule: Two names, one principle.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: Why do the authors prefer the name Principle of Least Knowledge to Law of Demeter?
options: The name is more intuitive, and 'Law' suggests no exceptions
Demeter is the name of a different principle altogether
The word Principle is shorter to write in code and comments
The Law of Demeter was invented by the authors themselves
optionExplain: Right: those are the two reasons the book gives.
The book says the two are the same.
Length of the name is not a reason the book gives.
The book does not say the authors invented it.
questions.explain: A name can carry a wrong message: 'law' implies no exceptions, which misdescribes a guideline.
questions.rule: Names signal how strictly to apply a rule.
questions.teaches: Words carry implications: calling a guideline a law suggests it has no exceptions, which would misdescribe how it is meant to be used.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: A prototype is due Friday. An engineer proposes writing a forwarding wrapper for every chained call in it. Which point from the book applies?
options: Every chained call must be wrapped, since the principle is a law
Wrappers never cost anything, so write them all
Weigh the extra wrappers and time against the benefit
Chains are never a problem, so ignore the principle
optionExplain: The book says no principle is a law.
The book says wrappers add complexity and development time.
Right: the book says the principle has costs, so apply it where it helps.
The book still values the principle; it asks for judgment.
questions.explain: A deadline raises the price of development time, which belongs in the weighing.
questions.rule: Weigh cost against benefit before applying.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: True or false: The claim 'the principle has no downside, since fewer dependencies is better' is consistent with the book's account.
questions.explain: The book names costs: more wrapper classes, with added complexity and development time, and possibly slower runtime.
questions.rule: A benefit does not cancel a cost.

questions.section: Keeping your method calls in bounds...
questions.q: A colleague notes that code in your logs calls System.out.println, which the book names as a common violation of the principle. Which response follows the authors' attitude?
options: Decide by weighing trade-offs in your case, not by the violation label
Rewrite every logging call at once, since any violation is a bug in the code
Ignore the book's principle, since the example proves it wrong
Remove the logging, since it cannot be fixed in any other way
optionExplain: Right: a flagged violation is a prompt to weigh, not a verdict.
Treating a violation as a bug turns the principle into a law.
One example of a common violation does not refute the principle.
Removing logging throws away something useful.
questions.explain: The authors pose the question 'Should you care?' as one to answer by judgment.
questions.rule: A flagged violation starts the weighing; it does not end it.
questions.teaches: A flagged violation of a principle is a prompt to weigh costs and benefits in the case at hand, not a verdict.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: How does the Facade Pattern help a client follow the Principle of Least Knowledge?
options: The facade deletes the components from the system
The facade forces the client to call every component directly
The facade lets the client call objects returned by components
The client deals with one facade, not with each component
optionExplain: The components remain; the facade only stands in front of them.
That is the opposite: calls to every component would widen the circle.
Calls on returned objects are what the principle limits.
Right: the client's circle of friends shrinks to the facade.
questions.explain: A facade shrinks what the client knows. The card next puts the two together.
questions.rule: A facade lets a client talk to one friend instead of every component, which keeps the client within the Principle of Least Knowledge.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: A facade not only simplifies an interface, it ____ a client from a subsystem of components.
questions.explain: The book says a facade decouples the client from the subsystem.
questions.rule: A facade decouples clients from the subsystem.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: Under the four guidelines, why is the facade allowed to call each component of its subsystem?
options: Facades are exempt from the principle, as a special case of the pattern
Its components are held in its instance variables, so they are its own
Each component is passed in as a parameter of every client call
The components are objects that other calls return to the facade
optionExplain: Nothing in the book exempts a facade.
Right: components referenced by instance variables are among its friends.
The facade holds its components in fields rather than receiving them each time.
Objects returned from other calls are the ones that are off limits.
questions.explain: The facade follows the principle itself: it calls only its own components.
questions.rule: Holding the parts makes them friends.
questions.teaches: The facade obeys the principle too, because the components it calls are its own, held in instance variables.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: A mobile app screen calls six classes of a payments subsystem. Which change brings the screen closer to the Principle of Least Knowledge?
options: Add a seventh payments class that the screen also calls directly
Add a PaymentsFacade over the six, and have the screen call only it
Have the screen call the six classes through their getters instead
Copy the six payments classes into the screen's own package
optionExplain: A seventh class widens the circle.
Right: the screen's circle of friends becomes one.
Getters lead to returned objects, which are off limits.
Copying keeps the screen dependent on all six.
questions.explain: The facade collects the knowledge, so the screen needs only one friend.
questions.rule: Fewer known classes through one facade.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: True or false: After the payments company adds a seventh class behind PaymentsFacade, each screen that uses the facade must learn about the new class.
questions.explain: The screens know the facade only. The new class is the facade's business, so growth behind the facade stays behind it.
questions.rule: Growth behind the facade stays behind it.

questions.section: The Facade and the Principle of Least Knowledge
questions.q: A team adds a facade over a tangled subsystem and says its coupling problem is solved. What has actually changed?
options: The subsystem's classes no longer depend on one another inside it
The subsystem has been removed from the system by the facade
Clients now depend on more classes than they did before the facade
Clients depend on the facade, but the subsystem's own ties remain
optionExplain: The facade does not change how the subsystem's classes relate.
The subsystem is still there and used by the facade.
Clients depend on fewer classes, not more.
Right: the facade shields clients; it does not untangle the subsystem.
questions.explain: The facade moves the coupling that clients carry to one place. Whatever tangle exists inside the subsystem is untouched.
questions.rule: A facade shields clients; it does not clean the subsystem.
questions.teaches: A facade shields clients from the subsystem's coupling but does not reduce the coupling inside the subsystem itself.

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: True or false: In a clean Coffee and Tea design, the order of the recipe steps should be written separately in each subclass.
questions.explain: Written separately, the same order would appear twice and every change would have to be made twice. The card next shows how the authors approach it.
questions.rule: Repeated code is a design smell.

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: True or false: In the book's first redesign, boiling water and pouring into the cup are moved into a shared base class.
questions.explain: Those two steps are identical in both drinks, so the first redesign puts them in the base class. The book notes they are already abstracted there.
questions.rule: Move identical steps up first.

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: A cafe app has SandwichOrder and SaladOrder. Both check stock, take payment and print a receipt in identical ways, but they assemble the food differently. What does the first redesign step do here?
options: It leaves all three steps in both classes because the assembly step differs
It moves the assembly step up, since assembly is the main work of an order
It moves the stock check, payment and receipt into a common base class
It makes SaladOrder a subclass of SandwichOrder so it can reuse the checks
optionExplain: Different assembly does not stop the identical steps from being shared.
Assembly is the part that differs, so it cannot be written once.
Right: these steps are identical, so they go to the base class and the assembly stays with each class.
A salad is not a kind of sandwich; a shared base class avoids that false link.
questions.explain: Identical steps move to a common base class; steps that differ stay behind.
questions.rule: Share what is identical, leave what differs.

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: After the identical methods move up, both subclasses still contain a recipe method that calls the steps in the same order. What does this show?
options: Some duplication remains: the order of the steps is written twice
Nothing remains to fix, since every step method now sits in one class
The subclasses are working as intended, since each recipe must be its own
The base class has grown too many methods and should hand some back
optionExplain: Right: the sequence itself is a repeated piece of knowledge even though no single method is copied.
It feels done because no method body is copied, but the call order is copied in each class.
Each recipe is only identical in its order here; there is no reason to keep two copies.
The count of methods is not the issue; the repeated sequence is.
questions.explain: Duplication can hide in the order of calls, not only in method bodies.
questions.teaches: Duplication can hide in the sequence of calls around methods, not only in copied method bodies, so a design with no copied method can still repeat knowledge.
questions.rule: Look for duplication in the order of calls too.

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: True or false: If Coffee and Tea ran their shared helper methods in different orders, moving the order into the base class would still remove all the duplicated knowledge.
questions.explain: There would be no single shared order to move. The saving comes from the sequence being the same in both classes.
questions.rule: Moving the order up only helps when the order is shared.
questions.hint: What would the base class write down if the two orders differ?

questions.section: Whipping up some coffee and tea classes (in Java)
questions.q: Two board-game classes, ChessGame and CheckersGame, each run a turn as: announce the player, make the move, check for a winner, announce the end of turn. The move and the winner check work differently in each game. Which steps could be moved into a shared base class as they stand? Select all that apply.
options: Announce the player
Make the move
Check for a winner
Announce the end of turn
optionExplain: Right: it is identical in both games, so it can be written once.
It has the same purpose in both games, but the work differs, so it cannot be moved up unchanged.
The purpose matches but the rule differs in each game, so the code is not identical.
Right: it is identical in both games, so it can be written once.
questions.explain: Only the announcements are identical. The move and the winner check match in purpose but not in work.
questions.teaches: Steps that share a purpose but differ in their work cannot be moved up as they stand; they first need a common name, which the next idea covers.
questions.rule: Same purpose with different work needs a common name first.

questions.q: Coffee and Tea already share boiling water and pouring into a cup. What else do they share that the authors want you to see?
options: Nothing more, because the remaining methods have different names and bodies
The same ingredients, which can be put in the base class
The same constructor, which sets up water and cup
The overall sequence of steps in the recipe
optionExplain: Different names hide that the steps play the same roles.
The ingredients differ between coffee and tea.
The book does not discuss constructors as a shared piece.
Right: both follow the same four-step algorithm.
questions.explain: The card next lays out the four steps both recipes follow.
questions.rule: Look for a shared sequence.

questions.q: The book lists four steps for both drinks: boil water, extract with the hot water, pour into a cup, and add the appropriate ____.
questions.explain: The fourth step adds the condiments: sugar and milk for coffee, lemon for tea.
questions.rule: Same four steps, different details.

questions.q: NewEmployee and Contractor classes each run four steps: create an account, assign equipment (different kit for each), send a welcome email, and schedule orientation (different content for each). What does the shared-algorithm view say?
options: Only the account and email steps are shared, so nothing more can move up
Both follow one four-step sequence, so the sequence can move up
The classes are unrelated, since the equipment and orientation steps differ
Contractor should be rewritten as a subclass of NewEmployee instead
optionExplain: Steps that differ in work still sit in the same place in the sequence.
Right: the steps play the same roles in both, so the sequence is shared even where the work inside a step differs.
Different details do not make the algorithms different.
Neither class is a special case of the other; they share a sequence.
questions.explain: A sequence can be shared even when some steps differ inside.
questions.rule: Compare roles and order, not only code.

questions.q: Brewing coffee grounds and steeping a tea bag are different actions. Why does the book still treat them as the same step of the algorithm?
options: Both are written with the same code inside the base class
Both take the same number of minutes to finish in practice
Both are required by Java to share a name in sibling classes
Both play the same role: they extract the drink with hot water
optionExplain: If the code were identical it would already be in the base class; it is not.
The book does not compare timings.
Java imposes no such rule.
Right: the book calls them analogous because of their role in the recipe.
questions.explain: Steps are analogous when they play the same role, even if the work differs.
questions.teaches: Two steps are analogous when they fill the same role in the algorithm, even when their actions and code differ; spotting this is how you find that two classes share one algorithm.
questions.rule: Steps are analogous when they play the same role.

questions.q: True or false: If Tea added its condiment before brewing while Coffee added it after, the two recipes would still follow the same sequence of steps.
questions.explain: A sequence is a list of steps in a given order. Swapping two steps in one class gives a different sequence.
questions.rule: A different order is a different algorithm.
questions.hint: Does the shared algorithm list steps in an order?

questions.q: A bakery has BreadLoaf and Muffin classes. Sort each step by whether it is the same in both or only the same in role.

items.t: Preheat the oven
Mix the dough or the batter
Bake at the set temperature
Shape the loaf or fill the tin
Cool on a rack
Decorate with seeds or glaze

questions.explain: Preheating, baking and cooling are identical. Mixing, shaping and decorating share their place in the recipe but not their work.
questions.teaches: The analogous steps mark where subclasses will differ, so they are the places a shared algorithm has to leave open.
questions.rule: Analogous steps are where subclasses will differ.

questions.q: Coffee's recipe calls brewCoffeeGrinds and Tea's calls steepTeaBag. What would let one recipe method work for both?
options: Checking the drink type with an if inside the recipe
Calling both through one general method name
Copying the recipe into each class and renaming the calls
Renaming steepTeaBag to brewCoffeeGrinds in Tea
optionExplain: It works but spreads the knowledge of every drink into the recipe.
Right: a shared name lets one sequence call either version.
That keeps the duplication.
A tea bag is not brewed from grounds; the name would mislead.
questions.explain: The card next shows the names the authors chose.
questions.rule: One name for analogous steps.

questions.q: The book's neutral names for the steps that differ are brew() and ____().
questions.explain: Adding sugar and milk, or lemon, are both condiments, so the second neutral name is addCondiments.
questions.rule: Name the role, not the drink.

questions.q: SmsAlert and EmailAlert each run: build the message, deliver it (sendSmsText or sendEmailMessage), then log the result. Which name for the delivery step lets one shared sequence call it?
options: deliver, a name for the purpose of the step
sendSmsText, because SMS was written first
sendSmsOrEmail, so both channels are named
sendEmailMessage, because email is the richer channel
optionExplain: Right: it describes what the step is for and fits both channels.
That name belongs to one channel, so the other would be misdescribed.
It names the channels, so a third channel would need a new name again.
It is tied to one channel as well.
questions.explain: Naming the delivery step by its purpose, deliver, lets one shared sequence call it for both channels, whereas a name tied to SMS or email would misdescribe the other channel.
questions.rule: A good shared name describes purpose, not one variant.

questions.q: Only Coffee and Tea know how to brew, yet the shared recipe in CaffeineBeverage has to call brew. How can that work?
options: CaffeineBeverage contains a full brew that both subclasses must then copy
The recipe asks each subclass to run its own complete recipe instead
brew is declared in CaffeineBeverage with no body, and each subclass fills it in
The client passes the right brewing code into the recipe each time
optionExplain: Then both drinks would brew the same way, which they do not.
That would drop the shared sequence again.
Right: the superclass names the step so it can call it, and each subclass supplies the work.
Nothing in the chapter passes brewing code through the client.
questions.explain: A step with varying work is declared in the superclass and implemented by subclasses.
questions.teaches: A step whose work varies is declared in the superclass as an abstract method with no body, so the shared sequence can call it while each subclass supplies the work.
questions.rule: A varying step is declared in the superclass and implemented by subclasses.

questions.q: Which pair of steps is a poor candidate for sharing one general name?
options: brewCoffeeGrinds and steepTeaBag, which both extract the drink
boilWater and addCondiments, which have different roles
addSugarAndMilk and addLemon, which both add condiments
sendSmsText and sendEmailMessage, which both deliver an alert
optionExplain: These are the book's own analogous pair.
Right: a common name is only honest when the steps fill the same role, and these two do not.
This is the book's second analogous pair.
These deliver the same thing over different channels.
questions.explain: Share a name only between steps with the same role.
questions.rule: Same role, same name.

questions.q: Two payroll classes, HourlyStaff and SalariedStaff, run similar steps. Match each step to the treatment it needs.
pairs: Give both one neutral name, such as computeBasePay
Give both one neutral name, such as addExtras
transferToBank, written the same in both
Needs no new name; it can stay in the base class
questions.explain: Renaming is for steps that differ in work but share a role. A step that is already identical needs no new name.
questions.teaches: A step that is already identical in all classes needs no neutral name; it simply lives in the base class, and renaming is only for steps that differ.
questions.rule: Rename only the steps that differ.

questions.q: True or false: In a good Coffee and Tea design, each subclass should contain its own copy of the method that runs the recipe steps in order.
questions.explain: Copies of the order would repeat the same knowledge in each subclass. The card next shows where the book puts it.
questions.rule: The order is written once.

questions.q: In the book's redesign, which class contains the method prepareRecipe?
options: Coffee, with Tea calling it through Coffee
Tea, because tea is the simpler recipe
Both Coffee and Tea, each with its own copy
CaffeineBeverage
optionExplain: Tea and Coffee are siblings; neither is the home of the recipe.
Simplicity does not decide where it lives.
Copies would bring the duplication back.
Right: the template method lives in the superclass.
questions.explain: The recipe sits in the common superclass.
questions.rule: The template method is in the superclass.

questions.q: A base class for tests has a template method that runs setUp, runTest and tearDown. Which of these belong in that base class rather than in each test class? Select all that apply.
options: The order in which setUp, runTest and tearDown are called
The body of runTest for a login test
The call that cleans up after each test
The data a payment test loads in setUp
optionExplain: Right: the order is the shared algorithm.
This is the part that varies, so it belongs in the test class.
Right: the call to the cleanup step belongs to the template, though the cleanup work itself may vary.
This is specific to one kind of test.
questions.explain: The base class holds the order and the calls. Each test class holds the work specific to it.
questions.rule: The base class holds the order and the calls.

questions.q: A client holds a variable of type CaffeineBeverage that may refer to a Coffee or a Tea. What must the client do to get the right drink?
options: Check which subclass it is, then call that subclass's own recipe method
Call brew, pourInCup and the other steps itself, in the right order
Call prepareRecipe on it; the object's own brew and addCondiments run inside
Pass the drink type to prepareRecipe so that it can choose the steps
optionExplain: That would defeat the point of the shared recipe.
The client would then own the order that the template exists to hold.
Right: the inherited template method works for any subclass object.
The object already knows its own steps.
questions.explain: One call to the template serves every subclass.
questions.teaches: The client calls the inherited template method on any subclass object, and that object's own versions of the varying steps run inside it, so the client never needs to know the subclass.
questions.rule: One call to the template serves every subclass.

questions.q: A developer adds a new step, tidyUp(), to prepareRecipe in CaffeineBeverage and declares it as a step the subclasses must implement. What happens to Coffee and Tea?
options: Both must now provide tidyUp before they are complete
Nothing, because the superclass supplies the step for them
Only Tea is affected, because it has the longer recipe
Both lose their other steps, which move to the superclass
optionExplain: Right: every concrete subclass has to define all the steps left abstract.
That would be true only if tidyUp had a body in the superclass.
The recipe length does not matter.
The existing steps stay as they are.
questions.explain: Abstract steps must be implemented by every concrete subclass.
questions.rule: Abstract steps bind every subclass.

questions.q: True or false: A calendar app has Meeting, which runs create, invite and notify, and Reminder, which runs notify and then create. One template method in a shared superclass can serve both by letting each subclass fill in the steps.
questions.explain: A template fixes one order. Classes that need different orders cannot share one template by only filling in its steps.
questions.rule: A template fixes the sequence for all subclasses.
questions.teaches: A template method fixes one sequence for every subclass, so classes that need different sequences cannot share one template by filling in steps alone.

questions.q: When a Tea object's prepareRecipe runs, whose code starts the sequence of steps?
options: The prepareRecipe in CaffeineBeverage
Tea's own code, because the object is a Tea
A client class that calls each step in turn
Whichever class defines brew
optionExplain: Right: Tea inherits the template, which begins in the superclass.
Tea has no recipe of its own to start with.
The client makes one call, not one per step.
Defining a step does not give a class control of the sequence.
questions.explain: The card next traces the steps.
questions.rule: The template starts in the superclass.

questions.q: Put these events in the order they happen when a Tea makes its drink.
items: prepareRecipe is called on the Tea object
boilWater runs, in CaffeineBeverage
brew runs, in Tea
pourInCup runs, in CaffeineBeverage
addCondiments runs, in Tea
questions.explain: The template begins, the superclass boils, the subclass brews, the superclass pours, and the subclass adds condiments.
questions.rule: Superclass and subclass take turns, in the superclass's order.

questions.q: A ReportBase template calls loadData, formatBody and printFooter. HtmlReport overrides only formatBody. When an HtmlReport runs the template, whose code runs formatBody and printFooter?
options: ReportBase's code for both, since the template lives in ReportBase
HtmlReport's code for both, since the object is an HtmlReport
HtmlReport's code for formatBody, then ReportBase's for printFooter
ReportBase's code for formatBody, then HtmlReport's for printFooter
optionExplain: The template lives there, but the step it calls is overridden.
HtmlReport did not override printFooter.
Right: each call goes to the version defined for that step.
This reverses which class supplied which step.
questions.explain: Each step runs in whichever class supplies it.
questions.rule: Overridden steps run in the subclass; the rest in the superclass.

questions.q: When Tea's brew finishes, how does pourInCup get called next?
options: Tea's brew calls pourInCup when it reaches its end
The client calls pourInCup after prepareRecipe starts
The language runs the next method in the class by itself
The template method in CaffeineBeverage calls it
optionExplain: That would put the sequence into the subclass.
The client makes a single call to the template.
Methods do not chain automatically.
Right: the subclass step ends and the superclass carries on.
questions.explain: Subclass steps return; the superclass moves on.
questions.teaches: A subclass step does its own part and returns control; because the sequence is driven from the superclass, subclass step code does not decide what runs next.
questions.rule: The superclass drives the sequence; subclass steps return.

questions.q: Suppose we trace a Coffee object instead of a Tea object. Which steps run in CaffeineBeverage's own code?
options: Only boilWater, because Coffee has a longer brew
boilWater and pourInCup, the same two as for Tea
All four steps, since Coffee overrides nothing
brew and addCondiments, since Coffee uses them most
optionExplain: pourInCup is shared too.
Right: changing the subclass changes the supplied steps, not the shared ones.
Coffee supplies brew and addCondiments, so those run in Coffee.
Those two are the ones the subclass supplies.
questions.explain: Shared steps stay shared whatever the subclass.
questions.rule: Only the open steps change with the subclass.

questions.q: A game engine's base class runs each frame: read input, update the world, draw the frame, then wait to hold the frame rate. Each game supplies its own update and draw. Sort the work by which class's code runs it.

items.t: Reading input
Moving the enemies
Drawing the player sprite
Waiting to hold the frame rate
Deciding that drawing comes after updating
Choosing what an enemy looks like

questions.explain: The base class owns the order and the shared steps. The game owns the content of its own steps.
questions.teaches: Decisions about order and timing belong to the base class, and decisions about content belong to the subclass.
questions.rule: Order and timing belong to the base class; content to the subclass.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: Compared with each drink class holding its own recipe, what is the main gain of one recipe in a superclass?
options: Each drink can freely change the order of its own steps
Fewer classes are needed because Coffee and Tea merge
A change to the recipe is made once for every drink
The subclasses no longer need any methods of their own
optionExplain: The superclass fixes the order; that is what keeps it consistent.
Coffee and Tea stay as classes; they supply the varying steps.
Right: the algorithm lives in one place.
They still supply brew and addCondiments.
questions.explain: The card next lists the gains the book names.
questions.rule: One algorithm, one place.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: Match each design with how the book describes it.
pairs: The old Coffee and Tea design
Each subclass runs its own algorithm
The superclass runs the algorithm and protects it
Adding a drink to the old design
Takes a lot of work, with duplicated code
Adding a drink to the new design
Takes a couple of methods to plug in
questions.explain: The table contrasts subclasses in control with the superclass in control, and heavy work to add a drink with a few methods.
questions.rule: The superclass takes control.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: A firm has twelve invoice classes, one per country, each copying the same six-step process. A law change adds a seventh step that is the same in every country. After a Template Method redesign, in how many places does the new step go?
options: One: the template method in the base class
Twelve, one in each country class
Six, one beside each existing step
Two: the base class and one example country
optionExplain: Right: the algorithm lives in one place, so one edit reaches all twelve.
That is the cost in the old design, before the redesign.
The steps are not copies in the redesign; there is one sequence.
No sample class is needed when the step is the same everywhere.
questions.explain: After the redesign the six-step sequence lives once in the base class's template method, so the seventh step is added in that one place and all twelve countries pick it up.
questions.rule: Edit the template, not every subclass.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: True or false: Because the superclass holds the knowledge of the algorithm, someone who reads only the Tea class learns the full recipe.
questions.explain: Tea shows only the steps that vary. The whole recipe is in the superclass's template method.
questions.rule: Read the template for the algorithm; read the subclass for what varies.
questions.teaches: Gathering the algorithm in one class also helps readers: the template tells the whole story, and each subclass shows only what is special about it.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: A bug is found in the order of the steps: condiments should go in before pouring. How many classes need a change in the old design with five drinks, and in the new one?
options: One in the old design and one in the new design
Five in the old design, one in the new
Five in the old design and five in the new design
One in the old design, five in the new
optionExplain: The old design repeated the order in every class.
Right: each old class held its own order; the new design holds it once.
The new design holds the order once.
This reverses the two designs.
questions.explain: Duplicated order means duplicated fixes.
questions.rule: Fix once where the algorithm lives.

questions.section: What did the Template Method get us?
questions.q: A travel agency has three trip types whose booking processes have almost nothing in common. A developer proposes one template method for all three. What does the book's table of gains suggest about this plan?
options: Large gain, because any shared superclass reduces duplication
Large gain, because the superclass will protect each trip's own process
No effect, because the table's gains are independent of the algorithm
Little gain, because the gains come from a really shared algorithm
optionExplain: With nothing shared, there is no duplication to remove.
The superclass would only force one sequence on trips that need different ones.
Each gain in the table relies on the algorithm being common.
Right: the reuse and local change come from the sequence being shared.
questions.explain: Gains follow shared structure.
questions.rule: No shared algorithm, no template.
questions.teaches: A template pays off only when the variants share an algorithm; with little in common, forcing a single sequence adds constraint without adding reuse.

questions.q: Under the Template Method Pattern, what may a subclass do with an algorithm owned by its superclass?
options: Rewrite the whole algorithm in any shape it likes
Choose at runtime which algorithm object to use
Decide which concrete class the superclass creates
Redefine certain steps while the structure stays
optionExplain: That would leave nothing fixed in the superclass.
This describes a different pattern, which swaps whole algorithms.
This describes another pattern, which defers object creation.
Right: this is the heart of the definition.
questions.explain: The card next gives the official wording.
questions.rule: Subclasses change steps, not structure.

questions.q: True or false: The Template Method Pattern lets subclasses redefine certain steps of an algorithm without changing its structure.
questions.explain: That is the second half of the book's definition: the skeleton stays and some steps are redefined.
questions.rule: Same skeleton, different steps.

questions.q: A data-import base class has a method that runs: open the source, read records, check each record, save, close. CsvImport and JsonImport differ only in how they read records. Is the method that lists the five steps a template method?
options: Yes, it fixes the steps and defers reading to the subclasses
No, because a template method must itself be abstract
No, because it sits in the same class as the steps it calls
Yes, but only if each subclass also overrides it
optionExplain: Right: it fixes the steps and leaves one of them to subclasses.
The template is the concrete method; the deferred steps are the abstract ones.
Being in the same class as the steps is how the pattern is built.
Overriding it would replace the structure.
questions.explain: A method that fixes the steps and defers some is a template method.
questions.rule: Fixed steps plus deferred steps.

questions.q: In the book's discussion of the class structure, the abstract steps that the template method calls are called primitive ____.
questions.explain: The template method is built from primitive operations, which are the steps subclasses supply.
questions.rule: Primitive operations are the steps.
questions.teaches: The book calls the steps that the template method calls, and that subclasses implement, primitive operations.
questions.hint: The word is also used for basic actions of a machine.

questions.q: What happens to the pattern's guarantee if a subclass is able to override the template method itself?
options: The guarantee would be stronger, since the subclass knows its own needs
The guarantee that the structure stays unchanged would no longer hold
Nothing, because structure is only a naming convention
The steps would become hooks instead of abstract methods
optionExplain: The subclass would own the order, so the guarantee is weaker.
Right: the subclass could replace the sequence.
The structure is the fixed sequence, not just names.
Overriding the template does not change what kind the steps are.
questions.explain: A template that can be replaced guarantees nothing.
questions.rule: Protect the structure.

questions.q: A meal-kit company has a base class that packs every order. Sort each change by whether a subclass may make it under the Template Method Pattern.

items.t: Pack a vegan box differently
Reorder the steps for one site
Change how the quality check is carried out
Add an extra step between two existing ones
Use a different label printer at one site
Replace the whole sequence with its own

questions.explain: Subclasses may change how a step is done. Reordering, adding a step in the sequence, or replacing the sequence changes the structure.
questions.teaches: The structure is made of which steps exist and the order in which they run; subclasses change how a step is done, not whether it exists or when it runs.
questions.rule: Subclasses change how a step is done, not which steps run or when.

questions.q: In a class built around a template method, which kind of method does every concrete subclass have to implement?
options: The concrete methods
Every method, including those already written
The abstract methods
The hooks, since they are part of the algorithm
optionExplain: Concrete methods are already written.
Methods that already have bodies need no rewrite.
Right: abstract methods have no body in the abstract class.
Hooks are optional steps with a default, so subclasses need not implement them.
questions.explain: A subclass must implement the abstract methods, which have no body in the abstract class. Concrete methods are already written and hooks are optional. The card next sets out the three kinds.
questions.rule: Abstract means the subclass must supply it.

questions.q: Match each kind of method with how the book describes it.
pairs: Written in the abstract class and shared by all subclasses
Left for each subclass to implement
Empty or default in the abstract class; a subclass may override it
questions.explain: The three kinds differ in who writes the body and whether it is required.
questions.rule: Shared, required, optional.

questions.q: A converter base class has these methods. Sort each by whether every subclass must implement it.

items.t: an abstract method readSource
a concrete method openInputFile
a hook afterConvert with an empty body
an abstract method convertBody
a concrete method closeFiles
a hook writeTitle with default text

questions.explain: Only abstract methods are required. Concrete methods are already written and hooks have defaults.
questions.rule: Only abstract methods are compulsory.

questions.q: The template method is itself a method of the abstract class. Which of the three kinds is it?
options: An abstract method, because subclasses supply it
A hook, because subclasses may change it
A concrete method, with a body that runs the steps
None of the three kinds, since it is the pattern itself
optionExplain: Subclasses supply the steps, not the template.
Hooks are called by the template, not the template itself.
Right: it has a body and is shared by all subclasses.
It is a method like the others and fits the concrete kind.
questions.explain: The template is the concrete method that calls the other kinds.
questions.rule: The template is concrete.
questions.teaches: The template method is itself a concrete method of the abstract class; it is the part subclasses are meant to leave unchanged.

questions.q: A developer changes one abstract step into a hook with an empty default. What changes for the existing subclasses?
options: They keep working, with no duty to provide that step
They stop compiling, because the step is no longer abstract
They must each provide the step in a different new way
They lose the ability to override the step at all
optionExplain: Right: an optional step no longer binds subclasses.
An empty default means subclasses need not change.
Nothing forces a new form of the step.
Hooks can still be overridden.
questions.explain: A hook makes the step optional.
questions.rule: Abstract to hook relaxes the duty.

questions.q: A text editor's plugin base class has a template that calls loadPlugin, initialize, renderToolbar and unload. loadPlugin and unload are written once. Every plugin must give its own initialize. renderToolbar draws nothing unless overridden. How are the four steps best described?
options: loadPlugin and unload are hooks, initialize is concrete, renderToolbar is abstract
All four are abstract, since all four are part of the algorithm
initialize and renderToolbar are abstract; loadPlugin and unload are hooks
loadPlugin and unload are concrete, initialize is abstract, renderToolbar is a hook
optionExplain: This swaps the kinds around.
That would force every plugin to write all four.
renderToolbar is optional, and the shared steps are not hooks.
Right: each kind matches who supplies the body.
questions.explain: Match the kind to who supplies the body.
questions.rule: Kind follows supply.
questions.teaches: The template method calls a concrete step, an abstract step and a hook in the same way; the kind only decides who supplies the body.

questions.q: True or false: Unless the design prevents it, a subclass of CaffeineBeverage could replace the template method with a recipe of its own.
questions.explain: Ordinary methods can be overridden, so the structure is only protected if something prevents it. The card next shows what the book advises.
questions.rule: Protection has to be asked for.

questions.q: To prevent subclasses from changing the algorithm, the book says to declare the template method ____.
questions.explain: A final method cannot be overridden by a subclass.
questions.rule: Final template, open steps.

questions.q: A payment base class has processPayment, which calls validate, authorise, capture and receipt. The team wants no subclass, such as CardPayment or WalletPayment, to reorder these. What does the book advise?
options: Declare each step final as well, so no subclass can touch any of them
Declare processPayment final
Make processPayment abstract so each subclass writes its own
Leave it as it is and trust the subclasses to keep the order
optionExplain: Final steps could not be overridden, so the subclasses could not supply them.
Right: this fixes the sequence while the steps stay open.
Then each subclass would own the order.
Trust is exactly what the pattern replaces with structure.
questions.explain: Declaring processPayment final fixes the sequence of validate, authorise, capture and receipt, so CardPayment and WalletPayment cannot reorder it, while they stay free to supply the individual steps.
questions.rule: Final on the template, not on the steps.

questions.q: The template method is final. Can a subclass still supply its own version of the abstract steps and the hooks?
options: No, because final locks the whole class against overriding
No, because the steps become part of the template method
Yes, but only the hooks, since abstract steps are locked as well
Yes, since final covers the template method, not the steps it calls
optionExplain: Final on a method locks that method.
The steps remain separate methods.
Abstract steps must be implemented; they cannot be locked.
Right: the template is closed and the steps stay open.
questions.explain: The template is closed; the steps stay open.
questions.rule: Closed sequence, open steps.
questions.teaches: A final template with open steps gives the pattern its mix of a fixed structure and flexible content; locking the steps too would leave subclasses nothing to supply.

questions.q: True or false: A subclass overrides a template method that is not final and leaves out addCondiments. The algorithm's structure still holds for that subclass.
questions.explain: The overriding version replaces the superclass sequence, and a missing step changes the structure. Without final, the structure is only a convention.
questions.rule: Final turns the convention into a rule.

questions.q: A base class has a final method run(). A new subclass needs one extra step between two existing steps. What does the final modifier imply for the team?
options: The subclass overrides run() and adds the step there
The change goes into run() in the base class and reaches every subclass
The language inserts the step when the subclass asks for it
The subclass adds the step by marking that step final too
optionExplain: Final forbids overriding run().
Right: a closed template can only be changed at its source.
Nothing in the pattern inserts steps automatically.
Final does not add steps.
questions.explain: Structure changes go to the superclass.
questions.rule: Change the template, not the subclass.
questions.teaches: A final template pushes any structural change into the superclass, where it is made once and reaches every subclass; this suits a shared structure but is a cost if one subclass truly needs its own sequence.

questions.q: A superclass has a method with an empty body at one point of its algorithm. What is its likely purpose?
options: To let subclasses add behaviour there if they wish
It is an unfinished method that the programmer forgot
It forces every subclass to fill in the step
It stops subclasses from acting at that point
optionExplain: Right: an empty default invites optional extension.
An empty body can be deliberate.
A required step would be abstract.
A subclass can still override it.
questions.explain: The card next calls this a hook.
questions.rule: Empty can mean optional.

questions.q: A hook is a method with an empty or default ____ in the abstract class, which a subclass may override or ignore.
questions.explain: A hook has a default, so a subclass that does not override it still works.
questions.rule: Hooks are optional.

questions.q: A document editor's base class saves a file with a template that validates, writes, then calls a hook named afterSave, which is empty. A word-count plugin wants to update its count after each save, and other plugins do nothing. What does the word-count plugin do?
options: It overrides the save template and adds the count
It asks the editor's authors to call its counter from the base class
It overrides afterSave
Nothing, because a hook cannot be overridden
optionExplain: That replaces the structure the hook was meant to protect.
That would couple the base class to one plugin.
Right: the hook is the extension point for this need.
Hooks exist to be overridden.
questions.explain: afterSave is an empty hook, so the word-count plugin overrides just that method to join in after each save, while the other plugins leave it alone.
questions.rule: Join at the hook.

questions.q: A team adds a new hook with an empty default to a template method. What happens to the subclasses already written?
options: Each must be edited to implement the hook
They keep working without any change
Each must be recompiled with a new template
Each loses the steps it had before
optionExplain: That would be true of a new abstract step.
Right: the default covers every existing subclass.
Recompiling is not an edit they have to make by hand.
Their steps stay as they were; adding a hook removes nothing.
questions.explain: A new hook comes with an empty default, so every existing subclass keeps compiling and behaves as before. Adding a hook is safe for old subclasses.
questions.rule: New hooks do not disturb old subclasses.
questions.teaches: Adding a hook with a default to a template leaves existing subclasses working, whereas adding a new abstract step breaks every subclass until it implements the step.

questions.q: What if a subclass overrides a hook but the template method does not call it?
options: The override runs anyway when the object is first created
The override takes the place of the template method
The language calls the override at the end of the algorithm
The override has no effect, since the template decides when hooks run
optionExplain: Nothing runs a hook by itself.
The template stays as it is.
There is no automatic call.
Right: a hook runs only where the template calls it.
questions.explain: The template controls the hook.
questions.rule: Hooks run when the template says so.

questions.q: True or false: A base class for bank transfers makes the debit step a hook with an empty default, because some subclasses may not need it.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a transfer that skips the debit cannot be right. The step is required, so it belongs among the abstract methods.
questions.rule: Required steps are abstract, not hooks.
questions.teaches: A step with no safe default must not be a hook, because an empty default would let a subclass silently skip essential work.

questions.q: How might a subclass use a hook to affect whether a step of the algorithm runs?
options: By deleting the step from the template method
By calling the step directly before the template starts
By overriding a hook whose answer the template checks
By declaring the step private in the subclass
optionExplain: Subclasses cannot edit the template.
The step belongs inside the sequence.
Right: the hook gives the subclass a say without changing the template.
Access modifiers do not decide whether the step runs.
questions.explain: The card next lists the uses of hooks.
questions.rule: The hook answers; the template acts.

questions.q: Match each use of a hook with an example.
pairs: A subclass implements the hook only if it wants that step
A hook like justReOrderedList runs after a list is reordered
A hook's answer controls whether the template adds condiments
questions.explain: The three uses are optional steps, reactions to events, and decisions that the template acts on.
questions.rule: Optional, react, decide.

questions.q: A card game's base class runs a turn: draw a card, play a card, then call a hook. A subclass for a shared-screen game uses that hook to hide the player's hand after each turn. Which use of a hook is this?
options: Reacting to a step that has already happened
Making a step optional
Deciding for the base class whether to run a step
Replacing the template method
optionExplain: Right: the hook runs after the turn and the subclass responds.
Nothing is skipped here.
The hook returns no answer for the base class to act on.
The template is untouched.
questions.explain: A hook after a step is a reaction.
questions.rule: After-step hooks are reactions.

questions.q: The condiment hook has a default answer in the abstract class. Why give a decision hook a default?
options: So subclasses with no opinion can leave it alone and the algorithm still works
So the template can skip calling the hook when it is in a hurry
So that subclasses are forced to override it before they work
So that the hook turns into an abstract method in the end
optionExplain: Right: the default is the common case.
The template decides to call it each time.
A forced override would make it abstract.
A default makes it a hook.
questions.explain: A decision hook needs a default.
questions.rule: Default to the common answer.
questions.teaches: A decision hook needs a sensible default, usually the common case, so that subclasses with no opinion still get a working algorithm.

questions.q: A subclass overrides the condiment hook so that it answers no. What does the template do?
options: It stops the whole recipe before the next step
It adds the condiments anyway and ignores the answer
It skips the condiment step and goes on with the rest
It asks the hook again until the answer is yes
optionExplain: Only one step depends on the answer.
The template honours the answer.
Right: the answer controls that one step.
The template asks once.
questions.explain: The hook's answer controls only the condiment step, so answering no skips that step and the recipe carries on with the rest.
questions.rule: No answer, no step.

questions.q: A checkout base class calls a hook wantsGiftWrap before a wrapping step. Which statements fit the book's use of a decision hook? Select all that apply.
options: The template calls wantsGiftWrap and wraps only when it answers yes
A subclass for a gift shop overrides wantsGiftWrap to answer yes
A subclass calls the wrapping step itself after checkout ends
Every subclass must override wantsGiftWrap
optionExplain: Right: the template acts on the hook's answer.
Right: the subclass supplies the answer.
The subclass would be running steps on its own and bypassing the template.
A hook is optional, so a default exists.
questions.explain: The subclass answers the question and the template does the acting.
questions.teaches: With a decision hook the subclass only answers a question, and the template keeps control of what to do with the answer.
questions.rule: The subclass answers; the template acts.

questions.q: A step of an algorithm is optional for some subclasses. How should the abstract class declare it?
options: As an abstract method, so every subclass is reminded of it
As a final method, so none can change it
As a private helper that the template skips
As a hook with an empty or default body
optionExplain: That forces every subclass to write it.
A final method cannot be overridden.
A skipped step would never run.
Right: optional steps suit hooks.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's rule.
questions.rule: Optional means hook.

questions.q: True or false: A concrete subclass has to implement every abstract method of the abstract class.
questions.explain: Each concrete subclass gives a complete implementation of the undefined steps.
questions.rule: Abstract means compulsory.

questions.q: A report base class has these steps: fetchRows (every report needs its own query), addWatermark (some reports want one) and formatTotals (every report formats differently). Which choice fits the book's rule?
options: All three abstract, so every report decides each one for itself
fetchRows and formatTotals abstract, addWatermark a hook
addWatermark abstract, and the other two steps hooks
All three hooks, so subclasses are never burdened at all
optionExplain: That would force an empty watermark in many reports.
Right: two steps are required and one is optional.
This reverses which steps are required.
Required steps with empty defaults would be skipped silently.
questions.explain: Required means abstract; optional means hook.
questions.rule: Ask whether the step is required.

questions.q: A team makes all ten steps of a template abstract, and most subclasses leave seven of them empty. What does this choice cost?
options: The template can no longer be declared final by the team
Subclasses lose the ability to vary any of the steps
Every subclass must write all ten, seven of them empty
The superclass can no longer call the steps it declares
optionExplain: Final and abstract concern different methods.
Subclasses can still vary all of them.
Right: abstract methods bind every subclass.
The template can still call them.
questions.explain: Abstract for optional steps burdens subclasses.
questions.rule: Do not use abstract for optional steps.
questions.teaches: The cost of a wrong choice is empty boilerplate in every subclass when abstract is used for optional steps, or silent omissions when a hook is used for required ones.

questions.q: What if a required step is made a hook with an empty default and a new subclass forgets it?
options: It compiles and runs, but silently skips that work
The subclass fails to compile until it adds the step
The template stops with an error at that step
The superclass supplies the missing work in its place
optionExplain: Right: the default hides the omission.
That happens for an abstract step, not a hook.
A hook default does not raise an error.
An empty default does no work.
questions.explain: A hook has a default, so a subclass that forgets it still compiles and runs, silently skipping the work. A hook cannot enforce a duty, which is why a required step should be abstract.
questions.rule: Duty needs abstract.

questions.q: A form-processing framework runs a template for each form type. Sort each step by whether the designer should make it an abstract method or a hook.

items.t: Parse the submitted fields (every form differs)
Log a message after saving (few forms care)
Choose the table to write to (no default exists)
Send an optional confirmation email
Show a custom error page (a standard page exists)
Validate the data (rules differ and are required)

questions.explain: Steps that every form must do, with no default, are abstract. Steps that few forms need, or with a standard default, are hooks.
questions.teaches: A useful test is whether a safe default exists: if the algorithm stays correct with an empty or standard step, a hook fits.
questions.rule: Ask whether a safe default exists.

questions.q: A designer splits an algorithm into thirty small abstract steps so subclasses can vary anything. What is the main drawback?
options: The template method can no longer be declared final
Each subclass must implement all thirty steps
Subclasses lose the ability to vary any of the steps
The superclass cannot call so many separate methods
optionExplain: Final and step count are unrelated.
Right: every abstract step is work for every subclass.
More steps give more flexibility, not less.
A method can call as many steps as it needs.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's advice.
questions.rule: Many abstract steps mean much work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, making the steps coarser gives subclasses more flexibility.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: less granularity means less flexibility.
questions.rule: Coarse steps, less flexibility.

questions.q: A plugin template has 25 abstract steps, and most plugins vary only 3 of them. Which fix eases the burden while keeping the flexibility?
options: Make all 25 steps final
Merge all 25 steps into one abstract step
Drop the template and let each plugin write its own algorithm
Turn the 22 optional steps into hooks
optionExplain: Final steps could not be supplied.
That leaves subclasses little structure and removes the choice of what to vary.
That loses the reuse the template gives.
Right: hooks spare subclasses without removing the chance to vary.
questions.explain: Use hooks to lighten the load.
questions.rule: Optional steps become hooks.

questions.q: True or false: Merging three neighbouring abstract steps into one gives subclasses less work, and also less control over each of the three parts.
questions.explain: Coarser steps cut effort and control together, which is the trade-off the authors describe.
questions.rule: Coarsening cuts work and control together.
questions.teaches: Merging steps trades control for effort; it suits steps that tend to vary together, since subclasses lose little by writing them as one.

questions.q: What if the algorithm had a single abstract step that covers nearly all of the work?
options: Subclasses write less code and also gain more control of each part
The template would gain more shared code to reuse among subclasses
The abstract step would turn into a hook with a default body
Subclasses write one method but redo nearly all the work, and the template shares little
optionExplain: Less work comes with less control, not more.
Less code is left in the template, not more.
Size does not turn a step into a hook.
Right: the coarsest step is easy to name and removes the benefit of the template.
questions.explain: A very coarse step leaves little to share.
questions.rule: Too coarse, little reuse.

questions.q: Rank these designs of one template from the least to the most flexible for subclasses.
items: One abstract step covering the whole algorithm
Three abstract steps
Seven abstract steps
Fifteen abstract steps
questions.explain: More steps give subclasses more places to vary. The same order also ranks the effort needed to write a subclass.
questions.teaches: The same order also ranks the effort of writing a subclass, so flexibility and effort rise together and the choice is a point on one scale.
questions.rule: Flexibility and effort rise together.

questions.q: In a layered system, what harm comes from high-level and low-level components that depend on each other in a tangle?
options: No one can easily see how the system is designed
Every call between the components runs more slowly
Components can no longer be inherited from by others
The compiler refuses to build a system with such calls
optionExplain: Right: the tangled dependencies hide the design.
Speed is not the issue the authors raise.
Inheritance is unaffected.
Tangled dependencies still compile.
questions.explain: The card next names this problem.
questions.rule: Tangled dependencies hide the design.

questions.q: The Hollywood Principle says: don’t call us, we’ll ____ you.
questions.explain: Low-level components wait to be called by high-level ones.
questions.rule: High-level components do the calling.

questions.q: A game engine, the high-level part, lets enemy scripts, the low-level part, plug in. Which arrangement follows the principle?
options: Each script calls into the engine's loop whenever it likes
The engine calls each script's update at the times it chooses
Scripts and engine call each other by name wherever convenient
Scripts start the engine and decide when each frame runs
optionExplain: That hands control to the low-level parts.
Right: the high-level part decides when the low-level part runs.
That is the tangle the principle warns about.
That also puts the low-level parts in charge.
questions.explain: The framework calls the plug-ins.
questions.rule: Plug-ins wait; the engine calls.

questions.q: A subclass step calls a method that it inherits from its own superclass. Is it breaking the Hollywood Principle?
options: Yes, because any call from a low level to a high level is forbidden
Yes, because inherited methods are always high-level components
No, since calling an inherited method is allowed; explicit cycles are the concern
No, because the principle applies only between unrelated classes
optionExplain: The principle does not go that far.
Inheritance itself does not make a component forbidden.
Right: low-level components often call methods above them through inheritance.
The principle applies within hierarchies too.
questions.explain: Inherited calls are fine; circular dependencies are the target.
questions.rule: Avoid explicit cycles, not every upward call.
questions.teaches: A low-level component often ends up calling a method defined above it through inheritance, and that is acceptable; the principle aims to avoid explicit circular dependencies between low-level and high-level components.

questions.q: A low-level component calls a high-level one, which in turn calls the low-level one back by name. Which problem grows?
options: Nothing, because both components are in the same system
Slower start-up, since both must be loaded first
Dependency rot, since each now depends on the other
Loss of the inheritance link between the two
optionExplain: Being in one system does not remove the tangle.
Loading time is not the concern.
Right: a circular dependency is the start of rot.
Inheritance is not affected.
questions.explain: When the low-level component calls the high-level one and the high-level one calls it back by name, each depends on the other, which is dependency rot. Cycles like this are what the Hollywood Principle helps avoid.
questions.rule: Do not let levels depend on each other.

questions.q: In a web server framework, sort each interaction by whether it follows the Hollywood Principle.

items.t: The framework calls a handler when a request arrives
A handler starts the framework's event loop
The framework decides when to load each plug-in
A plug-in calls three other plug-ins by name, which call it back
A page widget waits to be called when its section is drawn
A widget decides for itself when the framework draws it

questions.explain: The framework is in charge and calls your code at points it chooses. Code that takes control or forms call cycles breaks the principle.
questions.teaches: In a framework your code does not run the program; the framework does, and calls your code at the points it chooses.
questions.rule: The framework calls your code at points it chooses.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: In the CaffeineBeverage design, who decides when Tea's brew method runs?
options: The template method in CaffeineBeverage
Tea itself, when its own object is created
The client program, calling each step in turn
The Java runtime, when the program starts up
optionExplain: Right: the superclass calls the subclass step when its turn comes.
A Tea object does not start its own steps.
The client makes one call to the template.
The runtime does not know the recipe.
questions.explain: The card next ties this to the Hollywood Principle.
questions.rule: The superclass calls the subclass.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: Match each part of the drinks design with its role under the Hollywood Principle.
pairs: High-level component that controls the algorithm
Low-level components called when a step is needed
Don’t call us, we’ll call you
questions.explain: The superclass is high-level and in control, the subclasses wait for their turn.
questions.rule: High-level controls, low-level waits.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: A base class Job runs three steps: start, execute and finish. ReportJob supplies execute. Which statement shows the Hollywood Principle?
options: ReportJob's execute calls Job's start and finish in its own order
ReportJob starts Job and then supplies each step in turn
A scheduler calls execute directly and skips Job
Job's template calls ReportJob's execute when its turn comes
optionExplain: That puts the subclass in control of the order.
That also hands control to the subclass.
That bypasses the template that holds the structure.
Right: the high-level class decides when the low-level step runs.
questions.explain: The template calls; the subclass answers.
questions.rule: Template Method is Hollywood in action.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: How does the book relate the Hollywood Principle to the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: They are the same principle under two different names
Both aim at decoupling; Dependency Inversion is stronger and more general
The Hollywood Principle is the more general of the two
The Hollywood Principle is about concrete classes, the other about call order
optionExplain: They are related but not identical.
Right: they share a goal but differ in scope.
The book gives that role to Dependency Inversion.
This swaps the two: Dependency Inversion is the one about concrete classes, and the Hollywood Principle is about who calls whom.
questions.explain: Both principles aim at decoupling, but the Dependency Inversion Principle makes the stronger and more general statement about avoiding dependencies, while the Hollywood Principle is a technique for letting low-level components hook into a system. They share a goal but differ in scope.
questions.rule: Dependency Inversion is broader.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: What if a subclass called its superclass's steps itself, in an order it chose, instead of waiting for the template to call it?
options: Nothing would change, since the same steps would still run
The superclass would gain control of the order of the steps
Dependency rot would become impossible in the design
The subclass would hold the control, and the order would not be fixed in one place
optionExplain: The order would belong to each subclass.
The control would move away from the superclass.
It makes cycles more likely.
Right: whoever calls the steps owns the sequence.
questions.explain: If subclasses called the steps themselves, each would own its own sequence and nothing would fix the order in one place. The template keeps control by calling the subclass, not the other way round.
questions.rule: Keep control in the superclass.

questions.section: The Hollywood Principle and Template Method
questions.q: True or false: A subject that notifies its registered observers when its state changes follows the Hollywood Principle.
questions.explain: The observers do not poll the subject; the subject calls them when it chooses, which fits the principle.
questions.rule: Notification is calling, not being called.
questions.teaches: Other patterns use the principle too; the book names Factory Method and Observer as examples and asks the reader to find more.

questions.q: Java arrays cannot be subclassed, yet Arrays.sort needs a way to compare items. How did the designers supply the missing step?
options: Each array type gets its own subclass of Arrays
The items being sorted supply a comparison that sort calls
Sort guesses an order from the values themselves
The caller passes in the whole sorting algorithm
optionExplain: Arrays cannot be subclassed, which is the constraint here.
Right: the comparison is deferred to the items.
A guess could not order arbitrary objects.
The algorithm stays inside sort.
questions.explain: The card next gives the book's account.
questions.rule: The items supply the comparison.

questions.q: To sort ducks with Arrays.sort, the Duck class implements the Comparable interface and its ____ method.
questions.explain: That gives sort the piece it needs to finish the algorithm.
questions.rule: Implement compareTo.

questions.q: You want to sort an array of Invoice objects with Arrays.sort. What must you do?
options: Make Invoice implement Comparable with a compareTo method
Write a subclass of Arrays that overrides the sort steps
Write your own sort that calls the library's swap
Make a subclass of the array type to hold the comparison
optionExplain: Right: sort needs the comparison from the items.
Arrays offers sort as a static method, not a class to subclass.
The library's sort already contains the algorithm.
A Java array cannot be subclassed.
questions.explain: Supply the missing step through the interface.
questions.rule: The items complete the algorithm.

questions.q: What if the Duck class does not implement the comparison that sort relies on?
options: Sort falls back to ordering the ducks by name
Sort orders the ducks by their position in memory
Sort lacks the piece it needs and cannot complete the ordering
Sort finishes, but the ducks stay in the original order
optionExplain: Sort has no such default.
Memory position is not an order the method uses.
Right: without compareTo the algorithm is incomplete.
The method does not silently succeed.
questions.explain: Without a comparison such as compareTo on Duck, sort lacks the piece it needs to order the ducks and cannot complete the ordering. The algorithm is incomplete without it.
questions.rule: The deferred step is required.

questions.q: A reviewer says Arrays.sort is a textbook template method. How does the book assess that claim?
options: It is textbook, because the sort method calls the comparison step
Not textbook, as it uses no subclassing, but it follows the spirit
It is not Template Method at all, because it has no abstract class
It is really Strategy, because it uses object composition
optionExplain: The textbook form uses a superclass and subclasses.
Right: the form differs, the intent is the same.
The book says it is in the spirit of the pattern.
The book answers that Strategy composes with a complete algorithm, and sort's is incomplete.
questions.explain: Judge a pattern by its intent as well as its shape.
questions.rule: Spirit over diagram.

questions.q: True or false: Because a Java array cannot be subclassed, a pattern that depends on subclassing cannot be adapted to arrays at all.
questions.explain: Arrays.sort keeps the idea of a fixed algorithm with a deferred step, and swaps subclassing for a static method and an interface.
questions.rule: Keep the intent and change the mechanism.
questions.teaches: When a language constraint blocks the textbook form, designers can keep the intent and change the mechanism; real code seldom matches a pattern's diagram.

questions.q: JFrame has a paint method that draws nothing unless you override it. What role does it play?
options: An abstract method that every frame must implement
A final template method that cannot be changed at all
A constructor that builds the frame and its contents
A hook where your own drawing joins JFrame's algorithm
optionExplain: It does nothing by default, so it is optional.
It is the thing you override, so it is not final.
It draws, it does not construct.
Right: a default that does nothing is a hook.
questions.explain: The card next explains the hook.
questions.rule: Empty default, so a hook.

questions.q: A JFrame's paint method does nothing by default because it is a ____, so an override is optional.
questions.explain: A method with an empty default that a subclass may override is a hook, so an applet or frame is not required to implement it.
questions.rule: Hooks are optional.

questions.q: A web framework's Page class calls an onLoad method, empty by default, each time a page is shown. Your ContactPage should focus the name field when it appears. What do you do?
options: Edit Page so it focuses the field
Call Page's display steps yourself from a constructor
Override onLoad in ContactPage
Override the method that shows the page
optionExplain: That would put your page's needs in the framework.
That bypasses the framework's control of when things run.
Right: the hook is where your code joins in.
That replaces the framework's algorithm.
questions.explain: Use the hook that the framework offers.
questions.rule: Override the hook.

questions.q: Why would a framework like Swing make paint a hook instead of an abstract method?
options: Most frames need no custom drawing, so it would burden subclasses
Hooks run faster than abstract methods when the frame is drawn
Abstract methods cannot be called from inside a template method
A hook can be called more than once for every frame drawn
optionExplain: Right: optional behaviour suits hooks.
Speed is not what separates them.
Templates call abstract methods all the time.
Call counts do not distinguish them.
questions.explain: Optional behaviour suits hooks.
questions.rule: Hooks for what most users skip.
questions.teaches: Frameworks lean towards hooks for behaviour most users never change, so that an ordinary subclass has nothing to write.

questions.q: True or false: Overriding a hook lets you change when the framework calls it.
questions.explain: The framework decides when the hook runs. You change only what happens there.
questions.rule: You choose the content, not the timing.

questions.q: A plugin host calls start() and stop() on every plugin, and the base class gives both empty bodies. Which description fits?
options: A template with hooks: the host sets the timing, and plugins override what they need
A set of abstract methods, because every plugin must implement both
A Strategy, because the plugins can be swapped at runtime by the host
A final template with no room for any plugin behaviour at all
optionExplain: Right: the host drives the life cycle and the plugins hook in.
Empty bodies mean the plugins are not forced.
Swapping is not the point here; the host calls at set times.
The hooks are the room for plugin behaviour.
questions.explain: Life-cycle callbacks are hooks.
questions.rule: The host calls; the plugin reacts.
questions.teaches: Life-cycle callbacks are a common form of hooks: the framework drives the stages and your code reacts at each one.

questions.q: Both Template Method and Strategy encapsulate algorithms. What is the difference in how they do it?
options: Template Method uses composition; Strategy uses inheritance
Both use inheritance, but at different depths of the hierarchy
Template Method uses inheritance; Strategy uses object composition
Template Method uses interfaces; Strategy uses static methods
optionExplain: This reverses the two.
Strategy composes objects instead.
Right: the chapter's summary says one encapsulates by inheritance and one by composition.
Neither is described that way.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the contrast.
questions.rule: Inheritance versus composition.

questions.q: Match each pattern with what the book says it does.
pairs: Subclasses decide how to implement steps in an algorithm
Encapsulates interchangeable behaviors and delegates to the chosen one
Subclasses decide which concrete classes to instantiate
