questions.q: True or false: The three named variants are the only forms the Proxy Pattern takes.
questions.explain: Many other variants exist, such as caching proxies.
questions.rule: The list is open.

questions.q: A proxy keeps the results of earlier requests and returns them instead of fetching again. Which family does the book place it in?
options: A caching proxy, a specialised virtual proxy
A protection proxy that decides based on access rights
A remote proxy that forwards calls to a cache in another JVM
A decorator that adds behaviour
optionExplain: Right: the book calls it a caching proxy.
It does not check rights.
Remote is not the point.
It controls access, not adds behaviour.
questions.explain: Caching is a form of virtual proxy.
questions.rule: Pick the proxy by what it guards: a remote object, an expensive resource or a resource needing rights.
questions.teaches: A caching proxy is a specialised virtual proxy that keeps previously created objects and returns them when it can.

questions.q: What does a virtual proxy often do about creating an expensive object?
options: It creates the object twice, once as a safety copy
It creates the object in another JVM on the network
It delays creating the object until it is needed
It declines to create the object, whether needed or not
optionExplain: Duplicates are not the idea.
Another JVM describes a remote proxy.
Right: deferred creation.
The object is still created when needed.
questions.explain: The card next describes before and after creation.
questions.rule: Defer the cost.

questions.q: A virtual proxy often ____ creating the object until it is needed.
questions.explain: Deferring creation is the common use.
questions.rule: Defer creation.

questions.q: Once the real object exists, what does a virtual proxy do with requests?
options: It keeps answering them itself with its stand-in text
It destroys the real subject
It delegates them directly to the real subject
It refuses them until the client asks again
optionExplain: Its stand-in role ends once the object exists.
It does not destroy what it just built.
Right: after creation it passes requests on.
It has no reason to refuse.
questions.explain: Stand in first, delegate later.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
questions.teaches: A virtual proxy changes its behaviour over time: first it is a stand-in, then a plain pass-through to the real subject.

questions.q: A map app's RoutePlanner takes seconds to build, yet the screen must open at once. Which design matches a virtual proxy?
options: A planner proxy sends every request over the network to a planner in another JVM
A planner proxy answers at once, then builds the planner when a route is asked for
A planner proxy refuses to give routes to users who have no paid plan
A planner proxy logs every request it receives and then does nothing more
optionExplain: That is a remote proxy.
Right: stand in, create on demand, then delegate.
That is a protection proxy.
Logging alone does not stand in.
questions.explain: Match the symptom to the variant.
questions.rule: Costly creation suggests a virtual proxy.

questions.q: True or false: If no request needs the real object, a proxy that defers creation would not build it.
questions.explain: Deferring means creating only when needed.
questions.rule: No need, no creation.

questions.q: A proxy stands in for a report object that does not exist yet when the proxy is first used. Which statement fits?
options: That fits a remote proxy, whose subject must already exist elsewhere
That fits a protection proxy, whose subject must already be created
That cannot be a proxy, since a proxy needs an existing subject
That fits a virtual proxy, whose subject may not exist yet
optionExplain: A remote proxy's subject exists elsewhere.
Protection does not concern creation.
A virtual proxy can precede its subject.
Right: a virtual proxy can come first.
questions.explain: A virtual proxy can exist before its subject.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy stands in until the costly object is needed, creates it then, and afterwards passes requests straight through.
questions.teaches: A remote proxy's subject already exists elsewhere, whereas a virtual proxy's subject may not exist yet.

questions.q: What should a CD viewer do while a cover image is still downloading?
options: Show a placeholder message and stay responsive
Freeze the whole window until the image arrives
Skip the cover and leave the space empty for good
Download every single cover before showing any screen
optionExplain: Right: placeholder and responsiveness.
Freezing hangs the app.
The cover should eventually appear.
That makes the wait longer.
questions.explain: The card next shows how a proxy delivers this.
questions.rule: Show something, stay responsive.

questions.q: While the image loads, the proxy displays a message asking the user to ____.
questions.explain: The proxy displays Loading CD cover, please wait... until the image arrives.
questions.rule: A placeholder message covers the wait.

questions.q: In the Swing design, what does the virtual proxy take the place of?
options: The menu of CD titles in the application
The icon that would load the image
The online service that supplies the covers
The network connection used for the download
optionExplain: The menu of CD titles is a separate part of the application and is not replaced.
Right: it stands in for the icon.
The service stays where it is.
The connection is not replaced.
questions.explain: In the Swing design the virtual proxy stands in for the icon that would load the image, so it fills the icon's place until the cover has arrived.
questions.rule: The virtual proxy stands in for the slow icon.
questions.teaches: The proxy takes the icon's place, so the viewer treats it as an ordinary icon without knowing about the loading.

questions.q: A recipe app shows one photo per dish, and the photos load slowly. Which design matches the chapter's approach?
options: The app loads every one of the photos before showing any screen
The app shows no photos at all until a later release
The app moves all photo files onto the user's phone first
A stand-in per photo shows a message and loads in the background
optionExplain: That is exactly the freeze to avoid.
The photos are still wanted.
Moving files does not address the wait.
Right: stand in and load in the background.
questions.explain: Stand in, load, then hand over.
questions.rule: Placeholder now, real thing later.

questions.q: True or false: If the viewer loaded the image directly inside the display call, the whole application could hang while it waits.
questions.explain: The authors say they do not want to hang up the entire application while it waits.
questions.rule: Waiting in the display call risks hanging.

questions.q: Sort each task by who does it.

items.t: Shows the loading message
Paints the finished image
Manages the loading in the background
Holds the downloaded picture

questions.explain: The proxy handles the waiting; the real icon handles the finished picture.
questions.rule: The proxy handles the waiting; the real icon handles the picture.
questions.teaches: The work divides in two: the proxy covers the period before the image exists, and the real icon takes over once it does.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: What happens when the user asks for a new CD cover?
options: A new proxy is created and the process starts over
The old proxy swaps in the new URL and carries on
The old image is kept and the new request is ignored
The whole application restarts from the beginning
optionExplain: Right: a new proxy for a new image.
The book creates a new proxy.
The new request is honored.
The application does not restart; only a new proxy is created for the new cover.
questions.explain: A request for a new CD cover creates a new proxy, and the process starts over. The card next gives the four steps.
questions.rule: New image, new proxy.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: Put ImageProxy's four steps in order.
items: Create an ImageIcon and start loading it from the URL
Display the loading message while bytes arrive
Delegate all calls to the icon once it is loaded
Create a new proxy when the user asks for a new image
questions.explain: The proxy moves from loading to delegating, then starts over for a new image.
questions.rule: Load, show message, delegate, restart.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: Once the image is loaded, which calls does ImageProxy delegate to the icon?
options: Only paintIcon(), since painting is its main job
Only the calls that would change the loaded image
All calls, getWidth() and getHeight() included
None, since the proxy paints the image by itself
optionExplain: Sizes are delegated too.
Nothing here changes the image.
Right: after loading, the proxy forwards every call, getWidth() and getHeight() included.
The proxy does not paint the image itself.
questions.explain: Once the image is loaded, ImageProxy forwards every call to the real icon, getWidth() and getHeight() as well as paintIcon().
questions.rule: Once loaded, the proxy delegates every call.
questions.teaches: After loading, the proxy forwards every call to the icon, sizes included, and not only the painting.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: A slideshow shows a large PDF through a proxy that has finished loading. The user selects a different PDF. By the chapter's design, what happens next?
options: The existing proxy is reused with a different address
The finished PDF is deleted from memory first
A new proxy is created for the new PDF
The application waits for the old proxy to expire
optionExplain: The book creates a new proxy.
Deletion is not described.
Right: a new proxy per image.
No expiry is described.
questions.explain: The design uses one proxy per image: when the user selects a different PDF, a new proxy is created for it rather than reusing the finished one.
questions.rule: One proxy per item.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: True or false: While the bytes are still arriving, calls such as paintIcon() are delegated to the finished ImageIcon.
questions.explain: Before loading is complete the proxy shows its loading message; delegation starts after.
questions.rule: Delegation starts after loading.

questions.section: How ImageProxy is going to work
questions.q: A music app's TrackProxy offers the same methods as Track and hides a track that is still downloading. How does its structure compare with a remote proxy's?
options: The structure is the same; what differs is why the real object is hidden
The structures differ, because a virtual proxy has no real subject
The structures differ, because a virtual proxy changes the interface
The structures are the same, and so is the reason
optionExplain: Right: same structure, different reason.
A virtual proxy has a real subject.
Both implement the same interface.
The structures are the same but the reasons differ: one hides loading delay, the other hides distance.
questions.explain: A virtual proxy has the same structure as a remote proxy: it implements the real subject's interface and holds a real subject. What differs is why the real object is hidden, because it is still loading rather than on another machine.
questions.rule: Same structure as a remote proxy, but the reason for hiding differs.
questions.teaches: The class diagram looks like the remote proxy's; the difference is that the proxy hides an object that is expensive to create, not one that lives elsewhere.

questions.q: Which pattern does the book suggest for tidying ImageProxy's conditionals?
options: The Decorator Pattern
The Template Method Pattern
The Adapter Pattern
The State Pattern
optionExplain: Decorating adds behaviour.
Template Method fixes a sequence.
Adapter changes an interface.
Right: ImageLoaded and ImageNotLoaded become states.
questions.explain: The card next gives the redesign.
questions.rule: Two situations suggest State.

questions.q: In the redesign, the proxy starts in the ImageNotLoaded state and moves to ____ once the ImageIcon is retrieved.
questions.explain: The state changes when the image has been retrieved.
questions.rule: Start unloaded, then switch.

questions.q: What moves into the two state classes?
options: The network connection to the image server
The code from the if statements
The URL of the image to be loaded
The menu of titles in the viewer
optionExplain: The network connection stays with the proxy and is not moved into the states.
Right: the code from the if statements moves into the states, so each state holds its own case.
The image URL stays with the proxy, which the states use when they need it.
The menu of titles is part of the viewer outside the proxy, so it does not move.
questions.explain: The code from the if statements moves into the two state classes, so each state holds its own case and the proxy delegates to the current one.
questions.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
questions.teaches: Each state class holds the behaviour for one situation, so the repeated condition checks disappear.

questions.q: A document-upload widget repeats 'if uploaded ... else ...' inside four methods. Which clean-up fits the puzzle?
options: Move each situation's behaviour into its own state class
Merge the four methods into one long method with a switch
Add a fifth method that checks the flag for the others
Copy the widget into two subclasses that repeat its code
optionExplain: Right: states replace the checks.
A long method keeps the condition.
Another check adds more.
Subclasses duplicate code.
questions.explain: State replaces repeated conditions.
questions.rule: Repeated condition, consider State.

questions.q: True or false: If the proxy also had to handle a failed download, the redesign would add a third state class.
questions.explain: Each situation has its own state, so a third situation adds a third class.
questions.rule: A new situation is a new state.

questions.q: A ticket class repeats the same check of whether it is paid inside four methods. What does the puzzle suggest?
options: Four methods need four separate conditions
The ticket class should be turned into a proxy for another object
The same check in every method signals state-dependent behaviour
The paid flag should be removed from the class and the checks dropped
optionExplain: Four separate conditions would miss the point: the repeat of one condition is the clue.
Turning the ticket into a proxy for another object does not address the repeated check.
Right: this is the State signal.
Removing the flag loses information.
questions.explain: The same paid check repeated in four methods signals state-dependent behavior, which the State pattern removes by giving each state its own class. Spot the repeated condition.
questions.rule: When one internal condition is tested in several methods, consider moving each condition's behaviour into a state.
questions.teaches: A condition tested in every method is a sign that the object's behaviour depends on its state, which is where the State Pattern fits.

questions.q: When does the real image replace the loading message?
options: At the instant the user picks a title from the menu
Before the download of the image has begun
Only after the whole window has been closed
At the next paint after the ImageIcon is created
optionExplain: At the instant the user picks a title nothing has loaded yet, so there is no image to show.
Before the download has begun there is no image to show, so that is too early.
Waiting until the window closes is too late, because the image should appear as soon as it is ready.
Right: the image replaces the message at the next paint after the ImageIcon is created.
questions.explain: The real image replaces the loading message at the next paint after the ImageIcon is created, not before the download begins or after the window closes. The card next walks through it.
questions.rule: Next paint after loading.

questions.q: Put the events in order.
items: paintIcon() is called and the proxy starts a thread
The thread retrieves the image
The ImageIcon is fully created
The next paintIcon() delegates to the ImageIcon
questions.explain: The first paint starts the work; the later paint shows the result.
questions.rule: Start, load, create, delegate.

questions.q: Why can the user resize the window while the image is loading?
options: The window is closed for the duration of loading
A separate thread does the loading work
The image has already been loaded by that time
The proxy deletes the loading message from the screen
optionExplain: The window stays open.
Right: the thread keeps the window responsive.
The image has not arrived yet.
The message is still shown.
questions.explain: A thread keeps the display alive.
questions.rule: The first paint starts a background load; the first paint after it finishes shows the real image.
questions.teaches: The retrieval runs in a separate thread, so the window stays responsive while the image loads.

questions.q: A photo finishes loading at 3 seconds. The display next paints at 5 seconds. When does the real photo appear?
options: At 3 seconds, before any paint
At the first paint, before loading
Only when the proxy is recreated
At the 5 second paint
optionExplain: Arrival alone does not paint.
That paint showed the message.
No recreation is needed.
Right: the next paint after loading.
questions.explain: The paint call delivers the image.
questions.rule: Paint delivers the image.

questions.q: True or false: If loading ran on the same thread that paints the display, the window could hang while waiting.
questions.explain: That is the hang the thread avoids.
questions.rule: A thread avoids the hang.

questions.q: In a virtual proxy, who decides when the costly real subject gets created?
options: The remote registry creates it as soon as the program starts
The proxy creates it itself, once the first real need arrives
The client must create it before it builds the proxy
The real object creates itself and then tells the proxy
optionExplain: A registry belongs to remote proxies; it does not decide when a virtual proxy's subject is created.
Right: the proxy owns the decision and creates the real subject only when the first real need arrives.
If the client created it first, the creation cost would be paid up front and the proxy would have nothing to delay.
The real object does not exist yet, so it cannot create itself or tell the proxy anything.
questions.explain: The virtual proxy owns the creation decision: it stands in at first and creates the real subject only when a real need, such as the first paint, arrives. That is how it avoids the creation cost until then.
questions.rule: The virtual proxy decides when to create the real subject.
questions.teaches: A virtual proxy itself decides when to create the real subject, doing so on the first real need instead of at construction.

questions.q: A decorator and a proxy both forward calls to another object. What mainly separates them?
options: Their position in the class hierarchy of the program
Whether they implement an interface of their own
Their purpose: one adds, the other controls access
The number of methods that they forward to the subject
optionExplain: The hierarchy does not decide it.
Both implement the same interface.
Right: intent decides.
Method count does not separate them.
questions.explain: The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Intent separates them.

questions.q: A decorator adds ____ to a class, while a proxy controls access to it.
questions.explain: Adding behaviour is the decorator's job.
questions.rule: Decorator adds; proxy controls.

questions.q: Which statement fits the authors' view of the loading message in ImageProxy?
options: It adds behaviour, but its main role is controlling access
It makes ImageProxy a decorator, since it adds behaviour
It shows that the proxy has no real subject of its own to guard
It proves a proxy must change the interface
optionExplain: Right: the main role is access control.
The authors say the more important role is access control.
ImageProxy does have a real subject to guard, which is the icon it loads.
The proxy keeps the interface.
questions.explain: ImageProxy's loading message adds behavior, but the authors see its more important role as controlling access to the icon, so it remains a proxy rather than becoming a decorator.
questions.rule: The authors judge by main intent: access control.
questions.teaches: The proxy decouples the client from the icon: the client need not wait for each image before painting its whole interface.

questions.q: One wrapper adds spell-check highlights to any text box. Another wrapper checks that the user has edit rights before passing a call to the text box. Which is which?
options: The first is a proxy and the second is a decorator
The first is a decorator; the second is a proxy
Both are decorators, since both wrap an object
Both are proxies, since both control access
optionExplain: That swaps them: the highlighting wrapper adds behavior and the rights check controls access.
Right: adds behaviour versus controls access.
The second wrapper controls access, which makes it a proxy, so both cannot be decorators.
The first wrapper adds behavior, which makes it a decorator, so both cannot be proxies.
questions.explain: A wrapper that adds spell-check highlights adds behavior, so it is a decorator, while one that checks edit rights before passing a call on controls access, so it is a proxy.
questions.rule: Behaviour is decorating; rights are proxying.

questions.q: True or false: Because a decorator and a proxy both implement the same interface as the object they forward to, the interface alone shows which one you have.
questions.explain: Both share the interface; the purpose tells them apart.
questions.rule: Purpose separates them.

questions.q: Sort each wrapper by the pattern it is.

items.t: Adds a timestamp to every message
Hides that the service runs on another machine
Shows a placeholder while a photo loads
Adds compression to a data stream
Restricts a record to its owner
Adds toppings to a drink order

questions.explain: Adding behaviour is decorating; controlling access is proxying.
questions.rule: Sort each wrapper by its intent.
questions.teaches: A proxy does not always wrap an existing object: its subject can be on another machine or not yet created, so wrapping is only an informal word for it.

questions.q: Which pattern changes the interface of the object it wraps?
options: Proxy
Decorator
State
Adapter
optionExplain: A proxy keeps the interface.
A decorator keeps the interface.
State is not a wrapper in this sense.
Right: an adapter converts the interface.
questions.explain: The card next compares the four.
questions.rule: Adapter changes the interface.

questions.q: Match each pattern to its description.
pairs: Wraps an object and adds behaviour
Wraps several objects to simplify their interface
Wraps an object to control access to it
Wraps an object and gives it a different interface
questions.explain: Each pattern has its own purpose.
questions.rule: Know the purposes.

questions.q: How can the book make clients use a proxy rather than the real subject?
options: A factory that wraps the subject in a proxy before returning it
Rename the subject so that clients can no longer find it
Make each client check whether it holds a proxy or the subject
Copy the proxy class into the code of every client
optionExplain: Right: the factory hands out the proxy.
Renaming does not redirect clients.
The client is meant not to care.
Copies spread the code.
questions.explain: A factory can return the proxy.
questions.rule: Same interface and access control is Proxy; different interface is Adapter; added behaviour is Decorator; simplified interface is Facade.
questions.teaches: A factory that creates the subject can wrap it in a proxy before returning it, so the client never knows.

questions.q: A class wraps a legacy PhoneBook so that it can be used where a Contacts interface is expected, converting method names. Which pattern is it?
options: Proxy
Decorator
Adapter
Facade
optionExplain: A proxy would keep the interface.
A decorator would add behaviour.
Right: it converts the interface.
A facade would simplify several objects.
questions.explain: A new interface means an adapter.
questions.rule: Different interface, Adapter.

questions.q: True or false: A protection proxy that exposes only some of a subject's methods can look similar to an adapter.
questions.explain: The book notes the resemblance for partial interfaces.
questions.rule: Partial interfaces blur the line.

questions.q: A class wraps five home-cinema objects and offers one method, startMovie(). Which pattern is it?
options: Adapter
Proxy
Facade
Decorator
optionExplain: No interface conversion is described.
No access control is described.
Right: it simplifies the interface of several objects.
No behaviour is added to one object.
questions.explain: Many objects, one simple interface, is a facade.
questions.rule: Same interface and access control is Proxy; different interface is Adapter; added behaviour is Decorator; simplified interface is Facade.
questions.teaches: Wrappers share forwarding, so the pattern is decided by what the wrapper is for, not by how it is built.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: Where would you put custom behaviour for a proxy class that Java generates at runtime?
options: In the source code of the proxy class itself
In a handler object that the proxy calls
In the interface that the proxy class implements
In the class loader that loads the proxy class
optionExplain: There is no source for the generated class.
Right: the handler holds the behaviour.
An interface holds no behaviour here.
The loader finds classes.
questions.explain: The card next explains the handler.
questions.rule: Behaviour goes in the handler.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: Java creates the proxy class at ____, which is why it is called a dynamic proxy.
questions.explain: The class does not exist until the program runs.
questions.rule: Dynamic means created at runtime.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: In RMI, what is the remote object's stub, according to the book's note?
options: A hand-written class that the rmic tool generated
A copy of the service's own source code sent to the client
An instance of the UnicastRemoteObject class
A Proxy instance from java.lang.reflect with a handler
optionExplain: Static stubs are deprecated.
Source is not shipped.
UnicastRemoteObject is the service's superclass.
Right: the stub is a dynamic proxy.
questions.explain: RMI itself uses a dynamic proxy.
questions.rule: RMI's stub is itself a dynamic proxy with a handler.
questions.teaches: Java's dynamic proxy is the mechanism RMI uses for its stub, so the remote proxy of this chapter is itself a dynamic proxy with an invocation handler.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: A team wants one access rule applied to calls on three different service interfaces without writing three proxy classes. Which Java feature fits?
options: A dynamic proxy with one handler applying the rule
Three subclasses of the real services, one per interface
A registry that holds the rule for each service
A serializable copy of each service on the client
optionExplain: Right: the handler holds the rule.
Three subclasses repeat the access rule in each class, which is the repeated work to avoid.
The registry maps names to stubs.
Serializable copies on the client carry no access rule at all.
questions.explain: A dynamic proxy with one handler applying the rule can be created for each of the three interfaces, so the rule is written once rather than in three proxy classes.
questions.rule: One handler can serve several proxies.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: True or false: To change what a dynamic proxy does, you edit the generated proxy class.
questions.explain: You change the handler; the proxy class is generated.
questions.rule: Change the handler.

questions.section: Using the Java API’s Proxy to create a protection proxy
questions.q: Before a program runs, does a proxy class for a Thermostat interface exist?
options: Yes; it is compiled ahead of time together with the interface
No; it is created on demand from the interfaces
Yes; it is stored in the registry beforehand
No; only the handler class exists
optionExplain: It is not compiled in advance.
Right: the proxy class is created on demand at runtime from the interfaces.
The registry does not store classes.
The proxy class does exist once it has been created, so more than the handler exists.
questions.explain: The proxy class for Thermostat does not exist before the program runs; it is created on demand from the interfaces, which is why it is called dynamic.
questions.rule: A dynamic proxy class does not exist until runtime.
questions.teaches: The proxy class does not exist before the program runs; it is created on demand from the set of interfaces you pass.

questions.q: On what does a protection proxy base its decision to let a call through?
options: The size of the object being called
The network speed between the two sides
The age of the object in memory
The access rights of the caller
optionExplain: The size of the object being called does not decide who may call it.
Network speed is a concern for remote proxies, not for protection proxies.
The age of the object in memory plays no part in access decisions.
Right: the caller's access rights decide whether a call goes through.
questions.explain: A protection proxy decides whether to let a call through by the access rights of the caller. The card next gives the idea.
questions.rule: Rights decide.

questions.q: A protection proxy controls access to an object based on access ____.
questions.explain: Different callers have different rights.
questions.rule: Rights decide.

questions.q: Match each caller to what the matchmaking service should allow.
pairs: May set own information, not own rating
May set the rating, not other information
questions.explain: The same method can be allowed for one caller and refused for another.
questions.rule: Rules depend on caller and method.
questions.teaches: The same method, setHotOrNotRating, is refused to the owner and allowed to others, so one rule list for everyone cannot work.

questions.q: A hospital record object lets a nurse read and add notes, a doctor also change the diagnosis, and a clerk read contact details only. Which proxy fits?
options: A protection proxy giving each role its rights
A virtual proxy deferring creation of the record
A remote proxy that reaches a record server
A caching proxy that keeps copies of old records
optionExplain: Right: rights per role.
Nothing here is about creation.
Nothing here is about distance.
Nothing here is about reuse.
questions.explain: Roles and rights point to protection.
questions.rule: Roles and rights mean protection.

questions.q: True or false: If every proxy allowed every call, a customer could rate himself.
questions.explain: That is the problem the protection proxy removes.
questions.rule: Without rules, anyone can rate.

questions.q: A designer hides setHotOrNotRating from everyone to stop self-rating. What is wrong with that?
options: The method has no effect on the stored ratings
Hiding methods from callers is not possible in Java
Other customers must still be able to rate
Ratings must be settable by every single caller
optionExplain: The method sets the stored rating, so it does have an effect on the ratings.
The issue is not what Java allows; the rule must depend on who is calling.
Right: the rule depends on the caller.
Some callers are not allowed.
questions.explain: Hiding setHotOrNotRating from everyone also stops other customers from rating, so the rule must depend on the caller as well as on the method.
questions.rule: A protection proxy lets each caller reach only the methods their role allows.
questions.teaches: Protection rules depend on both caller and method, so a single allow or deny list for everyone cannot do the job.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: How many proxies does the book create to protect PersonBean?
options: One proxy that serves all callers
Three, one for each of the getters
Two: one for owners, one for non-owners
None, since a handler alone is enough for this
optionExplain: One proxy cannot apply two rule sets.
The book does not create a proxy per getter; it makes one per relationship.
Right: two situations, two proxies.
A handler does nothing without a proxy that calls it, so a proxy is still needed.
questions.explain: The book creates two proxies to protect PersonBean, one for owners and one for non-owners, because there are two situations with different rules. The card next gives the plan.
questions.rule: Two situations, two proxies.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: Put the three steps in order.
items: Create two InvocationHandlers
Write the code that creates the dynamic proxies
Wrap any PersonBean in the appropriate proxy
questions.explain: Handlers first, then proxy creation, then wrapping.
questions.rule: Handlers, proxies, wrapping.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: What decides which proxy wraps a PersonBean when it is used?
options: Whether the user is the owner or a non-owner
Which getter happens to be called first
The size of the bean in memory when used
Which JVM the PersonBean object is running in
optionExplain: Right: the relationship decides.
Getters are allowed for both owners and non-owners, so the first getter does not choose a proxy.
The size of the bean in memory is not part of any access rule.
Which JVM the bean runs in is not what decides the proxy; the user's relationship is.
questions.explain: The choice of proxy depends on the user's relationship to the PersonBean, owner or non-owner. Getters are allowed in both, and size or location are not rules.
questions.rule: Make one proxy for the owner and another for the non-owner, and wrap the bean in whichever fits the situation.
questions.teaches: The same underlying bean is wrapped with a different proxy depending on who is looking at it.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: A library has members viewing their own accounts and staff viewing members' accounts, with different rights. By the book's approach, how many handlers does it need?
options: One, covering every kind of user
One for each method of the interface
None, since the handlers are enough
Two, one for each kind of relationship
optionExplain: One cannot hold both rule sets.
A handler covers all the methods of an interface, so one per method is unnecessary.
Handlers carry the rules, so having none is wrong.
Right: one per relationship.
questions.explain: The book's approach needs one handler per relationship, so a library with members and staff needs two handlers, one for each rule set.
questions.rule: One handler per relationship.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: True or false: If a third kind of user, such as an administrator, needed different rights, a third handler would be the natural addition.
questions.explain: Each distinct rule set gets its own handler.
questions.rule: New rule set, new handler.

questions.section: Big Picture: creating a Dynamic Proxy for the PersonBean
questions.q: Which of the three steps does Java do for you?
options: It writes the handlers for each relationship
It creates the proxy class and object
It decides who is an owner or a non-owner
It wraps each bean in the correct proxy for it
optionExplain: Handlers are supplied by you.
Right: Java creates the proxies.
The developer chooses.
Wrapping is done in your code.
questions.explain: You supply handlers; Java makes the proxy.
questions.rule: Make one proxy for the owner and another for the non-owner, and wrap the bean in whichever fits the situation.
questions.teaches: Java generates the proxy class and object, while the developer supplies the handlers and decides which proxy to use.

questions.q: When a method is called on a dynamic proxy, which method does the proxy call on its handler?
options: invoke()
The method with the same name
A method named forward()
The constructor of the handler
optionExplain: Right: invoke() receives every call.
The proxy does not call a method of the same name on the handler; it calls invoke().
No method named forward() exists in the handler interface.
The handler's constructor runs once when it is created, not on each call.
questions.explain: Every call on a dynamic proxy is passed to the handler's invoke() method, which receives the method and its arguments. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: One entry point.

questions.q: The InvocationHandler interface has one method, ____.
questions.explain: Every call arrives at invoke().
questions.rule: One method, invoke().

questions.q: What does the book's non-owner handler do with a call to setName()?
options: It passes the call on to the person object
It returns the person's name to the caller
It throws an IllegalAccessException
It restarts the proxy and tries the call again
optionExplain: Only setHotOrNotRating and getters pass.
setName is a set method.
Right: other set methods are refused.
Restarting is not described.
questions.explain: Allow get and the rating; refuse other sets.
questions.rule: The non-owner handler refuses by throwing.
questions.teaches: The non-owner handler lets get methods and setHotOrNotRating through, and refuses every other set method by throwing an IllegalAccessException.

questions.q: A guest handler lets methods starting with view through and refuses those starting with edit. Following the book's handler, what should it do on a call to editTitle()?
options: Pass the call to the document
Return the title of the document
Call invoke() again
Throw an IllegalAccessException
optionExplain: Passing the call to the document would allow the edit the guest must not make.
Returning the title would answer a different call and would not refuse editTitle().
Calling invoke() again would loop back into the same handler without refusing anything.
Right: a refused call throws an IllegalAccessException, as in the book's handler.
questions.explain: For a refused call such as editTitle(), the book's handler throws an IllegalAccessException instead of passing the call on. Throwing tells the caller the access is not allowed.
questions.rule: Refuse by throwing.

questions.q: True or false: A call to setName() on the proxy leads to a method called setName() on the invocation handler.
questions.explain: Every call arrives at invoke().
questions.rule: Names are not mirrored.

questions.q: Sort each call by whether the matchmaking handlers let it through.

items.t: A non-owner calls getName()
A non-owner calls setHotOrNotRating()
A non-owner calls setName()
An owner calls getName()
An owner calls setName()
An owner calls setHotOrNotRating()

questions.explain: Both handlers allow the getters; they differ in which setters pass.
questions.rule: invoke() lets some calls through and refuses others.
questions.teaches: Both handlers allow the getters; they differ only in which setters they let through.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: What makes a dynamic proxy dynamic?
options: Its handler is chosen at runtime
Its class is created when the program runs
It is instantiated while the program runs
It can change its interface later
optionExplain: The handler is chosen in code when the proxy is created, which is not what makes it dynamic.
Right: the class itself is created at runtime.
Any object is instantiated at runtime.
A dynamic proxy does not change its interface later; the interfaces are fixed at creation.
questions.explain: A dynamic proxy is dynamic because its class is created when the program runs, not because its handler or instance appears at runtime. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Dynamic means the class is made at runtime.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: The static method that creates a dynamic proxy is Proxy.____().
questions.explain: newProxyInstance returns the proxy.
questions.rule: newProxyInstance creates it.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: Which three things does newProxyInstance receive in the book's solution?
options: The registry, the stub and a socket to the server
The interface, the class and the skeleton
A name, an address and a port
The class loader, the interfaces and a handler
optionExplain: The registry, stub and socket belong to RMI, not to newProxyInstance.
The interface, class and skeleton mix unrelated parts and are not the arguments.
A name, address and port belong to an RMI lookup, not to creating a dynamic proxy.
Right: the class loader, the interfaces and a handler are the three arguments.
questions.explain: newProxyInstance receives the class loader, the interfaces to implement and the handler that will take the calls.
questions.rule: newProxyInstance takes loader, interfaces and handler.
questions.teaches: Because the proxy is built from the interfaces of the person's class, the result can be cast to PersonBean and used anywhere a PersonBean is expected.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: To protect a Thermostat object, which arguments should the creation call take?
options: The registry address, the thermostat's name and a port number
Its class loader, its interfaces and a handler for it
The skeleton, the stub and a socket for the thermostat
A Thermostat subclass, a handler and a state object to pass in
optionExplain: The registry address, name and port are lookup details, not arguments for creating the proxy.
Right: the thermostat's class loader, its interfaces and a handler are the three arguments.
The skeleton, stub and socket are RMI parts, not dynamic proxy arguments.
A subclass is not passed to the creation call; the proxy's class is generated from the interfaces.
questions.explain: The same three arguments, a class loader, the interfaces and a handler, are used to create a protecting proxy for any bean, including a Thermostat.
questions.rule: Loader, interfaces, handler.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: True or false: To switch from an owner proxy to a non-owner proxy for the same bean, only the handler argument needs to change.
questions.explain: The two methods differ only in the handler they pass.
questions.rule: Swap the handler.

questions.section: Step two: creating the Proxy class and instantiating the Proxy object
questions.q: A colleague says dynamic means the proxy's handler is attached at runtime. What does the book say?
options: The colleague is right; dynamic means a runtime handler
It is dynamic because the interfaces change at runtime
It is dynamic because the class is made at runtime
It is dynamic because the proxy runs in a new thread
optionExplain: The Q&A rejects this reading, so the colleague is not right.
The interfaces are fixed when the proxy is created and do not change at runtime.
Right: the class is created at runtime.
Threads are not mentioned as the reason for the name dynamic.
questions.explain: The book's Q&A says that dynamic refers to the class being created at runtime, not to a handler attached at runtime. So the colleague's reading is not what the book says.
questions.rule: Dynamic refers to the class made at runtime.
questions.teaches: Dynamic refers to the class, not the instance, so before the program runs there is no proxy class at all.

questions.q: True or false: newProxyInstance accepts both classes and interfaces in the array it is given.
questions.explain: Only interfaces are allowed. The card next lists the restrictions.
questions.rule: Interfaces only.

questions.q: The static method Proxy.____() returns true if a class is a dynamic proxy class.
questions.explain: isProxyClass tells you whether a class is a proxy class.
questions.rule: isProxyClass tests it.

questions.q: How does the book describe the InvocationHandler's relation to the proxy?
options: It is a class the proxy dispatches to, not a proxy itself
It is the proxy itself, implementing all the target's methods
It is the interface that the proxy class extends from
It is the class loader used to build the proxy
optionExplain: Right: the proxy dispatches to the handler.
The handler implements none of the target's methods.
The proxy implements the interfaces.
The loader is a separate argument.
questions.explain: The proxy is generated; the handler is yours.
questions.rule: Pass only interfaces, keep non-public ones in one package, and avoid interfaces with clashing methods.
questions.teaches: The handler does not implement the target's methods, which is why it can seem a strange proxy, since it is only the class the proxy dispatches to.

questions.q: Two interfaces, Printer and Scanner, both declare void start(). A developer passes both to newProxyInstance. What does the book's list of restrictions say?
options: It works, since interfaces cannot conflict with each other
It breaks the rule against clashing method signatures
It fails only if both of the interfaces are public
It works as long as one of them is turned into a class
optionExplain: Interfaces can conflict when they declare the same method signature, as Printer and Scanner do.
Right: clashing signatures are not allowed.
Public status is not the issue.
Only interfaces may be passed, so turning one into a class does not help.
questions.explain: Two interfaces that both declare void start() have a clashing method signature, which the book's list of restrictions does not allow in a single dynamic proxy.
questions.rule: No clashing signatures.

questions.q: True or false: Passing a public class instead of an interface is accepted by newProxyInstance.
questions.explain: Only interfaces are allowed, no classes.
questions.rule: No classes.

questions.q: Which of these requests break the documented restrictions? Select three.
options: Passing a concrete class in the array
Passing two interfaces whose methods share a signature
Passing two non-public interfaces from different packages
Passing one public interface
optionExplain: Right: only interfaces are allowed.
Right: clashes are not allowed.
Right: non-public ones must share a package.
A single public interface is acceptable.
questions.explain: The array may hold only interfaces, free of clashes, with non-public ones from one package.
questions.rule: Pass only interfaces, keep non-public ones in one package, and avoid interfaces with clashing methods.
questions.teaches: Because the book gives only the major restrictions and refers to the javadoc, you should check the fine print before relying on an unusual combination.

questions.q: True or false: Remote, virtual and protection proxies are the full list of proxy variants.
questions.explain: The book names several more. The card next gives the list.
questions.rule: The family is open.

questions.q: Like any wrapper, proxies will increase the number of ____ and objects in your designs.
questions.explain: More wrappers mean more classes and objects.
questions.rule: Wrappers add classes.

questions.q: What does the Proxy Zoo invite readers to do?
options: Replace the three named variants with a new one
Remove the cost of wrapping from large designs
Ban proxies from all large designs
Add their own observations of other proxies
optionExplain: The three named variants stay in the Zoo; readers add to them rather than replace them.
The cost of wrapping remains in large designs; the Zoo does not remove it.
The Zoo suggests no ban on proxies in large designs; it only invites more observations.
Right: field notes for further proxies.
questions.explain: The Proxy Zoo invites readers to add their own observations of other proxies, so the catalogue of variants is open rather than closed.
questions.rule: The family of proxies is open to readers' additions.
questions.teaches: The authors expect readers to meet proxy variants beyond those in the chapter, so the catalogue is deliberately left open.

questions.q: A team wants a proxy in front of every object in its app, because proxies are a pattern. Which point from the toolbox applies?
options: Each wrapper adds classes and objects, so be selective
Proxies remove classes and objects from a design
Proxies cost nothing once the first one exists in the design
A proxy should wrap each object ten times to be safe
optionExplain: Right: every wrapper adds classes and objects, so the team should be selective and weigh the cost.
Proxies add classes and objects to a design; they do not remove them.
Each additional proxy adds weight, so the cost does not vanish after the first.
Repeated wrapping is a warning sign.
questions.explain: Each proxy adds classes and objects, so a team should weigh the range of uses against the price of wrapping rather than wrap everything.
questions.rule: Use a proxy where access control earns it.

questions.q: True or false: If a design wraps many subjects in proxies, the number of classes and objects in the design grows.
questions.explain: That is the cost the toolbox names.
questions.rule: Wrappers add weight.

questions.q: A blog says Proxy has exactly three forms: remote, virtual and protection. Which chapter evidence shows that claim is incomplete?
options: The chapter shows only the remote proxy in any detail at all
The chapter says that virtual proxies are rare in practice
The toolbox lists caching and firewall proxies too
The chapter shows that protection proxies are really decorators
optionExplain: Detail is not the evidence.
Rarity is not claimed.
Right: other variants are listed.
That is not the book's view.
questions.explain: Check a claim against the chapter's own list.
questions.rule: The named three are examples, not an exhaustive list.
questions.teaches: A fair summary of Proxy treats remote, virtual and protection proxies as examples within a larger family, not as the whole of it.

questions.q: A design has several different recurring problems to solve. How might patterns be used?
options: Only one pattern can be used per design, because patterns compete for the same classes
Several patterns can be combined in one design, each handling a different part
Patterns work only when each one lives in a separate program from the others
The patterns must first be merged into one new class before they can cooperate
optionExplain: It sounds tidy, but patterns do not compete for classes; they are routinely layered.
Right: patterns can coexist and cooperate within the same solution.
Separation is not required; the chapter combines them in one program.
Patterns cooperate through their objects and interfaces; no merging step is needed.
questions.explain: Patterns are often combined in one design. The card next shows how the chapter does this.
questions.rule: Patterns can be used together in one design.

questions.q: Patterns are often used ____ and combined within the same design solution.
questions.explain: The chapter opens by saying patterns are often used together within one design solution.
questions.rule: Patterns are often used together.

questions.q: A museum app must show exhibits from an old catalogue format, and the team also wants every lookup counted. Which description fits the chapter's idea of patterns working together?
options: Choose either the converting pattern or the counting pattern, since one design holds only one
Build two separate apps so that the two patterns never have to meet each other
Replace both patterns with one large class that does the conversion and counting
One pattern converts the catalogue format and another does the counting
optionExplain: Nothing limits a design to one pattern; the chapter layers several.
Patterns are meant to meet; splitting the app avoids the lesson rather than applying it.
A single large class loses the separation each pattern gives.
Right: each need is met by a pattern suited to it, and the two live together.
questions.explain: The conversion need and the counting need are different, so each gets its own pattern, and the two work side by side.
questions.rule: Match each need with a fitting pattern and let them coexist.

questions.q: True or false: In the duck simulator, the patterns were introduced one at a time, each in response to a new request.
questions.explain: The goose, the counting, the missing wrap, the flock management and the observing each arrived as a new request, and each got its own pattern.
questions.rule: Patterns enter a design as needs appear.
questions.teaches: Patterns in the chapter appear in response to concrete requests (a goose, a counter, flock management), so each pattern can be traced back to the need it answered.

questions.q: A ticket gate class from an old system is adapted to a new Entry interface, and a logging wrapper that also implements Entry is placed around it. Why can the logging wrapper be placed around the adapted gate?
options: The adapter makes the gate an Entry, which the wrapper accepts
Both patterns come from the same pattern family, so they always stack
The gate class was changed to contain logging code first
The wrapper reads the gate's internals directly, skipping the interface
optionExplain: Right: patterns combine when the output of one is a type the next expects.
Family membership is not the reason; the shared interface is.
No change to the gate is needed; that is the benefit of wrapping.
A wrapper works through the interface, not by reading internals.
questions.explain: The adapter turns the old gate into something of the Entry type, and the wrapper can wrap any Entry. This shared interface is what lets the patterns stack.
questions.rule: Patterns stack when each one presents the interface the next one expects.
questions.teaches: Patterns combine smoothly when each presents the common interface the next expects, so an adapted object can still be wrapped by a decorator.

questions.q: A task is small and one ordinary class with clear methods solves it fully. What does the chapter's advice suggest about adding patterns?
options: Add several patterns anyway, so the design shows its quality
Add exactly one pattern per class, so that the design stays balanced across classes
Good object-oriented design may be enough; more patterns may be overkill
Wait until the code is finished, then wrap it in patterns
optionExplain: Patterns added for show add complexity without a need.
Counting patterns per class has no basis in the chapter.
Right: the authors warn that some parts of their own simulator would be overkill with patterns.
Patterns are applied where a need appears, not wrapped around finished code.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the rule has a boundary: patterns serve needs. When plain good design covers the need, more patterns only add weight.
questions.rule: Use a pattern only where a real need calls for it.

questions.q: What makes a group of patterns a compound pattern rather than patterns used together in one design?
options: It contains at least five patterns, so it is large enough to count
It was built by one team for one particular application
It solves a general problem that recurs across many designs
It was planned fully before any code was written
optionExplain: Size is not the test; the problem the combination solves is.
A one-off is exactly what is not compound.
Right: a compound pattern is a combination applied to a recurring or general problem.
Planning order does not decide what a pattern is.
questions.explain: The difference is generality. The card next gives the definition.
questions.rule: A compound pattern answers a general problem.

questions.q: A compound pattern combines two or more patterns into a solution that solves a recurring or ____ problem.
questions.explain: The definition ends with a recurring or general problem.
questions.rule: Compound means a combination applied to a general problem.

questions.q: A bookshop team uses an adapter for its payment service, a decorator for gift wrapping and a factory for orders, all tailored to that one shop. How do the authors' terms describe it?
options: Patterns working together, but not compound, as it serves one shop
A compound pattern, because it uses more than two patterns
A compound pattern, because the team wrote the code with great care
Neither, because patterns cannot be combined in a single shop
optionExplain: Right: it is a tailored combination, not a general-purpose solution.
Counting patterns does not decide it.
Care in writing is not the test.
Patterns can be combined; the shop just has no general problem.
questions.explain: The combination answers one shop's specific needs. It lacks the general-purpose quality that defines a compound pattern.
questions.rule: Ask whether the combination solves a general problem.

questions.q: Why do the authors treat Model-View-Controller as a compound pattern but not the duck simulator?
options: MVC combines more patterns than the simulator does in its design
MVC is older than each of the other patterns that it combines
The simulator contains several bugs that MVC does not have
MVC is reused in many designs; the simulator served one case
optionExplain: The simulator uses more patterns (six against three), so this cannot be the reason.
Age is not what the authors point to.
Bugs are not the issue; the point is generality.
Right: reuse across many designs for a general problem is what earns the name.
questions.explain: The authors describe MVC as a collection of a few patterns used over and over in many designs. Reuse for a general problem is what makes it compound.
questions.rule: A combination becomes compound by proving useful again and again.
questions.teaches: MVC uses only three patterns while the simulator uses six, which shows that the number of patterns plays no part in being compound.

questions.q: Sort each combination: patterns working together for one system, or a compound pattern.

items.t: An adapter plus a decorator around one firm's legacy label printer
A factory plus a singleton tuned for one game's level loader
A mix reused across many apps to keep display, input and data apart
A mix of observer and strategy documented as the standard answer to a widespread problem

questions.explain: The first two serve a single system. The last two answer a problem that recurs across many systems, which is what compound means.
questions.rule: Ask what problem the combination solves, and how widely that problem recurs.
questions.teaches: Test a combination by the problem it answers: a problem specific to one system gives a one-off, while one that recurs across systems can be named and reused.

questions.q: Which feature does NOT help decide whether a combination is a compound pattern?
options: Whether it combines at least two different patterns
Whether it has more than three patterns
Whether the problem it solves is recurring
Whether the solution is general-purpose
optionExplain: Two or more is part of the definition, so this does help decide.
Right: the count of patterns is not part of the definition.
A recurring problem is part of the definition.
General-purpose is the heart of the definition.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the definition needs two or more patterns and a general, recurring problem. Beyond two, the number of patterns does not matter.
questions.rule: Count of patterns is irrelevant; generality is not.

questions.q: A simulator must treat mallards, duck calls and rubber ducks alike, yet each makes its own sound. What helps most?
options: A shared interface that each class implements its own way
One big class with a switch on the duck type to pick the sound
Copying the same quack code into every one of the duck classes
Making every duck class inherit directly from the simulator
optionExplain: Right: one interface, many implementations.
It works but must be edited for every new duck; the interface avoids that.
Copies make each change a chore and do not give a common type.
The simulator is the user of ducks, not their parent.
questions.explain: A common interface lets the simulator treat all the ducks alike. The card next shows it.
questions.rule: One interface, many behaviors.

questions.q: In the rebuilt simulator, every duck, duck call and rubber duck implements the ____ interface.
questions.explain: The chapter starts by creating a Quackable interface for everything that can quack.
questions.rule: Things that can quack implement Quackable.

questions.q: A garden-irrigation program must switch on sprinklers, drip lines and misters, each in its own way. What fits the duck chapter's approach?
options: Write one controller method per device type, and edit it for each new type
Make all devices copy the same on code, even if they differ
Give them a shared interface with an on method, each implementing it
Ask the user to pick each device's code at install time
optionExplain: It grows with every device, which the shared type avoids.
The devices differ, so a copy would be wrong for some.
Right: a shared interface lets the controller treat them alike.
The user is not the right place to choose behavior.
questions.explain: The shared interface lets calling code stay the same while each device does its own thing, as with the ducks.
questions.rule: Program to the shared interface.

questions.q: The simulator calls quack() on a Mallard Duck and on a Rubber Duck. What does the chapter's example show about the results?
options: Both produce an identical sound, since they share the interface
Both are called through one interface; each sounds different
Only the first one quacks, because the interface allows one caller
The simulator must know each duck's class to call the correct sound
optionExplain: The interface shares the call, not the behavior.
Right: same call, different behavior.
The interface lets many classes respond.
The simulator does not need to know; the interface hides it.
questions.explain: The note in the chapter says all implement the same interface, but implementations allow them to quack in their own way. The caller never checks which kind it has.
questions.rule: Same call, different behavior.
questions.teaches: Because callers depend only on the interface, a new kind of quacker can be added without editing the simulator.

questions.q: A cafe app has a Drink interface with a price() method. A new seasonal drink is added. What must change in the till code that totals orders?
options: Every place that totals orders must add a case for the new drink
The Drink interface must be split in two
The till must be rewritten to ask each drink for its class name
Nothing, since the till works through the Drink interface
optionExplain: That is what the interface removes.
No reason to split it for a new implementer.
Asking for the class name ties the till to concrete types.
Right: new implementers do not disturb code written against the interface.
questions.explain: Code written to the interface keeps working when a new implementer arrives. This matters later, when wrappers are made to look like ducks too.
questions.rule: New implementers do not disturb code that uses the interface.
questions.teaches: Wrappers that implement the same interface can be dropped in anywhere a real object is expected, which the next ideas use repeatedly.

questions.q: True or false: A Goose class with a honk() method, but no quack() method, can be placed in the simulator's list of Quackables as it is.
questions.explain: The simulator only knows Quackable. A class that does not implement it does not fit until something adapts it.
questions.rule: A shared interface covers only what implements it.

questions.q: A Goose class has a honk() method, but the simulator only calls quack(). What would help the goose join in without changing Goose?
options: Rename honk() to quack() in the Goose class itself
A small class that has quack() and calls honk()
Teach the simulator to call honk() when it meets a goose
Keep geese out of the simulator for good
optionExplain: It would work here, but the goose would then be altered, and it may be used elsewhere.
Right: that is an adapter.
The simulator would need special cases for every foreign class.
The chapter wants geese in; the goal is to fit them.
questions.explain: A wrapper that translates the call is the pattern, covered next.
questions.rule: Wrap to translate.

questions.q: The class that makes a goose look like a Quackable follows the ____ Pattern.
questions.explain: The chapter says we need a goose adapter that adapts a goose to a duck.
questions.rule: An adapter translates between interfaces.

questions.q: A weather dashboard expects sensors with a read() method. A new thermometer library offers measure(). Which choice follows the chapter?
options: Edit the library code to rename measure() to read()
Change the dashboard so it calls measure() on thermometers only
Make the dashboard skip any sensor lacking read()
Write a wrapper with read() that calls measure()
optionExplain: Library code is often not yours to change.
The dashboard would need a special case for each foreign sensor.
The new sensor would then never show up.
Right: the adapter implements the expected interface and delegates.
questions.explain: The wrapper hides the difference and leaves both the dashboard and the library untouched.
questions.rule: Adapt, do not edit.

questions.q: After the goose is wrapped in its adapter and added to the list of Quackables, what does a quack() call on the adapter produce?
options: A honk, since the adapter passes the call to the goose
A silent result, because geese cannot quack
A normal duck quack, because the adapter holds duck code
An error, since Goose lacks quack()
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says the wrapped goose will honk.
The adapter translates the call, so there is a sound.
The adapter holds no duck code; it holds the goose.
The adapter supplies quack(), so no error occurs.
questions.explain: The adapter turns quack() into the goose's own sound. The simulator never learns it is talking to a goose.
questions.rule: The adapter hides which class is behind the interface.
questions.teaches: The client cannot tell an adapted object from a native one, which is what lets foreign classes mix in with native ones.

questions.q: A fitness app expects every Workout to have start() and stop(). A third-party rowing machine class has begin() and end(). Which adapter design is sound?
options: A subclass of the machine that overrides begin() so that it behaves as start()
A new Workout interface that takes begin() and end() in place of the old calls, for every workout
A Workout class that holds the machine and maps start() and stop() to it
A flag in the app that treats rowing as a special case
optionExplain: This adds start() but the machine may be final or in use elsewhere, and it does not implement Workout.
Changing the interface forces every other workout to change.
Right: it implements the expected interface and delegates to the machine.
Special cases spread through the app, the opposite of adapting.
questions.explain: The adapter is one small class; the app and the machine class both stay as they were.
questions.rule: The adapter lives between the client and the foreign class.
questions.teaches: An adapter holds the foreign object and delegates to it, so the foreign class stays unchanged and can still be used on its own elsewhere.

questions.q: True or false: If the adapter is given a Goose that has no honk() method, the adapter can still make it honk.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: an adapter translates calls to methods the wrapped object has. It cannot give the goose abilities it lacks.
questions.rule: An adapter reshapes the call, not the capability.

questions.q: You need to count every call to quack() on dozens of duck classes without editing them. What helps most?
options: Add a counting line to each of the duck classes by hand
Ask the Quackologists to count them by listening closely
A wrapper that counts, then passes the call to the duck
Make all ducks quack only once
optionExplain: It works but means editing every class, and the next new duck needs it too.
Listening is not a design and is unreliable.
Right: that is the decorator idea.
It stops the counting from being meaningful.
questions.explain: Wrapping adds the behavior outside the duck. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Add behavior by wrapping.

questions.q: The QuackCounter adds counting by ____ the duck it decorates.
questions.explain: A decorator wraps the object and delegates the call to it.
questions.rule: A decorator wraps and delegates.

questions.q: A bakery system has an Oven interface with bake(). The owner wants a count of bakes without editing the oven classes. Which fits?
options: An Oven class that counts, then calls the wrapped oven's bake()
An Oven class that counts bakes but does not call the wrapped oven
A new Oven interface with a counter added to the interface
A global counter that each oven class increments itself
optionExplain: Right: count, then delegate.
Without delegating, nothing is baked.
Every oven class would then need to change.
Each oven class would need editing.
questions.explain: The counter wraps an existing oven, adds one, and passes bake() through to the real thing.
questions.rule: Count first or after, but always delegate.

questions.q: True or false: The QuackCounter must call the wrapped duck's quack() or the duck will not quack.
questions.explain: The decorator delegates the quack to the Quackable it wraps. Without delegation the wrapped duck is never asked to quack.
questions.rule: A decorator must pass the call on.
questions.teaches: A decorator that forgets to delegate swallows the call, so the decorated object silently stops doing its own job.

questions.q: A streaming app wants to time how long each video load takes, without editing the loader classes that share a Loader interface. Which design follows the chapter?
options: A timing class that replaces each loader and reimplements the loading itself
A timing method added to every loader class
A timing class outside the Loader type that watches the screen for changes
A Loader that starts a clock, calls the wrapped loader, then stops it
optionExplain: It would duplicate loading logic in one place and drop the loaders.
It edits every class, which decorating avoids.
It would not see the calls.
Right: it adds timing around the delegated call.
questions.explain: Behavior added around a delegated call is the decorator idea, whether it counts quacks or times loads.
questions.rule: Wrap, add behavior, delegate.
questions.teaches: A decorator can add behavior before the delegated call, after it, or both, so counting and timing are the same shape.

questions.q: True or false: A duck that is created and left unwrapped by a QuackCounter still has its quacks counted.
questions.explain: Only wrapped objects get the decorated behavior. An unwrapped duck quacks uncounted, which the next idea takes up.
questions.rule: Only wrapped objects are decorated.

questions.q: You add counting through a wrapper. What is the risk when ducks are created in many places in the code?
options: The wrapper will count each of the quacks twice over
Some ducks may be created unwrapped, so their quacks go uncounted
The ducks will stop quacking when they are wrapped
The wrapper changes the duck classes permanently
optionExplain: Wrapping does not double the count by itself.
Right: you have to decorate objects to get decorated behavior.
A wrapped duck still quacks; the issue is missing wrappers.
Wrappers do not change the duck classes.
questions.explain: The weakness is forgetting to wrap. The card next shows the fix.
questions.rule: Wrapping can be forgotten.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about wrapping ducks in QuackCounter? Select all that apply.
options: Every Quackable must be wrapped when created
An unwrapped duck still quacks but is not counted
A wrapped duck stops being a Quackable
Wrapping is optional, since all quacks are counted anyway
optionExplain: Right: otherwise it is not counted.
Right: it works but makes uncounted quacks.
It stays a Quackable, which is why the wrapper fits.
Counting only happens through wrappers.
questions.explain: The decorator only counts what it wraps. So every creation site must wrap.
questions.rule: Count only what is wrapped.

questions.q: A school system adds an audit wrapper to each Grade-change handler. Handlers are created in six different screens. What is the main risk?
options: A screen that makes a handler without the wrapper skips auditing
The audit wrapper will change the grades that it records
The screens will all share one handler, causing conflicts
The handler interface will stop working for every screen
optionExplain: Right: each creation site is a place to forget.
The wrapper only records; the risk is missing wrappers.
Nothing here shares handlers.
The interface is unaffected.
questions.explain: With creation in six places, any one can forget. Localizing creation removes that risk.
questions.rule: The more creation sites, the more chances to forget.

questions.q: What do the authors propose to make sure every duck gets wrapped?
options: Add a rule in the team handbook that says to remember the wrapping
Move the counting into each duck class instead
Create and decorate ducks in one place
Stop creating ducks and reuse one duck instead
optionExplain: A rule can be forgotten as well as the wrapper.
This reintroduces editing every duck.
Right: encapsulate creation and decoration together.
One duck cannot represent a flock.
questions.explain: The text says to take creation and decorating and encapsulate them in one place. The next idea names the pattern.
questions.rule: Put creation and decoration in one place.
questions.teaches: Putting construction and decoration in one place turns a convention people must remember into a structure that does it for them.

questions.q: A game wraps every enemy in a Shield wrapper when it spawns, but enemies spawn from eight scripts. Which change best removes the weakness the chapter describes?
options: Ask each script author to add the shield themselves
Create every enemy through one spawn function that adds the shield
Give enemies a shield attribute that each script may choose to ignore
Remove the shields from the game
optionExplain: Eight authors can each forget.
Right: one place creates and decorates, so nothing is missed.
Optional behavior is the weakness again.
Drops the feature instead of securing it.
questions.explain: A single creation point makes the wrapping automatic. This is the job of the factory in the next idea.
questions.rule: Centralize creation to centralize decoration.
questions.teaches: A central creation point means the decorating rule exists in one place, so a change to it takes effect everywhere at once.

questions.q: True or false: The risk of an unwrapped duck is smallest when one function creates every duck and applies the wrapper itself.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the risk grows with the number of places that create objects. With a single creation point, no site is left to forget.
questions.rule: One creation point removes the risk.

questions.q: Every duck must come out of creation already wrapped in a counter. Where should the wrapping happen?
options: At every single place in the code that needs a duck
Inside each duck class's own constructor
In a note that tells the Quackologists to wrap them
Inside one factory that creates the ducks and wraps them
optionExplain: Every place then has a chance to forget.
A duck cannot wrap itself in an outside object.
Notes can be ignored; a factory cannot be bypassed if used.
Right: a factory that creates and wraps leaves nothing to forget.
questions.explain: A single creating place can do the wrapping. The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: Create and wrap in one place.

questions.q: The CountingDuckFactory is an example of the ____ Factory Pattern.
questions.explain: The chapter calls it the Abstract Factory Pattern: a family of products, here duck types.
questions.rule: Abstract Factory makes families of related objects.

questions.q: A shop sells phone cases in plain and gift-wrapped variants. The ordering code should work with either kind. Which design follows the chapter?
options: Give the ordering code a flag, and test the flag before each case it makes
Give the ordering code a factory, plain or gift-wrapping, to use
Write one copy of the ordering code per variant
Let customers wrap the cases after delivery
optionExplain: The flag spreads through the code, and each new variant needs more tests.
Right: the same code gets a different product from a different factory object.
Copies drift apart and double the maintenance.
It moves the wrapping outside the design and may not happen.
questions.explain: The ordering method is polymorphic in the factory. Passing a different factory selects a different product family.
questions.rule: Swap the factory, keep the code.

questions.q: In the simulator, simulate() now receives a factory. How can the same simulate() produce counted ducks in one run and uncounted in another?
options: It reads a counting setting from each of the ducks that it creates
It checks whether the Quackologists are watching at the time
It rewrites its own code between the two runs of the program
It gets a CountingDuckFactory in one run, a DuckFactory in another
optionExplain: The ducks do not decide; the factory does.
Observers play no part in creation.
Code does not rewrite itself here.
Right: the factory chooses the product family.
questions.explain: Because simulate() asks the factory for ducks, which factory it holds decides whether ducks are wrapped. The method itself is unchanged.
questions.rule: The factory object picks the family.
questions.teaches: Choosing behavior by handing in a different factory means the creating code can stay unchanged while whole families of objects change.

questions.q: A messaging app builds Message objects. For a test run, all messages should be recorded, and for the live app they should not. Which design matches the chapter?
options: Give the message builder a recording factory in tests, a plain one live
Add a recording flag to the Message class and check it inside each of its methods
Have testers record the messages by hand
Build the live app and the test app from two unrelated code bases that never share
optionExplain: Right: the same builder code, a different factory per setting.
It mixes testing logic into the class itself.
Manual recording is slow and unreliable.
Two code bases double the work and drift apart.
questions.explain: The factory keeps the choice of wrapped or plain objects out of the building code. This is the same shape as counting and plain duck factories.
questions.rule: Keep the choice of product family in the factory.
