questions.teaches: A factory can also build test or recording variants of a whole family, so swapping the factory swaps the environment without touching the user of the objects.

questions.q: True or false: A duck made by calling new MallardDuck() directly inside simulate() is wrapped by the CountingDuckFactory.
questions.explain: The factory only wraps ducks it creates. A duck made directly with new never goes through it.
questions.rule: A factory protects only what it creates.

questions.q: A duck factory wraps every duck, but geese are created directly in the simulator. What is the gap?
options: Geese cannot be adapted to Quackable by any means
The factory makes too many ducks at one time
Geese avoid the factory, so they miss its treatment
The simulator no longer compiles without errors
optionExplain: They can; the chapter does this with an adapter.
The gap is about what the factory leaves out.
Right: only objects created through the factory benefit from it.
It compiles; the issue is coverage.
questions.explain: The factory covers ducks only. The card next shows what the authors suggest.
questions.rule: Objects outside the factory miss its protection.

questions.q: The authors suggest adding a createGoose____ method to the existing duck factories.
questions.explain: The method is createGooseDuck(): it returns a goose already wrapped to behave like a duck.
questions.rule: Add creation methods to cover all products.

questions.q: A café has a CupFactory that sleeves every cup it produces, but lids are made directly by staff. What would the chapter's approach do?
options: Stop sleeving cups to match the lids
Ask staff to be more careful whenever they make or fit the lids
Add a lid method to the factory, or make a separate lid factory
Make the cup factory return lids in place of the cups it makes now
optionExplain: This drops the feature rather than covering the gap.
Care is not a structure, and the point is to stop relying on it.
Right: bring the leftover products under a factory.
It would break the cup factory.
questions.explain: The authors give two options: extend the factory, or add a separate one. Either brings the missed objects under creation control.
questions.rule: Cover every product with a factory.

questions.q: Which pair of fixes do the authors give for creating goose ducks through a factory?
options: Add a goose-duck method to the duck factories, or make a goose factory
Delete the goose adapter, or rename honk() to quack() in the Goose class
Create geese in the Quackologist class, or in each duck class
Wrap each goose in a counter by hand, or ban geese from the simulator
optionExplain: Right: the solution lists exactly these two routes.
Neither fix addresses how geese are created.
Neither location is suggested, and both scatter creation.
Hand wrapping is what the factory exists to avoid.
questions.explain: The authors accept either route. Both put goose creation under a factory so the wrapping cannot be missed.
questions.rule: More than one design can close the same gap.
questions.teaches: A gap in coverage can be closed more than one way, here by extending the existing factories or adding a separate one, so a critic should name the gap rather than insist on one fix.

questions.q: A hospital app wraps every Prescription in an audit record through a factory, but Lab Orders are created directly in many screens. What is the critique?
options: The design is complete, since prescriptions are audited
The audit record is useless, because factories cannot audit orders
The prescriptions should be created directly like the Lab Orders
The audit guarantee has a gap: Lab Orders escape the factory
optionExplain: The gap is in what is left out.
A factory can wrap; the issue is coverage.
It would remove the guarantee for prescriptions too.
Right: the design is incomplete until Lab Orders pass through creation control.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a guarantee made by a factory holds only for objects it creates. Finding what is left out is a way to judge a design's completeness.
questions.rule: Look for objects that escape the guarantee.
questions.teaches: Judging a design for completeness means listing the objects it should cover and checking each one passes through the mechanism.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter's own duck factory already covers every object in the simulator.
questions.explain: The authors point out that geese are still created by concrete classes, which leaves a gap they ask the reader to close.
questions.rule: Check coverage before calling a design complete.

questions.q: You want to tell a whole group of ducks to quack with a single call, and group them into families. What helps?
options: A loop in the main program that handles ducks one by one every time
A group that is itself quackable and passes calls to its members
A giant duck class that quacks many times at the same moment
A list the Quackologists maintain by hand
optionExplain: It repeats everywhere and cannot hold family sub-groups.
Right: that is a composite.
It cannot represent distinct members or sub-groups.
A hand list does not respond to quack().
questions.explain: A group object that looks like a single duck is the composite. The card next gives the pattern.
questions.rule: Groups can look like single items.

questions.q: A Flock implements Quackable and holds a list of ____.
questions.explain: The flock holds Quackables, which may be ducks or other flocks.
questions.rule: A composite holds components of its own type.

questions.q: A photo app has Photo and Album, where an Album holds photos or other albums. The user taps Print on any of them. What does the composite design say happens for an Album?
options: The album passes the print call to every photo and sub-album
The album prints a cover page and then ignores its whole contents
The app must check each item's type before printing
Only the first photo in the album prints, then it stops
optionExplain: Right: the call goes down through the children.
A composite exists to apply operations to the whole set.
The common interface removes that check.
The call must reach every member.
questions.explain: The Album implements the same print as a Photo. It delegates to its members, which may be albums themselves.
questions.rule: Pass the call to every child.

questions.q: In a flock, one member is itself a flock of mallards. When quack() is called on the outer flock, what happens?
options: Only the outer flock's direct ducks quack
The inner flock counts as one quack, whatever its size
The inner flock gets the call and passes it to its mallards
The call is blocked because a flock cannot contain another flock inside it
optionExplain: The inner flock is a member, so it gets the call.
It passes the call on rather than counting once.
Right: the call recurses down the nesting.
Nesting is the whole point; flocks can contain flocks.
questions.explain: Because a flock is itself a Quackable, it can be a member of another flock. Calls travel down through every level.
questions.rule: Nesting works because a composite looks like a component.
questions.teaches: Because a composite is itself a component, nesting to any depth needs no extra code; each level simply passes the call down.

questions.q: A company chart has Employee and Department, where a Department holds employees or sub-departments. Payroll must compute total salary for any of them. Which composite design fits?
options: Only Employee has totalSalary(), and the app loops to add up departments
Both have totalSalary(); a department adds up its members' totals
Department ignores sub-departments and sums only direct employees
Each Department stores a number that is typed in by hand
optionExplain: The app then handles each level separately.
Right: the same call works on an employee or a whole department.
Totals would miss nested members.
A typed number drifts away from the real members.
questions.explain: The department treats its members like the employee does, and sums what they return. The caller needs no knowledge of structure.
questions.rule: Give parts and wholes the same interface.
questions.teaches: A composite can combine results as well as pass calls down, such as summing a value over all members.

questions.q: True or false: A goose wrapped in its adapter can be added to a flock, and it honks when the flock is told to quack.
questions.explain: The adapted goose is a Quackable, and a flock holds Quackables, so the call reaches it and it honks.
questions.rule: Anything that is a Quackable can join a flock.

questions.q: In a composite, should leaf objects have the same add() method as composite objects?
options: Yes, because composites need the same methods on all of their nodes
No, never, because leaves have no children
It does not matter, because clients never call add()
It depends on weighing safety against uniform treatment
optionExplain: Uniformity has a cost: nonsense calls become possible.
Removing it costs transparency, which can matter more.
Clients do call add(); that is where the choice shows.
Right: each choice gains one thing and loses the other.
questions.explain: There is a trade-off. The card next names the two sides.
questions.rule: Each choice has a price.

questions.q: Match each design choice with what it gives.
pairs: Safer: nonsense calls cannot be made
Transparent: the client need not know which it holds
Must know the object is a Flock
questions.explain: Safety comes from keeping add() off leaves; transparency comes from keeping the same methods everywhere.
questions.rule: Safety and transparency pull in opposite directions.

questions.q: In a drawing app, Shape and Group (which holds shapes) share a draw() call. The designer must decide whether Shape also gets an addChild() method. Which choice favors safety?
options: Both have addChild(), and Shape throws an error when it is used
Only Group has addChild(), so a plain Shape cannot be given a child
Neither has addChild(), and groups cannot be edited
Both have addChild(), and Shape silently ignores the call
optionExplain: The error appears at run time, and the call is still possible.
Right: nonsense calls are blocked.
Groups then become unusable.
Allowed nonsense calls hide mistakes.
questions.explain: Keeping addChild() on Group alone stops meaningless calls from being written at all. That is the safer design.
questions.rule: Safety means impossible mistakes.

questions.q: What does a client of the safe flock design need to know that a client of the fully uniform design does not?
options: How many ducks the flock contains right now
Which sound each of the ducks makes
The order in which all of the ducks were created
Whether the Quackable it holds is a Flock
optionExplain: The size is not needed in either design.
Sounds are hidden behind the interface in both.
Order of creation is not at issue.
Right: that is the lost transparency.
questions.explain: The uniform design lets the client treat any node alike, leaf or composite. The safe design makes the client check, or know, before adding.
questions.rule: Safety costs knowledge in the client.
questions.teaches: In a fully uniform design, a meaningless call such as add() on a leaf can be written, so the safe design buys protection at the price of a client that must know what it holds.

questions.q: A form builder has Field and Section (which holds fields). Many developers will use it, and a mistaken addChild() on a Field would be costly. The team decides mistakes matter more than uniform treatment. Which choice fits the safety side of the authors' trade-off?
options: Leaning toward safety, so only Section can add children
Leaning toward transparency, so Field gets a matching addChild() that throws
Leaning toward neither, since one choice is correct for every design
Deciding at random, since the choice has no consequences
optionExplain: Right: when mistakes are costly, prefer to make them impossible.
The mistake would still be possible, and found only at run time.
The authors say trade-offs exist in every design.
It does have consequences, as the card describes.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the trade-off is settled by what matters more in your design. Here, costly mistakes tip it toward safety.
questions.rule: Let the cost of mistakes guide the choice.
questions.teaches: There is no universal answer; the balance between safety and transparency is a decision about which cost your own design can better bear.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the safe design is better than the transparent design in every case.
questions.explain: They say there are trade-offs in OO design and the choice must be considered for your own composites.
questions.rule: Weigh the trade-off; there is no automatic winner.

questions.q: Researchers want to be told each time a given duck quacks, without polling the duck. What helps?
options: The researchers ask every duck once a minute whether it quacked
The duck writes its quacks into a file that nobody reads
The duck keeps registered watchers and notifies them per quack
The duck waits until the researchers ask it to quack
optionExplain: Polling wastes effort and can miss quacks.
Unread output tells no one.
Right: that is the Observer Pattern.
The researchers want to follow natural quacks.
questions.explain: Registering watchers is the pattern. The card next gives its parts.
questions.rule: Register once, hear every time.

questions.q: An Observable needs methods for registering and ____ observers.
questions.explain: The text says an Observable needs methods for registering and notifying observers.
questions.rule: Observables register and notify.

questions.q: A trading app lets screens register with a Stock object so that they update when its price changes. Which role does Stock play?
options: Observer, the object that waits to be told when things change
Decorator, the wrapper that adds new behavior to an object
Observable, the watched object that notifies the screens
Adapter, which converts one interface into another one
optionExplain: The screens are the observers.
Nothing here wraps another object.
Right: Stock is the thing observed.
No interface translation is happening.
questions.explain: The screens register interest, and Stock tells them. That makes Stock the observable and the screens the observers.
questions.rule: The observed object notifies; observers register.

questions.q: True or false: In the chapter's version, a Quackologist that has not registered with a duck is still notified when the duck quacks.
questions.explain: Only registered observers are notified. Registration is how an observer says which observable it wants to follow.
questions.rule: Register to be notified.
questions.teaches: Observers choose their subjects by registering, so one Quackologist can follow some ducks and ignore others.

questions.q: A smart-home hub has doors that report when they open. A lamp, an alarm and a logger each want to know. Which design matches the chapter?
options: Each door keeps registered devices and notifies them on opening
Each device checks every door constantly to see if it opened
The door calls only the alarm, which then calls the others by hand
The door stores a log and each device reads it once a day
optionExplain: Right: one event, many registered listeners.
The devices poll, which is what observers avoid.
The door would depend on one chosen device.
Notifications would arrive far too late.
questions.explain: The door does not need to know what its watchers do. It tells all registered ones, and adding a new device means registering it.
questions.rule: The observable knows only that it has observers.
questions.teaches: The observable needs no knowledge of what its observers do with the news, so new kinds of observers can be added by registering them.

questions.q: A new Quackologist registers with a duck after the duck has already quacked twice. According to the registration model, what will it be told?
options: Both earlier quacks and every later one
Nothing at all, since the duck has already quacked
Only the first earlier quack
Only the quacks made after it registered
optionExplain: Registration does not replay history.
Later quacks will still notify it.
There is no rule that replays any past quack.
Right: notifications go to those registered at the time.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Notifications happen at the time of each quack, to whoever is then registered. A late registrant hears only what follows.
questions.rule: Observers hear what happens after they register.

questions.q: Twelve classes must each let observers register and be notified. How can the registering code be written only once?
options: Paste the same code into each one of the twelve classes
Put it in a helper that each class holds and delegates to
Make the twelve classes share one global list of observers
Make the observers poll all twelve classes
optionExplain: It works at first, and then each fix must be made twelve times.
Right: composition with delegation.
All observers would hear about every class.
The point is to be told, not to poll.
questions.explain: A helper holds the code once. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Write the shared part once.

questions.q: Each Quackable is composed with a helper Observable and ____ registration and notification to it.
questions.explain: The Quackable classes delegate the real work to the helper.
questions.rule: Delegate to the helper.

questions.q: A shared Counter helper holds the code for counting events. Six sensor classes should use it. Which design fits the chapter?
options: Each sensor holds a Counter and delegates count calls to it
Each sensor copies the Counter code into its own class
Each sensor extends Counter and so cannot extend anything else
The sensors share one static count that nobody owns
optionExplain: Right: composition plus delegation.
Six copies defeat the purpose of the helper.
Inheritance for reuse ties each class to one parent.
One shared count mixes all sensors together.
questions.explain: The helper keeps the code in one place. Each sensor only needs a field and a few delegating methods.
questions.rule: Compose with a helper rather than copy it.

questions.q: When Quackable is changed to extend QuackObservable, what must happen to the QuackCounter decorator?
options: Nothing, because decorators are exempt from interface changes
It must be removed, since it cannot be observed
It must implement the observable methods too, as a Quackable
It must be turned into a Duck class first
optionExplain: A decorator implements the interface, so it must follow.
It can be observed once it implements the methods.
Right: every class implementing Quackable must follow the change.
It stays a decorator.
questions.explain: The QuackCounter is a Quackable too, so changing the interface forces a change to it, as the solution to the exercise says.
questions.rule: Interface changes reach every implementer.
questions.teaches: A change to a widely implemented interface reaches every implementer, including wrappers such as decorators, so widening an interface is not free.

questions.q: A document editor has twelve widget classes that need undo support. A shared UndoLog class has the logic. Why might the team prefer holding an UndoLog over copying its code?
options: A widget with its own copy runs noticeably slower
A fix is made once and every widget gets it
Copied code cannot be compiled twice in one project
Widgets must be unrelated to each other to hold helpers
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue.
Right: one copy of the code means one place to fix.
Copies compile fine; they just drift.
Relatedness plays no role.
questions.explain: With delegation, there is one place to repair a bug or add a feature. With copies, each class must be edited.
questions.rule: Delegation keeps shared code in one place.
questions.teaches: Putting shared code in one helper means a defect is fixed once, whereas copies must each be found and fixed.

questions.q: True or false: If one Quackable class forgets to delegate its register call to the helper, observers who register with that class will still be notified.
questions.explain: Registration would never reach the helper that holds the list, so there would be nothing to notify.
questions.rule: Delegation must be complete for the helper to work.

questions.q: A flock contains ducks and a smaller flock. A researcher registers with the outer flock. What should the researcher be notified about?
options: Only the quacks of the ducks directly in the outer flock
Only the quack of the first duck in the flock's list
The number of ducks in the flock, but no quacks
Quacks of every duck in the outer flock and the smaller one
optionExplain: The smaller flock is also inside the outer one.
There is no reason to single out one duck.
The researcher wants the quacks.
Right: observing a composite means observing everything in it.
questions.explain: Registering with a composite covers its members. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Observe the whole by registering with the composite.

questions.q: When you register with a flock, the flock registers you with all its ____.
questions.explain: The solution says the flock makes sure you get registered with all its children.
questions.rule: The composite passes registration down.

questions.q: A school has a Building made of Floors, each made of Rooms, and a monitor can register for door-open events. The monitor registers with Building. What reaches the monitor?
options: Door-open events from the building's main entrance only
Door-open events from every room on every floor
Events only from floors, not from rooms
No events, since a monitor must register with each room
optionExplain: Only the top-level object would be covered.
Right: registration passes down to all members.
Rooms are children of floors and are covered too.
Registering with the composite saves doing so room by room.
questions.explain: The composite hands the registration down through floors to rooms, so the monitor hears about every room.
questions.rule: One registration covers the whole composite.

questions.q: How does a Quackologist's registering code for a flock compare with its code for a single duck?
options: It is longer, since the Quackologist must list each member of the flock
It is impossible, since only individual ducks can be observed
It is shorter, since flocks do not notify anyone
It is the same, since a flock is itself an observable Quackable
optionExplain: The flock handles the members, so the Quackologist lists none.
The chapter shows that flocks can be observed.
A registered observer is notified of the members' quacks.
Right: the flock presents the same interface as a duck.
questions.explain: A flock is a Quackable, and Quackable extends the observable interface, so the Quackologist treats a flock like a duck. The flock does the fan-out.
questions.rule: A composite lets one registration stand for many.
questions.teaches: Because the composite looks like a single observable, the observer's code does not change as flocks grow or nest more deeply.

questions.q: A shop chain has Region objects holding Store objects (and sub-regions). A manager wants every sale in a region. Which design echoes the chapter?
options: Registering with the region covers every store inside it
The manager registers with each store individually
The region alone reports sales and the stores stay silent about them
The manager polls every store in the chain each night
optionExplain: Right: registration is passed down through the composite.
It works, but nothing makes the composite useful.
The region has no way to know of sales except via stores.
Polling replaces the observer idea.
questions.explain: The region is a composite, so registering with it is the same as registering with each member beneath it.
questions.rule: Composite and observer fit together.
questions.teaches: Two patterns can cooperate on one request: the composite supplies the structure and the observer supplies the notification.

questions.q: True or false: A duck added to a flock before an observer registers with the flock will be covered by that registration.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Registration is passed down to the flock's members as they are at that time, and that includes ducks already in the flock.
questions.rule: Registration covers current members.

questions.q: A flock passes quack() to each member in turn. Which pattern is involved in stepping through the members?
options: Singleton, which keeps one instance only
Strategy, which swaps in alternative algorithms
Iterator, which walks through a collection
Proxy, which controls access to an object
optionExplain: Nothing here limits instances.
The flock's walk is not interchangeable behavior.
Right: the flock uses an iterator over its list.
No access control is involved in walking a list.
questions.explain: Walking a collection is the iterator's job. The card next shows where it appears.
questions.rule: Walking a collection is Iterator.

questions.q: The flock uses the Iterator Pattern through java.util's iterator in an ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says the Composite implementation uses the iterator of an ArrayList.
questions.rule: A collection class often provides the iterator.

questions.q: Which parts of the finished simulator step through a collection of objects, according to the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The goose adapter calling honk()
The factory creating a Mallard Duck
The flock passing quack() to its members
The Observable helper notifying its observers
optionExplain: It makes one call to one goose, with no collection.
It creates one object and walks nothing.
Right: the Composite implementation uses the iterator.
Right: iterator is used again there.
questions.explain: Both the flock and the Observable helper visit every element of a list. That is the iterator at work.
questions.rule: Iterator appears wherever code visits each item.

questions.q: True or false: The authors count the Iterator among the six patterns that came together in the finished simulator.
questions.explain: The recap lists Adapter, Decorator, Abstract Factory, Composite, Iterator and Observer, so Iterator is one of the six even though it answered no request of its own.
questions.rule: A pattern can be counted in a design without being a design decision.
questions.teaches: Five of the six patterns were chosen to answer visible requests, while the sixth, Iterator, came along with the collection classes, so a pattern can be present without anyone choosing it.

questions.q: A music app stores playlists in a list and plays each track by looping through it. A reviewer says the app uses a pattern without naming it. Which is the most plausible one?
options: Adapter, since the list converts one type of object into another type
Decorator, since each track gets some extra behavior as it plays
Iterator, as the loop visits each element, hiding the storage
Abstract Factory, since the loop creates the tracks it plays
optionExplain: Nothing is being converted.
Nothing wraps the tracks.
Right: stepping through a collection element by element is the Iterator idea.
The loop visits existing tracks.
questions.explain: The loop hides the storage details of the list while visiting every item. That is the essence of Iterator.
questions.rule: A loop over a collection is often Iterator.
questions.teaches: Familiar everyday code, such as a loop over a list, can be an instance of a named pattern, which is why learning patterns changes how you read existing code.

questions.q: Which statement fits the way the chapter treats the Iterator?
options: It works inside the Composite and Observer code, answering no request
It was added to the simulator in order to solve the problem with the goose
It replaces the Composite Pattern in the flock and takes over its work
It is the only pattern that the simulator needs for its design
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says iterator was used in both implementations.
The goose was solved by the Adapter.
It supports Composite; it does not replace it.
The chapter names several patterns.
questions.explain: The text says Composite uses the iterator of ArrayList and that iterator appears again in Observer. It supports those patterns.
questions.rule: Some patterns work inside others.

questions.q: In the duck simulator, which pattern was added so that quacks could be counted without changing the ducks?
options: Adapter
Composite
Observer
Decorator
optionExplain: The Adapter brought the goose in.
The Composite groups ducks into flocks.
The Observer lets Quackologists be notified of quacks, which is not the same as counting them.
Right: a QuackCounter wraps each Quackable.
questions.explain: The counter is a wrapper, so Decorator. The card next lines up all the patterns.
questions.rule: Match each need to its pattern.

questions.q: Match each request in the simulator with the pattern that answered it.
pairs: A goose wants to act like a Quackable
Make sure ducks always get wrapped
Manage ducks and geese as flocks
questions.explain: Each request has its own pattern. The Observer came last, for notifications.
questions.rule: One need, one pattern.

questions.q: Put the patterns in the order the chapter introduces them as new requests arrive.
items: Adapter
Decorator
Abstract Factory
Composite
Observer
questions.explain: The goose comes first (Adapter), then counting (Decorator), then protecting the wrap (Abstract Factory), then flocks (Composite), then notification (Observer).
questions.rule: Each pattern answers the latest request.

questions.q: What feature of the design lets the adapted goose, the counter, the flock and the observable all work together?
options: They are all created by the same developer on the team
They all present the Quackable interface
They all inherit from one base duck class
They all contain the same counting code inside them
optionExplain: Authorship has no effect on how objects connect.
Right: a shared interface lets them stack.
The adapter and the flock are not ducks and do not inherit from one.
Only the counter counts.
questions.explain: The adapter, decorator and composite are each a Quackable, so each can take the place of a duck. That is why the patterns could be layered.
questions.rule: A shared interface is the glue.
questions.teaches: The simulator holds together because every wrapper and group is itself a Quackable, so the interface acts as the glue between patterns.

questions.q: A parcel firm describes its system: foreign carrier feeds fitted to one interface, every request wrapped with timing, a factory to apply the timing, depot groups containing sub-depots, and managers notified of each delivery. Which list of patterns does it match?
options: Adapter, Decorator, Abstract Factory, Composite, Observer
Observer, Singleton, Adapter, Proxy, Iterator, Bridge
Strategy, Command, Template Method, State, Visitor, Facade
Facade, Bridge, Flyweight, Prototype, Memento
optionExplain: Right: the same chain in a new domain.
Singleton and Proxy have no counterpart in the description.
None of these are described.
None of these are described.
questions.explain: Fitting feeds is Adapter, timing wrappers are Decorator, the applying factory is Abstract Factory, nested depots are Composite, and managers told of deliveries are Observers.
questions.rule: Read a system as a chain of needs and patterns.
questions.teaches: Describing a design as a chain of needs and their patterns works for any system, which is a quick way to state its unity in a few sentences.

questions.q: True or false: In the simulator, the Decorator Pattern was used to let geese act as Quackables.
questions.explain: Geese were fitted in by an adapter. A decorator adds behavior to something that is already a Quackable.
questions.rule: Adapter changes the interface; Decorator keeps it and adds behavior.

questions.q: According to the authors of this chapter, how should you approach a design problem?
options: Keep applying patterns to the problem until a solution appears
Start by choosing the patterns you most want to use
Apply patterns where they make sense, not for their own sake
Avoid patterns altogether in any serious design that is large
optionExplain: The authors call this the wrong approach.
This is using patterns for their own sake.
Right: that is what they say.
They are not against patterns; they are against forced use.
questions.explain: The authors give clear advice on this. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Need first, pattern second.

questions.q: The authors call the design of the Duck Simulator forced and ____.
questions.explain: They describe it as forced and artificial, but fun and useful for seeing how patterns fit together.
questions.rule: The simulator is a demonstration, not a model of how to design.

questions.q: A team is building a small contact-list app. A member suggests adding Abstract Factory, Observer and Decorator because the book chapter used them. What does the chapter's advice suggest?
options: Add all three, since a design with more patterns is better
Add a pattern only if a real need in the app calls for it
Add none, since patterns are only for large systems
Add them now and decide later what they are for
optionExplain: More patterns do not make a design better.
Right: apply patterns where they make sense.
The advice is about need, not size.
This is using patterns for their own sake.
questions.explain: The test is a real need in the app. Without one, the patterns would be overkill.
questions.rule: Let the need call for the pattern.

questions.q: The authors say that for parts of the simulator the patterns were overkill. What might have solved those parts well enough?
options: A larger number of patterns applied more carefully
A different programming language for the whole simulator
Removing the Quackable interface from the design
Good object-oriented principles on their own
optionExplain: More patterns would add to the overkill.
Language is not part of their argument.
The interface is a basic good-design move, not the overkill.
Right: they say sometimes good OO principles are enough.
questions.explain: The authors do not set patterns against good design; sound OO principles are where a design starts, and a pattern is added where those are not enough.
questions.rule: Principles first, patterns where needed.
questions.teaches: Good object-oriented principles come first and patterns come in where those principles alone leave a recurring problem unsolved.

questions.q: A review of a ticketing codebase finds a factory, a decorator and an observer wrapped around a single function that formats a date. Which critique fits the authors?
options: The date function needs yet more patterns before it is complete
The patterns were used for show; the function needed none
Three patterns on one function is the right amount of design for it
Patterns have no place around functions
optionExplain: This repeats the mistake.
Right: forced use of patterns where a simple design would do.
The count is not a measure of quality.
They are not banned; they are used when needed.
questions.explain: The authors warn against using patterns for their own sake. Judging a design in this way means asking what need each pattern answers.
questions.rule: Ask what need each pattern answers.
questions.teaches: A fair critique of a design asks what need each pattern answers, and a pattern with no answer is a sign of overdesign.

questions.q: True or false: The authors advise giving up patterns, because the simulator showed how fragile they are.
questions.explain: The authors still call patterns powerful and say the simulator fun and instructive. Their advice is to apply patterns where and when they make sense.
questions.rule: The caution is about forced use, not about patterns.

questions.q: In a music player, which part holds the song database and decides how it changes?
options: The view
The controller
The speakers
The model
optionExplain: The view displays; it does not own the data.
The controller interprets input and calls the model, but the logic lives in the model.
Hardware is not a role in MVC.
Right: the model keeps data, state and application logic.
questions.explain: The model holds the data and logic. The card next gives all three roles.
questions.rule: Model: data and logic.

questions.q: Match each MVC part with its job.
pairs: Holds data, state and application logic
Presents the model to the user
Interprets user actions and manipulates the model
questions.explain: Each part has one responsibility, which keeps the others free to change.
questions.rule: One job per part.

questions.q: In a recipe app, the user taps Scale to 4 servings. Which part works out what that tap means and asks for the change?
options: The controller
The view, which shows the model
The model, which holds the data
The database, which stores the data
optionExplain: Right: it interprets the action and manipulates the model.
The view reports the tap and shows results; it does not decide what it means.
The model carries out the change; it does not interpret the tap.
It stores data and is not an MVC role.
questions.explain: The view passes on the tap, the controller decides what it means, and the model changes its state.
questions.rule: The controller interprets; the model changes.

questions.q: The BeatModel later in the chapter makes no assumptions about its views. What does this allow?
options: Each view to rewrite the model in the way that it likes
The model to be used only with one view
Different views to be attached to the same model
The controller to be left out
optionExplain: The model does not take orders from its views.
The point is the opposite.
Right: the model stays the same whatever views watch it.
The controller still has its role.
questions.explain: A model that knows nothing about its views can serve any of them. That is why the chapter talks about reuse.
questions.rule: A model that knows no view can serve many.
questions.teaches: Because the model assumes nothing about its views, new views such as a lightshow can be added without touching the model.

questions.q: A step-counter app has a counting model. A new watch face is to be added with a different layout. Which part has to be written?
options: A new model, because every layout needs its own data
A new controller and a new model, in every case
A new view, while the counting model stays as it is
Nothing, since the old view cannot be replaced
optionExplain: Layouts do not need separate data.
The model is not tied to the layout.
Right: the display changes while the data and logic stay.
Views can be replaced; that is part of the design.
questions.explain: Separate roles let one part change without the others. A new layout is a new view of the same model.
questions.rule: Change the part that varies, and leave the rest.
questions.teaches: Separating the roles means a change in presentation touches only the view, which is the practical payoff of MVC.

questions.q: True or false: In MVC, the view alters the model directly whenever the user clicks a button.
questions.explain: The view tells the controller what the user did, and the controller manipulates the model. The view only uses the model's state to display it.
questions.rule: The controller, not the view, changes the model.

questions.q: A user clicks Play in a music app built with MVC. Which part receives that click first?
options: The view
The model
The speakers
The database
optionExplain: Right: you interact with the view, and it tells the controller.
The model is reached only via the controller.
Speakers are output hardware, not an MVC part.
It sits behind the model, not at the front.
questions.explain: The user touches the view. The card next gives the full order.
questions.rule: The user touches the view.

questions.q: Put the steps in the order MVC performs them when the user clicks.
items: The user acts on the view
The view tells the controller what happened
The controller asks the model to change
The model notifies the view of the change
The view asks the model for the state to show
questions.explain: The action goes in through view and controller to the model. The change comes back through a notification and a request for state.
questions.rule: Action goes in; the update comes back.

questions.q: In a library app, a user clicks Renew. After the controller has asked the model to renew the loan, what makes the due date on the screen change?
options: The controller writes the new date onto the screen itself
The user must press Refresh in order to see the new date
The view guesses the new date from the click
The model notifies the view, which then asks for the date
optionExplain: The controller may adjust the view, but the displayed model state comes from the model.
The model notifies; no refresh is needed.
The view takes its state from the model.
Right: update flows from model to view, and the view pulls the state it shows.
questions.explain: The model tells the view that its state changed, and the view fetches what it needs to display.
questions.rule: Notify first, then the view asks for state.

questions.q: True or false: The controller may also ask the view to change, such as disabling a menu item, as well as asking the model to change.
questions.explain: The text lists this as step three: when the controller receives an action it may tell the view to change, for example to enable or disable buttons.
questions.rule: The controller can act on both the model and the view.
questions.teaches: A controller can adjust the view's controls directly, as when it disables Start after the beat begins, while the displayed model data still arrives from the model.

questions.q: A bus-tracking app is built on MVC. A bus arrives at a stop on its own, and no user taps anything. What reaches the screen?
options: Nothing, until the user taps something on the screen
The model notifies the view, which asks for new arrival data
The controller, which must first receive a tap from a user
The view, which polls the bus every second
optionExplain: The model's own changes notify the view as well.
Right: the model also notifies when something other than a user action changes it.
The controller is not needed for a change that starts inside the model.
The view is told by notification instead.
questions.explain: The text says the model notifies when its state changes from a user action or from some other internal change.
questions.rule: The model announces its own changes.
questions.teaches: Not every update starts with the user: changes that start inside the model notify the view with no controller involved.

questions.q: If the model did not notify the view when it changed, what would happen on screen after a click?
options: The model would change but the display would stay old
The display would update anyway, from the controller alone
The click would be ignored by the controller entirely and lost
The model would undo its own change
optionExplain: Right: the view finds out about changes from the notification.
The controller does not feed model state to the view.
The controller would still act.
No rule says so.
questions.explain: Without the notification, the view has no signal to ask for the new state, so it stays stale.
questions.rule: No notification, no refresh.

questions.q: A team puts the code that decides how to change the data right inside the screen class. What is the main cost?
options: The screen can no longer be shown to any of its users
The data will be lost every time that there is a click
The screen is tied to that data model and has two jobs
The program can no longer be compiled
optionExplain: It can still be shown; the problem is design.
Nothing is lost.
Right: coupling and mixed responsibilities.
It compiles fine.
questions.explain: Mixing the two ties the view to the model. The card next gives the authors' reasons.
questions.rule: Keep control logic out of the view.

questions.q: Which two reasons do the authors give for having a controller rather than putting its code in the view? Select all that apply.
options: The view would be tightly coupled to the model
Controllers make programs run faster
The model cannot be reached from a view at all
The view would take on two responsibilities
optionExplain: Right: reuse with another model would be lost.
Speed is not mentioned.
A view can reach the model for state; the issue is control.
Right: interface and control logic.
questions.explain: The two reasons are mixed responsibilities and tight coupling.
questions.rule: Two reasons: two jobs, tight coupling.

questions.q: A dashboard screen contains the code that decides how a Reset click changes the sales data. Management wants the same screen for the warehouse data next quarter. What is the problem?
options: The warehouse data has too many rows for any one screen to show
The screen is tied to the sales model by its control code
The screen cannot show two kinds of data in a single working day
The Reset button needs a different color
optionExplain: Size is not the issue.
Right: tight coupling blocks reuse.
The coupling is the issue, not time.
Color has nothing to do with it.
questions.explain: Control logic inside the view ties the view to the sales model. A controller would let the screen be reused with another model.
questions.rule: Decoupling enables reuse.

questions.q: True or false: The controller is responsible only for passing user input straight to the model.
questions.explain: The authors say it interprets the input and manipulates the model based on it; it does more than forward.
questions.rule: The controller interprets.
questions.teaches: The controller's work is interpretation, such as turning a click into the right model call, even when each interpretation is small.

questions.q: A game has one scoreboard view. The team wants a practice mode and a tournament mode that react differently to the same buttons. What does the controller idea offer?
options: Two copies of the scoreboard view with different code
One big if statement inside the view for the two modes
Two models that differ only in their buttons
Two controllers can give one view different behavior
optionExplain: Duplicating the view is what the controller avoids.
It mixes control logic back into the view.
The buttons are in the view, not the model.
Right: the control logic lives outside the view, so it can be swapped.
questions.explain: Because control logic sits in the controller, the view stays the same while the controller is swapped, which the next ideas call the Strategy Pattern.
questions.rule: Swap the controller, keep the view.
questions.teaches: Because control is outside the view, one view can be given different behavior by changing its controller.

questions.q: When does the extra controller class buy the least?
options: A screen that must work with several models
A throwaway screen with one fixed model and no reuse
A screen whose behavior must vary by mode of use
A screen that several teams will keep changing over time
optionExplain: Here decoupling is valuable.
Right: reuse and swapping are the benefits, and they are not needed here.
Swapping controllers helps.
Separate jobs ease change.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the reasons for a controller are reuse and flexibility. A screen with neither need gains little.
questions.rule: Weigh the benefit against the extra class.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: Which pattern lets a model keep several screens up to date without knowing what they are?
options: Singleton
Adapter
Factory
Observer
optionExplain: It limits instances, not notification.
It translates interfaces and does not notify.
It creates objects and does not notify.
Right: the model notifies registered observers.
questions.explain: Observer is the pattern for it. The card next maps all three parts.
questions.rule: Model: Observer.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: Match each MVC part with the pattern it uses.
questions.explain: The model notifies, the controller is the swappable strategy for the view, and the view is built from nested components.
questions.rule: Observer, Strategy, Composite.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: In a chat app, the message list notifies screens when new messages arrive. Which MVC part is it playing?
options: The model, using Observer to notify the views
The controller, which uses Strategy for the view
The view, which uses Composite for its parts
The controller, which uses Observer on the model
optionExplain: Right: notification of state changes is the model's Observer role.
The controller supplies behavior for the view.
The view is the one being notified.
The authors give Observer to the model.
questions.explain: The thing that holds state and tells watchers when it changes is the model.
questions.rule: State holder plus notifier: the model.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: Why does the text call the controller the strategy for the view?
options: It decides which patterns the view uses for its display
It stores the view's colors and fonts for every window
It supplies the view's behavior and can be swapped
It must be created before the model can exist
optionExplain: The controller does not choose patterns.
Appearance is not the controller's job.
Right: a swappable behavior is a strategy.
Creation order is not the point.
questions.explain: The controller is the behavior of the view and is exchangeable, which is the Strategy idea.
questions.rule: Swappable behavior is Strategy.
questions.teaches: The view is the context and the controller the strategy, so one view can be paired with different controllers for different behavior.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: A photo-editing app has a canvas made of layers, each containing shapes or groups of shapes, and a swappable handler for mouse behavior, plus a document that tells open panels when it changes. Which MVC reading fits?
options: Canvas is the model, handler the view, document the controller
Canvas as the controller (Observer), handler as the model (Composite), document as the view (Strategy)
Canvas is the view, handler the controller, document the model
There is no MVC reading, since photo editors do not use patterns
optionExplain: The roles are scrambled.
The patterns are on the wrong parts.
Right: each part carries its MVC pattern.
The reading depends on structure, not on the domain.
questions.explain: Nested layers and groups are Composite and belong to the view. A swappable input handler is a Strategy for the view. A document that notifies panels is an Observer model.
questions.rule: Look for the structure, not the domain.
questions.teaches: MVC can be spotted in any program by looking for a notifying data holder, a swappable behavior object and a nested display.

questions.section: Looking at MVC through patterns-colored glasses
questions.q: True or false: In MVC, the Strategy Pattern is applied to the model, and the Observer Pattern to the controller.
questions.explain: The model uses Observer, and the controller is the Strategy for the view.
questions.rule: Keep the pairs straight: model-Observer, controller-Strategy, view-Composite.

questions.q: A model should update any number of screens when it changes, without depending on those screens. What works?
options: The model keeps registered observers and notifies them on change
The model keeps a reference to each screen class and calls it by name
Each screen asks the model for changes in a tight loop
The controller copies model data to the screens
optionExplain: Right: that is the Observer approach.
The model would depend on every screen.
Polling is wasteful and can lag.
The controller then does the model's notifying.
questions.explain: Observers register, and the model notifies. The card next shows the details.
questions.rule: Register and notify.

questions.q: The model uses the Observer Pattern so it can keep observers updated yet stay ____ from them.
questions.explain: The bullet points say the model keeps observers updated yet stays decoupled from them.
questions.rule: Observer keeps the model decoupled.

questions.q: A weather model should drive a bar chart and a text readout. Neither the chart nor the readout should be known to the model by name. How is that arranged?
options: The model calls the chart and the readout by name after each change
The chart and the readout copy the model's code
The model is merged into the chart class
Both register as observers, and the model notifies them on change
optionExplain: The model would know the screens.
Copying the model code produces two independent models.
The readout would be left without a model.
Right: registration keeps the model unaware of the specific screens.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Registration inverts the dependency: the screens know the model, not the other way round.
questions.rule: Observers know the model; the model knows only that it has observers.

questions.q: True or false: The model could send its state along with the notification instead of waiting for the view to ask for it.
questions.explain: The authors say a push model is possible, and the Model 2 JSP does exactly this by receiving the model in a bean. They also mention disadvantages covered in the Observer chapter.
questions.rule: Notification can pull or push state.
questions.teaches: State can travel with the notification (push) or be requested after it (pull); the DJ view pulls, and the web view in Model 2 gets its state pushed in a bean.

questions.q: A logistics app model signals a Delay event. A map view, an SMS sender and an audit log register. Next month, a fourth watcher is wanted. What must change in the model?
options: The model must be edited to call the new watcher
Nothing, as the new watcher registers like the others
The three existing watchers must be edited
The model must be rewritten as a brand new class
optionExplain: That would couple the model to each new watcher.
Right: the model only knows it has observers.
They are unaffected by a new observer.
No rewrite is needed.
questions.explain: Adding an observer is registering it. The model's code stays the same.
questions.rule: New observers need no change to the model.
questions.teaches: Open-ended extension is the payoff of decoupling: the number and kind of watchers can grow without changing the observed model.

questions.q: Which is true of the controller in some MVC designs, according to the authors?
options: It registers with the model and is notified
It is not permitted to observe the model at any time
It is the one and only observer of the model
It owns the data that the model holds
optionExplain: Right: they say the controller sometimes observes the model.
The authors say that in some designs it does.
Views are the main observers.
The model owns the data.
questions.explain: In some designs the controller registers with the model, so it can ask the view to enable or disable controls when the model demands it.
questions.rule: Controllers may observe too.

questions.q: A screen must act differently on button clicks in two modes, without changing the screen code. What helps?
options: The screen contains a switch statement for the modes
Two separate screens are written with different code
The screen hands clicks to a swappable object behind an interface
The user is asked to restart the program for each mode
optionExplain: Every new mode needs the screen edited.
The screen code is duplicated.
Right: that is the Strategy idea.
It does not solve the design problem.
questions.explain: An exchangeable behavior object is a strategy. The card next shows it in MVC.
questions.rule: Swappable behavior is Strategy.

questions.q: Because the DJ view implements the Strategy Pattern, we need an ____ for any strategy that might be plugged into it.
questions.explain: The text says we need an interface for any Strategy plugged into the DJ View, called ControllerInterface.
questions.rule: Strategies share an interface.

questions.q: A map app's view passes touch gestures to a GestureHandler interface. The team wants a left-handed mode with mirrored gestures. What follows the chapter's approach?
options: Copy the view and mirror its code
Write a second GestureHandler and plug it in, leaving the view
Edit the view to branch on a left-handed flag
Change the interface so that the handler becomes optional for the view
optionExplain: This duplicates the view.
Right: a new controller gives new behavior.
The view then holds control logic.
Weakens the contract and gives no new behavior.
questions.explain: The view calls the interface, so any implementer can be plugged in.
questions.rule: New behavior is a new controller.

questions.q: The DJ view and its controller are given as an example of which relation?
options: The controller is the context, and the view is its strategy
The model is the strategy for the controller to use
The controller and the view are the same object
The view is the context; the controller is its strategy
optionExplain: The roles are the other way round.
The model is not a strategy here.
They are separate objects.
Right: the Strategy Pattern in MVC.
questions.explain: The text says the controller is the strategy plugged into the view to give it some smarts. The view holds the strategy.
questions.rule: The view holds the controller as its strategy.
questions.teaches: In Strategy terms the view is the context, so asking which object holds which is a way to read any MVC code.

questions.q: A chess app's board component hands moves to an interface. A tutoring mode lets only legal moves through; a free mode lets everything through. What does this show about the board?
options: The board must be rewritten for each of the two modes
Its behavior changes by swapping the handler
The board contains both rule sets and picks one of them
The two modes need two different boards to be used
optionExplain: It is not rewritten.
Right: the Strategy shape.
The rule sets live in the handlers.
They share one board.
questions.explain: The rules live in the exchangeable handler, so the board draws and delegates the same way in both modes.
questions.rule: Put varying rules in the strategy.
questions.teaches: Anything that varies by mode or user, such as rules, permissions or gesture mappings, can be placed in the swappable controller.

questions.q: True or false: A controller with a different set of method names and signatures can be plugged into the DJ view as it is.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the view is written against ControllerInterface. A controller outside that interface must be rewritten or adapted to fit first.
questions.rule: A strategy must fit the context's interface.

questions.q: A screen is built from windows holding panels holding buttons. Which pattern describes treating containers and buttons alike?
options: Observer
Singleton
Template Method
Composite
optionExplain: It describes notification, not nesting.
It limits instances.
It fixes steps of an algorithm in a base class.
Right: containers and leaves share an interface.
questions.explain: Nested parts treated alike are a composite. The card next places it in MVC.
questions.rule: Nested parts, treated alike: Composite.

questions.q: The view uses the ____ Pattern to implement a user interface made of nested components like panels, frames and buttons.
questions.explain: The bullet points say the view uses Composite for the nested user interface.
questions.rule: View: Composite.

questions.q: A report page has sections, which hold tables, which hold rows. A Print command is called on the page. How does a composite view handle it?
options: Each container passes the call down to what it holds, to every row
The page alone prints and ignores what it holds
The program checks the type of every part and prints each differently
Only the last row prints, since it is the deepest
optionExplain: Right: the call propagates through the nesting.
Contained parts would be skipped.
The common interface avoids this.
Every part takes part.
questions.explain: A composite treats containers and leaves alike. Calls to the top travel through each level.
questions.rule: Calls travel down the tree.

questions.q: Why do the authors say the Composite is hard to see in a modern MVC program?
options: Composite is no longer used in graphical interfaces
Modern views are made of a single flat component with no nesting
GUI packages and browsers manage the nesting for us
The pattern was removed from MVC in some of its later versions
optionExplain: They say it is still there.
Views are still nested.
Right: the library hides the structure.
No such change is mentioned.
questions.explain: The authors answer a reader who doubts that Composite is present: GUI packages have become sophisticated enough to hide the internal structure.
questions.rule: Hidden is not absent.
questions.teaches: A pattern may be present in a library rather than in your own code, so your program can use Composite without ever writing it.

questions.q: A web page is written in HTML as nested elements: a body holding divisions holding lists holding items. A browser renders it. How do the authors read this?
options: There is no composite, since HTML is only text
The server builds a composite of the page for the user to edit
Underneath, the browser most likely builds a composite
The page is the model, so the Composite does not apply to it
optionExplain: The text is turned into objects for display.
The text speaks of the browser rendering.
Right: they say an object system underneath most likely forms a composite.
The page is the view in Model 2.
questions.explain: Even when the interface is defined in markup, the browser builds nested components from it, which most likely form a composite.
questions.rule: Nested display, even from markup, is Composite.
questions.teaches: A pattern can live in the structure the browser builds from a document, so it does not need to appear in the author's own classes.

questions.q: True or false: If a GUI package changed to hide its component structure completely, the view would stop being a composite.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Hiding the structure only hides it from you; the nested components still exist inside the package.
questions.rule: Hiding a structure does not remove it.

questions.q: In the DJ tool, what should the code that generates the beat sounds belong to?
options: The model, which holds the beat state and logic
The view, since the user listens to it
The controller, since it starts the beat
The Observer helper, since it sends notifications
optionExplain: Right: state and application logic are the model's.
The view displays; the sound is the model's business.
The controller asks; the model does.
It only notifies.
questions.explain: The model owns the state and logic. The card next describes the BeatModel.
questions.rule: Logic belongs in the model.

questions.q: Which things does the BeatModel contain or offer, according to the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Code that draws the beat bar on the screen
State holding the current beats per minute
Methods to let observers register and be notified
An interface for the controller to manipulate the beat
optionExplain: Drawing belongs to the view.
Right: it keeps the BPM.
Right: it uses Observer.
Right: the controller drives it through the interface.
questions.explain: The model has state, logic and an interface with observer methods. It does not draw anything.
questions.rule: The model has no display code.

questions.q: A team writes a TemperatureModel for a greenhouse. Which of these belongs in it?
options: The code that draws the temperature gauge
The code that reads which button was clicked by the user
A reference to the specific gauge class that shows the reading
The reading, the heating rules and observer methods
optionExplain: Drawing is for the view.
Clicks are interpreted by the controller.
The model should not know its views.
Right: state, logic and observer methods.
questions.explain: The model holds state and logic and announces changes. Display and input interpretation go elsewhere.
questions.rule: State, logic, observer methods.

questions.q: The authors suggest a lightshow driven by the beat and a text view naming the genre from the BPM. What does this suggest about the BeatModel?
options: It must be changed whenever each new view is added
It can serve very different views
It can serve only one view at a time, never two
It must contain code for the lightshow and for each view
optionExplain: It was built not to need that.
Right: it makes no assumptions about its views.
Many observers can register.
Display code belongs in the views.
questions.explain: Both views would register and read state through the model's interface. The model needs no change.
questions.rule: Many views, one model.
questions.teaches: A text view can derive new information from a model's raw state, such as a genre from the BPM, so views may interpret the same state in different ways.

questions.q: A parking model holds the number of free spaces and notifies observers. A signboard shows the number. A new feature should show Nearly full above 90 percent. Where is the check best made?
options: In a view, which reads the numbers
In the model, which would then know about the signboard
In the controller, which polls the model every minute
In a new model for each wording
optionExplain: Right: how to present the state is the view's concern.
The model should not know its views.
The controller does not feed the display.
Wording is presentation.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the model reports raw state. Turning it into words such as Nearly full is presentation, like naming a genre from a BPM.
questions.rule: Presentation choices belong to views.
questions.teaches: Interpretation for display belongs in the view, so the model stays reusable by views that present the same data differently.

questions.q: True or false: If the lightshow view is added, the BeatModel must be changed to know about it.
questions.explain: The model only knows that it has observers. The lightshow registers like any other view.
questions.rule: Adding a view does not change the model.

questions.q: In the DJ tool, a user presses the Increase button. What should the view do?
options: Change the BPM in the model directly
Generate the MIDI beat itself
Tell the controller what the user did
Ignore the press, since it is not the view's job
optionExplain: The controller manipulates the model, not the view.
The model generates the beat.
Right: the view reports actions to the controller.
It must be reported.
questions.explain: The view reports and the controller acts. The card next shows the view's structure.
questions.rule: The view reports to the controller.

questions.q: The DJ view registers as an ____ of the model, so it is told when the BPM or the beat changes.
questions.explain: The view registers with the model as an observer.
questions.rule: The view observes the model.

questions.q: A game's score panel must show the current score and update on its own. How should the panel get the score?
options: Poll the controller for the score once every second
Register with the score model, then read the score
Keep its own private copy of the score and add to it
Let the controller write the score into the panel itself
optionExplain: The controller does not own the score.
Right: observer registration plus pulling the state.
A private copy can drift from the model.
The view takes its state from the model.
questions.explain: The panel registers as an observer. On notification, it asks the model for the score.
questions.rule: Register, be told, then ask.

questions.q: In the DJ tool, a user changes the BPM with the controls. What updates the display of the BPM?
options: The control itself, which writes the number to the display directly
The controller, which writes the number to the display itself
A timer in the view that runs every second
The model's notification, then the view asking for the BPM
optionExplain: The display has no logical link to the controls.
The display takes its number from the model.
A timer is not how the chapter does it.
Right: the display reflects the model, not the control.
questions.explain: The chapter points out the display reflects the changes despite no logical link to the controls. It follows the model.
questions.rule: The display follows the model.
questions.teaches: Because the display is driven by the model alone, any path that changes the model, not just the on-screen controls, updates the display.

questions.q: A smart-speaker app has a volume slider (control) and a volume bar (display). The volume can also be changed from a wall remote. What should the bar show?
options: The slider's position, so that it ignores any remote change
The model's volume, so slider and remote both show
The last press that the controller received from either input
A separate number kept for each input device in the room
optionExplain: It would be wrong after a remote change.
Right: the display follows the model, whichever way it was changed.
The controller may not have seen the remote.
The model has one volume.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: If the display is tied to the model, every source of change is shown. A display tied to a control shows only that control.
questions.rule: Tie the display to the model, not to the controls.
questions.teaches: A display tied to the model stays correct for every source of change, whereas a display tied to a control shows only that control's changes.

questions.q: True or false: In the DJ view, the two windows must be two separate classes.
questions.explain: The chapter says both parts live together in one class, DJView, and that the split is only for showing the code.
questions.rule: Roles are not the same as files.

questions.q: The user chooses Start in the DJ tool. What should the controller do?
options: Generate the MIDI events by itself in the controller
Wait for the model to ask it what it should do
Draw the beat bar on the view
Tell the model to start and update the menu items
optionExplain: Generating the beat is application logic and belongs in the model.
The controller acts on view actions.
Drawing belongs to the view.
Right: act on the model and adjust the view.
questions.explain: The controller translates and adjusts. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Translate the action, then adjust the view.

questions.q: The controller does not implement application logic; that lives in the ____.
questions.explain: The application logic is the code that manages and manipulates your data, and it lives in the model.
questions.rule: Logic lives in the model.

questions.q: In a recipe app, the controller receives a Double click. Which of these is the controller's job?
options: Choosing which model call doubles the quantities
Doing the arithmetic of doubling every ingredient amount
Storing all of the recipes in a database for the app
Drawing the new quantities
optionExplain: Right: it chooses and makes the model call.
Arithmetic on the data is application logic.
Storage is part of the model.
Drawing is the view's job.
questions.explain: The controller works out which model method to call, and the model does the actual work.
questions.rule: The controller chooses the call; the model does the work.

questions.q: After Start, the DJ controller disables the Start menu item. Which part of MVC does it ask to change?
options: The model, whose state holds the menu
The Observer helper class of the model
The view, whose controls it adjusts
The speaker that plays the sound
optionExplain: The menu is part of the view.
The helper plays no part here.
Right: the controller may ask the view to change.
The controller does not address hardware.
questions.explain: The controller asks the view to enable or disable controls as a result of the action it received.
questions.rule: The controller can adjust the view's controls.
questions.teaches: Which controls are enabled follows from the action just taken, so it is controller behavior and not application logic held in the model.

questions.q: A ticket app's controller receives Buy. Where should the rule that no more than four tickets may be bought at once be placed?
options: In the controller, which refuses the click
In the view, which removes the Buy button
In the model, with the application logic
In each view that shows tickets
optionExplain: This is application logic and belongs to the model.
The view only presents.
Right: rules about the data are application logic.
It would be repeated and could be missed.
questions.explain: The authors say the controller may work out which calls to make, but the rules that manage data live in the model.
questions.rule: Rules about the data live in the model.
questions.teaches: Putting rules in the model means they hold no matter which controller or view is attached, whereas rules in a controller disappear when it is swapped.

questions.q: True or false: If the controller were swapped for another that implements ControllerInterface, the model would need to change.
questions.explain: The model is independent of the controller. Only the behavior offered to the view changes.
questions.rule: Controllers can be swapped without touching the model.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: In the DJ tool, a user clicks Increase. Which is the correct path to the changed display?
options: The view reports to the controller, which changes the model, which notifies
The view changes the display itself, then tells the model about it
The controller writes the new number onto the display itself
The model changes the display directly
optionExplain: Right: control, controller, model, notification, view.
The display follows the model, not the click.
The display takes its number from the model.
The model does not know the view.
questions.explain: The path runs through the controller and the model. The card next confirms it.
questions.rule: Follow the path.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: Order the events after the user clicks Increase BPM in the DJ tool.
items: The view tells the controller about the click
The controller sets a higher BPM on the model
The model notifies its observers
The view reads the new BPM from the model and shows it
questions.explain: The click goes in via the controller to the model; the update comes back via the notification.
questions.rule: Follow the path in order.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: A user changes the volume in a player built like the DJ tool. The label does not update. Where should you look first?
options: Whether the volume button is wired directly to the label
Whether the controller draws the label on the screen
Whether the user clicked hard enough
Whether the label observes the model and reads it
optionExplain: The label should have no link to the button.
Drawing is the view's job.
Not a design question.
Right: the label depends on notification and on reading the model.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the label follows the model through observation, so a stale label points to registration or reading.
questions.rule: Stale display: check the observer link.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: At the start, the DJ view shows offline, and after Start it shows the default BPM of 90. What does the display follow?
options: The label the controller sets on the Start menu
The BPM the model reports after Start
A number the user typed before
A constant written in the view
optionExplain: The menu and the display are separate.
Right: the display follows the model's state.
The user typed nothing at that point.
The view reads the model.
questions.explain: On Start the model sets the BPM to its default and notifies. The view shows what the model reports.
questions.rule: The display shows model state.
questions.teaches: The model's state changes on its own, such as to the default BPM at Start, and the display follows without the controller writing any numbers.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: A lighting app built like the DJ tool shows brightness. Bob moves a slider, and later a timer dims the lights on its own. What does the display do?
options: It follows the model both times, as both change it
It follows the slider only, because the slider is a control
It follows the timer only, because timers are faster
It shows neither, until the user presses Refresh
optionExplain: Right: the view follows the model whatever changed it.
The display has no logical link to the controls.
Speed is not at issue.
The model notifies.
questions.explain: The display is an observer of the model, so any change to the model updates it.
questions.rule: One display, many sources of change.
questions.teaches: Because the display depends only on the model, the number of ways to change the model can grow without any change to the view.

questions.section: And now for a test run...
questions.q: In the test run, the beat bar keeps up with the beat because it is an ____ of the model.
questions.explain: The text says the beat bar always keeps up with the beat since it is an observer of the model, notified on each beat.
questions.rule: Observers keep up by being notified.

questions.q: A display calls getBPM(), but a new device offers getHeartRate(). How can the display be reused without editing it?
options: Edit the display so that it calls getHeartRate() as well
Rename the display's method to getHeartRate()
Wrap the device in a class with getBPM() that calls getHeartRate()
Write a brand new display from scratch for the device
optionExplain: The display would then be tied to the device.
It would break the display's other users.
Right: that is an adapter.
It throws away a working view.
questions.explain: A wrapper that translates calls adapts the device to the view. The card next gives the case.
questions.rule: Adapt the model, keep the view.

questions.q: The HeartAdapter's getBPM() method calls the heart model's ____ method.
questions.explain: The adapter translates getBPM() calls into getHeartRate() calls.
questions.rule: The adapter translates calls.

questions.q: A battery gauge view calls getLevel(). A new power cell class has chargePercent(). What fits the chapter?
options: Change the gauge to call chargePercent() from now on instead
An adapter with getLevel() that returns chargePercent()
Change the power cell class so that it renames its own method
Use a flag in the gauge to pick which call is made
optionExplain: It would no longer work with the old cells.
Right: adapt the model to the view's interface.
The cell may not be yours to change.
It adds special cases to the view.
questions.explain: The adapter hides the difference, so the gauge and the cell both stay as they are.
questions.rule: Adapt, do not edit.

questions.q: In the heart example, what do the authors adapt, and what do they leave as it was?
options: They adapt the view to the heart model and rewrite it
They adapt the controller and discard the old view
They adapt nothing and rewrite both
They adapt the model to BeatModel; the view is reused
optionExplain: The view is reused.
The view is kept; a new controller is added.
An adapter is used.
Right: the adapter sits on the model side.
questions.explain: The text says to adapt a model to work with existing controllers and views. Here the view stays and the model is wrapped.
