questions.rule: In MVC, adapt the model to the existing view.
questions.teaches: In MVC the adapter typically wraps the model, because the view and controller are the stable parts that expect one model interface.

questions.q: A theme-park queue display calls getWait() on ride objects. A new ride-sensor library returns waiting time in a call named estimate(). The display must be reused. Which design fits?
options: A second display written specially for the library
An adapter with getWait() that delegates to estimate()
A subclass of the display that overrides getWait()
A copy of the library code with estimate() renamed to getWait()
optionExplain: It duplicates a working view.
Right: adapt the library to the display's interface.
The display is the stable part; adapting the supplier is what the chapter shows.
Copying the library creates a fork to maintain.
questions.explain: The adapter implements what the display calls and delegates to the library.
questions.rule: Adapt the supplier to the consumer.
questions.teaches: Adapting the supplier rather than changing the consumer is the same move whether the supplier is a heart monitor, a library or a sensor.

questions.q: True or false: The adapter can make the heart model start a beat, as the BeatModel does.
questions.explain: The heart model has no beat generator to start, and the HeartAdapter's on(), off() and setBPM() do nothing.
questions.rule: An adapter can only translate calls to things that exist.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: A view with Start, Stop, Increase and Decrease buttons is reused with a read-only heart monitor. What is a likely rough edge?
options: The monitor will not display anything on the screen at all
The view must be rewritten from scratch for the monitor
The monitor will start generating beats
Buttons that the monitor cannot use remain on the screen
optionExplain: It displays the rate fine.
The view is reused as is.
It only reports a rate.
Right: the view keeps the controls it was built with.
questions.explain: The controls the model cannot use stay in the view. The card next shows how the chapter handles this.
questions.rule: Unused controls remain.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: In the HeartController, the buttons that have no meaning for a heart are implemented as ____.
questions.explain: The text says the controller implements no ops for them.
questions.rule: Unwanted actions can be no-ops.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: A kitchen-timer view with Start, Pause and Reset is reused for a clock that only shows the time. The new controller disables Start and ignores Pause and Reset. What does the user see?
options: Pause and Reset buttons that do nothing when pressed
Pause and Reset buttons that disappear from the screen
Pause and Reset buttons that start the clock
An error message each time one of them is pressed
optionExplain: Right: the controller makes them no-ops.
The view would need to change to hide them.
The controller ignores them.
A no-op gives no message.
questions.explain: Like the heart example, the buttons stay on screen and do nothing.
questions.rule: No-op controllers leave dead buttons.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: What improvement do the authors say could be made to remove the dead buttons?
options: Change the model to include a Start function of its own
Make the controller draw replacements for the missing buttons
Change the view so it can disable unsupported controls
Delete the heart monitor from the program altogether
optionExplain: The heart model has no beat to start.
Drawing is the view's task.
Right: they say the view could be changed to support the disabling of these items.
It does not address the buttons.
questions.explain: The fix lies in the view, which is the part that holds the controls.
questions.rule: Unused controls are a view concern.
questions.teaches: Reuse can leave cosmetic gaps, and the remedy is a small change to the reused part, here letting the view disable items, rather than abandoning the reuse.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: A review of a reused invoice screen says: Reuse worked, but Export and Email buttons do nothing for the new data source. How does this compare with the heart example?
options: It is a different case, since the heart monitors have no buttons at all
It shows that the screen cannot be reused for the new data at all
The same gap: controls the new controller ignores, fixable in the view
It shows the model must be rewritten
optionExplain: The heart view has buttons that do nothing.
Reuse worked.
Right: the same pattern of reuse with leftover controls.
The model is not the problem.
questions.explain: The invoice screen shows the same pattern as the heart view: the controller ignores some controls, which stay visible.
questions.rule: Check what remains of the old view's controls.
questions.teaches: A reuse review should list what the new controller does not support, since those controls need hiding or disabling in the view.

questions.section: Now we’re ready for a HeartController
questions.q: True or false: The chapter claims the heart example is a finished product with nothing left to improve.
questions.explain: The authors point out the dead buttons and say the view could be changed to disable them.
questions.rule: Look for what a reuse leaves unfinished.

questions.q: On the web, which part usually plays the role of the controller in Model 2?
options: A servlet that receives the HTTP request
The browser that sends the request
The database that stores the data
The HTML form that is on the page
optionExplain: Right: the servlet is the controller.
The browser displays the page and sends requests.
It is usually the model.
It is part of the view.
questions.explain: The servlet takes the request and acts on the model. The card next gives the full path.
questions.rule: Servlet: controller.

questions.q: Match each web part with its MVC role in Model 2.
pairs: Database with a bean holding the result
questions.explain: The servlet controls, the JSP presents, and the data sits in the model, passed along in a bean.
questions.rule: Servlet, JSP, model.

questions.q: Put the Model 2 steps in order for one request.
items: The browser sends an HTTP request
The servlet parses it and acts on the model
The servlet forwards control to the JSP
The JSP builds the page, which is returned to the browser
questions.explain: The request enters at the servlet, which works with the model and hands off to the view; the page then returns to the browser.
questions.rule: Request, controller, view, response.

questions.q: In Model 2, how does the JSP learn the model's state?
options: It registers with the model as an observer and is told continually
It reads the browser's history
It asks the user to type the state
The controller passes it a JavaBean holding the model's state
optionExplain: The view is no longer an observer in the classic sense.
History plays no part.
The page is built from the bean.
Right: the result is bundled into a bean.
questions.explain: The controller gives the view a bean, which is how the view obtains the state it needs.
questions.rule: On the web the controller hands the state to the view.
questions.teaches: On the web the state reaches the view through the controller in a bean, so an update arrives only when a response page is made.

questions.q: A recipe site: the browser posts a rating, a script saves it and then hands the result to a page template that returns the updated recipe page. In Model 2 terms, what is the script?
options: The view, since it is the part that produces the page
The controller, as it handles the request and passes it on
The model, since it is the part that saves the rating
The observer, since it is the part that reacts to the post
optionExplain: The template produces the page.
Right: it plays the servlet's role.
The store holds the rating; the script handles the request.
Observers are notified by the model.
questions.explain: It receives the request, works with the model and forwards to the view. That is the controller's role.
questions.rule: The controller handles the request and forwards.
questions.teaches: The Model 2 shape does not depend on Java; any request handler that processes input, calls the model and hands over to a page template plays the controller.

questions.q: True or false: In Model 2, the view can push a new page to the browser at any time, without a request.
questions.explain: The view only creates a page when the controller forwards control to it, and the page returns as an HTTP response.
questions.rule: The web model is request and response.

questions.q: Besides a cleaner design, what practical gain does separating a web app into controller and view give a team?
options: People who know HTML can work on pages without touching the logic
The pages load at twice the speed they had before
All developers can edit every file in the project more freely
The database becomes unnecessary for the application
optionExplain: Right: it separates production responsibilities.
Speed is not claimed.
The opposite is claimed.
The model remains.
questions.explain: The separation also splits who works on which part. The card next gives the authors' account.
questions.rule: Design separation can mean job separation.

questions.q: Model 2 separates components in design and also in ____ responsibilities.
questions.explain: The authors say it provides a separation in production responsibilities.
questions.rule: Separate design, separate jobs.

questions.q: A newspaper site has designers who know HTML and developers who know servlets. Using Model 2, how should the work be split?
options: Designers own the servlets, and developers edit the JSPs
Everyone edits everything in the project
Developers own servlets; designers edit simple JSPs
Developers own both and designers send requests
optionExplain: The roles are reversed.
It brings back the chaos.
Right: the producers work on simple JSPs.
It leaves the producers out.
questions.explain: Developer jobs go to the people who know servlets, and producers work on simple JSPs.
questions.rule: Give each group the files it understands.

questions.q: In Model 2, what does a web producer have access to in a simple JSP?
options: The servlet's code and the database
HTML and simple JavaBeans
Only the browser
Every Java class in the project
optionExplain: Those belong to the developers.
Right: that is all they need for the view.
The browser is not a file they edit.
That brings back the problem.
questions.explain: The producers get HTML and simple JavaBeans, so they can shape the page but cannot alter the logic.
questions.rule: Limit access to what the role needs.
questions.teaches: Limiting a role to a small, safe slice of the system is itself a design benefit, because it prevents mistakes by people who work on other things.

questions.q: A mobile-game studio has artists who edit level layout files and programmers who write game rules. Which design carries the Model 2 lesson?
options: Put layouts and rules together, so that artists can adjust both
Let programmers draw the layouts
Merge the artists' files into the programmers' source code
Keep layouts in simple files apart from the rules code
optionExplain: It exposes the rules to mistakes.
It wastes the artists' skill.
It removes the protection.
Right: separation of responsibilities protects the logic.
questions.explain: The lesson is separation by responsibility, not just by technology.
questions.rule: Separate what different people own.
questions.teaches: Model 2's lesson applies beyond web pages: wherever different people own different parts, separate the parts so each group can work without risk to the other.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Model 2 is only a clean design and has no effect on how teams are organized.
questions.explain: They say Model 2 is more than just a clean design: it also separates production responsibilities.
questions.rule: Check for effects on people as well as on code.

questions.q: A model is moved from a desktop program to a web application. Under what condition does it need no change?
options: It is written in a newer language than the controller
It depends on no view or controller classes
It is small enough to fit on a single page
It has been tested by many users
optionExplain: Language age is irrelevant.
Right: it is decoupled from the setting.
Size is not the criterion.
Testing does not affect dependencies.
questions.explain: Independence from views and controllers makes the model portable. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No dependencies, no changes.

questions.q: In MVC, the model is totally ____: it knows nothing about the views or controllers.
questions.explain: The text says that in MVC the model doesn't know anything about the views or controllers.
questions.rule: The model is decoupled.

questions.q: A shop's StockModel was written for a desktop till. It only holds stock counts and offers get, set and register-observer methods. The shop wants a web storefront. What must be done to the model?
options: Rewrite all of its code for the web from the start
Add some servlet code to it for the web setting
Copy it and then rename the copy for the web
Nothing, as it does not depend on desktop views
optionExplain: Not needed.
It must not know about the controller.
Copying gains nothing.
Right: it can be used off the shelf.
questions.explain: A model that offers only an interface and observers is ready for any new setting.
questions.rule: Reuse a decoupled model as is.

questions.q: In Model 2 the servlet and JSP are new. Which part stays exactly the same?
options: The BeatModel, used off the shelf
The servlet, which reuses the DJ controller
The JSP, which reuses the Swing view
Nothing, since all three parts were rewritten
optionExplain: Right: it needed no change.
The servlet is a new controller.
The JSP is a new view.
The model stayed.
questions.explain: The text says to use the BeatModel off the shelf without changes.
questions.rule: The model carries over; controller and view change.
questions.teaches: When a program moves between settings, expect the controller and view to be rewritten while the decoupled model carries over, which is where MVC pays off.

questions.q: A team moves a game from a phone to a smart TV. The score logic lives in a ScoreModel that imports nothing from the phone interface. Which plan fits MVC?
options: Rewrite ScoreModel from the start for the TV
Keep the phone view and port it to the TV
Keep ScoreModel as it is; write a TV view and controller
Merge the controller into ScoreModel in order to save time
optionExplain: It has no phone dependencies to remove.
The view is screen-specific.
Right: only the screen-specific parts change.
It couples the model to input again.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the model has no ties to the phone, so only view and controller need to be rewritten.
questions.rule: Port the view and controller, keep the model.
questions.teaches: The cost of porting a program shrinks to the view and controller when the model is kept free of screen and input code.

questions.q: True or false: Had the BeatModel imported a Swing class to draw its beat bar, it could still move to the web without any change.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a model with a tie to a desktop interface class depends on something the web setting lacks, so it would need changes.
questions.rule: One hidden dependency is enough to break reuse.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: In Model 2, how does the view learn about changes in the model?
options: By registering with the model as an observer of changes
By watching the database directly for any changes
Indirectly, when the controller passes it the model's state
It never learns about changes in the model at all
optionExplain: That is the classic form, not Model 2.
The view only uses the bean.
Right: the equivalent of a notification.
It receives state each time a page is built.
questions.explain: Notification happens through the controller. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Indirect notification.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: Match each pattern with how it appears in Model 2.
pairs: The view gets state indirectly from the controller
The servlet provides behavior but is not composed with the view
The browser builds nested components from HTML
questions.explain: Each pattern is present in an adapted form.
questions.rule: The patterns persist, adapted.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: A page is delivered to a browser at 10:00. The model changes at 10:05. In Model 2, what shows the new state?
options: The next response page, built on the next request
The same page at 10:05, updated at once by the model
The servlet, which edits the page after delivery
The model, which updates the browser directly
optionExplain: Right: state is incorporated only when a page is made.
Notification at other times would be pointless here.
It cannot edit a delivered page.
The model does not know the view.
questions.explain: The authors say the view only needs an update when an HTTP response is returned.
questions.rule: Update on response.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: In Model 2 the controller servlet is not directly composed with the view. Why do the authors still call it the strategy?
options: It is declared inside the view class as a field
It was written by the same developers who wrote the view
It generates the HTML for the page that is returned
It implements the view's behavior and could be swapped
optionExplain: It is not composed with the view.
Authorship is irrelevant.
The JSP does that.
Right: the role of the strategy remains.
questions.explain: The text says the controller still provides the view's behavior even when the two are not joined by object composition.
questions.rule: A pattern is its role, not its wiring.
questions.teaches: A pattern is defined by the role its parts play, so it can survive when the original wiring, such as object composition, changes.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: A team's framework has controllers chosen by URL and views rendered from templates; the framework passes a data object to the template when it renders. A newcomer asks if the Observer idea is present. What fits the chapter?
options: No, since the view does not register with the model at all
Yes, adapted: the controller hands the view fresh state
No, since observers exist only in desktop programs and nowhere else
Yes, since the view registers with the model as before
optionExplain: Missing registration does not mean the role is missing.
Right: indirect notification at render time.
The authors show the web adaptation.
The view does not register in this setup.
questions.explain: The data object plays the role of the notification and state in one. The framework differs from the classic wiring, but the role is there.
questions.rule: Look for the role, not the wiring.
questions.teaches: When reading an unfamiliar framework, search for each role of the pattern, such as a way to learn about state changes, rather than for the textbook classes.

questions.section: Model 2 is an adaptation of MVC to the Web
questions.q: True or false: In Model 2, the view still registers with the model as an observer in the classic sense.
questions.explain: The authors say it no longer does; it receives the equivalent of notifications indirectly from the controller.
questions.rule: Adaptation keeps the roles, not the wiring.

questions.q: What do the Observer, Strategy and Composite patterns achieve together in MVC?
options: They decouple the model, view and controller
They remove the need for a model in the design
They merge the three parts into a single class
They make the program run on any kind of server
optionExplain: Right: that keeps the design clear and flexible.
The model is still required.
The point is to keep them apart.
Portability of servers is not claimed.
questions.explain: The patterns together decouple the three players. The card next adds the loose ends.
questions.rule: MVC decouples.

questions.q: The ____ Pattern can be used to adapt a new model to an existing view and controller.
questions.explain: The bullet points say Adapter can fit a new model to the existing view and controller.
questions.rule: Adapter fits a new model.

questions.q: In a reporting tool, the view has full access to all model methods, including those that change data. The team wants the view to read but not change. What do the authors point to?
options: Trust the view not to call the methods that change data
Remove the changing methods from the model altogether
Adapt the model to a narrower, read-only interface
Give the view its own separate copy of the data
optionExplain: Trust is the weakness being fixed.
The controller needs them.
Right: a pattern can present a subset of an interface.
A copy will drift from the model.
questions.explain: The authors ask whether you can think of a pattern that adapts an interface to offer a subset. The Adapter does.
questions.rule: Adapt an interface to narrow what a part can do.

questions.q: Why is the controller not a true mediator between the view and the model, according to the authors?
options: The controller does not exist inside the model
The view holds a model reference to read state
Mediators cannot be used with views of any kind
The controller never talks to the model itself
optionExplain: That has no bearing on mediation.
Right: a true mediator would route the state reads too.
No such rule is stated.
It does, to change it.
questions.explain: The view never sets state through the model directly, but it does read the model. For a pure mediator, the view would go through the controller for state too.
questions.rule: A mediator would keep two objects from referring to each other at all.
questions.teaches: A mediator keeps two objects from referring to each other explicitly, so a view that holds a model reference falls short of it.

questions.q: In a hospital app, the display screen holds a reference to the patient model and could call setDosage() by mistake. Which critique fits the authors' reasoning?
options: The design is perfect, since the view does not call setDosage() now
The model should be merged into the view to avoid the problem
The controller should read the dosage and pass it to the view
The view has more access than it needs; a read-only face fixes it
optionExplain: Today's behavior is no guarantee.
It removes decoupling.
The view reads from the model in MVC.
Right: the same loose end as the DJ code.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Access that is not needed is a risk. Narrowing it with an adapter fits the authors' hint.
questions.rule: Give each part the narrowest access it needs.
questions.teaches: A design can be judged by how much each part is allowed to reach, not just by how the parts are named.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the loose ends make MVC unsound as a design.
questions.explain: They mention them as simplifications and open points. Their conclusion is that the patterns working together decouple the parts and keep designs flexible.
questions.rule: Loose ends are places to tighten, not reasons to drop MVC.

questions.q: In the definition of a design pattern as a solution to a problem in a context, what does the context refer to?
options: The recurring situation in which the pattern applies
The programming language and tools the solution is written with
The list of classes and their roles that make up the solution
The goal the designer is trying to reach
optionExplain: Right: the context is the situation where the pattern applies, and it should recur.
Code is written in some language, but the context is a situation, not a tool.
The classes belong to the solution, which is a separate part of the definition.
The goal belongs to the problem part, so this mixes up two parts.
questions.explain: The context names the situation in which the pattern applies. The card next shows how it differs from the problem and the solution.
questions.rule: Context means the situation where the pattern applies.

questions.q: A pattern is a solution to a problem in a ____.
questions.explain: The definition has three parts: a context, a problem and a solution. The context is the situation in which the pattern applies.
questions.rule: Pattern = solution to a problem in a context.

questions.q: Which of these statements describes a context rather than a problem or a solution?
options: Appointments must be read in date order without letting callers see how the list is stored
Put the list behind a separate class that hands out one appointment at a time
The clinic wants fast lookups but has a small budget
A clinic keeps a list of appointments
optionExplain: This is a goal with a constraint, so it is the problem part.
This is a design that answers a problem, so it is the solution part.
This is a goal plus a constraint, so it also belongs to the problem.
Right: it only sets the scene, like the book's collection of objects.
questions.explain: A context sets the scene: there is something in place, and nothing has gone wrong or been decided yet. Goals and constraints make the problem, and the design answering them is the solution.
questions.hint: Which statement has no goal, constraint or design in it?
questions.rule: A context has no goal and no fix in it.

questions.q: The book gives a mnemonic that begins: if you find yourself in a context with a problem. What job does the context do in that sentence?
options: It is the design that finally gets applied once the problem is clear
It is the full list of constraints that shape the problem
It is the condition you recognise before you reach for a design
It is the person who documents the pattern for the catalog
optionExplain: The design comes at the end of the sentence, as the 'then'.
Constraints belong to the problem, which the sentence mentions separately.
Right: the sentence works as an if-then rule, and the context is the recognisable 'if'.
The sentence is about using a pattern, not about who wrote it down.
questions.explain: The mnemonic reads like a rule: if you are in this context with this problem, then apply this design. The context is the part you notice first.
questions.rule: Spot the context, then check the problem, then apply the design.
questions.teaches: The book's mnemonic turns the definition into an if-then rule: if you are in a context with a problem, you can apply a design that resolves it, so recognising the context comes first.

questions.q: A cookbook editor files recipes by situation, such as cooking for forty guests or cooking with one pan. Which part of a pattern does this filing resemble, and what does it let a cook do?
options: The solution; a cook can see which recipe has the most steps and tools
The problem; a cook can compare how hard each dish is to make for guests
The name; a cook can learn what other cooks call each dish
The context: a cook can search by situation before knowing the answer
optionExplain: Steps belong to the solution, but the filing is by situation, not by method.
Difficulty is not the filing key here; the situation is.
Names matter, but the filing key described is the situation.
Right: situations work like contexts, and a context lets you find help by matching where you are.
questions.explain: Situations such as feeding forty guests play the role of contexts. Because a context says where something applies, it can serve as an index: you start from your situation, not from the answer.
questions.rule: Start from your situation to find the pattern.
questions.teaches: Because a context says where a pattern applies, it works as a search key: you can look up help by describing your situation before you know the solution.

questions.q: True or false: A team has a context and a working solution for a problem that happened once, to one project. The book's definition says the situation should recur, so this is a poor basis for a pattern.
questions.explain: The definition asks for a recurring situation. A one-off situation can have a good local fix, but nothing about it can be reused.
questions.rule: No recurrence, no context for a pattern.

questions.q: Pattern writers talk about forces. In the pattern definition, what are the forces?
options: The pressure from managers to deliver a design quickly and cheaply
The goals and the constraints that together make up the problem
The strength of the coupling between a pattern's classes and objects
The number of classes the solution adds to the design
optionExplain: Deadlines can be a constraint, but forces is a wider term for the whole problem.
Right: forces are the two sides of the problem, goals and constraints.
Coupling is a design property; forces describe the problem, not the solution.
Class count is a feature of the solution, not of the problem.
questions.explain: Forces is the pattern writers' name for the goal and constraints of the problem. The card next explains why they are called that.
questions.rule: Forces = goal + constraints.

questions.q: Match each term from the pattern definition to its meaning.
pairs: What you are trying to achieve in the context
A limit on how the goal may be reached
The goals and constraints taken together
questions.explain: The problem has two ingredients, a goal and constraints. Forces is the pattern writers' word for the two together.
questions.rule: Problem = goal plus constraints.

questions.q: A bakery must deliver 500 loaves by 6 a.m., but the oven only holds 50 at a time and the staff cannot start before 3 a.m. Which sorting uses the book's terms?
options: The oven size is the goal; the 500 loaves by 6 a.m. and the start time are constraints
The 3 a.m. start is the solution; the 500 loaves is the context of the bakery
The 500 loaves by 6 a.m. is the goal; oven size and start time are constraints
All three are constraints, since a goal has to be reachable before it counts
optionExplain: The oven limits how the goal is reached, so it is a constraint, not a goal.
A start time limits the plan; a solution is a design that answers the problem.
Right: the target is the goal, and the two limits narrow how it can be reached.
A problem always has something to reach for; the goal is what the constraints are limiting.
questions.explain: The goal is what you are trying to achieve. Constraints are the limits on achieving it. Together they are the forces, and a plan must respect both.
questions.rule: Ask what you want, then what limits you.

questions.q: According to the book, where do a problem's constraints come from?
options: The designer adds them while choosing and building the solution
They occur in the context, so they come with the situation
They are written into the pattern's name when it is first coined
They are set by the catalog's template for describing patterns
optionExplain: A designer may add limits, but the book places constraints in the context itself.
Right: the book says the problem refers to constraints that occur in the context.
A name labels the pattern but does not carry its constraints.
Templates organise a description; they do not create constraints.
questions.explain: The definition links the parts: the problem lives in a context, and the constraints are part of that context. This is why a solution that is good in one context may fail in another.
questions.rule: Constraints come with the context.
questions.teaches: The book places constraints inside the context, so they are conditions of the situation, not extras the designer chooses later; the same goal in another context can face other constraints.

questions.q: A hospital needs every shift covered (goal), and no nurse may work more than 12 hours (constraint). A proposed rota covers every shift by having two nurses work 16 hours. What does the force idea say about it?
options: It is a sound solution because the goal is the main force in a pattern
It meets the goal but breaks a constraint, so the forces are unbalanced
It balances the forces because the goal has been fully reached in practice
It is outside the idea because forces only apply to software designs
optionExplain: The book names both sides as shaping the solution; the goal does not outrank the constraints.
Right: a useful solution has to respect both sides, and this one ignores a constraint.
Reaching the goal is only one side of the balance.
The book uses the idea for design patterns, but it works wherever there is a goal and limits.
questions.explain: A candidate solution must be checked against every constraint as well as against the goal. Covering every shift at the price of 16-hour days fails one side of the balance.
questions.rule: Check the goal and every constraint.
questions.teaches: Testing a candidate solution means checking it against each constraint one by one, as well as against the goal; passing the goal alone does not make it acceptable.

questions.q: True or false: In the book's collection example the constraint is hiding how the collection is stored. If that constraint were dropped, designs that were ruled out only by it, such as exposing the storage, would become acceptable.
questions.explain: Constraints narrow the acceptable solutions. Remove one and designs that it alone excluded come back into play, while the goal stays the same.
questions.hint: Which designs were ruled out only by the dropped limit?
questions.rule: Fewer constraints, more acceptable solutions.

questions.q: In the pattern definition, which of these best describes the solution part?
options: The finished code from one successful project in a real system
A description of the situation in which the problem occurs again
A general design that anyone can apply to resolve the forces
A list of the benefits the team hopes to gain from the design
optionExplain: Code from one project is a specific answer; the definition asks for something others can reuse.
That describes the context, a different part of the definition.
Right: the solution is a general design, not tied to one program.
Benefits may follow, but the solution is the design itself.
questions.explain: The solution is a general design that anyone can apply. The card next shows what general means here.
questions.rule: Solution = a general design that resolves the forces.

questions.q: Put the parts of the book's collection example in the order of the definition: context, problem, solution.
items: You have a collection of objects
You need to step through the objects without exposing the collection's implementation
Encapsulate the iteration into a separate class
questions.explain: The context comes first, then the problem with its goal and constraint, then the solution that resolves them.
questions.rule: Context, problem, solution.

questions.q: A library wants one routine that any branch can follow when a book is returned damaged, whatever its forms look like. Which description fits the book's idea of a solution?
options: Written steps and roles that each branch can adapt to its own forms
The exact wording of the damage form that the main branch uses today
A promise by the head librarian to review every damaged book herself
A list of all the damaged books found across branches last year
optionExplain: Right: it is a general design others can apply to their own case.
One branch's form is a specific artifact, not a general design.
A promise is not a design that others can apply.
A list of cases records the situation, not a way to resolve it.
questions.explain: A solution in the book's sense is a design that other people can take and use on their own case. A routine of steps and roles can travel; one form cannot.
questions.rule: General means others can apply it to their own case.

questions.q: Why can the same solution, encapsulating the iteration into a separate class, be reused for unrelated collections?
options: Because every collection stores its objects the same way
Because the class is copied unchanged into each program
Because the solution ignores the constraints of each collection
Because it is a general design, not the code for one program
optionExplain: The book's constraint is precisely that the storage stays hidden, so storage may differ.
Copying code is reuse of an artifact, not of a design.
A solution still has to respect the constraints; ignoring them breaks it.
Right: a design describes an arrangement that fits many programs.
questions.explain: The solution describes how to arrange things so that the goal and constraints are resolved. Because it does not depend on one collection's code, it can be applied to any collection in that context.
questions.rule: Reuse a design, not a file.
questions.teaches: A general design can be applied over different kinds of objects because it describes the arrangement, not one program's code.

questions.q: A school writes down how to run a fire drill: roles, order of steps and a roll call. A rival school with a different building uses the same outline. Which feature of a pattern's solution does this show?
options: The design is general enough to be applied to another case
The design had to be copied word for word to work elsewhere
The design is only valid in the school that wrote it down
The design avoids having any constraints to meet at all
optionExplain: Right: another building can apply it because it is a general design.
If it worked only by being copied word for word, it would not be general.
Reuse by a rival school shows the opposite.
The drill still has to respect constraints such as exits and time.
questions.explain: The outline works for a second building because it describes roles and steps, not one building's corridors. That is what makes a solution general in the book's sense.
questions.rule: Hand it to someone else; can they use it?
questions.teaches: The test of a general solution is handing it to someone with a different case: if they can apply it to their own, it is general.

questions.q: True or false: A fix that resolves the goal but only works with one project's own classes is not yet the general design that the definition asks for.
questions.explain: The definition asks for a general design that anyone can apply. A fix tied to one project's classes is a local answer, not yet a pattern's solution.
questions.rule: Tied to one project means not yet general.

questions.q: True or false: Any description that has a context, a problem and a working solution is a design pattern.
questions.explain: The book shows a description with all three parts that is still not a pattern. The card next shows its counter-example.
questions.rule: Three parts are necessary, not sufficient.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A pattern needs a solution that can be applied over and over to a ____ problem.
questions.explain: The book's test: the problem must recur and the solution must be applicable again and again.
questions.rule: Recurring problem, repeatable solution.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A tenant wants to reach a spare key and climbs through a window, which has to be replaced afterwards. The tenant describes a context, a problem and a solution. Which test does this fail?
options: The context is missing, because lockouts of this kind are rare
The solution does not work, so the problem remains unsolved
There is no goal, so there are no forces
The solution cannot be repeated, so it is not a pattern
optionExplain: The context exists: a locked-out situation. The weakness is in the solution.
The solution does reach the key; it works once but not repeatably.
Reaching the key is the goal, so the forces are present.
Right: replacing a window each time is not a repeatable solution, as with the book's car.
questions.explain: As in the book's car example, every part is present and the solution works, but it cannot be applied over and over at a reasonable cost.
questions.rule: Works once is not the same as repeatable.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Why does the book say that breaking the car window cannot be applied over and over?
options: Balanced against cost, it is unlikely to be worth repeating
Windows can only be broken once, so there is nothing to repeat
Getting to work on time is not a goal that designers care about
Keys are never locked in the same car more than once
optionExplain: Right: the book weighs the goal against another constraint, cost.
Windows can be replaced; the point is what repeating it would cost.
The goal is real; the book accepts it and questions the solution.
The book notes an absent-minded person might lock keys often, so repetition of the problem is possible.
questions.explain: The book's wording is that breaking the window is not likely to be applied repeatedly once the goal is balanced against cost. So repeatability depends on the constraints.
questions.rule: Repeatable means affordable to repeat.
questions.teaches: Whether a solution can be repeated depends on the constraints: a solution that works once but is too costly to repeat fails the recurrence test.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Bakers often face dough that sticks. Baker A chills the dough before shaping it each time. Baker B once fixed a batch by mixing in a glue-like paste that spoiled the loaves. Which cure is closer to the book's idea of a pattern's solution?
options: A's, because it can be applied again and again without harm
B's, because it solved the sticking problem in that one batch
Neither, because dough problems are not design problems
Both, because each was applied to a real baking problem
optionExplain: Right: it can be repeated at acceptable cost, which is what recurrence needs.
It worked once, but ruining the loaves means it cannot be repeated.
The idea of a pattern was born outside software; the test is repeatability.
Applying to a real problem is needed but not enough; B's cure fails on repeatability.
questions.explain: A cure that damages something else each time cannot be applied over and over, whatever it did for one batch. Repeatability is judged by the whole result, including costs.
questions.rule: Judge the fix by everything it costs.
questions.teaches: Repeatability is judged on the whole result: a fix that solves the stated problem but damages something else each time is not a repeatable solution.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Which statements follow from the book's car-window example? Select all that apply.
options: Cost never matters when judging whether a solution is repeatable
A person who often locks keys in the car has thereby found a pattern
A solution that worked once can still fail the recurrence test
Having a context, a problem and a solution is necessary but not enough
optionExplain: The book weighs the goal against cost, so cost does matter.
The book says an absent-minded person may repeat the problem, but the solution is still not repeatable.
Right: working once is different from being applicable over and over.
Right: the example has all three parts and still fails.
questions.explain: The example shows that the three parts are not a complete test and that recurrence of the solution matters. Frequent lockouts do not make breaking a window a pattern.
questions.rule: Test for recurrence of the solution, not just of the problem.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Besides recurrence, which weaknesses does the book name in the keys-in-the-car description? Select all that apply.
options: It has no goal to measure the solution against
It has no name that could join a shared vocabulary
It is not easy to hand to someone else to apply to their own problem
It was written down too late to be useful
optionExplain: The example does state a goal, getting to work on time.
Right: the book points out that the description has not even been given a name.
Right: a pattern description has to be usable by others.
Timing of writing is not among the book's complaints.
questions.explain: The book names two faults beyond recurrence: it cannot easily be handed over, and it has no name. The card next explains each.
questions.rule: Hand-over and name.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, a pattern needs a name so that it can become part of a vocabulary shared with other developers.
questions.explain: The book says the missing name is important: without it the pattern cannot become part of a shared vocabulary.
questions.rule: No name, no shared vocabulary.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A support team documents a fix for jammed printers in clear steps that other teams use on their own printer models. Everyone calls it that thing Dana did. Which of the book's faults remains?
options: It cannot be handed to anyone else to apply to their own printers
It does not describe a recurring problem that teams face
It has no name, so it cannot join a vocabulary the teams share
It has no context, since jams happen on printers everywhere
optionExplain: Other teams do apply it, so the hand-over test is met.
Printer jams do recur, so recurrence is fine.
Right: the steps travel well, but nobody can refer to it by a shared name.
The context, printers that jam, is present.
questions.explain: The fix passes the hand-over test because other teams apply it to their own printers. What it lacks is a name that people can use in conversation.
questions.rule: A pattern is something you can refer to by name.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Two teams both know the pattern name Observer. What does the name let one developer do when talking to the other?
options: Skip reviewing the design, because the name guarantees its quality
Avoid documenting how their version differs from the classic design
Refer to a whole design in a word without describing its classes
Prove that the design is the best possible choice for the job
optionExplain: A name shows both know the design, not that it suits the problem.
The book still asks for documentation of differences.
Right: a shared name carries the whole design in a word.
A name does not rank designs.
questions.explain: A name compresses a design into a word that both sides understand. That is why the book treats the missing name in the car example as a real fault.
questions.rule: A name is a shortcut for a design.
questions.teaches: A shared name packs a whole design into a word, so a team can discuss it without describing each class.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Two hospitals want to share a method for handing patients between shifts. Which description is more likely to let a stranger apply it to their own ward?
options: A name, when it applies, the steps, and the trade-offs of using it
A detailed list of the steps used on one ward on one night
A name with a note that it worked well, signed by the ward manager
A photograph of the ward where the method was first used
optionExplain: Right: when it applies and what it costs, as well as the steps, let a stranger judge whether it fits.
Steps from one night record what happened but not when or why to use them.
A name and praise do not tell a stranger what to do.
A photograph shows a place, not a method.
questions.explain: Catalog entries add intent, applicability and consequences to the bare steps for exactly this reason: someone with a different problem needs to know whether and how the solution fits.
questions.rule: Say when, why and at what cost, as well as how.
questions.teaches: A description that others can apply states when the solution applies and what it costs, not only its steps; this is why catalog entries have sections beyond the solution.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Priya says: I named my one-off workaround Plan Bee and gave it to a friend, so it is a pattern. Which parts of her reasoning fail? Select all that apply.
options: Handing a fix to a friend makes it less likely to be a pattern
Naming and handing over are required but are not sufficient by themselves
A name does not turn a one-off fix into a solution that applies over and over
A pattern may not be given a name until it has been published
optionExplain: Handing it to others is what the book asks for.
Right: the book lists them as needs, not as a full test.
Right: recurrence is still missing.
The book does not say names wait for publication.
questions.explain: Priya has a name and a hand-over, which the car example lacked, but she has not shown that the solution is repeatable or general. The tests add up; none replaces the others.
questions.rule: Recurrence, hand-over and name are all needed.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: A pattern's classic structure must be followed exactly, or the design no longer counts as using the pattern.
questions.explain: The book treats patterns as guidelines you can alter to fit your needs. The card next adds what it asks you to do when you do.
questions.rule: Patterns are guidelines.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Like design principles, patterns are not meant to be laws or rules; they are ____ that you can alter to fit your needs.
questions.explain: The book calls patterns guidelines, in the same spirit as design principles.
questions.rule: Guidelines, not laws.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A team uses a well-known pattern but removes one of its classes because their application does not need it. What does the book advise?
options: Restore the class, since patterns are laws
Document how the design differs from the classic one
Rename the design so nobody thinks it is the pattern
Say nothing, because the adapted version becomes the new classic
optionExplain: The book says patterns are not laws, so changing them is allowed.
Right: the book advises documenting how your pattern differs from the classic design.
A name still helps; the better step is to record the difference.
Silence leaves later readers unsure what changed.
questions.explain: Adapting is fine; what the book adds is documenting the difference so that others recognise the pattern and the departure.
questions.rule: Adapt, then say how.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: What does documenting the difference from the classic design let other developers do?
options: Treat the adapted version as the official classic from then on
Skip reading the code, because the pattern's name explains everything
Recognise the pattern quickly and see where this version departs
Prove that the adaptation is better than the classic design
optionExplain: Documentation records a difference; it does not make the version official.
The name helps, but the code still shows the details.
Right: they keep the pattern's name as a clue and learn exactly what changed.
Documentation says what differs, not whether it is better.
questions.explain: The note works twice: the name tells readers which pattern to expect, and the note tells them where reality departs from it.
questions.rule: Name for what to expect, note for what changed.
questions.teaches: A note on differences keeps a pattern name useful after adaptation: the name tells readers what to expect and the note tells them what changed.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A team lead says: our code matches no textbook pattern exactly, so we are not using patterns. What view does the book offer?
options: The lead is right, since only exact matches of the classic design count
Real-world uses often depart from classic designs, which is expected
The team should rewrite its code to match the classic designs exactly
Patterns apply only to textbook problems, not to real software
optionExplain: The book treats patterns as adaptable guidelines, so exactness is not required.
Right: the book notes that many real-world examples do not fit the classic designs.
Rewriting to match is the rule-following the book argues against.
The book wants patterns used in real work, with adaptation.
questions.explain: The book itself says that a lot of real-world examples do not fit the classic pattern designs. A close-but-adapted use still counts, and the difference should be documented.
questions.rule: A near match with notes is still use of the pattern.
questions.teaches: Real-world uses often fail to match the classic design exactly, so a close fit with documented differences is normal, not a failure to use the pattern.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: Even though the book allows patterns to be adapted, it still advises documenting how a version differs from the classic design.
questions.explain: The book says that when you adapt a pattern it never hurts to document the difference. Freedom to adapt is a reason to document it, so others can follow.
questions.rule: More freedom, more reason to document.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A pattern catalog describes each pattern with the same set of sections. What is the main benefit of that?
options: Every pattern ends up looking equally suitable for your problem
You know where to look for the same information in every entry
You can skip reading the sections that describe consequences
The patterns are guaranteed not to overlap with one another
optionExplain: A template organises information; it does not make patterns equally suitable.
Right: a fixed template means the answer to a given question is in a known place.
The consequences section is one of the most useful, so skipping it defeats the purpose.
Related patterns are described precisely because patterns relate and can overlap.
questions.explain: A shared template makes entries comparable and lets you jump straight to the part you need. The card next lists the sections.
questions.rule: Same template, same place to look.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Match each catalog section to what it tells you.
pairs: What the pattern is, like a definition
When and where the pattern might be used
The classes in the design and their roles
The good and bad effects of using the pattern
questions.explain: Intent says what the pattern is, Motivation and Applicability say when it fits, Participants name the classes and roles, and Consequences list the effects.
questions.rule: What, when, who, cost.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: You are choosing between two patterns and want to understand how they differ. Which part of a catalog entry helps most?
options: The sample code section showing how one version is written
The list of participants and the roles they play in the design
The pattern's name and the picture of its class diagram
The section on how the pattern relates to other patterns
optionExplain: Sample code shows one implementation, not how patterns compare.
Participants list classes and roles of this pattern only.
A name labels the pattern but does not compare it.
Right: the book says each entry describes the relationship to other patterns, such as how two patterns differ.
questions.explain: Entries describe relationships to other patterns, which is why the book calls this one of the most useful sections for telling similar patterns apart.
questions.rule: Look under related patterns to compare.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A catalog entry lists the bad effects of a pattern as well as the good ones. What does that make possible?
options: A reader can ignore the intent section
A reader can alter the pattern without documenting it
A reader can guarantee the pattern has no side effects
A reader can decide not to use the pattern
optionExplain: Intent remains the first check of what the pattern is.
Documentation of differences is a separate need.
Listing effects shows them; it does not remove them.
Right: an entry that shows costs supports a choice against the pattern.
questions.explain: Consequences cover both sides, so reading them is how you find unintended effects before committing. A pattern's benefits come with costs.
questions.rule: Read the costs before the code.
questions.teaches: A catalog entry lists the bad effects of a pattern next to the good ones, so reading it can lead you to choose against the pattern.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A gardening guide lists each plant with the parts below. Match each part to the catalog section it resembles.
pairs: What the plant is good for
Soils and climates where it thrives
questions.explain: The guide has the same kinds of parts as a pattern catalog: name, purpose, where it applies and what it costs. Any collection of reusable solutions can use such a template.
questions.rule: A template travels beyond software.
questions.teaches: Any collection of reusable solutions can be organised with the same kind of template: a name, a purpose, where it applies and what it costs.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Sort each question by the part of a catalog entry that answers it.

items.t: Does my situation fit this pattern?
Where might I use it?
Will it add effects I did not intend?
What will I pay in complexity?
When was the pattern meant to be used?
What are the drawbacks of applying it?

questions.explain: Motivation and Applicability say when and where the pattern fits. Consequences say what comes with using it, good and bad.
questions.rule: Fit before cost: applicability, then consequences.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: You think a catalog pattern fits your problem. What should you check before working it into your design?
options: Its motivation, applicability and consequences
Its sample code, in order to copy it into the design
Its name, to see if it sounds right for the problem
Its class diagram, to count the classes it will add
optionExplain: Right: confirm the fit and the effects before investing in details.
Sample code is a later step and is not a test of fit.
A name may suggest a fit but does not confirm one.
The structure matters after the fit is confirmed.
questions.explain: A fit check comes first. The card next gives the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Fit first, details later.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Put the steps of Jim's routine in the order he follows them.
items: Get familiar with the patterns and their relationships
Check Motivation and Applicability
Review Consequences
Read Structure and Participants
Work the pattern into your design with alterations
Review Implementation and sample code
questions.explain: Jim confirms the fit and effects first. Only after that does he study the structure, work it into his design and read the implementation notes.
questions.rule: Fit, effects, structure, adapt, implement.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: An engineer reading a catalog of building-safety patterns finds one that might suit a stairwell. Following Jim's routine, what comes before studying the diagrams?
options: Copying the sample solution straight into the plan as drawn
Checking where the pattern applies and what effects it has
Asking colleagues which pattern is the most popular these days
Building a small model first to see how the structure looks
optionExplain: Sample solutions come at the end of the routine.
Right: motivation, applicability and consequences come before structure.
Popularity is not part of the routine.
Models come later, if at all, after the fit is checked.
questions.explain: Jim reads the diagram and participants only after he knows the pattern is right and what it will do to the rest of the design.
questions.rule: Is it right? What will it do? Then how is it built?
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: Why does Jim review the Consequences section before he reads the structure?
options: Because the structure section cannot be understood without it
Because the consequences section also contains the sample code
To rule out unintended effects on his design before details
Because the catalog forbids anyone from reading structure first
optionExplain: Structure is understandable on its own; the order is about risk.
Consequences list effects, not code.
Right: he wants to be sure there will be no unintended effect on his design.
The routine is Jim's habit, not a catalog rule.
questions.explain: Reading effects early protects the rest of the design: if the costs are unacceptable, the details never need studying.
questions.rule: Check the costs before the details.
questions.teaches: Reviewing consequences before adopting a pattern is how you protect the rest of the design from unintended effects.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A paramedic memorises emergency protocols before any call. In the call, a quick look at a card confirms which to use. Which part of Jim's routine is this like, and why does it help?
options: Reviewing consequences, so that no protocol is ever used in practice
Getting familiar first, so a lookup only has to confirm a choice
Reading sample code, so that each protocol is copied exactly as written
Alteration of the structure, so that every protocol is changed
optionExplain: Consequences are reviewed to avoid bad effects, not to avoid using protocols.
Right: prior familiarity means that, when a need arises, you already have an idea of what to look up.
Samples are a late step and the paramedic is not copying code.
Alterations come when working a choice into a design.
questions.explain: Jim gets to know all the patterns and their relationships first, so that when a need arises he has some idea of what he is looking for and the catalog confirms it.
questions.rule: Learn the options before the need.
questions.teaches: Knowing the options in advance turns a catalog from something you search blindly into something that confirms a choice you already have in mind.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: After Jim confirms a pattern is right, he works it into his design, making any alterations needed to make it fit.
questions.explain: In the dialogue he works the pattern into his design, making any alterations needed to make it fit. Adapting the structure is part of the routine.
questions.rule: Adapt the structure to your design.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: How do a fundamental patterns catalog and a domain-specific one differ?
options: Fundamental catalogs are written for beginners, domain ones for experts
Domain catalogs describe anti-patterns, fundamental ones describe patterns
Domain catalogs cover one area, fundamental ones cover general design
Fundamental catalogs cover only creational patterns
optionExplain: Audience level is not the distinction the book draws.
Anti-patterns are a different topic; both kinds of catalog describe patterns.
Right: scope is the difference.
The fundamental catalog covers several categories of patterns.
questions.explain: The difference is scope: general design versus a specific area. The card next gives the classic example.
questions.rule: Fundamental catalogs are general; domain catalogs are specific.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: The classic GoF catalog lays out ____ fundamental patterns.
questions.explain: The GoF catalog lays out 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.rule: GoF: 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A team building a service that handles many simultaneous users wants patterns for that kind of system. Which kind of catalog does the book suggest?
options: Only the GoF catalog, since it has every pattern ever described
A catalog of anti-patterns, since concurrent systems are risky
None; patterns do not exist for systems of that kind
A domain-specific catalog, such as one on concurrent systems
optionExplain: The GoF catalog holds fundamental patterns, not every domain's.
Anti-pattern catalogs warn about bad solutions; the team wants good ones.
The book says domain catalogs are being published.
Right: the book says catalogs exist for domains such as concurrent systems.
questions.explain: Domain-specific patterns concern problems in specific domains, and catalogs for them exist.
questions.rule: Domain problem, domain catalog.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: What does the book say about catalogs other than the fundamental one?
options: None exist yet, so the fundamental catalog is all there is to use
They replace the fundamental patterns with newer, improved versions of them
New ones are appearing for areas such as enterprise and business systems
They are limited to a single programming language or platform
optionExplain: The book says the opposite.
They add domain patterns; they do not replace the fundamentals.
Right: the book says many catalogs are starting to be published in such areas.
The book names areas of work, not languages.
questions.explain: The book mentions enterprise software, concurrent systems and business systems as areas where catalogs are starting to appear.
questions.rule: The catalog shelf keeps growing.
questions.teaches: Catalogs are being published for areas such as enterprise software, concurrent systems and business systems, so the set of catalogs is still growing.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: A law student owns a textbook of general contract principles and a handbook on shipping contracts only. Which book plays the part of a domain-specific catalog?
options: The shipping handbook, because it covers one area's problems
The general textbook, because it is the most definitive of the two
Neither, because law has no recurring problems to document
Both, because any book on a topic is a catalog
optionExplain: Right: scope to one area is what makes a catalog domain-specific.
The general book plays the part of the fundamental catalog.
Law has recurring problems, which is why handbooks exist.
Scope, not being a book, is what defines each kind.
questions.explain: A narrow handbook mirrors a domain catalog and a general textbook mirrors a fundamental one. You turn to the narrow one when the area has recurring problems of its own.
questions.rule: General first, specific when the area demands it.
questions.teaches: Turn to a domain catalog when your area has recurring problems of its own that general patterns do not address.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: True or false: A designer meets a recurring problem in a specialised area that none of the 23 GoF patterns addresses. This means the problem cannot have a pattern.
questions.explain: The GoF catalog covers fundamental patterns only. Domain-specific catalogs exist for problems particular to an area.
questions.rule: Not in GoF is not the same as no pattern.
questions.section: Looking more closely at the Design Pattern definition

questions.q: According to the book, how do design patterns come into existence?
options: They are invented at a desk by experienced designers and then tested
They are voted on each year by the publishers of catalogs
They are generated step by step from the design principles
They are discovered in solutions that recur, then described
optionExplain: Invention is the opposite of the book's view.
Publishers collect and publish patterns; they do not make them.
Principles guide design, but patterns are found in practice.
Right: the book says patterns are discovered, not created.
questions.explain: The book says patterns are discovered, not created. The card next adds who can discover one and why few do.
questions.rule: Patterns are found, not made.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, anyone can discover a pattern and write its description, although it takes commitment.
questions.explain: The book says anyone can discover a pattern and write its description, though it is not easy and takes commitment.
questions.rule: Anyone can, but it takes commitment.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A hospital pharmacist notices that the same safe-dispensing routine solves a problem that recurs on many wards. How does the book describe her situation?
options: She has created a pattern, since she thought of the routine and wrote it down
She has nothing, because only software can have patterns at all
She has a pattern as soon as she gives it a name of her own
She has found a possible pattern in practice; describing it takes commitment
optionExplain: The book speaks of discovery, not creation.
The idea of patterns started outside software.
A name is only one need; the other tests still apply.
Right: it is a candidate found in recurring practice, and writing it up is real work.
questions.explain: A routine that works and recurs is the raw material of a pattern. Describing it well and testing it still lie ahead.
questions.rule: Found in practice, proven later.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: The book says the majority of people do not write patterns; they use them. What follows?
options: People who use patterns without writing them have not really understood them
Using patterns without writing one is the normal way to benefit
Only people who write patterns can contribute to the pattern community
Using patterns is a stage everyone must pass before writing
optionExplain: Understanding does not depend on authoring.
Right: the book presents using as the common, fine way to take part.
The book lists other ways to take part, such as joining the community.
Nothing in the text makes writing a required next step.
questions.explain: Writing is a choice with a cost, not a duty. Most people gain by using what others have written.
questions.rule: Use first; write only with a reason.
questions.teaches: Using patterns without writing any is the normal way to benefit; authoring is optional and worth doing only for a reason.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Which of these would the book count as good reasons for someone to start writing patterns? Select all that apply.
options: Having found a solution to what seems a recurring problem
Working in a specialised domain where new patterns would help
Wanting to join the patterns community and add to its work
Wanting a name for a one-off fix to spare the effort of documenting it
optionExplain: Right: a recurring problem with a solution is the raw material.
Right: the book names specialised domains as a reason.
Right: contributing to the growing body of work is a reason.
A name for a one-off fix does not meet the recurring test, and avoiding documentation is not a reason the book gives.
questions.explain: The book lists three reasons: a specialised domain, a recurring problem with a solution you found, and wanting to be part of the community.
questions.rule: Write with a reason.
questions.teaches: The book gives three reasons to write patterns: a specialised domain, a found solution to a recurring problem, or wanting to join the community.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Which statement matches the book's view of where a new pattern comes from?
options: A writer notices a solution already recurring in practice and describes it
A writer designs a new structure first and then looks for problems it solves
A writer renames an existing pattern and publishes it as new
A writer asks a community which patterns it would like
optionExplain: Right: patterns are discovered in recurring solutions.
Designing first is creating, which the book says is not how patterns arise.
Renaming does not discover anything.
Patterns come from practice, not wish lists.
questions.explain: Discovery starts from practice: a recurring problem and a solution people already use. The writer's job is to see it and describe it.
questions.rule: Start from practice, not from the drawing board.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: According to the book, when can a candidate solution be called a design pattern?
options: As soon as its author documents it in a standard template
When a catalog publisher accepts it for publication
After it has been applied once, successfully, in one large project
After it has been applied in real solutions at least three times
optionExplain: Documentation is needed but is not the test of being a pattern.
The book does not tie being a pattern to a publisher.
One use does not show a solution recurs; the rule asks for three.
Right: the Rule of Three sets this test.
questions.explain: The book gives a numeric rule. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Three real-world uses.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A candidate can be called a pattern only if it has been applied in a real-world solution at least ____ times.
questions.explain: The Rule of Three: at least three applications in real-world solutions.
questions.rule: Rule of Three.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A teacher has used her classroom routine in two real classes and it worked both times. A colleague says she can publish it as a pattern. What does the Rule of Three say?
options: Yes: two successes show that the routine recurs in practice
Yes: a routine used by its own author counts as a pattern
Not yet: it needs at least three real-world applications
No: routines used in classrooms can never be patterns
optionExplain: Two is below the minimum in the rule.
The book says others should have used it and found it works.
Right: two uses fall short of three.
The rule is about the number of applications, not the subject area.
questions.explain: The rule sets three real-world applications as the minimum before a candidate is called a pattern; two are a good start but not enough.
questions.rule: Two is a good start, not the threshold.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Why does the rule ask for applications in real-world solutions?
options: Real-world solutions are always simpler than classroom examples would be
Three is the number of categories in the standard scheme of patterns
Publishers only accept patterns that already appear in shipping products
A pattern is shown by use that worked, not by an author's confidence
optionExplain: Complexity is not the reason.
The number of categories is unrelated.
Publishing is not what the rule is about.
Right: the book says you do not have a pattern until others have used it and found it to work.
questions.explain: A candidate becomes a pattern through proof in use. Real-world use shows that it solves the problem under real constraints.
questions.rule: Proof comes from use.
questions.teaches: The rule treats pattern status as earned by successful use in real conditions; the author's belief that the design is good does not count.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A chef's technique works well in her own kitchen only. Which step would move it toward pattern status in the book's sense?
options: Other cooks use it in real kitchens, at least three times
The chef gives it a catchy name and lists it on the menu of her restaurant
The chef demonstrates it three times in her own kitchen for guests
Critics write praise of the dishes that the technique produces
optionExplain: Right: others applying it in real settings is what the rule asks for.
A name helps, but use is the test.
Her own kitchen is one place; the book says others have to use it.
Praise is not the same as being applied by others.
questions.explain: The book ties pattern status to others having used the solution and found it works. Three demonstrations in one kitchen are one setting repeated.
questions.rule: Others, in real settings.
questions.teaches: The uses that count come from others, in separate real solutions; repeating a technique in the author's own setting does not meet the standard.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: True or false: A candidate has been applied successfully in two real-world solutions, and a third is under way. It has not yet met the Rule of Three.
questions.explain: The rule asks for at least three applications that have happened. Until the third is done and found to work, the candidate has not passed.
questions.rule: Count completed, successful uses.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: A developer believes she has found a brand-new pattern. What does the book expect to be true of most such finds?
options: They turn out to need a new category of their own in the catalog
They turn out to be correct and complete as first written
They turn out to be variants of patterns that already exist
They turn out to be too complicated for any catalog to hold
optionExplain: Nothing in the text suggests new categories are the usual outcome.
The book expects patterns to need refining.
Right: the book says most apparently new patterns are variants.
Complexity is not the issue the book raises.
questions.explain: A newcomer's find usually has an older relative. The card next explains why that matters before writing anything.
questions.rule: Most new patterns are variants.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: Most patterns that appear to be new are, in fact, ____ of existing patterns.
questions.explain: The book says most apparently new patterns are variants of existing patterns.
questions.rule: Variants of known patterns.
questions.section: So you wanna be a Design Patterns writer

questions.q: An architect thinks she has invented a new way to arrange hospital wards for recurring emergencies. What does the book's advice to would-be writers say to do first?
options: Publish it quickly before someone else publishes the same idea
Learn the existing arrangements, since hers may be a variant
Replace the older arrangements with hers on every ward at once
Wait to see whether anyone else notices the same problem
optionExplain: Speed is not the book's concern; being well versed is.
Right: study first, since most new-looking patterns are variants.
Replacing existing patterns is not part of the advice.
Waiting is not the advice; the book says to study and to reflect.
questions.explain: A well-versed writer can tell whether the idea is new or a variant, and learns how it relates to existing ones.
questions.rule: Know the field before claiming to extend it.
