The other developer need not know any patterns for the name to work
optionExplain: Right: the name stands for a design both understand.
Names do not change speed.
A shared name does not replace review.
The benefit depends on both knowing the name.
questions.explain: A shared name is a compact way to describe a design and keeps misunderstandings down.
questions.rule: A name carries a design.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: How do the OO design principles help when you meet a pattern that is new to you?
options: You can skip reading the new pattern's catalog description entirely
You can assume the new pattern is sound without checking its fit
You can understand the pattern's motivation and workings from them
You can rename the pattern to suit the habits of your own team
optionExplain: The principles help you read the description; they do not replace it.
Understanding is not the same as assuming it is sound.
Right: the book says the principles let you understand the motivation and workings of any new pattern.
Renaming would damage the shared vocabulary.
questions.explain: Principles are the common ground behind the patterns, so a new pattern can be read in their light.
questions.rule: Principles unlock new patterns.
questions.teaches: The OO principles give you a base from which to understand the motivation and workings of any new pattern.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Jazz musicians call a chord sequence by a name, and a band of strangers can play it at once. Why does the book say it is worth spreading pattern names to colleagues?
options: Names are valuable only to the person who first coined them
Its value rises as more of your colleagues know the names
Spreading names replaces the need to learn the patterns
A name works even if nobody else on the team knows it
optionExplain: The point of a vocabulary is that it is shared.
Right: a shared vocabulary improves as more people share it.
Names stand for patterns that must still be learned.
The vocabulary needs shared knowledge.
questions.explain: The musicians' name works because everyone knows it. The book says to spread the word so that more colleagues can use the vocabulary.
questions.rule: Spread the vocabulary.
questions.teaches: Sharing the vocabulary is itself worthwhile, since its value rises as more colleagues know it.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: True or false: A developer who is the only person on a team who knows the pattern names gets the full benefit of a shared vocabulary.
questions.explain: A shared vocabulary needs more than one person who shares it. The book urges you to spread the word so that fellow developers use it too.
questions.rule: A vocabulary needs speakers.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: What does the book say using patterns in design meetings helps a team do?
options: Skip discussion of the requirements and move straight on to code
Stay in the design longer without getting bogged down in details
Finish meetings sooner by having everyone vote on which patterns to use
Avoid the need for any documentation of the design afterwards
optionExplain: Requirements still need discussion.
Right: the vocabulary keeps the talk at the level of design.
Voting is not part of the advice.
Documentation is a separate setting for the vocabulary.
questions.explain: Pattern names lift a discussion above implementation detail. The card next lists all five settings.
questions.rule: Patterns keep talk in the design.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Match each setting to what the book says patterns do there.
pairs: Keep the team in the design and prevent misunderstandings
Reduce the amount of documentation needed
Let readers quickly see the pattern behind the code
Share knowledge, for example in a brown-bag lunch
questions.explain: Each setting has a benefit: staying in the design, shorter documentation, quick understanding of code, and wider knowledge.
questions.rule: Five settings, five benefits.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer names a class after the pattern behind it and notes the pattern in a comment. Which of the book's five ways is this?
options: Design meetings, where the team talks
Code comments and naming conventions
Architecture documentation for the whole system
Talks to groups of interested developers
optionExplain: Meetings are a spoken setting.
Right: the book recommends naming and commenting to reveal the pattern.
Architecture documents are separate from code.
Talks are to groups.
questions.explain: Names and comments in code reveal the pattern, so later readers understand the implementation quickly.
questions.rule: Let names reveal patterns.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Why does mentioning a pattern in architecture documentation reduce the amount of writing needed?
options: The reader is expected to guess the design from the name and context
Patterns cannot be described in writing, so documents leave them out
The documentation replaces the code as the real source of the design
The name stands for a design the reader knows, so fewer words suffice
optionExplain: Guessing is the opposite of a shared vocabulary.
The catalog describes patterns in writing.
Documentation supports code; it does not replace it.
Right: a shared name carries a design in a word.
questions.explain: The name does work that sentences would otherwise do, provided the reader knows it.
questions.rule: A name saves words.
questions.teaches: A pattern name in documentation conveys a whole design in a word, so fewer words give the reader a clearer picture, if the reader knows the name.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A hospital procedure manual names its routines, such as a two-person check, and uses those names in forms and on wall charts. Which advice in the book does this resemble?
options: Hiding the procedure behind general terms that suit every ward
Writing nothing in the manual and teaching by word of mouth
Using a different name for the same routine on every ward
Choosing names that reveal what is underneath so readers understand
optionExplain: Hiding is the opposite.
The book asks for documentation.
Different names would break the shared vocabulary.
Right: names that reveal the pattern help readers understand quickly.
questions.explain: Where a name appears in the places people read, the vocabulary does its job. The hospital's checks work like pattern names in code and comments.
questions.rule: Put names where readers look.
questions.teaches: Where a shared name appears in the places people actually read, such as comments, class names and charts, it lets readers understand the structure at once.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: A developer's plan for sharing patterns has these parts. Which conflict with the book's advice? Select all that apply.
options: Offer a short talk to a local user group
Never mention patterns in comments
Name every class Manager, whatever pattern it follows
Explain pattern names in design meetings
optionExplain: No conflict: this is the book's fifth suggestion.
Conflict: the book says to identify patterns in comments.
Conflict: the book says to choose names that reveal the pattern underneath.
No conflict: this is the book's first suggestion.
questions.explain: The first two parts hide the patterns, which defeats the vocabulary. The others follow the book.
questions.rule: Reveal, do not hide.
questions.section: Don’t forget the power of the shared vocabulary

questions.q: Which person is a member of the Gang of Four?
options: Erich Gamma
Christopher Alexander
Ward Cunningham
Elisabeth Robson
optionExplain: Right: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides are the GoF.
Alexander was the architect with whom patterns began, a different group.
Cunningham runs the Portland Patterns Repository.
Robson is a co-author of this Head First book.
questions.explain: The GoF are four authors of the first catalog. The card next names them and their book.
questions.rule: GoF: Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: The GoF book, Design Patterns, kicked off the field of design patterns when it was released in ____.
questions.explain: The book says the GoF book kicked off the field in 1995.
questions.rule: The GoF book appeared in 1995.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: A colleague says: check what GoF says about this before we decide. What is she pointing you to?
options: A catalog of the anti-patterns found in many real projects
A catalog of domain-specific patterns for a single named industry
A list of the coding standards used across the whole company
The first and most definitive catalog of fundamental patterns
optionExplain: Anti-patterns are described elsewhere.
The GoF catalog covers fundamental patterns, not one industry's.
The GoF catalog is about patterns, not standards.
Right: GoF means the Gang of Four's catalog.
questions.explain: GoF is shorthand for the authors and their book of 23 fundamental patterns.
questions.rule: GoF = the first catalog.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: What is the relation between the GoF book and the patterns in this Head First book?
options: This book replaces the GoF set with a newer set of patterns
The two books share no patterns, as they cover different fields
The GoF book is the basis for the patterns used here
This book describes only the patterns the GoF left out
optionExplain: It uses the GoF set, not replaces it.
They share the patterns.
Right: the book says GoF is the basis for its set.
It covers the GoF patterns.
questions.explain: The book builds on the GoF catalog and points you to it for the full treatment.
questions.rule: This book is based on GoF.
questions.teaches: The patterns taught in this book are drawn from the GoF catalog, which is why the GoF book is the natural next read.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: A new field has a founding textbook that is still the standard reference decades later. What attitude does the book's description of GoF suggest toward such a text?
options: Treat it as the last word on patterns, so nothing further is needed
Treat it as outdated and ignore it in favour of newer, shorter books
Treat it as useful only to its authors and the people who know them
Treat it as the definitive starting point, expecting later growth
optionExplain: The book says it is not the last word.
It remains a recommended start.
It is for all readers of the field.
Right: the book calls GoF first and most definitive, but not the last word.
questions.explain: A founding text is a good start. Its value does not shut out later work.
questions.rule: Start with the founders; keep reading.
questions.teaches: A founding text deserves reading as the starting point of a field, and later work should be expected to extend it.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: True or false: The book presents the GoF book as the last word on design patterns.
questions.explain: The book says the field has grown substantially since the GoF book was published; it is the first and most definitive, but not the last word.
questions.rule: First, not last.
questions.section: Cruisin’ Objectville with the Gang of Four

questions.q: Where did the idea of patterns begin?
options: In the GoF book of 1995, which gathered the first catalog
In building architecture, with Christopher Alexander
In the Portland Patterns Repository wiki run by Ward Cunningham
In the first multi-tier systems built for the early web
optionExplain: The GoF book brought patterns to software but did not begin them.
Right: patterns started with Alexander's work on buildings.
The wiki is a later community resource.
The book says patterns started in architecture of buildings, not systems.
questions.explain: Patterns began outside software. The card next names the source.
questions.rule: Patterns began in building architecture.

questions.q: Match each resource to what the book says about it.
pairs: A wiki run by Ward Cunningham where anyone can take part
A central resource for patterns work, with articles, books, mailing lists and tools
A conference called Pattern Languages of Programs
The ACM Conference on Object-Oriented Systems, Languages and Applications
questions.explain: The wiki and the Hillside site are online resources. PLoP and OOPSLA are conferences.
questions.rule: Wiki, site, two conferences.

questions.q: A software developer asks why she should read A Pattern Language, a book about towns and buildings. What does the book give as the reason?
options: It lists the 23 fundamental software patterns with sample code
It replaces the GoF catalog with a newer and much fuller catalog
It teaches the object-oriented principles behind the software patterns
It shows the true beginnings of patterns and analogies with software
optionExplain: That is the GoF catalog.
It is not a software catalog.
Principles are taught elsewhere.
Right: the book recommends it for the origins and the analogies.
questions.explain: Alexander's books are the roots of the idea. Reading them shows what software patterns borrowed.
questions.rule: Read the roots.

questions.q: What does it suggest about patterns that their originator was an architect rather than a computer scientist?
options: The idea of patterns is not tied to software
Software patterns are older than architectural ones
Patterns apply only to buildings
Computer scientists should not write patterns
optionExplain: Right: patterns began outside software.
The book says patterns started in architecture.
The book lists several domains.
The book invites participation.
questions.explain: Because patterns began in architecture, the concept carries to other fields, as the next idea shows.
questions.rule: Patterns are not only for software.
questions.teaches: Patterns began in building architecture, so the concept is not tied to software and can carry to other fields.

questions.q: A hospital manager wants to discuss shared routines with people from many fields, on a site where anyone can take part and every topic can be raised. Which resource in the book fits?
options: The Hillside Group conference list
The GoF book
The Portland Patterns Repository
The Timeless Way of Building
optionExplain: The Hillside site lists conferences and resources, not an open wiki.
The GoF book is a catalog, not a discussion site.
Right: it is a wiki open to anyone, with threads on every topic related to patterns and OO systems.
That is a book by Alexander.
questions.explain: Of the resources named, the wiki is the open discussion space.
questions.rule: An open wiki for open discussion.
questions.teaches: The Portland Patterns Repository is an open wiki, so anyone can join discussions on patterns and object-oriented systems.

questions.q: True or false: According to the book, Christopher Alexander was a computer scientist who invented software patterns.
questions.explain: The book says Alexander was an architect, a professor of architecture at Berkeley, who invented patterns for buildings and towns.
questions.rule: Alexander was an architect.

questions.q: Which of these does the book's Patterns Zoo include as a domain of patterns? Select all that apply.
options: Compiler optimisation patterns
User interface patterns
Business process patterns
Organizational patterns
optionExplain: Not in the book's zoo.
Included: designing interactive software.
Included: interaction between businesses, customers and data.
Included: structures and practices of human organizations.
questions.explain: The zoo covers more than code design. The card next lists each domain.
questions.rule: Patterns reach beyond code.

questions.q: Match each pattern domain to what it addresses.
pairs: Interaction between businesses, customers and data
Structures and practices of human organizations
questions.explain: Each domain applies the pattern idea to a different kind of recurring problem.
questions.rule: Domain, then problem.

questions.q: A designer wants guidance on laying out an interactive screen for a mobile app. Which pattern domain in the zoo covers this?
options: Architectural patterns
Business process patterns
User interface patterns
Domain-specific patterns for real-time systems
optionExplain: Architectural patterns concern buildings and towns.
Business processes concern interactions between businesses and customers.
Right: designing interactive software is the user interface domain.
Real-time systems are a different specific domain.
questions.explain: User interface patterns address how to design interactive software programs.
questions.rule: Screens: user interface patterns.

questions.q: What does the book say about application patterns?
options: They concern only buildings, towns and cities, where patterns first began
They concern system-level architecture; MVC has been known to pass for one
They are the same as the creational patterns in the GoF classification
They are limited to concurrent systems and other real-time software
optionExplain: That is the architectural domain.
Right: this is the book's description.
Creational is a different, purpose-based category.
That is a domain-specific example.
questions.explain: Application patterns work at the level of the whole system, and the book notes that MVC can pass for one.
questions.rule: Whole-system architecture: application patterns.
questions.teaches: Application patterns work at the level of the whole system, and MVC has been known to pass for an application pattern.

questions.q: Sort each concern into the kind of pattern the zoo would file it under.

items.t: Problems of concurrent systems
How to make and communicate decisions effectively
Problems of real-time systems
Interaction between businesses and customers
Problems particular to a specialised technical field
How data and decisions flow between a business and its clients

questions.explain: Domain-specific patterns concern a particular technical domain. Business process patterns concern how businesses, customers and data interact.
questions.rule: Technical field, or business interaction?
questions.teaches: Patterns can describe how people and companies work together, as well as how code is built.

questions.q: True or false: The book's Patterns Zoo lists every domain in which patterns can be used.
questions.explain: The book says the zoo shows a few domains, and leaves space for the reader's own field notes.
questions.rule: The zoo is a sample.

questions.q: What does an anti-pattern tell you?
options: How to remove a pattern from a design safely
How to test whether a pattern is correct in code
How to name a pattern so others can find it
How to go from a problem to a bad solution
optionExplain: Removing patterns is a separate topic.
Testing a pattern is a different job.
Naming is a feature of patterns and anti-patterns alike.
Right: it documents a recurring bad solution.
questions.explain: An anti-pattern is the mirror of a pattern. The card next explains why it is worth writing.
questions.rule: Anti-pattern: problem to bad solution.

questions.q: Avoiding bad solutions can be as ____ as finding good ones.
questions.explain: The book says documenting bad solutions prevents others from repeating the mistake, which is as valuable as finding good solutions.
questions.rule: Avoiding is as valuable as finding.

questions.q: A finance team keeps applying the same Friday patch that fixes this week's complaint and breaks next week's reports. A colleague writes up why the patch keeps being chosen and why it fails. What is the write-up closest to?
options: An anti-pattern: a recurring bad solution, documented to be avoided
A design pattern, since the patch does solve the weekly complaint
A refactoring, since it changes the structure of the finance reports
A catalog, since it lists each of the reports that the patch breaks
optionExplain: Right: a recurring, attractive bad solution documented to prevent repetition.
A pattern is a good solution; this one fails.
Refactoring improves structure; the write-up changes no code.
A catalog describes many patterns.
questions.explain: The patch recurs, looks good up front and fails later. Documenting it so others can avoid it is the anti-pattern's job.
questions.rule: Recurring and attractive and bad.

questions.q: Which statement about anti-pattern types is supported by the book?
options: Like patterns, they come in several types, such as organizational ones
They exist only for development work in large software companies today
They exist only for organizations, the teams inside them, and management
They exist only for one programming language and its libraries
optionExplain: Right: the book lists these types.
The book names more than one type.
The book names more than one type.
The book names areas of work, not a language.
questions.explain: Anti-patterns mirror patterns, which also exist in many domains.
questions.rule: Anti-patterns have domains too.
questions.teaches: Anti-patterns, like patterns, exist in several domains: development, object-oriented design, organizations and specific fields.

questions.q: Airlines publish reports on recurring pilot errors and on the conditions that tempt crews into them. Which idea in the book does this resemble?
options: Removing a pattern from a design once its flexibility is no longer needed
Documenting recurring failures and why they tempt, so others avoid them
Reading a catalog's consequences section before using a pattern in a design
Spreading a shared vocabulary in meetings, documents and code comments
optionExplain: Removal is about unneeded flexibility.
Right: a recurring failure documented as a warning.
Catalog reading is about choosing patterns.
Vocabulary is about communication.
questions.explain: The reports turn individual mistakes into shared lessons, which is what documenting an anti-pattern does.
questions.rule: Failures documented are lessons shared.
questions.teaches: Documenting recurring failures as carefully as successes turns individual mistakes into lessons that others can use.

questions.q: True or false: Any bad solution, even a one-off, counts as an anti-pattern.
questions.explain: An anti-pattern is a recurring bad solution to a common problem, documented so that others avoid it. A one-off mistake does not recur, and so does not qualify.
questions.rule: Recurring is required, here too.

questions.q: Which elements should a complete anti-pattern include? Select all that apply.
options: Why the bad solution is attractive
Other patterns that may give good solutions
The name of the developer who first made the mistake
Why it is bad in the long term
optionExplain: Included: it must show the appeal.
Included: it points toward good solutions.
Not included: the focus is on the solution, not the person.
Included: it shows where you will get into trouble.
questions.explain: A good anti-pattern explains the appeal, the later cost and the better route. The card next gives the book's wording.
questions.rule: Appeal, cost, alternatives.

questions.q: Match each element of an anti-pattern to its job.
pairs: Alerts you to the seductive aspect of the solution
Why it is bad in the long term
Shows where you will get into trouble down the road
questions.explain: Each element does one job: it shows the appeal, the later cost or the way forward.
questions.rule: Appeal, cost, way forward.

questions.q: A write-up warns that copying a rival's pricing is a bad idea, but says nothing else. Which elements of an anti-pattern is it missing?
options: Why copying is attractive, and which better approaches exist
Only the name of the bad solution, which the write-up does have
Only the author's name and the date on which it was written
Nothing, since a clear warning on its own is already complete
optionExplain: Right: it gives the verdict but not the appeal or the alternatives.
The write-up has a name for the idea.
Authorship is not an element.
The book wants the appeal and the way forward as well.
questions.explain: A warning alone does not tell you why people fall for the bad solution or what to do instead.
questions.rule: Warn, explain the appeal, point onward.

questions.q: Which job does the book call one of the biggest jobs of an anti-pattern?
options: Listing the names of the people who made the mistake before
Naming the best programming language for solving the problem
Alerting you to the seductive aspect of the solution
Replacing the need for patterns and for any design principles
optionExplain: People are not the focus.
Language is not at issue.
Right: the book says this is one of its biggest jobs.
Anti-patterns point toward patterns.
questions.explain: A bad solution persists because it looks good. Knowing the appeal is the best protection against falling for it.
questions.rule: Know the temptation.
questions.teaches: Understanding why a bad solution is appealing is the main protection against choosing it, which is why the book calls this one of the anti-pattern's biggest jobs.

questions.q: A sales pitch lists only the benefits of a tool. What does the structure of an anti-pattern do that the pitch does not?
options: It hides the cost of the bad solution so that readers stay relaxed
It gives the appeal and the long-term cost, and points to alternatives
It removes the appeal so that readers feel nothing about the option
It leaves the choice entirely in the hands of the seller of the tool
optionExplain: An anti-pattern states the cost.
Right: a fair account shows both the appeal and the cost.
It states the appeal, because it explains the temptation.
It informs the reader's own choice.
questions.explain: A one-sided pitch persuades without balance. An anti-pattern pairs appeal with cost and points to better routes.
questions.rule: Read the appeal and the cost together.
questions.teaches: A fair account of any option states both its appeal and its long-term cost; presenting only the appeal is persuasion without balance.

questions.q: True or false: An anti-pattern's only job is to warn against the bad solution; suggesting other patterns is outside its scope.
questions.explain: The book says an anti-pattern also suggests other patterns that may give good solutions. To be helpful it must point in the right direction.
questions.rule: Warn and point onward.

questions.q: In the Golden Hammer anti-pattern, what is the supposed solution?
options: Use the familiar technology anyway, even where it is a poor fit
Pick the newest technology for every project the team starts
Hire developers who know only one technology, to save on training costs
Avoid choosing any technology until a vendor recommends one
optionExplain: Right: the familiar technology is applied obsessively.
The anti-pattern is about clinging to the familiar, not chasing the new.
Hiring is not the supposed solution.
The problem is choosing technologies, so avoiding is not a solution.
questions.explain: The supposed solution is the comfortable choice. The card next gives the whole write-up.
questions.rule: The supposed solution is the familiar one.

questions.q: Match each part of the Golden Hammer write-up to its content.
pairs: Choosing technologies while believing exactly one must dominate the architecture
Reasons the team finds the familiar technology attractive
Use the familiar technology anyway, even where it is inappropriate
Widen developers' knowledge through education and training
questions.explain: The write-up follows the anti-pattern elements: problem, the forces that tempt, the bad solution and the way out.
questions.rule: Problem, forces, supposed solution, cure.

questions.q: An accounting team that knows only spreadsheets builds a real-time inventory tracker out of spreadsheet macros. Which anti-pattern does this match?
options: Golden Hammer, using the familiar tool where it fits poorly
The Rule of Three, applying a pattern in three real projects
KISS, choosing the simplest tool that meets the need at hand
Refactoring, improving structure without changing the behavior
optionExplain: Right: familiarity drives the choice of the wrong tool.
The Rule of Three is about proving a pattern.
KISS is about simplicity for the need, not familiarity.
Refactoring does not add a new system.
questions.explain: The team's comfort and its fear of unfamiliar tools drive the choice, which is the Golden Hammer pattern.
questions.rule: Comfort choosing the tool is the hammer.

questions.q: Which situation does the book give as an observed example of Golden Hammer?
options: Teams drop all patterns from their designs after a long design review
Developers switch to a new language for every project they start, to learn
Companies publish internal catalogs of patterns for use by their own staff
Web companies keep maintaining homegrown caches despite open source options
optionExplain: The anti-pattern is not about dropping patterns.
Constant switching is the opposite of the hammer.
Publishing catalogs is not an anti-pattern.
Right: this is the book's example.
questions.explain: The example shows the pattern at work: familiar, homegrown tools are kept even when better options exist.
questions.rule: Examples show where it was seen.
questions.teaches: Anti-pattern write-ups record real examples of where the bad solution has been observed, as in the homegrown caches kept alongside open source options.

questions.q: A teacher who loves lectures uses lectures for lab skills and gets poor results. Which remedy matches the Golden Hammer's refactored solution?
options: Ban lectures from the school and replace them with lab sessions
Tell the teacher to repeat the same lectures again, more slowly
Move the lab skills to another teacher without any discussion
Widen the teacher's knowledge of other methods through training
optionExplain: The method is not bad everywhere, only where it does not fit.
More of the same does not widen options.
The cause, limited knowledge, remains.
Right: the cure widens knowledge so that the familiar option is not the only one.
questions.explain: The book's cure targets the cause, limited familiarity, not the familiar tool itself.
questions.rule: Widen the options.
questions.teaches: The cure for a golden hammer targets its cause, limited familiarity with alternatives, not the familiar tool itself.

questions.q: True or false: If more of the team learned other technologies, one of the forces behind Golden Hammer would weaken.
questions.explain: Two of the forces are that the team is unfamiliar with other technologies and sees them as risky. Training reduces both, which is why it is the book's refactored solution.
questions.rule: Knowledge weakens the forces.

questions.q: Which is among the book's closing bullet points?
options: Use a pattern in every design, to keep all the designs consistent
Let patterns emerge in your designs instead of forcing them in
Treat each pattern as a fixed rule that cannot be adapted by anyone
Learn the categories by heart before studying any pattern
optionExplain: The closing advice is the simplest solution that meets the need.
Right: this is the first closing point.
The book says patterns can be adapted.
The book says to study patterns and their relationships and to use classifications when they help.
questions.explain: The closing points restate the chapter's themes. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Emerge, do not force.

questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it is consistent with the book's closing advice.

items.t: Let patterns emerge as the design progresses
Force a pattern in so the design uses one
Adapt a pattern to meet your needs
Treat a pattern as a law
Use the simplest solution, even without a pattern
Assume every design needs several patterns

questions.explain: The closing advice favours emergence, adaptation and simplicity. Forcing, rigidity and pattern counts run against it.
questions.rule: Emerge, adapt, simplify.

questions.q: A team lead reviews a design for a small tool that contains five patterns. Which closing advice applies first?
options: Build the team's shared vocabulary of pattern names before anything else
Study more catalogs of patterns before the next design review begins
Use the simplest solution that meets the need, even without a pattern
Adapt each of the five patterns further to reduce their complexity
optionExplain: Vocabulary helps communication but does not address the over-use.
Study does not address the over-use.
Right: five patterns for a small tool suggests the simplest solution has been missed.
More adaptation does not address the over-use.
questions.explain: The lead should first ask whether the design is as simple as it can be and whether each pattern answers a real need.
questions.rule: Ask if it is as simple as the need allows.

questions.q: A newcomer is put off by the jargon on a patterns forum. What does the book say?
options: Learn the whole vocabulary of the community before you post there
Avoid forums like this one until you have become a recognised expert
Ask the other members to avoid the jargon when you are present
Do not let the lingo hold you back; you know most of it now
optionExplain: The book says you already know most of it.
The community is described as friendly and welcoming.
The vocabulary is an asset, not a problem.
Right: this is the book's closing encouragement.
questions.explain: Every community has its own lingo. The book says you have already learned most of this community's.
questions.rule: You already know most of the lingo.
questions.teaches: The patterns community has its own lingo, but a reader of this book already knows most of it, so it need not be a barrier.

questions.q: A teammate wants to use an elegant pattern for a feature, though the simple code already meets every requirement. Which closing points settle the question?
options: Always prefer the more elegant design, whatever it costs to build
Adapt the pattern until it looks simple enough to keep in the design
Use the simplest solution that meets the need; let patterns emerge
Wait until the whole team has studied the whole catalog thoroughly
optionExplain: The book's emphasis is need, not elegance.
Adapting does not remove the unneeded complexity.
Right: these two points favour the simple code unless a need emerges.
Study is not the deciding point.
questions.explain: When the simple code meets the requirements, the closing advice favours it. If a need appears, a pattern can then emerge.
questions.rule: Simple wins until a need emerges.
questions.teaches: When the closing points conflict with enthusiasm for a pattern, the simplest solution that meets the need wins, and a pattern is added only if a need emerges.

questions.q: Which of these statements contradict the book's closing points? Select all that apply.
options: Learn the categories by heart before using any pattern
A shared vocabulary is one of the most powerful benefits of patterns
Apply every pattern exactly as the classic design shows
Most patterns you meet are adaptations of existing ones
optionExplain: Contradicts: the book says to use classifications when they help.
Consistent: the book says this.
Contradicts: patterns are not set in stone.
Consistent: the book says this.
questions.explain: The closing points favour adaptation and the practical use of classifications. The other two statements are the book's own.
questions.rule: Adapt; use categories when they help.

questions.q: You face nine unfamiliar patterns and have ten minutes to find one that suits a problem. What is the best first move?
options: Read the opening purpose line of each pattern and rule most out
Read the full scenario of the first pattern, then the next, in order
Read only the drawbacks of every pattern and pick the cheapest one
Pick the pattern whose name sounds closest to your problem
optionExplain: Right: purpose lines are short and sort the nine patterns fast.
This is thorough but slow, and it spends most of your time on patterns that do not fit.
Drawbacks help later, but they do not say what a pattern is for.
Names can mislead; two different patterns may sound similar.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The card next shows why the opening line is the best place to start.
questions.rule: Start with the purpose line.

questions.q: The appendix says its goal is to give you a high-level ____ of what each pattern is about.
questions.explain: The appendix aims for a high-level idea of each pattern, not full detail, which is why a quick first pass over each opening line is enough.
questions.rule: Aim for a high-level idea first.

questions.q: Match each need to the pattern whose purpose sentence fits it.
pairs: Return an object to a previous state
Make new instances by copying existing ones
Give more than one object a chance to handle a request
Centralize complex communication between related objects
questions.explain: Each purpose sentence names one problem. The matches follow from those sentences without reading the scenarios.
questions.rule: Match need to purpose line.

questions.q: Builder and Prototype both concern creating objects. What in their opening lines tells them apart?
options: Builder is used only for composites, while Prototype is used only for graphics
Builder constructs a product in steps, Prototype copies when creation is costly
Builder copies existing objects, while Prototype builds them in several steps
They do not differ, because both patterns are about creating objects
optionExplain: Composites are a common use of Builder, not a rule, and Prototype is not tied to graphics.
Right: the condition in each line differs even though both mention creating objects.
This swaps the two descriptions.
Sharing a topic word is not sharing a purpose; read the condition that follows it.
questions.explain: Both patterns create objects, but Builder is aimed at multistep construction of a complex product and Prototype at copying when new instances are expensive or complicated. The condition decides, not the topic.
questions.rule: Compare the condition, not the topic word.
questions.teaches: Two patterns can share a topic such as creating objects and still answer different problems, so the condition in the opening line separates them.

questions.q: True or false: If an opening line matches your problem, you can choose that pattern without reading its scenario or drawbacks.
questions.explain: The opening line is only a lead. Scenarios and drawbacks can show that the pattern costs more than it gives for your case, or that a similar pattern is closer.
questions.rule: Confirm a lead before you commit.

questions.q: A new library's reference pages each open with one sentence beginning use this when. How should the appendix's habit carry over?
options: Read the pages in alphabetical order so that no page is missed along the way
Memorize every opening sentence before using the library for anything
Skim the sentences to shortlist pages, then read those pages closely
Skip the sentences, since only code samples are reliable
optionExplain: Order has nothing to do with relevance, and it spends time on every page.
Memorizing is heavier than needed; the point is to find the right page when you need it.
Right: a purpose sentence is a cheap filter, and close reading is kept for the shortlist.
Samples show how, but not whether the thing fits your problem.
questions.explain: The habit is a two-pass reading: a fast pass over purposes, then a careful pass over the few that matter. It works for any reference material that states a purpose up front.
questions.rule: Skim purposes, then read a shortlist.
questions.teaches: Any reference that states a purpose up front can be read in two passes, a fast pass over the purposes and a careful pass over a shortlist.

questions.q: A product has controls that will keep being redesigned and must run on several kinds of hardware. How would you shape its classes?
options: Write one subclass for every combination of control design and hardware
Fix the controls now and vary only the hardware classes
Put a large conditional on hardware type inside the control classes
Keep a hierarchy for the controls and another for the hardware
optionExplain: It works at first but multiplies classes as either side grows.
This ignores that the controls will change, the dilemma in the scenario.
It hides the variation in one place instead of separating it, and every new hardware type edits the control classes.
Right: two things vary, so each gets its own hierarchy.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next shows how the appendix answers this.
questions.rule: Two changing things, two hierarchies.

questions.q: Bridge allows the implementation and the abstraction to vary by placing the two in separate class ____.
questions.explain: Two hierarchies are the core of the pattern: one for the abstraction, one for the implementation.
questions.rule: Separate hierarchies for separate variation.

questions.q: A reporting tool has 4 report layouts that will be redesigned and 5 output formats. Counting concrete classes only, how many does Bridge need?
options: 9, from 4 abstraction classes plus 5 implementation classes
20, one for every pair of layout and output format
5, one for each output format and nothing for layouts
1, since a single report class can hold both layouts and formats
optionExplain: Right: the two hierarchies add up instead of multiplying.
20 is the count for a single combined hierarchy, the design Bridge avoids.
This counts only one side and leaves the layouts without classes.
One class cannot vary two independent things without conditionals.
questions.explain: Each side needs one concrete class per variant: 4 plus 5. A combined hierarchy needs 4 times 5.
questions.rule: Two hierarchies add; one hierarchy multiplies.
questions.hint: Count each hierarchy separately.

questions.q: A reporting tool has 4 report layouts and 5 output formats. A sixth output format is added. How many new concrete classes does each design need, combined hierarchy first and Bridge second?
options: 1 in the combined design and 1 in Bridge
4 in the combined design and 1 in Bridge
6 in the combined design and 6 in Bridge
5 in the combined design and 4 in Bridge
optionExplain: This holds only for Bridge; the combined design still needs one class per layout.
Right: the combined design needs one for each of the 4 layouts, while Bridge needs one implementation class.
Nothing in either design needs six new classes.
This mixes up the two counts.
questions.explain: In a combined hierarchy each new format needs a class per layout. With Bridge it needs one class on the implementation side.
questions.rule: A new variant costs one class under Bridge.
questions.teaches: Under Bridge a new variant on one side costs one class, while in a single combined hierarchy it costs one class for each variant on the other side.

questions.q: A game has character types (warrior, mage) that will keep changing and several graphics back ends. According to the authors, which kind of system especially suits Bridge?
options: Systems that build objects from many optional parts in steps
Systems where each request must find its one handler
Graphics and windowing systems that run on several platforms
Systems with thousands of identical, similar objects in memory
optionExplain: That describes Builder.
That describes Chain of Responsibility.
Right: the appendix names graphics and windowing systems over multiple platforms as a use.
That describes Flyweight.
questions.explain: The appendix lists graphics and windowing systems over many platforms, and any case that needs to vary an interface and an implementation in different ways.
questions.rule: Look for two independent axes of change.
questions.teaches: The signal for Bridge is two axes of change that vary independently, such as character kind and rendering back end.

questions.q: True or false: Bridge is a good choice for a class whose implementation stays fixed for its whole life.
questions.explain: Bridge pays for its flexibility with extra complexity. If the implementation never varies, that cost buys nothing.
questions.rule: Add Bridge only where both sides vary.

questions.q: A trip plan may hold a hotel, many tickets and several dinners, or only dinners. Where should the code that assembles such plans live?
options: Inside every client that needs a plan
In the plan's constructor, with a parameter for each possible part
In a one-step factory that returns a finished plan
In a separate object that assembles the plan step by step
optionExplain: Each client would repeat the same complex assembly.
The parameter list grows with every part and many calls would pass empty values.
A single call cannot express a varying, multistep process.
Right: construction is moved out so clients stay simple.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Move assembly into its own object.

questions.q: Builder allows an object to be constructed in a multistep and ____ process, unlike one-step factories.
questions.explain: The appendix contrasts Builder's multistep, varying process with one-step factories.
questions.rule: Builder is multistep.

questions.q: A tool produces contracts where the number of schedules and the optional clauses differ for every customer. Which design follows Builder?
options: A builder receives one step per clause and returns the finished contract
One contract class with a constructor that takes twelve parameters
One subclass of contract for every possible combination of clauses
A single static method that returns one fixed contract template
optionExplain: Right: the varying steps are encapsulated in the builder.
The list grows with every clause and stays awkward for optional parts.
The number of combinations grows quickly.
A fixed template cannot vary.
questions.explain: A builder takes the variable assembly steps and hides the contract's internal structure from the client.
questions.rule: Varying parts, builder steps.

questions.q: The vacation planner must now also be produced as a printable booklet using the same ordering steps. What lets the client stay unchanged?
options: The client code is rewritten so that it builds the booklets directly itself
The client sees only an abstract builder, so another builder can be swapped in
The planner classes are copied and then edited into booklet classes
The client calls the booklet's internals to fill each part in itself
optionExplain: That moves the construction back into the client, the problem Builder avoids.
Right: the appendix says product implementations can be swapped because the client only sees an abstract interface.
Copying leaves two versions to maintain.
That would expose the product's representation, which Builder hides.
questions.explain: Because the client talks to an abstract builder, a different concrete builder can produce a different product from the same steps.
questions.rule: Swap the builder, keep the client.
questions.teaches: Since the client sees only the abstract builder, one set of client steps can produce different products by swapping in a different concrete builder.

questions.q: Sort each case by what it needs.

items.t: Assemble a document from an optional cover, a varying number of sections and an optional appendix
Return a circle, square or triangle object by shape name
Compose a meal order from a varying number of dishes, drinks and extras
Return a ready-made logger for either console or file output
Build an itinerary of days, each holding different activities
Create a standard currency object from a code

questions.explain: Builder suits products assembled in several varying steps; a factory is enough when one call decides what to make.
questions.rule: Many steps, builder; one call, factory.

questions.q: A team replaces a factory call with a builder for report objects. Which new burden falls on the calling code, according to the authors?
options: The callers must now keep the report's fields hidden themselves
The callers can no longer swap one report type for another one
The callers need more domain knowledge, since they must know the steps to request
The callers must wait until every step has been completed by another thread
optionExplain: Hiding the internals is what the builder does for the client.
Builder keeps swapping possible through the abstract interface.
Right: the appendix says constructing objects requires more domain knowledge of the client than a factory does.
Nothing in the appendix mentions threads.
questions.explain: A factory decides everything inside one call; a builder hands the sequence of steps to the client, which must know them.
questions.rule: The client chooses the steps.
questions.teaches: Choosing a builder moves part of the decision about what to build from the factory to the client, which needs to understand the steps.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: Incoming mail may be spam, fan mail, a complaint or a request. Which design keeps the mail sender from knowing which department handles each kind?
options: The sender checks the kind and then calls the right department
One big handler class with a conditional for every kind
Each department keeps polling the inbox for its own mail
A line of handlers, each taking the mail or passing it on
optionExplain: The sender then knows every department.
The sender is shielded, but one class has to know all the rules and grows with each new kind.
Departments would each need access to the inbox and a way to avoid taking the same mail twice.
Right: the sender only hands the mail to the first handler.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names this pattern.
questions.rule: The sender hands off to the first handler.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: Each handler in the chain has a ____ object to which it forwards a request it cannot handle.
questions.explain: The appendix says each handler has a successor and forwards the request to it when it cannot handle it.
questions.rule: Handle, or forward to the successor.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: An expense claim goes first to a manager, who approves claims up to a limit and otherwise sends them to a director, who approves up to a higher limit and otherwise sends them to a finance chief. Which description fits?
options: A chain in which each approver approves or forwards to the next
A mediator that holds all of the approval rules in one object
A flyweight that shares one approver among many separate claims
A builder that assembles an approval one step at a time
optionExplain: Right: each object examines the request and either handles it or passes it on.
A mediator coordinates peers; here the claim moves along a line.
A flyweight shares one instance for many virtual instances.
A builder constructs a product, not a path for a request.
questions.explain: The approvers are handlers in a line, and each has the next one as its successor.
questions.rule: Check, then handle or forward.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: Two handlers in a chain would both accept the same email. What decides which one acts?
options: Their names, which are compared in alphabetical order
Their order, since the first handler to accept it stops the pass
The sender, who picks one of the handlers in advance
Both act, since each handler in turn receives the email
optionExplain: Names play no role in how the request is passed.
Right: the request is passed along until a handler takes it, so order decides.
The pattern's point is that the sender does not choose.
A handler that handles the request does not forward it.
questions.explain: Because a handler either handles or forwards, the order of the chain sets which handler acts when more than one could.
questions.rule: Order is a design decision.
questions.teaches: When more than one handler could accept a request, the order of the chain decides the outcome, so reordering the chain changes the behaviour.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: A support chatbot chain has a refund bot, a shipping bot and an account bot. A message about gift wrapping matches none of them. What happens?
options: It is handled by the refund bot, since that bot comes first in the chain
The chain reports an error automatically and then stops working
It reaches the end unhandled unless a catch-all is placed last
It is handled by whichever bot happens to have the least work
optionExplain: The first bot passes on what it cannot handle.
The pattern does not guarantee any reporting.
Right: execution is not guaranteed, and a final catch-all handler is one way to cover it.
The chain contains no load balancing.
questions.explain: A request can fall off the end of the chain. Whether that is acceptable depends on the need, and a last handler that accepts everything closes the gap.
questions.rule: Plan for requests that nobody takes.
questions.teaches: If every request must be handled, end the chain with a catch-all handler, since the chain itself gives no guarantee.

questions.section: How to use the Chain of Responsibility Pattern
questions.q: True or false: With a chain in place, every request is guaranteed to be handled by some object.
questions.explain: The appendix notes that a request may fall off the end if no object handles it, which can be an advantage or a disadvantage.
questions.rule: No guarantee of handling.

questions.q: A landscape app slows down with 100000 tree objects that each store a location and an age and draw the same way. What idea would help most?
options: Give every tree object its own separate thread to draw itself
Cache a rendered picture inside each tree object to save work
Delete the oldest trees from the landscape design to lighten it
Keep one shared tree and store each tree's location and age elsewhere
optionExplain: Threads add overhead and leave the object count the same.
Each cached picture still takes memory per tree.
This changes what the user designed instead of the design of the code.
Right: this cuts the instance count while keeping every tree on the screen.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next shows this idea.
questions.rule: Fewer instances, shared state elsewhere.

questions.q: Flyweight reduces the number of object ____ at runtime, saving memory.
questions.explain: The appendix lists reducing the number of instances as the first benefit.
questions.rule: Fewer instances, less memory.

questions.q: A game shows 20000 coins that differ only in position. Which design follows Flyweight?
options: One coin object and a manager holding all the positions
A coin object for each position, each running its own thread
A single coin object that draws every coin at the same spot
20000 coin objects, each with its drawing code compressed
optionExplain: Right: one shared coin, with the differing state held centrally.
That keeps all 20000 objects.
The shared object cannot show distinct positions if it keeps none of that state.
Compressing code does not reduce the instance count.
questions.explain: The coins can all be controlled identically, so one instance can stand for all, with state kept by a client object.
questions.rule: Share the object, centralize the state.

questions.q: In the shared design, a single tree must draw itself at different ages. Where must each tree's age be kept?
options: Inside the one shared Tree object itself, as a single field
In the client object that holds the state of all trees
In the operating system's memory manager, outside the app
Nowhere, since age is not needed for drawing
optionExplain: One shared object cannot hold a different age for each tree.
Right: the appendix puts the state of all trees in a client object.
The pattern does not rely on the operating system.
The scenario says trees draw themselves depending on age.
questions.explain: Whatever differs between trees cannot live in the one shared object, so it is held by the client and used when a tree is drawn.
questions.rule: What differs lives outside the shared object.
questions.teaches: Because the shared object cannot store every tree's own values, whatever differs between the virtual instances must be kept by the client object.

questions.q: A shooter has 5000 identical bullets and one player who has an inventory and health of his own. Which parts suit Flyweight?
options: Both do, since everything in a game can be shared by instances
Only the player does, since he is the largest object in the game
Bullets suit it, the player does not, as he needs state of his own
Neither does, since games need unique objects for everything
optionExplain: Sharing means identical control, which fails for a unique player.
Size is not the criterion; many identically controlled instances are.
Right: many objects controlled identically suit it, and an object that behaves independently does not.
The bullets have no individual behaviour.
questions.explain: Flyweight applies to the mass of identical objects. A single character that needs independent behaviour stays an ordinary object.
questions.rule: Mix shared objects with ordinary ones.
questions.teaches: One program can use Flyweight for a crowd of identical objects and keep ordinary independent objects for the few that need their own behaviour.

questions.q: True or false: Flyweight is worth using for an application that shows 12 trees.
questions.explain: The problem began with lots and lots of trees. With 12 the memory saving is small, and the pattern's cost remains.
questions.rule: Match the pattern to the scale of the problem.

questions.q: Beginners will steer a simulated animal with a tiny language you design. What is the cleanest way to represent the language's rules in code?
options: Write one long function that scans the text for every rule
Store each program as a plain string and run it unchanged
Ask each user to type Java
Give each rule its own class, mirroring the grammar
optionExplain: One function mixes all the rules and gets hard to change.
A string is only text; nothing interprets it.
That removes the point of a small language.
Right: the class structure follows the grammar, so it is easy to change.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: One rule, one class.

questions.q: Match each term in the Interpreter pattern to what it is.
pairs: The rules for how sentences of the language look
The class that represents one rule of the grammar
Holds the input stream of the program being parsed
Matches the input and evaluates it
questions.explain: The grammar is written first. Each rule gets a class, and interpret works on the context.
questions.rule: Grammar, classes, context.

questions.q: A thermostat language has three rules: a schedule is a list of entries, an entry is a time followed by a temperature, and a temperature is a number. How many classes does Interpreter use for it?
options: Three, one for each rule
One, for the schedule as a whole
Two, since numbers need no class
Six, one for each word in a typical program
optionExplain: Right: the classes map directly to the rules of the grammar.
One class would hide the rules inside a single block.
The appendix says each rule gets a class.
Classes follow rules, not the words in a particular program.
questions.explain: The pattern maps each rule to a class, so three rules give three classes.
questions.rule: Count rules to count classes.

questions.q: The thermostat language gains a new rule for holiday settings. What does Interpreter ask you to do?
options: Rewrite the whole interpreter from the start
Add the rule to the grammar and add one class for it
Leave the classes unchanged and add a conditional to interpret
Replace the classes with a parser generator
optionExplain: The structure is built to avoid a rewrite.
Right: because the classes mirror the grammar, the language is easy to extend.
A conditional spreads the new rule through the old code.
A generator is for large grammars, as the appendix notes.
questions.explain: The grammar and the classes correspond one to one, so a new rule becomes a new class.
questions.rule: Grammar change, class change.
questions.teaches: Because the classes mirror the grammar, the grammar works as the design document: extending the language means extending the grammar and the classes together.

questions.q: The robot-cleaner language works. The teacher also wants every program printed in tidy form. According to the authors, how can this be done?
options: By writing a second grammar for the printing alone
By replacing the classes with plain strings of text
By adding a method for it to the existing classes
By asking each class to run the program twice over
optionExplain: The same grammar and classes already exist.
Strings carry no structure to print from.
Right: methods added to the class structure can give new behaviour such as pretty printing.
Running twice does not format anything.
questions.explain: The appendix lists pretty printing and program validation as behaviour you can add to the class structure beyond interpretation.
questions.rule: Same classes, more methods.
questions.teaches: Since each rule is a class, you can add other methods to the same classes, such as printing or validation, in addition to interpretation.

questions.q: True or false: For a language with hundreds of grammar rules, the authors still consider Interpreter the best fit.
questions.explain: The appendix says the pattern becomes cumbersome with many rules and that a parser or compiler generator may be more appropriate.
questions.rule: Simple grammar, simple pattern.

questions.q: An alarm clock, a coffee maker and a sprinkler each hold rules about the others, and each new rule means edits in several classes. What change would help?
options: Copy each rule into every appliance that might need it later
Merge all the appliances together into one large class instead
Add a new subclass of appliance for every new rule that arrives
Move the coordination into one object they all report to
optionExplain: Copies drift apart and multiply the edits.
A single class loses the separate objects altogether.
Subclasses do not say where cross-object rules live.
Right: coordination in one place makes the rules findable and the appliances simpler.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names this pattern.
questions.rule: One place for the coordinating rules.

questions.q: True or false: With a Mediator in place, the appliance objects still need to know about one another.
questions.explain: The appendix says the appliances become completely decoupled from each other; they talk only to the mediator.
questions.rule: Peers talk to the mediator, not to each other.

questions.q: On a flight booking form, choosing one way must disable the return date and change the price shown. Where should those rules live under Mediator?
options: In a form controller object that the widgets report to
In the return-date field, which watches the other widgets
In each widget, with copies of the rules
In the database that stores bookings
optionExplain: Right: widgets report changes and the mediator decides what each should do.
That ties the field to every other widget.
Copies would diverge when a rule changes.
Storage is a different concern from coordinating widgets.
questions.explain: The appendix says Mediator is commonly used to coordinate related GUI components.
questions.rule: Widgets report, mediator decides.

questions.q: Six appliances all know about each other. A seventh is added. How many new links does it need in that design and with a Mediator, in that order?
options: 1 new link, and 6 with a Mediator
6 new links, and 1 with a Mediator
7 new links, and 7 with a Mediator
6 new links, and 6 with a Mediator
optionExplain: This reverses the two designs.
Right: it must connect to each of the six, but to the mediator only once.
It does not need a link to itself.
The mediator needs only one link.
questions.explain: When every object knows every other, links grow quickly with each addition. With a mediator each new object adds one link.
questions.rule: Links grow by one under a mediator.
questions.teaches: When every object must know every other, the number of links grows quickly with each new object, whereas with a mediator each new object adds one.

questions.q: A team wants to reuse the coffee-maker object in a different house with different rules. Which design makes that easiest, according to the authors?
options: The coffee maker holds copies of the rules for the other appliances
It calls the alarm clock directly whenever it needs to know the time
A Mediator holds the rules, so the coffee maker knows no other appliance
It inherits from the sprinkler to share the rules it needs
optionExplain: Copied rules come along into the new house.
Direct calls tie it to the alarm clock.
Right: the appendix says a Mediator increases the reusability of the objects by decoupling them.
Inheritance ties it to another appliance.
questions.explain: Since the coffee maker only talks to the mediator, a different house can supply a different mediator.
questions.rule: Decoupled objects are reusable objects.
questions.teaches: Because only the mediator knows the rules of one system, an object can move to another system by being given a different mediator.

questions.q: Which statements about Mediator are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Centralizing control logic simplifies maintenance
The mediator object cannot become complex, since it only forwards messages
It reduces the variety of messages sent between objects
The objects supported by a mediator must each know all the others
optionExplain: Right: the rules are found in one place.
Wrong: the appendix warns that without proper design the mediator can become overly complex.
Right: objects send simple messages to the mediator.
Wrong: they are decoupled from each other.
questions.explain: Mediator simplifies the peers and the messages, but moves the complexity into one object that needs care.
questions.rule: Simpler peers, busier mediator.

questions.q: Which problem is about a sender that should not know which of several objects will answer?
options: A product whose screens and hardware both keep changing
A group of peers whose rules about each other are scattered
A complex object that has to be built in many steps
A request that must reach a handler able to deal with it
optionExplain: That is about two things that vary, abstraction and implementation.
That is about peers that know each other.
That is about construction, not about links.
Right: that is the sender and receivers problem.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next compares three patterns.
questions.rule: Sender and receivers.

questions.q: Match each pattern to what it separates.
pairs: An implementation from the interface it would be bound to
The sender of a request from its receivers
questions.explain: Each pattern loosens a different link.
questions.rule: Know which link each one loosens.

questions.q: Sort each situation by the pattern that fits better.

items.t: A refund request moves from a clerk to a supervisor if the clerk cannot approve it
A group of form fields enable and disable one another through a shared controller
An email is examined by one filter after another until one claims it
Smart-home devices report changes to one hub that decides how others should react
A moderation queue gives each post to the first checker that can rule on it
Chat-room participants send messages through a room object instead of to each other

questions.explain: A request passed along a line fits Chain. Peers that communicate through a central object fit Mediator.
questions.rule: Line of handlers or central hub.

questions.q: Chain and Mediator both remove direct links between objects. Which statement about how they differ is correct?
options: Chain passes a request along until one object takes it, Mediator centralizes control logic
Chain centralizes the control logic in one object, while Mediator passes a request along a line of objects
Chain separates an interface from its implementation, while Mediator separates a sender from receivers
They work in the same way, and differ only in their names and diagrams
optionExplain: Right: Chain forwards, and Mediator centralizes.
This swaps the two.
This swaps in the descriptions of Bridge and Chain.
Their structures differ.
questions.explain: In a chain each handler knows only its successor. In a mediator the logic is in the mediator.
questions.rule: Forwarding versus centralizing.

questions.q: In which of the two does a single object end up holding the knowledge of the whole system's rules?
options: In Chain, whose first handler knows every later handler in the line
In Mediator, whose object holds the control logic
In neither, since both patterns spread the rules out evenly
In Bridge, whose abstraction holds all of the system's rules
optionExplain: The appendix says a chain simplifies an object because it need not know the chain's structure.
Right: the mediator contains the control logic, while a handler needs only its successor.
Mediator centralizes rules deliberately.
Bridge separates two hierarchies.
questions.explain: Mediator concentrates the rules, which is why it can grow complex, while Chain keeps each handler small.
questions.rule: Centralize or distribute.
questions.teaches: Mediator concentrates the rules in one object, while in a chain the rules are spread across handlers that each know only their successor.

questions.q: Document kinds (letter, invoice) and printer models (laser, inkjet) change independently. Which pattern fits?
options: Chain, because a document must find a printer
Mediator, because documents and printers must talk
Bridge, because two independent things vary
Flyweight, because there are many documents
optionExplain: Chain is about a request seeking a handler.
Mediator is about peers that coordinate, not about two independent variations.
Right: separate hierarchies for the two varying sides.
Flyweight is about sharing identical instances.
questions.explain: The deciding clue is two axes of variation, not a need to communicate.
questions.rule: Look for two independent axes.
questions.teaches: Many systems have objects that talk to each other, but that alone does not call for Mediator; Bridge is signalled by two independent axes of variation.

questions.q: True or false: Because all three patterns reduce coupling, any one of them can replace another in a design.
questions.explain: Each separates a different pair, and each has its own cost. The pattern follows the kind of tangle you have.
questions.rule: Pick the pattern for the tangle.

questions.q: A player's progress must be restorable after the character dies. Which approach keeps the player class focused on gameplay?
options: Add a list of old copies of every field inside the player class itself
Let any class read and change the player's fields whenever it needs
Restart the player at level one, since saving adds too much complexity
Keep saved snapshots in a separate object used to restore the player
optionExplain: That puts the history and gameplay together in one class.
That breaks the player's encapsulation.
That drops the feature the players asked for.
Right: the saving is a different job and lives in a separate object.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Saved state gets its own object.

questions.q: The separate object that holds the saved state is called the ____ object.
questions.explain: The appendix names the object that holds saved state the Memento object.
questions.rule: The saved state is the memento.

questions.q: A drawing program needs undo. Which design follows Memento?
options: Canvas snapshots are kept in separate objects, and undo restores from the latest
The canvas keeps an ever longer list of its own old field values inside it
Undo redraws everything from the beginning of the session each time
A global variable holds one copy of the canvas data for the whole program
optionExplain: Right: the saved state sits outside the canvas, and restoring uses it.
That mixes saving into the canvas class and makes it less cohesive.
That is slow and does not save state.
A global variable exposes the data to the whole program.
questions.explain: The memento holds state apart from the key object, which keeps the canvas cohesive.
questions.rule: Snapshot out, restore in.

questions.q: Why not let outside code copy the player's fields directly to save them?
options: It is impossible to copy fields from outside the class at all
It would expose the player's internals, breaking encapsulation
It would make the saved game load too quickly to be useful
Fields cannot be restored once they have been copied out
optionExplain: Copying is possible, but it requires access to the details.
Right: Memento aims to save state while keeping the key object encapsulated.
Speed is not the concern here.
Restoring is possible; the concern is exposure.
questions.explain: Memento's two goals pull apart. Saving is easy if you open everything up, but that costs encapsulation.
questions.rule: Save state without exposing it.
questions.teaches: Saving state and keeping it hidden pull in opposite directions, and Memento exists to achieve both at once.

questions.q: True or false: If a game saves a very large state every second, a Memento design is likely to become slow.
questions.explain: The appendix names the cost of saving and restoring state as a drawback. A larger state saved more often makes that cost bigger.
questions.rule: Big state, frequent saves, slow design.

questions.q: A multi-step order form lets users go back a step and find their entries as they were. Which pattern's purpose does this match?
options: Flyweight, since many forms look like each other
Interpreter, since a form has a grammar
Memento, since it returns the form to an earlier state
Chain of Responsibility, since each step passes the order on
optionExplain: Flyweight shares one instance among many virtual ones.
The form is not a language to be interpreted.
Right: the purpose is returning to a previous state, and undo is only one example.
Steps are not handlers examining a request.
questions.explain: The appendix says to use Memento when you need to return an object to one of its previous states, with undo as an example.
questions.rule: Any return to an earlier state.
questions.teaches: Memento is about returning to any earlier state, so it covers back buttons and revert commands as well as undo.

questions.q: A game needs hundreds of monster kinds, and players can design their own. How should new monsters be created?
options: By writing a new class for every monster a player designs
By building each monster from scratch with a long constructor
By asking the player to restart the game
By copying a prepared monster of the wanted kind
optionExplain: Players cannot add classes while the game runs.
Each build repeats the setup work.
That does not make monsters.
Right: copying avoids a class per monster and a long construction each time.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Copy something already set up.

questions.q: In Java, Prototype typically uses the ____ method to copy an object.
questions.explain: The appendix says in Java this typically means using the clone method.
questions.rule: Copy with clone.

questions.q: A slide editor has a duplicate button for any slide a user selects. Which design follows Prototype?
options: The editor copies the selected slide and places the copy elsewhere
The editor builds a new slide from the title of the old one only
The editor asks the user to retype every element on the slide
The editor keeps a different class for every slide that exists
optionExplain: Right: a new instance is made by copying an existing one.
That loses the slide's other content.
That does not copy anything.
That needs a class per slide.
questions.explain: A duplicate command is a copy of an existing object, with the details left to the object.
questions.rule: Duplicate means copy.

questions.q: Which Java technique does the appendix mention when a copy must be a deep one?
options: Method overloading
Deserialization
Reflection on the class name
Static initializers
optionExplain: Overloading chooses among methods and does not copy.
Right: the appendix says clone or deserialization when you need deep copies.
Reflection would need to know the class name, which Prototype avoids.
Static initializers run once per class.
questions.explain: Deserialization can rebuild the whole object graph, so the copy shares nothing with the original.
questions.rule: Deep copies need more care.
questions.teaches: A plain copy may leave the new object sharing inner objects with the original, which is one reason copying can be complicated and deep copies need more care.

questions.q: A drawing tool must let users duplicate any shape on the canvas, including shape kinds added later by plug-ins. What does Prototype give the tool?
options: The ability to count how many shapes of each class exist
The ability to hide the shapes from the user's view
The ability to copy a shape without knowing its class
The ability to turn every shape into one common class
optionExplain: Prototype does not count anything.
Visibility is not the concern.
Right: client code makes new instances without naming their class.
Shapes stay as they are.
questions.explain: Since the tool only asks a shape to copy itself, a plug-in's new shape works without any change to the tool.
questions.rule: The client does not name the class.
questions.teaches: Because the client only asks an object to copy itself, new kinds of objects can be added later without changing the code that makes copies.

questions.q: True or false: The appendix says that copying an object is more efficient than creating a new one in every case.
questions.explain: The appendix says only that in some circumstances copying can be more efficient, and that copying can sometimes be complicated.
questions.rule: Copying is not always cheaper.

questions.q: A word processor needs undo and a duplicate-slide button. Which pairing of patterns fits?
options: Prototype for undo and Memento for the duplicate button
Memento for both
Prototype for both
Memento for undo and Prototype for the duplicate button
optionExplain: This swaps the two purposes.
Duplicate makes a new object, not a restored one.
Undo restores an old state instead of making a new object.
Right: undo restores an earlier state, and duplicate makes a new object by copying.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next sets out the difference.
questions.rule: Restore, or reproduce.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the pattern it describes.

items.t: Returns an object to one of its previous states
Makes new instances by copying existing ones
Keeps the key object's data encapsulated while saving it
Lets the client create objects without knowing their class
Its cost is the time to save and restore state
Its cost is that a copy can be complicated to make

questions.explain: Memento is about restoring one object, and Prototype is about producing new ones.
questions.rule: Restore or reproduce.

questions.q: A CAD tool must reset a part's dimensions to those saved yesterday. Which pattern's purpose does that match?
options: Memento, since the part returns to a saved state
