Prototype, since a part is copied to make a new one
Interpreter, since the part has a grammar of its own
Flyweight, since many parts share a single shape
optionExplain: Right: the same object is restored to a saved state.
No new part is created.
There is no language to interpret.
Nothing here concerns sharing one instance for many.
questions.explain: Resetting to saved dimensions brings back an earlier state of the same part.
questions.rule: Same object, earlier state.

questions.q: A teammate says that Memento creates new objects from templates and Prototype restores old states. What is the correct fix?
options: Both descriptions are correct, and only the names of the patterns differ
The descriptions are swapped: Prototype copies, and Memento restores an earlier state
Memento is described correctly, but Prototype also restores old states
The statement is correct, since both patterns work by copying state
optionExplain: The descriptions are different problems.
Right: each pattern's goal is the other's description.
Prototype makes new instances, not restorations.
Both involve state but have different goals.
questions.explain: The patterns share the idea of state being copied but serve different goals.
questions.rule: Goal decides.

questions.q: Java serialization is mentioned for saving state in Memento, and deserialization for deep copies in Prototype. What follows?
options: Serialization shows that Memento and Prototype are really the same pattern
Serialization is only valid inside Memento, and Prototype must avoid it
The same mechanism can serve either pattern, so purpose says which one it is
A pattern is identified by the library call or technique its code uses
optionExplain: Same mechanism does not make the same pattern.
The appendix names it for both.
Right: look at what the code is for.
The call is a means, not the pattern.
questions.explain: Memento uses serialization to save state, and Prototype uses deserialization to copy deeply. The patterns differ in goal.
questions.rule: Judge by purpose, not mechanism.
questions.teaches: A pattern is identified by the problem it solves, so the same technique such as serialization can appear inside different patterns.

questions.q: A level editor lets designers duplicate an enemy and also undo edits. Which patterns does the editor use? Select all that apply.
options: Prototype for the duplicate command
Memento for the undo command
Interpreter for the duplicate command
Mediator for the undo command
optionExplain: Right: duplicate makes a new object by copying.
Right: undo returns to an earlier state.
Wrong: no language is involved.
Wrong: undo restores a state rather than coordinating peers.
questions.explain: One system can use both patterns, each for its own purpose.
questions.rule: Match each feature to its purpose.
questions.teaches: Features map to patterns by purpose, so one system can combine Memento for one feature and Prototype for another.

questions.q: Customers want calorie totals now, allergen lists next month and prices later, all for a menu made of items and sub-menus. Where should the new operations go?
options: As a new method added to every menu class each time
In the order form that the customer fills in at the table
In a single menu method that grows with every new request
In separate objects that walk through the menu classes
optionExplain: Every addition then edits every class.
The form cannot see the menu structure.
A single method becomes unwieldy.
Right: the menu classes stay stable while operations are added elsewhere.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: New operations live outside.

questions.q: Match each role to what it does.
pairs: Knows how to navigate to all objects in the Composite
Collects state as it is guided and performs operations
Asks the visitor to perform operations on the gathered state
The structure of objects the operations run over
questions.explain: The traverser walks, the visitor collects and operates, and the composite is left alone.
questions.rule: Traverser walks, visitor works.

questions.q: A file system tree needs a new report that counts files by type. Under Visitor, what is added?
options: A new visitor, with the folder and file classes unchanged
A new method in the folder class and one in the file class
A new traverser class written for each type of file
A new subclass of the client that wants the report
optionExplain: Right: only the visitor is enhanced.
That is the approach Visitor avoids.
The traverser is the same for all reports.
The client is not where operations go.
questions.explain: New functionality means a new visitor, since the visitor carries the operations.
questions.rule: One visitor per new operation.

questions.q: Visitor makes adding operations easy. Which change is made harder by it?
options: Adding a second operation of the same kind
Changing the structure of the composite itself
Reading the code for one operation in one place
Running an operation over the whole structure
optionExplain: Adding operations is the easy case.
Right: the appendix lists this as a drawback.
The operations' code is centralized.
Running over the structure is the visitor's job.
questions.explain: The cost moves from adding operations to changing the structure.
questions.rule: Cheap operations, costly structure changes.
questions.teaches: Visitor shifts cost: operations become cheap to add and structural changes become expensive, the reverse of putting each operation inside the classes.

questions.q: A menu structure has two classes. Three operations are added by putting a method in each class. How many existing-class edits are needed, and how many with Visitor?
options: 3 edits, and 3 with Visitor
2 edits, and none with Visitor
6 edits, and none with Visitor
6 edits, and 6 with Visitor
optionExplain: Each operation needs an edit in both classes.
That counts each class once instead of each operation.
Right: each operation touches each of the two classes, but the visitor holds the operations separately.
Visitor does not edit the structure's classes.
questions.explain: The book's concern was that each new method must be added in each place. Visitor keeps the structure unchanged.
questions.rule: Operations times classes, versus none.

questions.q: A web page is a tree of elements. Which statement describes using Visitor to produce a word count and a link check?
options: Each one is written as a method in every element class
Both share one visitor that must count and check links together
Each is run by editing the structure of the tree each time
Each gets its own visitor that walks the same tree
optionExplain: That is the approach Visitor avoids.
One visitor per operation keeps them separate.
Visitor leaves the structure unchanged.
Right: each visitor collects state as it goes through the structure.
questions.explain: The same traverser can guide different visitors, and each gathers its own result.
questions.rule: One tree, many visitors.
questions.teaches: One composite can be walked by many different visitors, each gathering its own result, without any change to the composite.

questions.q: True or false: Using a Visitor keeps the composite classes' encapsulation intact.
questions.explain: The appendix says encapsulation is broken, which is why Visitor suits cases where encapsulation is not important.
questions.rule: Visitor trades encapsulation for flexibility.

questions.q: Before adopting an unfamiliar pattern from a summary, what quick check is most useful in addition to reading its benefits?
options: Read its listed drawbacks to see whether the cost fits
Count how many classes the pattern's diagram shows on a page
Check how famous the pattern's original inventors have become
Read only its first benefit and stop there to save time
optionExplain: Right: the drawbacks tell you what you will pay.
Class counts do not say what it costs you in your case.
Fame says nothing about fit.
One benefit leaves out the price.
questions.explain: A guess is fair. The card next lists the drawbacks.
questions.rule: Read the price as well.

questions.q: Match each pattern to its drawback.
pairs: Single instances cannot behave independently of the others
Saving and restoring state can be time consuming
The composite classes' encapsulation is broken
Making a copy of an object can sometimes be complicated
Cumbersome when the number of grammar rules is large
questions.explain: Each pattern's cost comes from what it does.
questions.rule: Know each pattern's price.

questions.q: A dashboard has 50000 widgets that each respond differently to events. A teammate proposes Flyweight to save memory. Which drawback argues against it?
options: It increases complexity because there are two separate hierarchies
Its instances cannot behave independently of one another
It needs much more domain knowledge in the calling client
It may leave a request unhandled if no object takes it
optionExplain: That is Bridge's drawback.
Right: the widgets must act on their own, which Flyweight does not allow.
That is Builder's drawback.
That is Chain's drawback.
questions.explain: Flyweight suits instances that can all be controlled identically.
questions.rule: Match the drawback to the need.

questions.q: The appendix says that a request falling off the end of a chain can be an advantage or a disadvantage. When is it an advantage?
options: When every request must be answered by someone in time
When the chain is long and hard to debug at runtime
When requests nobody wants can be safely ignored, such as junk
When a request must reach two or more handlers at once
optionExplain: That would make it a disadvantage.
Debugging difficulty is a separate drawback.
Right: leaving a request unhandled costs nothing if nobody needs it handled.
The chain stops at the handler that handles it.
questions.explain: Whether a drawback matters depends on the requirement it meets.
questions.rule: A drawback depends on your need.
questions.teaches: Whether a listed drawback is a problem depends on what the system needs, so the same property can be an advantage in one case and a disadvantage in another.

questions.q: A developer is choosing between two code libraries. What would the appendix's habit suggest?
options: Choose the library with the longer list of features
Choose the library that has been released most recently
Read the sample code of only the first library you meet
Skim each library's limitations next to its features
optionExplain: A longer feature list says nothing of the price.
Newness does not show fit.
One library's samples cannot compare the two.
Right: reading costs beside benefits shows whether the price fits.
questions.explain: The habit of reading drawbacks beside benefits applies to any choice among tools.
questions.rule: Weigh price with benefit.
questions.teaches: Reading the costs next to the benefits is a habit for choosing any tool, not only a design pattern.

questions.q: Which statements about the appendix's drawbacks are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Chain of Responsibility can be hard to observe and debug at runtime
Bridge decreases complexity
Mediator can itself become overly complex
Builder needs less domain knowledge in the client than a Factory
optionExplain: Right: this is listed as a drawback.
Wrong: Bridge increases complexity.
Right: without proper design the mediator can become overly complex.
Wrong: it needs more domain knowledge than a Factory.
questions.explain: Reading the lists accurately matters, since a reversed drawback leads to a wrong decision.
questions.rule: Read the drawback as written.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a programmer who knows abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism will automatically build flexible, reusable and maintainable systems.
questions.explain: The authors call this belief one of the true misunderstandings of object-oriented development. The card next shows what the book adds to the basics.
questions.rule: The basics are not enough.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: The authors say that with patterns you get reuse of experience instead of reuse of ____.
questions.explain: A pattern gives a general solution that you apply to your own application, not code you link in.
questions.rule: Patterns reuse experience, not code.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A study-group leader must tell new members in one sentence what this book is about. Which sentence states its unity, and not only its kind or its style?
options: It is a Java book in a lively Head First style, full of puzzles, pictures and dialogue between characters.
It is a reference that lists the patterns, each with ready-made code you can paste into your application.
It is a course in object-oriented basics, such as abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
It teaches proven answers to recurring design problems, and the principles behind them.
optionExplain: This describes the book's style and kind, not what the book is about.
The book says patterns do not give you code; they give general solutions to apply.
The authors say the basics alone do not make a good designer, so the basics are not the subject.
Right: it says what the author is up to, covers patterns and principles, and keeps the adaptation point.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a statement of unity says what the book is about, not what kind of book it is or how it is written.
questions.rule: State what the book is about, not its kind.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A developer cannot find any pattern that matches her problem. What does the guru in the opening chapter say will help her?
options: Waiting for the patterns community to publish a new pattern for her kind of problem
The object-oriented basics, which the guru says are enough on their own
The object-oriented principles that underlie the patterns
Combining two patterns until one of them happens to fit the problem
optionExplain: The guru does not suggest waiting; the principles can be used now.
The guru says the basics do not make a good designer, so they are not enough alone.
Right: the guru says the principles underlie the patterns and help you cope when no pattern matches.
Nothing in the dialogue suggests forcing patterns to fit.
questions.explain: The guru names the principles as the fallback. They also explain why the patterns work, which is why the book teaches them alongside.
questions.rule: No matching pattern? Use the principles.
questions.teaches: The principles are useful on their own: when no pattern matches a problem, they guide the design directly.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: True or false: This statement of the book's unity is accurate: 'The book gives programmers finished code for the common design problems, so they can reuse it and skip design work.'
questions.explain: The error is the claim of ready-made code. The book says patterns do not give you code but general solutions that you apply to your own application, which still takes design work.
questions.rule: Experience reuse, not code reuse.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A town-planning handbook collects proven street layouts for recurring problems, such as a junction that jams. Its editor says most layouts exist so that one district can grow without rebuilding the others. Which claim in this book's unity does that second remark mirror?
options: Patterns are discovered from practice and are not invented by their authors
Most patterns and principles address change, so one part can vary alone
Patterns give a team a shared language for talking about designs
Knowing the object-oriented basics does not make you a good designer
optionExplain: True in the book, but the handbook remark is not about where layouts come from.
Right: the handbook's growth-without-rebuilding is the book's thread of change.
True in the book, but the remark is not about naming or talking.
True in the book, but the remark is about growth, not about basic knowledge.
questions.explain: The book says most patterns and principles address issues of change and let some part of a system vary independently of all other parts. A unity statement should carry that thread.
questions.rule: Change is the thread through the patterns.
questions.teaches: Most patterns and principles in the book are about change: they let one part of a system vary or grow without disturbing the rest.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most patterns allow some part of a system to vary independently of all other parts.
questions.explain: That is the authors' summary of what the patterns have in common. The card next lists what varies in several of them.
questions.rule: Most patterns let one part vary on its own.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: Match each pattern with the part of a system it lets vary.
pairs: A step inside a fixed algorithm
How a collection is walked through
questions.explain: Each pattern puts one changing part behind its own boundary: a behavior object, a creation step, a deferred step, an iterator object.
questions.rule: Each pattern isolates one varying part.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A language-learning app scores lessons in different ways: some courses count correct answers, others weight hard questions, others reward speed. Each course gets one method when it is created, and the lesson-delivery code must stay unchanged. Which part varies, and which pattern lets it vary?
options: The scoring calculation, handled by Strategy
The set of listeners, handled by Observer
The order of lesson steps, handled by Iterator
The extra features added to a lesson, handled by Decorator
optionExplain: Right: the scoring methods are interchangeable alternatives, each a complete calculation, so they are a family of algorithms.
Nothing here asks who is told about changes.
Nothing here asks how lessons are walked through.
Nothing is being added to a lesson in layers; one whole method is chosen.
questions.explain: Each course picks one complete scoring calculation, which is what Strategy encapsulates and makes interchangeable.
questions.rule: A swappable whole calculation points to Strategy.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A newsroom's alert system must let reporters and editors subscribe to a story feed or leave it at any time, without changes to the code that publishes stories. Which part varies here?
options: The algorithm that decides which stories get published
The concrete class created for each new story
The behavior of the publisher at different times of day
The parties that depend on the publisher's updates
optionExplain: How stories are chosen is not what the subscribing and leaving concerns.
Creation of stories is not what changes when someone subscribes.
Nothing in the scenario depends on the publisher's own condition.
Right: subscribers come and go, and the publisher's code is not touched.
questions.explain: In Observer the varying part is who depends on the subject. Because the subject knows its dependents only through a shared interface, they can change without editing the publisher.
questions.rule: Observer: the dependents vary.
questions.teaches: What varies is hidden behind an interface: the subject knows its observers only as implementers of the Observer interface, so the set can change freely.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: True or false: In the ride-hailing example, if the city rules turn out to be fixed for good, the first principle still asks you to move the pricing rule into its own classes.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the principle is about what varies, not about everything. With one fixed rule there is nothing to separate, and extra classes would add structure without benefit.
questions.rule: Encapsulate what varies, not everything.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A bakery franchise bakes every loaf in the same sequence: mix, prove, shape, bake, cool. Only the shaping step differs by loaf. Head office wants the sequence kept in one place, with each loaf type supplying its own shaping. What varies, and which pattern does that point to?
options: The whole baking procedure; Strategy
The kind of oven that is created; Factory Method
One step of a fixed procedure; Template Method
The way loaves are counted at the end; Iterator
optionExplain: Strategy swaps a whole algorithm, but here only one step changes.
Nothing in the scenario creates different ovens.
Right: only one step differs, so the outline stays and the step is deferred to subclasses.
Counting is not the point; the shaping step is.
questions.explain: The sequence is fixed and only one step differs, which fits Template Method. The varying part can be as small as one step.
questions.rule: One varying step in a fixed outline: Template Method.
questions.teaches: What varies can be as small as a single step of an algorithm, not only a whole behavior or a whole object.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: Which principle is summed up by the slogan: Don't call us, we'll call you?
options: The Hollywood Principle
The Principle of Least Knowledge
The Open-Closed Principle
The Dependency Inversion Principle
optionExplain: Right: high-level components decide when to call low-level ones.
Least Knowledge is summed up as talking only to your immediate friends.
Open-Closed is about extension without modification.
Dependency Inversion is about depending on abstractions.
questions.explain: The slogan names the Hollywood Principle. The card next ties it and the other principles to the patterns that show them.
questions.rule: Know each principle by its slogan.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: Match each principle with the pattern whose chapter shows it best.
pairs: Loosely coupled designs between interacting objects
Open for extension, closed for modification
Don't call us, we'll call you
A class should have one reason to change
questions.explain: Each principle is introduced in the chapter where a pattern makes it concrete.
questions.rule: Each principle has a home pattern.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A ticketing class keeps the list of events and also prints schedules in several layouts. Layout changes keep breaking the list handling. Which principle does this situation violate?
options: Talk only to your immediate friends
A class should have only one reason to change
Don't call us, we'll call you
Strive for loosely coupled designs between objects that interact
optionExplain: Least Knowledge concerns how many classes one object talks to, which is not the problem here.
Right: the class changes when the list changes and when a layout changes, so it has two reasons to change.
The Hollywood Principle concerns who decides when to call whom.
Loose coupling is about objects that interact; here one class holds two jobs.
questions.explain: Two responsibilities mean two areas of change. The principle says each responsibility belongs to one class.
questions.rule: Two jobs in a class means two reasons to change.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: The chapter on Adapter and Facade shows a pattern that helps a design follow the Principle of Least Knowledge. Which pattern is it?
options: Singleton, because only one object exists for others to know
Facade, because a client then talks to one friend
Template Method, because the superclass calls the subclass
Observer, because the subject knows nothing of its observers
optionExplain: One instance does not reduce how many classes a client talks to.
Right: the facade is the one object the client deals with; it holds the components.
That is the Hollywood Principle, which is about who calls whom.
That is loose coupling, a different principle.
questions.explain: A client that uses a facade no longer calls each component of the subsystem. The facade may call them all, because they are its own.
questions.rule: A facade keeps a client to one friend.
questions.teaches: A pattern can serve a principle: Facade lets a client keep to Least Knowledge by dealing with one object instead of a subsystem's many components.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a design that purposely departs from a design principle after weighing the effect must be a mistake.
questions.explain: The authors call Composite a classic case of tradeoff: it trades the one-reason-to-change principle for transparency. They say designers are guided by principles but must observe the effect they have.
questions.rule: Principles guide; observe their effect.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: A photo editor loads filter plug-ins. The editor decides when each plug-in runs and hands it the image. The plug-ins do not reach into the editor's internals. Which principle is about this question of who decides when a low-level part is called?
options: The Open-Closed Principle
The Principle of Least Knowledge
The Hollywood Principle
A class should have only one reason to change
optionExplain: New plug-ins do extend the editor, but extension is not the question asked.
Least Knowledge limits how many classes one object talks to, not who initiates calls.
Right: the high-level editor calls the plug-ins when it needs them, and they hook themselves in.
One reason to change concerns the responsibilities inside a class.
questions.explain: The principle settles who is in charge of the flow. The authors show it in frameworks too, such as the hooks in a JFrame and in applets.
questions.rule: High-level parts decide when low-level parts are called.
questions.teaches: The Hollywood Principle describes frameworks and plug-in hosts in general, not only Template Method.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Putting the book in one view

questions.q: True or false: If two patterns have the same class diagram, they are the same pattern under two names.
questions.explain: The authors say State and Strategy have the same class diagram and still differ. The card next shows what tells them apart.
questions.rule: Same diagram does not mean same pattern.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: State and Strategy have the same class diagram, yet they differ in ____.
questions.explain: The authors argue that the two patterns differ in intent: who picks the behavior object and why it changes.
questions.rule: Same structure, different intent.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A class implements the same interface as a SmartLock. It holds the real lock and, before passing each unlock call on, checks that the caller is on the household's guest list. What is the wrapper doing?
options: Adding a responsibility, so it is a Decorator
Converting the interface, so it is an Adapter
Simplifying a subsystem, so it is a Facade
Controlling access, so it is a Proxy
optionExplain: The check can look like added behavior, but its job is to allow or refuse the call.
The interface is the same, so nothing is being converted.
Only one object is wrapped and the interface is not simplified.
Right: the check decides whether the call goes through, which is control of access.
questions.explain: A wrapper that keeps the interface and decides whether a call may pass is a protection proxy. Its intent is access control.
questions.rule: Same interface plus a gate: Proxy.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: Many developers say Decorator belongs with the behavioral patterns because it adds behavior. What reasoning do the authors give for placing it among the structural patterns?
options: Its focus is how objects are composed, by wrapping one in another
It changes how objects communicate with one another while the program runs
It depends on inheritance, which is a structural feature of languages
It decides which concrete class to create, which is a structural task
optionExplain: Right: the authors look at what the pattern is about, and Decorator is about dynamic composition.
Communication between objects is what behavioral patterns are about, and Decorator is not.
Decorator is built on composition, with inheritance used only for the shared type.
Deciding what to create is creational, not structural.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: the authors place a pattern by its focus. Decorator's focus is composing objects by wrapping, not the communication between objects.
questions.rule: Intent often decides the category.
questions.teaches: Intent also decides a pattern's category: Decorator is structural because it is about how objects are composed, though the placement can be argued.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: If an adapter is changed to wrap three classes instead of one, it becomes a facade.
questions.explain: The book says an adapter may adapt many classes and a facade may simplify one class. What changes the pattern is the intent: converting an interface versus simplifying one.
questions.rule: Count does not decide; intent does.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: In a lift controller, the lift hands every button press to an object for its present condition (Idle, Moving, DoorsOpen), and those objects set the next condition themselves. In a parking system, each zone is given a pricing-rule object at setup and keeps it unless an operator replaces it. Which pairing is right?
options: Lift controller: Strategy; parking system: State
Lift controller: State; parking system: Strategy
Both are State, because both hold an object and delegate to it
Both are Strategy, because both delegate behavior to an object
optionExplain: This swaps them: the lift moves itself through conditions, and the zone is configured.
Right: the lift's objects change as the lift's own condition changes, while the zone's rule is configured from outside.
Both do delegate, but delegation is shared by the two patterns and cannot tell them apart.
The zone fits Strategy, but the lift's objects change by themselves, which is not Strategy.
questions.explain: Both designs delegate, which is why they look alike. The difference is who changes the behavior object and why: the context's own condition in State, a client's choice in Strategy.
questions.rule: State changes itself; Strategy is configured.
questions.teaches: One way to apply the intent test: ask whether the behavior object changes as a consequence of the context's own condition (State) or because a client chose it and keeps it (Strategy).
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A wrapper implements the same interface as the object it wraps and adds a log line before forwarding each call. Which pattern is closest?
options: Decorator
Adapter
Facade
Proxy
optionExplain: Right: it keeps the interface and adds behavior.
An adapter would change the interface.
A facade would simplify the interface of a group of objects.
A proxy would control access, which logging does not do.
questions.explain: Same interface plus added behavior describes a decorator. The card next gives the full sort.
questions.rule: Same interface, added behavior: Decorator.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: Match each purpose with the pattern that has it.
pairs: Converts an interface into the one a client expects
Adds responsibilities while keeping the interface
Offers a simpler interface to a group of objects
questions.explain: The four wrappers are separated by their purpose, not by the fact that they wrap.
questions.rule: Purpose sorts the four wrappers.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A cinema's new booking code expects an object with reserve(Seat). The old seat-hold service offers holdSeat(row, number). A new class implements reserve(Seat) and calls holdSeat inside. Which pattern is it?
options: Decorator
Facade
Proxy
Adapter
optionExplain: It does not keep the old interface and add to it.
It does not simplify a group of objects; it translates one interface.
It does not control who may call or when the service is created.
Right: it converts the old interface into the one the client expects.
questions.explain: The wrapper presents a different interface from the one it wraps and exists to match what the client expects, which defines an adapter.
questions.rule: Different interface, converted to the expected one: Adapter.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: Because a facade simplifies a subsystem, clients can no longer call the subsystem's classes directly.
questions.explain: The book says facades do not encapsulate the subsystem classes. They provide a simplified interface while the classes stay available to clients that need them.
questions.rule: A facade simplifies; it does not seal off the subsystem.
questions.teaches: A facade does not hide the subsystem: clients that need its full power can still use the classes directly.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A wrapper implements the same interface as a document store and logs every call before forwarding it. The team then changes it so that it refuses calls from users who lack a role, and it no longer logs. Which pattern does it become?
options: Adapter, because its behavior now differs from the document store's
Facade, because it now hides part of the document store
Proxy, because its purpose changed to controlling access
It stays a Decorator, because it still wraps the document store
optionExplain: The interface did not change, so there is no conversion.
It does not simplify a group of objects.
Right: the interface is the same and the wrapper now gates access.
Wrapping is shared by all four, so it cannot decide; the purpose changed.
questions.explain: Both versions keep the interface. The first added behavior (Decorator); the second decides who may call (a protection proxy).
questions.rule: Same shape, new purpose, new pattern.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A video editor shows a placeholder frame for each clip and loads the large clip file only when the user starts scrubbing. The placeholder implements the same interface as the clip. Which statement is right?
options: It is a Decorator, because it adds a placeholder to the clip
It is an Adapter, because a placeholder differs from a clip
It is a Proxy, and the clip it stands for may not exist yet
It is a Facade, because it simplifies loading the clip
optionExplain: The placeholder looks like added behavior, but its main role is to control access to the clip.
The interface is the same as the clip's, so nothing is converted.
Right: it controls access by standing in until the real subject is needed.
It does not simplify a group of objects.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: a virtual proxy decides when the real object is created and stands in before then. That is control of access even though nothing is wrapped yet.
questions.rule: A virtual proxy stands in before its subject exists.
questions.teaches: A proxy can exist before its real subject, so it is a stand-in that decides when the subject comes into being, not only a wrapper around an existing object.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A class holds an object that implements an algorithm interface, and its caller can replace that object. Which pattern is this?
options: Strategy
Template Method
Singleton
Iterator
optionExplain: Right: a family of interchangeable algorithms used through composition.
Template Method keeps the algorithm in a superclass and varies steps through subclasses.
Singleton limits instances; it does not swap algorithms.
Iterator walks a collection.
questions.explain: Replaceable algorithm objects held by a class describe Strategy. The card next compares it with State and Template Method.
questions.rule: Swappable algorithm objects: Strategy.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: Sort each statement under the pattern it describes.

items.t: Swaps in a whole algorithm object
Behavior varies by composition
A client can switch it while the program runs
Subclasses supply the steps
Behavior varies by inheritance
The superclass keeps the outline of the algorithm

questions.explain: Both encapsulate algorithms: Strategy by object composition and Template Method by inheritance.
questions.rule: Strategy composes; Template Method inherits.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A leave-request object can be Submitted, Approved, Rejected or Cancelled. Its approve() and cancel() methods behave differently in each condition, and the code is a thicket of if tests on a status field. Which pattern does the book's reasoning reach for?
options: Strategy
Template Method
Decorator
State
optionExplain: Nobody from outside is choosing an algorithm for the request.
There is no fixed outline with one varying step.
Nothing is being layered onto the request.
Right: behavior depends on the object's own condition, and conditionals on that condition are piling up.
questions.explain: The authors present State as an alternative to many conditionals in the context: each condition becomes a class, and the object delegates to its current one.
questions.rule: Conditionals on internal state: State.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: In the authors' fireside dialogue between the two patterns, what does Template Method claim in its favor against Strategy?
options: It lets the client swap algorithms while the program runs
It needs fewer objects and is a little more efficient
It needs no superclass, so nothing is inherited
It lets every subclass change the order of the steps
optionExplain: That is Strategy's claim in the dialogue, not Template Method's.
Right: those are the claims Template Method makes.
Template Method relies on a superclass that holds the outline.
The outline stays in the superclass, so subclasses do not reorder it.
questions.explain: Strategy is more flexible because a client can change algorithms at runtime. Template Method is leaner, but the choice is made by the subclass you pick.
questions.rule: Strategy: flexibility. Template Method: economy.
questions.teaches: The trade between the two is flexibility against economy: Strategy can change at runtime but needs more objects, while Template Method is leaner but the subclass fixes the choice.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: A report class built with Template Method, whose output format must now be switched while one report object is running, is a better fit for Strategy.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: With Template Method the subclass chosen fixes the format. Holding a replaceable format object, as Strategy does, lets one object change format at runtime.
questions.rule: Runtime switching points to composition.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A sort method owns the sorting algorithm but defers one step, comparing two items, to the items themselves, which implement a compare method. A Java array cannot be subclassed. How do the authors judge this design?
options: In the spirit of Template Method, with the algorithm in one place
It is Factory Method, because each item decides which class to create
It is Observer, because items are told when to compare themselves
It is no pattern at all, because nothing is subclassed
optionExplain: Right: a method that owns an algorithm and defers one step fits the pattern's purpose.
Nothing is created by the items; they only compare.
Nothing is announced to dependents.
The authors say it is not the textbook form but still in the spirit of the pattern.
questions.explain: The sort method fixes the algorithm and needs one piece from outside, which is what Template Method is for, even without subclassing.
questions.rule: Judge by what the code is for, not only by the textbook form.
questions.teaches: A pattern can be present without its textbook structure: a method that owns an algorithm and defers one step is Template Method in spirit even where subclassing is impossible.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: Which factory form is handed to a client as an object and creates a family of related products?
options: Factory Method
Simple Factory
Abstract Factory
Singleton
optionExplain: Factory Method works through subclasses and usually makes one product.
Simple Factory is a separate creator object but does not make families that belong together.
Right: it uses composition and makes related products together.
Singleton limits instances; it is not a factory.
questions.explain: An object that creates a family of related products is an Abstract Factory. The card next sets the three forms side by side.
questions.rule: Family of products by composition: Abstract Factory.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: Match each name with what the book says about it.
pairs: A separate creator object; an idiom, not a pattern
Subclasses decide which concrete product is created
An object that creates a family of related products
The pattern of which Factory Method is a specialization
questions.explain: Each form places the creation step differently, and Factory Method is the one that is a Template Method whose varying step creates.
questions.rule: Know where the creation step lives.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A strategy game gives each of three kingdoms its own weapons, shields and armor. Mixing pieces from different kingdoms would be a bug, and the game code must not name concrete classes. Which form fits?
options: Simple Factory, one creator object for all pieces
Abstract Factory, one factory per kingdom
Factory Method, with one subclass of the game per piece
No factory is needed, because the kingdoms are fixed
optionExplain: A single creator object offers no way to guarantee that pieces match one kingdom.
Right: a family of matching products is what Abstract Factory is for.
Factory Method makes one product per method; the matching of the family would be left unchecked.
The code must avoid concrete class names, which a factory achieves.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Pieces that belong together must be created together. A factory per kingdom keeps the family consistent while the game depends only on abstractions.
questions.rule: Matching families call for Abstract Factory.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A team using Abstract Factory adds a fourth product type, a banner, to each kingdom's set. According to the authors' interview with the two patterns, what does this cost?
options: Nothing changes, because clients depend only on abstractions
Only the client changes, because it must ask for banners
Only the new product classes change, and nothing else
The interface and every concrete factory must change
optionExplain: The abstraction itself has grown, so the classes that implement it must change.
The client changes too, but that is not the whole cost.
The product classes are needed, but the factories must also create them.
Right: a new product type means a new method in the interface and in every subclass.
questions.explain: Abstract Factory needs a big interface because it makes whole families. Growing the family changes the interface and every factory, which people dislike.
questions.rule: A growing family costs interface changes.
questions.teaches: The price of Abstract Factory's family is a large interface: adding a product type means changing the interface and every concrete factory.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: A Factory Method creator that has only one concrete subclass gives no benefit, because nothing varies.
questions.explain: The book says that even with one concrete creator the pattern decouples the product's implementation from its use, so products can change without affecting the creator.
questions.rule: Decoupling pays even before variety exists.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A page-rendering class has a fixed procedure: collect the fields, create an input widget for each, lay them out. The widget-creating step is abstract, and each subclass returns its own widget type. Which description fits?
options: Abstract Factory, because the class makes widgets for a family
Simple Factory, because creation sits in one place
Template Method with no connection to the factory patterns
Factory Method: subclasses choose the product
optionExplain: Abstract Factory exists purely to create families; this class also runs a procedure.
Simple Factory puts creation in a separate object, not in subclasses.
The book says Factory Method is a specialization of Template Method, so they are linked.
Right: the creation step is deferred to subclasses and used inside a fixed procedure.
questions.explain: The class has a fixed outline that uses a product, and its subclasses decide which one to make. That is Factory Method, a Template Method whose varying step creates an object.
questions.rule: A procedure that needs a product, made by subclasses: Factory Method.
questions.teaches: In Factory Method the creator usually holds code that uses the product, while an Abstract Factory exists purely to create products.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: According to the authors, what should you try first when you meet a design problem?
options: The most flexible pattern in the catalog, to be safe
A survey of every pattern, to find the best match
A simpler solution, to see whether it is enough
A rewrite of the design from first principles
optionExplain: Flexibility is not the first aim; the simplest solution that meets the need is.
Surveying patterns comes after a simpler solution has been ruled out.
Right: the book says to give a simpler solution a chance first.
The book does not call for a rewrite at this point.
questions.explain: The authors say to introduce a pattern when you are sure it addresses a problem, and to give a simpler solution a chance first. The card next gives the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Simpler solution first.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: Match each symptom with the candidate pattern the book associates with it.
pairs: Many objects must follow one object's changes
Conditionals pile up on an object's internal state
A request must be separated from the code that performs it
An interface does not match what the client expects
Clients must treat parts and wholes in the same way
questions.explain: Each symptom is the problem statement of one pattern's chapter.
questions.rule: A symptom gives a candidate.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: In a clinic's booking code, many places name concrete appointment classes with new, and every new appointment type forces edits in all of them. Which candidate does the book link to this symptom?
options: A factory, to move creation out of the using code
State, to replace the appointment types with state objects
Observer, to tell each place when a type is added
Facade, to give the places one simpler interface
optionExplain: Right: concrete dependencies are the symptom the book ties to factories.
State is for behavior that depends on an object's own condition.
Observer notifies dependents of changes in one object, which is not the problem.
A facade simplifies a subsystem, but the problem is who creates what.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Using new on concrete classes ties the code to them. A factory moves that choice into one place and lets the rest depend on abstractions.
questions.rule: Concrete dependencies suggest a factory.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: According to the authors, when is it natural to look for the symptoms that suggest a pattern?
options: Only at the start of a project, before any code exists
During refactoring, when code is being reorganized
Only after a pattern has already been chosen for the design
Only when users report that the program has become slow
optionExplain: Early designs can use patterns, but the book singles out refactoring as the moment.
Right: refactoring improves structure, so it is a good time to ask whether patterns would organize the code better.
The point is to find the need before choosing the pattern.
Slowness is not the symptom the authors name; conditionals and concrete dependencies are.
questions.explain: The authors give two signs for refactoring time: code full of conditionals may call for State, and concrete dependencies may be cleaned up with a Factory.
questions.rule: Refactoring time is patterns time.
questions.teaches: Refactoring is a good moment to look for these symptoms, because it improves structure without changing behavior, so a pattern added then must not alter what the code does.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: Put the book's steps for choosing a pattern in order.
items: Try a simpler solution
State the problem with its constraints
Match it to a pattern by intent and applicability
Check the consequences for the rest of the design
questions.explain: The sequence moves from the cheapest option to the commitment: simple solution, problem and constraints, match by intent, then consequences.
questions.rule: Simple, constrain, match, check.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a simpler solution would work, you should use it even when you expect parts of your system to vary in practice.
questions.explain: The book names one exception: when you expect aspects of your system to vary, a pattern can be right even if a simpler solution would work. The change must be practical and likely.
questions.rule: Likely variation is the one exception.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: A team believes a pattern fits its problem and now opens the catalog entry for it. In what order does the book's dialogue suggest reading the parts of the entry?
options: Fit and consequences first, then structure, then implementation
Structure and participants first, then sample code, then the consequences
Sample code first, so the idea is concrete, then motivation and structure
Consequences only, since the other parts repeat what the team knows
optionExplain: Right: confirm the fit and consequences before studying the structure.
Studying structure before confirming the fit risks adopting the wrong pattern.
Code comes last, once the pattern is known to fit.
Consequences matter, but the fit must be confirmed first and the structure still has to be studied.
questions.explain: The routine moves from whether the pattern fits, to what it costs, to how it is built and coded.
questions.rule: Fit and consequences before structure.
questions.teaches: Reading a catalog entry has an order: confirm the fit, review the consequences, and only then study structure, adapt it and read the implementation notes.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: Which pattern is meant for bringing an existing object back to an earlier state, as in undo?
options: Prototype
Mediator
Memento
Bridge
optionExplain: Prototype makes a new object by copying an existing one.
Mediator centralizes the coordination between peers.
Right: it saves and restores state while keeping the object's data encapsulated.
Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementations.
questions.explain: Restoring an object to an earlier state is Memento's job. The card next compares it with similar patterns.
questions.rule: Restore the same object: Memento.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: Match each pattern with what it separates or does.
pairs: Separates an abstraction from its implementations
Separates a sender from several possible receivers
Separates peers that each know the others
Restores an object to an earlier state
questions.explain: Naming what is tangled in the problem is the quickest way to the right candidate.
questions.rule: Name the tangled pair.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: A help-desk ticket may be handled by the first of several teams able to deal with it, and the sender should not know which team will respond. Which pattern separates the sender from the receivers?
options: Mediator, which coordinates peers that know one another
Bridge, which splits abstraction from implementation
Prototype, which makes new objects by copying
Chain of Responsibility, which passes requests on
optionExplain: Mediator coordinates peers that know one another, not a sender and its receivers.
Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementations.
Prototype copies objects.
Right: each handler either deals with the request or passes it to its successor.
questions.explain: The tangled pair is a sender and possible receivers, which is what the chain separates.
questions.rule: Sender and receivers: Chain of Responsibility.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: True or false: The book's appendix says a request that falls off the end of a chain, because no object handles it, can be an advantage in some applications and a disadvantage in others.
questions.explain: The appendix lists this under the pattern's drawbacks and adds that it can be an advantage or a disadvantage. Whether it matters depends on whether an unhandled request is acceptable.
questions.rule: A drawback is a risk to weigh in context.
questions.teaches: A listed drawback is a risk, not a verdict: whether it hurts depends on the application, so judge it against your need.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: A game needs a Duplicate command that copies an enemy, and an Undo command that restores an enemy's earlier stats. What do the appendix descriptions of Prototype and Memento suggest?
options: Memento for both, since both work with an enemy's state
Prototype for Duplicate and Memento for Undo
Prototype for both, since both produce an enemy with certain stats
Neither, since copying and restoring are the same job
optionExplain: Memento restores the same object; a duplicate is a new object.
Right: a new object like an old one is Prototype, and the same object back in an earlier state is Memento.
Prototype makes copies; undo wants the same enemy back, not a copy.
The jobs differ in what you want at the end, and the book treats them as separate patterns.
questions.explain: Beyond the book's wording, but sound: Ask what you want at the end: another object (Prototype) or the same object restored (Memento). Here the game wants one of each.
questions.rule: New like the old: Prototype. Old again: Memento.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: A recipe app keeps a flat list of recipes and wants to step through them without exposing the list type. Later it must hold folders that contain recipes and other folders, and treat all of them alike. Which patterns fit the two stages?
options: Iterator for the flat list, then Composite for the nested folders
Composite for the flat list, then Iterator for the folders
Mediator for the flat list, then Chain of Responsibility for the folders
Iterator for both stages, since a folder is only a longer list
optionExplain: Right: a flat collection needs an iterator, and a tree of parts and wholes calls for Composite.
This reverses them: a flat list has no part-whole structure to compose.
Neither pattern separates what is tangled in these stages.
Nested folders are a tree, not a longer list, and clients must treat parts and wholes alike.
questions.explain: The first stage is traversal without exposure. The second is a part-whole hierarchy. The book keeps Iterator as part of the Composite solution, to walk the tree.
questions.rule: Flat: Iterator. Nested: Composite.
questions.teaches: The two patterns work together: Composite does not replace Iterator, because the book still uses an iterator to traverse the whole structure.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Choosing a pattern for a situation

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the more patterns a design uses, the better the design.
questions.explain: The authors call this the beginner's belief and say designs should be as simple as possible. The card next shows what to ask instead.
questions.rule: More patterns is not better design.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: The authors abbreviate their advice to solve things in the simplest way possible as KISS, which stands for keep it ____.
questions.explain: The goal is simplicity, not how to apply a pattern to the problem.
questions.rule: Aim for simplicity, not for patterns.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A school's timetable script has one report format, no plan to add others, and runs once a term. A teammate proposes a Strategy for report formats. What does the book's advice suggest?
options: Add the Strategy, because patterns are tested by many developers
Add the Strategy, in case a second format is ever wanted
Add an Observer instead, because it is the safer pattern
Keep the single format in plain code, since nothing varies
optionExplain: Being well tested does not mean a pattern fits; it still adds classes.
A reason that is only hypothetical does not justify a pattern.
Swapping one pattern for another does not answer whether any is needed.
Right: nothing varies, so the simplest solution meets the need.
questions.explain: The authors say to resist patterns for hypothetical change. With one format and no plan for more, the pattern would add complexity and nothing else.
questions.rule: No practical variation, no pattern.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A pattern was added to a system two years ago to give flexibility that nobody has used. What does the book say about it?
options: Keep it, because removing a pattern is a sign of a failed design
Keep it, since its flexibility may still be used one day
Remove it if a simpler solution without it would be better
Remove every pattern in the system for consistency
optionExplain: The authors say no one talks about removal, as if it were blasphemy, and that we can take it.
A hope for future use is the hypothetical reason the book warns against.
Right: the book says not to be afraid to remove a pattern whose flexibility is not needed.
Patterns that still handle real change earn their place; only unneeded ones go.
questions.explain: Complexity that buys no flexibility is a cost with no benefit. The authors say to remove a pattern when the flexibility it was added for is not needed.
questions.rule: Remove a pattern whose flexibility is unused.
questions.teaches: Taking a pattern out is legitimate: when the flexibility it was added for is not needed, a simpler solution without it is better.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: In the school example, if the board has now asked for three more report formats next term, a pattern can be justified.
questions.explain: The book's one exception is expected variation: change that is practical and likely, not hypothetical. A request for three more formats is a practical need.
questions.rule: Practical, likely change justifies a pattern.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A start-up developer has a function that sends one welcome email. She plans to add a Template Method, a Factory and an Observer so that the design is ready for anything. Which of the book's warnings does this match?
options: The Golden Hammer, where one familiar technology is applied everywhere
The beginner's belief that more patterns make a better design
Dependency rot, where high-level and low-level parts call each other
Using a well-tested pattern without thinking through its consequences
optionExplain: The Golden Hammer is about forcing one familiar technology on a problem, not about stacking patterns.
Right: three patterns are added for a design that nothing requires.
Dependency rot is the Hollywood Principle's concern and is not the issue here.
That is the magic-bullet warning; this plan is driven by a wish for readiness, not by trust in a track record.
questions.explain: Nothing in the function varies, so the patterns respond to no need. The authors say the temptation to build a design ready for change from any direction is natural, and that the answer is to resist.
questions.rule: Resist building for hypothetical change.
questions.teaches: The pull to build an architecture ready for change from any direction is natural for developers, and the book's answer is to resist it unless the need is practical.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a design that purposely departs from a design principle has necessarily done something wrong.
questions.explain: The authors say we are guided by design principles but always need to observe the effect they have on our designs. The card next gives their example.
questions.rule: Principles guide; they are not laws.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: The authors say Composite takes the single-responsibility principle and trades it for ____.
questions.explain: Transparency means a client can treat composites and leaves uniformly, without knowing which it holds.
questions.rule: Composite trades a principle for transparency.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A file-manager design puts add(), remove() and getChild() on the interface shared by files and folders, so both can be handled the same way. A reviewer objects that a file has no children. Which response matches the authors' reasoning?
options: It is a mistake, and the interface must be split before anything else
It is a tradeoff: uniformity is gained and some safety lost
It is fine, because principles apply only to the first version of a design
It is fine, because a file manager has no need for safety
optionExplain: The authors treat it as a design decision with a cost, not as an error to be fixed at once.
Right: this is the same tradeoff the authors describe for Composite.
The book does not limit principles to a first version.
Safety is the cost being accepted; the reviewer's worry is real.
questions.explain: Putting everything on one interface buys transparency at some cost in safety. The authors note that seeing a leaf as a node with zero children softens the apparent violation.
questions.rule: Name the gain and the cost of the choice.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: The safer alternative to the single shared interface in Composite separates child management into its own interface. What does the book say it costs?
options: Nothing, since inappropriate calls are then caught for free
The tree can no longer hold folders inside folders
Transparency is lost, and clients must check types
The leaf classes must each store a list of children
optionExplain: Safer, yes, but the price is paid in transparency.
Nesting still works; what changes is how clients treat the elements.
Right: the client must test what kind of element it has before using it.
Leaves would not need children under the safer design.
questions.explain: Neither design is free. The shared interface is transparent but less safe; the separated interfaces are safer but clients must check types.
questions.rule: Each side of a tradeoff has a price.
questions.teaches: The safer design has its own price: separating the interfaces catches inappropriate calls, but clients lose transparency and must check types.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: True or false: For a throwaway demo with three states, the authors accept that a class for each state may not pay back its cost.
questions.explain: The authors say more classes are often the price of flexibility, and they advise paying it unless the code is a one-off you will throw away.
questions.rule: Weigh cost against how long the code will live.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole

questions.q: A team adapts a well-known design by dropping one class their application does not need. They add a comment saying which class was dropped and why. Which advice from the book does this follow?
options: Adapt a pattern to your needs and record how yours differs
Keep a pattern exactly as published, because patterns are laws and not guidelines
Rename the pattern, since a changed design is a different pattern
Remove the comment, since good code needs no explanation
optionExplain: Right: adapting is allowed, and the note lets the next developer see where the version departs.
The authors say patterns are guidelines you can alter to fit your needs.
The book does not ask for a new name; it asks that the departure be documented.
Without the note, another developer cannot tell which pattern is in use or how it differs.
questions.explain: The authors say patterns, like principles, are guidelines you may alter. They add that documenting how yours differs lets others quickly recognise the pattern and see the change.
questions.rule: Adapt, then write down the difference.
questions.teaches: When you adapt a pattern, documenting how your version differs from the classic design lets other developers recognise the pattern and see where yours departs.
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
